claims.subject: iatrogenic-medicine
claims.question: What is the average lifespan of doctors?
claims.answer_short: Startlingly short. An 1895 JAMA report put it at 55 years, and Wallach says a century of medicine added only three more — doctors average about 58, still dying younger than the ~75.5-year-old average American.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that doctors are strikingly short-lived for people who advise everyone else on health. An 1895 edition of the Journal of the American Medical Association put the average life of a doctor at just 55 years, and when Wallach checked whether that gap had closed a century later, he found it had narrowed by only three years. By his figures doctors today still average only about 58 years, far short of the roughly 75.5 years the average American reaches — the founding observation behind 'Dead Doctors Don't Lie.'
claims.verbatim:
what he discovered, in an 1895 edition of the Journal of the American
Medical Association was that the average life of doctors was just 55 years. Anticipating this gap to
be much closer today than 100 years ago, he researched it further. What he found was that today, the
gap is closer-but only by three years.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: Does copper deficiency cause gray hair?
claims.answer_short: Yes; Wallach says copper deficiency shows up first as white, gray, or silver hair because copper is the cofactor needed to make hair pigment.
claims.answer: Premature gray, white, or silver hair is, in Wallach's reading, the first visible sign of copper deficiency — because copper is the cofactor the body needs to manufacture hair pigment. He backs it with a favorite story: a flock of turkeys dying of ruptured aortic aneurysms whose deaths stopped once copper was doubled in the feed, since copper also builds the strong elastic fibers in artery walls. Other copper-shortage signs he lists include skin wrinkles, spider and varicose veins, and an iron-resistant anemia.
claims.verbatim:
Copper deficiency in human beings presents itself first as white, gray, or
silver hair.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: How was it discovered that copper deficiency causes aneurysms?
claims.answer_short: In 1950s turkeys: half a flock on copper-poor feed pellets died of ruptured aortic aneurysms, a pathologist pinned it on copper deficiency (copper builds arteries' elastic fibers), and doubling the feed's copper the next year stopped the deaths entirely.
claims.answer: It was discovered in turkeys during the 1950s. When turkeys were switched to a new 'complete' feed-pellet ration, fully half of them died within the first thirteen weeks, and autopsies showed almost all had died of a ruptured aortic aneurysm. A pathologist reasoned it had to be copper deficiency, because copper is required to manufacture the heavy elastic fibers in artery walls — and when the copper in the feed was doubled the next year, not a single turkey died of a ruptured aneurysm.
claims.verbatim:
In the first thirteen weeks on the original
complete pellet ration, fully half of the turkeys on this ration died. Farmers
were picking them up by the bushel baskets full and taking them to the state
diagnostic lab to see what they died from.
At autopsy, it was obvious that almost all of the dead turkeys had died from
a ruptured aortic aneurysm. One clever pathologist said, “This has got to be
due to a copper deficiency, because copper is required to manufacture the
heavy elastic fibers found in arteries.” The next year the amount of copper
was doubled in the feed pellets and not a single turkey died from a ruptured
aneurysm.

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: What causes age spots and liver spots?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reads 'liver spots' or 'age spots' as an early outward sign of selenium deficiency and only the visible tip of ceroid lipofuscin deposits he says build up throughout the organs and sharply raise the risk of cancer, Alzheimer's, and heart disease.
claims.answer: Wallach reads the common 'liver spots' or 'age spots' on older skin as an early outward sign of selenium deficiency — and warns they are only the visible tip. When someone shows ten age spots on the skin, he says, they carry millions of the same deposits throughout the brain, eyes, heart, liver, and other organs. This 'pigment of aging,' known scientifically as ceroid lipofuscin, is essentially accumulated rancid fat (free radicals) that clogs cell function and, in his view, sharply raises the risk of cancer, Alzheimer's disease, and heart disease.
claims.verbatim:
Another early symptom of selenium deficiency in older humans is the
appearance of “liver spots” or “age spots.”

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Can selenium prevent and reverse disease?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says selenium prevents an entire family of deficiency diseases, from cardiomyopathy and muscular dystrophy to cystic fibrosis, and in many cases reverses or cures them, all for a few pennies a day in livestock.
claims.answer: Yes. Wallach says selenium was universally thought to be toxic until 1957, when it was found to be an essential trace nutrient. Selenium deficiency causes a whole family of diseases — infertility, miscarriages, cystic fibrosis of the pancreas, animal Sudden Infant Death Syndrome, liver cirrhosis, stiff lamb disease, white muscle disease, muscular dystrophy, anemias, encephalomalacia (which he equates with Alzheimer's disease), cardiomyopathy, and mulberry heart disease. In each case, selenium supplementation prevented the disease and in many cases reversed or cured it — the livestock industry does this for a few pennies a day.
claims.verbatim:
For example, the mineral selenium was universally thought to be toxic until
1957 when it was found to be an essential nutrient in trace amounts in
laboratory animals and livestock. Selenium deficiency causes infertility,
miscarriages, cystic fibrosis of the pancreas, Sudden Infant Death
Syndrome in animals, liver cirrhosis, stiff lamb disease, white muscle
disease, muscular dystrophy, anemias, encephalomalacia (Alzheimer’s
disease), cardiomyopathy heart disease, and mulberry heart disease. In each
case, selenium supplementation prevented the disease and in many cases
reversed or cured existing diseases, which were all significant causes of
animal losses to the livestock industry.

claims.subject: diabetes
claims.question: How did Wallach first connect diabetes to a mineral deficiency?
claims.answer_short: From the autopsy table: he saw zoo marmosets, alligators and shrews die of diabetes caused by chromium and vanadium deficiency.
claims.answer: Zoo marmosets and shrews died of diabetes attributed to chromium and vanadium deficiency (observed at autopsy).
claims.verbatim:
I saw marmosets, alligators, and
shrews that died of diabetes, a chromium and vanadium deficiency.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What diseases can calcium deficiency cause?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties calcium deficiency to as many as 147 different diseases, from osteoporosis and arthritis to Bell's palsy, tinnitus, and trigeminal neuralgia.
claims.answer: Calcium deficiency alone can result in as many as 147 different diseases (osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, Bell's palsy, tinnitus, trigeminal neuralgia, spinal stenosis, and more).
claims.verbatim:
Calcium deficiency alone could result in as many as 147 different diseases
ranging from osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, osteomalacia, degenerative
arthritis, Bell’s Palsy, tinnitus, trigeminal neuralgia, and spinal stenosis to
name a few.

claims.subject: cancer
claims.question: What happens if a trace mineral deficiency is left untreated?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says untreated trace-mineral deficiency reaches a 'clinical phase' of full-blown disease — cardiomyopathy, diabetes, cancer, liver cirrhosis, even death — that doctors rarely recognize as a mineral shortage, though simply replacing the missing element can bring improvement in as little as 48 hours to 30 days.
claims.answer: Wallach describes trace-mineral deficiency as a cascade that ends in what he calls the 'clinical phase' — the point where the body can no longer compensate and full-blown disease sets in, including cardiomyopathy, diabetes, cancer, and liver cirrhosis, and even death. His pointed twist: these clinical deficiencies are almost never diagnosed as mineral shortages by conventional doctors, yet the 'cure' is often simply replacing the missing element, with positive responses sometimes appearing in as little as 48 hours to 30 days.
claims.verbatim:
The clinical phase of trace mineral deficiencies is characterized by the onset
of full-blown disease states and even death—i.e., cardiomyopathy, diabetes,
cancer, liver cirrhosis.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: How much germanium should I take a day?
claims.answer_short: The recommended maintenance dose is 20 to 30 mg per day; 50 to 100 mg per day is common when serious illness calls for higher oxygen levels in the body.
claims.answer: The recommended maintenance dose for germanium is 20–30 mg per day (50–100 mg/day is used for serious illness requiring increased oxygenation).
claims.verbatim:
Twenty to 30 mg per day is the recommended maintenance dose for
germanium. Fifty to 100 mg per day doses are commonly used when an
individual has a serious illness that requires an increased oxygen level in
the body.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: What are the signs of germanium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: A crashing immune system is the hallmark — Wallach also ties a germanium shortfall to arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy, and cancer.
claims.answer: Germanium deficiency is typified by reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy, and cancer.
claims.verbatim:
A severely reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy, and
cancer typify deficiencies of germanium.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: How much silver can you take per day?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says humans can take about 400 micrograms of silver a day, and that a silver deficiency results in an impaired immune system.
claims.answer: Wallach treats silver as an essential trace mineral with a germ-killing role. Humans can take about 400 micrograms of silver a day, he says, and a silver deficiency results in an impaired immune system. He describes silver as an antibacterial, antiviral, and antifungal agent that works by disabling the enzymes microorganisms use to breathe — the same property that once led people to drop a silver dollar into milk to keep it from spoiling. He cites Dr. Robert Becker's The Body Electric linking low tissue silver both to more illness and to poor tissue repair.
claims.verbatim:
Humans can
consume 400 mcg of silver per day. A silver “deficiency” results in an
impaired immune system.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: How does silver kill germs?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains silver acts as an antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal 'anti-metabolite' that disables the enzymes microorganisms use for respiration, in effect suffocating them.
claims.answer: Silver's power against germs comes down to a specific mechanism, Wallach explains: it acts as an antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal 'anti-metabolite' that disables the very enzymes microorganisms rely on for respiration — in effect, it suffocates them. He notes this is why silver sulfadiazine is still used in most American burn centers to prevent infection, and why silver was dropped into milk and onto wounds long before modern antibiotics existed.
claims.verbatim:
Silver is an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-metabolite that
disables specific enzymes that microorganisms use for respiration.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: How many Americans are deficient in chromium?
claims.answer_short: Almost everyone — the USDA's Richard Anderson put it at 90% of all Americans.
claims.answer: Per USDA researcher Richard Anderson, 90 percent of Americans are deficient in chromium.
claims.verbatim:
According to Richard Anderson, USDA, “Ninety percent of
all Americans are deficient in chromium.”

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Does chromium supplementation extend lifespan?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach cites Gary Evans' study showing chromium lengthened lab animals' lifespan by 33.3%, upending the belief that only severe calorie restriction could extend life.
claims.answer: Yes. Wallach cites work by Gary Evans of Bemidji State University, Minnesota, which clearly showed a 33.3 percent increase in the lifespan of laboratory animals supplemented with chromium. He frames it as a landmark: before this study, gerontologists led by Roy Walford believed a severe restriction of calories was the only way to extend life past the expected average — Evans showed that a single trace mineral could do it.
claims.verbatim:
Gary Evans, Bemidji State University, Minnesota, very clearly showed an
increased life span in laboratory animals by 33.3 percent when they were
supplemented with chromium. Prior to this study gerontologists, led by Roy
Walford, felt a severe restriction of calories was the only way to extend life
past the expected average.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Can a chromium deficiency shorten your life?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says chromium deficiency causes a wide variety of clinical diseases and a shortened life expectancy, made worse by a concurrent vanadium deficiency.
claims.answer: Chromium deficiency produces a wide range of clinical diseases (low blood sugar, type II diabetes, elevated triglycerides/cholesterol, coronary vessel disease, infertility) and a shortened lifespan, aggravated by concurrent vanadium deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of chromium in humans are
characterized by a wide variety of clinical diseases as well as a shortened
life expectancy. The clinical diseases of chromium deficiency are
aggravated by concurrent vanadium deficiencies.

claims.subject: cesium
claims.question: What is high-pH therapy for cancer?
claims.answer_short: Cesium chloride pushed into the cancer cell to make its interior alkaline — the 'high-pH' approach used in alternative cancer programs.
claims.answer: Cesium chloride is used in alternative cancer therapy ('high-pH therapy'), entering the cancer cell to produce an alkaline environment.
claims.verbatim:
Cesium chloride is used as part of alternative cancer therapy programs.
Cesium provides “high ph therapy” for cancer by entering the cancer cell
and producing an alkaline environment.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What is pica a sign of?
claims.answer_short: It's a red flag for iron deficiency — the compulsion to eat ice, dirt, or lead paint.
claims.answer: Pica (a compulsion to eat ice, dirt, or lead paint) is a specific sign of iron deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Experimental evidence shows very clearly that “pica” is a specific sign of
iron deficiency. Pica can drive children and adults to eat ice (pagophagia),
dirt (geophagia), or lead paint.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What are the symptoms of iron deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Low iron shows up as tiredness and listlessness, a pounding heart on exertion, fuzzy thinking and memory slips, a sore tongue, and a pale, small-cell (hypochromic microcytic) anemia.
claims.answer: Iron deficiency symptoms include fatigue, heart palpitations on exertion, reduced cognition and memory, sore tongue, and hypochromic microcytic anemia.
claims.verbatim:
Symptoms of iron deficiency
include listlessness, fatigue, heart palpitations on exertion, reduced
cognition, memory deficits, sore tongue, angular stomatitis dysphagia, and
hypochromic microcytic anemia.

claims.subject: absorption
claims.question: What helps or blocks iron absorption?
claims.answer_short: Stomach acid and vitamin C boost iron absorption; clays and phytates block it — so low stomach acid or a high-fiber, high-phytate diet leaves you absorbing far less.
claims.answer: Iron absorption is governed by the gut environment: stomach hydrochloric acid is required for optimal absorption of iron, and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) increases it, while clays and phytates decrease it. Wallach adds that impaired absorption from high-fiber, high-phytate diets makes the standard 18 mg RDA too low for people eating that way.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Can too much iron be harmful?
claims.answer_short: Yes — too much iron can drive cirrhosis, pancreatic fibrosis, diabetes, and heart failure, not by direct toxicity but by raising the body's need for selenium, copper, and zinc.
claims.answer: Yes. Excess iron can cause cirrhosis of the liver, fibrosis of the pancreas, diabetes, and heart failure. Wallach's key point is the mechanism: these diseases are not the direct toxic effects of iron itself, but the result of the excess iron raising the body's needs for selenium, copper, zinc, and other nutrients — so the harm is really a driven deficiency of those minerals.
claims.verbatim:
Excesses of iron can cause cirrhosis of the liver, fibrosis of the pancreas,
diabetes, and heart failure. These diseases are not the direct toxic affects of
iron, but rather the increased iron results in the increased needs of selenium,
copper, zinc, etc.

claims.subject: iodine
claims.question: What does iodine do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Iodine combines with the amino acid tyrosine to build the thyroid hormone thyroxin, and it is essential to all vertebrates.
claims.answer: Iodine's whole reason for being essential, Wallach explains, is that the body combines it with the amino acid tyrosine to manufacture thyroxin, the main thyroid hormone that sets the body's metabolic rate. He warns iodine intake is usually low to begin with, and that Americans cutting back on salt at their doctors' urging have pushed goiter and hypothyroidism toward epidemic levels — all the more since iodine is freely lost in sweat.
claims.verbatim:
In combination with the amino acid tyrosine,
iodine is manufactured into the thyroid hormone thyroxin.

claims.subject: iodine
claims.question: Does cutting back on salt cause goiter and hypothyroidism?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says that since Americans began restricting salt on doctors' advice, goiter and hypothyroidism have become epidemic, because iodized salt was a key source of iodine.
claims.answer: Since Americans began restricting salt intake on doctors' advice, goiter and hypothyroidism have become epidemic (iodized salt was a key iodine source).
claims.verbatim:
Iodine intake is
usually low to begin with, but since Americans have begun restricting their
salt intake at the advice of their doctors, goiter and hypothyroidism has
become epidemic.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: Can copper deficiency cause goiter?
claims.answer_short: Yes — because copper is the cofactor the body needs to use iodine, a copper shortage can produce goiter even when iodine in the soil and diet is adequate.
claims.answer: Copper is a required cofactor to utilize iodine; copper deficiency can drive an iodine-deficiency (goiter) state even where soil iodine is adequate.
claims.verbatim:
A severe copper deficiency
in the soils of the north and the south cause the deficiency state because
copper is a required cofactor to utilize iodine.

claims.subject: manganese
claims.question: What diseases does manganese deficiency cause?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls manganese deficiency striking, causing birth defects like congenital ataxia and deafness, plus asthma, convulsions, stunted growth, skeletal defects, and joint disorders like TMJ and carpal tunnel.
claims.answer: Manganese deficiency causes birth defects (congenital ataxia, deafness), asthma, convulsions, skeletal defects, and joint problems including temporomandibular joint (jaw) disorder, repetitive motion syndrome, and carpal tunnel syndrome.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiency diseases of Mn are very striking, ranging from severe birth
defects (congenital ataxia, deafness, chondrodystrophy), asthma,
convulsions, retarded growth, skeletal defects, disruption of fat and
carbohydrate metabolism to joint problems in children and adults (i.e. TMJ,
Repetitive Motion Syndrome, Carpal Tunnel Syndrome).

claims.subject: manganese
claims.question: Why does manganese matter for the ears and joints?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes manganese as an essential mineral that activates numerous enzyme systems — including glucose metabolism, energy production and superoxide dismutase — and is structurally part of the three fragile ear bones and joint cartilage.
claims.answer: Manganese is an essential mineral with both an enzymatic and a structural role. Wallach notes it activates numerous enzyme systems — including those for glucose metabolism, energy production and the antioxidant superoxide dismutase — and is a major constituent of the body's metalloenzymes, hormones and proteins. Structurally, he says it is part of both the developmental process and the finished form of the three fragile ear bones (the ossicles) and of joint cartilage.
claims.verbatim:
Manganese is part of the developmental process and the structure
of the three fragile ear bones and joint cartilage.

claims.subject: molybdenum
claims.question: Why is molybdenum essential to the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains molybdenum is essential because it forms part of at least three enzymes the body relies on: xanthine oxidase, aldehyde oxidase, and sulfite oxidase.
claims.answer: Molybdenum earns its 'essential' status, Wallach explains, by forming an integral part of at least three enzymes the body relies on: xanthine oxidase, aldehyde oxidase, and sulfite oxidase. It is a clear illustration of how a mineral present in only trace amounts can still be indispensable — each of these enzymes depends on its molybdenum atom to do its job at all.
claims.verbatim:
Molybdenum is known to be an integral part of no less
than three essential enzymes: Xanthine oxidase, Aldehyde oxidase, and
Sulfite oxidase.

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: How does selenium work as an antioxidant?
claims.answer_short: Selenium is the body's most efficient antioxidant: acting through the glutathione peroxidase enzyme system, it stops fats from peroxidizing — that is, from going rancid inside your cells.
claims.answer: Selenium is the most efficient antioxidant, working in the glutathione peroxidase enzyme system to keep body fats from going rancid.
claims.verbatim:
Selenium is the most efficient antioxidant (anti-peroxidant).
It’s used at the subcellular level in the glutathione peroxidase enzyme
system and metalloamino acids (selenomethionine, etc.).

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Is vegetable oil bad for your heart?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says lots of vegetable oil plus low selenium is the fastest path to heart attack and cancer, because polyunsaturated oils (especially heated or hydrogenated into trans fats) go rancid and free-radical-damage your cells.
claims.answer: Wallach's answer is yes, especially alongside low selenium. He calls high intakes of vegetable oils — salad dressings and cooking oils — together with a selenium deficiency the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer. The reason is the oils' polyunsaturated structure: when heated or hydrogenated into trans fatty acids they go rancid, inflicting free-radical damage on cellular fat — the very peroxidation that selenium, the body's antioxidant, normally prevents.
claims.verbatim:
High intakes of vegetable oils,
including salad dressing and cooking oils, concurrent with a selenium
deficiency is the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer. The polyun‐
saturated configuration of the oils when heated or treated with hydrogen
(“trans fatty acids”) literally causes the rancidity (“free radical” damage) of
cellular fat

claims.subject: tin
claims.question: Does tin deficiency cause hair loss?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's account, rats deprived of tin grew poorly and developed hearing loss and bilateral male-pattern hair loss — the basis for his link between tin deficiency, male-pattern baldness, and hearing loss.
claims.answer: Tin deficiency in rats produced poor growth, hearing loss, and bilateral (male-pattern) hair loss; Wallach links tin to male-pattern baldness and hearing loss.
claims.verbatim:
Rats fed tin at 17.0 ng/gm show poor growth, reduced feeding efficiency,
hearing loss, and bilateral (male pattern) hair loss, while rats fed 1.99
|ng/gm were physiologically and anatomically normal.

claims.subject: strontium
claims.question: Can a strontium deficiency cause osteoporosis?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach ties a strontium shortage to the stubborn forms of osteoporosis and arthritis that don't respond to calcium and boron alone.
claims.answer: Strontium deficiency is associated with certain calcium- and boron-resistant forms of osteoporosis and arthritis.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of strontium are associated with certain types of Ca and boron
resistant osteoporosis and arthritis.

claims.subject: strontium
claims.question: What is strontium?
claims.answer_short: A bone-seeking trace mineral that can stand in for calcium. Wallach considers it essential in mammals and ties its deficiency to calcium- and boron-resistant osteoporosis and arthritis.
claims.answer: Strontium is a trace mineral most highly concentrated in mammalian bone. Wallach says it can replace calcium in many organisms, including man, and that there is considerable evidence it is essential in mammals. He associates a strontium deficiency with certain calcium- and boron-resistant forms of osteoporosis and arthritis.
claims.verbatim:
Strontium
can replace calcium in many organisms, including man. There is
considerable evidence for essentiality in mammals including man.
Deficiencies of strontium are associated with certain types of Ca and boron
resistant osteoporosis and arthritis

claims.subject: diabetes
claims.question: How does vanadium help with diabetes?
claims.answer_short: Vanadium mimics insulin — it makes the cell's insulin receptors more sensitive, helping the body handle glucose and carbohydrates.
claims.answer: Vanadium appears to function like insulin by altering cell-membrane function for ion transport — making the membrane's insulin receptors more sensitive to insulin, and benefiting people with glucose and carbohydrate intolerance.
claims.verbatim:
Vanadium appears to function
like insulin by altering cell membrane function for ion transport.

claims.subject: vanadium
claims.question: Can vanadium help with diabetes and low blood sugar?
claims.answer_short: Yes — vanadium mimics insulin, sensitizing cell receptors and normalizing blood sugar (diabetic rats fed vanadium matched normal controls). Wallach says it could reduce or even eliminate most adult-onset diabetes.
claims.answer: Yes. Wallach says vanadium (proven essential in 1971) functions like insulin: it stimulates blood-sugar (glucose) oxidation and transport, and in diabetic rats fed vanadium the blood glucose matched normal controls despite low serum insulin. It works by making the cell-membrane insulin receptors more sensitive to insulin, which benefits glucose and carbohydrate intolerance such as hypoglycemia and prediabetes. He states vanadium supplementation could reduce or even eliminate most cases of adult-onset diabetes, and cites a 1985 University of Vancouver statement that 'vanadium will replace insulin for adult onset diabetics.'
claims.verbatim:
Vanadium supplementation can have a major positive
economic impact by reducing or even eliminating most cases of adult onset
diabetes.

claims.subject: vanadium
claims.question: Can vanadium help prevent cancer?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says vanadium is anticarcinogenic: in mice it blocked mammary tumor induction, cut tumor incidence and count, and extended cancer-free time without harming the animals' health.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that vanadium has known anticarcinogenic properties. In mice, feeding 25 micrograms of vanadium per gram of diet blocked the induction of mammary tumor growth; the vanadium supplement reduced tumor incidence, lowered the average tumor count per animal, and prolonged the median cancer-free time — all without inhibiting the animals' overall growth or health.
claims.verbatim:
Vanadium has known
anticarcinogenic properties. Feeding 25 |ng of vanadium per gram of diet
blocked induction of mouse mammary tumor growth.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Why is zinc so important in the body?
claims.answer_short: At least 70 metalloenzymes require zinc as a working cofactor — including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, and carboxypeptidase — and zinc also sits inside RNA (the 'zinc fingers') and drives DNA synthesis and cell division.
claims.answer: Zinc's importance is easy to underestimate until you count the enzymes that depend on it: at least 70 metalloenzymes require zinc as a working cofactor, Wallach notes — among them carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, and carboxypeptidase, which handle jobs from carbon-dioxide transport to protein digestion. Zinc also sits inside the RNA molecule itself (the 'zinc fingers') and drives DNA synthesis and cell division, which is why a shortage reaches into so many systems at once.
claims.verbatim:
There are no less than 70 metalloenzymes that require Zn as a
functional cofactor.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: What role does zinc play in DNA and cell division?
claims.answer_short: Zinc forms the 'metallic fingers' built into RNA and drives cell division and DNA synthesis; the DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and thymidine kinase are both zinc-dependent enzymes.
claims.answer: Zinc is central to the cell's genetic machinery. Wallach says it takes part in the metabolism of nucleic acids and the synthesis of proteins, and is an integral part of the RNA molecule itself — providing the 'metallic fingers' that take part in cell division and the synthesis of DNA. He notes that DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and thymidine kinase are both zinc-dependent enzymes.
claims.verbatim:
Zinc participates in the metabolism of nucleic acids and the synthesis of
proteins. Zinc is also an integral part of the RNA molecule itself where Zinc
provides the “metallic fingers” and participates in cell division and
synthesis of DNA. The DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is a zinc-dependent enzyme, as is thymidine kinase

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: What birth defects are linked to zinc deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties zinc deficiency in pregnancy to birth defects including Down's syndrome, cleft lip and palate, brain and eye malformations, spina bifida, and clubbed or webbed limbs, plus degenerative diseases across all age groups.
claims.answer: Zinc deficiency, in Wallach's account, produces an unusually wide range of diseases — from congenital birth defects present at birth to degenerative diseases across every age group. He ties a striking list of birth defects specifically to zinc shortage during pregnancy, including Down's syndrome, cleft lip and palate, brain and eye malformations, spina bifida, and clubbed or webbed limbs. He notes zinc concentrates in the kidney, prostate, and eye, and that its essentiality for humans was recognized only about twenty years before he wrote.
claims.verbatim:
Zinc deficiency
produces a wide range of diseases including congenital birth defects and
degenerative diseases of all age groups.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: What blocks zinc absorption?
claims.answer_short: Wallach warns that too much dietary copper and iron, plus high-phytate vegan diets, all cut down how much zinc the body can actually take up.
claims.answer: Getting enough zinc isn't only about how much you eat — Wallach flags what blocks it: an excess of dietary copper or iron, and high-phytate diets (he singles out vegan eating), all reduce the availability of the zinc you take in, because they compete for or bind the mineral in the gut. He notes zinc is also lost heavily in sweat, which puts unsupplemented athletes at particular risk of deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Excesses of dietary copper and iron and high phytate diets (vegans) will
reduce availability of dietary zinc.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: Can vitamin A deficiency cause blindness?
claims.answer_short: In children, vitamin A deficiency caused keratitis and corneal ulcers that could progress to blindness, the eye being one of the first tissues to fail without it.
claims.answer: From his years as a barefoot doctor among the Zulu, Wallach watched textbook nutritional deficiencies play out in children. Vitamin A shortage, he recounts, caused keratitis and corneal ulcers that could progress all the way to blindness — the eye being one of the first tissues to fail without it. He lists it beside the other deficiencies he treated there: calcium (bone disease), iodine and copper (goiter and miscarriage), and folic acid or zinc (spina bifida and cleft palate).
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin A deficiencies in
children caused keratitis, corneal ulcers, and blindness.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: What deficiency causes spina bifida and cleft palate in babies?
claims.answer_short: A folic-acid and/or zinc deficiency (also B12) in the mother. Wallach calls these 'birth defects' simple mineral deficiencies, not true genetic flaws — and preventable by supplementing before conception.
claims.answer: Wallach says spina bifida and cleft palate are not true 'genetic' defects but the visible fingerprint of a simple nutritional deficiency — chiefly a lack of folic acid and/or zinc (and vitamin B12) in the mother's diet. He produced these very defects in animals by feeding pregnant mothers diets deficient in zinc, B12, and folic acid, and prevented up to 98% of them by supplying the proper nutrients before conception. In infants he attributes spina bifida and serious cleft palates to folic acid or zinc deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
I studied dozens of congenital birth defects in laboratory and farm animals
and what nutritional deficiencies produced them. What we found was that,
in most instances, “genetic defects” are simple mineral deficiencies that
leave a repeatable “fingerprint” on a specific gene, in a specific location, on
a specific chromosome. They are no more complicated in concept than a
deficiency of zinc resulting in a cleft palate or spina bifida in a farm animal

claims.subject: vitamin-b1
claims.question: What is beriberi and what causes it?
claims.answer_short: Beriberi is the classic vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency disease — weakness in the limbs plus congestive heart failure. Wallach ties it to diets of polished white rice that stripped away the thiamine.
claims.answer: Beriberi is the classic thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency disease. Wallach describes it as a common disease of the Asian rice cultures (the name is Sinhalese for 'I cannot'), characterized by weakness in the legs, hands, and arms together with congestive heart failure, with death from pulmonary edema and abdominal 'dropsy.' He identifies the cause as a thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency — historically appearing where the diet was polished white rice with its thiamine-bearing bran removed.
claims.verbatim:
Beriberi with resultant congestive
heart failure was common, the result of a thiamin or vitamin B1 deficiency.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: Why is vitamin B12 red?
claims.answer_short: Because of cobalt — the single cobalt atom bound at the center of the B12 molecule is what gives the water-soluble crystal its red color.
claims.answer: Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble red crystalline substance; its red color comes from the cobalt atom at its center.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline substance that is water soluble. The red
color is due to the cobalt in the molecule.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: Does cooking destroy vitamin B12?
claims.answer_short: About 30 percent of vitamin B12's activity is lost during cooking, whether by electric, gas, or microwave heat, because B12 is fragile and slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances.
claims.answer: About 30 percent of vitamin B12's activity is lost during cooking, whether by electric, gas, or microwave heat, according to Wallach. He explains why it is so fragile: B12 is a water-soluble, red crystalline vitamin — its color comes from the cobalt atom at its center — and it is slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances, so ordinary heat degrades a meaningful share of it.
claims.verbatim:
About 30 percent of B12 activity is lost during cooking
(electric, gas, or microwave).

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Can chromium prevent or cure diabetes?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says supplemental chromium has prevented and treated both diabetes and hypoglycemia since 1958. He counts adult-onset diabetes a chromium (and vanadium) deficiency, so the mineral corrects the root cause.
claims.answer: Yes. Wallach says it has been known since 1958 that supplemental chromium will prevent and treat both diabetes and hypoglycemia, and points to Walter Mertz (director of USDA field services), who published the chromium-diabetes facts in Federation Proceedings. He calls diabetes the ultimate case of a whole medical specialty that could be wiped out by universal chromium supplementation, because in his framework adult-onset diabetes and hypoglycemia are fundamentally deficiencies of chromium and vanadium — so supplying those minerals corrects the root cause.
claims.verbatim:
Since
1958, it has been known that supplemental chromium will prevent and treat
diabetes as well as hypoglycemia. Just ask any health food storeowner or
N.D.! Walter Mertz (the director of the U.S.D.A. field services) published
the facts associated with chromium and diabetes in the Federation
Proceeding. Here is the ultimate case of a whole specialty of medicine
which could be wiped out by universal chromium supplementation

claims.subject: vanadium
claims.question: Can vanadium replace insulin for diabetes?
claims.answer_short: Yes. Wallach says vanadium acts like insulin -- keeping blood sugar normal even when insulin is low -- and can reduce or eliminate most adult-onset diabetes; he cites a 1985 University of Vancouver statement that it 'will replace insulin.'
claims.answer: Wallach holds that vanadium can act as a substitute for insulin. He reports that despite low serum insulin, diabetic animals fed vanadium held the same blood glucose as normal controls, because vanadium functions like insulin by altering cell membrane function for ion transport. On that basis he argues that vanadium supplementation can reduce or even eliminate most cases of adult-onset (type 2) diabetes, and cites a 1985 statement from the medical school at the University of Vancouver, BC that vanadium will replace insulin for adult onset diabetics.
claims.verbatim:
the medical school at the
University of Vancouver, BC, Canada stated that “vanadium will replace
insulin for adult onset diabetics.”

claims.subject: diabetes
claims.question: How does Wallach treat diabetes?
claims.answer_short: Start with chromium and vanadium at 250 mcg a day in the early stages — carefully, to avoid dropping blood sugar too fast ('insulin shock').
claims.answer: Wallach's diabetes program opens with the two minerals he ties to blood-sugar control — chromium and vanadium — at 250 micrograms a day in the early stages. He adds a caution: introduce them carefully, because as they sharpen the body's own glucose handling, a diabetic still taking the old dose of insulin or pills can be tipped into 'insulin shock,' a sudden, dangerous drop in blood sugar. The answer is to keep testing and taper the medication as levels come down.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of diabetes should include chromium and vanadium at 250
mcg/day in the initial stages to prevent “insulin shock”

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: Is niacin important for blood sugar or diabetes?
claims.answer_short: Yes — niacin is part of the GTF (glucose tolerance factor), so Wallach's diabetes protocol makes a point of including it.
claims.answer: The diabetes regimen also includes zinc 50 mg three times daily, B-complex 50 mg three times daily (with niacin), EFAs 5 g three times daily, B12 1,000 mcg/day, quercetin 150 mg/day, copper 2-3 mg/day, lecithin 2,500 mg three times daily, and glutathione 100 mg/day.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of diabetes should also include zinc at 50 mg t.i.d., B-complex at
50 mg t.i.d. (be sure to include niacin which is part of the GTF “glucose
tolerance factor”), essential fatty acids at 5 gm t.i.d., B12 at 1,000 mcg/day,
bioflavonoids including quercetin at 150 mg/day, copper at 2-3 mg/day,
lecithin at 2,500 mg t.i.d., and glutathione at 100 mg/day.

claims.subject: arthritis
claims.question: What causes osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?
claims.answer_short: Two very different causes: the wear-and-tear kind (osteoarthritis / degenerative arthritis) is a cluster of nutritional deficiencies, while rheumatoid arthritis is really a chronic Mycoplasma infection -- not the autoimmune mystery 'orthodox' medicine claims.
claims.answer: Osteoarthritis and degenerative arthritis are a complex of nutritional deficiencies; rheumatoid arthritis's overt cause is chronic Mycoplasma infection.
claims.verbatim:
osteoarthritis and degenerative arthritis are a complex of
nutritional deficiencies. In the case of rheumatoid arthritis, a chronic
infection with a Mycoplasma spp. is the overt cause.

claims.subject: arthritis
claims.question: How do you treat arthritis with supplements?
claims.answer_short: Rebuild the joint, don't just kill the pain: calcium 2,000 mg/day (more with meat), magnesium 800-1,000 mg/day, and glucosamine/chondroitin cartilage 1,000 mg three times daily, over the full vitamin-mineral base -- and for rheumatoid arthritis add an antibiotic to clear the Mycoplasma.
claims.answer: Wallach's arthritis protocol rebuilds joint tissue nutritionally rather than just masking pain. The core is calcium at 2,000 mg/day (more if you eat meat two or three times a day), magnesium at 800-1,000 mg/day, and cartilage -- collagen, glucosamine sulfate and chondroitin sulfate -- at 1,000 mg three times a day. He adds vitamin C to bowel tolerance, B6 100 mg twice daily, B3 450 mg twice daily, vitamin E 1,000 IU/day, copper 2 mg/day, selenium 300 mcg/day and zinc 50 mg three times daily, favoring plant-derived colloidal minerals (up to 98 percent absorbable). For rheumatoid arthritis he additionally treats the underlying Mycoplasma infection -- low-dose tetracycline or minocycline for a year (or oral food-grade H2O2) plus IV EDTA/H2O2 chelation.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of arthritis should include calcium at 2000 mg/day and more if
you eat meat two or three times per day. Also take magnesium at 800-1000
mg/day, and cartilage (collagen, glucosamine sulfate and
chondroitin sulfate) at 1000 mg t.i.d. For
rheumatoid arthritis, add tetracycline or minocycline at the low dose acne
therapy level daily for one year, or oral food grade H2O2 to deal with the
Mycoplasma infection.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What is the ideal calcium to phosphorus ratio?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says a 2:1 dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio is ideal but impossible to reach on an unsupplemented diet, and the more meat you eat the more calcium supplementation you need.
claims.answer: A dietary calcium:phosphorus ratio of 2:1 is ideal but impossible to attain on an unsupplemented diet; the more meat eaten, the more calcium supplementation needed.
claims.verbatim:
A dietary calcium/phosphorus ratio of 2:1 is ideal yet impossible to attain in
an unsupplemented diet.

claims.subject: absorption
claims.question: Are some 'diseases' really just malabsorption?
claims.answer_short: Yes. Wallach says celiac-type gut damage can wipe out most of the intestine's absorptive surface, so conditions like diabetes, cancer, asthma and muscular dystrophy are often malabsorption in disguise -- the body starving for minerals despite a decent diet.
claims.answer: Yes -- Wallach reframes many named 'diseases' as malabsorption in disguise. He argues that celiac-type damage to the intestinal lining (from wheat gluten, cow's-milk albumen or soy protein) can destroy up to 85-90 percent of the absorptive surface, so the body starves for minerals even on an adequate diet. On that basis he calls celiac disease the basic cause of many diseases, including diabetes (malabsorption of chromium and vanadium), cancer (malabsorption of zinc, vitamin A and selenium), and muscular dystrophy / cystic fibrosis (malabsorption of selenium). He describes asthma the same way -- a disease of malabsorption with deficiencies of essential fatty acids, manganese and magnesium -- and atopic dermatitis as a malabsorption syndrome.
claims.verbatim:
Asthma is a
disease of malabsorption with essential fatty acid deficiencies and
deficiencies of manganese and magnesium.

claims.subject: cor_pulmonale
claims.question: How do you treat cor pulmonale?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats cor pulmonale by resolving the underlying lung disease plus oxygen, IV hydrogen peroxide, and selenium at 500-1,000 mcg per day for adults.
claims.answer: Cor pulmonale treatment includes resolving the lung disease plus oxygen, intravenous (into a vein) hydrogen peroxide, and selenium at 500-1,000 mcg/day for adults.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of cor pulmonale includes resolving the precipitating lung
disease and oxygen, IV hydrogen peroxide, and selenium at 500-1,000 mcg
per day for adults.

claims.subject: cradle_cap
claims.question: How do you treat cradle cap?
claims.answer_short: Loosen the greasy scale with regular shampooing, then fix the deficiency underneath -- vitamin B6 10-25 mg/day and zinc 15-25 mg/day -- and pulse-test for the food allergies that can drive it.
claims.answer: Wallach treats cradle cap (seborrheic dermatitis of infants) by loosening the greasy scale and correcting the deficiencies underneath it. His protocol is regular shampooing to loosen the greasy crust, vitamin B6 at 10-25 mg/day, and zinc at 15-25 mg/day, plus a pulse test for food allergies, which can contribute to the problem. Because he classes cradle cap as a seborrheic dermatitis that can arise from celiac-type intestinal lesions and a malabsorption syndrome, he also supports it with biotin (100 mcg three times daily), folic acid, more B6, vitamin E, essential fatty acids and vitamin A.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of cradle cap includes shampooing regularly to loosen the greasy
scale, B6 at 10-25 mg per day, and zinc at 15-25 mg per day. Food allergies
can contribute to this problem—do a pulse test.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: Can you overdose on beta-carotene?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says it is almost impossible to overdose on beta-carotene, the first sign being dry skin, and he uses it at a vitamin A equivalent of about 300,000 IU per day.
claims.answer: Cancer prevention includes beta-carotene at ~300,000 International Units/day (vitamin A equivalent) and selenium at 250-500 mcg/day, alongside a low-fat, high-fiber, fried-food-free diet.
claims.verbatim:
Try to OD on beta-carotene
(almost impossible—first sign is dry skin) at about a vitamin A equivalent
of 300,000 IU per day. Use selenium at 250 to 500 mcg per day.

claims.subject: cancer
claims.question: Has cancer survival improved in the last 20 years?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites the US government that the five-year cancer survival rate has not changed in 20 years despite new surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, and that untreated patients as a group survived longer.
claims.answer: Per the US government, the five-year cancer survival rate has not changed in 20 years despite new surgery/radiation/chemotherapy — untreated patients as a group survived longer.
claims.verbatim:
CHEMOTHERAPY—IN FACT, UNTREATED
PATIENTS, AS A GROUP, SURVIVED LONGER!

claims.subject: osteoporosis
claims.question: Can osteoporosis be prevented and reversed?
claims.answer_short: From personal experience Wallach says osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure with stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) and calcium — the real problem is often too little stomach acid to absorb calcium, not too little calcium — and he rejects the conventional estrogen-and-fluoride approach.
claims.answer: Osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure, Wallach claims from personal experience, with two unglamorous things: stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) and calcium. His logic is that the real problem is often not too little calcium in the diet but too little stomach acid to absorb it — so supplementing HCl unlocks the calcium a person already eats. He dismisses the conventional estrogen-and-fluoride approach as failing to touch that root absorption problem.
claims.verbatim:
In our personal experience
osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure with proper supplementation of
stomach acid (HCl) and calcium.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Can osteoporosis be cured?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach calls it easy to prevent and cure. Estrogen and fluoride miss the point; the fix is restoring stomach acid (HCl) plus calcium and magnesium so the bone can actually be rebuilt.
claims.answer: Yes -- Wallach says osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure. He argues the orthodox push for estrogen and fluoride supplementation does not solve it, because the real problem is failure to absorb and supply calcium. In his experience it prevents and reverses with proper supplementation of stomach acid (HCl) and calcium: betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes 75-200 mg three times daily before meals, plus calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg/day (or more for the first 30 days), with plant-derived colloidal minerals supplying calcium, magnesium and boron. He also recommends a pulse test for the food allergies that cause celiac-type malabsorption.
claims.verbatim:
The big push by the “orthodox”
doctors is for estrogen and fluoride supplementation, yet these two
compounds alone do not solve the problem. In our personal experience
osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure with proper supplementation of
stomach acid (HCl) and calcium.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: How much magnesium does Wallach recommend a day?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's standard pairing is calcium at 2,000 mg and magnesium at 1,000 mg a day — a two-to-one combination he prescribes for osteoporosis and other bone and mineral problems.
claims.answer: Osteoporosis treatment includes betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes (75-200 mg three times daily before meals) plus calcium and magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000 mg/day or more for the first 30 days.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of osteoporosis should include betaine HCl and pancreatic
enzymes at 75-200 mg t.i.d. 15 minutes before meals, and calcium and
magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day or more for the first 30 days.

claims.subject: estrogen
claims.question: Is estrogen therapy safe for osteoporosis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach opposes estrogen for osteoporosis: it can cause breast and uterine cancer, and he treats the disease as a mineral/absorption failure — betaine HCl, calcium, magnesium and colloidal minerals — not a hormone deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach considers estrogen the wrong treatment for osteoporosis, and a risky one: it may be contraindicated because of a carcinogenic effect — it is known to cause breast and uterine cancer. His deeper objection is that he does not see osteoporosis as an estrogen-deficiency disease at all, but as a mineral-and-absorption failure — his program corrects stomach acid with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes and supplies calcium, magnesium and the plant-derived colloidal minerals (including boron) that bone actually needs. In that view hormone replacement treats a symptom while missing the real deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Estrogen may be contraindicated because of the potential carcinogenic
effect: it is known to cause breast and uterine cancer.

claims.subject: otitis
claims.question: Are ear infections caused by milk allergy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach claims 95 percent of all otitis (ear inflammation) is the result of a milk allergy rather than a primary infection, and urges a pulse test, strict avoidance of cow's milk, and eardrops instead of antibiotics and ear tubes.
claims.answer: Wallach makes a striking claim about earaches: in reality, he says, 95 percent of all otitis (inflammation of the ear) is the result of a milk allergy rather than a primary infection. Instead of the conventional route of antibiotics and surgically inserted ear tubes, he urges a pulse test to confirm the food trigger, strict avoidance of cow's milk in every form, and local relief with hydrogen-peroxide or mullein eardrops alongside the baseline nutritional program. Left uncorrected, he warns, a milk allergy can drive high fever, severe earaches, and even burst eardrums.
claims.verbatim: In reality, 95 percent of all otitis (earaches) is the result of a milk allergy.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Which fatty acids does Wallach say are actually essential?
claims.answer_short: Of the three EFAs — linoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic — only linoleic and linolenic are truly essential, since the body can make arachidonic acid from linolenic.
claims.answer: The essential fatty acids are linoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic acids; 3% of total daily calorie intake should come from EFAs (linoleic and linolenic are strictly essential).
claims.verbatim:
Three polyunsaturated fatty acids (linoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic acids)
are known as essential fatty acids (EFA). Three percent of the total daily
calorie intake is required from EFA.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: What do essential fatty acids do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains essential fatty acids are the raw material the body uses to make prostaglandins, which help regulate blood pressure, heart rate, blood-vessel and airway dilation, clotting, and central nervous system function.
claims.answer: EFAs are the raw material the body uses to manufacture prostaglandins, which regulate blood pressure, heart rate, vascular and bronchial dilation, blood clotting, and central nervous system (CNS) function.
claims.verbatim:
EFA’s are also the raw material for the human body to
manufacture prostaglandins that help regulate blood pressure, heart rate,
vascular dilation, blood clotting, bronchial dilation, and central nervous
system (brain and spinal cord) function.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: What are the signs of essential fatty acid deficiency in infants?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports essential fatty acid deficiency in infants causes poor growth, eczema, and lowered resistance to infectious disease.
claims.answer: Essential fatty acids matter most where growth is fastest, and Wallach flags their deficiency in infants specifically: it results in poor growth, eczema, and lowered resistance to infectious disease. He frames these good fats as far more than fuel — they lower serum cholesterol and are the raw material for prostaglandins, the local hormones that help regulate blood pressure, heart rate, blood-vessel and airway width, clotting, and brain and spinal-cord function.
claims.verbatim:
EFA deficiency in human infants
results in a poor growth rate, eczema, and lowered resistance to infectious
diseases.

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: Is taurine an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Wallach adds taurine to the classic list of essential amino acids, saying that over the long haul it helps prevent a specific disease — macular degeneration.
claims.answer: Wallach adds arginine, taurine, and tyrosine to the classic essential amino acids — over the long haul these three help prevent cancer, macular degeneration, and goiter respectively.
claims.verbatim:
To the classic list of essential amino
acids, I would add arginine, taurine, and tyrosine. Over the long haul, these
three amino acids help prevent certain specific diseases. Respectively, those
diseases are cancer, macular degeneration, and goiter.

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: What do amino acids like tryptophan turn into in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lays out amino-acid conversions: tryptophan is the precursor of niacin (B3) and serotonin, phenylalanine gives rise to thyroxin and epinephrine (adrenaline), and methionine forms choline and creatine phosphate — all classic essential amino acids the body cannot make and must get from the diet.
claims.answer: Beyond building protein, several amino acids are the raw material for other key body chemicals, and Wallach lays out the conversions: tryptophan is the precursor of niacin (vitamin B3) and serotonin (the mood neurotransmitter); phenylalanine gives rise to thyroxin (a thyroid hormone) and epinephrine (adrenaline); and methionine is used to form choline and creatine phosphate. It comes from his table of the classic essential amino acids — the ones the body cannot make for itself and must take in from the diet each day.
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan precursor of niacin and serotonin
Phenylalanine precursor of thyroxin and epinephrine
Methionine formation of choline and creatine phosphate

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: What is cholesterol used for in the body?
claims.answer_short: Cholesterol is structural to cell walls, brain and spinal cord (myelin), and is the raw material the body uses to make vitamin D, bile acids, adrenal cortical hormones, estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone.
claims.answer: Cholesterol is structural to cell walls and to the brain and spinal cord (myelin), and is the raw material for vitamin D, bile acids, adrenal cortical hormones, estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone.
claims.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential part
of the structure of cell walls, brain and spinal cord (myelin), the raw
material for the production of vitamin D in the human body, bile acids,
adrenal cortical hormones, estrogen (a cholesterol deficiency makes
menopause a living hell), progesterone, and testosterone

claims.subject: infertility
claims.question: Can infertility be cured with nutrition?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds that infertility is usually caused by a nutritional deficiency and reports curing several hundred cases with supplementation of vitamins, minerals, trace minerals, and digestive aids.
claims.answer: Infertility is usually caused by a nutritional deficiency; Wallach reports curing several hundred cases with supplementation of vitamins, minerals, trace minerals, and digestive aids.
claims.verbatim:
INFERTILITY (curable inability to have children) is usually caused by a
nutritional deficiency of some nutrient. We have “cured” several hundred
cases of infertility by simple supplementation of vitamins, minerals, trace
minerals, and digestive aids.

claims.subject: infertility
claims.question: What supplements does Wallach recommend for infertility?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's infertility protocol is essential fatty acids, L-arginine, zinc, selenium, vitamin A (100,000 IU/day for 30 days then 25,000), and germanium.
claims.answer: Infertility protocol: EFA 5 g three times daily, L-arginine 500 mg three times daily, zinc, selenium 250 mcg/day, vitamin A 100,000 International Units/day for 30 days then 25,000 International Units/day, and germanium 50 mg/day.
claims.verbatim:
EFA at 5 gm t.i.d., l-arginine at 500 mg t.i.d., zinc at 15 mg t.i.d., selenium
at 250 mcg/day, vitamin A at 100,000 IU/day for 30 days then drop to
25,000 IU/day, germanium at 50 mg/day

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Can selenium prevent muscular dystrophy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says selenium prevents muscular dystrophy in all its forms, and that a preconception woman's selenium level matters for both maintaining pregnancy and preventing muscular dystrophy.
claims.answer: Selenium prevents muscular dystrophy in all its forms (and Keshan disease, heart muscular dystrophy); preconception selenium levels matter for both pregnancy maintenance and muscular-dystrophy prevention.
claims.verbatim:
The selenium levels in
preconception women is important to the maintenance of pregnancy as well
as the prevention of muscular dystrophy in all of its forms

claims.subject: muscular_dystrophy
claims.question: Can muscular dystrophy be cured with selenium and vitamin E?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says that if selenium and vitamin E are given by intramuscular or intravenous injection at the very first onset of symptoms, muscular dystrophy can be arrested or even cured.
claims.answer: Given selenium and vitamin E (intramuscular [injected into a muscle] or intravenous [into a vein]) at the very first onset of symptoms, muscular dystrophy can be arrested or even cured.
claims.verbatim:
If selenium and vitamin E were to
be given IM or IV at the very first onset of symptoms, the disease will be
arrested or maybe even “cured.”

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Why do I keep getting muscle cramps and charley horses?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls a muscle cramp a 'mini-convulsion' in the muscle, caused by deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, potassium, and selenium.
claims.answer: Muscle cramps (charley horse) are a mini-convulsion in the muscle resulting from deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, potassium, selenium, and/or vitamin E.
claims.verbatim:
MUSCLE CRAMPS (Charley horse) are a “mini” convulsion that is taking
place in the muscle as a result of deficiencies of calcium, magnesium

claims.subject: insomnia
claims.question: How do you treat insomnia naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's insomnia treatment is to avoid caffeine and offending food allergens and to supplement calcium (especially plant-derived colloidal) plus chromium and vanadium.
claims.answer: Insomnia treatment includes avoiding caffeine and food allergens, calcium (especially plant-derived colloidal), and chromium + vanadium at 25-200 mcg three times daily.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment for insomnia includes avoidance of caffeine and offending food allergens, calcium
(especially plant derived colloidal calcium), chromium and vanadium at 25-200 mcg t.i.d.

claims.subject: angina
claims.question: How do you treat angina naturally?
claims.answer_short: For angina, Wallach says calcium, magnesium, and essential fatty acids help prevent disease progression, and that lifestyle change with supplementation can reverse cardiovascular disease.
claims.answer: For angina, calcium 2,000 mg/day, magnesium 800 mg/day, and essential fatty acids help prevent disease progression; lifestyle change and supplementation can reverse cardiovascular disease.
claims.verbatim:
Calcium (2000 mg/day) and magnesium (800 mg/day) and essential fatty
acids can help prevent progress of current disease

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Can zinc deficiency cause loss of smell?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says a lasting loss of smell (anosmia) is most often from zinc deficiency, and zinc supplementation (50 mg three times a day) is very effective at restoring it — except when the cause is an injury, stroke, or tumor.
claims.answer: A lasting loss of the sense of smell — known medically as anosmia — is most often the result of a zinc deficiency, Wallach says. He separates this chronic loss from the temporary kind caused by a cold or nasal inflammation, and notes that zinc supplementation (he uses 50 mg three times a day) is very effective at restoring smell — except where the underlying cause is an injury, stroke, or tumor.
claims.verbatim:
Chronic loss of the sense of
smell is most frequently the result of a zinc deficiency.

claims.subject: anxiety
claims.question: How do you treat anxiety and panic attacks naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach advises avoiding caffeine and sugar and taking chromium and vanadium, high-dose vitamin B6 and B3, L-tryptophan, calcium, and magnesium.
claims.answer: Anxiety/panic treatment: avoid caffeine and sugar; chromium + vanadium 200-300 mcg/day, B6 100 mg three times daily, B3 450 mg three times daily, L-tryptophan, calcium 2,000 mg/day, magnesium 800 mg/day.
claims.verbatim:
Take chromium and vanadium
200-300 mcg/day, B6 100 mg t.i.d., B3 450 mg t.i.d. as time-release tablets,
Bl, B2, and B5 at the rate of 50 mg t.i.d., L-tryptophan 10 grams t.i.d.,
calcium 2000 mg/day, and magnesium at 800 mg/day.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: What deficiency causes loss of appetite or anorexia?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties poor appetite to zinc and lithium deficiency, and argues anorexia nervosa is often a severe food allergy — treated by correcting the deficiency, finding the offending food, and supporting digestion with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes.
claims.answer: Wallach ties poor appetite to mineral status, not just psychology: deficiencies of the minerals zinc and lithium are associated with anorexia (loss of appetite). In the same discussion he goes further, arguing that anorexia nervosa — usually treated as a psychiatric disease — is often a manifestation of a severe food allergy, since sufferers commonly feel better when they don't eat. His answer is to correct the deficiency, hunt down the offending food (frequently cow's milk, wheat, eggs, or corn), and support digestion with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes alongside the baseline vitamin-mineral program.
claims.verbatim: Deficiencies of zinc and lithium are associated with anorexia.

claims.subject: canker_sores
claims.question: How do you treat canker sores?
claims.answer_short: Wallach uses folic acid, B12, iron, and zinc as adjuncts to allergen-avoidance diets for canker sores.
claims.answer: Canker sores (aphthous stomatitis): folic acid 5 mg three times daily, B12 1,000 mcg/day, iron 15 mg/day, and zinc 50 mg three times daily as adjuncts to allergen-avoidance diets.
claims.verbatim:
Folic acid at 5 mg ti.d., B12 at 1000 mcg/day, iron at 15 mg/day and zinc at
50 mg t.i.d. are effective adjuncts to avoidance diets.

claims.subject: arsenic_toxicity
claims.question: How do you remove arsenic from the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says IV chelation and oral colloidal or chelated selenium effectively remove the body's load of arsenic.
claims.answer: For arsenic toxicity, intravenous (into a vein) chelation and oral colloidal/chelated selenium effectively remove the body's arsenic load.
claims.verbatim:
IV chelation is very effective in removing
the body load of arsenic, as is the oral use of colloidal or chelated selenium.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Does magnesium deficiency cause hardening of the arteries?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says magnesium deficiency produces a 'malignant calcification' of the large elastic arteries and may be the very cause of arteriosclerosis, the hardening of the arteries.
claims.answer: This is one of Wallach's signature cardiovascular claims: magnesium deficiency, he says, produces a 'malignant calcification' of the elastic arteries — the aorta and other large vessels — and may be nothing less than 'the cause' of arteriosclerosis, the hardening of the arteries. In his framing the calcium hardening the artery wall is a downstream sign of a missing mineral, magnesium, rather than the primary villain — a direct challenge to the conventional cholesterol-centered story of heart disease.
claims.verbatim:
Magnesium deficiencies produce “malignant calcification” of
elastic arteries and are perhaps “the cause” of arteriosclerosis.

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: Can too much vitamin D be dangerous?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach teaches that vitamin D toxicity is angiotoxic, targeting the elastic arteries and causing fibrosis of arterial smooth muscle and calcification of blood vessel walls.
claims.answer: Vitamin D toxicity (angiotoxicity) targets the elastic arteries, causing fibrosis of the vascular smooth muscle and calcification of the vessel wall.
claims.verbatim:
The target tissue of vitamin D toxicity is the
elastic arteries and the specific result is fibrosis of the vascular smooth
muscle and calcification of the blood vessel wall

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: What causes an enlarged prostate?
claims.answer_short: A zinc deficiency. As the prostate enlarges with age its tight outer capsule squeezes down on the neck of the bladder, producing the classic urgency and frequency.
claims.answer: Age-related prostate enlargement (benign prostatic hyperplasia) is usually the result of a zinc deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
As the prostate
enlarges with age (usually the result of a zinc deficiency)

claims.subject: benign_prostatic_hyperplasia
claims.question: How do you treat an enlarged prostate naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate) with zinc, flaxseed-oil essential fatty acids, a high-fiber diet with pumpkin seeds, vitamin A as beta-carotene, and selenium.
claims.answer: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate) treatment: zinc 50 mg three times daily, flaxseed-oil EFAs 9 g/day, high-fiber diet with pumpkin seeds, 300,000 International Units vitamin A as beta-carotene/day, and selenium 250 mcg three times daily.
claims.verbatim:
Benign prostatic hypertrophy is treated with zinc at 50 mg t.i.d., essential
fatty acids as flaxseed oil at 9 grams per day, high fiber diets including
pumpkin seeds and alfalfa, 300,000 IU vitamin A as beta carotene per day

claims.subject: bells_palsy
claims.question: How do you treat Bell's palsy?
claims.answer_short: Bell's palsy is a facial nerve pinched by bone loss (osteoporosis), so Wallach rebuilds the bone: B12 (1,000 mcg/day up to 20,000 mcg total), calcium/magnesium at 2,000/800 mg, and EFAs 5 g three times daily -- treated properly, up to an 80 percent chance of significant recovery.
claims.answer: Bell's palsy treatment: B12 1,000 mcg/day to a total of 20,000 mcg, calcium/magnesium 2,000 and 800 mg/day, and essential fatty acids 5 g three times daily.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment is B12 at 1000 mcg/day for a total of 20,000 mcg, calcium/
magnesium at 2,000 mg and 800 mg per day, essential fatty acids at 5 gm
t.i.d.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Does taking calcium cause kidney stones?
claims.answer_short: No — Wallach says kidney and bladder stones are ironically caused by calcium and magnesium deficiency, with the stone minerals coming from your own bones.
claims.answer: Kidney/bladder stones are ironically caused by a calcium- and/or magnesium-deficient diet — the stone minerals come from your own bones.
claims.verbatim:
BLADDER STONES (kidney stones, cystic calculi) are ironically caused
by a calcium and/or a magnesium deficient diet

claims.subject: kidney_stones
claims.question: How do you prevent kidney stones?
claims.answer_short: The stones form because a calcium/magnesium-deficient diet leaches those minerals out of your own bones — so you prevent them by supplying calcium (2,000 mg) and magnesium (1,000 mg) and cutting meat to right the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that bladder and kidney stones are, ironically, caused by a calcium- and/or magnesium-deficient diet together with raging osteoporosis — the minerals that form the stones are pulled from your own bones. Prevention therefore means correcting that deficiency rather than avoiding calcium: he calls calcium at 2,000 mg and magnesium at 1,000 mg daily imperative to stop the calcium loss from the bones, and adds reducing meat intake (shifting toward the vegetarian scale) to bring the dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio back in order.
claims.verbatim:
BLADDER STONES (kidney stones, cystic calculi) are ironically caused
by a calcium and/or a magnesium deficient diet and when you
have raging osteoporosis. The minerals in the
“stones” come from your own bones

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: What deficiency causes easy bruising or bleeding under the skin?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says easy bruising or bleeding under the skin can signal a vitamin E or vitamin K deficiency — or an overdose of prescription blood thinners — and he distinguishes it from bleeding in the stool, which needs real diagnostic follow-up.
claims.answer: Easy bleeding or bruising under the skin can be a nutritional clue, Wallach notes: it may point to a vitamin E or vitamin K deficiency — both vitamins tied to normal blood clotting — or to an overdose of prescription blood thinners. He is careful to separate this from bleeding in the stool, which he warns is a different and potentially serious sign that calls for real diagnostic follow-up.
claims.verbatim:
Bleeding under the skin may indicate vitamin E or vitamin K
deficiencies

claims.subject: menopause
claims.question: What causes hot flashes and night sweats in menopause?
claims.answer_short: In a normal, gradual menopause the adrenals and liver step up estrogen output to replace lost ovarian function, and hot flashes and night sweats occur when that output falls short.
claims.answer: In a normal gradual menopause, the adrenals and liver increase female-hormone (estrogen) output to make up for lost ovarian function; insufficient output produces hot flashes and night sweats.
claims.verbatim:
the adrenals and liver increase their
output of female hormones (primarily estrogen) and make up the difference
from the lost ovarian function.

claims.subject: estrogen
claims.question: Should you take estrogen during menopause?
claims.answer_short: Wallach advises against estrogen in menopause — it raises breast/uterine cancer risk — treating menopause as a normal transition to support: as the ovaries wind down, the adrenals and liver take over, aided by calcium, magnesium, diet and herbs.
claims.answer: On menopause, Wallach's stance is that estrogen supplements should not be used, because they raise the risk of inducing breast and uterine cancer. He treats menopause not as a disease needing hormone 'treatment' but as a normal transition to support: as the ovaries wind down, the adrenals and liver take over female-hormone production, and the aim is to smooth that shift — with the base-line supplement program plus extra calcium and magnesium, two eggs and red meat daily, a monthly liver flush, betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes, and herbs such as lady's mantle, motherwort and St. John's wort.
claims.verbatim:
Estrogen supplements should not be used as
they increase the breast and uterine cancer induction risk.

claims.subject: menopause
claims.question: Should women take estrogen supplements for menopause?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats menopause as a normal transition to support, not a disease, and he pointedly avoids estrogen supplements -- arguing they raise the risk of breast and uterine cancer. Instead he pairs the baseline supplement program with calcium and magnesium and traditional women's herbs.
claims.answer: For menopause — which Wallach frames as a normal transition needing 'support,' not a disease to 'treat' — his plan pairs the baseline supplement program with calcium at 2,000 mg and magnesium at 1,000 mg a day, plus traditional women's herbs such as lady's mantle, motherwort, and St. John's wort. He pointedly avoids estrogen supplements, arguing they raise the risk of breast and uterine cancer, and leans on nutrition to smooth the change and head off the osteoporosis that can follow.
claims.verbatim:
Use the base line supplement program, plus calcium and magnesium
at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day

claims.subject: common_cold
claims.question: Why is there no vaccine for the common cold?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains there is no cold vaccine because the common cold is caused by more than 100 different viruses, so no single shot can cover them all; colds are self-limited to 7-14 days and best met with heavy vitamin C, not antibiotics.
claims.answer: Wallach's explanation for why there is still no cold vaccine is simple: the common cold (nasal catarrh, or coryza) isn't one illness but the work of more than 100 different viruses, so no single shot can cover them all. He notes colds run a self-limited 7 to 14 days regardless of treatment, arrive fast after a short 1-to-3-day incubation, and are best met with heavy vitamin C rather than antibiotics, which do nothing against a virus.
claims.verbatim:
COLDS (nasal catarrh, coryza) are caused by more than 100 different
viruses, this is why no vaccine has been made available.

claims.subject: common_cold
claims.question: How do you treat a common cold naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats the common cold with vitamin C to bowel tolerance, bioflavonoids, garlic, the baseline supplement program, and chicken-rice soup.
claims.answer: Common-cold treatment: vitamin C to bowel tolerance, bioflavonoids 150 mg three times daily, garlic, the baseline supplement program, and chicken-rice soup.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of the “common cold” should include vitamin C to bowel
tolerance, bioflavonoids at 150 mg t.i.d., garlic, gelatin capsules t.i.d.

claims.subject: salt
claims.question: Why does Wallach say to salt your food?
claims.answer_short: Salt (NaCl) is the raw material for stomach acid; salt-restricted diets breed achlorhydria and failed absorption -- so his treatment starts with salting your food to taste.
claims.answer: Wallach identifies salt (sodium chloride) as the raw material the stomach needs to manufacture its acid, so people on salt-restricted diets are more prone to achlorhydria (loss of stomach acid). Achlorhydria brings 'burp, belch, and bloat,' lets intestinal bacteria and yeast ferment high-carbohydrate foods in the stomach, and leads to B12, calcium, and protein deficiencies plus new adult-onset food allergies from absorbing partly digested proteins -- so his treatment starts with putting salt back on your food.
claims.verbatim:
Sodium chloride is the
raw material required to manufacture stomach acid, so it follows that people
on a salt restricted diet are more likely to
develop achlorhydria.
Symptoms include “burp, belch, and bloat” after eating. The reduction or
absence of acid in the stomach allows intestinal bacteria and yeast (Candida
albicans) to enter the stomach and ferment high carbohydrate foods (i.e.
juice, fruit, breads, etc.). Failure to deal with achlorhydria will result in
B12, calcium, and protein deficiencies and the onset of new food allergies
acquired later in life as a result of absorption of partially digested
polypeptides (relatively large protein fragments) which trigger an allergic
response.
Treatment of achlorhydria includes salting your food to taste and
supplementation of betaine HCl at the rate of 75-250 mg 15-20 minutes
before each meal.

claims.subject: dietary_oils
claims.question: Why does Wallach say heated vegetable and cooking oils are dangerous?
claims.answer_short: Heating or hydrogenating polyunsaturated oils turns them into trans fats and free-radical damage; with low selenium that's 'the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer.'
claims.answer: Wallach warns that a diet high in vegetable oils (salad dressing, cooking oils) combined with low selenium is the fastest path to heart attack and cancer, because heating or hydrogenating the polyunsaturated oils turns them into trans fats and rancid, "free radical"-damaged cellular fat.
claims.verbatim:
High intakes of vegetable oils,
including salad dressing and cooking oils, concurrent with a selenium
deficiency is the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer.

claims.subject: dietary_oils
claims.question: What causes age spots (liver spots), and how does Wallach treat them?
