claims.answer_short: Age spots are rancid fat (ceroid lipofuscin / trans fatty acids) from cell walls surfacing in the skin — a cancer and heart-disease red flag; he cuts all fried foods and vegetable oils.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that age spots (liver spots) are rancid fat — ceroid lipofuscin or trans fatty acids — from cell walls accumulating under the skin; ten on the back of the hand mean millions in the organs, and they flag a high risk of cancer and heart disease. Because they are reversible, his treatment is to eliminate all fried foods and vegetable oils (salad dressing, cooking oils, margarine) plus sugar, with selenium and vitamin E.
claims.verbatim:
These unsightly brown
spots are caused by rancid fat (ceroid lipofuscin or trans fatty acids)from
cell walls accumulating under the skin. If you have ten on the back of your
hand, you have millions in your brain, heart, liver, kidney, lungs, etc. They
interfere with cell function, shorten your life, and are a red flag warning for
high risk of cancer and heart disease (i.e. cardiomyopathy). The nice thing
about age spots is that they are reversible. When they go away on the
outside, they are going away on the inside.
Treatment includes eliminating all fried foods, vegetable oils (i.e. salad
dressing, cooking oils, margarine, etc.), and sugar from the diet.

claims.subject: dietary_oils
claims.question: What does Wallach say causes fibromyalgia?
claims.answer_short: He calls fibromyalgia a multiple-deficiency disease driven by a high intake of fried foods and vegetable oils plus low selenium, vitamin E and sulfur amino acids.
claims.answer: Wallach frames fibromyalgia (which he equates with white muscle disease / stiff lamb disease / adult-onset muscular dystrophy, eliminated in livestock in 1957) as a multiple-deficiency disease caused by a high intake of fried foods and vegetable oils together with deficiencies of selenium, vitamin E, and the sulfur amino acids.
claims.verbatim:
FIBROMYALGIA (stiff lamb disease, white muscle disease, adult onset
muscular dystrophy) is a disease that was eliminated from lambs, calves,
and pigs in 1957. It is a multiple deficiency disease caused by a high intake
of fried foods and vegetable oils (margarine, cooking oils, and salad
dressing) and deficiencies of selenium, vitamin E, and sulfur amino acids
(methionine, cysteine, cystine).

claims.subject: eggs
claims.question: How does Wallach say to cook eggs, and how much red meat, for Alzheimer's?
claims.answer_short: Soft-scrambled (not fried) eggs every day and 72 oz of red meat each month, to replace cholesterol needed to rebuild myelin.
claims.answer: For Alzheimer's, Wallach says to replace the cholesterol the brain needs to rebuild myelin by eating soft-scrambled (not fried) eggs every day plus 72 oz of red meat each month.
claims.verbatim:
500 mcg
selenium daily and IV chelation will be of value. Eat soft-scrambled (not
fried) eggs every day and 72 oz. red meat each month to replace cholesterol
needed to rebuild myelin.

claims.subject: eggs
claims.question: Are fried eggs bad, according to Wallach?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach says fried eggs precipitate 93% of gallbladder attacks (with fried onions, fried potatoes and pork close behind).
claims.answer: Wallach warns that fried eggs trigger 93 percent of all gallbladder attacks (with fried onions, fried potatoes and pork close behind) -- a reason to poach, boil or soft-scramble eggs rather than fry them.
claims.verbatim:
the base line
nutritional supplement including 5 gm of EFA t.i.d. Fried eggs are known to
precipitate 93 percent of all gallbladder attacks, followed closely by fried
onions, fried potatoes, and pork.

claims.subject: meat
claims.question: How often does Wallach say to eat meat, eggs and poultry for blood sugar?
claims.answer_short: Three to six times a day (cutting sugar and refined carbs) to stabilize blood sugar early in diabetes therapy.
claims.answer: For the early stage of treating diabetes, Wallach says to cut all natural and processed sugar and refined carbs and instead eat meat, eggs and poultry three to six times a day to stabilize blood sugar.
claims.verbatim:
No natural
or processed sugar and carbohydrates should be consumed. Eat meat, eggs,
and poultry three to six times per day to stabilize blood sugar in the
beginning stages of the therapy.

claims.subject: meat
claims.question: Why does Wallach say eggs and red meat are critical for MS, and what foods should be avoided?
claims.answer_short: Myelin is almost pure cholesterol, so eggs and red meat are vital; avoid fried foods and margarine and use fish/flax oil.
claims.answer: For MS and ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease), Wallach says avoiding fried foods and margarine (plus taking fish or flax oil) raises survival, and that eating the cholesterol in eggs and red meat is critically important because the myelin sheath is made almost entirely of cholesterol.
claims.verbatim:
It is known that avoidance of fried foods and margarine
and a relatively high consumption of flaxseed oil or fish oil (cod liver oil or
salmon oil) at 5 gm t.i.d. will increase your survival rate by 50 percent. The
consumption of cholesterol (eggs and red meat) is of extreme importance as
the myelin sheath that disappears in MS is made almost exclusively of
cholesterol.

claims.subject: cruciferous_vegetables
claims.question: Should people with hypothyroidism avoid cabbage and other cruciferous vegetables?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's hypothyroidism protocol begins by eliminating all goitrogenic foods such as nitrates and cabbage, then adds thyroid support.
claims.answer: For an underactive thyroid, Wallach's first dietary step is to cut out goitrogenic foods — including cruciferous vegetables like cabbage — before adding thyroid support.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of hypothyroidism includes eliminating all goiterogenic
substances such as nitrates, cabbage, etc. Supplement with U.S. Armour
thyroid at 1 to 3 grains each morning.

claims.subject: water
claims.question: Should you drink distilled water or filtered water?
claims.answer_short: Drink filtered water, not distilled - distilled water is 'hungry' and leaches minerals from your bones over long-term use.
claims.answer: For everyday drinking Wallach recommends filtered water over distilled: distilled water is 'hungry' water, and used long-term it leaches minerals out of your bones, thinning them.
claims.verbatim:
drink filtered —not distilled—water. Distilled water
is “hungry” water and will demineralize your bones over a long period of
usage.

claims.subject: carbonated_beverages
claims.question: Are carbonated soft drinks bad for you?
claims.answer_short: Yes - Wallach says all carbonated soft drinks are loaded with phosphates that cause osteoporosis over the long haul.
claims.answer: Wallach warns against carbonated soft drinks: every one of them is loaded with phosphates, and over the long haul those phosphates drive osteoporosis - a special concern for anyone already on a restricted diet.
claims.verbatim:
avoid carbonated soft drinks which ALL are loaded with phosphates which
will cause osteoporosis over the long haul especially when you are already
on a restricted diet

claims.subject: butter
claims.question: Is there ever a reason to cut back on butter?
claims.answer_short: Yes — the one cautionary note. For cerebrovascular disease (where Wallach calls vitamin D angiotoxic and a driver of arterial calcification), he says hold total vitamin D under 400 IU/day, and flags butter — alongside animal fat, cholesterol, milk, cereals, supplements and sunshine — as a notable dietary vitamin D contributor that makes staying under the cap difficult.
claims.answer: The one cautionary note: for cerebrovascular disease (where Wallach calls vitamin D angiotoxic and a driver of arterial calcification) he says hold total vitamin D under 400 IU/day, and flags butter — alongside animal fat, cholesterol, milk, cereals, supplements and sunshine — as a notable dietary vitamin D contributor that makes staying under the cap difficult.
claims.verbatim:
Reduce the amount of vitamin D intake to a maximum of 400 IU/day (this
is a real toughie when you consider animal fat, cholesterol, milk, butter,
various prepared cereals and snack bars, supplements, and sunshine).
Optimal levels of all nutrients including magnesium can also prevent
“malignant calcification.”
Treatment of cerebrovascular disease

claims.subject: butter
claims.question: Did the long-lived, disease-free cultures Wallach admires eat butter?
claims.answer_short: Yes — emphatically. In Wallach's analysis of the Hunza, the people he holds up as relatively disease-free and living well past 100, butter is a staple, not an afterthought: they put it in their tea and used it as a cooking shortening, and it sits among their core fat sources alongside whole milk, ghee, apricot oil and animal fats. Wallach lists it among the 14 Hunza practices he credits for their longevity.
claims.answer: Yes — emphatically. In Wallach's account of the Hunza, the people he describes as relatively disease-free and living well past a hundred, butter is a staple rather than an afterthought: they put it in their tea and use it as a cooking shortening, and it sits among their core fat sources alongside whole milk, ghee, apricot oil and animal fats. He lists those fat sources as one of the 14 Hunza practices that contribute to their longevity.
claims.verbatim: Fat sources include whole milk, butter, ghee, apricot oil, and animal fats.

claims.subject: beef
claims.question: How much red meat does Wallach recommend eating during menopause?
claims.answer_short: For menopause, Wallach's protocol includes eating red meat once each day, plus 2 eggs daily and a monthly liver flush, on top of the base-line supplements and calcium/magnesium.
claims.answer: For menopause, Wallach's protocol has the person eat red meat once each day, plus 2 eggs daily and a monthly liver flush, on top of the base-line supplement program with calcium and magnesium.
claims.verbatim:
Eat two eggs
every day, red meat once each day, and the liver flush at least once per
month. Use the base line supplement program, plus calcium and magnesium
at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day

claims.subject: beef
claims.question: Why does Wallach tell some people to cut back on red meat?
claims.answer_short: Because red meat is heavy in phosphorus relative to calcium; for bone/phosphorus-driven conditions like Paget's disease he says to reduce or eliminate red meat to correct the calcium/phosphorus ratio, the same logic that recurs for periodontal disease, triglycerides and hypertension.
claims.answer: Wallach tells some people to cut back on red meat because it is heavy in phosphorus relative to calcium; for phosphorus-driven bone conditions like Paget's disease he says to reduce or eliminate red meat to correct the calcium/phosphorus ratio.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of Paget’s Disease should include a vigorous effort to correct the
dietary calcium/phosphorus ratio, reduce or eliminate red meat intake, avoid
phosphate containing soft drinks, avoid all phosphate containing
supplements

claims.subject: pork
claims.question: Is fried pork bad for you according to Wallach?
claims.answer_short: Wallach credits the longer average lifespan of Mormons and Seventh-Day Adventists partly to their avoidance of fried foods, and he lists fried pork first among the fried foods to skip.
claims.answer: Wallach credits the longer average lifespan of Mormons and Seventh-Day Adventists partly to their avoidance of fried foods, and he lists fried pork first among the fried foods to skip.
claims.verbatim:
Mormons and Seventh Day Adventists live to be 82
years of age on the average because they avoid caffeine (i.e. coffee, soft
drinks, tea, iced tea, etc.), alcohol, smoking, and fried foods (i.e. pork,
catfish, shrimp, lard shortening, etc).

claims.subject: eggs
claims.question: Is egg a high-quality protein compared to other foods?
claims.answer_short: Whole egg tops Wallach's protein chart with a chemical score of 100 and 94% utilization, higher than human milk, cow's milk, or soybean, making it his benchmark for usable protein.
claims.answer: Whole egg tops Wallach's protein-quality chart with a chemical score of 100 and 94% utilization, higher than human milk, cow's milk, or soybean, making it his benchmark for usable protein.
claims.verbatim:
The availability and usability of N from various foods are
quite different and must be considered when choosing N sources.
Nitrogen/Protein Utilization Values of Common Foods
Nitrogen Source (Protein) Chemical Score % Utilization
Whole egg 100 94
Human milk 100 87
Cow’s milk 95 82
Soy bean 74 65

claims.subject: fish
claims.question: Does fish contain germanium?
claims.answer_short: Yes, but only a trace — and it is not a reason to eat tuna. Germanium is a trace element Wallach prizes as an immune booster (it stimulates natural killer cells, interferon, macrophages and T-suppressor cells) and an oxygen-utilization cofactor, with deficiency typified by a severely reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy and cancer. But tuna carries only about 2.3 ppm of germanium — actually less than ordinary beans at 4.67 ppm, and far below the germanium-rich healing herbs and foods like garlic, ginseng and shiitake mushrooms (100 to 2,000 ppm). So fish is a minor incidental source at best — not a meaningful way to get germanium.
claims.answer: Yes, but only a trace — and it is not a reason to eat tuna. Germanium is a trace element Wallach prizes as an immune booster (it stimulates natural killer cells, interferon, macrophages and T-suppressor cells) and an oxygen-utilization cofactor, with deficiency typified by a severely reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy and cancer. But tuna carries only about 2.3 ppm of germanium — actually less than ordinary beans at 4.67 ppm, and far below the germanium-rich healing herbs and foods like garlic, ginseng and shiitake mushrooms (100 to 2,000 ppm). So fish is a minor incidental source at best — not a meaningful way to get germanium.
claims.verbatim:
Food plants and animals contain small amounts of germanium (i.e. beans—
4.67 ppm, tuna—2.3 ppm).

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: How much omega-3 or essential fatty acids should I take per day?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says essential fatty acids should make up 3 percent of your total daily calories, or be supplemented at 9 grams per day in capsule form.
claims.answer: Essential fatty acids are required every day at 3% of total daily calorie intake, or 9 g per day when supplemented in capsule form. The 9 g is one combined amount for the essential fatty acids together, not 9 g of each.
claims.verbatim:
Essential fatty acids are a
must and should be consumed at the rate of 3 percent of your total daily
calorie consumption or supplemented at the rate of 9 grams per day in
capsule form.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Where did plant-derived colloidal minerals come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach traces the whole category to Mineral Toddy — a liquid he found at Hospital Santa Monica, drawn from a prehistoric plant deposit that never became oil, coal, or stone.
claims.answer: Wallach's origin story for plant-derived colloidal minerals. He credits a specific product — Mineral Toddy, made by a company called Rockland U.S.A. — that he came across at Hospital Santa Monica. What made it work, he says, was where it came from: a prehistoric deposit of buried plant matter that had never turned into oil, coal, or stone. That escape from geological compression is why the minerals in it were still in the form the original plants had made them, ready for the body to use, rather than trapped back inside rock.
claims.verbatim:
Mineral Toddy was produced by Rockland U.S.A. from a unique prehistoric
plant deposit that had never been compressed into oil or coal. It had never
been fossilized or petrified.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Why does he say plant-derived beats ground-up rock?
claims.answer_short: Two claims in one sentence: 77 minerals in the bottle (more than the 60 he counts as essential), and up to 98% absorbable — because plants made them, not a mill.
claims.answer: Two claims about the same liquid, side by side. First: it carries 77 different minerals — more than the 60 Wallach counts as essential to a human body, so a single bottle covers the full essential spectrum and then some. Second: up to 98% of what you swallow is 'bio-available,' meaning the body can actually absorb and use it rather than pass it straight through. Both, in his framing, follow from the same fact: these minerals were built by living plants, not milled out of rock. A mineral's usefulness, to him, depends on which of those two things made it.
claims.verbatim:
The value of this tea colored liquid was that it
contained 77 minerals in the plant derived colloidal form. Because they
were plant derived colloidal minerals instead of from ground up rocks, they
were up to 98 percent bio-available.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Why do plants matter to your minerals?
claims.answer_short: The single step at the heart of his whole framework — plants pull rock minerals out of the soil and rebuild them inside their own cells into the form living cells can actually use. A step your body can't do for itself.
claims.answer: The single step at the heart of Wallach's whole mineral framework — and the reason he cares about the source. Rock ground into fine dust and suspended in water is real minerals, but in a form that living cells can't take in. Plants can. Their roots pull those rock minerals up from the soil and rebuild them inside their own cells into a different chemical form — the form every living cell of every plant, animal, and human is actually built out of. So a mineral in a rock and the same mineral in a piece of broccoli, he argues, are not the same nutrient. A plant is the factory that does the one step your body can't do for itself, which is why he says the source matters.
claims.verbatim:
Plants, including wild forms and crops such as grains, vegetables, fruits,
and nuts, take up these inorganic metallic colloids and convert them into
intracellular (within the cell) organically bound plant colloids. These
organic plant colloids are the form of minerals found in and used by all
living cells of plants, animals, and humans.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: What do the world's longest-lived peoples all share?
claims.answer_short: Not genes — what grows in their fields. Every "Age Beater" culture settled below a glacier and built canals to bring its mineral-rich meltwater ('glacial milk') to their crops, which converted those inorganic minerals into plant-derived colloidal form.
claims.answer: 'Age Beaters' is Wallach's shorthand for the eight unrelated long-lived cultures he tracks — populations where reaching 100+ in good health is common rather than exceptional. What ties them together, he argues, is what grows in their fields: each settled by chance in a high arid valley below a glacier and built canals to bring the glacier's mineral-rich meltwater ('glacial milk') to their crops, which converted those inorganic minerals into plant-derived colloidal form. Those plant-derived colloidal minerals in their food, he says, are the common thread behind the shared longevity — and why he calls them, flatly, the Fountain of Youth.
claims.verbatim:
It is the plant derived colloidal minerals in their grains,
vegetables, fruits, and nuts that are their common threads giving the Age Beaters their health and longevity. It is the plant derived colloidal
minerals that are in fact the Fountain of Youth!

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: What can these minerals NOT do on their own?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's own honest limit on Mineral Toddy: every mineral in it is present only in tiny amounts. To hit even mainstream RDAs for calcium, magnesium, manganese, zinc, and potassium, you need a separate major-mineral source alongside it.
claims.answer: Wallach's own honest limit on Mineral Toddy, stated a few sentences after listing what it fixed. The colloidal liquid, he says, carries every mineral only in trace amounts. That is enough for the trace minerals the body needs in tiny amounts, but to even come close to the mainstream Recommended Daily Allowances it has to be paired with a separate source of what he calls the "major minerals and electrolytes": calcium, magnesium, manganese, zinc, and potassium. In the same passage he put the minerals in calcium-enriched orange juice, which both masked their harsh astringent taste and provided a significant amount of additional calcium — one of those lacking majors. On his own account the colloidal minerals were never meant as a stand-alone mineral supplement — a piece of the picture, not the whole picture.
claims.verbatim:
The colloidal
minerals were all present in trace amounts. They required an additional
source of the major minerals and electrolytes such as calcium, magnesium,
manganese, zinc, and potassium to even come close to the published RDAs.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Where is Wallach's “Fountain of Youth”?
claims.answer_short: Under our feet the whole time — it's minerals. After millennia of chasing longevity, Wallach says the answer is almost anticlimactic: the plant-derived minerals in the ground.
claims.answer: Wallach's punchline to the entire search for longevity. For all of recorded history people have poured out resources, money, and even their lives chasing a Fountain of Youth — and his answer is almost anticlimactic: it was under our feet the whole time. The Fountain of Youth is minerals.
claims.verbatim:
The search for health and longevity is as old as man himself. We have
expended resources, money, energy, and have in fact died in droves looking
for the Fountain of Youth. Literally the Fountain of Youth has been under
our feet since the beginning of time. The answer is almost anticlimactic; it’s
minerals.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: What does the liquid mineral supplement taste like?
claims.answer_short: Intensely astringent — Wallach says drunk straight it would “shrink wrap your lips over your teeth,” so it's taken stirred into juice.
claims.answer: What the raw liquid actually tastes like. Plant-derived colloidal minerals are intensely astringent — Wallach says that taken straight, undiluted, they would 'shrink wrap your lips over your teeth.' That is why they are taken stirred into juice rather than drunk on their own.
claims.verbatim:
The plant derived colloidal minerals were very astringent. Taken “straight,”
they’d “shrink wrap your lips over your teeth” if you drank
them without juice.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: How did Wallach discover colloidal minerals?
claims.answer_short: He'd never heard of them until he met the liquid being served to patients at Hospital Santa Monica, then spent three months reading everything then known about colloids.
claims.answer: How Wallach came to colloidal minerals. He had never even heard of them until he encountered the liquid being served to patients at Hospital Santa Monica. Excited by the new tool, he gathered every book and article ever written on colloids, and within three months had absorbed essentially everything then known about them.
claims.verbatim:
I got excited about this new-found nutritional tool, and I gathered every
piece of information that I could find on plant derived colloidal minerals. I
had never heard of colloidal minerals until this moment in my professional
career so I began to educate myself. I gathered every book and every article
that had ever been written on colloidal minerals and within three months I
was familiar with just about everything historically and currently known
about colloids and plant derived colloidal minerals.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Does the source of plant-derived minerals matter — and what if a maker cuts corners?
claims.answer_short: Yes — quality tracks the source deposit. Wallach tells how a product went black and green batch-to-batch after its bottler switched to a cheaper source, and how he fixed it by going back to the original deposit under his own label.
claims.answer: Wallach's own account of the fight to keep plant-derived colloidal minerals high-quality — and a hard lesson about companies that cut corners. The minerals he built his products on came from one particular prehistoric deposit. When the company then bottling them, Eagle, quietly switched to a cheaper source to save about a dollar a gallon, the liquid changed batch to batch: one day thin and tasteless with its astringency gone, the next black like India ink, the next green. Every product built on those minerals suffered, and customers began complaining that 'the minerals didn't work anymore.' When Wallach objected, Eagle denied anything had changed, and in early 1997 terminated his distributorship, wanting a quieter corporate image. Rather than accept a degraded product, Wallach founded his own company, American Longevity, and went straight back to Elmer Heinrich of Rockland — the original deposit the minerals had come from since 1991 — relaunching them as 'Virgin Earth' plant-derived colloidal minerals. He went back to the proven source. The lasting lesson for anyone buying these minerals: the source deposit is what makes them work, and a cheaper source is not the same product.
claims.verbatim:
The Mineral Toddy, however, was beginning to change. One day you could
drink a quart of Toddy minerals like water because the astringent character
of the minerals was gone. The next batch of Mineral Toddy was black like
India Ink. The next batch was green. The obvious changes in the Mineral
Toddy negatively affected all of the products that used the minerals as a
base.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Why does Wallach point to the long-lived cultures as proof?
claims.answer_short: He treats them as a living “control group” — five ancient peoples with disease-free longevity from steady access to all 90 essential nutrients, chiefly plant-derived colloidal minerals — and promises you can do the same.
claims.answer: Wallach's opening thesis, framed as science. He treats the world's long-lived cultures as a living 'control group' — five ancient, very different peoples who all reached healthful, disease-free longevity, with steady access to all ninety essential nutrients the body needs. The secret they shared, he says, was unique natural sources of plant-derived colloidal minerals, and his promise is that anyone who taps that same accumulated knowledge can do the same.
claims.verbatim:
This control group of five
ancient and highly diverse cultures share common denominators that
include healthful, disease-free longevity, and unlimited access to adequate
levels of all ninety essential nutrients required by humans. One of the
secrets they shared includes access to unique natural sources of plant
derived colloidal minerals. My promise to you is that if you plug into the
thousands of years of accumulated knowledge of these long-lived peoples,
you and yours can make it too!

claims.subject: microplastics
claims.question: How do I detox microplastics and plastics from my body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach never wrote about microplastics, but they're a xenobiotic — a foreign chemical the body must clear — and he endorses selenium's role in the 'detoxification of metals and certain xenobiotics.'
claims.answer: Microplastics are a modern problem Wallach's books never take up. But they fall squarely into a category he does address: xenobiotics — the foreign compounds the body has to recognize and clear. In a selenium review he quotes approvingly across several books, the mineral is described as 'involved in detoxification of metals and certain xenobiotics,' one of the body's built-in tools for handling foreign chemicals. From there his general defense against toxin load is consistent: keep selenium up (he runs 250 to 500 mcg a day in his prevention programs), lean on plant-derived colloidal minerals to 'reduce your risk of damage from heavy metals and pollution,' filter your home's water and air, and run a periodic detox. None of this is Wallach speaking about plastics specifically — it is his framework for foreign-chemical exposure, which microplastics now fall under.
claims.verbatim:
selenium acts as an acceptor of
biogenic methyl groups, and is involved in detoxification of metals and
certain xenobiotics. Selenium also has immunopotentiating properties.

claims.subject: detox
claims.question: What is Wallach's routine for detoxing and clearing toxic metals?
claims.answer_short: Take alfalfa daily as a detoxifier, do a monthly apple-juice liver flush, and get a yearly hair analysis to track your toxic-metal load.
claims.answer: As part of his cancer-prevention program, Wallach lays out a simple ongoing detox routine: take alfalfa daily 'in some form as a detoxifier,' do a liver flush once or twice a month by drinking apple juice for three days, and get a hair analysis each year — which he uses both to monitor toxic-metal load and to check how well you're absorbing minerals (if absorption is poor, he notes, all your mineral levels run low). It sits inside a broader daily regimen for keeping toxins down: dietary fiber at every meal, filtered (not distilled) water, 2 to 3 bowel movements a day, biodegradable household cleaners, and organic food wherever possible. The hair analysis is the feedback loop — it is how he would tell whether the metals are actually coming down.
claims.verbatim:
Take alfalfa daily in some form
as a detoxifier. Do a liver flush once or twice each month by drinking apple
juice for three days. Do a hair analysis each year to monitor toxic metal
load as well as absorption capability.

claims.subject: digestion
claims.question: Does everyone get low stomach acid as they age?
claims.answer_short: Largely yes — Wallach calls achlorhydria a natural process of aging and “perhaps the most significant aging phenomenon,” and puts the number at 75 percent of people over 50 needing supplemental stomach acid. He names stress as the other cause, and says it lowers acid rather than raising it.
claims.answer: Achlorhydria — what causes it, and how common it is. Achlorhydria means the loss of the stomach's hydrochloric acid (HCl). Wallach names two causes, and says both run opposite to what most people assume. The first is stress — contrary to popular belief it does not raise stomach acid, it shuts acid production down, and he pins the moment: once stress passes the point of decompensation, where the body can no longer compensate. The second is age itself, a natural process he calls perhaps the most significant aging phenomenon, at 75 percent of people over 50 requiring supplemental stomach acid. A third contributor is dietary: ordinary salt (sodium chloride) is the raw material the stomach uses to manufacture its acid, so people on salt-restricted diets are more likely to become achlorhydric. The everyday sign is 'burp, belch, and bloat' after eating.
claims.verbatim:
ACHLORHYDRIA (loss of stomach acid—hydrochloric acid): Contrary
to popular belief, stress will result in loss of stomach acid production.
Achlorhydria is also a natural process of aging and perhaps the most
significant aging phenomenon. Seventy-five percent of people over the age
of 50 years require supplementation of stomach acid.

claims.subject: digestion
claims.question: Is indigestion actually serious?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls dyspepsia probably the most common “disease” in the western world and the most costly — but says the money is the smaller cost, because chronic indigestion leads on to food allergies, osteoporosis, anemia, a debilitated immune system and degenerative disease.
claims.answer: Chronic dyspepsia — what it costs if you leave it. Dyspepsia means poor digestion, and Wallach describes it by its everyday signs: belching, burping, bloating and 'acid stomach.' His explanation inverts the usual one — the trouble is not too much acid but that the stomach's acid is not acid enough, so food ferments and the gas is burped back up. He calls it probably the most common 'disease' in the western world and certainly the most costly, measured by what people spend on relief — but says the real cost is what it becomes: food allergies, osteoporosis, anemia, a debilitated immune system, degenerative disease. Prevention is reduced stress, exercise, healthful diet habits and reasonable food volumes; and because stomach-acid production falls as we age — an unforgiving event, and the main cause of dyspepsia in seniors — the regular use of digestive aids.
claims.verbatim:
Dyspepsia is probably the most common
“disease” in the western world and is certainly the most costly from the
amount of money spent on “relief.” Even more costly is the secondary
results of chronic dyspepsia: food allergies, osteoporosis, anemia,
debilitated immune system, degenerative disease. Prevention includes
reduced stress levels, exercise, healthful diet habits, and reasonable food
volumes. An unforgiving event as we age is a decrease in stomach acid
production, the main cause of dyspepsia in seniors. Prevention in this case
includes the regular use of digestive aids.

claims.subject: digestion
claims.question: Are antacids bad for you?
claims.answer_short: In an emergency, no — Wallach calls them a good temporary fix. As a habit, yes: regular use will eventually damage you by reducing the nutrients you absorb, because the underlying problem is usually too little stomach acid, not too much.
claims.answer: Antacids versus digestive aids. Wallach's position on antacids is split, and the split follows from his account of indigestion. In an emergency they are a good temporary fix. As a regular habit they harm you — regular use will eventually damage you by reducing the nutrients you absorb — because the stomach's acid is already not acid enough, so neutralizing it further undercuts the digestion and absorption that acid exists to drive. What he prescribes instead is replacement rather than suppression: 75 to 200 mg of betaine hydrochloride (a supplemental form of stomach acid) with pancreatic enzymes, three times a day, 15 to 30 minutes before each meal. His herbal preventions and remedies are papaya, common barberry, and bitters such as gentian — and in some cases a glass of wine or several ounces of vinegar before meals will help.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of dyspepsia includes supplementation of 75-200 mg betaine
HCl and pancreatic enzymes t.i.d. 15-30 minutes before each meal.
“Antacids” are a good “temporary fix” in an emergency, but regular use will
eventually damage you by reducing the nutrients you absorb.

claims.subject: digestion
claims.question: Should I be taking digestive enzymes?
claims.answer_short: Wallach’s rule of thumb: as you grow older, take betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal decline in stomach-acid production — and be sure to take them if you are under stress.
claims.answer: Who should take digestive aids, and why. Wallach gives this instruction as part of preventing candidiasis — the Candida albicans overgrowth he ties to chronic fatigue syndrome — and the reasoning is what makes the advice land. Candida is a normally harmless yeast living on the skin, mouth, vagina and intestine. It turns pathological when the gut's competing normal bacteria are killed off by long-term antibiotic use, or when low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, usually the result of salt restriction) lets it move up into the stomach — a location it does not normally occupy. Stress reduces stomach acid once it reaches the point of decompensation, and food allergies change the lining of the gut in a way very similar to celiac disease, raising the nutrient concentration in the gut into a 'hyperfertilized' environment the yeast finds attractive; eventually the overgrowth spills into the bloodstream. So his prevention starts with knowing your own digestive and absorptive patterns: pulse-test for food allergies, avoid long-term antibiotics, and as you grow older take betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal decrease in stomach-acid production. He is emphatic on two more points — take these digestive aids if you are under stress, and deal aggressively with any disease that lowers your immune capacity.
claims.verbatim:
Prevention includes being aware of your intestines and knowing your
digestive and absorptive abilities and patterns. Do pulse tests for food
allergies, avoid long term use of antibiotics, and as you grow older take
betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal
decrease in production of stomach acid. Be sure to take these digestive aids
if you are under stress; deal aggressively with any disease that lowers your
immune capacity!

claims.subject: digestion
claims.question: Why do I get bloated after eating?
claims.answer_short: Because the stomach isn’t acidic enough to stay sterile. Wallach says low stomach acid lets bacteria and yeast from the small intestine migrate up into the stomach, where they ferment the carbohydrates and sugars in your meal — and that fermentation is the gas.
claims.answer: Gastric bloating — where the gas actually comes from. Bloating is the accumulation of gas in the stomach, and Wallach's explanation turns on a fact most people don't know: a healthy stomach is sterile, and it stays that way because it is so acidic. When hypochlorhydria — low stomach acid — sets in, that sterility fails, and bacteria and yeast from the small intestine migrate upward into the stomach, a place they do not belong. There they ferment the carbohydrates and sugars you have eaten, and the gas that fermentation produces is the 'bloat.' It is the same picture he draws for achlorhydria, where the symptom triad is 'burp, belch, and bloat,' and it explains why his treatment goes after the missing acid — colloidal minerals, betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals — rather than after the gas.
claims.verbatim:
BLOATING (gastric) is the accumulation of gas in the stomach. Normally
the stomach is sterile because of the acid environment; however, when
hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid) occurs, bacteria and yeast from the
small intestine migrates up into the stomach. The bacteria in the stomach
now “ferments” carbohydrates and sugars that are eaten and produce gas or
“bloat.”

claims.subject: digestion
claims.question: Why do pancreatic enzymes stop working?
claims.answer_short: They need an alkaline environment. Wallach explains it through dumping syndrome — when the stomach empties into the small intestine all at once it overloads the intestine’s natural buffer, and the acid conditions that result stop pancreatic enzymes from working properly.
claims.answer: Dumping syndrome — why an acid intestine disables your enzymes. Dumping syndrome is the sudden emptying of stomach contents into the small intestine all at once, overloading the intestine's natural buffer system. That matters because of where the body's acid is meant to sit: the stomach is supposed to be strongly acidic, the small intestine is not, and pancreatic enzymes require an alkaline environment to function — so when unbuffered acid floods in, they stop working properly. Wallach notes it is a common side effect of stomach surgery, and that anemia and osteoporosis are its common secondary diseases, which is what you would expect from a stretch of gut that can no longer digest and absorb. His treatment works with the mechanism rather than against it: any of the classic bitters such as gentian, folic acid at 3 to 5 mg a day, pectin at half an ounce in water before meals, high animal-protein diets, six to eight small meals a day rather than a few large ones, and lying down for half an hour after eating.
claims.verbatim:
DUMPING SYNDROME is the sudden “dumping” of stomach contents
into the small intestine all at once, thus overloading the natural intestinal
buffer system. The resulting acid condition in the intestine prevents proper
functioning of pancreatic enzymes, which require an alkaline environment.
Dumping syndrome is a common side effect of stomach surgery. Anemia
and osteoporosis are common secondary diseases of the dumping
syndrome.

claims.subject: digestion
claims.question: What is the pH of stomach acid?
claims.answer_short: About 1.0. Wallach gives the body’s secretions as running from 1.0 in stomach acid up to 8.2 in pancreatic juice — a deliberately wide spread, in contrast to blood, which is held in the narrow band of 7.36 to 7.44.
claims.answer: How acidic your stomach is supposed to be. Wallach draws a sharp line between the body's internal chemistry and its secretions. Internally, acidity is policed within a very narrow range: healthy blood runs 7.36 to 7.44, below 7.30 is acidosis, above 7.44 is alkalosis, and anything below 6.8 or above 7.8 is rapidly fatal. Secretions and excretions are the opposite — deliberately variable, running from about 1.0 in stomach acid at one end to 8.2 in pancreatic juice at the other, with alkaline urine in vegans. That spread is the point rather than a flaw. The stomach is meant to be strongly acidic: it is the acid environment that keeps the stomach sterile and that activates protein digestion. The pancreatic juice meeting food further down the tract is meant to be alkaline — which is why acid conditions in the small intestine disable pancreatic enzymes.
claims.verbatim:
In contrast to the internal body, the pH
of secretions and excretions can be more variable and range from 1.0 in
stomach acid to 8.2 in pancreatic juice and alkaline urine in vegans.

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Why does Wallach warn about vegetable oils?
claims.answer_short: Because, in his framework, polyunsaturated vegetable oils plus a selenium deficiency are a lethal pairing — together he calls them “the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer.”
claims.answer: Selenium's job is to keep the fats in your cells from oxidizing; vegetable oils are polyunsaturated fats that oxidize easily — especially once heated or hydrogenated into trans fats. So Wallach's warning is about the combination: flood the body with rancidity-prone oils while selenium (the antioxidant that would protect them) runs low, and the oils go rancid inside your cells, driving free-radical damage. He calls high vegetable-oil intake concurrent with selenium deficiency “the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer,” and ties the same pairing — including too much fish oil — to birth defects, arteriosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, and sudden cardiac death. The practical point: to him these oils aren't just empty calories, they actively consume the protection selenium is meant to provide.
claims.verbatim:
High intakes of vegetable oils,
including salad dressing and cooking oils, concurrent with a selenium
deficiency is the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer.

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: What causes fibromyalgia, according to Wallach?
claims.answer_short: Wallach equates fibromyalgia with the adult form of muscular dystrophy — the same “white muscle disease” vets eliminated in livestock in 1957 — and calls it a multiple-deficiency disease, not a mystery pain syndrome.
claims.answer: To Wallach, fibromyalgia isn't an unexplained chronic-pain condition but a nutritional muscle disease under a modern name — the same thing veterinarians call white muscle disease or stiff lamb disease, and what he terms adult-onset muscular dystrophy. He notes it was eliminated from lambs, calves, and pigs back in 1957 through nutrition. In humans he frames it as a multiple-deficiency disease with a dietary trigger: a high intake of fried foods and vegetable oils (margarine, cooking oils) combined with deficiencies of selenium, vitamin E, and the sulfur-bearing amino acids. The logic mirrors his selenium thesis throughout — rancidity-prone oils flooding in while the antioxidants that would protect the muscle are missing — so his answer to the pain is to correct the deficiencies and cut the oils, not to mask symptoms with muscle relaxants.
claims.verbatim:
FIBROMYALGIA (stiff lamb disease, white muscle disease, adult onset
muscular dystrophy) is a disease that was eliminated from lambs, calves,
and pigs in 1957. It is a multiple deficiency disease caused by a high intake
of fried foods and vegetable oils (margarine, cooking oils, and salad
dressing) and deficiencies of selenium, vitamin E, and sulfur amino acids

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Does selenium affect fertility and pregnancy?
claims.answer_short: Strongly, in Wallach's view. He ties selenium deficiency to male sterility, infertility, miscarriage, low birth weight, and SIDS — and says a woman's selenium level before conception helps determine whether a pregnancy holds.
claims.answer: Wallach treats selenium as a reproductive mineral on both sides of conception. In men, he lists sterility as a direct sign of selenium deficiency. In women, he emphasizes preconception status: adequate selenium in the diet and supplements before conceiving is, in his framing, key both to maintaining the pregnancy and to preventing birth defects like muscular dystrophy and cystic fibrosis in the child. On the deficiency side he links low selenium to infertility, low birth weight, high infant mortality, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). It's consistent with his cystic-fibrosis thesis — that the mother's trace-mineral status in the first months of pregnancy shapes the child's lifelong health — and it's why “preconception nutrition” recurs throughout his prevention advice.
claims.verbatim:
The selenium levels in
preconception women is important to the maintenance of pregnancy as well
as the prevention of muscular dystrophy in all of its forms

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: What is selenium?
claims.answer_short: Selenium is an essential trace mineral -- needed in only tiny amounts, yet in Wallach's framework it's the body's most efficient antioxidant and the hidden deficiency behind diseases from cystic fibrosis to Keshan heart failure.
claims.answer: Selenium is a trace mineral — an essential nutrient the body needs in only tiny (microgram) amounts, with Wallach's daily target around 200 mcg. Its importance is out of all proportion to that amount because of what it does: he calls it the most efficient antioxidant there is, the front-line defense that stops the fats inside your cells from oxidizing, or 'going rancid.' It is also the mineral Wallach is most identified with — his 1977 finding that cystic fibrosis is a selenium deficiency, and his framing of Keshan-disease heart failure, muscular dystrophy, and much of cancer as selenium-deficiency diseases, all trace back to this one element. The catch, in his telling: selenium is spread unevenly through the world's soils, so entire regions are deficient, and a gut damaged by gluten cannot absorb it even when food supplies it.
claims.verbatim:
Selenium is a trace mineral that has been investigated very intensively as a
cancer preventative and as therapeutic nutrition.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: What is zinc?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's framework, zinc is a foundational essential trace mineral the body must be given every day: no fewer than 70 metalloenzymes cannot function without it, so a shortage ripples across the body's whole chemistry.
claims.answer: Wallach counts zinc among the foundational essential minerals — a nutrient the body cannot make and has to be supplied daily. The adult body holds only about 1.4 to 2.3 grams of it, stored mainly in the liver, pancreas, kidney, bone, and muscle, yet that small amount does outsized work: no fewer than 70 metalloenzymes — including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, and carboxypeptidase — require zinc as a cofactor before they can work at all. Zinc is also built into the RNA molecule (the 'zinc fingers') and is needed for cell division, DNA synthesis, growth, immunity, wound healing, taste and smell, and healthy skin, hair, and nails. Because it touches so many systems, Wallach ties a long list of deficiency signs and birth defects to a shortage of it, and he includes zinc as a daily essential in his Base Line supplement program.
claims.verbatim:
There are no less than 70 metalloenzymes that require Zn as a
functional cofactor.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: How much zinc is in the human body and where is it stored?
claims.answer_short: Wallach puts the adult body's total zinc at 1.4 to 2.3 grams, held mostly in the liver, pancreas, kidney, bone, and muscle, with smaller stores in the eye, prostate, and semen.
claims.answer: Wallach states that the adult human contains between 1.4 and 2.3 grams of zinc. The largest reserves sit in the liver, pancreas, kidney, bone, and skeletal muscles, while lesser amounts are found in the eye, prostate gland, semen, skin, hair, fingernails, and toenails. That spread across so many tissues mirrors how many jobs zinc does — and, in his framework, why a deficiency can surface in places as different as the prostate, the skin, and the hair.
claims.verbatim:
There are 1.4 to 2.3 grams of Zn in the adult human. The liver, pancreas,
kidney, bone, and skeletal muscles have the greatest reserves of Zn. Lesser
amounts are found in the eye, prostate gland, semen, skin, hair, fingernails,
and toenails.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: What are the signs and symptoms of a zinc deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists a wide range — loss of taste and smell, wounds that won't heal, weak immunity, poor growth, hair loss, anemia, depression, and even odd cravings like eating dirt.
claims.answer: Wallach catalogs a broad set of zinc-deficiency signs and diseases: loss of the sense of smell and taste, infertility, failure of wounds and ulcers to heal, immune failure, poor growth and short stature, high infant mortality, hypogonadism, anemia, and hair loss (alopecia). He also lists pica or cribbing — abnormal cravings to eat things like dirt, wool, or hair. In his framework these are not separate mysterious illnesses but the visible fingerprint of one missing mineral.
claims.verbatim:
Symptoms and Diseases of Zinc Deficiency
• Pica/Cribbing (geophagia, wool eating, hair eating, etc.)
• Loss of sense of smell
• Loss of sense of taste
• Infertility
• Failure of wounds and ulcers to heal
• Immune status failure
• Poor growth (short stature)
• High infant mortality
• Hypogonadism (small poorly functioning ovaries and testes)
• Perpetual prepubic state
• Anemia
• Alopecia (hair loss)

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Do men lose zinc when they ejaculate?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach states that men lose 420 mcg of zinc with each ejaculation, which is why he calls sex without ejaculation a zinc-conserving practice.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that men lose 420 micrograms of zinc per ejaculation. He raises this while discussing Taoist sexual practice, observing that enjoying sex without ejaculation is, in mineral terms, a zinc-conserving practice.
claims.verbatim:
Men lose 420 mcg of zinc per ejaculation. The
ability to enjoy the ecstasy of sex without ejaculation is a zinc conserving
practice.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Does zinc help with hair loss?
claims.answer_short: Wallach includes zinc at 50 mg three times a day in his treatment for alopecia (hair loss).
claims.answer: In his entry on alopecia (hair loss), Wallach says hair loss occurring with eczema is often caused by an essential-fatty-acid deficiency and responds to IV interlipids and/or oral flaxseed oil (9 grams per day), and that zinc at 50 mg three times a day is also indicated. He also cites tin deficiency in male-pattern baldness. Zinc is one of his nutritional levers for alopecia.
claims.verbatim:
Alopecia that occurs with eczema is
often caused by essential fatty acid deficiency and will respond to IV
interlipids and/or oral flaxseed oil at the rate of 9 grams per day. Zinc at 50
mg t.i.d. is also indicated.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Is zinc oxide good for sunburn and burns?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recommends zinc oxide ointment to shield the skin — especially the nose — from sunburn, and to cover second-degree burns.
claims.answer: Wallach points to zinc oxide ointment as a topical skin protector, noting that the nose in particular may need its special protection against sunburn. For a second-degree burn with blisters, he lists covering the area with zinc oxide — or bathing it in vitamin E oil or colloidal silver — as part of care. Here zinc works from the outside as a physical barrier and skin protectant rather than as an oral supplement.
claims.verbatim:
Prevention of sunburn is easy with modern “sun
screen” products. The nose may need the special protection of zinc oxide
ointment.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Can zinc improve Down's syndrome?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says treating Down's syndrome children with zinc (15 mg three times a day) plus his full nutrient program can raise IQ by 15–20 points and improve physical features — gains that are lost if the program is stopped.
claims.answer: Wallach's treatment for Down's syndrome is zinc at 15 mg three times a day together with his base line nutritional supplement program, plus pulse-testing to find and avoid food allergies that block absorption. He claims that on this program you can expect an increase in IQ of 15 to 20 points and an improvement in physical features, as long as it is followed consistently. He is equally blunt about the reverse: withdrawing from the program results in the loss of all the physical and IQ gains.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of Down’s syndrome should include zinc at 15 mg t.i.d. and the
base line nutritional supplement program. Do pulse test in Down’s patients
to determine the presence of food allergies and avoid offending foods. You
can expect an increase in IQ of 15-20 points and an improvement in
physical features as long as the program is followed. Withdrawal from the
program results in loss of all the physical and IQ gains.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Does zinc help shrinking testicles or low sex drive in men?
claims.answer_short: Zinc leads Wallach's treatment for testicular atrophy — the shrinking of the testicles seen in aging men or after mumps that can bring on decreased sex drive and feminization.
claims.answer: Wallach describes testicular atrophy — a shrinking of the testicles common in aging men or following a bout of mumps — as something that can lead to decreased sexual drive and feminization. His treatment for it leads with zinc at 20 mg three times a day, alongside plant-derived colloidal minerals, ginseng (Panax ginseng), saw palmetto and an herbal combination mixed with testosterone (Zumbani). He does not present zinc as a cure on its own, but he places it first among the nutrients he uses to address the problem.
claims.verbatim:
TESTICULAR ATROPHY is not uncommon in aging men or following
an episode of mumps. Testicular atrophy may result in decreased sexual
drive and feminization.
Treatment of testicular atrophy should include zinc at 20 mg t.i.d., plant
derived colloidal minerals, an herbal combination mixed with testosterone
(Zumbani), ginseng (Panax ginseng), and saw palmetto (Serenoa serrulata).

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Can a zinc deficiency cause cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach links cancer to malabsorption of zinc, along with vitamin A and selenium, caused by celiac-type gut damage.
claims.answer: Wallach frames celiac disease — gut damage from wheat gluten, cow's milk, or soy — as the basic cause of many major diseases because it blocks nutrient absorption. In his account, cancer results specifically from the malabsorption of zinc, vitamin A, and selenium, just as diabetes follows from malabsorbed chromium and vanadium. So he treats a chronic zinc shortfall not as trivial but as one of the nutritional roots of cancer.
claims.verbatim:
Celiac disease is, therefore, the basic cause of many diseases including
diabetes (i.e. malabsorption of chromium and vanadium), cancer (i.e.
malabsorption of zinc, vitamin A, and selenium), and muscular dystrophy
and cystic fibrosis (i.e. malabsorption of selenium in the pregnant mother
resulting in damage to the fetus).

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: What is the relationship between calcium and magnesium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says calcium and magnesium are antagonists in muscle contraction — calcium is the stimulator, magnesium the relaxer — so too much calcium can trigger signs of magnesium deficiency, while too much magnesium blocks bone calcification.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, calcium and magnesium play opposite roles in normal muscle contraction: calcium acts as the stimulator and magnesium as the relaxer. Because they balance each other, an excessive amount of calcium can induce the signs of a magnesium deficiency. He also warns that the reverse imbalance matters — an excess of magnesium will inhibit bone calcification.
claims.verbatim:
AN EXCESS OF
MAGNESIUM WILL INHIBIT BONE CALCIFICATION. Calcium and
Mg have antagonistic roles in normal muscle contraction, calcium acting as
the stimulator and Mg as the relaxer. An excessive amount of Ca can induce
signs of Mg deficiency.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Does magnesium help keep calcium in your bones?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says magnesium is needed to hold calcium in the bones, and running short can let bony calcium leak out (showing up as tartar on the teeth).
claims.answer: Wallach explains that magnesium is needed to hold calcium in your bones. He raises this in the context of tartar (dental calculus): the calcium that hardens into tartar is actually your own bony calcium being lost into the saliva, and when that's happening you may need more magnesium to keep calcium in the bones and to correct a badly skewed dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio. In other words, magnesium isn't just about calcium intake — it helps keep the calcium you already have where it belongs.
claims.verbatim:
When
this happens you may need more magnesium to hold calcium in the bones
and correct a severe dietary calcium/ phosphorus ratio problem.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Can low magnesium cause heart palpitations?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists a magnesium deficiency among the nutritional shortfalls that can trigger palpitations, or an irregular heartbeat.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework, palpitations — an irregular heartbeat — aren't always a sign of organic heart disease. Once that's ruled out with an EKG, he points to other causes: food allergies (like a reaction to MSG), hypoglycemia, and nutritional deficiencies. Among those deficiencies he specifically names magnesium, alongside B1, B3, selenium and potassium. In his view a simple mineral shortfall can leave the heart beating irregularly.
claims.verbatim:
PALPITATIONS (irregular heartbeat) can be the result of organic heart
disease. This is easily determined by an EKG or ECG. Other causes: food
allergies (i.e. Chinese Restaurant Syndrome or allergy to MSG), nutritional
deficiencies (i.e. Bl, B3, selenium, magnesium, potassium, etc.), and/or
hypoglycemia.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Can magnesium help mitral valve prolapse?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says magnesium deficiency is a common cause of mitral valve prolapse, and if that's the cause you can expect significant improvement within 30 to 60 days of correcting it.
claims.answer: Wallach identifies magnesium deficiency as a common cause of mitral valve prolapse, the progressive change in the heart's mitral valve. His treatment pairs magnesium at 1,000 mg with selenium, salmon oil, hawthorn, and the base line nutrition program. The encouraging part: if the prolapse is genuinely due to a magnesium deficiency, he says you can expect significant improvement within 30 to 60 days of correcting it.
claims.verbatim:
Magnesium deficiency
is a common cause of mitral valve prolapse.
Treatment of mitral valve prolapse should include selenium at 500-1,000
mcg/day, magnesium at 1,000 mg ti.d., salmon oil at 1-5 gm ti.d., and
English hawthorne (Crataegus oxyacantha). Don’t forget the base line
nutrition program. If the prolapse is due to a magnesium deficiency you can
expect a significant improvement within 30-60 days.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Can sweating deplete your magnesium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach warns that if you sweat out your calcium, magnesium and sulfur and don't replace them, you're at high risk of arthritis, osteoporosis and kidney stones — and he notes high-performance athletes lose a lot of magnesium in sweat.
claims.answer: Wallach cautions that heavy sweating drains minerals, and that if you sweat out all of your calcium, magnesium and sulfur without replacing them by supplementation, you are at high risk of developing arthritis, osteoporosis and kidney stones. Elsewhere in the same book he notes that high-performance athletes lose a considerable amount of magnesium in sweat. This is part of why he argues athletes in particular need to supplement rather than assume food covers the loss.
claims.verbatim:
If you sweat
out all of your calcium, magnesium, and sulfur and don’t replace them by
supplementation, you are at high risk of developing arthritis, osteoporosis,
and kidney stones.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Can a magnesium deficiency cause memory loss or dementia?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists magnesium deficiency — along with low vitamin B1 and cholesterol — as one of the common nutritional causes of dementia, which he says is not a true result of aging.
claims.answer: Wallach rejects the idea that dementia (senile memory loss) is a natural part of getting old. He names nutritional deficiencies — specifically magnesium, vitamin B1, and cholesterol — alongside arteriosclerosis and alcoholism as the common causes. His answer is good nutrition and the base line supplement program rather than accepting memory loss as inevitable.
claims.verbatim:
DEMENTIA (memory loss, as in senile) is a common symptom yet not a
true result of aging. Nutritional deficiencies (magnesium, vitamin B1,
cholesterol), arteriosclerosis, and alcoholism are the common causes of
dementia.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Can a magnesium deficiency cause bones to break easily?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says fractures can result from malnutrition — including calcium/magnesium deficiency — and that good mineral status in your bones prevents most 'spontaneous' fractures and fractures from simple falls.
claims.answer: Wallach lists calcium/magnesium deficiency, a poor calcium-to-phosphorus ratio, and osteoporosis as forms of malnutrition that can lead to fractures, right alongside outright trauma. His key point is preventive: good mineral status in your bones will prevent most 'spontaneous' fractures, compression fractures, and fractures from simple falls. He recommends the base line nutritional supplements — his Pig Arthritis Formula with calcium and magnesium (2,000 and 1,000 mg per day) plus digestive aids — as an almost sure guarantee against non-trauma fractures.
claims.verbatim:
FRACTURES (broken bones) can result from malnutrition (i.e.
calcium/magnesium deficiency, improper calcium/phosphorus ratio,
osteoporosis) and severe trauma (i.e. a blow during a fight, auto accident,
fall, etc.). Good mineral status in your bones will prevent most types of
“spontaneous” fractures, compression fractures, and fractures from simple
falls.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: What actually causes kidney stones?
claims.answer_short: Contrary to what mainstream doctors believe, Wallach says kidney stones are caused by calcium and magnesium DEFICIENCY, which pulls calcium out of your bones — and that bone calcium is what ends up in the stone.
claims.answer: Wallach turns the usual advice on its head: he says kidney stones aren't caused by too much calcium but by calcium and magnesium deficiency. When you're short on these minerals, calcium is depleted from your bones, and that lost bone calcium is the very source of the calcium that forms the stone. He adds that magnesium deficiency also produces 'malignant calcification' in the small arteries of the kidney, and that excess vitamin D taken alongside a calcium deficiency speeds the depletion and raises stone risk. His prevention is adequate supplemental calcium and magnesium plus cutting phosphorus intake.
claims.verbatim:
Kidney stones, contrary to popular
belief by the “orthodox” doctor, are caused by calcium and magnesium
deficiencies which cause a depletion of calcium from your bones, which is
the source of the calcium found in kidney stones.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Did Wallach see magnesium deficiency cause disease in animals?
claims.answer_short: Yes — in his zoo autopsies Wallach found osteoporosis and osteoarthritis from calcium-and-magnesium deficiency, and arteriosclerosis in plant-eating animals from magnesium deficiency, across species from parrots to rhinos.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts finding the same magnesium-related diseases across many zoo species. He saw lions, wolves, woolly monkeys, alligators, iguanas and parrots with osteoporosis, which he attributed to a calcium and magnesium deficiency, and sheep, monkeys, rhinos and kangaroos with osteoarthritis from the same combined deficiency. In vegetarian animals such as pheasants, parrots and kangaroos he found arteriosclerosis, which he attributed specifically to a magnesium deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
There were lions, wolves, woolly monkeys,
alligators, iguanas, and parrots with osteoporosis, a calcium and magnesium
deficiency. There was arteriosclerosis in vegetarian animals such as
pheasant, parrots, kangaroo, a magnesium deficiency. There were even
sheep, monkeys, rhino, and kangaroos with osteoarthritis, a calcium and
magnesium deficiency.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: What do essential fatty acids do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says EFAs have vitamin-like roles in fat transport and metabolism and in keeping cell walls (the bilipid membranes) intact, and they form part of the cholesterol esters and phospholipids in the blood.
claims.answer: Wallach describes essential fatty acids as having vitamin-like functions in fat transport and metabolism and in maintaining the integrity of cell walls — the bilipid layer membranes. He adds that they are part of the fatty acids of cholesterol esters and phospholipids found in plasma lipoproteins and mitochondrial lipoproteins.
claims.verbatim:
EFA’s have essential vitamin-like functions in fat transport and metabolism, and in maintaining the
integrity of cell walls (bilipid layer membranes). They are also part of the
fatty acids of cholesterol esters and phospholipids in plasma lipoproteins
and mitochondrial lipoproteins.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Is eczema related to omega-3 or essential fatty acids?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says atopic dermatitis (eczema) is part of the 'atopic' syndrome — which also includes asthma, hair loss and lowered immunity — and is a condition of essential fatty acid malabsorption.
claims.answer: Wallach describes atopic dermatitis, or eczema, as one part of the 'atopic' patient syndrome, which also includes asthma, alopecia (hair loss), and a lowered immune response. He attributes this whole syndrome to malabsorption of essential fatty acids, linking the skin, lungs, hair, and immune system to the same underlying fat-absorption problem.
claims.verbatim:
ATOPIC DERMATITIS (eczema) is part of the “atopic” patient syndrome
which includes asthma, alopecia (hair loss), and lowered immune response.
This syndrome is one of malabsorption of essential fatty acids

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Why is the cystic fibrosis sweat test positive?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the positive CF 'sweat test' results from essential fatty acid deficiency, which causes a secondary shortage of prostaglandins that control the sodium, chloride and potassium levels of sweat.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the positive 'sweat test' used to diagnose cystic fibrosis is the result of an essential fatty acid deficiency. That deficiency causes a secondary shortage of prostaglandins — very short-lived hormones — which normally control the sodium, chloride, and potassium levels of the sweat. He presents the abnormal sweat chemistry as tracing back to a fatty-acid deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
It has been learned recently that the positive “sweat test” is the result of an
essential fatty acid deficiency that causes a secondary deficiency of
“prostaglandin” (very short lived hormones) that control the sodium,
chlorides, and potassium levels of the sweat!!!

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Does an omega-3 or essential fatty acid deficiency cause acne?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says acne is primarily the result of an essential fatty acid deficiency combined with eating too much saturated and polyunsaturated fat from fried foods and margarine.
claims.answer: Wallach breaks with the idea that acne is just a teenage hormone or hygiene problem: he calls it primarily the result of an essential fatty acid deficiency, made worse by eating too much saturated and damaged polyunsaturated fat — the kind in fried foods and margarine. His fix is to cut the fast food, supply the missing good fats (essential fatty acids at about 3% of daily calories, or 9 grams a day), and check for food allergies, rather than reaching first for antibiotics.
claims.verbatim:
Acne is primarily the result of an essential
fatty acid deficiency with a concurrent intake of too much saturated fat and
polyunsaturated fatty acids (fried foods and margarine).

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: What are the best sources of omega-3 or essential fatty acids?
claims.answer_short: Wallach points to flaxseed oil and salmon oil as the essential fats to take, and advises avoiding as much of the other polyunsaturated fats as possible.
claims.answer: Wallach tells people to pay special attention to their essential fatty acids while avoiding as much of the other polyunsaturated fats as they can, naming flaxseed oil and/or salmon oil as 'the essentials' to consume. In his heart-disease guidance these two oils are the go-to sources, set apart from the polyunsaturated oils he warns against.
claims.verbatim:
Pay special attention to EFA, avoid as much of
the polyunsaturated fatty acids as you can (other than the essentials— i.e.
flaxseed oil and/or salmon oil)

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Is dry skin a sign of omega-3 or essential fatty acid deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says dry skin, cracked cuticles and hangnails signal essential fatty acid deficiency that can lead to cardiovascular disease; he sums it up as 'dry skin means essential fatty acids.'
claims.answer: Wallach treats dry skin — along with cracked cuticles, hangnails, and a cracked index finger and thumb — as more than a cosmetic issue: he calls it a signal of essential fatty acid deficiency that can result in cardiovascular disease such as thrombosis, stroke, and heart attack. He warns that the deeper consequences of this deficiency can be sudden and deadly, and coins the shorthand 'DSM/EFA,' meaning 'dry skin means essential fatty acids.'
claims.verbatim:
DRY SKIN (cracked cuticles, hang nails, cracked
index finger and thumb) is a common malady in the western world. In itself,
it is a cosmetic problem. It is a signal of a potentially more serious problem
— essential fatty acid deficiency that can result in cardiovascular disease
(i.e.—thrombosis, stroke, heart attack, etc.). Superficial creams will
temporarily deal with the superficial problem, but the more ominous results
of the body’s deficiency of essential fatty acids can be sudden and deadly!!!
DSM/EFA or “dry skin means essential fatty acids”!!!

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: How much vitamin C should I take?
claims.answer_short: For treating abrasions, Wallach recommends taking vitamin C orally to bowel tolerance — anywhere from 1 to 5 grams.
claims.answer: In his home-care first-aid entry for abrasions, Wallach recommends taking vitamin C orally 'to bowel tolerance,' which he gives as anywhere from 1 to 5 grams.
claims.verbatim:
Take Vitamin C orally to bowel tolerance
(anywhere from 1-5 grams).

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Should people with MS avoid vitamin C supplements?
claims.answer_short: For multiple sclerosis (and ALS), Wallach advises avoiding large-dose vitamin C supplements and getting vitamin C from green vegetables and juices instead.
claims.answer: In his multiple sclerosis protocol, Wallach makes an exception to his usual high-dose vitamin C advice: he recommends avoiding large doses of vitamin C supplementation and instead eating green vegetables and juices as a natural source of vitamin C. He notes the same treatment regimen has proved effective for ALS (Lou Gehrig's Disease). This is a distinctive, condition-specific caution rather than general guidance.
claims.verbatim:
avoid large doses of vitamin C
supplementation. Eat green vegetables and juices as a natural source of
vitamin C.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: What causes night blindness?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says night blindness is caused by a vitamin A deficiency, from a poor diet, fat malabsorption, or a zinc shortage that blocks the liver from converting carotene to vitamin A.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that night blindness (xerophthalmia) is caused by a vitamin A deficiency, which can arise several ways. It can come from an outright dietary shortage, from fat-malabsorption syndromes (vitamin A is fat-soluble), or from a zinc deficiency that leaves the liver unable to convert carotene into vitamin A. Conditions such as cystic fibrosis, celiac disease, and food allergies that damage the intestine and block absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, as well as a lack of essential fatty acids, can also cause it. He treats night blindness very specifically with 25,000 to 300,000 IU of vitamin A per day as beta-carotene plus zinc at 15 to 50 mg three times a day.
claims.verbatim:
NIGHT BLINDNESS (xerophthalmia) is caused by a vitamin A deficiency
which can be overt dietary deficiency, fat malabsorption syndrome (vitamin
A is fat soluble), zinc deficiency which results in poor conversion of
carotene to vitamin A by the liver, cystic fibrosis, celiac disease and various
food allergies resulting in intestinal changes that prevent absorption of fat
soluble vitamins (i.e. vitamin A, vitamin E, vitamin D and vitamin K), as
well as a deficiency of essential fatty acids.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: Why do I have rough bumpy skin on my arms?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says rough, sandpaper-like 'shark skin' (keratosis) is caused by a deficiency of vitamin A and zinc, often from a low-animal-protein diet.
claims.answer: Wallach identifies 'shark skin' (keratosis) as a deficiency of vitamin A and zinc, usually resulting from a low-animal-protein diet. It shows up as cracks in the corners of the mouth (cheilosis), oral lesions often secondarily infected with Candida, a 'geographic' tongue, and skin lesions with hard granular plugs of sebaceous and keratinized material in the hair follicles that give a sandpaper-like surface.
claims.verbatim:
SHARK SKIN (keratosis) is caused by a deficiency of vitamin A and zinc
(usually as a result of low animal protein diets). Shark skin is characterized
by cracks in the corners of the mouth (cheilosis), oral lesions that are often
secondarily infected by Candida albicans (per
leche), “geographic” tongue, and skin lesions characterized by hard
granular plugs resulting from collections of sebaceous and keratinized
material in hair follicles which gives a sandpaper-like surface (shark skin).

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: How does Wallach use vitamin A to fight cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says beta-carotene with vitamin E can be taken at up to 600,000 IU of vitamin A equivalent in cancer therapy, helping the thymus make antibodies and making laetrile more effective.
claims.answer: For cancer therapy programs, Wallach says beta-carotene taken together with vitamin E can be used at as much as 600,000 IU of vitamin A equivalent. He considers this of significant benefit, especially for carcinomas. He adds that the vitamin A provided this way also helps the thymus gland produce antibodies and makes laetrile more effective.
claims.verbatim:
Beta-carotene taken with vitamin E can be taken at as much as 600,000 IU
vitamin A equivalent! This will be of significant benefit in cancer therapy
programs, especially CARCINOMAS. The vitamin A thus provided will
also help the thymus gland produce antibodies and make laetrile more
effective.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: How does Wallach treat acne with vitamin A?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recommends vitamin A at 300,000 units a day as beta-carotene for five months, then dropping to 25,000 a day, along with B6, zinc, and topical vitamin E oil.
claims.answer: For acne, Wallach recommends a regimen of vitamin A at 300,000 units per day as beta-carotene for five months, then reducing to 25,000 per day. He pairs it with vitamin B6 at 100 mg three times a day and zinc at 50 mg three times a day for 30 days, and suggests vitamin E oil applied topically to the acne lesions. He treats acne primarily as an essential-fatty-acid problem, so this vitamin A protocol sits on top of correcting fats and food allergies.
claims.verbatim:
A regimen of Vitamin A 300,000 units/day (as beta-carotene)
for five months, then reduce to 25,000 i per day B6 100 mg t.i.d., zinc 50
mg t.i.d. for 30 days, and vitamin E oil may be applied topically to acne
lesions is also recommended.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: What is keratomalacia?
claims.answer_short: Keratomalacia is a severe vitamin A deficiency disease in which the cornea turns hazy, dry, and ulcerated, and if untreated it can cause permanent blindness.
claims.answer: Wallach describes keratomalacia (xerophthalmia) as a hazy, 'bluish,' dry cornea, the clear dome on the front of the eye, that becomes ulcerated. Its symptoms include extreme dryness of the eyes with constant blinking to keep them moist, conjunctivitis, and night blindness, and fat-like 'Bitot's spots' can appear on the white of the eyeball. He warns that untreated keratomalacia can result in permanent blindness.
claims.verbatim:
KERATOMALACIA (xerophthalmia) is recognized as a hazy “bluish” dry
cornea (the domed clear bulge on the front of the eye) that becomes
ulcerated. Symptoms include extreme dryness of the eyes with blinking in
attempts to keep the eyes moist, conjunctivitis, and night blindness. Fat-like
spots (Bitots spots) can be found on the “white” of the eyeball. Untreated
keratomalacia can result in permanent blindness.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: Can vitamin A deficiency cause miscarriage or birth defects?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says miscarriage is usually due to deficiencies of vitamins, trace minerals, or protein, and names vitamin A, zinc, folic acid, selenium, and complete proteins as essential to maintaining a pregnancy.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that miscarriage (spontaneous abortion) is usually caused by deficiencies of vitamins, trace minerals, and/or protein.
