extracellular colloidal P in combination with carbohydrates, lipids, protein,
and a wide variety of other biologically active organic compounds including
the blood’s major buffer system. B-complex vitamins function as
coenzymes to intracellular metabolic functions only when combined with
phosphorus.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: How much phosphorus do we eat and how well is it absorbed?
claims.answer_short: Adults eat 1,000-1,500 mg of phosphorus a day, but absorb only 3-5% of metallic phosphorus, 40-50% of chelated forms, and up to 98% of organically bound colloidal phosphorus.
claims.answer: Wallach puts the average adult dietary intake of phosphorus at 1,000 to 1,500 mg per day. Absorption depends heavily on form: metallic phosphorus is limited to about three to five percent in adults and older children (up to 8-12 percent in infants), mixed chelated dietary sources reach 40 to 50 percent, and organically bound colloidal phosphorus is absorbed up to 98 percent. He adds that optimal absorption of metallic and chelated phosphorus occurs when the dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio is 1:1.
claims.verbatim:
The average adult human dietary intake of P is 1,000 to 1,500 mg/day. In
adults and older children, the absorption of metallic P is limited to about
three to five per cent and as high as eight to 12 percent in infants. Mixed
dietary sources of chelated P may be absorbed at the rate of 40 to 50
percent. Optimal absorption of metallic and chelated P occurs when the
dietary Ca:P ratio is 1:1. Organically bound colloidal P is absorbed up to 98
percent.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: Which foods have too much phosphorus compared to calcium?
claims.answer_short: All the basic foods are lopsided — grain 1:8, red meat and fish 1:12, carbonated drinks 1:8, and organ meat as extreme as 1:44 calcium to phosphorus.
claims.answer: Wallach says a dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio of 2:1 is ideal yet impossible to attain on an unsupplemented diet. The calcium-to-phosphorus ratios of everyday foods are consistently and wildly off: grain 1:8, red meat 1:12, fish 1:12, carbonated drinks 1:8, and organ meat (liver, kidney) as extreme as 1:44. None of these are anywhere near correct, so they increase calcium loss from the body, bones and teeth — meaning the more meat you eat, the more calcium supplementation you need.
claims.verbatim:
The calcium/phosphorus ratios of
food items is consistent: FOOD CALCIUM PHOSPHORUS
grain 1 8
red meat 1 12
organ meat 1 44
(liver, kidney)
fish 1 12
carbonated drinks 1 8
It is easily seen that none of the calcium/phosphorus ratios of the basic
foods are anywhere near correct. These increase the calcium loss from the
body including the bones and teeth. The more meat you eat, the more
calcium supplementation you need.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: Does phosphorus in grains block absorption of other minerals?
claims.answer_short: Yes — phosphorus in grains occurs as phytates, and phytic acid in unleavened bread binds calcium, iron, zinc and other minerals, lowering their absorption.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that phosphorus is present as phytates in cereals and whole grain flours. When bread is made from unleavened flours, the phytic acid complexes with calcium, iron, zinc and other minerals in the gut, further lowering their absorption rate. This is why phosphorus in grain form can work against the very minerals the body needs.
claims.verbatim:
Phosphorus is
present as phytates in cereals and whole grain flours, therefore, if bread is
made from unleavened flours, the phytic acid will complex with Ca, Fe, Zn,
and other minerals further lowering their absorption rate.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: What happens if you are deficient in phosphorus?
claims.answer_short: Phosphorus deficiency is widespread and ultimately fatal, collapsing ATP synthesis into complete metabolic energy failure with neuromuscular, skeletal, blood and kidney disease.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that phosphorus deficiency has long been recognized in livestock — where its signs include pica, cribbing and fractures — but has only recently been recognized in humans. Because phosphorus underlies so many biological functions, its deficiency is widespread, universal and ultimately fatal, largely through a decrease in adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis that amounts to complete metabolic energy failure. The result carries associated neuromuscular, skeletal, blood and kidney disease.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of P have long been recognized in livestock. Symptoms of P
deficiency include the behavior of pica and cribbing and fractures.
Phosphorus deficiency has only recently been recognized in humans. The
widespread, universal, and ultimately fatal results of P deficiency are the
result of its widespread biological functions, significantly as the result of a
decrease in ATP synthesis (complete metabolic energy failure) with
associated neuromuscular, skeletal, blood, and kidney disease.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: Do Americans get too much phosphorus?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says most American diets run 15 to 20 parts phosphorus to 1 part calcium, the reverse of the healthy 2:1 calcium-to-phosphorus ratio.
claims.answer: Wallach's distinctive position is that the correct dietary ratio is 2 parts calcium to 1 part phosphorus, but most American diets are inverted to 15-20 parts phosphorus per 1 part calcium. He treats gum and jaw disease as osteoporosis of the face and jaw, driven by this imbalance. Correcting it is impossible without supplementing calcium and consciously cutting phosphorus — giving up soft drinks and reducing meat intake.
claims.verbatim:
The correct calcium/phosphorus ratio is 2 calcium/1
phosphorus (most American diets are 15-20 phosphorus/ 1 calcium) and it
is impossible to achieve without supplementation of calcium and
consciously reducing the phosphorus intake (i.e. give up soft drinks, reduce
meat intake, etc.).

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: Why do phosphorus-deficient animals chew on bones and wood?
claims.answer_short: A 'phosphate appetite' drives phosphorus-deficient cattle to anxiously search pastures for discarded bones (osteophagia) and to gnaw on wood and each other's horns.
claims.answer: Wallach cites LeVaillant's 1796 description of 'phosphate appetite' — the anxious search by cattle in phosphate-deficient South African pastures for discarded animal bones, a behavior called osteophagia. Phosphorus-deficient cattle also chewed on wood and each other's horns. He notes this bone-chewing has been reported across many wild herbivore species, including reindeer, caribou, red deer, camels, giraffe, elephant and wildebeest.
claims.verbatim:
Phosphate appetite was described by LeVaillant (1796) as the anxious
search by cattle in phosphate deficient South African pastures for discarded
animal bones (osteophagia). Phosphorous deficient cattle also chewed on
wood and each others horns.
Osteophagia has been reported in many wild species of herbivores
including reindeer, caribou, red deer, camels, giraffe, elephant, and
wildebeest.

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: Which proteins in the body contain sulfur?
claims.answer_short: Sulfur is built into hemoglobin, hormones such as insulin and the adrenal cortical hormones, enzymes, and antibodies.
claims.answer: Wallach lists the sulfur-containing proteins that work in indirect ways to keep you alive: hemoglobin, hormones (including insulin and the adrenal cortical hormones), enzymes, and antibodies. Sulfur also turns up in carbohydrates such as heparin, a natural anticoagulant concentrated in the liver, and in chondroitin sulfate, a component of cartilage. Even the vitamins thiamine (B1) and biotin carry sulfur bound in their molecules.
claims.verbatim:
Sulfur-containing proteins work in indirect ways to maintain life:
• Hemoglobin
• Hormones (insulin, adrenal cortical hormones) • Enzymes • Antibodies
Sulfur also occurs in carbohydrates such as heparin, an anticoagulant that is
concentrated in the liver and other tissues, and chondroitin sulfate
(cartilage, gelatin). The vitamins thiamine (Bl) and biotin have S bound in
their molecule.

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: Why are my fingernails brittle?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reads brittle fingernails as a sign of sulfur amino acid and protein deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach treats the fingernails as barometers of absorption and nutritional status. Brittle nails, in his reading, point to sulfur amino acid and protein deficiencies, while white spots signal zinc deficiency and ridges can indicate iron or calcium deficiency. He advises correcting the underlying nutrition, including the base-line supplements, rather than treating the nail alone.
claims.verbatim:
FINGERNAILS (white spots, ridges, brittle) are good barometers of
absorption and nutritional status. Bluish fingernails indicate chronic lung
conditions (i.e. not enough oxygen); white spots indicate zinc deficiency;
ridges can indicate iron and/or calcium deficiency; brittle nails indicates
sulfur amino acid and protein deficiencies.

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: Why do farts smell like rotten eggs?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the rotten-egg smell is sulfur released when unabsorbed proteins reach the colon and are fermented by bowel organisms.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, foul bowel gas usually comes from digested but poorly absorbed food reaching the colon, where bowel organisms ferment it. Food sensitivities to wheat, gluten, and dairy can trigger celiac-type changes in the small intestine that cause this malabsorption. The unabsorbed proteins then reach the colon and become the source of the sulfur that smells like rotten eggs.
claims.verbatim:
FARTING (bowel gas) is usually caused by digested but poorly absorbed
food reaching the colon and being fermented by bowel organisms. Some
foods such as beans, garlic, and onions are legendary for their production of
bowel gas. Food sensitivities to wheat, wheat gluten, and dairy can cause
celiac disease type changes in the small intestine, which results in
malabsorption. The unabsorbed proteins reach the colon and are the source
of sulfur that smells like rotten eggs.

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: Can sulfur treat scabies?
claims.answer_short: For scabies, Wallach recommends a 5-10% sulfur ointment for infants, in place of the adult chemical treatments, to avoid potential neurotoxicity.
claims.answer: In treating scabies, an infestation by the microscopic mite Sarcoptes scabiei, Wallach lists total-body application of 1 percent gamma benzene hexachloride and 25 percent benzyl benzoate cream for adults, but recommends a 5-10 percent sulfur ointment for infants to avoid potential neurotoxicity. He notes that poke (Phytolacca decandra) may also be used topically as a natural alternative.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of scabies includes total body application of 1 percent gamma
benzene hexachloride, 25 percent benzyl benzoate cream in adults, and 5-10
percent sulfur ointment in infants to avoid potential neurotoxicity; poke
(Phytolacca decandra) may be used topically as a natural alternative.

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: What are the symptoms of sulfur deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says a sulfur deficiency produces degenerative arthritis and cartilage breakdown, weakened ligaments and tendons, lupus, sickle cell anemia, and other collagen diseases.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, a deficiency of sulfur drives degenerative types of arthritis marked by the breakdown of cartilage, including osteoarthritis and degenerative arthritis, along with weakened ligaments and tendons. He also ties sulfur deficiency to systemic lupus erythematosus, sickle cell anemia, and various collagen diseases.
claims.verbatim:
A deficiency of sulfur results in
degenerative types of arthritis involving degeneration of
cartilage, osteoarthritis, degenerative arthritis, weakened ligaments,
weakened tendons, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, sickle cell anemia, and
various “collagen diseases.”

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: Is lupus caused by a nutritional deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach argues lupus features multiple mineral deficiencies of sulfur, copper, and selenium, and that its autoimmune damage is a result of the disease, not its cause.
claims.answer: Wallach rejects the orthodox view that systemic lupus erythematosus is fundamentally an autoimmune disease in which the body attacks itself. He argues the autoimmune defect appears as a result of the disease and of abnormal proteins, rather than being its cause. Characteristically present, he says, are multiple mineral deficiencies of sulfur, copper, selenium, and others.
claims.verbatim:
The “orthodox” theory is that
SLE is an “autoimmune” disease that causes the patient’s own antibodies to
attack themselves. The fact is the autoimmune defect occurs as a result of
the disease and the presence of abnormal proteins rather than being the
cause. Multiple mineral deficiencies of sulfur, copper, selenium, etc. are
characteristically present.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: What is Chloride?
claims.answer_short: Chloride is an essential mineral and one of the body's three key electrolytes; Wallach says its most important job is supplying the raw material your stomach uses to make hydrochloric acid.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework, chloride is essential to every living species — it drives electrochemical and catalytic reactions and activates numerous enzymes. He groups it with sodium and potassium as one of three indispensable electrolytes that govern water balance, osmotic equilibrium, acid-base balance, and muscular function. Its single most important role, though, is serving as the basic raw material the stomach uses to manufacture hydrochloric acid (HCl) — the stomach acid that digests protein via pepsin, activates intrinsic factor for vitamin B12 absorption, and lets the body absorb minerals. Ordinary table salt (sodium chloride) is the universal source of chloride ions.
claims.verbatim:
Chlorine is essential for all living species’ electrochemical and catalytic
functions, activates numerous enzymes, and is the basic raw material for
our stomachs to make stomach acid (HCl) for protein digestion by pepsin,
B12 absorption (intrinsic factor activation), and absorption of minerals.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: What does chloride actually do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Chloride is the raw material your stomach uses to make hydrochloric acid; it is essential to all living things and activates numerous enzymes.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that chlorine (chloride) is essential to every living species for electrochemical and catalytic functions and that it activates numerous enzymes. It also serves as the basic raw material the stomach uses to manufacture stomach acid (HCl), which drives protein digestion by pepsin, activates intrinsic factor for vitamin B12 absorption, and enables the absorption of minerals. He notes that sodium chloride (NaCl), or common table salt, is the universal source of chloride ions for all living things.
claims.verbatim:
Chlorine is essential for all living species’ electrochemical and catalytic
functions, activates numerous enzymes, and is the basic raw material for
our stomachs to make stomach acid (HCl) for protein digestion by pepsin,
B12 absorption (intrinsic factor activation), and absorption of minerals.
Sodium chloride (NaCl) or salt is the universal source of chloride ions for
all living things.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: How much of the body is chloride, and what does it do with sodium and potassium?
claims.answer_short: Chlorine makes up three percent of the body's total mineral content and works with sodium and potassium as one of three indispensable electrolytes.
claims.answer: Wallach groups sodium, chlorine, and potassium as three indispensable electrolytes so intimately associated that they are presented together. By his figures sodium makes up two percent, potassium five percent, and chlorine three percent of the body's total mineral content, with sodium and chloride living mainly outside the cells (extracellular) and potassium inside them. Together the three run at least four physiological jobs: maintaining normal water balance and distribution, osmotic equilibrium, acid-base balance, and muscular irritability.
claims.verbatim:
Sodium, chlorine, and potassium are three indispensable “electrolytes” so
intimately associated in the body that they can be presented together.
Sodium makes up two percent, potassium five percent, and chlorine three
percent of the total mineral content of the human body. All three are widely
distributed throughout the body tissues and fluids, however, Na and CI are
primarily extracellular (outside the cell), while K is an intracellular (inside
the cell) mineral. Sodium, potassium, and chlorine are involved in at least
four important physiological functions in the body: 1. Maintenance of
normal water balance and distribution.
2. Maintenance of normal osmotic equilibrium.
3. Maintenance of normal acid-base balance.
4. Maintenance of normal muscular irritability.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: What does the sweat test measure and is it really specific to cystic fibrosis?
claims.answer_short: It measures sodium, chloride, and potassium in sweat; Wallach says it is nonspecific, turning positive in 17 different diseases.
claims.answer: Wallach describes the sweat test as a nonspecific test that measures the amount of electrolytes—sodium, chlorides, and potassium—in sweat. Though originally thought to be a specific genetic indicator for cystic fibrosis, he says it is now known to be positive in 17 different diseases plus food allergies, starvation, kwashiorkor, and celiac disease. He attributes the mechanism to essential fatty acid deficiencies and the resulting lack of prostaglandins that control sweat electrolyte levels in the skin.
claims.verbatim:
SWEAT TEST a nonspecific test that measures the amount of electrolytes
(i.e. sodium, chlorides, and potassium) in sweat. Originally it was thought
to be a specific genetic indicator for cystic fibrosis (CF). However, today it
has been found to be positive in 17 different diseases, food allergies,
starvation, kwashiorkor, celiac disease, etc. The mechanism is related to
EFA deficiencies and thus the lack of certain prostaglandins (short-lived
hormone-like substances) which control sweat electrolyte levels in the skin.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Can a low-salt diet cause low stomach acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach says sodium chloride is the raw material for stomach acid, so a salt-restricted diet makes achlorhydria more likely.
claims.answer: Because sodium chloride is the raw material the body needs to manufacture stomach acid, Wallach argues that people on a salt-restricted diet are more likely to develop achlorhydria, the loss of stomach acid. He calls achlorhydria a natural process of aging and perhaps the most significant aging phenomenon, noting that 75 percent of people over age 50 require supplementation of stomach acid. This ties salt and its chloride directly to the ability to digest protein and absorb nutrients.
claims.verbatim:
Achlorhydria is also a natural process of aging and perhaps the most
significant aging phenomenon. Seventy-five percent of people over the age
of 50 years require supplementation of stomach acid. Sodium chloride is the
raw material required to manufacture stomach acid, so it follows that people
on a salt restricted diet are more likely to
develop achlorhydria.

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: How much arginine does Wallach recommend for infertility?
claims.answer_short: For infertility, Wallach's protocol includes l-arginine at 500 mg three times a day (t.i.d.).
claims.answer: In Wallach's infertility program, l-arginine is dosed at 500 mg three times a day (t.i.d.). It is one part of a broader plan that includes a high-protein diet of up to 200 g/day, essential fatty acids, zinc, and selenium.
claims.verbatim:
Eat high protein diets (up to 200 gm/day),
EFA at 5 gm t.i.d., l-arginine at 500 mg t.i.d., zinc at 15 mg t.i.d., selenium
at 250 mcg/day

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: How much arginine is used for cataracts?
claims.answer_short: For cataracts, Wallach's protocol includes l-arginine at 300 mg per day.
claims.answer: Wallach's cataract protocol includes l-arginine at 300 mg per day. It sits alongside other targeted nutrients such as glycine, l-glutamine, l-cysteine, and glutathione, on top of the baseline vitamin/mineral supplement.
claims.verbatim:
bioflavonoids at 300 mg, glycine at 200 mg, l-glutamine at 200 mg,
l-arginine at 300 mg/day, l-cysteine at 400 mg/day, and glutathione at 40
mg/day.

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: Should I avoid arginine if I get cold sores or herpes?
claims.answer_short: Yes—for herpes, Wallach says to avoid high-arginine foods like chocolate, nuts, seeds and grains, and to eat high-lysine foods instead.
claims.answer: As part of treating herpes, Wallach advises avoiding high-arginine foods—chocolate, peanuts, nuts, seeds, and grains—and eating high-lysine foods such as meat, potatoes, milk, yeast, fish, chicken, beans, and eggs. Other measures include applying ultraviolet light directly on the lesion for 1–6 minutes per day.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment includes ultra violet light directly on lesion for 1-6 minutes per
day, avoid high arginine foods (i.e. avoid chocolate, peanuts, nuts, seeds,
grains), eat high lysine foods (i.e. meat, potatoes, milk, yeast, fish, chicken,
beans, eggs)

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: How much taurine should I take for macular degeneration?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's macular degeneration protocol includes taurine at 2 to 5 grams per day, alongside all 90 essential nutrients.
claims.answer: For macular degeneration — a free-radical degeneration of the retina and a common cause of blindness in aging individuals — Wallach's treatment approach includes taurine at 2 to 5 grams per day. It is paired with eliminating all fried foods, margarine, and all sugar, supplementing with all 90 essential nutrients (including selenium, vitamin E, and methionine), and taking the 60 essential minerals in plant-derived colloidal form.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment approach includes elimination of all fried foods and
margarine, elimination of all sugar (natural and processed), supplement with all 90 essential nutrients
(including selenium—500 mcg., vitamin E—1,200 iu., methionine), taurine 2-5 grams per day, and
the 60 essential minerals in the plant derived colloidal form.

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: Does taurine help with epilepsy or seizures?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists taurine at 500 mg three times a day among the nutrients indicated for epilepsy.
claims.answer: In Wallach's nutritional approach to epilepsy, taurine at 500 mg three times a day is one of the indicated nutrients. It sits alongside vitamin B6 (which he says frequently 'cures' epilepsy at 50-100 mg), calcium and magnesium, folic acid, B12, manganese, zinc, essential fatty acids, choline, and dimethyl glycine. He adds that high-fat, high-cholesterol diets often help resolve acquired seizure disorders not related to trauma.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B6 alone will frequently “cure” epilepsy at 50-100
mg ti.d.. Long-term administration can cause some numbness and tingling
in the face or hands. Adding Calcium magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000
mg/day, folic acid at 15-25 mg/day and B12 at 1,000 mcg/day IM can also
be curative. Manganese at 50 mg/day, zinc at 50 mg t.i.d., essential fatty
acids at 5 gm t.i.d., choline at 4 gm/day, taurine at 500 mg t.i.d., and
dimethyl glycine at 100 mg b.i.d. are also indicated.

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: Does taurine help with gallstones or gallbladder problems?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's treatment for gallbladder disease and gallstones includes taurine at 500 mg three times a day.
claims.answer: For gallbladder disease and gallstones, Wallach's treatment includes taurine at 500 mg three times a day. It is combined with a high-fiber diet aimed at 2-3 bowel movements per day, lecithin at 2,500 mg, essential fatty acids, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, and selenium.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of gallbladder disease and gallstones includes the use of high
fiber diets (i.e. make sure you are having 2-3 bowel movements per day),
lecithin at 2,500 mg t.i.d., EFA at 5 gm t.i.d., vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per
day, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, selenium at 200 mcg t.i.d., and taurine at
500 mg t.i.d.

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: What is the treatment for absence seizures (petit mal)?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's treatment for absence attacks (petit mal) includes taurine at 500 mg three times a day.
claims.answer: Absence attacks (petit mal) are brief episodes in which a person stops what they are doing and rapidly blinks, then resumes the activity where they left off. Wallach's recommended treatment includes taurine at 500 mg three times a day, along with choline, dimethyl glycine, phosphatidyl choline, and vitamin B6.
claims.verbatim:
ABSENCE ATTACKS {petit mal): patient stops what he is doing and rapidly
blinks eyes then starts the activity again where he left off. Treatment should
include choline 4 gm/day, taurine 500 mg t.i.d., dimethyl glycine 100 mg
b.i.d., phosphytidyl choline, and B6 100-300 mg/day.

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: How much tryptophan for depression?
claims.answer_short: For depression, Wallach's program uses dl-phenylalanine, L-tryptophan, and L-tyrosine at 2 grams three times a day each, on top of the base-line supplement program.
claims.answer: Wallach's depression protocol pairs L-tryptophan with dl-phenylalanine and L-tyrosine, each taken at 2 grams three times a day (t.i.d.). This sits on top of the base-line supplement program and steps to address food allergies and hypoglycemia, together with chromium/vanadium, B vitamins, vitamin C, calcium and magnesium, potassium, and essential fatty acids.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of depression should include dealing with the food allergies (i.e.
avoidance, rotation diets) and hypoglycemia (i.e. hypoglycemia diet). In
addition to the base line supplement program, also use chromium/vanadium
supplementation at 50-200 mcg t.i.d, iron at 15 mg/day, B6, B2, Bl at 50 mg
t.i.d., B12 at 1,000 mcg/day, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, calcium and
magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg/day, potassium at 250 mg q.i.d.,
essential fatty acids at 5 gm t.i.d., and dl-phenylalanine, l-tryptophan, and
l-tyrosine at 2 gm t.i.d. each.

claims.subject: phenylalanine
claims.question: How much phenylalanine does Wallach recommend for insomnia?
claims.answer_short: For insomnia, Wallach's protocol includes dl-phenylalanine at 250 mg three times a day, along with avoiding caffeine, plus calcium, chromium, l-tryptophan, inositol and niacinamide.
claims.answer: For insomnia, Wallach's treatment starts with avoiding caffeine and any offending food allergens, then layers in a set of nutrients and amino acids: dl-phenylalanine at 250 mg three times a day, calcium (especially plant-derived colloidal calcium), chromium and vanadium at 25-200 mcg three times a day, l-tryptophan at 1,000 mg three times a day, inositol at 500 mg a day, and niacinamide at 1,000 mg at bedtime, plus acupuncture and homeopathy. He notes that food allergies and hypoglycemia can themselves cause insomnia, and recommends the pulse test and a six-hour glucose tolerance test to find them.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment for insomnia includes avoidance of caffeine and offending food allergens, calcium
(especially plant derived colloidal calcium), chromium and vanadium at 25-200 mcg t.i.d.,
acupuncture, homeopathy, dl-phenylalanine at 250 mg t.i.d., l-tryptophan at 1,000 mg t.i.d., inositol
at 500 mg/day, niacinamide at 1,000 mg at bedtime

claims.subject: tyrosine
claims.question: Is tyrosine an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Mainstream science calls tyrosine non-essential, but Wallach adds it to the essential list because, over the long haul, a deficiency causes a specific disease -- goiter.
claims.answer: Conventional nutrition recognizes nine classically essential amino acids -- histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine -- which the body cannot make and must take in daily. Wallach argues that list is incomplete. He adds three more, arginine, taurine, and tyrosine, on the grounds that over the long haul a deficiency of each produces a specific disease: cancer for arginine, macular degeneration for taurine, and goiter for tyrosine. So while tyrosine is technically 'non-essential' because the body can synthesize it, Wallach treats it as essential in practice, because going without it long-term has real disease consequences.
claims.verbatim:
To the classic list of essential amino
acids, I would add arginine, taurine, and tyrosine. Over the long haul, these
three amino acids help prevent certain specific diseases. Respectively, those
diseases are cancer, macular degeneration, and goiter.

claims.subject: tyrosine
claims.question: How does tyrosine relate to the thyroid and goiter?
claims.answer_short: Tyrosine combines with iodine to build the thyroid hormone thyroxin, so a shortage of tyrosine, along with iodine, copper, or molybdenum, is one cause of goiter.
claims.answer: The thyroid is Wallach's main reason for calling tyrosine essential. In combination with the mineral iodine, tyrosine is the amino acid the body manufactures into the thyroid hormone thyroxin, which governs metabolism. Because of that, Wallach lists goiter -- an enlarged, struggling thyroid -- as a simple deficiency disease caused by a shortage of nutrients including iodine, copper, molybdenum, and the amino acid tyrosine. Supply the missing raw materials, tyrosine among them, and the thyroid has what it needs to make its hormone.
claims.verbatim:
GOITER (colloid goiter, hypothyroid) is caused by a simple deficiency of
nutrients (i.e. iodine, copper, molybdenum, the amino acid tyrosine, etc.).

claims.subject: lysine
claims.question: What foods are high in lysine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists meat, potatoes, milk, yeast, fish, chicken, beans, and eggs as high-lysine foods, recommending them (while avoiding high-arginine foods) for people dealing with herpes.
claims.answer: Wallach names meat, potatoes, milk, yeast, fish, chicken, beans, and eggs as foods rich in lysine. He recommends loading up on these high-lysine foods while avoiding high-arginine foods such as chocolate, peanuts, nuts, seeds, and grains, as part of managing herpes outbreaks.
claims.verbatim:
eat high lysine foods (i.e. meat, potatoes, milk, yeast, fish, chicken,
beans, eggs)

claims.subject: lysine
claims.question: How much lysine does Wallach recommend for shingles?
claims.answer_short: For shingles, Wallach's treatment of choice includes lysine at 5 grams a day, along with the antivirals Isoprinosin and Ribavirin, vitamin B12, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, vitamin E, and zinc.
claims.answer: Shingles produces skin lesions that follow a regular pattern because the virus travels along the nerves. Wallach's treatment of choice combines the antivirals Isoprinosin at 500-1,500 mg/day and Ribavirin at 250-500 mg/day with high-dose nutrients: vitamin B12 at 1,000 mcg/day, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU/day, lysine at 5 grams/day, and zinc at 15 mg three times a day.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of choice for shingles is Isoprinosin at 500-1,500 mg/day,
Ribavirin at 250-500 mg/day, vitamin B12 at 1,000 mcg/day, vitamin C to
bowel tolerance, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU/day, lysine at 5 grams/day, and
zinc at 15 mg t.i.d.

claims.subject: valine
claims.question: What is valine's function in the body?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's essential-amino-acid chart, valine's function is protein production—it serves as one of the raw building blocks the body uses to make its proteins.
claims.answer: In Wallach's chart of the classic essential amino acids, valine's function is listed as protein production—it is one of the amino acids the body strings together as a raw building block to make its proteins. Valine shares this straightforward 'protein production' role with lysine, threonine, leucine, and isoleucine, while other essentials in the same chart play more specialized parts: tryptophan as a precursor of niacin and serotonin, phenylalanine of thyroxin and epinephrine, methionine in forming choline and creatine phosphate, and histidine in forming histamine.
claims.verbatim:
Amino acid Function
Valine protein production
Lysine protein production
Threonine protein production
Leucine protein production
Isoleucine protein production
Tryptophan precursor of niacin and serotonin
Phenylalanine precursor of thyroxin and epinephrine
Methionine formation of choline and creatine phosphate
Histidine formation of histamine

claims.subject: histidine
claims.question: What does histidine do in the body?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's amino-acid function table, histidine's job is the formation of histamine — the compound the body releases during allergic reactions and immune responses.
claims.answer: In Wallach's table of the essential amino acids and their functions, histidine is assigned a single job: the formation of histamine. Histamine is the signaling compound the body releases during allergic reactions and immune responses, so histidine is the raw material the body draws on to produce it. Wallach lists this same histidine-to-histamine function consistently across his books.
claims.verbatim:
Methionine formation of choline and creatine phosphate
Histidine formation of histamine

claims.subject: isoleucine
claims.question: What does isoleucine do in the body?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's essential amino-acid function table, isoleucine's role is protein production—it serves as a direct building block for the body's proteins.
claims.answer: In Wallach's table of the classic essential amino acids and their functions, isoleucine's listed role is protein production. Like valine, lysine, threonine, and leucine, it works as a direct building block for the body's proteins, rather than serving as a precursor to a hormone or neurotransmitter the way tryptophan (precursor of niacin and serotonin) or phenylalanine (precursor of thyroxin and epinephrine) do.
claims.verbatim:
Amino acid Function
Valine protein production
Lysine protein production
Threonine protein production
Leucine protein production
Isoleucine protein production
Tryptophan precursor of niacin and serotonin
Phenylalanine precursor of thyroxin and epinephrine
Methionine formation of choline and creatine phosphate
Histidine formation of histamine

claims.subject: threonine
claims.question: What does threonine do in the body?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's function table, threonine's role is protein production—it's a building block the body uses to manufacture its proteins, alongside valine, lysine, leucine, and isoleucine.
claims.answer: When Wallach lays out what each essential amino acid actually does, he assigns threonine a single, foundational role: protein production. It sits in the same group as valine, lysine, leucine, and isoleucine—the amino acids whose listed job is simply building protein—rather than the specialists like tryptophan (a precursor of niacin and serotonin) or phenylalanine (a precursor of thyroxin and epinephrine). In other words, threonine is raw material: the body strings it together with the other amino acids to manufacture the proteins that make up its tissues.
claims.verbatim:
The classic essential amino acids are:
Amino acid Function
Valine protein production
Lysine protein production
Threonine protein production
Leucine protein production
Isoleucine protein production
Tryptophan precursor of niacin and serotonin
Phenylalanine precursor of thyroxin and epinephrine
Methionine formation of choline and creatine phosphate
Histidine formation of histamine

claims.subject: carbon
claims.question: Are minerals carbon-based?
claims.answer_short: No — Wallach teaches that minerals are the body's non-carbon raw materials that come from the soil, while the carbon-based nutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins and vitamins) are built using the sun's energy.
claims.answer: Wallach draws a fundamental line between the two kinds of raw materials the body must take in. The carbon-based nutrients — the macronutrients (carbohydrates, fats and proteins) together with micronutrients such as vitamins — are built using the energy of the sun. The non-carbon materials, chiefly the minerals, are not manufactured by living things at all; their only source is the earth's crust, the soil. Because a soil's mineral make-up varies so widely from place to place, Wallach notes that people with the same basic genetics do not all get the same opportunity for health and longevity.
claims.verbatim:
The sun provides the energy to manufacture the
carbon-based macronutrients (carbohydrates, fats, and proteins) and
micronutrients like vitamins. The earth’s crust—the soil— is the source of
all our non-carbon based raw materials like minerals.

claims.subject: oxygen
claims.question: What is oxygen and why does the body need it?
claims.answer_short: Oxygen is one of the three obvious raw materials every living thing needs to sustain life, and unlike food it is a 'non-variable' — the same everywhere on earth.
claims.answer: Wallach lists oxygen, water, and food as the obvious raw materials every living organism needs to sustain life, maintain and repair tissues and organs, reproduce, and support longevity. He draws a sharp line between them: clean oxygen and water, free of pathogens and pollution, are 'non-variables' — the same in China, Germany, Brazil, Nigeria, Canada, and all fifty U.S. states. Food, by contrast, is the variable, because all nourishment ultimately comes from the soil and depends on its mineral composition. In his framework oxygen is essentially a given; the real problem to solve is the mineral-depleted food supply.
claims.verbatim:
Raw materials are required by all living organisms. The obvious raw
materials to sustain life, maintain and repair tissues and organs, support
reproduction, and support longevity, are oxygen, water, and food. Clean
oxygen and water, free of pathogens and pollution, are non-variables.
Oxygen and water are the same in China, Germany, Brazil, Nigeria,
Canada, and all fifty states in the United States.

claims.subject: strontium
claims.question: Does the body need strontium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds there is considerable evidence that strontium is an essential mineral in mammals, including humans.
claims.answer: Wallach classes strontium among the essential minerals the body requires, holding that there is considerable evidence for its essentiality in mammals including man. He backs this with strontium's ability to replace calcium in many organisms and its high concentration in mammalian bone. In his framework strontium is a genuine nutritional need — one of many minerals that meet the criteria for an essential nutrient even though they are not 'classically' considered essential.
claims.verbatim:
There is
considerable evidence for essentiality in mammals including man.

claims.subject: strontium
claims.question: What is strontium-90, and is it natural?
claims.answer_short: Strontium-90 is a man-made radioactive product of atomic-bomb fission — the great biohazard scare of the Cold War — and, unlike natural strontium, it does not occur in nature.
claims.answer: Wallach is careful to separate two things that share a name. Strontium-90 is not the natural strontium the body uses in place of calcium — it is a man-made radioactive product of the fission atomic explosions, and Wallach calls it the greatest biohazard fear of the Cold War. Unlike natural strontium, which is found throughout rocks, soil, plants and animals, strontium-90 does not occur in nature at all; it exists only because humans split atoms.
claims.verbatim:
Strontium 90, the man-made product of
fission atomic explosions and the greatest biohazard fear during the cold
war, does not occur in nature.

claims.subject: tin
claims.question: Does tin help regrow hair?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says tin deficiency causes male-pattern baldness in lab animals, and he personally regrew a considerable amount of hair using plant-derived liquid colloidal tin.
claims.answer: In his entry on alopecia, Wallach ties male-pattern baldness to tin. He states that deficiencies of the mineral tin have been shown to cause male-pattern baldness in lab animals, and he offers his own experience as evidence: he personally had considerable hair regrowth after using plant-derived liquid colloidal tin. It is one of the clearest places he connects a single trace mineral to both hair loss and hair regrowth.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies
of the mineral tin have been shown to cause male pattern baldness in lab
animals. I personally have had considerable hair regrowth following the use
of plant derived liquid colloidal tin.

claims.subject: korsakoff
claims.question: What is Korsakoff's syndrome?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's "false Alzheimer's": recent-memory loss driven by a vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency — often from alcoholism plus sugar — and reversible with high-dose thiamine.
claims.answer: Korsakoff's syndrome is a form of recent-memory loss that Wallach calls a "false Alzheimer's disease": the person can still perform detailed tasks they learned before the illness began, but can no longer record or store new memories or learn even the simplest new task. A telltale feature is confabulation — inventing imaginary experiences to fill in for memories that can't be recalled. Wallach traces it to a single vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, usually caused by chronic alcoholism combined with a diet heavy in sugar and simple carbohydrates; it can also follow a blow to the head. Because it is a thiamine deficiency and not true Alzheimer's, he considers it reversible — patients are routinely misdiagnosed with Alzheimer's yet can be cured within a week once given megadoses of thiamine. His treatment centers on high-dose vitamin B1 (100 mg three times a day) along with lecithin, strict avoidance of alcohol and sugar, chromium and vanadium, betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes, and other memory-supporting agents. When alcohol has actually damaged the brain tissue, the alcoholic form is called Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and is harder to treat.
claims.verbatim:
KORSAKOFF’S SYNDROME (recent memory loss, false Alzheimer’s
Disease) is characterized by an inability to record and store new memory.
The patient can perform detailed tasks learned before onset but cannot learn
the simplest of new tasks.

claims.subject: protein
claims.question: What is the best quality protein?
claims.answer_short: Whole egg is the highest-quality protein Wallach lists — a chemical score of 100 and 94% utilization; animal proteins outrank plant proteins, and mixing plant sources fills in the missing amino acids.
claims.answer: Wallach ranks protein quality with two measures — a 'chemical score' (how well a food's amino-acid pattern matches the body's needs) and '% utilization' (how much of it the body actually uses). Whole egg is the gold standard, scoring 100 with 94% utilization, the highest of any source he lists. Animal proteins sit at the top: human milk 100/87 and cow's milk 95/82. Plant proteins score lower — cotton seed 81/59, soy bean 74/65, rice 67/59, peanut 65/47, millet 63/44, wheat 53/48, sesame 50/54, and corn (maize) 49/52 — because each is short on or missing certain amino acids. Mixing plant sources (beans with rice, wheat with legumes) or combining vegetable with animal protein raises the usable value and makes up for the missing amino acids. Quality matters because protein repairs and builds tissue, forms enzymes, hormones, and antibodies, and holds blood fluid and acid-base balance in check; a shortfall of complete protein leads to poor growth, weakened immunity, edema, and Kwashiorkor.
claims.verbatim:
The availability and usability of N from various foods are
quite different and must be considered when choosing N sources.
Nitrogen/Protein Utilization Values of Common Foods
Nitrogen Source (Protein) Chemical Score % Utilization
Whole egg 100 94
Human milk 100 87
Cow’s milk 95 82
Soy bean 74 65
Sesame 50 54
Peanut 65 47
Cotton seed 81 59

claims.subject: testosterone
claims.question: How can I raise my testosterone naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's main lever for testosterone is the mineral boron — he says the body needs it to keep testosterone (and estrogen) at normal levels, and that supplementing boron doubles testosterone.
claims.answer: Dr. Wallach ties testosterone directly to the trace mineral boron. He says the body requires boron to maintain normal blood levels of both estrogen and testosterone, and that boron supplementation actually doubles testosterone levels. He describes the effect as fast and measurable: within 8 days, supplementing boron cut urinary mineral losses (40% less calcium, 33% less magnesium, and less phosphorus) and doubled a key estrogen (estradiol) to the levels seen in women on estrogen-replacement therapy — with testosterone likewise doubling. So in Wallach's framework, low testosterone is in part a boron-deficiency problem, and boron is a direct nutritional lever to raise it.
claims.verbatim:
Boron is required for the maintenance of bone density and normal blood
levels of estrogen and testosterone. Within eight days of supplementing
boron, women lost 40 percent less calcium, 33 percent less magnesium, and
less phosphorus through their urine. Women receiving boron
supplementation had blood levels of estradiol 17B doubled to “levels found
in women on estrogen replacement therapy.” Levels of testosterone also
double with Boron supplementation.

claims.subject: testosterone
claims.question: Do you need cholesterol to make testosterone?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says the body builds testosterone out of cholesterol, and warns that driving cholesterol too low can leave a man 'totally disinterested in sex.'
claims.answer: Wallach frames cholesterol as an essential raw material, not merely a villain: the body uses it to build cell walls, the myelin of the brain and spinal cord, vitamin D, bile acids, and hormones — including the adrenal-cortical hormones, estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone. Because testosterone is manufactured from cholesterol, he warns that pushing cholesterol too low backfires on men: a cholesterol deficiency, in his words, 'will turn hubby into a TV watching steer who is totally disinterested in sex.' So in Wallach's view, adequate cholesterol is a prerequisite for normal testosterone and male sex drive.
claims.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential part
of the structure of cell walls, brain and spinal cord (myelin), the raw
material for the production of vitamin D in the human body, bile acids,
adrenal cortical hormones, estrogen (a cholesterol deficiency makes
menopause a living hell), progesterone, and testosterone (a cholesterol
deficiency will turn hubby into a TV watching steer who is totally
disinterested in sex).

claims.subject: testosterone
claims.question: Does Wallach recommend taking testosterone for impotence or low libido?
claims.answer_short: Yes — among his impotence remedies Wallach lists 'oral testosterone,' which he specifies as glandular food supplements plus testosterone by injection (IM), alongside herbs like ginseng and saw palmetto.
claims.answer: For impotence, Wallach's plan starts with the non-nutritional basics — relaxation, time with your mate, and setting up romantic situations — then adds acupuncture, homeopathy, and herbs such as ginseng, nux vomica, sarsaparilla, saw palmetto and Zumbani. Notably it also includes 'oral testosterone,' which he specifies as glandular food supplements plus testosterone given by injection (IM, intramuscular). This is a notable case where Wallach endorses supplying testosterone directly, rather than only raising it through a mineral like boron. He adds that the drug Viagra can help maintain an erection but comes with side effects, and reminds readers to keep up the base-line nutrition program with plant-derived colloidal minerals.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of impotence should include relaxation, spending time with your
mate, and setting up romantic situations. The interpretation of the word
romantic is an individual thing: flowers excite some people and turn others
off, alcohol excites some people and anesthetizes others.
Also, acupuncture, homeopathy, and herbs to include ginseng (Panax
ginseng), nux vomica (Strychnos nux vomica), sarsapilla (Smilax
officinalis), saw palmetto (Serenoa serrulata), Zumbani, and oral testosterone
(i.e. glandular food supplements and testosterone IM), can be of value.

claims.subject: korsakoff
claims.question: Has Wallach's memory-loss treatment actually restored anyone's memory?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach cites his multi-drug Korsakoff protocol (nootropics like centrophenoxine and piracetam, plus IV chelation, vitamin B1, lecithin and chromium/vanadium) as the exact program used to restore the memory of Princess Diana's bodyguard.
claims.answer: Wallach caps his drug protocol for Korsakoff's syndrome — IV chelation and IV hydrogen peroxide, vitamin B1 at 100 mg three times a day, lecithin, chromium and vanadium, betaine HCl with pancreatic enzymes, and the memory nootropics hydergine, vasopressin nasal spray, centrophenoxine and piracetam — with a real-world result: he says this is the exact program used to restore the memory of Princess Diana's bodyguard. He offers it as evidence that the recent-memory loss he calls a 'false Alzheimer's' is treatable rather than permanent.
claims.verbatim:
centrophenoxine at 4.4-8.0 gm per day, and piracetam
(Dinagen) at 1.6-4.8 gm per day. This is the drug treatment program used to
restore Princess Di’s bodyguard’s memory.

claims.subject: memory_loss
claims.question: What causes memory loss, and how does Wallach treat it?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says memory loss has many causes, not one -- so check each, including food allergies and low blood sugar -- then treats it by cutting allergens/sugar/fried food/margarine/alcohol and adding chromium, vanadium, selenium, vitamin E, B-complex, and the memory agents Diapid, Lucidril, Dinagen (with choline), and hydergine.
claims.answer: Wallach treats memory loss as an umbrella covering senile dementia, Korsakoff's syndrome, and Alzheimer's, and stresses it has a variety of causes rather than one -- so each possible cause should be looked up separately, including food allergies and hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). He recommends a pulse test to find food sensitivities and a six-hour glucose tolerance test (GTT) to confirm or rule out hypoglycemia. His treatment: avoid the offending food allergens plus sugar, fried food, margarine, and alcohol; then supplement chromium and vanadium at 25-200 mcg three times a day, selenium at 200-1,000 mcg a day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU a day, and B-complex at 50 mg three times a day. He adds the memory agents Diapid (vasopressin nasal spray) at 12-16 units a day, Lucidril (centrophenoxine) at 4.4-8.0 gm a day, Dinagen (piracetam) at 1.6-4.8 gm a day taken with choline, and hydergine at 9-20 mg a day. In Wallach's words: "MEMORY LOSS (senile dementia, Korsakoff's syndrome, Alzheimer's) can be much more devastating than a physical disability. There are a variety of causes of memory loss and it is suggested that you look up each one separately including food allergies and hypoglycemia."
claims.verbatim:
MEMORY LOSS (senile dementia, Korsakoff’s syndrome, Alzheimer’s)
can be much more devastating than a physical disability. There are a variety
of causes of memory loss and it is suggested that you look up each one
separately including food allergies and hypoglycemia. You should do the
pulse test to determine allergies or sensitivities to various foods and do a
six-hour GTT to rule in or rule out hypoglycemia.
Treatment of memory loss should include avoidance of offending food
allergens, sugar, fried food, and margarine, avoidance of alcohol, the taking
of chromium and vanadium at 25-200 mcg t.i.d., selenium at 200-1,000
mcg per day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, B-complex at 50 mg t.i.d.,
Diapid (vasopressin) at 12-16 U/day (this is a nasal spray), Lucidril
(centrophenoxine) at 4.4-8.0 gm/day, Dinagen (piracetam) at
1.6-4.8 gm/day (should take choline with this product), and hydergine at 9-
20 mg per day.

claims.subject: memory_loss
claims.question: What causes senile dementia?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties senile dementia to cerebrovascular disease: the brain's main artery hardens and starves the brain of oxygen -- and he blames cholesterol-linked and (in his view) vitamin-D-driven arterial scarring plus magnesium-deficiency 'malignant calcification.'
claims.answer: Wallach describes cerebrovascular disease -- what he equates with senile dementia -- as more common in the United States than anywhere else. It develops when the middle cerebral artery (the brain's main blood supply) 'hardens,' cutting oxygen to the brain and producing loss of memory and the typical 'senile' changes. As with arteriosclerosis elsewhere in the body, that hardening comes from smooth-muscle scarring followed by calcification and fatty cholesterol deposits. He flags elevated blood cholesterol as a risk factor because cholesterol is a building block of vitamin D, which he considers angiotoxic (toxic to blood vessels) -- in his view it scars arterial smooth muscle and drives further calcification. He adds that magnesium deficiency causes 'malignant calcification' of the cerebral arteries, so optimal magnesium (with all nutrients) is protective. In Wallach's words: "CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE (senile dementia) is more common in the United States than anywhere else. The “hardening” of the middle cerebral artery (the main blood supply to the brain) results in poor oxygen supply to the brain, which causes loss of memory and typical “senile” changes."
claims.verbatim:
CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE (senile dementia) is more common in
the United States than anywhere else. The “hardening” of the middle
cerebral artery (the main blood supply to the brain) results in poor oxygen
supply to the brain, which causes loss of memory and typical “senile”
changes. As with arteriosclerosis, the “hardening” of the arteries is caused
by smooth muscle scaring, followed by calcification and fatty cholesterol
deposits. The risk factors include elevated blood cholesterol which is a
building block of vitamin D. Vitamin D is angiotoxic (toxic to blood
vessels) causing scaring of arterial smooth muscle and subsequent
calcification. Magnesium deficiency also results in “malignant
calcification” of cerebral arteries.

claims.subject: alzheimers
claims.question: What is Alzheimer's disease and what causes it, according to Wallach?
claims.answer_short: Wallach defines Alzheimer's as a physician-caused disease of progressive memory loss, first identified in 1979, caused by a cholesterol and fat deficiency -- and in his view not genetic.
claims.answer: Wallach defines Alzheimer's disease as a 'physician-caused' disease -- one he blames on the medical campaign against dietary cholesterol and saturated fat (what he calls 'cholesterol and saturated fat bashing'). He describes it as a progressive loss of memory, with difficulties in arousal and motor function appearing in the disease's later stages. He says it was identified in 1979 and holds that it results from a cholesterol and fat deficiency, not from genetics -- stating flatly that 'Alzheimer's disease is not genetic.' In his framing the brain needs cholesterol to rebuild myelin, so a diet stripped of cholesterol and fat starves it of that raw material.
claims.verbatim:
ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE appears to be a physician-caused disease
(resulting from cholesterol and saturated fat bashing) in which those
afflicted suffer from a progressive loss of memory. Difficulties with arousal
and motor function appear in the later stages of the disease. Identified in
1979, it appears to be due to a cholesterol and fat deficiency. Alzheimer’s
disease is not genetic.

claims.subject: gmo_foods
claims.question: What does Wallach think of GMO foods?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls genetically engineered crops "Frankenstein Food" and argues that manipulating genes without supplying the body's basic essential nutrients is a faulty, greedy premise.
claims.answer: Wallach calls the 1990s corporate drive to patent genetically engineered crops "Frankenstein Food," and lumps it together with patented enzymes, hormones, bacteria, and cloned animals and humans as a "heroic, if not greedy" effort by entrepreneurial scientists to further what he calls the "cult of allopathy." His core objection is that genetically manipulated living cells cannot develop, maintain themselves, reach their genetic potential for longevity, or perform without "the basic stuff of life" — the essential nutrients. He likens the whole enterprise to expecting a Mercedes to be driven full-speed from San Diego to Los Angeles without any oil or coolant: genetic potential without the raw nutritional materials to support it is, in his view, faulty in its premise.
claims.verbatim:
The 90s drive to patent genetically engineered crops (“Frankenstein Food”),
enzymes, hormones, bacteria, cloned animals (a* la Dolly the cloned lamb),
and even humans (identical humans can now be cloned at the embryonic
stage: “The Boys from Brazil” are here!), has been a heroic, if not greedy, effort
by our entrepreneurial scientists to further the cult of allopathy. But
expecting genetically manipulated living cells to develop, maintain
themselves, reach their genetic-potential for longevity, and perform without
the basic stuff of life

claims.subject: ginger
claims.question: Does ginger help with motion sickness?
claims.answer_short: Dr. Wallach lists ginger among the herbs that are useful for preventing motion sickness such as carsickness, seasickness, and air sickness.
claims.answer: Dr. Wallach names ginger among the herbs that are useful for motion sickness — the carsickness, seasickness, and air sickness brought on when repetitive angular and linear movement occur at the same time, producing a "green at the gills" feeling with vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. He lists ginger as a helpful herbal option for preventing motion sickness, alongside the conventional over-the-counter measures of scopolamine transdermal patches (which can be worn behind the ear) and Dramamine.
claims.verbatim:
Prevention of motion sickness includes the use of scopolamine transdermal
patches (can be worn behind the ear) or Dramamine (both medications can
be purchased at the pharmacy without a prescription). Herbs that are useful
for motion sickness include ginger.

claims.subject: emory_university
claims.question: What did Dr. Wallach do at Emory University?
claims.answer_short: Wallach worked as a comparative pathologist at Emory University's Yerkes Regional Primate Research Center in Atlanta, a center administered by Emory and funded by the NIH and NASA, across the street from the CDC.
claims.answer: Dr. Wallach's connection to Emory University came through the Yerkes Regional Primate Research Center in Atlanta, Georgia, where he worked as a comparative (veterinary) pathologist after a four-year stint at the Brookfield Zoo. The primate center was administered by Emory University and funded by a variety of agencies including the NIH and NASA, and it sat directly across the street from the Centers for Disease Control — which Wallach describes as a dream position for a comparative pathologist. His job was to help the investigators understand everything about their primates, their diets, and their deaths, with nutritional deficiencies in monkeys, apes, and humans studied closely.
claims.verbatim:
After a four year stint at the Brookfield Zoo, I wound up at the Yerkes
Regional Primate Research Center in Atlanta, Georgia. The primate center
was administered by Emory University and funded by a variety of agencies
including NIH and NASA. Physically the center was located across the
street from the Centers for Disease Control, a dream position for a
comparative pathologist.

claims.subject: honey
claims.question: Can honey cause hyperactivity in kids?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts a dyslexic child who followed the Feingold Diet except for honey and reacted so severely he was found on top of a 40-foot dome.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that even the Feingold Diet is not a complete shield, because many foods and additives it does not exclude can 'set off some kids like skyrockets.' He recounts one dyslexic child patient who followed every Feingold requirement except eliminating honey; the reaction was so extreme they found the boy on top of a 40-foot dome. The lesson he draws is that a natural sugar like honey can trigger dramatic behavioral reactions in sensitive children, and the whole family must eat the same clean way for it to work.
claims.verbatim:
There are
many foods and food additives not excluded by the Feingold program that
will set off some kids like skyrockets. We had one dyslexic child patient
that did everything the Feingold Diet required except eliminate honey. We
found him on top of a 40-foot dome!

claims.subject: nobel_prize_nomination
claims.question: Was Dr. Wallach nominated for a Nobel Prize?
claims.answer_short: In 1990 the Association of Eclectic Physicians forwarded a nomination to the Nobel Committee in Stockholm, nominating Wallach for the 1991 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his work linking cystic fibrosis to a maternal selenium deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that his Chinese study comparing the microscopic tissue changes of Keshan disease to cystic fibrosis led the Association of Eclectic Physicians to award him the Wooster Beach Gold Medal, and that in 1990 that same body formally forwarded a nomination to the Nobel Committee in Stockholm, Sweden, nominating him for the 1991 Nobel Prize in Medicine for establishing the basic understanding of the relationship between the genesis of cystic fibrosis and a maternal deficiency of the trace mineral selenium.
claims.verbatim:
The results of the Chinese study prompted the awards committee of the
Association of Eclectic Physicians to bestow upon me the Wooster Beach
Gold Medal. In 1990, they formally forwarded a nomination to the Nobel
Committee in Stockholm, Sweden and nominated me for the 1991 Nobel
Prize in Medicine for establishing the basic understanding of the
relationship between the genesis of cystic fibrosis and a maternal deficiency
of the trace mineral selenium.

claims.subject: nobel_prize_nomination
claims.question: How did Wallach react to his Nobel Prize nomination?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls the 1991 Nobel nomination the pinnacle of his scientific career, but says it stirred jealous rage from many conventional and alternative-medicine doctors who resented that a maverick was so honored.
claims.answer: Wallach describes the 1991 Nobel Prize nomination as the pinnacle of his scientific career, saying he was honored and humbled that peers and colleagues held his work in such high regard. He adds that the nomination also provoked a jealous rage in later years from many conventional medical doctors and even fellow doctors of alternative medicine, who questioned how a maverick like Wallach could deserve such a hallowed and coveted honor.
claims.verbatim:
I was honored and humbled by the nomination. The fact that peers and
colleagues held my work in such high regard was the pinnacle of my
scientific career. The nomination for the Nobel Prize in Medicine, however,
only created a jealous rage from many medical doctors and fellow doctors
of alternative medicine in later years. After all, who was Wallach, and how
could such a maverick deserve such a hallowed and coveted nomination?

claims.subject: msg
claims.question: Can MSG feel like a heart attack?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says that in people sensitive to MSG, eating it (the 'Chinese restaurant syndrome') can trigger sudden palpitations alarming enough to be mistaken for a heart attack -- a real food-allergy reaction that passes quickly. He counts MSG among the food allergens sensitive people should pin down (with his pulse test) and then avoid.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that a reaction to MSG can be alarming enough to feel like a heart attack. Many patients struck by sudden irregular heartbeat and palpitations from the 'Chinese restaurant syndrome' (sensitivity to MSG) have called an ambulance believing they were having a heart attack — yet by the time it arrives the symptoms have already passed. The giveaway, he says, is a history of eating out, especially at a Chinese restaurant.
claims.verbatim:
The classic for this syndrome is the “Chinese
restaurant syndrome” which is caused by sensitivity to MSG. Many a
patient with sudden irregular heartbeat and palpitations has called the
ambulance thinking they had a “heart attack.” By the time the ambulance
arrived, they no longer had symptoms. A history of eating out, especially at
a Chinese restaurant, is the give away.

claims.subject: twenty_thousand_autopsies
claims.question: What did Wallach's autopsies conclude?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's autopsies led him to conclude that every animal and every human dying of natural causes dies of a nutritional deficiency disease.
claims.answer: After more than twelve years of autopsies on 17,500 animals across over 454 species and 3,000 humans for comparison, Wallach reached the central conclusion of his life's work: every animal and every human who dies of natural causes dies of a nutritional deficiency disease. He presents the autopsy findings as so consistent and profound that this pattern 'stood out like a beacon.'
claims.verbatim:
After spending 12 plus years doing autopsies on 17,500 animals of over 454
species and 3,000 humans for a comparison, it was apparent that every
animal and every human who dies of natural causes dies of a nutritional
deficiency disease.

claims.subject: twenty_thousand_autopsies
claims.question: Why don't doctors find nutritional deficiencies at autopsy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says only about 5% of hospital deaths are autopsied (to limit malpractice data), and pathologists never record the nutritional deficiency behind the disease.
claims.answer: Wallach states that autopsies are performed on only about five percent of people who die in hospitals, kept low primarily to avoid collecting data that would support malpractice suits. When a human autopsy is done, the pathologist limits the report to organ size and color, gross, microscopic and laboratory findings, and a 'cause of death,' and never lists the underlying nutritional deficiency that causes aneurysms, diabetes, blood clots, heart attacks, cancer, Alzheimer's, or even osteoporosis. Because of this frequent omission, he argues, clinical nutrition in human medicine never progresses.
claims.verbatim:
However, autopsies are only done on five percent
of people who die in hospitals primarily to avoid the collection of data that
would support malpractice suits.
The human pathologist looks for pneumonia, trauma, ruptured aneurysms,
blood clots, perforating gastric ulcers, heart attacks, cancer, and might do a
chemical or drug screen if the clinical case history suggests a need. The
human pathologist limits the data on the autopsy report to the size and color
of organs, gross findings, microscopic and laboratory findings and a “cause
of death.” The human pathologist never lists the nutritional deficiency which
causes aneurysms, diabetes, blood clots, heart attacks, cancer, Alzheimers,
even osteoporosis.

claims.subject: ma_lan
claims.question: How did Dr. Wallach meet his wife?
claims.answer_short: Wallach met Ma Lan at the Jones Medical Library, courted her through fishing and sailing, and married her on Valentine's Day, 1987.
claims.answer: Wallach met Ma Lan at the Jones Medical Library, where they sat across the reading table from each other; he describes her as a very tall, beautiful, happy, and intelligent Chinese medical doctor. They shared interests in helping people with their health, the outdoors, sailing, and fishing, and their dates consisted of fishing and eating their catch. After six months of courting they were married on Valentine's Day, 1987.
claims.verbatim:
It was during one visit to the Jones Medical Library that I came
across that very tall, very beautiful, very happy and very intelligent Chinese
lady named Ma Lan. Let me tell you more about our courtship now.
Ma Lan and I sat across the library reading table from each other.

claims.subject: ma_lan
claims.question: How did Ma Lan survive the Chinese Cultural Revolution?
claims.answer_short: Arrested as an academic and sent to forced labor in the rice fields, Ma Lan kept herself alive by adding river grass and mud to her meals.
claims.answer: While in medical school during the Chinese Cultural Revolution, Ma Lan was arrested along with all academics and sent to a forced-labor program in the countryside rice fields. For three years the captives were restricted to a simple diet of corn meal, pork fat, and salt; many millions died, but Ma Lan kept herself alive by adding river grass and mud to her meals.
claims.verbatim:
Ma Lan was in medical school during the Chinese Cultural Revolution. She
was arrested along with all academics and put in the countryside in a forced
labor program in the rice fields. She, along with the other captives, was
restricted to a simple diet of corn meal, pork fat, and salt for three years.
Many millions died, but Ma Lan kept herself alive by adding river grass and
mud to her meals.

claims.subject: ma_lan
claims.question: Was Ma Lan a surgeon?
claims.answer_short: As a microsurgeon Ma Lan achieved a 95 percent success rate repairing arteries and veins as thin as a human hair, versus the typical 65 percent.
claims.answer: Ma Lan was an expert microsurgeon, a skill refined over a seven-year tenure as a general surgeon at the Canton Air Force Hospital and further honed through numerous military wound repairs during the Vietnam War. Whereas most microsurgeons reported a respectable 65 percent success rate joining together the major arteries and veins, Ma Lan boasted a 95 percent success rate because of her ability to repair small arteries and veins the diameter of a human hair, in addition to repairing the larger vessels.
claims.verbatim:
While most
micro-surgeons reported a respectable success rate of 65 percent by joining
together the major arteries and veins, Ma Lan boasted a 95 percent success
rate because of her ability to repair small arteries and veins the diameter of
human hair, in addition to repairing the larger vessels.

claims.subject: ma_lan
claims.question: Why did Ma Lan eat fish bones?
claims.answer_short: Ma Lan ate fish bones and simmered bones in vinegar to leach out calcium, magnesium, manganese, boron, copper, and sulfur, which is how the dairy-free Chinese get their calcium.
claims.answer: On their fishing dates Ma Lan cooked the catch in traditional Chinese fashion and ate the fish bones herself, giving Wallach the steamed or baked fillets. She simmered the bones of fish, chicken, pork, and beef in a vinegar solution, which leaches calcium, magnesium, manganese, boron, copper, sulfur, and other minerals out of the bones into the soup. Wallach notes that the Chinese as a culture do not eat dairy yet still require calcium like everyone else, and get their calcium from animal bones.
claims.verbatim:
Fishing was our recreation. Ma Lan would cook our catch in traditional
Chinese fashion in the galley of The Elixir. The fish and shrimp were fresh,
the taste was great, and Ma Lan ate the fish bones! Ma Lan gave me the
steamed or baked fish fillets. I was very surprised when she simmered the
bones of fish, chicken, pork, and beef in a vinegar solution. The vinegar
would leach the calcium, magnesium, manganese, boron, copper, sulfur,
and other minerals out of the bones into the soup.

claims.subject: colonics
claims.question: Why do colonics during a candida or parasite cleanse?
claims.answer_short: Wallach uses colonics (with liver flushes), especially in the first two weeks of therapy, to detoxify the toxins produced as organisms die off during treatment.
claims.answer: Wallach uses colonics as a detoxification tool during treatment for chronic infections. In his Chronic Fatigue Syndrome protocol he directs the patient to detoxify with liver flushes and colonics, especially during the first two weeks of therapy, in order to cope with the toxins generated as the offending organisms die off.
claims.verbatim:
Detoxify with liver flushes and colonics (especially for the first
two weeks of therapy) to cope with toxins generated by organism die-off.

claims.subject: colonics
claims.question: Can you use an enema to restore acidophilus or good bacteria?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says reimplanting Lactobacillus acidophilus is useful in any Candida program, using a retention enema of 4 ounces of warm water containing 10 billion organisms (twenty 500,000-organism capsules).
claims.answer: In treating Candida (candidiasis), Wallach says replanting Lactobacillus acidophilus - a friendly resident of the gut and a primary competitor to Candida albicans - is a useful part of any treatment program. He recommends doing this with a retention enema of 4 ounces of warm water containing 10 billion organisms, prepared by emptying twenty 500,000-organism capsules into the water.
claims.verbatim:
Replantation of Lactobacillus acidophilus, a friendly resident of the gut and
a primary competitor to Candida albicans, is a useful part of any treatment
program. Use the retention enemas with 4 oz. of warm water containing 10
billion organisms (empty twenty 500,000 organism capsules into the water).

claims.subject: shark_cartilage
claims.question: How does shark cartilage fight cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says shark cartilage contains angiostatin and endostatin, which stop the new capillaries a metastatic tumor needs to feed itself — an effect he says Harvard and Yale proved over 25 years of research.
claims.answer: Wallach says shark cartilage (and shark liver oil) contain angiostatin and endostatin, substances that stop the formation of the new capillaries — tiny blood vessels — that a spreading, metastatic cancer must build to feed itself. He states that Harvard Medical School and Yale Medical School have done 25 years of solid research on shark cartilage's effect on the rate of cancer metastasis, and proved that angiostatin and endostatin do in fact retard the growth of the capillaries needed to support cancer growth. Cut off the tumor's new blood supply, the reasoning goes, and its growth is starved.
claims.verbatim:
Harvard Medical School and Yale Medical School
have done 25 years of solid research on the effects of shark cartilage on the
rate of cancer metastasis and have proved that angiostatin and endostatin do
in fact retard the growth of capillaries that are necessary for the support of
cancer growth.

claims.subject: shark_cartilage
claims.question: How much shark cartilage does Wallach recommend for cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says to start shark cartilage at 70 grams per day if you have cancer; he claims it shrinks metastases, reduces pain, and can make a growth smaller than a grape disappear.
claims.answer: For someone who already has cancer, Wallach's protocol is to start shark cartilage at 70 grams per day. He states that if you already have metastasis — cancer that has spread — the shark cartilage will shrink the metastasis and reduce pain, and that a metastatic growth smaller than a grape may disappear altogether. He argues there is no need to wait for a genetically engineered, prescription version of angiostatin or endostatin, because the natural shark cartilage delivering those substances is available now.
claims.verbatim:
If you already have metastasis, the shark cartilage will shrink
the metastasis and reduce pain. If the metastatic growth is smaller than a
grape it may
disappear altogether. You don’t need to wait for the genetically engineered
angiostatin or endostatin to appear on your doctor’s prescription pad; if you
have cancer start using shark cartilage at 70 grams per day.

claims.subject: shark_cartilage
claims.question: Why does mainstream medicine call shark cartilage quackery?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says orthodox medicine dismissed shark cartilage — used by the Chinese for 5,000 years against cancer — as quackery, but now that angiostatin and endostatin can be patented, the same idea is rebranded as profitable 'science.'
claims.answer: Wallach uses shark cartilage as his prime example of what he sees as mainstream medicine's hypocrisy. He notes that angiostatin and endostatin occur naturally in shark cartilage, which the Chinese have used in cancer therapy for five thousand years, and that the medical profession dismissed shark cartilage cancer therapy as quackery. His point: now that the genetic-engineering industry has found a patentable way to produce angiostatin and endostatin, the very same idea is promoted as legitimate science — which he mocks as science with a capital Stock Option. The reversal, he argues, is driven by patent profit, not by new evidence.
claims.verbatim:
A great example is the hype over “angiostatin” and “endostatin” as a cancer
“cure.” These substances are found naturally in shark cartilage, which has
been used in cancer therapy by the Chinese for five-thousand years. The
medical profession discounted the concept of using shark cartilage as a
cancer therapy with the usual exclamation: it’s quackery!
Now that the genetic engineering industry has found a way to produce
angiostatin and endostatin in a patentable way, the hype is on. It is no
longer “quackery”—it is “science” with a capital “Stock Option!”

claims.subject: ginkgo
claims.question: Is ginkgo good for angina?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says ginkgo and English hawthorn are specific for relieving angina by increasing blood flow through the coronary arteries.
claims.answer: Wallach names ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba), alongside hawthorn (Crataegus oxyacantha), as specific for relieving angina - the sharp, debilitating chest pain of arterial heart disease that reduces the heart's oxygen supply - by increasing blood flow through the coronary arteries. He presents ginkgo as part of a broader nutritional and herbal approach (chelation, calcium, magnesium, essential fatty acids, lifestyle change, and nitroglycerin for symptoms) that he says can reverse cardiovascular disease, rather than relying on coronary bypass surgery.
claims.verbatim:
English hawthorn (Crataegus oxyacantha)
and ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba) are specific for relieving angina by increasing the
blood flow through coronary arteries.

claims.subject: ginkgo
claims.question: Does ginkgo help memory?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists ginkgo among the useful herbs in his treatment of dementia and memory loss.
