claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: What are the signs of vitamin B6 deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's signs of pyridoxine (B6) deficiency include depression and mental confusion, inflammation and lesions of the oral mucous membranes, nausea, vomiting, PMS, seborrheic dermatitis, carpal tunnel syndrome, TMJ problems, peripheral neuritis, ataxia, head tics (Tourette's syndrome), and seizures.
claims.answer: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is converted to pyridoxal phosphate, the coenzyme for transamination and other reactions in amino-acid, lipid, and nucleic-acid metabolism, and for glycogen phosphorylase. Wallach lists the health problems of pyridoxine deficiency: depression and mental confusion, inflammation and lesions of the oral mucous membranes, nausea, vomiting, premenstrual syndrome, seborrheic dermatitis, itchy scaly skin, carpal tunnel syndrome, temporomandibular joint problems, peripheral neuritis, ataxia (instability), hyperirritability, head tic (Tourette's syndrome), seizures, and convulsions.
claims.verbatim:
Pyridoxine (B,) deficiency health problems include:

Depression, mental confusion

Inflammation of the oral mucus membranes
Nausea

Vomiting

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: What are the symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency?
claims.answer_short: B12 deficiency causes pernicious anemia, dementia and neuropsychiatric changes, nerve demyelination and neuropathy, a sore tongue, general weakness, and liver disease.
claims.answer: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) works with folate to synthesize DNA and RNA, supports bone marrow and the production of myelin (the nerve-fiber insulation), and is required to release folate from its bound form -- so a B12 deficiency causes a folic-acid deficiency even when folate intake is optimal. Wallach notes the deficiency can be dietary or secondary to hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid), salt deficiency, or gluten intolerance, and lists its health problems: pernicious anemia (macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia), dementia, neuropsychiatric behavior, demyelination of the brain, spinal cord, optic nerve, and peripheral nerves, neuropathy, a sore tongue, general weakness, and liver disease.
claims.verbatim:
Pernicious anemia (macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia)

Dementia

Neuropsychiatric behavior

Brain, spinal cord, optic nerve and peripheral nerve demyelination
Neuropathy

Sore tongue

General weakness

Liver disease

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: What does folic acid do and what happens if you're deficient?
claims.answer_short: Folate is needed to make DNA, RNA, and red blood cells and works with vitamin B12; deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, birth defects like spina bifida, failure to thrive, diarrhea, bleeding gums, weight loss, and irritability.
claims.answer: Folic acid (folate, vitamin B9) is required for the synthesis of DNA, RNA, and red blood cells and works interdependently with vitamin B12; a deficiency of either produces a megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia. Wallach notes the deficiency arises from a diet lacking green leafy vegetables and from malabsorption (gluten intolerance, celiac disease, leaky gut syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome), and lists its health problems: impaired cell division, birth defects (neural tube defects such as spina bifida), failure to thrive, anemia, diarrhea, bleeding gums, weight loss, and irritability.
claims.verbatim:
Birth defects (Neural tube defects (hydroencephaloceole, spina bifida, etc.)
Failure to thrive

Anemia

Diarrhea

Bleeding gums

Weight loss

claims.subject: biotin
claims.question: What are the signs of biotin deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists biotin (B7) deficiency signs including eczema and dermatitis, baldness, muscle pain, fatigue, fatty liver, depression, insomnia, appetite loss, gray or white hair, and hallucinations.
claims.answer: Biotin (vitamin B7, or vitamin H) is required for glucose metabolism and the production of fatty acids; its conversion to the active coenzyme depends on magnesium and adenosine triphosphate. Wallach lists the health problems of biotin deficiency: eczema and dermatitis, alopecia (baldness), myalgia (muscle pain), fatigue, fatty liver, inborn errors of metabolism, depression, hyperesthesia and paresthesia, blepharitis, gray, silver, or white hair, loss of appetite (anorexia), insomnia, weight loss, and hallucinations.
claims.verbatim:
Biotin-deficiency health problems can result in:

Eczema, dermatitis
Alopecia (baldness)

Myalgia (muscle pain)
Fatigue

Fatty liver

Inborn errors of metabolism
Depression

Hyperesthesia, paraesthesia

Blephritis
Gray, silver or white hair
Anorexia

Insomnia.

Weight loss

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: What are the signs of vitamin C deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin C deficiency can cause bleeding gums, loose teeth, bruising, dry rough skin, poor growth, slow wound healing, elevated cancer risk and scurvy.
claims.answer: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a required cofactor for producing collagen, connective tissue, cartilage, bones, teeth, blood-vessel walls, and capillaries, and it increases the absorption of inorganic iron and supports white blood cells, immune responses, and wound healing. Wallach lists the health problems of vitamin C deficiency: bleeding gums, loose teeth, bruising, dry rough skin, loss of appetite (anorexia), poor growth, elevated cancer risk, slow wound healing, scurvy, skin hemorrhages, swollen joints (particularly the wrists and ankles), and rib and cartilage fractures.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin C deficiency can result in:

Bleeding gums
Loose teeth

Bruising

Dry rough skin

Anorexia

Poor growth

Elevated cancer risk

Slow wound healing

Scurvy

Skin hemorrhages

Swollen joints (particularly wrist and ankles)
Rib and cartilage fractures

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: What are the signs of choline deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Choline deficiency can cause fatty liver, liver cirrhosis, kidney hemorrhage, Alzheimer's disease, dementia, tardive dyskinesia and Huntington's disease, with no known overdose.
claims.answer: Choline is a major structural component of phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) -- essential to all cell membranes, plasma lipoproteins, and lung surfactant -- and, in the central nervous system, of sphingomyelin and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Wallach lists the health problems of choline deficiency: fatty liver, liver cirrhosis, kidney hemorrhage, Alzheimer's disease and dementia, tardive dyskinesia, and Huntington's disease.
claims.verbatim:
Fatty liver
Liver cirrhosis,

Kidney hemorrhage
Alzheimer's disease, dementia
Tardive dyskinesia
Huntington's disease

claims.subject: inositol
claims.question: What diseases does inositol deficiency cause?
claims.answer_short: Inositol deficiency can result in fat metabolism problems, fatty liver, diabetes, diabetic neuropathy, slow nerve conduction, and renal failure.
claims.answer: Inositol (myo-inositol) is a major constituent of the phospholipids in cell biomembranes, and its triphosphate form is a second messenger for receptor-mediated hormonal stimuli that mobilizes intracellular calcium; it also appears to have a lipotrophic (fat-handling) function. Wallach lists the health problems of inositol deficiency: fat-metabolism problems, intestinal lipodystrophy, fatty liver, diabetes mellitus, diabetic neuropathy, slow nerve-conduction velocity, renal failure, and galactosemia.
claims.verbatim:
Fat metabolism problems
Intestinal lipodystrophy

Fatty liver

Diabetes mellitus

Diabetic neuropathy

Slow nerve conduction velocity
Renal failure

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: What are the signs of a bioflavonoid deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists capillary hemorrhage, easy bruising, nosebleeds, hemorrhoids, venous insufficiency, leg ulcers, weakened immunity, higher cancer risk, and a shortened lifespan.
claims.answer: Flavonoids (bioflavonoids), once called vitamin P for their role in small-blood-vessel permeability, are antioxidant, anti-inflammatory plant compounds that support vascular and capillary function and lower cardiovascular-disease risk. Wallach lists the health problems of bioflavonoid deficiency: capillary hemorrhage, reduced immune capacity, widespread free-radical injury and inflammation, hemorrhoids, venous insufficiency, leg ulcers, bruising, nosebleeds, increased cancer risk, shortened lifespan, and reduced telomere length and viability.
claims.verbatim:
Bioflavonoids deficiency can result in:

Capillary hemorrhage
Reduced immune capacity

Widespread free radical injury and inflammation
Hemorrhoids

Venous insufficiency

Leg ulcers

Bruising

Nosebleeds

Increased cancer risk

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: Is arginine used for erectile dysfunction?
claims.answer_short: Yes—arginine is commonly used together with proanthocyanidins or yohimbine to relieve erectile dysfunction.
claims.answer: Arginine is required for complete cell division, wound healing, the excretion of ammonia, immune support, and the synthesis of nitric oxide -- and supplementing it makes more adenosine triphosphate (cellular fuel) available. Wallach notes oral arginine reduces healing time after trauma (especially bone trauma), lowers blood pressure, and increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels; an 8% arginine toothpaste relieves dental pain by depositing a calcium-phosphate dentin-like material, and arginine is commonly used (with proanthocyanidines or yohimbine) for erectile dysfunction.
claims.verbatim:
Arginine is commonly employed concurrently with proanthocyanidines or
yohimbine for the relief of erectile dysfunction

claims.subject: histidine
claims.question: What is histidine?
claims.answer_short: Histidine is an amino acid whose imidazole side chain works in enzyme active sites and binds metals; Wallach also notes it's required for hemoglobin, aiding oxygen binding and resisting carbon monoxide.
claims.answer: Histidine, an amino acid with an imidazole side chain, is a coordinating ligand of metalloproteins and part of the catalytic sites of certain enzymes (acting in catalytic triads and as a proton shuttle). Wallach notes histidine is required for hemoglobin in helices E and F, where it stabilizes oxyhemoglobin and destabilizes carbon-monoxide hemoglobin -- so that carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far less tightly (less than 200 times stronger) than it binds free heme (20,000 times stronger).
claims.verbatim:
Histidine is also required
for haemoglobin in helices E and F. Histidine supports the stabilization of
oxyhaemoglobin and the destabilization of CO (carbon monoxide) haemoglobin.

claims.subject: isoleucine
claims.question: How does the body use isoleucine for energy—is it glucogenic or ketogenic?
claims.answer_short: Isoleucine is both glucogenic and ketogenic: part of it can be turned into glucose, while another part is routed into ketone bodies or fatty acids for fuel.
claims.answer: Isoleucine is a hydrophobic amino acid that is both glucogenic and ketogenic. Wallach explains that after transamination its carbon skeleton can be converted to succinyl coenzyme A and fed into the citric-acid (Krebs) cycle for oxidation or routed to oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis (glucose production), while its acetyl coenzyme A portion -- which mammals cannot convert back to carbohydrate -- is used to make ketone bodies or fatty acids.
claims.verbatim:
Isoleucine is both a glucogenic and ketogenic amino acid. Following
transamination with alphaketogluterate, the carbon skeleton can be converted
into Succinyl CoA, and then fed into the TCA cycle for oxidation, or converted
into oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis (ie, glucogenic).

claims.subject: leucine
claims.question: What is leucine?
claims.answer_short: Leucine is a branched-chain essential amino acid Wallach says is solely responsible for building muscle protein—a catalyst for muscle growth that also switches on the mTOR kinase controlling cell growth.
claims.answer: Leucine, a branched-chain amino acid, has major roles in the liver, adipose tissue, and muscle; in muscle and adipose tissue it is used to synthesize sterols, and it is solely responsible for the synthesis of muscle proteins -- a catalyst for muscle growth that also activates the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase regulating cell growth. Wallach notes that leucine toxicity, as in decompensated Maple Syrup Urine Disease, produces delirium and neurologic compromise and can be life-threatening, and that excessive leucine intake can produce a clinical pellagra (the 'four Ds': diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death).
claims.verbatim:
Leucine is solely responsible

for the synthesis of muscle proteins.

claims.subject: lysine
claims.question: How does lysine help build collagen, elastin, and healthy veins?
claims.answer_short: Through its derivative allysine, lysine lets the enzyme lysyl oxidase form the crosslinks that stabilize collagen and elastin, which Wallach says helps prevent and repair spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids, and aneurysms.
claims.answer: Lysine is required, via its derivative allysine, for the production of elastin and collagen: the enzyme lysyl oxidase (which needs a copper cofactor) acts on lysine to form the crosslinks that stabilize collagen and elastin. Wallach states that lysine consumption contributes to the prevention and repair of spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids, and aneurysms.
claims.verbatim:
Lysine
consumption contributes to the prevention and repair of spider veins, varicose
veins, hemorrhoids, and aneurysms.

claims.subject: methionine
claims.question: What is methionine?
claims.answer_short: Methionine is a sulfur-containing essential amino acid; its derivative SAM is the body's main methyl donor, and it's the raw material the body uses to build cysteine, carnitine, taurine, lecithin and phosphatidylcholine.
claims.answer: Methionine is a sulfur-containing amino acid whose derivative S-adenosyl methionine serves as a methyl donor, and it is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of cysteine, carnitine, taurine, lecithin, and phosphatidylcholine. Wallach reports that laboratory rats fed a methionine-free diet developed steatohepatitis (fatty liver disease), anemia, and lost two-thirds of their body weight over five weeks -- all of which were resolved by methionine supplementation.
claims.verbatim:
Laboratory rats fed a methionine-free diet developed steatohepatitis (fatty
liver disease), anemia, and lost two thirds of their body weight over five weeks.
Supplementation with methionine resolved all of the disease problems of the
study group.

claims.subject: phenylalanine
claims.question: What does phenylalanine turn into in the body?
claims.answer_short: Phenylalanine is the precursor to tyrosine and, through it, the signaling molecules dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine, plus the pigment melanin (a step that needs copper).
claims.answer: Phenylalanine is a precursor for tyrosine and, through it, the signaling molecules dopamine, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and epinephrine (adrenaline), plus the skin and hair pigment melanin (which requires a copper cofactor). Wallach explains that the inborn error phenylketonuria -- the inability to metabolize phenylalanine, which he says is falsely believed to be genetically transmitted -- is managed by avoiding phenylalanine (including the sweetener aspartame), and that the DL-phenylalanine form is marketed as a sleep aid, antidepressant, and analgesic (pain reliever).
claims.verbatim:
Phenylalanine is a precursor for tyrosine, the monoamine signaling molecules
dopamine, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and epinephrine (adrenaline), and the
skin and hair pigment melanin (this procedure requires the cofactor copper).

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: What does taurine deficiency cause?
claims.answer_short: A taurine deficiency can produce cataracts and retinal damage; taurine is also needed to maintain skeletal muscle and healthy blood pressure.
claims.answer: Taurine -- a sulfonic-acid amino acid that conjugates bile acids, acts as an antioxidant, and modulates calcium signaling -- is essential to the cardiovascular system, skeletal muscle, the retina, and the central nervous system. Wallach states that taurine is required for the maintenance of skeletal muscle and healthy blood pressure, and that taurine deficiency can produce cataracts and retinal damage; he also notes that doses above 2 grams per day have been shown to contribute to psoriasis.
claims.verbatim:
Taurine is required for the maintenance of skeletal muscle and the
maintenance of healthy blood pressure. Taurine deficiency can produce cataracts
and retinal damage.

claims.subject: threonine
claims.question: What is threonine?
claims.answer_short: Threonine is a polar, protein-building essential amino acid that, with serine, is one of only two amino acids carrying an alcohol group—making it a site for chemical modification and energy production.
claims.answer: Threonine is a polar amino acid that, together with serine, is one of only two protein-building amino acids bearing an alcohol group, making it a site for post-translational modification (glycosylation and phosphorylation by threonine kinase). Wallach notes threonine is converted to pyruvate via threonine dehydrogenase, and through intermediates can yield acetyl coenzyme A and glycine or alpha-ketobutyrate feeding into the succinyl-coenzyme A pathway.
claims.verbatim:
Threonine (Thr) is an alpha amino acid that is classified as polar; its codons
are ACU, ACA, ACC, and ACG. Together with serine, threonine is one of only
two proteinogenic amino acids that bear an alcohol group.

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: Can gluten intolerance cause depression?
claims.answer_short: Yes; gluten intolerance, lactose intolerance, and fructose malabsorption all reduce tryptophan absorption from the gut, lowering blood tryptophan and producing clinical depression.
claims.answer: Tryptophan is the biochemical precursor of the neurotransmitter serotonin (which can be converted to the sleep hormone melatonin), and niacin is also synthesized from it. Wallach explains that fructose malabsorption, lactose intolerance, and gluten intolerance reduce tryptophan absorption from the intestine, lowering blood tryptophan and producing clinical depression, and that tryptophan supplements are sold as sleep aids while its metabolite 5-hydroxytryptophan has been suggested for seizure disorders and depression.
claims.verbatim:
The disorders, fructose malabsorption, lactose intolerance, and gluten
intolerance cause a reduced state of tryptophan absorption from the intestine,
therefore causing reduced levels of tryptophan in the blood and clinical
depression. Tryptophan supplements are sold as sleep aids.

claims.subject: tyrosine
claims.question: What is tyrosine good for?
claims.answer_short: Tyrosine is the precursor for dopamine and norepinephrine, and Wallach reports studies show it helps with stress, fatigue, colds, grief, long work hours, and sleep deprivation, easing stress hormones and boosting mental and physical performance.
claims.answer: Tyrosine is a precursor for the neurotransmitters dopamine and norepinephrine and serves in cellular signal transduction (as a receiver of phosphate groups via protein kinases). Wallach reports that several studies show tyrosine to be of benefit for colds, stress, fatigue, the loss of a loved one or divorce, prolonged work hours, and sleep deprivation -- reducing stress-hormone levels and stress-related weight loss and improving cognitive and physical performance -- though because tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme its effects are less than those of L-Dopa.
claims.verbatim:
Tyrosine is a precursor for the synthesis of neurotransmitters, and particularly
for dopamine and norepinephrine. Several studies have shown tyrosine to be of
benefit for colds, stress, fatigue, loss of a loved one or divorce, prolonged work
hours, and sleep deprivation, with reductions of stress hormone levels

claims.subject: valine
claims.question: What is valine?
claims.answer_short: Valine is a branched-chain amino acid Wallach counts among the essentials—it supports cognitive function, builds and maintains muscle, and aids exercise recovery and endurance.
claims.answer: Valine is a branched-chain amino acid (named for the plant valerian) that functions in the nervous system to support cognitive function, and in the function and maintenance of muscle, muscle-tissue recovery and metabolism after exercise, and increased exercise endurance. Wallach notes that in sickle-cell disease valine substitutes for the water-loving amino acid glutamic acid in hemoglobin; because valine is water-repelling (hydrophobic), the hemoglobin is then more likely to aggregate.
claims.verbatim:
It functions in the nervous
system to support cognitive function, function and maintenance of muscle, and
the muscle tissue recovery and metabolism post-exercise and for increasing
exercise endurance.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: What diseases does essential fatty acid deficiency cause?
claims.answer_short: Wallach states essential fatty acid deficiency produces thrombosis (including stroke), skin diseases like eczema and psoriasis, respiratory diseases like asthma, and depression, with low omega-3 linked to depression and suicide.
claims.answer: The two classically essential fatty acids -- alpha-linolenic acid (an omega-3) and linoleic acid (an omega-6) -- cannot be synthesized and must be consumed daily, in proper omega-3 to omega-6 ratio, to make eicosanoids, endocannabinoids, and other signaling molecules and to regulate inflammation. Wallach states that essential fatty acid deficiency produces thrombosis (cerebral stroke, coronary thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and deep vein thrombosis), skin disease (dry/cracked skin, dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, rosacea, acne), respiratory disease (asthma, chronic bronchitis, unremitting cough), and depression -- and that low omega-3 (docosahexaenoic acid) is associated with increased depression and suicide.
claims.verbatim:
Essential fatty acid deficiencies will produce thrombosis (i.e., cerebral stroke,
coronary thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and deep vein thrombosis), skin
disease (including dry/cracked skin, dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, rosacea acnea,
etc,), respiratory disease (including asthma, chonic bronchitis, unremitting cough,
etc,), and depression.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Why are the minerals in ordinary supplement tablets so poorly absorbed?
claims.answer_short: Because of their form. Wallach says metallic minerals (the gluconate/carbonate/oxide forms in most tablets, plus eggshell, oyster shell, dolomite and antacids) are only 8–12% absorbable — and just 3–5% after age 35–40. Chelated minerals absorb better, but plant-derived colloidal minerals are the most usable, which is why he calls them the most critical of the 90 essential nutrients.
claims.answer: Wallach describes three basic forms of minerals and their very different bioavailability. Metallic minerals (eggshell, oyster shell, calcium carbonate, dolomite, antacids such as Rolaids and Tums, and the gluconate/carbonate/oxide forms in most tablets) are, despite claims to the contrary, only 8 to 12 percent absorbable by humans -- dropping to roughly 3 to 5 percent after age 35 to 40. Chelated minerals (created by the livestock industry in the 1960s, the mineral wrapped in an amino acid such as EDTA) absorb better, and colloidal minerals -- ultra-fine plant-derived particles suspended in liquid -- are the most usable, which is why he calls plant-derived colloidal minerals the most critical of the 90 essential nutrients.
claims.verbatim:
Metallic minerals, despite wild claims to the contrary, are only eight percent
to twelve percent biologically available to all vertebrates, including humans; after
attaining the age of 35 to 40 years the absorptive availability to humans is


reduced to somewhere around three to five percent.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What does calcium deficiency cause?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says calcium — 99% held in the bones and teeth — is tied to no fewer than 147 deficiency diseases, and that high dietary calcium actually lowers the risk of kidney stones rather than causing them.
claims.answer: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body, with about 99% in the bones and teeth (as hydroxyapatite) and the rest used as a cofactor for blood clotting, muscle contraction, and the heart's electrical conduction. Wallach states that, contrary to the medical belief that high calcium causes kidney stones, a high dietary calcium intake actually reduces the risk of nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcemia, and kidney stones, and that no fewer than 147 deficiency diseases are attributed to calcium deficiency or imbalance. His Common Calcium-Deficiency Diseases include: osteoporosis (with kyphosis, scoliosis, Dowager's hump, lordosis, spontaneous fractures), receding gums, osteomalacia, myelosclerosis, arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, bone spurs, kidney stones, nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, hypertension, insomnia, calcium deposits (vascular, restless leg, atrial fibrillation), cramps and twitches (Tourette's syndrome), premenstrual syndrome, low-back pain (sciatica), neuropathy (Bell's palsy, trigeminal neuralgia), tetany with convulsions, and panic attacks.
claims.verbatim:
NSH (nutritional hyperparathyroidism) : Same as osteoporosis

Hypertension (high blood pressure) : Same as osteoporosis

Insomnia (sleep apnea, snoring, etc.) : Same as osteoporosis

Calcium deposits (vascular, tendons, ligaments, restless leg, atrial-fibrillation, etc.) : Same as osteoporosis

Cramps & twitches (Tourette's syndrome, foot, calf, hamstring, eyelids, etc.) : Same as osteoporosis

PMS (emotional & physical symptoms) : Same as osteoporosis

Low back (sciatica, spasm, disc, etc.) : Same as osteoporosis

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: What diseases are caused by chromium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties chromium to blood-sugar control through glucose tolerance factor and lists its deficiency diseases — from low blood sugar, pre-diabetes and type-2 diabetes to hyperactivity, ADD/ADHD, depression, bipolar disorder, high triglycerides and cholesterol, coronary artery disease and infertility.
claims.answer: Chromium is a key component of the glucose tolerance factor (GTF) and is essential to insulin function and blood-sugar control; Wallach notes a USDA spokesperson stated 90% of Americans are deficient, that dietary sugar loads raise urinary chromium loss by 300% for 12 hours, and that chromium-supplemented animals lived 33% longer. Chromium-deficiency diseases (aggravated by concurrent vanadium deficiency and dietary sugar) include: low blood sugar, reactive hypoglycemia, bed-wetting, pre-diabetes, type-2 diabetes, hyperinsulinemia, hyperactivity, learning disability, attention deficit disorder (ADD/ADHD), hyperirritability, depression, manic depression (bipolar disorder), 'Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde' rages, impaired growth, peripheral neuropathy, negative nitrogen balance (protein/muscle loss), elevated triglycerides (over 200) and cholesterol (over 270), coronary artery disease, aortic cholesterol plaque, infertility (anovulation and low sperm count), and a shortened lifespan.
claims.verbatim:
Low blood sugar
Reactive hypoglycemia

Bed wetting
Pre-diabetes

Diabetes (Type 2)

Hyperinsulinemia

Hyperactivity

Learning disability

ADD/ADHD

Hyperirratability

Depression

Manic depression

“Bi-polar” disease

Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde rages ("Bad Seeds")
Impaired growth

Peripheral neuropathy

Negative nitrogen balance (protein/muscle loss)
Elevated blood triglycerides (> 200)

Elevated blood cholesterol (> 270)

Coronary artery disease

Aortic cholesterol plaque

Infertility (anovulation and low sperm count)

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: Can copper deficiency cause violent or aggressive behavior?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists violent behavior, blind rage, explosive behavior, and criminal behavior among the symptoms of copper deficiency.
claims.answer: Copper is a universally important cofactor for hundreds of metalloenzymes -- required for the pigment melanin (hair and skin color), for lysyl oxidase that gives blood vessels, skin, and discs their tensile strength, and for oxygen handling in respiration; Wallach calls copper deficiency widespread and notes it underlies several diseases the medical community wrongly blames on prions or infection. Copper-deficiency diseases include: white/gray/silver and dry brittle hair, ptosis (sagging eyelids, skin, breasts, belly), hernias, varicose and spider veins (hemorrhoids), aneurysms, Kawasaki disease, Marfan's syndrome, anemia, hypo- and hyperthyroid, arthritis, ruptured and bulging discs, liver cirrhosis, violent/blind-rage/explosive/criminal behavior, learning disabilities, cerebral palsy with cerebellar hypoplasia (congenital ataxia), high cholesterol, iron-storage disease, reduced glucose tolerance (hypoglycemia, reactive hypoglycemia), and neutropenia.
claims.verbatim:
Ptosis (ie., sagging tissue—eye lids, skin, breasts, belly, etc.)
Hernias (congenital and acquired)

Varicose veins/ spider veins (hemorrhoids)

Aneurysms (aortic, cerebral, coronary, gastric, etc.)

Kawasaki Disease (congenital aneurysms with streptococcal infection)
Marfan's syndrome

Anemia (vegan and high milk diets)

Hypo and Hyper thyroid

Arthritis (especially when growth plate is involved)

Ruptured & bulging vertebral discs

Liver cirrhosis

Violent behavior, blind rage, explosive behavior, criminal behavior
Learning disabilities

Cerebral palsy and hypoplasia of the cerebellum (congenital ataxia)
High blood cholesterol

Iron storage disease (hemosiderosis)

Reduced glucose tolerance (hypoglycemia, reactive hypoglycemia)

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: What happens if you don't get enough silver?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says a silver deficiency results in an impaired immune system with more illness such as colds and flu, and that silver also stimulates the growth and repair of injured tissue.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that although silver is not required by any known biological system, many researchers consider it an essential element for its role as a systemic disinfectant and immune-system support. He cites it as a broad-spectrum antibacterial, antiviral, and antifungal agent that disables the enzymes microbes use for respiration, notes that humans can safely consume 400 mcg of silver per day, and states that a silver 'deficiency' results in an impaired immune system with a higher rate of illness such as colds and influenza. Drawing on Dr. Robert Becker's The Body Electric, he adds that silver also stimulates the growth and repair of injured tissue.
claims.verbatim:
A silver “deficiency”
results in an impaired immune system. In the Body Electric Dr. Robert Becker
identified a relationship between low levels of tissue and dietary silver and the
rate of illness (such as flu, colds, etc.)

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Does aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach rejects the popular fear that aluminum causes Alzheimer's, citing a 1992 Oxford study that found identical brain-aluminum levels in patients and controls and the Alzheimer's Society's 2013 position that no causal link is demonstrated, and calls aluminum remarkably nontoxic at dietary levels.
claims.answer: Wallach identifies aluminum's known biological function as activating the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase and increasing newborn survival, and reports that Professor Gerhard Schrauzer (former chair of chemistry at the University of California, San Diego) argues it should be classed as an essential mineral for all vertebrates including humans. He stresses that aluminum is remarkably nontoxic at dietary levels -- far less toxic than heavy metals -- and that it competes with calcium absorption, so excess can reduce skeletal mineralization. He explicitly rejects the popular fear that aluminum causes Alzheimer's disease, citing the 1992 Oxford study (Frank Watt and colleagues, in Nature) that found identical brain-aluminum levels in Alzheimer's patients and controls, and the Alzheimer's Society's 2013 position that no causal link has been demonstrated.
claims.verbatim:
The known biological function of aluminum is to activate the enzyme succinic
dehydrogenase; it increases the survival rate of the newborn

claims.subject: arsenic
claims.question: Can arsenic be used as medicine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach presents arsenic as an essential trace element and notes low-dose arsenic trioxide is effective against acute promyelocytic leukemia (FDA-approved in 2000) and Fowler's solution was used for psoriasis, distinguishing organically-bound arsenic from far-more-toxic metallic arsenic.
claims.answer: Wallach presents arsenic as an essential trace element -- known to be essential for survivability of the newborn and for neonatal growth. He notes arsenic promotes the growth rate of chicks, that the growth and metamorphosis of tadpoles is enhanced by its presence, that in combination with choline it prevents 100 percent of perosis ('slipped tendon') in poultry, and that its role in human physiology lies in methyl-group metabolism and polyamine synthesis. He distinguishes organically-bound arsenic from metallic arsenic, which carries 65 times greater toxicity potential, and recounts that low doses of arsenic trioxide are effective against acute promyelocytic leukemia, a cancer of the blood and bone marrow, with FDA approval of the compound in 2000 and 'Fowler's solution' used for psoriasis.
claims.verbatim:
Arsenic promotes the growth rate of chicks at 90 to 120 ppm. The rate of
growth and metamorphosis of tadpoles is enhanced by the presence of arsenic.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Is the gold leaf in fancy foods and drinks good for you?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says elemental gold leaf is biologically inert -- tasteless, unabsorbed and passed unchanged in the feces -- so the gold in gourmet foods and $1,000 cocktails is purely decorative with no nutritional value.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that elemental gold is biologically inert -- tasteless, unabsorbed, and passed unchanged in the feces with no nutritional value -- so the gold leaf in gourmet foods and liqueurs is purely decorative. Gold compounds (gold sodium thiomalate, aurothioglucose), by contrast, are given by conventional physicians as an add-on anti-inflammatory for rheumatoid arthritis: effective against active joint inflammation but not for advanced destructive disease, and anti-inflammatory rather than pain-relieving. He notes the standard intramuscular schedule (10 milligrams rising to 50 milligrams weekly to a one-gram total), warns it is contraindicated in liver, kidney, and blood disease and in lupus, and lists toxic reactions including itching, dermatitis, mouth inflammation, gastrointestinal upset, blood in the urine, aplastic anemia, and hepatitis.
claims.verbatim:
Gold has been reported only to be effective against active joint
inflammation and is not usually helpful for advanced destructive rheumatoid
arthritis,

claims.subject: barium
claims.question: Why do you have to drink barium before an X-ray?
claims.answer_short: Because barium sulfate is dense and blocks X-rays, it outlines the digestive tract on film — the basis of the 'barium meal' and 'barium enema.'
claims.answer: Wallach notes that barium's essentiality in mammals was established in 1949 (Rygh). Most naturally-occurring barium minerals (barite, witherite) are water-insoluble, and barium sulfate has very low toxicity together with high X-ray opacity -- which is why it serves as the contrast medium (the 'barium meal' and 'barium enema') for upper and lower gastrointestinal X-ray studies of the digestive system.
claims.verbatim:
Barium sulfate has a very low toxicity and relatively high density and has
a high opacity to X-rays. It is used as a contrast media in X-ray imaging of
the digestive system

claims.subject: beryllium
claims.question: Is beryllium toxic?
claims.answer_short: Yes - Wallach warns that pure powdered beryllium and its compounds must be handled carefully because they can cause acute beryllium disease or chemical pneumonitis.
claims.answer: Although beryllium appears on Wallach's list of essential minerals, the stance he records here is a safety caution: pure powdered beryllium and its compounds should be handled with care because of the risk of acute beryllium disease or chemical pneumonitis (first reported in Europe in 1933 and in the United States in 1943), and chronic berylliosis resembles pulmonary sarcoidosis.
claims.verbatim:
Pure powdered beryllium and its compounds should be handled with care
because of the potential for acute beryllium disease or chemical pneumonitis

claims.subject: bismuth
claims.question: What is bismuth used for?
claims.answer_short: Bismuth subsalicylate is the antidiarrheal active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol; combined with tetracycline it was FDA-approved in 1994 to cure H. pylori gastric ulcers -- the bacterial cause Marshall and Warren proposed in 1983.
claims.answer: Wallach describes bismuth (which chemically resembles arsenic and antimony) and its medicinal use: bismuth subsalicylate is the antidiarrheal active ingredient in 'Pink Bismuth' compounds such as Pepto-Bismol, as well as the 2004 reformulation of Kaopectate. He recounts that a combination of bismuth subsalicylate, bismuth subcitrate, and the antibiotic tetracycline -- used in pigs since 1952 to treat gastric ulcers -- was approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration in 1994 for curing gastric ulcers in humans. Stress, he notes, has historically been blamed for stomach and peptic ulcers of the stomach and duodenum; however, the same bacterium that causes gastric ulcers in pigs, Helicobacter pylori, has been proven to be the cause in humans -- the bacterial cause Australian gastroenterologist Barry Marshall, M.D. and pathologist J. Robbin Warren proposed in 1983.
claims.verbatim:
Bismuth subsalicylate is used as an antidiarrheal; it is the active ingredient
in “Pink Bismuth” compounds such as Pepto-Bismol

claims.subject: bromine
claims.question: What is bromine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes bromine as a halogen related to iodine, fluorine and chlorine; its compounds like potassium bromide were used as sedatives until the FDA pulled over-the-counter bromide sedatives such as Bromo-Seltzer in 1975, and a bromine overdose can cause acne-like skin eruptions.
claims.answer: Wallach describes bromine as a halogen related to iodine, fluorine, and chlorine. Bromine compounds such as potassium bromide were used as sedatives through the 19th and 20th centuries, until the United States Food and Drug Administration pulled over-the-counter bromide sedatives such as Bromo-Seltzer from sale in 1975, and he notes that toxic reactions from a bromine overdose can resemble acne-like skin eruptions.
claims.verbatim:
Bromine compounds, such as potassium bromide, were used as sedatives in
the 19th and 20th centuries.

claims.subject: carbon
claims.question: What does carbon do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes carbon as the essential structural atom of every organic molecule — including the genes themselves — and notes it is present at very high concentrations in living tissue.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that carbon -- one of the few elements known since antiquity -- functions as the essential structural atom for all organic molecules, including the genes themselves, and is present at very high concentrations in living tissue (around 454,000 parts per million in land plants and 465,000 in land animals, with roughly 280,000 in bone).
claims.verbatim:
Carbon
functions as an essential structural atom for all organic molecules

claims.subject: cadmium
claims.question: Does cadmium have any biological function in the body?
claims.answer_short: Despite being a toxic heavy metal, cadmium has real biological roles: it can substitute for zinc in zinc-deficient enzymes, it triggers the hatching of nematode (worm) cysts, and cadmium-bound proteins occur naturally in molluscs and horse kidney.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that cadmium -- a soft metal chemically similar to zinc, best known as a kidney-accumulating heavy metal -- nonetheless has biological functions: it can substitute for zinc in zinc-deficiency states by activating some zinc-dependent enzymes (such as carbonic anhydrase in marine diatoms), it stimulates the hatching of nematode (worm) cysts, and cadmium-bound proteins have been isolated from molluscs and horse kidney. He adds the historical note that the 1907 British Pharmaceutical Codex listed cadmium iodide as a therapy for enlarged joints, scrofulous (tuberculous) glands, and chilblains.
claims.verbatim:
Cadmium can substitute for zinc in zinc deficiency states by its ability
to activate some zinc dependent enzymes

claims.subject: cerium
claims.question: Does cerium act like calcium in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says cerium can function much like calcium in all organisms — it deposits in bone and has been shown to stimulate metabolism.
claims.answer: Wallach describes cerium -- the most abundant of the rare-earth elements -- as able to function in a manner similar to calcium in all organisms: it is deposited in bone and has been shown to stimulate metabolism. He notes cerium nitrate is used as a topical disinfectant for severe burn victims.
claims.verbatim:
Cerium can function in a similar fashion to calcium an all organisms, so it is
deposited in bones and has been shown to stimulate metabolism.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Why is chloride essential and what does it do?
claims.answer_short: Wallach presents chloride as essential to all living organisms — it activates many enzymes and is the raw material the stomach's cells use to make hydrochloric acid, which keeps the stomach sterile and aids digestion and absorption of minerals and vitamin B12; salt is the universal source.
claims.answer: Wallach presents chlorine (as chloride) as essential to all living organisms for electrochemical and catalytic functions: it activates numerous enzymes and is the basic raw material the stomach's gastric 'chief' cells use to manufacture hydrochloric acid -- which keeps the stomach sterile, boosts the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin, and improves absorption of minerals and vitamin B12 (via intrinsic factor). Salt (sodium chloride) is the universal source of chloride ions. He also recounts chlorine's public-health legacy: Labarraque's chlorinated-lime solutions and Semmelweis's 1847 chlorine hand-disinfection that ended the spread of childbed fever, and the 1918 mandate to chlorinate United States drinking water.
claims.verbatim:
Essential for all living organisms and electrochemical and catalytic functions,
activates numerous enzymes and is the basic raw material for the gastric “chief”
cells to manufacture HCl for stomach acidity

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: Why is cobalt essential?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains cobalt is essential as the metal at the center of vitamin B12, which helps transfer methyl groups to build DNA and RNA and to form myelin and red blood cells, and whose deficiency shows as pernicious anemia.
claims.answer: Cobalt is essential because it is the metal at the center of vitamin B12 (cobalamin): a single cobalt atom sits in B12's tetrapyrrole ring, and the vitamin acts as a cofactor for transferring methyl groups -- with folic acid, choline, and methionine -- to build RNA and DNA, and for myelin formation and red-blood-cell synthesis. Wallach recounts that cobalt's essentiality was discovered when veterinarians found the fatal 'bush sickness' in Australian and New Zealand livestock (emaciation, listlessness, anorexia, microcytic anemia) could be cured by cobalt supplementation, and that pernicious anemia and demyelination of the spinal cord are the classic signs of B12/cobalt deficiency in humans -- common in vegans, after stomach or ileum surgery, and with hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid). He prefers 250 to 400 micrograms a day (above the 3-to-4 microgram conventional allowance), notes calcium is required for B12 to cross the intestinal wall, and warns that cobalt excess (20 to 30 milligrams a day) can drive erythropoiesis; cobalt is also a cofactor for thyroid-hormone production.
claims.verbatim:
parasites (tapeworm), celiac disease, gluten intolerance, and other malabsorption
diseases. Pernicious anemia

claims.subject: cesium
claims.question: How does cesium work against cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes cesium as an alkaline mineral that behaves like sodium, potassium, and rubidium and enters the cancer cell to create an alkaline environment ('high pH therapy'), recommended for cancers including sarcomas, bronchiogenic carcinoma, and colon cancer.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that cesium is an alkaline mineral that behaves chemically like sodium, potassium, and rubidium, entering an ion-exchange complex with potassium (so extra dietary potassium speeds cesium's excretion). He records its use as a cancer treatment: cesium chloride is used as part of alternative cancer therapy, providing 'high pH therapy' by entering the cancer cell and producing an alkaline environment, and has been recommended for cancers including sarcomas, bronchiogenic carcinoma, and colon cancer.
claims.verbatim:
Cesium chloride is used as part of alternative cancer therapy. Cesium provides
“high pH therapy for cancer by entering the cancer cell and producing an alkaline
environment.” Cesium has been recommended for the treatment of many types
of cancer including sarcomas, bronchiogenic carcinoma, and colon cancer

claims.subject: dysprosium
claims.question: Where does the name dysprosium come from?
claims.answer_short: The name comes from the Greek word 'dysprositos,' meaning 'hard to get,' given by its discoverer after it was first identified in 1886.
claims.answer: In Epigenetics, Wallach's entry for dysprosium -- a rare-earth metal -- covers only its natural distribution (parts-per-million across igneous rocks, shale, sandstone and limestone, with animal concentrations highest in bone) and its discovery history; he assigns it no specific human deficiency disease or nutritional function here. Dysprosium was named in 1886 by the French chemist Paul Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran from the Greek 'dysprositos', meaning 'hard to get', and is never found free in nature.
claims.verbatim:
Dysprosium was first identified in 1886 by a French chemist, Paul Emile Lecoq
de Boisbaudran while he was studying holmium oxide. He gave it the name
dysprosium from the Greek word dysprositos meaning “hard to get,”

claims.subject: erbium
claims.question: Where does the name erbium come from?
claims.answer_short: Erbium is named for Ytterby, a village in Sweden, from the yttria that Carl Gustaf Mosander split into three fractions in 1843.
claims.answer: Wallach's Epigenetics entry for erbium -- a rare-earth metal -- records only its natural distribution (parts-per-million in rocks, plants and animals, concentrating in bone) and its discovery, plus that a large variety of medical applications in dermatology and dentistry use erbium; he assigns it no specific human nutritional deficiency or function. Erbium was discovered in 1843 by Carl Gustaf Mosander, who split 'yttria' from the mineral gadolinite into three fractions -- yttria, erbia and terbia -- and its oxide has a distinctive pink color.
claims.verbatim:
Erbium (for Ytterby, a village in Sweden) was discovered by Carl Gustaf
Mosander in 1843. Mosander separated “yttria” from the mineral gadolinite into
three fractions which he called yttria, erbia, and terbia.

claims.subject: europium
claims.question: Can europium help you live longer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports that europium doubled the lifespan of a laboratory species (the protozoan Tetrahymena pyriformis) -- a 100 percent increase over its normal expected lifespan.
claims.answer: Wallach's stance on europium -- a 'light' rare-earth metal: europium extended the lifespan of a laboratory species (the protozoan Tetrahymena pyriformis) by 100 percent over its normal expected lifespan. He also notes europium is found in higher concentrations in the breast milk of women in third-world countries than in American women. As with the other rare earths, he offers little element-specific detail beyond this life-extension observation and its natural distribution.
claims.verbatim:
Europium has extended the life of laboratory species (e.g., Tetrahymena
pyriformis) over their normal expected lifespan by 100%. Europium is found in
higher concentrations in breast milk from women in third world countries than in
American women.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: Does fluoride in drinking water cause cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach accepts fluoride as an essential trace mineral (proven 1972) yet ties water fluoridation to cancer: a 1990 National Toxicology Program study found oral squamous-cell carcinoma, a rare osteosarcoma, and thyroid and liver tumors in fluoride-fed rats.
claims.answer: Wallach holds a dual stance on fluorine/fluoride. On one hand he accepts it as an essential trace mineral: prior to 1972 fluoride was thought essential only for warding off dental caries (cavities) via tooth enamel, and in 1972 the researcher Schwarz proved fluoride to be a genuine essential mineral. On the other hand he treats water fluoridation as highly controversial and links it to cancer. Following 1977 epidemiological studies by Yiamouyiannis and Burk, full-scale congressional hearings examined the charge that 10,000 excess cancer deaths were caused by fluoridating certain public water systems. The resulting U.S. National Toxicology Program animal study, reported in 1990, found increased precancerous lesions and squamous-cell carcinoma of the oral mucous membranes, a rare osteosarcoma (bone cancer) at double the rate in males as females, and a significant increase in thyroid follicular-cell tumors and liver cancer. Clinical fluoride toxicity appears as dental fluorosis at 2 to 7 parts-per-million and osteosclerosis at 8 to 20 parts-per-million, with chronic systemic toxicity at 20 to 80 milligrams per day over years; the average American already takes in about 4.4 milligrams per day from food, toothpaste, supplements and water.
claims.verbatim:
In 1990 the results of the fluoride study showed an increase in rat
precancerous lesions in the oral mucus membrane cells; there was an increase
in cancers of the oral mucus membranes (squamous cell carcinoma); a rare
form of osteosarcoma appeared at double the rate in males as females;

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What does iron do, and what are the signs of low iron?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says iron is an essential mineral (a healthy adult carries 3 to 5 grams, mostly in hemoglobin and myoglobin) that carries oxygen, and its deficiency shows as pica, fatigue, palpitations, poor memory, sore tongue, and anemia.
claims.answer: Iron is an essential mineral; a healthy adult carries 3 to 5 grams, most of it in hemoglobin and myoglobin, where iron carries oxygen (iron is to hemoglobin what magnesium is to chlorophyll). Wallach stresses that pica -- obsessive cravings driving children and adults to eat ice (pagophagia), dirt (geophagia), lead-paint chips and high-calorie snack foods -- is a specific sign of iron deficiency, and that the snack-food form can cause weight gain and obesity. Iron deficiency arises from unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation, chronic infection, hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid from salt-restricted diets or proton-pump inhibitors), chronic diarrhea, chronic bleeding, and impaired absorption from high-fat or high-phytate diets and gluten intolerance. Its symptoms include listlessness, fatigue, heart palpitations on exertion, rapid pulse (tachycardia), reduced cognition and memory, sore tongue, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and hypochromic microcytic anemia. Stomach hydrochloric acid and vitamin C aid absorption; heme iron from meat is 10 percent absorbable versus 1 percent from plants (phytates bind it). He notes excess iron storage can be caused by deficiencies of selenium, copper or zinc and is falsely blamed for liver cirrhosis, pancreatic fibrosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes.
claims.verbatim:
tongue, angular stomatitis, dysphagia (pica), hypochromic microcytic anemia,
weight gain, obesity, etc.

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: Is gallium an essential mineral?
claims.answer_short: Wallach counts gallium among the essential elements, noting it was claimed essential in 1938 and again in 1958 and has metalloenzyme activity in the human brain.
claims.answer: Wallach's stance on gallium -- a trace element claimed to be essential in 1938 and again in 1958 -- centers on the brain and brain cancer. He states gallium has specific areas of metalloenzyme activity in the human brain and has been reported to specifically reduce the rate of brain cancer in laboratory animals, and that British research shows supplementing the diets of pregnant women will reduce the rate of brain cancer in their children. Gallium maltolate, an orally absorbable form of the gallium ion, is used in medical treatments for brain cancer, inflammation and certain infectious diseases. Because gallium and ferric (iron) salts behave similarly in biological systems, gallium ions often mimic iron ions in medical applications.
claims.verbatim:
Gallium was claimed to be essential in 1938 and again in 1958. Gallium
has specific areas of metalloenzyme activity in the human brain and has been
reported to specifically reduce the rate of brain cancer in laboratory animals.

claims.subject: gadolinium
claims.question: What is gadolinium?
claims.answer_short: Gadolinium is a rare-earth mineral Wallach counts among the trace elements, found naturally in rocks, plants and animals.
claims.answer: Wallach's Epigenetics entry for gadolinium (the book spells it 'Gadolium') -- a rare-earth mineral -- records only its natural distribution across igneous rocks, shale, sandstone, limestone, plants and animals, and the observation that land animals accumulate it in bone and liver very quickly after absorption; he assigns it no specific human deficiency disease or nutritional function.
claims.verbatim:
Gd - Gadolium, a rare earth mineral, is found in igneous rocks at 5.4 ppm; shale
at 4.3 ppm; sandstone at 2.6 ppm; limestone at 0.7 ppm; land plants at up to
70 ppm by Carya spp.; marine animals at 0.06 ppm; land animals accumulate
gadolium in bone and liver very quickly after absorption.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: What are the signs of germanium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Germanium deficiency is typified by a severely reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoarthritis, low energy, and cancer.
claims.answer: Wallach lists the fallout of a germanium deficiency as a severely weakened immune system, arthritis and osteoarthritis, low energy, and cancer — consistent with his view of germanium as an oxygen- and immune-supporting trace element. In the same passage he puts the maintenance dose at 20 to 30 mg a day, rising to 50 to 100 mg when a person is seriously ill and needs more oxygen carried to the tissues.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of germanium are typified by a severely reduced immune status,
arthritis, osteoarthritis, low energy, and cancer.

claims.subject: hydrogen
claims.question: What does hydrogen do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains hydrogen is the major constituent of water (about 70% of the body) and all organic molecules, and that the body's acid-base balance is really the regulation of hydrogen-ion (H+) levels.
claims.answer: Hydrogen is an essential structural element: it is the major constituent of water (about 70 percent of the human body is water) and of all organic molecules, and Wallach frames the body's acid-base balance as, in fact, the regulation of hydrogen-ion (H+) levels in cellular and extracellular fluids. Healthy blood pH ranges from 7.36 to 7.44; below 7.30 is acidosis and above 7.44 is alkalosis, while values below 6.8 or above 7.8 are rapidly fatal. The body controls hydrogen-ion concentration by dilution, buffering (reacting in fractions of a second), respiration (minutes) and the kidney (up to hours or days). Large amounts of hydrogen ions are generated or retained in disease states such as emphysema, diabetes, anxiety, chloride loss, cystic fibrosis and Addison's disease. He notes a practical corollary: bladder infections (cystitis) can often be controlled by acidifying the urine with unsweetened cranberry juice.
claims.verbatim:
Hydrogen functions as a major constituent of water (70% of the human body
is water) and all organic molecules. The regulation of the acid-base balance in the
human body is in fact the regulation of the hydrogen ion (H+) levels of cellular
and extracellular fluids.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: How much colloidal minerals should I take?
claims.answer_short: In Epigenetics Wallach recommends liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals at one ounce per 100 pounds of body weight per day, listing a parts-per-million profile that spans rare-earth, trace and bulk minerals.
claims.answer: In the supplement-recommendation section of Epigenetics -- following his vitamin and mineral daily-dose tables -- Wallach lists liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals at one ounce per 100 pounds of body weight per day. He gives the product's mineral profile as a table of concentrations in parts-per-million, covering the rare-earth elements alongside the trace and bulk minerals.
claims.verbatim: Liquid Plant Derived Coloidal Minerals One Ounce/ 100 pounds/day PPM

claims.subject: hafnium
claims.question: What is hafnium?
claims.answer_short: In Epigenetics, Wallach's hafnium entry gives only its natural distribution across rocks, sea water, soil, and plants and animals, assigning it no specific human deficiency disease or function.
claims.answer: In Epigenetics, Wallach's entry for hafnium -- a trace metal -- gives only its natural distribution: its concentration in parts per million (ppm) across igneous rocks, shale, sandstone, limestone, sea water, soil, and marine and land plants and animals. He assigns it no specific human deficiency disease or nutritional function here.
claims.verbatim:
Hf - Hafnium is found in igneous rocks at 3 ppm; shale at 2.8 ppm; sandstone
at 3.4 ppm; limestone at 0.5 ppm

claims.subject: mercury
claims.question: Is mercury in fish dangerous?
claims.answer_short: Methyl mercury from fish (highest in shark, tuna and swordfish) crosses the placenta and is chiefly neurotoxic -- tremors, depression, loss of coordination -- and Wallach notes selenium is mutually antagonistic, protecting against it.
claims.answer: Mercury occurs universally in living things and is a well-known toxic element; Wallach traces its accumulation to industry, mining, agriculture, dental amalgam fillings, and micro-organisms that convert it to methyl mercury in aquatic sediments. Methyl mercury (the form in fish) crosses the placenta easily and has a biological half-life of about 70 days; heavy fish eaters, especially of large predators such as shark, tuna and swordfish, can reach tissue levels up to 400 micrograms per kilogram. Direct mercury poisoning is primarily neurological -- tremors, vertigo, irritability, moodiness, depression, salivation, inflammation of the mouth (stomatitis) and diarrhea -- while poisoning with the more toxic alkyl mercury progresses to loss of coordination, vision and hearing. Wallach notes selenium and mercury are mutually antagonistic: selenium protects the kidney from mercury-induced tissue death (necrosis) and limits placental transfer. He cites the 1962 Minamata Bay disaster in Japan and a mass poisoning in Iran (bread from mercury-treated seed grain) as producing congenital brain defects, cerebral palsy and infant deaths, and relays the theory that dental-amalgam vapor is linked to multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, Lou Gehrig's disease) and Parkinson's disease.
claims.verbatim:
The manifestations of direct Hg poisoning are primarily neurological
(ie, tremors, vertigo, irritability, moodiness [suicidal], depression, salivation,
inflammation of the mouth [stomatitis] and diarrhea).

claims.subject: holmium
claims.question: What is holmium?
claims.answer_short: In Epigenetics, Wallach's holmium entry gives only its natural distribution across rocks, land plants (notably hickory), and marine and land animals where it appears in bone, with no specific human deficiency disease or function.
claims.answer: In Epigenetics, Wallach's entry for holmium -- a rare-earth metal -- gives only its natural distribution in parts per million (ppm) across igneous rocks, shale, sandstone, limestone, land plants (notably concentrated in hickory, Carya species), and marine and land animals, where it appears in bone. He assigns it no specific human deficiency disease or nutritional function here.
claims.verbatim:
Ho - Holmium, a Rare Earth, is found in igneous rocks at 1.2 ppm; in shale at
0.6 ppm; sandstone at 0.51 ppm; limestone at 0.17 ppm

claims.subject: iodine
claims.question: What happens if you don't get enough iodine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says iodine concentrates in the thyroid to make thyroxin, and low iodine causes hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's), with fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hair loss, depression, constipation, goiter, infertility, and cretinism in newborns.
claims.answer: Iodine is an essential mineral concentrated in the thyroid gland; combined with the amino acid tyrosine it is manufactured into the thyroid hormone thyroxin, which regulates digestion, heart rate, body temperature, sweat-gland activity, the nervous and reproductive systems, general metabolism and body weight. Wallach argues iodine intake is usually low to begin with, and that as Americans restrict their salt intake on medical advice, physician-caused goiter and hypothyroidism have become epidemic; copper is a required cofactor for using iodine, so copper-poor soils also drive goiter. Low iodine and thyroid function produce hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's disease) -- fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hair loss, depression, constipation, dry skin, poor memory, goiter, infertility, and congenital birth defects (cretinism in the newborn). He notes many foods act as goitrogens that interfere with thyroid function (dietary and waterborne nitrates, cruciferous vegetables, gluten intolerance) and that about 11 million Americans have an under- or over-active thyroid; the average American takes in only 170 to 250 micrograms of iodine per day, and metallic iodine is not toxic up to 2,000 micrograms per day.
claims.verbatim:
Symptoms of Hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's Disease)

Fatigue
Cold intolerance

Muscle aches & pains

Heavy or more frequent menstrual periods
Low sex drive

Brittle nails

Weight gain

Hair loss

Muscle cramps

Depression

Constipation

Elevated blood cholesterol

Puffy face

Dry skin and hair

Inability to concentrate

Poor memory

Goiter

Infertility

Congenital birth defects (Cretinism)

claims.subject: potassium
claims.question: What are the signs of low potassium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach states chronic potassium deficiency shows as muscular weakness and mental apathy, with hypokalemic cardiac failure its most serious event.
claims.answer: Potassium is essential to all organisms and is the major positively-charged ion (cation) inside cells, driving electrochemical and enzyme functions; it makes up about five percent of the body's total mineral content. With sodium, the other main electrolyte, potassium maintains normal water balance, osmotic equilibrium and acid-base balance, and works with calcium to regulate neuromuscular activity. It is easily absorbed but barely stored -- about 90 percent of ingested potassium is excreted in the urine -- so Wallach states a significant daily intake of 5,000 milligrams is required. Chronic potassium deficiency shows as muscular weakness and mental apathy, and its most serious event is hypokalemic (low-potassium) cardiac failure. Diuretics (both natural and prescribed), sweating from colds, flu or exercise, vomiting and diarrhea all increase the loss of potassium and other minerals.
claims.verbatim:

claims.question: Can a lithium deficiency cause depression, bipolar disorder, or autism?

claims.answer: Wallach presents lithium as an essential trace mineral for mental and behavioral health, not merely a pharmaceutical. He states that in humans, clinical depression, manic depression, 'bi-polar' disease and autism are hallmarks of lithium deficiency, and that hyperactivity, attention-deficit disorder (ADD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) belong to the same picture. Although psychiatrists describe depression and manic depression as rooted in negative feelings and self-recrimination, Wallach notes they nonetheless treat it successfully with the trace mineral lithium -- which to him shows the conditions are fundamentally a lithium deficiency, aggravated by high sugar or alcohol intake. He reports that the risk of clinical depression has nearly doubled with each generation since 1915 and that its age of onset keeps dropping. As supporting evidence he cites Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer (University of California, San Diego), whose study of 27 Texas counties (1978-1987) found that areas whose drinking water contained little or no lithium had significantly higher rates of suicide, homicide and drug-related arrests than counties with water-lithium levels of 70 to 170 micrograms per liter. He adds that normal individuals carry roughly 400 times more lithium in their hair than violent criminals do, that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) estimates a daily lithium intake of 650 to 3,100 micrograms (much of it metallic and poorly absorbed), and that lithium supplementation shifts serum vitamin B12 levels.

In humans, manic depression, clinical depression, “bi-polar” disease


autism are hallmarks of Li deficiency

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: What are the symptoms of magnesium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties a long list of problems to magnesium shortage — including asthma, menstrual migraines, depression, tetany and convulsions, tremors, muscular weakness, vertigo, ECG changes, and abnormal calcification of arteries and soft tissue.
claims.answer: Magnesium is essential to all living organisms, second only to potassium as an intracellular cation; the adult body holds 20 to 28 grams, about 60% of it in bone. It powers energy production and protein synthesis, muscle contractility and nerve excitability, is a cofactor for countless enzymes, and is a constituent of chlorophyll. Calcium and magnesium play antagonistic roles in muscle -- calcium the stimulator, magnesium the relaxer -- so an excess of calcium can induce magnesium-deficiency signs, and an excess of magnesium inhibits bone calcification. Wallach lists a wide range of magnesium-deficiency diseases and symptoms: asthma, anorexia, menstrual migraines, growth failure, electrocardiogram (ECG) changes, neuromuscular problems, tetany and convulsions, depression, muscular weakness, muscle tics, tremors, vertigo, and calcification of the small arteries and soft tissue. Absorption ranges from about 24% for metallic sources to 85% for plant-derived colloidal sources; fat, phytates and calcium reduce it while vitamin D has no effect. He notes there is no evidence of toxicity up to 6,000 milligrams per day when the kidneys are healthy.

claims.answer: Manganese is essential to all known living organisms; it activates numerous enzyme systems (including those for glucose metabolism, energy production and the antioxidant superoxide dismutase) and is a constituent of many metalloenzymes, hormones and proteins. Wallach stresses its role in building the fragile ear bones and joint cartilage. He describes the deficiency diseases as very striking, ranging from severe congenital birth defects -- congenital ataxia, congenital deafness, chondromalacia, chondrodystrophy and 'slipped tendon' -- to asthma, convulsions, retarded growth, skeletal defects, infertility (failure to ovulate, testicular atrophy), stillbirths/miscarriages, loss of libido, and defects of chondroitin-sulfate metabolism that show up as joint problems: temporomandibular joint disorder (TMJ), repetitive motion syndrome and carpal tunnel syndrome. He argues most carpal tunnel and repetitive-motion cases are really manganese deficiency, not a purely mechanical injury. Separately, an EXCESS of manganese (from some water supplies or industrial exposure) can instead produce a Parkinson-like syndrome or a schizophrenia-like psychiatric disorder ('locura manganica').

claims.answer_short: Wallach states classic protein (nitrogen) deficiency causes infertility, poor growth, lowered immune status, edema, and Kwashiorkor — the potbellied, thin children of third-world countries.
claims.answer: Nitrogen is essential to life as a structural atom in protein, nucleic acids (RNA and DNA) and a wide variety of organic molecules. Dietary nitrogen, supplied as protein, furnishes the amino acids the body uses to repair worn-out tissue, build new tissue, form enzymes, hormones and other secretions, maintain the blood's osmotic and acid-base balance, transport minerals and vitamins, and make the immunoglobulins (antibodies). Wallach states that classic protein (nitrogen) deficiency results in infertility, poor growth, lowered immune status, edema, and Kwashiorkor -- the potbellied, thin children of third-world countries. Because the availability and usability of nitrogen differs greatly between foods, protein sources must be chosen with that in mind.

claims.answer_short: Wallach explains that a sodium deficiency causes salt hunger, that Addison's disease brings weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss, and marked salt hunger, and that 'water intoxication' from low-sodium infant formula swelled babies' brains and killed them.
claims.answer: Sodium is one of the three indispensable electrolytes (with chloride and potassium); it makes up about two percent of the body's mineral content and, with chloride, is mainly extracellular. Together these electrolytes maintain normal water balance and distribution, osmotic equilibrium, acid-base balance, and muscular and nerve excitability, all under adrenal-cortex and pituitary hormonal control. Wallach explains that 'salt hunger' is one of the most basic cravings of animals and man, strongest in herbivores and human vegetarians because grains, vegetables and fruit contain little sodium chloride. Addison's disease (failure of the adrenal cortex) causes a loss of sodium and potassium retention with general weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss and a marked salt hunger, relieved by salt supplementation. Sodium-chloride deficiency arises mainly in hot weather or heavy exercise with profuse sweating; Wallach warns that 'water intoxication' killed infants fed low-sodium formulas -- their brains swelled from a simple sodium deficiency -- and that the treatment for sodium deficiency is water and salt, taken orally or as 0.9% intravenous saline.

claims.subject: absorption
claims.question: Is it what you eat, or what you absorb?
claims.answer_short: Wallach flips the old adage: your health isn't decided by what you eat but by what you actually absorb — the cornerstone of his two-pronged model (supply the 90, and fix the gut so they get in).
claims.answer: Wallach's core reframing of nutrition: your health is determined not by what you eat but by what you actually absorb. He calls the familiar adage 'you are what you eat' inaccurate and replaces it with 'you are what you absorb' -- the foundation of his two-pronged model, in which supplying the 90 essential nutrients only works if the gut is healthy enough to take them up.
claims.verbatim:
There is an old adage that states “you are what you eat.” Unfortunately, this old
adage is not correct. It is more correct and accurate to say “you are what you
absorb.”

claims.answer_short: About a third of Americans — 115 million people — are gluten intolerant per a 2009 Mayo Clinic study Wallach cites, and far more in high-grain communities.
claims.answer: Wallach cites a 2009 Mayo Clinic study finding that thirty-one percent of Americans -- almost a full third, 115 million people -- suffer from gluten intolerance, a prevalence he says runs far higher in high-grain communities.
claims.verbatim:
According to a 2009 study published by the Mayo Clinic, thirty-one percent,
almost a full third of Americans (115 million), suffer from gluten intolerance.

claims.answer_short: Two prongs together: go fully gluten-free AND supply the 90 essential nutrients (plus therapeutic doses of what you're most short on). Wallach says the combination resolves many chronic problems.

He argues this combination resolves many chronic health problems that a gluten-damaged gut had been quietly starving the body of.

Putting an afflicted individual on a gluten-free diet and supplementing the
person correctly with the basic platform of the 90 essential nutrients and
therapeutic levels of the deficient nutrient will solve many health problems

claims.question: Why does Wallach say phytates in nuts, grains, and seeds block calcium?
claims.answer_short: Phytic acid in nuts, grain bran, seeds, oatmeal and whole wheat binds calcium into insoluble calcium phytate the body can't absorb.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that phytic acid — a phosphorus-bearing compound concentrated in nuts, the bran of grains, seeds, and especially oatmeal and whole wheat — binds dietary calcium into calcium phytate, an insoluble complex the body cannot absorb, so a high-phytate diet is itself a cause of calcium deficiency.

phytate consumption (phytic acid is a phosphorus containing acid compound

many plants, especially oatmeal and whole wheat that combine with Ca to form
calcium phytate which is insoluble and thus unavailable to humans) all result

in a Ca deficiency.

claims.subject: phytates
claims.question: Which foods does Wallach say block calcium with oxalic acid?

Free radical damage resulting from the regular consumption of

they provided at least

claims.subject: fish
claims.question: Is it safe to eat a lot of fish — what about mercury?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's answer is nuanced, not a blanket 'avoid fish.' The mercury in fish is methyl mercury, and it bioaccumulates the more fish you eat — the real offenders being the large predator fish: shark, tuna, and swordfish. He lays the body-burden out in plain tiers: people who rarely eat fish carry very little mercury (about 2-5 ug/kg), moderate eaters sit 10 ug/kg, and heavy eaters of those big predators can climb to 400 ug/kg — on the order of 100 times the occasional eater. So the caution is aimed at loading up on the large predators, not at fish generally. Wallach also points to the protection built into his own framework: selenium and mercury are mutual antagonists, so keeping selenium adequate defends the body against the mercury it does take in.

The mercury in fish is methyl mercury, and it bioaccumulates the more fish you eat — the real offenders being the large predator fish: shark, tuna, and swordfish. He lays the body-burden out in plain tiers: people who rarely eat fish carry very little mercury (about 2-5 ug/kg), moderate eaters sit 10 ug/kg, and heavy eaters of those big predators can climb to 400 ug/kg — on the order of 100 times the occasional eater. So the caution is aimed at loading up on the large predators, not at fish generally. Wallach also points to the protection built into his own framework: selenium and mercury are mutual antagonists, so keeping selenium adequate defends the body against the mercury it does take in.
claims.verbatim:
Mercury in fish is present as methyl mercury. People who rarely eat fish have
very low levels of mercury (2-5 ug/kg); moderate fish consumers have 10 ug/kg;
high fish consumers (especially if they eat the large predator fish such as shark,
tuna, or swordfish) will typically have higher levels of up to 400 ug/kg.

claims.subject: fish
claims.question: Where did cod liver oil's reputation as a cure come from?
claims.answer_short: Scottish fishermen used cod-liver oil to prevent and cure rickets long before doctors accepted it; the French physician Trousseau confirmed it with cod-liver oil, sunshine, and butter — while orthodox medicine kept hunting for a 'rickets germ.'
claims.answer: Cod-liver oil earned its reputation as a rickets cure among Scottish fishermen long before doctors accepted it; the French physician Trousseau confirmed it with cod-liver oil, sunshine, and butter while orthodox medicine still hunted for a 'rickets germ.'
claims.verbatim:
Cod liver oil, the Scottish fisherman's treatment for rickets, continued to be

used by the lay community throughout the 19th century. Armand Trousseau, a
French physician, treated his rickets patients with cod liver oil, sunshine, and
butter—proving to himself that diet and sunshine played a vital role in the cause,
prevention, and cure of rickets.

claims.subject: fish
claims.question: What foods are high in vitamin A — is fish one?
claims.answer_short: Yes — fish liver is one of the richest sources of preformed vitamin A, the ready-to-use form called retinol, with cod-liver oil the classic example. Wallach draws the useful line here: this animal-derived retinol is already active, unlike the carotene (provitamin A) your body has to convert out of brightly pigmented plants. The same early vitamin-A research pointed to butter and egg yolk alongside cod-liver oil as the animal foods that reversed the deficiency — so fish sits with butter and eggs among the top preformed-A foods.
claims.answer: Yes — fish liver is one of the richest sources of preformed vitamin A, the ready-to-use form called retinol, with cod-liver oil the classic example. Wallach draws the useful line here: this animal-derived retinol is already active, unlike the carotene (provitamin A) your body has to convert out of brightly pigmented plants. The same early vitamin-A research pointed to butter and egg yolk alongside cod-liver oil as the animal foods that reversed the deficiency — so fish sits with butter and eggs among the top preformed-A foods.
claims.verbatim:
Retinol, a primary alcohol, is present in
high concentrations of marine fish liver (cod liver oil, etc.).

claims.subject: fish
claims.question: Do fish contain vitamin K / the fat-soluble 'Activator X'?
claims.answer_short: Yes, and it matters more than it first sounds. Fish livers and shellfish are one of the few sources of the fat-soluble factor Weston Price named 'Activator X' — now believed to be vitamin K2 — which every healthy traditional culture had in its diet. Its importance is all about absorption: Price found that the fat-soluble vitamins A, D and Activator X act as the catalysts that let the body actually take up minerals and use protein, and that without them a person cannot absorb minerals no matter how abundant they are in the food. Those primitive diets supplied roughly 10 times the fat-soluble vitamins of the modern American diet — which is a large part of why they were so free of degenerative disease.
claims.answer: Yes, and it matters more than it first sounds.
