Fish livers and shellfish are one of the few sources of the fat-soluble factor Weston Price named 'Activator X' — now believed to be vitamin K2 — which every healthy traditional culture had in its diet. The fat-soluble vitamins matter for absorption: Price found that A and D act as the catalysts that let the body actually take up minerals and use protein, and that without them a person cannot absorb minerals no matter how abundant they are in the food. Those primitive diets supplied at least 10 times the fat-soluble vitamins of the modern American diet — which is a large part of why they were so free of degenerative disease.
claims.verbatim:
Dr. Price discovered an additional fat-soluble nutrient, which he labeled
“Activator X," that is present in fish livers and shellfish, organ meats, and butter
made from milk from cows that eat rapidly growing green grass in the Spring and
Fall. All primitive cultures had a source of Activator X, now thought to be vitamin
K,, in their diets.

claims.subject: fish
claims.question: Can fish oil ever be harmful?
claims.answer_short: Wallach warns that a high intake of polyunsaturated oils including fish oil, if you're selenium-deficient, raises the risk of birth defects, arteriosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, sudden heart death, and cancer — because the unprotected oils go rancid in your cells.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that a high intake of polyunsaturated oils including fish oil, if you are selenium-deficient, raises the risk of birth defects, arteriosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, sudden heart death, and cancer — because the unprotected oils go rancid in your cells.
claims.verbatim:
High intake of dietary polyunsaturated oils (such as olive oil, coconut
oil, fish oil, etc,), salad dressings, margarine, and cooking oils concurrent with a
selenium deficiency will increase the risk and rate of birth defects (such as cystic
fibrosis, muscular dystrophy, etc), arteriosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, sudden heart
death, and cancer.

claims.subject: antioxidants
claims.question: Do flavonoids raise your ORAC?
claims.answer_short: Yes - Wallach lists raising ORAC antioxidant activity among the effects demonstrated clinically in people, not just in cell studies.
claims.answer: Wallach draws a line between test-tube results and whole-person results, and puts raising ORAC antioxidant activity on the whole-person side. In in-vivo studies he lists flavonoid supplementation as clinically effective for reducing or eliminating allergies, calming vascular and pulmonary inflammation, raising ORAC antioxidant activity, antimicrobial action against bacteria, viruses, yeast and fungus, improving gastrointestinal function, and supporting the immune system in cancer patients. Flavonoids themselves are plant pigments - the yellow, red and blue in flower petals.
claims.verbatim:
supplementation with flavonoids have demonstrated clinical
effectiveness for reducing or eliminating allergies, vascular and pulmonary
inflammation, for increasing ORAC antioxidant activity, antimicrobial properties

claims.subject: epigenetics
claims.question: What does Dr. Wallach mean by epigenetics?
claims.answer_short: Most diseases blamed on inherited ‘bad genes’ are really nutritional deficiencies that cripple how your DNA, RNA and enzymes work — fix the nutrition and you can prevent or reverse them.
claims.answer: Wallach's own one-line definition of epigenetics, and the idea behind his book's subtitle 'The Death of the Genetic Theory of Disease Transmission': most diseases that are thought to be genetically transmitted are, in fact, nutritional deficiencies that negatively impact the functions of DNA, RNA, and enzymes. His conclusion is that supplying all 90 essential nutrients lets medicine prevent and reverse most diseases, rather than writing them off as inherited fate.
claims.verbatim:
epigenetics (i.e., most diseases that are thought to be genetically transmitted are
in fact nutritional deficiencies that negatively impact the functions of DNA, RNA,
and enzymes)

claims.subject: epigenetics
claims.question: What is Wallach's duckling experiment?
claims.answer_short: His 1968 proof that nutrition beats genetics: 100 genetically identical ducklings split onto four diets — the ones fed a complete nutrient ration grew three-to-six times larger than their identical siblings fed only lettuce or barley grass.
claims.answer: The experiment Wallach credits as the origin of the field. In 1968, at the Center for the Biology of Natural Systems, he set out to show that 'genetic potential' is controlled by environment and nutrition. He took 100 genetically identical ducklings -- same mother and father -- and divided them into four groups of 25, each on a different diet: lettuce only; hydroponic barley grass only; Purina duck grower pellets only; or pellets plus barley grass. After one month the results were dramatic -- the two groups eating the nutritionally complete Purina pellets grew three to six times larger than the identical ducklings fed only lettuce or barley grass, which showed almost no growth at all. Same genes, different nutrition, radically different bodies.
claims.verbatim:
In 1968 Wallach, while at the Center for the Biology of Natural Systems,
designed a simple experiment that would demonstrate how “genetic potential”
can be affected by the environment and nutrition. Thus we have the field of
epigenetics.

claims.subject: epigenetics
claims.question: How did Wallach come up with the idea of epigenetics?
claims.answer_short: From cystic fibrosis. If CF were a recessive gene, every child of two CF parents would have it — but out of thousands of such babies Wallach found only one did, so the genetic theory couldn’t be right.
claims.answer: Where Wallach's rejection of the genetic theory began. Cystic fibrosis was taught to be the 'most classic' simple Mendelian recessive-gene disease, with a supposed one-in-four carrier rate. Wallach ran what he called a fourth-grade test: if CF were truly recessive, 100% of babies born to two CF parents would have CF. Instead, out of thousands of babies born to such couples, only one had CF -- and couples with one CF parent never produced the predicted one-in-four. The results did not match the theory; it was impossible for CF to be genetic. Coming to the question, in his words, as an empty slate untainted by dogma, Wallach concluded CF was not inherited but a congenital defect caused by a selenium deficiency in the mother.
claims.verbatim:
Wallach, on the other hand came to the table as an empty slate and untainted
by dogma, As a result, he "knew" that CF was not a genetically-transmitted
disease, and “epigenetics” was born!

claims.subject: epigenetics
claims.question: What's the scientific definition of epigenetics?
claims.answer_short: The textbook definition Wallach adopts: epigenetics is how the cell interprets its DNA — like a pianist interpreting a musical score — the study of heritable traits that don't change the DNA sequence itself. Wallach adds his own gloss: those traits are driven by nutritional deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach opens his Epigenetics chapter by adopting a textbook definition from Clifford Pickover's The Medical Book (2012): just as a pianist interprets the notes of a musical score — controlling volume and tempo — epigenetics governs how a cell interprets its DNA. It is the study of heritable traits that do not involve any change to the underlying DNA sequence. Wallach signals his agreement by inserting his own thesis directly into the borrowed definition — those heritable traits, he adds in parentheses, are 'caused by nutritional deficiencies.'
claims.verbatim:
Just as a pianist interprets the notes of a musical score, controlling the
volume and tempo, epigenetics affects the interpretation of DNA genetic
sequences in cells. Epigenetics usually refers to the study of ‘heritable
traits’ (caused by nutritional deficiencies), that do not involve changes to the
underlying DNA sequence of the cells.

claims.subject: epigenetics
claims.question: Why does Wallach say DNA is a script, not a blueprint?
claims.answer_short: Because a blueprint stamps out identical copies, but DNA doesn't. Wallach borrows Nessa Carey's metaphor: DNA is more like a script — two film versions of Romeo & Juliet used the same script yet came out completely different. Same genes, different 'production' — and what directs the difference, Wallach adds, is nutrition.
claims.answer: To explain the core idea, Wallach opens the chapter with a metaphor from Nessa Carey's The Epigenetics Revolution (2012): DNA is not a rigid template or blueprint that stamps out thousands of identical copies — it is more like a script. Carey compares it to Romeo and Juliet: two film versions made sixty years apart used the same Shakespearean script yet came out entirely different. Identical starting points, different outcomes. Wallach adopts and extends the metaphor, adding in his own words that the 'production' differs because the cell is reading a script from DNA that is nutritionally deficient — the difference is driven by diet and nutrition, not by any change to the genes themselves.
claims.verbatim:
But DNA isn’t really like that. It's more like a script. Think of Romeo
and Juliet, for example. In 1936 George Cukor directed Leslie Howard and
Norma Shearer in a film version. Sixty years later Baz Luhrmann directed
Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes in another movie version of this play.
Both productions used Shakespeare's script, yet the two movies are entirely
different. Identical starting points, different outcomes.

claims.subject: epigenetics
claims.question: Can I change my genes, or are they set in stone?
claims.answer_short: Not entirely — and that's the hopeful part. As Wallach quotes twin researcher Danielle Reed: your DNA is written in pen and can't be changed, but epigenetics is written in pencil — and for Wallach, nutrition is the eraser.
claims.answer: Answering whether your genes are your destiny, Wallach quotes twin researcher Danielle Reed (speaking in National Geographic, 2012): 'Mother Nature writes some things in pencil and some things in pen. Things written in pen you can't change — that's DNA. But things written in pencil you can — that's epigenetics.' The point Wallach draws is his optimistic thesis: the pen — your actual DNA sequence — is fixed, but the pencil — how those genes are expressed — can be rewritten. For Wallach, the pencil and eraser are nutrition.
claims.verbatim:
Mother Nature writes some things in pencil and
some things in pen... Things written in pen you can’t change. That's DNA. But
things written in pencil you can. That's epigenetics.

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: How did Wallach discover selenium causes cystic fibrosis?
claims.answer_short: In 1977, during a routine autopsy at Emory's Yerkes Primate Research Center, Wallach found textbook cystic-fibrosis lesions in a 6-month-old rhesus monkey — the first non-human case ever documented — and concluded CF isn't a genetic disease but a congenital selenium deficiency. Announcing it cost him his job.
claims.answer: The monkey, one of a group being studied for the space program, had died of unknown causes; in its pancreas, liver, and lungs Wallach found damage identical to human cystic fibrosis. Two independent pathologists confirmed it — Dr. Victor Nassar of Emory and Dr. John Easterly, a national CF authority in Chicago — and the finding held up: a 2005 retrospective in the ILAR Journal called it “a classic textbook case.” Because the lesions tracked with low selenium, Wallach argues CF is not the inherited genetic disease medicine assumed, but a congenital deficiency of the trace mineral selenium in the embryo or early infancy — and therefore preventable and reversible. Emory terminated him in April 1978; St. Louis University, which had just hired him, fired him before he moved into his office. He later autopsied 1,700 children in Keshan Province, China, and found that 35% of those who died of selenium-deficiency heart disease also carried the pancreatic and liver lesions of cystic fibrosis.
claims.verbatim:
When Wallach announced that cystic fibrosis was not a genetic disease, but
rather a congenital deficiency of the trace mineral selenium in the embryo or
early postnatal life, Wallach was summarily terminated in April of 1978 from his
Position at Yerke's without the ability to defend his observations

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Why do young athletes drop dead of heart failure?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's answer is blunt: the sudden cardiac death of a young athlete is Keshan disease — hypertrophic cardiomyopathy caused by a simple deficiency of the trace mineral selenium — and it's preventable.
claims.answer: Keshan disease is named for Keshan Province, China, where Wallach autopsied 1,700 children under ten and documented death by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — a thickened, failing heart muscle — traced to selenium deficiency in the local diet. He argues the collapses of seemingly healthy young athletes are the same disease: not a mysterious “silent” defect but selenium-starved heart muscle giving out under exertion. His prescription is equally direct — a complete 90-essential-nutrient program with extra selenium, and, he says, “the athlete can live.” It's the human echo of what he watched selenium do in livestock, where the identical heart-muscle disease (“mulberry heart disease”) was eliminated by simple selenium supplementation.
claims.verbatim:
In fact, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy,
sudden heart death of athletes, is KSD and is caused by a simple deficiency
of the trace element selenium. Supplement a complete 90 nutrient program
with extra selenium and the athlete can live.

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: What foods are high in selenium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach names liver, eggs, kidneys, and certain high-selenium varieties of rice as the everyday food sources — but warns a damaged gut may not absorb it no matter how much you eat.
claims.answer: The richest dietary selenium, in Wallach's telling, comes from organ meats — liver and kidneys — plus eggs and some high-selenium rice varieties (a plant's selenium depends heavily on the soil it grew in). He raises these specifically around cystic fibrosis, which he frames as a prenatal selenium deficiency: “Normal selenium levels in pregnant women will prevent CF.” But he attaches the caveat that runs through his whole framework — “you are not what you eat, you are what you absorb.” A gut damaged by gluten can't take up selenium even when it's on the plate, which is why he pairs selenium-rich food (or supplements) with a gluten-free diet rather than trusting diet alone.
claims.verbatim:
Wallach says the key to its prevention and cure is selenium, a trace
element found in liver, eggs, kidneys and some varieties of high selenium
rice.

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Can cystic fibrosis actually be cured?
claims.answer_short: Wallach makes a striking claim: that cystic fibrosis — conventionally a fatal genetic disease — is essentially 100% curable when caught within 30 days of birth, because in his view it's a selenium deficiency, not a genetic defect.
claims.answer: Conventionally, cystic fibrosis strikes about 1 in every 2,500 American children, is usually fatal in infancy, and fewer than half of those affected live past 21. Wallach's position overturns the premise: he argues CF isn't an inherited genetic disease but a congenital deficiency of selenium (with zinc and vitamin B12) during pregnancy — which makes it both preventable and curable. His specific claims are that normal selenium levels in a pregnant woman will prevent CF outright, and that the disease is “100 percent curable when diagnosed within 30 days of birth,” with recovery still possible even in teenagers and young adults. It's the therapeutic flip side of his 1977 discovery: if the pancreatic, lung, and intestinal damage of CF comes from missing selenium, then supplying it early enough should reverse it.
claims.verbatim:
Normal selenium levels in pregnant women will prevent CF,” Wallach
said, and tests on thousands of monkeys (their exaggeration) have shown
the disease is 100 percent curable when diagnosed within 30 days of birth

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: What does zinc actually do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says at least 70 different enzymes need zinc as a cofactor to work — including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, and carboxypeptidase.
claims.answer: In Wallach's account, zinc is a true workhorse mineral: no fewer than 70 metalloenzymes require zinc as a cofactor to function properly, among them carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase, and carboxypeptidase. Zinc helps lock these enzymes onto the substances they act on by holding the right spatial arrangement. Some enzymes bind zinc so tightly that they keep working even when the body is severely depleted.
claims.verbatim:
There are no less than 70 metalloenzymes that require Zn as a cofactor to
function properly. These include carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, lactic
dehydrogenase, and carboxypeptidase. Zinc helps to bind enzymes to substrates
by maintaining special and configurational relationships. Some enzymes bind
Zn so tightly that even during severe Zn depletion they can still function.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: How does zinc affect your DNA and genes?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says zinc is built right into the RNA molecule — the 'zinc fingers' — and is needed for protein synthesis, cell division, and making DNA.
claims.answer: Zinc plays a direct role in the body's genetic machinery, a central theme of Wallach's book Epigenetics. He describes zinc as an integral part of the RNA molecule — the 'zinc metallic fingers' — and says it takes part in the metabolism of nucleic acids and the synthesis of proteins. In the same passage he adds that zinc is required for cell division and the synthesis of DNA, and that the enzyme DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is itself zinc-dependent.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Can a zinc deficiency cause birth defects?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach links zinc deficiency to a long list of congenital birth defects, from cleft lip and palate and spina bifida to Down's syndrome and heart defects.
claims.answer: Wallach places zinc deficiency at the root of a striking list of congenital birth defects. Among those he associates with zinc deficiency are Down's syndrome, cleft lip and cleft palate, spina bifida, brain defects and cerebral palsy, small or absent eyes, clubbed or missing limbs, webbed fingers and toes (syndactyly), diaphragmatic and umbilical hernias, and heart, lung, and urogenital defects. In his epigenetic framework these trace to the mother's nutrition rather than to fixed genetic fate.
claims.verbatim:
Congenital Birth Defects Associated with Zinc Deficiency:

Down's syndrome

Cleft lip

Cleft palate

Brain defect (dorsal herniation, hydroencephaloceol, cerebral palsy, etc.)
Micro or anophthalmia (small or absent eyes)
Micro or agnathia jaw structure

Spina bifida

Clubbed limbs

Syndactyly (webbed fingers and toes)
Missing limbs and digits

Diaphragmatic hernia (hiatal hernia)
Umbilical hernias (gastroschisis)

Heart defects

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: How long have we known that zinc is essential?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes zinc was known to be essential for bread mold 125 years ago and for rats 70 years ago, but was recognized as essential for humans only 40 years ago.
claims.answer: Zinc's status as an essential nutrient came late for humans, in Wallach's telling. He notes it was known to be essential for bread mold 125 years ago and for rats 70 years ago, but that its essentiality for humans was recognized only 40 years ago. The lateness underscores how recently zinc's importance to people was accepted.
claims.verbatim:
Zinc was known to be an essential nutrient for bread mold 125 years ago, to
be essential for rats 70 years ago, and essential for humans 40 years ago.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Can a mother's zinc deficiency cause birth defects in her baby?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says yes — in his zoo work he traced birth defects across many animal species directly to the mother's zinc (and other) deficiencies during pregnancy.
claims.answer: Much of Wallach's conviction about zinc and birth defects came from his years as a zoo and veterinary pathologist. He describes a constant stream of congenital birth defects in animals that he traced directly to nutritional deficiencies in the mother before and during pregnancy: cerebral palsy in a llama from copper and zinc deficiency, spina bifida in a monkey from folic acid and/or zinc deficiency, cleft palates in arctic foxes from vitamin A and/or zinc deficiency, and a ventricular septal heart defect in a kangaroo. Once the mothers' diets were adjusted, he says, the defects were prevented — the same logic he applies to human pregnancy.
claims.verbatim:
Wallach saw a constant stream of congenital birth defects that could be
directly attributed to nutritional deficiencies in the mother prior to and during
her pregnancy: cerebral palsy in a llama (from a copper and zinc deficiency); spina
bifida in a monkey (from a folic acid and/or zinc deficiency); cleft palates in arctic
foxes (from a vitamin A and or a zinc deficiency); a ventricular septal heart defect
in a kangaroo (from a congenital vitamin A and or a zinc deficiency).

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Does the body need magnesium to use biotin?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach's book says converting biotin (vitamin H) into its active coenzyme form depends on magnesium and ATP being present.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that biotin, also called vitamin H, has to be converted into an active coenzyme form before the body can use it — and that this conversion depends on the presence of both magnesium and ATP (adenosine triphosphate). It is one example of how magnesium works behind the scenes as a partner to the B-vitamin system: without enough magnesium, even an adequate biotin intake cannot be fully activated.
claims.verbatim:
conversion of biotin to the active form of the coenzyme is dependent on the
presence of magnesium and adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Can you take too much magnesium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's book reports that with healthy kidneys there is no evidence of magnesium toxicity even up to 6,000 mg a day — though he cautions that a true excess of magnesium can inhibit bone calcification.
claims.answer: Wallach's book presents magnesium as very safe: if the kidneys are healthy, he states there is no evidence of toxicity at intakes up to 6,000 mg per day. For reference he cites the conventional RDA at 350 mg/day for adult men, 300 mg/day for women, and 450 mg/day in pregnancy and lactation. The one caveat he flags is that an actual excess of magnesium will inhibit bone calcification — a reminder that magnesium and calcium must stay in balance rather than either one running away.
claims.verbatim:
The RDA for Mg is 350 mg/day for adult males, 300 mg/day for adult females
and 450 mg/day for pregnant and lactating females. If kidneys are healthy there
is no evidence of toxicity at up to 6,000 mg/day.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: What causes arthritis according to Wallach?
claims.answer_short: Wallach found osteoarthritis to be a near-universal disease across animal species and attributes it to deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, sulfur and trace minerals — not simple wear and tear.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that osteoarthritis showed up as a universal disease across an enormous range of species he autopsied — iguanas, ducks, flamingos, pheasants, sheep, llamas, monkeys, rhinos and kangaroos among them. He attributes it to deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, sulfur and trace minerals rather than treating it as unavoidable aging or wear. In this view arthritis is a nutritional-deficiency disease, and magnesium is one of the minerals whose shortage helps drive it.
claims.verbatim:
was a universal disease found in all species, including iguanas, ducks, flamingos,
pheasants, sheep, llamas, monkeys, rhinos, and kangaroos (caused by calcium,
magnesium, sulfur, and trace-mineral deficiencies).

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: What is Omega-3?
claims.answer_short: Omega-3 is one of the two fatty acids Wallach classes as truly essential — alpha-linolenic acid — a fat the body cannot make and must get from the diet.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that of all the fats, only two are classically 'essential,' meaning the body cannot manufacture them and must obtain them from the diet: alpha-linolenic acid, the omega-3 fatty acid, and linoleic acid, an omega-6. He counts three essential fatty acids among the body's 90 essential nutrients. The 'omega-3' name marks where the fat's first double bond sits, counted three carbons in from the tail or methyl end of the chain; longer-chain omega-3s such as DHA and EPA belong to the same family. In his framework these fats are structural raw materials — they build the bilipid cell membranes and the prostaglandins that help steer blood pressure, blood clotting, and brain and nervous-system function — not merely a source of fuel.
claims.verbatim:
There are two fatty acids that are classically regarded as essential: alpha
linolenic acid (omega-3 fatty acid) and linoleic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid).

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Can omega-3 help with depression?
claims.answer_short: Low DHA (an omega-3) tracks with low brain 5-HIAA, which Wallach links to higher rates of depression and suicide.
claims.answer: Wallach identifies DHA and EPA as the omega-3 fatty acids the body needs for the enzyme pathways that metabolize long-chain polyunsaturated fats. He notes that low plasma DHA is a marker for low levels of 5-HIAA in the cerebral spinal fluid, and that low brain 5-HIAA is directly associated with increased rates of depression and suicide.
claims.verbatim:
Omega-3 fatty acids, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid
(EPA) are essential for enzymatic pathways required to metabolize long-chain
polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). Low plasma concentrations of DHA is a
marker for low cerebral spinal fluid levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (S-HIAA).
Low brain concentrations of 5-HIAA is directly associated with increased rates of

depression and suicide.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Does omega-3 slow aging?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites research in which omega-3 supplementation lengthened DNA telomeres and lowered inflammation in obese adults.
claims.answer: Wallach points to research published in the journal Brain, Behavior and Immunity showing that supplementing omega-3 fatty acids in sedentary, obese adults lengthened their DNA telomeres and reduced their inflammation markers.
claims.verbatim:
In an article
published in the journal Brain, Behavior and Immunity, research demonstrated
that supplementation of omega-3 fatty acids to sedentary, obese adults received
a benefit of lengthening of their DNA telomeres and a reduction in inflammation
markers.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Can low omega-3 cause blood clots or a heart attack?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists coronary thrombosis as a disease caused by omega-3 deficiency, not by genetics.
claims.answer: Wallach rejects the idea that cardiovascular disease is genetically inherited. He teaches it is a collection of diseases driven by free-radical damage (inflammation) to the artery lining and by specific nutritional deficiencies — pairing coronary thrombosis with omega-3 deficiency, cardiomyopathy with selenium deficiency, congestive heart failure with thiamine deficiency, and aneurysms with copper deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
cardiovascular disease is a
collection of diseases that are caused by free-radical damage to the lining of
the arteries (inflammation) and nutritional deficiencies (e.g., cardiomyopathy/
selenium deficiency; congestive heart failure/thiamine deficiency; coronary
thrombosis/omega-3 deficiency, aneurysms/copper deficiency, atrial fibrillation/
degenerative disc disease, and others).

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: What does omega-3 do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Essential fatty acids like omega-3 are the raw material for prostaglandins that regulate blood pressure, heart rate, blood clotting, airway opening, and brain neurotransmitters.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that the essential fatty acids, which include omega-3, are the raw material the body uses to manufacture prostaglandins. Those prostaglandins regulate blood pressure, heart rate, vascular dilation, blood clotting, and bronchial dilation — which he says prevents and reverses asthma — as well as the neurotransmitters of the central nervous system.
claims.verbatim:
EFA are also the raw material required by the human to manufacture
prostaglandins that regulate blood pressure, heart rate, vascular dilation,
blood clotting, bronchial dilation (prevents and reverses asthma), and
neurotransmitters of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord).

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: What is the ideal ratio of omega-3 to omega-6?
claims.answer_short: Wallach points out that traditional diets contained nearly equal amounts of omega-3 and omega-6 essential fatty acids.
claims.answer: Reviewing the common features of traditional and tribal diets, Wallach notes that they contained nearly equal amounts of omega-3 and omega-6 essential fatty acids. He observes that only four percent of those diets' calories came from polyunsaturated oils, with the remainder of the fat calories coming from saturated and monounsaturated fats.
claims.verbatim:
8. Traditional diets contained nearly equal amounts of omega-3 and
omega-6 essential fatty acids.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Why did Wallach take the FDA to court over omega-3?
claims.answer_short: Wallach was plaintiff in eight FDA lawsuits — up to the Supreme Court steps — to make information on omega-3, selenium, folic acid and antioxidants available to Americans.
claims.answer: Wallach has been the plaintiff or co-plaintiff in eight lawsuits and claims requests against the FDA in federal courts, reaching up to the steps of the U.S. Supreme Court. His aim was to ensure that proper information about supplementing with selenium, omega-3 essential fatty acids, folic acid, and antioxidants — nutrients he says can prevent and reverse human diseases — was available to all Americans.
claims.verbatim:
Dr. Wallach has been the plaintiff and/or co-plaintiff in eight lawsuits and claims requests lodged
against the FDA in federal courts (Federal District Courts, Federal Appellate Courts, and up to the steps
of the U.S. Supreme Court) to ensure that proper information regarding supplementation with selenium,
omega-3 essential fatty acids, folic acid, and antioxidants that could prevent and reverse human diseases
was available to all Americans.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Why is it called omega-3?
claims.answer_short: The '3' marks where the first double bond sits — three carbons in from the tail (methyl) end of the fatty acid.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the 'omega' number refers to the location of the first double bond, counted from the tail or methyl end of the fatty acid chain. In an omega-3 fatty acid that first double bond is at the third carbon; omega-6 and omega-9 are named the same way for double bonds farther along the chain.
claims.verbatim:
The location of the first double bond as counted from the “tail” or methyl end
of the fatty acid is referred to as the “omega” number (ie., omega-3, omega-6,
omega-9, etc).

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: What is Vitamin C?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a water-soluble antioxidant that most mammals make in their own bodies, but humans cannot -- so we must get it from food or supplements every day.
claims.answer: Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble antioxidant. Wallach explains that many mammals can synthesize their own vitamin C internally, but humans -- like guinea pigs -- cannot, so people must obtain it from the diet. It belongs to the water-soluble vitamin class (alongside the B-complex) and serves as a required cofactor for building collagen -- the protein behind connective tissue, cartilage, bones, teeth, and blood vessels. Its classic role is preventing and curing scurvy, the deficiency disease that plagued sailors and explorers for centuries.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin C is a water-soluble antioxidant that can be synthesized by many
mammals but not by guinea pigs or humans.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: What does vitamin C do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin C is a required cofactor for building collagen, connective tissue, cartilage, bones, teeth and blood vessels, and it improves iron absorption.
claims.answer: Wallach describes vitamin C as a required cofactor for producing collagen and connective tissue — the material that forms cartilage, bones, teeth, blood vessel walls and capillaries. Because so much of the body's structural framework depends on collagen, vitamin C is essential to keeping these tissues strong. It also increases the efficiency with which the body absorbs inorganic iron.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin C required cofactor for the production of collagen, connective tissue,
cartilage, bones, teeth, blood vessel walls, capillaries, and it also increases the
efficiency of absorption of inorganic iron.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Does vitamin C help the immune system?
claims.answer_short: Yes — vitamin C affects white blood cells, macrophages, immune responses, wound healing and allergic reactions.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, vitamin C affects the function of white blood cells and macrophages — the body's immune-defense cells — and influences immune responses. It is also tied to wound healing and to how the body handles allergic reactions.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin C also affects
the functions of white blood cells, macrophages, immune responses, wound
healing, and allergic reactions.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Can your body store vitamin C?
claims.answer_short: No — humans cannot store vitamin C, so it must be replenished from the diet every day.
claims.answer: Wallach points out that most plants and animals can store vitamin C, with the guinea pig being the exception among animals. Humans, by contrast, are unable to store vitamin C and therefore require a fresh source of it every day. This is why a steady daily supply from food or supplements matters.
claims.verbatim:
Most plants and animals (except for the guinea pig) can store vitamin C.
However, humans are unable to store vitamin C and require a daily source of it.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Can you take too much vitamin C?
claims.answer_short: Yes — too much vitamin C can cause oxalate crystal deposits, urinary tract inflammation, diarrhea, and breakdown of red blood cells.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that too much vitamin C is not harmless. Signs of overdose include tissue deposits of oxalate crystals, inflammation of the urinary tract, diarrhea, and lysis — the breaking apart of the cell walls — of red blood cells. Even a water-soluble vitamin can cause problems when taken far in excess.
claims.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: Too much vitamin C can result in tissue deposits of oxalate
crystals, urinary tract inflammation, diarrhea, lyses (breakage of cell walls) of red
blood cells,

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Who discovered the cure for scurvy?
claims.answer_short: Scottish naval surgeon James Lind proved in 1753 that lemons and oranges cured scurvy, in one of the first controlled experiments.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon, eliminated scurvy in the British navy after studying the legend of a marooned sailor's self-cure. In 1753, as recorded in his 'A Treatise on Scurvy,' Lind divided scurvy-stricken sailors into six groups and fed each different foods; only the sailors given lemons and oranges recovered rapidly and completely. Because Lind did not prescribe a specific treatment from his results, it took another forty-two years before the British navy adopted his findings.
claims.verbatim:
James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon, finally eliminated scurvy in the British
navy after researching the legend of Zoe and his miraculous self-cure. In 1753,
as he recorded in his A Treatise on Scurvy, Lind divided sailors with scurvy into
six separate groups. Each group was provided with different foods, and only the
sailors who consumed lemons and oranges recovered rapidly and completely.
Lind did not prescribe a specific treatment as a result of his study, so it took
another forty-two years before the British navy adopted his recommendations.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Who made vitamin C famous?
claims.answer_short: Linus Pauling — his 1970 book 'Vitamin C and the Common Cold' triggered a national surge in vitamin C use dubbed the 'Linus Pauling effect.'
claims.answer: Wallach describes how Linus Pauling popularized vitamin C. Pauling's 1970 best-seller 'Vitamin C and the Common Cold' won a Phi Beta Kappa Book Award, and a later edition, 'Vitamin C, the Common Cold and the Flu,' suggested vitamin C could fend off a swine flu pandemic. Sales quadrupled, pharmacies could not keep up with demand, and roughly fifty million Americans lined up to follow Pauling's vitamin C protocol — a response vitamin manufacturers called the 'Linus Pauling effect.'
claims.verbatim:
In 1970 Pauling's best-selling book, Vitamin C and the Common Cold, was
published. The book would be awarded the Phi Beta Kappa Book Award in
1971 as one of the most distinguished and important works published in 1970.
Paperback editions were published in 1971 and 1973, and a second edition,
Vitamin C, the Common Cold and the Flu published three years later suggested
that vitamin C could fend off a swine flu pandemic. Sales of vitamin C quadrupled
and pharmacies could not keep up with the demand. Fifty million Americans were
lining up to follow Pauling's vitamin C protocol. Vitamin manufacturers referred
to this massive response as the “Linus Pauling effect.”

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Why is vitamin C called ascorbic acid?
claims.answer_short: It was named 'ascorbic' — meaning 'without scurvy' — after Szent-Gyorgyi first jokingly proposed calling it 'ignosco' and 'godnose.'
claims.answer: Wallach relays the naming story: Albert Szent-Gyorgyi noticed the new vitamin resembled sugar and first proposed calling it 'ignosco' — Latin for 'I do not know' combined with the sugar suffix '-ose.' When a British journal editor rejected that, he offered the tongue-in-cheek alternative 'godnose.' The substance was ultimately dubbed hexuronic acid, and the name was later changed to ascorbic acid, meaning 'without scurvy.'
claims.verbatim:
Szent-Gyorgyi
knew that the vitamin had some similarities to sugar, and he initially proposed
that the substance be named “ignosco,” Latin for “I do not know” and “ose”
the suffix common to sugars. The editor of a British journal refused to accept
the name, prompting Szent-Gyorgyi to offer the alternative name of “godnose.”
Ultimately, when Szent-Gyorgyi’s article was published, the vitamin was dubbed
hexuronic acid and later the name was changed to ascorbic—"without scurvy"—
acid.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: What is Vitamin A?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin, isolated in 1913, that exists in several active forms — retinol, retinoic acid, and retinyl esters — and is essential for vision, healthy skin and mucous membranes, and strong bones and teeth.
claims.answer: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin, first isolated in 1913, that exists in several active forms — retinol, retinoic acid, and retinyl esters — plus precursors. Beta-carotene is the fat-soluble precursor the body converts into vitamin A. Wallach teaches that it is required to maintain vision and night vision, healthy skin and mucous membranes, and bones and teeth, and that it has been shown to reduce the risk of epithelial cancers. Because it is fat-soluble it is stored mainly in the liver and absorbed along with dietary fats, which is why a low-fat diet or any condition that blocks fat absorption can leave you short of it.
claims.verbatim:
This vitamin, isolated in 1913, which has many active forms including, retinol,
retinoic acid and retinyl esters and precursors.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: What is vitamin A?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin, isolated in 1913, that exists in several active forms and is essential for vision, skin, mucous membranes, bones, and teeth.
claims.answer: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin first isolated in 1913 that exists in several active forms, including retinol, retinoic acid, and retinyl esters, along with precursors. Beta-carotene is a fat-soluble precursor the body uses to make vitamin A, and it is required to maintain vision and night vision, healthy skin and mucous membranes, and bones and teeth. Wallach notes it has been shown to reduce the risk of epithelial cancers, and that the ancient Egyptians used beef liver juice, a natural source of vitamin A, to cure night blindness.
claims.verbatim:
This vitamin, isolated in 1913, which has many active forms including, retinol,
retinoic acid and retinyl esters and precursors. Beta carotene is a fat soluble
vitamin A precursor that is required for maintenance of vision and night vision
(the Egyptians employed beef liver juice, a natural source of vitamin A, to
cure night blindness in 2000 BC), to maintain healthy skin and healthy mucus
membranes, bones, and teeth; it has been shown to reduce the risk if epithelial
cancers.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: What does vitamin A do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin A drives growth, maintains epithelial tissues like the retina, gut lining, and skin, and helps make adrenal steroid hormones.
claims.answer: Wallach describes vitamin A as having a number of functions in the body. It plays an essential role in growth stimulation and in maintaining and running epithelial tissue, including the retina, the intestinal mucosa, and the skin. It is also involved in the synthesis of adrenocortical steroids, for example converting pregnenolone to progesterone, DHEA to androstenedione, and desoxycorticosterone to corticosterone.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin A has a number of functions in the body. It plays an essential role in
growth stimulation, the maintenance and function of epithelial tissue including
the retina, intestinal mucosa, and skin. Vitamin A is also known to function
in the synthesis of adrenocortical steroids, particularly in the conversions of
pregneno-lone to progesterone, of dehydroepiandrosterone to androstenedione,
and desoxycorticosterone to corticosterone.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: Can you absorb vitamin A on a low-fat diet?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says no, vitamin A is fat-soluble and is poorly absorbed on low-fat diets, and people without a gallbladder should take ox bile to absorb it.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that fat-soluble vitamins cannot be efficiently absorbed from the intestine when people eat low-fat diets, which matters directly for getting enough vitamin A. He advises that individuals who have had their gallbladder removed should supplement with ox bile to boost the bile salts needed for efficient absorption. This applies to all of the fat-soluble vitamins, A, D, E, and K.
claims.verbatim:
Fat soluble vitamins can not be efficiently absorbed from the
intestine when humans consume low fat diets. Individuals who have their gall
bladder removed should supplement with ox bile to increase the volume of bile
salts which are required for the efficient absorption of the fat soluble vitamins A,
D, E, and K.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: Can you take too much vitamin A?
claims.answer_short: Yes, sustained high intakes of retinol can be toxic, but Wallach says overdose signs generally appear only above about 50,000 IU of retinol a day in adults.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that too much vitamin A can cause overdose signs such as headaches, blurred vision, fatigue, painful menstruation, joint and bone pain, dry cracked skin, hair loss, itchiness, birth defects (for example, malformations of the cranium, face, heart, thymus, and central nervous system), and liver disease. He notes a 'pseudo-jaundice' in which the skin turns orange or yellow from high beta-carotene intake, but with no yellowing of the whites of the eyes. According to him, toxicity signs usually appear only with sustained daily intakes of 50,000 IU of retinol in adults and 20,000 IU in infants.
claims.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: too much vitamin A is indicated by headaches, blurred vision,
fatigue, dysmenorrhea, joint and bone pain, dry cracked skin, hair loss, itchiness,
birth defects (for example, malformation of the cranium, face, heart, thymus,
and central nervous system), liver disease, and pseudo-jaundice (when the skin
becomes orange or yellow as a result of high levels of beta carotene intake,
notably there is no yellowing or jaundice of the ocular sclera).

Signs of toxicity usually appear only with sustained daily intakes of 50,000 IU
of retinol for adults and 20,000 1U in infants.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: How was vitamin A discovered?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin A was discovered in 1913 when two research groups found that animals fed only lard developed a deficiency that was corrected by adding butter, egg yolk, and cod liver oil.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that vitamin A was discovered through experiment rather than mere observation, in 1913. Two groups working independently, Osborne and Mendel, and McCollum and Davis, reported that animals fed artificial diets using lard as their only source of fat developed a nutritional deficiency. That deficiency could be corrected by adding foods such as butter, egg yolk, and cod liver oil to the diet, revealing the missing factor now known as vitamin A.
claims.verbatim:
Experimental, rather than observational evidence, led to the discovery of
vitamin A in 1913. Two groups (Osborne and Mendel; McCollum and Davis)
independently reported that animals fed on artificial diets with lard as a
sole source of fat developed a nutritional deficiency that could be corrected
by the addition of foods such as butter, egg yolk, and cod liver oil to the
diet.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: Was cystic fibrosis first thought to be a vitamin A deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach notes that when cystic fibrosis was first described in 1933 it was thought to be a vitamin A deficiency, based on vitamin A deficiency changes seen in young celiac patients.
claims.answer: Wallach points out that when cystic fibrosis was first described in 1933, it was originally thought to be the result of avitaminosis A, a vitamin A deficiency. This was because specific vitamin A deficiency changes were found in a subgroup of young patients who had been clinically diagnosed with celiac disease. He raises this history as part of his broader argument challenging the purely genetic theory of cystic fibrosis.
claims.verbatim:
Initially described in 1933, CF was originally thought to be the result of
avitaminosis A (a vitamin A deficiency), because of specific vitamin A deficiency
changes found in a subgroup of young patients diagnosed clinically with celiac
disease.

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: What is Vitamin D?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin with two forms — D2 from plants and D3, which the body makes when sunlight converts cholesterol in the skin — and it is essential for depositing calcium and phosphorus in the bones and teeth.
claims.answer: Vitamin D exists in two active forms: D2, the plant source, and D3, the animal source, which the body creates by exposing the cholesterol deposits in the skin to UV light. In Wallach's framework it is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium and phosphorus in the bones and teeth, which makes it central to skeletal health. It works hand-in-hand with parathyroid hormone to govern how the body handles calcium and phosphorus, and many consider it a hormone in its own right because it is synthesized in one place, such as the skin, and acts on a distant target, such as bone.
claims.verbatim:
This vitamin has two active forms: D, the plant source and D; the animal source,
which is created by exposing the skin deposits of cholesterol to UV light. Vitamin
D is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium
and phosphorus in the bones and teeth.

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: Why is vitamin D deficiency so common today?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls the universal vitamin D deficiency of the 20th and 21st centuries a physician-caused disease driven by medical advice to avoid the sun and skip cholesterol and supplements.
claims.answer: Wallach argues that the universal deficiency of vitamin D in the 20th and 21st centuries is a physician-caused disease. He blames the medical community's instructions to avoid sun exposure, wear sunblock, wide-brimmed hats, long sleeves and gloves, avoid dietary cholesterol such as egg yolks, chicken skin, dairy and saturated fats, and not take vitamin-mineral supplements. He calls this combination the 'perfect storm' that created a universal vitamin D deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiency: The universal deficiency of vitamin D in the 20th and 21st
centuries is a physician-caused disease. The doctor's instructions dictated by
the medical community to the American people to avoid exposure to the sun,
wear sun blocker, wear wide-brimmed hats, long-sleeved shirts and gloves, avoid
cholesterol in the diet (including egg yolks, chicken skin, dairy products, saturated
fats, etc), and not to take vitamin-mineral supplements turned out to be the

“perfect storm” to create a universal vitamin D deficiency.

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: Is vitamin D a hormone?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes some consider vitamin D a hormone, since it is synthesized in one place, like the skin, and acts on a distant target, like bone, much like steroid hormones.
claims.answer: Wallach observes that some consider vitamin D a hormone because it behaves like one: synthesis can take place at one site, for example the skin, while the target organ is elsewhere, such as a bone. He notes its mechanism of action is similar to that of aldosterone, estrogens, and testosterone, thought to be linked to an action on DNA-directed synthetic processes. In this sense vitamin D blurs the line between a vitamin and a hormone.
claims.verbatim:
There are some who consider vitamin D a hormone, as there are similarities
between vitamin D and hormone activity. Synthesis can take place in one site
(for example, on the skin) and the target organ found elsewhere (a bone). Its
mechanism of action, similar to that of aldosterone, estrogens, and testosterone,
is thought to be linked to an action on DNA-directed synthetic processes.

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: How was vitamin D discovered to cure rickets?
claims.answer_short: Early 20th-century researchers proved both sunlight and diet cured rickets — Hulschinsky straightened deformed limbs with UV lamps, and Mellanby and McCollum showed cod liver oil cured it even after its vitamin A was destroyed.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that early in the 20th century two theories arose for the cause of rickets: one blamed environmental factors, especially lack of sunlight, the other revisited Trousseau's idea that diet was involved. Dr. Kurt Hulschinsky exposed rickets-deformed children from Berlin to mercury quartz lamps that duplicated the sun's ultraviolet light, and their limbs straightened out after two months. In England, Edward Mellanby confirmed the Scottish fishermen's tale that cod liver oil cured rickets, and McCollum of Johns Hopkins showed that destroying the vitamin A in cod liver oil with heat still left it able to cure and prevent rickets — pointing to a separate antirachitic factor.
claims.verbatim:
Early in the 20th century, two separate theories were developed for the
cause of rickets. One postulated that rickets was due to environmental factors,
especially lack of sunlight, the second revisited Trousseau’s theory that diet was
involved. Dr. Kurt Hulschinsky, exposed rickets-deformed children from Berlin
to mercury quartz lamps, duplicating the sun's ultraviolet light, and their limbs
straightened out after two months.

‘At the same time, in England, Edward Mellanby proved the Scottish
fishermen’s tale of curing rickets with cod liver oil to be correct. EV. McCollum
of Johns Hopkins destroyed the vitamin A in cod liver oil with heat, and it still
had antirachitic activity and cured and prevented rickets.

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: Is rickets making a comeback?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach reports rickets reappeared in the industrialized world in 2013 with a 400 percent increase between 1995 and 2011, which he blames on sun-avoidance, sunscreen, and fear of cholesterol.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that in 2013 rickets reappeared among children in the industrialized world, with a reported 400 percent increase between 1995 and 2011. He attributes this to fears of skin cancer from sun exposure, widespread use of sunscreens, and fear of cholesterol in egg yolks, which he calls a good source of vitamin D. To Wallach, the return of rickets is a physician-caused disease.
claims.verbatim:
In 2013 rickets reappeared in children in the industrialized world with a
reported increase of 400 percent between 1995 and 2011. This is a result of
fears of increased risk of skin cancer from skin exposure to the sun as well as

widespread use of sun screens, fear of cholesterol in egg yolks (a good source
of vitamin D)

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What is iron?
claims.answer_short: Iron is an essential mineral found in nearly every living thing; in the body it sits at the heart of hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in the blood, and a healthy adult holds about 3 to 5 grams of it.
claims.answer: Iron is a necessary element present in nearly all living organisms, and one of the 60 essential minerals Wallach says the body must obtain from diet or supplements. It works through iron-containing enzymes and proteins, many of them built around heme groups, that drive biological oxidation and oxygen transport, including hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochrome, and catalase. A healthy adult carries 3 to 5 grams of total iron, a newborn nearly double that per kilogram of body weight; roughly 60 to 70 percent is functional iron doing active work and 30 to 40 percent is held in storage. In Wallach's framework iron is the metal that lets blood carry oxygen, and running short of it, a deficiency he treats as common given how many everyday conditions drain it, drives fatigue, anemia, poor memory, and the strange cravings of pica.
claims.verbatim: Iron is a necessary element found in nearly all living organisms.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What is iron and what does it do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Iron is an essential element in nearly all living things; a healthy adult carries 3 to 5 grams of it, mostly in hemoglobin and other oxygen-handling proteins.
claims.answer: Iron is a necessary element found in nearly all living organisms, working through iron-containing enzymes and proteins that often carry heme groups to drive biological oxidation and transport. Examples in higher organisms include hemoglobin, cytochrome, and catalase. A healthy adult holds an average of 3 to 5 grams of total iron, and a newborn carries nearly double that amount per kilogram of body weight. Roughly 60 to 70 percent of tissue iron is essential or functional iron, while 30 to 40 percent is stored.
claims.verbatim:
Iron is a necessary element found in nearly all living organisms. Iron containing
enzymes and proteins, often containing heme prosthetic groups, participate in

many biological oxidations and in transport. Examples of iron containing proteins
found in higher organisms include hemoglobin, cytochrome, and catalase.

In a healthy adult human there is an average of 3 to 5 gms of total iron.
The newborn infant has nearly double the amount of iron per kg than adults.
Sixty to 70 percent of tissue iron is classed as essential or functional iron, and
30 to 40 percent as storage iron.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What causes iron deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Iron deficiency comes from unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation, chronic infections, low stomach acid, chronic diarrhea or bleeding, and impaired absorption from high-fat, high-phytate, or gluten-intolerant diets.
claims.answer: Wallach traces iron deficiency to a range of causes: an unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation, chronic infections, and hypochlorhydria, which is low stomach acid that he links to salt-restricted diets or the use of proton pump inhibitors. It also results from chronic diarrhea, chronic bleeding from illness such as cancer, ulcers, and parasites, and impaired absorption caused by high-fat diets, high-phytate diets, and gluten intolerance.
claims.verbatim:
Iron deficiency can result from an unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation,
chronic infections, hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid from salt-restricted diets
or use of proton pump inhibitors), chronic diarrhea, chronic bleeding (from illness
from cancer, uncers, parasites, etc.) and impaired absorption (caused by high-fat
diets, high phytate diets, gluten intolerance, etc).

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Is too much iron dangerous?
claims.answer_short: Wallach argues iron overload is falsely blamed for diseases like cirrhosis and diabetes; excess stored iron is actually caused by shortages of selenium, copper, and zinc.
claims.answer: Wallach's position is that excess storage of iron is itself caused by deficiencies of selenium, copper, zinc, and similar minerals, not simply by taking in too much iron. He says iron is falsely blamed for liver cirrhosis, fibrosis of the pancreas, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and diabetes. In his view these diseases are not the direct result of iron excess.
claims.verbatim:
Excess storage of iron can be caused by deficiencies of selenium, copper, zinc,
etc,, and is falsely blamed for liver cirrhosis, fibrosis of the pancreas, hypertrophic
cardiomyopathy and diabetes. These diseases are not the direct result of iron
excess.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: If I have iron-deficiency anemia, do I have other deficiencies too?
claims.answer_short: Almost certainly, Wallach says deficiencies rarely occur alone, so an obvious one like iron-deficiency anemia usually means others, maybe dozens, are present.
claims.answer: Wallach stresses that few nutritional deficiencies occur in the pure state. If there is one obvious clinical deficiency, such as iron-deficiency anemia, the odds are that others are present as well, maybe dozens. This is why he favors supplementing the full set of essential nutrients rather than chasing a single mineral in isolation.
claims.verbatim:
The clinical realities are that few nutritional deficiencies occur in the pure
state. In other words, if there is an obvious clinical deficiency, such as iron
deficiency anemia, the odds are that there are others, maybe dozens

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Can iron actually cure pica or ice-eating?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach cites trials where iron cured children of eating sand and made ice-eating disappear once the underlying anemia was corrected.
claims.answer: Wallach cites the research to show iron reverses pica. In a 1964 study by McDonald and Marshall, twenty-five children who ate sand were split into two groups, and after three to four months eleven of the thirteen given iron were cured of the behavior, compared with only three of twelve given saline. In a 1968 report by Reynolds and colleagues, thirty-eight anemic people showed pagophagia (ice-eating) as their most common form of pica, and twenty-two of them had it disappear once their iron-depletion anemia was corrected.
claims.verbatim:
McDonald and Marshall (1964) reported on twenty-five children who ate sand.
They divided the group in half, giving one group iron and the other group saline.
After three to four months, eleven of the thirteen children given iron were cured
of their pica behavior compared to three of the twelve given saline.

Reynolds et al. (1968) reported on thirty-eight people with anemia who
exhibited “pagophagia,” or ice eating, as the most common form of pica. Twenty-
two of the thirty-eight had their pica symptoms disappear after correcting an iron
depletion anemia.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Why did ancient people call iron the metal from the sky?
claims.answer_short: Because the first purified iron came from meteors, the Egyptians called iron 'the metal from the sky' and the Aztecs 'the gift of heaven.'
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that the taming of fire brought the mastery of metals, and iron was the primary key of that transition, lifting human life from a brutish hunter-gatherer existence toward civilization. This early history gave iron a special, almost supernatural quality, reinforced by the fact that the first purified iron was extracted from meteors that fell from the heavens. For that reason the ancient Egyptians called iron 'the metal from the sky,' and the Aztecs called it 'the gift of heaven.'
claims.verbatim:
The “taming” of fire by man brought the “mastery” of metals that eventually
led to human progress and civilization. Iron was the primary key of this transition,

which raised the quality of human life from a brutish animal-like hunter gatherer

existence to civilization. This early history of the ferrous metal was enough to
give iron a special supernatural quality. Additionally, the first purified iron was
extracted from meteors that fell from the heavens.

The ancient Egyptians referred to iron as “the metal from the sky,” and the
Aztecs referred to iron as “the gift of heaven.”

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How much calcium is in the human body and where is it stored?
claims.answer_short: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body—about 1,200 g in men and 1,000 g in women—with 99 percent of it stored in the bones and teeth.
claims.answer: Wallach states that calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body: the average man carries about 1,200 grams (roughly 3 pounds) and the average woman about 1,000 grams (roughly 2 pounds), around two percent of body weight and up to 39 percent of the body's total mineral reserve. Ninety-nine percent of that calcium is held in the bones and teeth. The remaining one percent circulates in blood, extracellular fluid, and cells, where it acts as a cofactor and activator for numerous chemical, DNA, and enzymatic reactions.
claims.verbatim:
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body. The average male
has 1,200 grams (approximately 3 pounds) and the average female has 1,000
grams (approximately 2 pounds), which makes up about two percent of the
human body weight (water makes up 65 to 75%) and up to 39 percent of the
total mineral reserves of the human body (ash). Ninety-nine percent of the total
body calcium is found in the bones and teeth, and the remaining one percent is.
found in the blood, extracellular fluid, and within cells where it is a cofactor and
activator for numerous chemical, DNA, and enzymatic reactions.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What does calcium do in the body besides build bones?
claims.answer_short: Beyond bone structure, calcium is required for muscle contraction, blood clotting, nerve transmission, hormone secretion, and regulating the heartbeat.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that in addition to being a major structural mineral, calcium releases energy from ATP (adenosine triphosphate) for muscular contraction and drives blood clotting—ionized calcium triggers thromboplastin release, converts prothrombin to thrombin, and helps form the fibrin web that traps red blood cells into a clot. Calcium also mediates transport across cell and organelle membranes, releases neurotransmitters at synaptic junctions, and governs the synthesis and secretion of hormones and enzymes. He adds that it helps regulate the heartbeat, muscle tone, and the muscle's responsiveness to nerve stimulation.
claims.verbatim:
In addition to being a major structural mineral, Ca is also required for the
release of energy from ATP for muscular contraction, blood clotting (ionized
Ca stimulates the release of thromboplastin from the platelets, converts


prothrombin to thrombin, and thrombin facilitates the conversion of fibrinogen
to fibrin. Fibrin creates the protein “web” that traps the RBCs to form blood clots);
Ca mediates the transport function of cell and organelle membranes; Ca effects
the release of neurotransmitters at synaptic junctions; Ca mediates the synthesis,
secretion and metabolic effects of hormones and enzymes; Ca helps to regulate
the heartbeat, muscle tone and muscle receptiveness to nerve stimulation and
communication.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Does calcium need vitamin D to be absorbed?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach says vitamin D is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium (and phosphorus) in the bones and teeth.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that calcium cannot do its job without vitamin D: vitamin D is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium and phosphorus in the bones and teeth. This is why he ties calcium deficiency and bone disease so closely to vitamin D status and sunlight exposure.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin
D is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium
and phosphorus in the bones and teeth.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Can bone spurs and calcium deposits be reversed?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach says bone spurs, heel spurs, and calcium deposits form during raging osteoporosis and can be reversed and eliminated by supplementing with significant amounts of chelated and colloidal calcium.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that bone spurs, heel spurs, and calcium deposits are not a sign of too much calcium but of raging osteoporosis: they always develop at the insertions of tendons and ligaments as the body loses bone mineral. Rather than being permanent, he says they can be reversed and eliminated by supplementing with significant amounts of chelated and colloidal calcium sources.
claims.verbatim:
Bone spurs, heel spurs, and calcium deposits always develop at the sites
of insertions of tendons and ligaments during a raging osteoporosis. Bone
spurs, heel spurs, and calcium deposits can be reversed and eliminated by
supplementing with significant amounts of chelated and colloidal calcium
sources.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How did Wallach discover that kidney stones come from too little calcium?
claims.answer_short: In zoo tortoises and iguanas fed diets with no added calcium, Wallach found the calcium in their kidney stones had been leached from their own bones and shells during raging osteoporosis—proof stones come from too little calcium, not too much.
claims.answer: Working with zoo reptiles, Wallach found that tortoises and iguanas fed fruit, eggs, meat, and lettuce with no added calcium universally developed kidney stones. The calcium in those stones, he determined, came from the animals' own bones, skeletons, and shells, dissolved by raging osteoporosis when the diet lacked calcium. Because the same phenomenon was already well documented in domestic animals, he could cite refereed references showing kidney stones develop from too little dietary calcium, not too much.
claims.verbatim:
Where did the calcium come from that was in the tortoise and iguana kidney
stones? It came from the bones of the iguana and the skeleton and shell of
the tortoise when they didn’t enough calcium in their diet and they had raging
osteoporosis! The fact that kidney stones developed as the result of too little
calcium in the diet was well documented in domestic animals, so it was easy to
find appropriate refereed references for another journal article and for the book.

claims.subject: vitamin-b1
claims.question: What is Vitamin B1?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a water-soluble B-complex vitamin and an essential cofactor for energy production and the metabolism of carbohydrates.
claims.answer: Vitamin B1, also called thiamine, is one of the water-soluble vitamins of the B-complex. In Wallach's framework it is essential throughout life for tissue respiration and energy production: thiamine combines with phosphorus to form the coenzyme thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), which drives the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate at the entrance to the Krebs cycle. Because carbohydrate metabolism depends on thiamine, the daily requirement rises with the amount of dietary sugar and starch. Discovered in 1897 and isolated in 1911, thiamine is also the vitamin from which the word 'vitamin' itself was coined.
claims.verbatim:
This water soluble vitamin was discovered in 1897 and isolated in 1911.
It is a cofactor required for energy production and optimal metabolism of
carbohydrates.

claims.subject: vitamin-b1
claims.question: What does vitamin B1 do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Thiamine is a cofactor for energy production; it forms the coenzyme TPP that drives the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate at the entry to the Krebs cycle.
claims.answer: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a water-soluble vitamin that acts as a cofactor required for energy production and the optimal metabolism of carbohydrates. It combines with phosphorus to form the coenzyme thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), which works as a cocarboxylase enzyme. TPP is required for the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate into active acetate and acetyl coenzyme A, the critical compound of the Krebs cycle. Wallach notes the vitamin was discovered in 1897 and isolated in 1911.
claims.verbatim:
This water soluble vitamin was discovered in 1897 and isolated in 1911.
It is a cofactor required for energy production and optimal metabolism of
carbohydrates. Thiamine combines with phosphorous to form the coenzyme
thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), which functions as a cocarboxylase enzyme. TPP
is required for the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to form active acetate
and acetyl coenzyme A, the critical compound of the Krebs cycle.

claims.subject: vitamin-b1
claims.question: Can vitamin B1 reverse memory loss or dementia?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cured a patient misdiagnosed with Alzheimer's — who actually had Korsakoff's syndrome, a single thiamine-deficiency disease — in one week using mega-doses of thiamine.
claims.answer: Wallach treats all four forms of dementia simultaneously because doctors get the diagnosis wrong about 65% of the time. In one case, a patient diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease was actually afflicted with Korsakoff's syndrome — a disease of a single vitamin deficiency (thiamine, B1), first diagnosed and solved in the late 1700s by a Japanese naval surgeon. Because mega-doses of thiamine were included in the treatment, the patient was cured in a week; had he continued on Alzheimer's drug programs alone, Wallach says he would have died of the complications of Alzheimer's.
claims.verbatim:
he was afflicted with Korsakoff’s syndrome, a disease of a single vitamin
deficiency (thiamin B,) first diagnosed and solved in the late 1700s by a
Japanese naval surgeon, Because mega doses of thiamine were included
in the treatment, the patient was cured in a week

claims.subject: vitamin-b1
claims.question: How was beriberi proven to be a dietary disease?
claims.answer_short: Japanese naval surgeon Takaki proved beriberi came from diet: one ship returned in 1883 with 25 dead and 144 stricken sailors, and correcting the diet on later voyages nearly eliminated it.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts the naval evidence that beriberi is a dietary deficiency disease. The Japanese ship Riuyo returned from an extended voyage in 1883 with 25 dead sailors and 144 others stricken with beriberi. In 1884 naval surgeon Kanekiro Takaki joined an identical voyage and proved that a diet built primarily on polished rice was the cause; by changing the diet to include sources of thiamine (vitamin B1), the disease could be prevented and cured.
claims.verbatim:
The Riuyo, a Japanese naval ship with a complement of 276 men, returned
from an extended voyage in 1883 with 25 dead sailors and 144 other crew
members stricken with beriberi. In 1884 Takaki was able to convince the Japanese
naval command to allow him to join the crew of a second ship going on an
identical voyage.

claims.subject: vitamin-b1
claims.question: Why are vitamins called vitamins?
claims.answer_short: The word 'vitamin' traces to thiamine: Funk's crystalline anti-beriberi substance was a basic (vital) amine, which he named a 'vital amine' — later shortened to vitamin.
claims.answer: The very word 'vitamin' traces back to thiamine (vitamin B1). Wallach explains that Funk produced a crystalline substance from rice polishings and yeast that could prevent and cure experimentally produced beriberi. Because the substance was a basic (high-pH) nitrogen compound — an amine essential to life — Funk called it a 'vit- (vital) amine.' The term was then accepted as a broad label for dietary substances deemed to be dietary essentials.
claims.verbatim:
Some years later, Funk produced a crystalline substance
from rice polishings and yeast that was effective in the prevention and cure
of experimentally produced beriberi. The substance contained a high pH (basic)
nitrogen (amine), so Funk called it a vit- (vital) amine. The term was accepted as a
broad label for dietary substances that were deemed to be dietary essentials.

claims.subject: vitamin-b2
claims.question: What is Vitamin B2?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) is a water-soluble B vitamin that acts as a cofactor for the flavin coenzymes FMN and FAD, which the body needs for energy production.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework, vitamin B2 — riboflavin — is a water-soluble B vitamin and a key cofactor for two flavin coenzymes, flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), that drive the oxidation-reduction reactions behind cellular energy production. Riboflavin-dependent enzymes also activate vitamin B6 and help convert tryptophan into niacin, and the vitamin is required to maintain healthy skin, mucous membranes, the cornea of the eye, and nerve sheaths. A shortage shows up early as cracks at the corners of the mouth (cheilosis), a sore burning tongue, and light-sensitive eyes.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B,, discovered in 1879 and isolated in 1932, is a key cofactor for
two flavin coenzymes that are required for oxidation-reduction reactions and

energy production flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide


(FAD).

claims.subject: vitamin-b2
claims.question: What does vitamin B2 (riboflavin) do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Riboflavin is a cofactor for the flavin coenzymes FMN and FAD that drive oxidation-reduction reactions and energy production.
claims.answer: Wallach describes vitamin B2 (riboflavin) as a key cofactor for two flavin coenzymes — flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) — that are required for oxidation-reduction reactions and energy production. Riboflavin-dependent enzymes also activate vitamin B6 (converting phosphorylated pyridoxine into its functional coenzyme) and help convert tryptophan into niacin. On top of that, it is needed to maintain healthy skin, mucous membranes, the cornea of the eye, and nerve sheaths.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B,, discovered in 1879 and isolated in 1932, is a key cofactor for
two flavin coenzymes that are required for oxidation-reduction reactions and

energy production flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide


(FAD). Among the enzymes that require riboflavin is the FMN-dependent oxidase
responsible for conversion of phosphorylated pyridoxine to functional coenzyme
and the FAD-dependent hydroxylase involved in the conversion of tryptophan to
niacin. Riboflavin is also required to maintain healthy skin, mucus membranes,
cornea of the eye, and nerve sheaths.

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: What is niacin (vitamin B3)?
claims.answer_short: Niacin, or vitamin B3, is a water-soluble B vitamin the body turns into the coenzymes NAD and NADP to release energy from food; a severe deficiency causes pellagra.
claims.answer: Niacin — vitamin B3 — is a water-soluble B vitamin that Wallach also names nicotinic acid, nicotinamide, or niacinamide. Isolated in 1900, it works in the body as part of two coenzymes, NAD and NADP (the pyridine nucleotides), which cells use to release energy from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. The body can also make its own niacin from the amino acid tryptophan. A severe niacin deficiency produces pellagra — the classic 'three Ds' of dermatitis, dementia, and diarrhea — and Wallach uses niacin at doses far above the RDA for problems ranging from high cholesterol to schizophrenia.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B,, isolated in 1900, functions in humans as a part of the coenzymes
nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide
phosphate (NADP), known as the pyridine nucleotides.

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: What does vitamin B3 (niacin) actually do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Niacin forms the coenzymes NAD and NADP, which cells use to release energy from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.
claims.answer: Niacin (also called nicotinic acid, nicotinamide, or niacinamide) was isolated in 1900 and works as part of two coenzymes: nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP), together known as the pyridine nucleotides. These coenzymes interact with the cell's respiratory enzymes and are essential to the oxidation-reduction reactions that release energy from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. In their reduced forms they become NADH and NADPH, and NAD is also required for glycogen synthesis.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B, (niacin, nicotinic acid, nicotinamide, niacinamide) function:

Vitamin B,, isolated in 1900, functions in humans as a part of the coenzymes
nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide
phosphate (NADP), known as the pyridine nucleotides. These coenzymes interact
with cellular respiratory enzymes. They are essential to the oxidation-reduction
reactions in the release of energy from carbohydrates, fats and proteins. These
coenzymes in their reduced forms are NADH and NADPH. In addition NAD is
required for glycogen synthesis.

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: Why does eating a lot of corn cause pellagra?
claims.answer_short: Corn is not poisonous, but the little niacin it contains is not easily used by humans, so a corn-heavy diet leaves people niacin-deficient.
