claims.answer: Corn itself is not poisonous, but the small amount of niacin it naturally contains is not easily used by the human body, so a high-corn diet produces the dermatitis, dementia, and diarrhea of classic pellagra. The Indians of the New World ate corn for centuries without harm because their diets also included beans, squash, chilies, and coffee — foods rich in niacin. In Mexico, women soaked the ground corn in lime water before making tortillas, which increased the availability of the little niacin the corn contained.
claims.verbatim:
Corn in of itself is not poisonous. However, the little niacin that occurs
naturally in corn is not easily used by humans and the resulting deficiency that
occurs in a high-corn diet produces the skin disease (dermatitis), dementia, and
diarrhea of classic pellagra.

The Indians of the New World subsisted on a corn-based diet for centuries
without ill effect because their diets also included beans, squash, chilies, and
coffee—common foods that are rich in niacin. In Mexico the Indian women soaked
the corn in lime water after they ground the grain for tortillas, which produced
increased availability of the small amounts of niacin naturally found in the corn.

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: How much tryptophan does the body need to make niacin?
claims.answer_short: By convention, 60 mg of the amino acid tryptophan equals 1 mg of niacin, though studies found the amount ranged from 39 to 86 mg.
claims.answer: The body can make its own niacin from the amino acid tryptophan. When niacin status was gauged by urinary metabolite levels, the amount of supplementary tryptophan needed to produce the same effect as one milligram of niacin ranged from 39 to 86 mg. By convention, 60 mg of tryptophan is treated as equivalent to one mg of niacin.
claims.verbatim:
When niacin status was gauged by urinary metablyte levels,
the quantities of supplementary tryptophan required to give the same response
as one mg of niacin ranged from 39 to 86 mg. Convention allows that 60 mg of
tryptophan is equivalent to one mg of niacin,

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: What are the side effects of too much niacin?
claims.answer_short: Overdosing on nicotinic acid can cause hot skin flushes, ulcers, liver disease, elevated blood sugar and uric acid, cardiac arrhythmia, and dry, itchy skin.
claims.answer: Wallach draws a sharp line: it is specifically the nicotinic-acid form of niacin (vitamin B3) that can cause overdose trouble. Too much brings on the hot skin 'flush' niacin is famous for, plus ulcers, liver disease, raised blood sugar and uric acid, cardiac arrhythmia, and dry, itchy skin. He points out the same high pharmacological doses (three to nine grams a day) are also what doctors use deliberately to lower cholesterol.
claims.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: Vitamin B; (nicotinic acid only) overdose can result in hot
flushes of the skin, ulcers, liver disease, elevated blood sugar and uric acid, cardiac
arrhythmia, and dry, itchy skin.

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: Who discovered that niacin cures pellagra?
claims.answer_short: Dr. Joseph Goldberger proved pellagra was a dietary deficiency, and in 1937 Conrad Elvehjem showed niacin (nicotinic acid) cured it.
claims.answer: Dr. Joseph Goldberger was one of the first physicians convinced pellagra was a deficiency disease. He fed children in a Mississippi orphanage on a corn-based diet meat, milk, and eggs, and their pellagra disappeared; in a classic 1915 experiment he induced pellagra in Mississippi prison-farm inmates fed a typical pellagra diet, then reversed it by adding meat, milk, or yeast. Physicians stayed skeptical until 1937, when Conrad Elvehjem at the University of Wisconsin reported that dogs with experimentally produced pellagra could be cured with a form of niacin called nicotinic acid.
claims.verbatim:
Dr.Joseph Goldberger, was one of the first physicians to be convinced that
pellagra was a deficiency disease. He began to experiment with the diets of
children in a Mississippi orphanage who were on a corn-based diet and suffered
from pellagra. After adding meat, milk, and eggs to their diets, pellagra
disappeared.

In 1915 Dr. Goldberger conducted a classic experiment in human nutrition. For
six months Goldberger fed prisoners in a Mississippi prison farm the typical diet
of people who were hard hit with pellagra. After they developed symptoms of the
disease he changed their diets to include meat, milk, or yeast and the symptoms
rapidly disappeared.

Physicians remained skeptical until 1937, when Conrad Elvehjem at the
University of Wisconsin reported that dogs with experimentally produced
pellagra could be cured with a form of “niacin” named nicotinic acid.

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: Where did pellagra come from and why did it appear in Europe?
claims.answer_short: Pellagra was unknown in Europe until Columbus brought corn from the New World; peasants who became dependent on corn developed the disease.
claims.answer: Wallach traces pellagra to the arrival of corn: the disease was unknown in Europe until Christopher Columbus brought the first corn seeds back from the New World. European peasants embraced corn as an easy 'miracle crop' and became dependent on it, and whole villages and towns then came down with what Wallach calls the 'four Ds' — dermatitis (skin disease), dementia, diarrhea, and death. That was pellagra.
claims.verbatim:
Pellagra is considered a “new disease” in the civilized world, as it was unknown
in Europe until Christopher Columbus delivered the first corn seeds from the
“New World" to Europe. The European peasant looked upon corn as an easy to
produce miracle crop; it spread quickly as a food crop and the peasants became
dependent on corn.

Corn was the beginning of the end for millions of people. Complete villages
and towns came down with a plague of skin disease (dermatitis), dementia,
diarthea, and death (the four Ds—pellagra had arrived.)

claims.subject: vitamin-b5
claims.question: Does vitamin B5 help make energy and hormones?
claims.answer_short: Yes — through coenzyme A, vitamin B5 helps release energy from carbohydrates and helps build fatty acids, steroid hormones, and acetylcholine.
claims.answer: As a component of coenzyme A, pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) drives acyl-group activation and transfer reactions. Wallach explains these reactions are essential for releasing energy from carbohydrates, for gluconeogenesis, for the synthesis and breakdown of fatty acids, and for making key compounds including sterols, steroid hormones, porphyrins, and acetylcholine. That places B5 at the heart of both energy production and the manufacture of hormones and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.
claims.verbatim:
that serves in acyl-group activation and transfer reactions. These reactions are
essential for the release of energy from carbohydrates; in gluconeogenesis; in
the synthesis and degradation of fatty acids; in the synthesis of such essential
compounds as sterols and steroid hormones, porphyrins, and acetylcholine; and
in acylation reactions.

claims.subject: vitamin-b5
claims.question: Can you take too much vitamin B5?
claims.answer_short: Only at extreme amounts — pantothenic acid at 10 to 20 grams a day can cause a relative thiamine deficiency, diarrhea, and edema.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) can be overdone at very high amounts. Signs of overdose appear at 10 to 20 grams per day and can include a relative deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1), diarrhea, and edema (fluid swelling). These are gram-level doses, far above the milligram amounts used for ordinary daily supplementation.
claims.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: Vitamin B, overdose (10 to 20 grams per day) can result in a
relative deficiency of thiamine, diarrhea, and edema.

claims.subject: vitamin-b5
claims.question: How was vitamin B5 discovered?
claims.answer_short: Scientists found pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) in the 1930s by accident, while searching for a nutrient that would make yeast grow.
claims.answer: Pantothenic acid, vitamin B5, was discovered in the 1930s essentially by accident. The scientists were not looking for the cause, prevention, or cure of any particular disease; they were searching for a nutrient that would stimulate the growth of yeast. Along the way they found a substance that supported yeast growth and that, when missing from animal diets, produced deficiency diseases. Wallach notes the vitamin was formally isolated in 1940.
claims.verbatim:
When scientists discovered pantothenic acid in the 1930s, they were not
searching for a cause, prevention, or cure for any particular disease. In fact, they
were looking for a nutrient that would stimulate the growth of yeast. Along the
way, investigators found a substance that would support the growth of yeast, that
when missing in animal diets would produce deficiency diseases.

claims.subject: vitamin-b5
claims.question: What happens to animals deficient in pantothenic acid?
claims.answer_short: Animals on pantothenic-acid-deficient diets showed stunted growth, anemia, nerve damage, weak immunity, gastric ulcers, and many birth defects.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that pantothenic acid deficiency looks different from one animal species to another, but common threads emerge. Animals placed on pantothenic acid-deficient diets demonstrated a reduced growth rate, anemia, nerve degenerative diseases, reduced immune functions, gastric ulcers, and a wide variety of birth defects. This animal evidence underscores how broadly the vitamin affects growth, the nervous system, immunity, and development.
claims.verbatim:
The symptoms of pantothenic acid deficiency varied from one animal species
to another. In general, however, animals that were placed on pantothenic acid-
deficient diets demonstrated a reduced growth rate, anemia, nerve degenerative
diseases, reduced immune functions, gastric ulcers, and a wide variety of birth
defects.

claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: What is Vitamin B6?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is a B-complex vitamin that occurs in three related forms — pyridoxine, pyridoxal, and pyridoxamine — which the body converts into active coenzymes for amino-acid, fat, and energy metabolism.
claims.answer: Vitamin B6, commonly called pyridoxine, is not a single molecule but a functional complex of three closely related compounds: pyridoxine, pyridoxal, and pyridoxamine. The body converts these into the active coenzymes pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) and pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP), which drive transamination — the building up and breaking down of amino acids — and act as essential cofactors in the metabolism of proteins, fats, and stored sugar. In Wallach's framework B6 is a workhorse nutrient: he considers shortfalls common in the population and reaches for it across a wide range of conditions, from epilepsy and pregnancy-related morning sickness to alcoholism.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin Bg, originally designated B3, is found as three chemically, metabolically,
and functionally related structures pyridoxine (pyridoxol, PN), pyridoxal (PL), and

pyridoxamine (PM). These structures are converted in the liver, red blood cells,
and other tissues to pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) and pyridoxamine phosphate
(PMP), which act primarily as coenzymes in transamination reactions.

claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: What does vitamin B6 do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Its active form PLP is a coenzyme for amino-acid, lipid and nucleic-acid metabolism and for glycogen phosphorylase.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the active form of B6, pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), participates in the decarboxylation and racemization of amino acids, in other transformations of amino acids, and in the metabolism of lipids and nucleic acids. Beyond amino-acid chemistry, B6 is the essential coenzyme for glycogen phosphorylase, the enzyme that releases stored sugar. That makes it central to how the body handles proteins, fats, and energy.
claims.verbatim:
PLP
also participates in decarboxylation and racemization of A in amino acids, in
other metabolic transformations of amino acids, and the metabolism of lipids
and nucleic acids. In addition, Bg is the essential coenzyme for glycogen
phosphorylase.

claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: Does vitamin B6 need other B vitamins to work?
claims.answer_short: Yes — riboflavin (B2) powers the enzyme that converts B6 into its active coenzyme form.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that among the enzymes requiring riboflavin (vitamin B2) is the FMN-dependent oxidase responsible for converting phosphorylated pyridoxine into its functional coenzyme. In practical terms, the body needs adequate B2 to activate vitamin B6 — an example of how the B vitamins work together rather than in isolation.
claims.verbatim:
Among the enzymes that require riboflavin is the FMN-dependent oxidase
responsible for conversion of phosphorylated pyridoxine to functional coenzyme

claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: Can you take too much vitamin B6?
claims.answer_short: Yes — excess B6 can cause peripheral neuropathy, with nerve damage in the fingers and legs.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that vitamin B6 can cause harm at excessive intakes. The sign of overdose is peripheral neuropathy — nerve damage that shows up in the fingers and legs.
claims.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: Vitamin B, overdose can result in peripheral neuropathies in
fingers and legs.

claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: Are most people deficient in vitamin B6?
claims.answer_short: A 1980 US survey found half of those surveyed consumed less than 70% of the RDA for pyridoxine.
claims.answer: Wallach cites the Nationwide Food Consumption Survey done in 1980, which found that US consumption of pyridoxine fell below 70% of the RDA in 50% of the individuals surveyed — that is, half of those surveyed took in less than 70% of the official RDA for vitamin B6.
claims.verbatim:
The Nationwide Food Consumption Survey done in 1980 revealed that the
US. consumption of pyridoxine fell below 70% of the RDA in 50% of the
individuals surveyed.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: What is folate?
claims.answer_short: Folate — vitamin B-9, also called folic acid or folacin — is an essential B vitamin the body needs to build DNA, RNA, and red blood cells. Wallach calls its deficiency perhaps the most common vitamin deficiency in humans.
claims.answer: Folate, known as vitamin B-9 and also called folic acid or folacin, is one of the essential B vitamins. Wallach explains that it was first identified in 1946 and is required for the synthesis of DNA and RNA and the formation of erythrocytes (red blood cells). Metabolically it acts as a coenzyme that shuttles single carbon units during amino acid metabolism and nucleic acid synthesis, working hand-in-hand with vitamin B12 — so a shortage of either vitamin produces the same megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia. Because folate builds the genetic material of every dividing cell, Wallach ties its deficiency to anemia, birth defects such as spina bifida, and a long list of other problems, and considers it perhaps the most common vitamin deficiency in humans.
claims.verbatim:
Folic acid was identified in 1946. It is required for the synthesis of DNA and RNA
and erythrocytes.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: What does folic acid do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Folic acid works as a coenzyme that shuttles single carbon units in amino acid and DNA/RNA synthesis, working hand-in-hand with vitamin B12.
claims.answer: Folic acid (folate) acts metabolically as a coenzyme that transports single carbon units from one compound to another during amino acid metabolism and the synthesis of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). Folate and vitamin B12 work interdependently, so a shortage of either vitamin produces the same kind of megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia. This role in building DNA and RNA makes folic acid essential to cell division and the formation of red blood cells.
claims.verbatim:
Folates act metabolically as coenzymes that transport single carbon units
from one compound to another in amino acid metabolism and nucleic acid (DNA
and RNA) synthesis. Folates and vitamin B,, work interdependently. A deficiency
of either vitamin produces a megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: Can you be deficient in folic acid even if you take enough of it?
claims.answer_short: Yes — because vitamin B12 is needed to release folate into a usable form, a B12 deficiency causes a folic acid deficiency even when folic acid intake is optimal.
claims.answer: Vitamin B12 plays a key role in folic acid metabolism: it is required to release free folate from its bound form so the folate can be absorbed, transported, and stored. Because of this, a deficiency of vitamin B12 will produce a folic acid deficiency even though the intake of folic acid is optimal. B12 also supports bone marrow function and the production of myelin, the insulating coating around nerve fibers.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B,, is required to support the function of bone marrow
and the production of myelin (nerve fiber insulation coating) and a key role in
folic acid metabolism. It is required to release free folate from its bound form so it,
can be absorbed, transported and stored. A deficiency of vitamin B,, will result in
a folic acid deficiency even though the intake of folic acid is optimal.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: What medications interfere with folic acid?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says many drugs block folic acid absorption and metabolism, including methotrexate, aspirin, oral contraceptives, anti-convulsants, anti-psoriatic drugs, and cancer chemotherapy.
claims.answer: Many medications interfere with folic acid absorption and metabolism, according to Wallach, including methotrexate, aspirin, oral contraceptives, anti-convulsives, anti-psoriatic drugs, and cancer treatment pharmaceuticals. People taking these drugs are therefore at greater risk of a folic acid deficiency. He notes that malabsorption conditions such as gluten intolerance, celiac disease, leaky gut syndrome, and IBS can also drive the deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Many medications interfere with folic acid absorption and metabolism

including methotrexate, aspirin, oral contraceptives, anti-convulsives, anti-
psoriatic, and cancer treatment pharmaceuticals.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: Can you take too much folic acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach warns that an overdose of folic acid can cause a relative zinc deficiency by impairing zinc absorption.
claims.answer: Wallach cautions that folic acid is not risk-free at high intake: an overdose of folic acid can cause a relative zinc deficiency by impairing absorption. In other words, taking too much folic acid can lower the body's zinc status even when zinc intake is unchanged.
claims.verbatim:
Overdose of folic acid: This can cause a relative zinc deficiency by impairing

absorption.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: Who discovered folic acid?
claims.answer_short: In 1930 Lucy Wills and her team reported that yeast contained a substance that could cure macrocytic anemia in pregnant women; folic acid itself was not isolated until 1946.
claims.answer: The discovery of folic acid traces to 1930, when Lucy Wills and her investigating team reported that yeast contained a substance that could cure macrocytic anemia in pregnant women. That substance, however, was not actually isolated as folic acid until 1946. Folic acid is a generic term for compounds chemically related to pteroylglutamic acid (PGA).
claims.verbatim:
In 1930 Lucy
Wills and her investigating team reported that “yeast contained a substance that
could cure macrocytic anemia in pregnant women. However, it was not until 1946
that folic acid was isolated.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: How are vitamin B12 and folic acid related?
claims.answer_short: B12 is required to release folate from its bound form, so a B12 deficiency creates a folic acid deficiency even when folate intake is high.
claims.answer: Vitamin B12 and folate are both required to synthesize the DNA and RNA that carry the human genome in every cell, and B12 plays a key role in folic acid metabolism. Specifically, B12 is needed to release free folate from its bound form so folate can be absorbed, transported, and stored. As a result, a deficiency of B12 produces a folic acid deficiency even when folic acid intake is optimal, and a deficiency of either vitamin produces the same kind of macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B,, and folate are both
required for the synthesis of DNA and RNA, which carry the human genome for
every living cell. Vitamin B,, is required to support the function of bone marrow
and the production of myelin (nerve fiber insulation coating) and a key role in
folic acid metabolism. It is required to release free folate from its bound form so it,
can be absorbed, transported and stored. A deficiency of vitamin B,, will result in
a folic acid deficiency even though the intake of folic acid is optimal. A deficiency
of either vitamin produces a similar form of macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: Where does vitamin B12 come from?
claims.answer_short: B12 comes from animal products and bacterial fermentation, because only bacteria, fungi, and algae can actually make it — plants and animals cannot.
claims.answer: Animal products and bacterial fermentation are the most common sources of vitamin B12. In meat the most common forms are adenosyl- and hydroxocobalamin, while in dairy products (including human breast milk) they are methyl- and hydroxocobalamin. The key reason B12 is essentially an animal-food nutrient is that only bacteria, fungi, and algae can synthesize it; yeast, higher plants, and all animals cannot make it themselves.
claims.verbatim:
Animal products and bacterial
fermentation are the most common sources of B,2. The most common forms
of By, in meat are adenosyl-and hydroxocobalamin; in dairy products (including
human breast milk) the most common forms are methyl-and hydroxocobalamin.

Bacteria, fungi, and algae can synthesize vitamin B,>. However, yeast, higher
plants and animals of all forms are unable to.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: What is the difference between cyanocobalamin and the natural forms of B12?
claims.answer_short: Cyanocobalamin is the primary commercial form of B12 in supplements; the body strips off the cyanide and converts it to the metabolically useful forms found in the tissues.
claims.answer: Cyanocobalamin is the primary commercial form of vitamin B12 found in vitamin pills and pharmaceuticals. It is water soluble and heat resistant, and once ingested or injected the body converts it, by removing the cyanide, into the forms that are actually useful in the tissues. In plasma and tissue the primary forms of B12 are methylcobalamin, adenosylcobalamin, and hydroxocobalamin.
claims.verbatim:
Cyanocobalamin is the primary commercial form of vitamin B;>
found in vitamin pills and pharmaceuticals. This form is water soluble and heat
resistant, and when it is ingested or injected it is converted (by the removal
of cyanide) to the forms that are metabolically useful in vertebrates including
humans.

In plasma and tissue, the primary forms of B,, are methylcobalamin,
adenosylcobalamin, and hydroxocobalamin.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: What causes vitamin B12 deficiency?
claims.answer_short: B12 deficiency comes from a poor diet, low stomach acid, salt deficiency, and gluten intolerance.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, a vitamin B12 deficiency can arise directly from an inadequate diet. It can also occur secondarily, driven by hypochlorhydria (a lack of stomach acid), by salt deficiency, and by gluten intolerance. This means B12 status is not just about how much you eat but about whether your stomach and gut can actually absorb it.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiency: The deficiency of cyanocobalamine can result from an overt dietary
deficiency as well as secondary to hypochlorhydria (lack of stomach acid), salt
deficiency, and gluten intolerance.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: Can you take too much vitamin B12?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports that no clear toxicity has been reported from daily oral B12 in doses of up to 100 mcg.
claims.answer: On the question of vitamin B12 overdose, Wallach reports that no clear toxicity has been documented — specifically, that 'no clear toxicity has been reported from daily oral consumption of B12 in doses of up to 100 ug' (100 micrograms).
claims.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: For vitamin B,, overdose: “No clear toxicity has been reported
from daily oral consumption of B,, in doses of up to 100 ug.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: How was vitamin B12 discovered?
claims.answer_short: The search began in 1926 after doctors found that eating a pound of raw liver a day cured pernicious anemia; the pure vitamin was finally isolated in 1948.
claims.answer: The hunt for vitamin B12 began in 1926, prompted by the observation that people with pernicious anemia could cure themselves by eating a pound of raw liver every day. Dr. William Castle theorized that liver held an 'antipernicious anemia' (APA) factor, and that sufferers were missing an 'intrinsic factor' needed to use it. The search dragged on for decades because humans store and recycle B12, until 1948, when two independent teams in the UK and the US finally isolated the pure vitamin, extracting just 20 mg from a ton of liver.
claims.verbatim:
The search for vitamin B,, began in 1926, following the observation that
individuals with pernicious anemia could cure the disease by consuming a pound


of raw liver per day.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: How does copper help the body use oxygen?
claims.answer_short: Copper proteins carry and process oxygen and drive cellular respiration; in mollusks the copper-based carrier hemocyanin even makes their blood blue.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that copper proteins play a wide role in biological electron transport and oxygen transportation, using the easy interconversion between copper's two forms. He notes copper's biological role began with the appearance of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere, and points to hemocyanin, the copper-based oxygen carrier in most mollusks and some arthropods like the horseshoe crab, which gives those animals blue blood rather than the red blood of hemoglobin-using vertebrates. Copper also partners with iron in cytochrome c oxidase for aerobic respiration and appears in the superoxide dismutases that break down damaging superoxides.
claims.verbatim:
Copper proteins have a wide role in biological electron transport and oxygen
transportation, processes that make use of the simple interconversion of Cu(!)
and Cu(ll). The biological role of copper started with the formation of oxygen in
the earth's atmosphere. The protein hemocyanin is the oxygen carrier for most
mollusks and some arthropods (such as the horseshoe crab, Limulus polyphemus).
Because hemocyanin is blue, these invertebrates have blue blood, not the red
blood found in vertebrates that use hemoglobin.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What causes Kawasaki disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says Kawasaki disease is not genetic but a congenital copper deficiency that leaves a baby with a weak coronary artery aneurysm, later infected by strep.
claims.answer: Wallach rejects the idea that Kawasaki disease is genetically transmitted, calling it a congenital copper deficiency with two parts. First, the infant is born with a congenital coronary artery aneurysm, a ballooning or separation of the artery layers, initiated by a copper deficiency because copper is required to build and maintain the elastic fibers in arteries. Second, a streptococcal infection sets up in the damaged artery wall. He considers the disease totally preventable with preconception supplementation of all 90 essential nutrients, extra copper, and antibiotics.
claims.verbatim:
Kawasaki Disease, thought by the medical community to be a genetically-
transmitted disease, is in fact a congenital copper deficiency that has two parts.
The human infant born with Kawasaki Disease is born with a congenital coronary
artery aneurysm (a separation of the middle and inner layers of the artery or
a ballooning of a weakened coronary artery), which is in fact initiated by a
congenital copper deficiency, copper being required to manufacture and maintain
elastic fibers in arteries as well as other tissues.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: Is mad cow disease caused by copper deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach argues that mad cow disease (BSE) and CJD are copper-deficiency diseases, not prion infections, pointing to identical brain lesions and copper-poor soils where cases cluster.
claims.answer: Wallach contends that BSE (mad cow disease) in cattle and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans are copper-deficiency diseases rather than infectious prion diseases. He points out that the brain lesions in sheep with enzootic ataxia, a known copper-deficiency disease, are identical to the lesions in cattle with BSE and humans with CJD, and that cases of BSE and CJD are typically diagnosed in geographic areas where the soils are copper deficient. He also notes that attempts to transmit the disease by injecting prions have failed to satisfy Koch's postulates.
claims.verbatim:
It is obvious that the brain lesions in sheep afflicted with enzootic ataxia,
a known copper-deficiency disease, are identical to the brain lesions in cattle
afflicted with BSE and also to the brain lesions in humans afflicted with CJD.
The preponderance of the cases of BSE in cattle and CJD in humans are typically
diagnosed in geographical areas where the soils are copper deficient.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: How do you test chromium levels, and how much is in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says hair analysis is far more accurate than blood for chromium because hair holds ten times more, and the body contains about 1.5 mg under optimal conditions.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that concentrations of chromium in human hair are ten times greater than in blood, which makes hair analysis a much more accurate view of chromium stores and function than a blood test. He puts the average amount in the human body at about 1.5 mg under optimal conditions. Hair analysis therefore gives a truer picture of a person's chromium status.
claims.verbatim:
Concentrations of chromium in human hair is ten times greater than in blood,
making hair analysis a much more accurate view of chromium stores and function
in the human (there is an average of 1.5 mg in the human body under optimal
conditions).

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: How much chromium do you actually absorb from food?
claims.answer_short: Very little — 50 to 100 mcg of inorganic chromium from food yields only 0.25 to 0.5 mcg usable, whereas 25 percent of chelated chromium is absorbed.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that the average daily intake of 50 to 100 micrograms of inorganic chromium from food supplies only 0.25 to 0.5 micrograms of usable chromium. By contrast, about 25 percent of chelated chromium is absorbed. This is why he favors well-absorbed chelated forms over the inorganic chromium found in ordinary food.
claims.verbatim:
The average human daily intake of 50 to 100 ug of inorganic Cr from food
supplies only 0.25 to 0.5 ug of usable chromium, by contrast 25% of chelated
chromium is absorbed.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Is type 2 diabetes genetic or caused by a mineral deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach insists type 2 diabetes is not genetically transmitted — it is in fact a simple mineral deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach argues that type 2 diabetes is not a genetically transmitted disease but a simple mineral deficiency. He points to Walter Mertz, director of the USDA field services, whose research in Federation Proceedings showed an entire medical specialty, endocrinology, could be wiped out by universally adding chromium to an otherwise perfect diet. In his view, supplying chromium addresses the real cause.
claims.verbatim:
an entire medical specialty (endocrinology) would be
wiped out by universally adding chromium to an otherwise perfect diet. Type 2
diabetes is not a genetically-transmitted disease—it is in fact a simple mineral
deficiency!

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: What was chromium used for in ancient times?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts that over 2,000 years ago the Chinese coated the Terracotta Army's bronze weapons with chromium oxide, which kept them from corroding.
claims.answer: Wallach relates that chromium oxide was used by the Chinese in the Qin dynasty over 2,000 years ago to coat the metal weapons found with the Terracotta Army at Xi'an. The bronze tips of crossbow bolts and swords at the site showed very little oxidation or corrosion because the bronze was deliberately coated with a thin layer of chromium oxide. He offers this as an early demonstration of chromium's corrosion resistance.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium oxide was employed by the Chinese in the Qin dynasty over 2,000
years ago in the late 34 century BC to coat the metal weapons found in Xi'an
with the Terracotta Army. The ancient bronze tips of crossbow bolts and swords
found at the site had very little oxidation or corrosion because the bronze was
deliberately coated with a thin layer of chromium oxide.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: What is Vitamin E?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant vitamin — actually a family of compounds called tocopherols — that protects cell membranes and red blood cells from oxidative damage.
claims.answer: Wallach describes vitamin E as a fat-soluble vitamin, first isolated in 1922, that is not a single molecule but a family of related compounds called tocopherols (specifically the alpha-tocopherols). Its core job is antioxidant protection: it shields cell membranes from oxidative inflammation and keeps red blood cells from rupturing (lysis). Working alongside the trace mineral selenium it also lowers the risk of certain cancers, slows the aging process, and helps preserve the length of telomeres. This antioxidant role is the foundation for its wider benefits across the heart, brain, muscles, and reproduction.
claims.verbatim:
This fat soluble vitamin, isolated in 1922, is actually a group of compounds
referred to as alpha-tocopherols. It has antioxidant functions, protects cell
membranes from oxidative inflammation, protects red blood cells from lyses,

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: What does vitamin E do for the body?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin E slows aging and preserves telomere length; combined with selenium it reduces the risk of certain cancers, and Wallach also links it to a lower risk of Alzheimer's disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, muscular dystrophy and cystic fibrosis.
claims.answer: Beyond its antioxidant role, Wallach credits vitamin E with slowing the aging process and helping preserve the length of telomeres, the protective caps on chromosomes tied to cellular aging. Working together with the trace mineral selenium, it can reduce the risk of certain cancers. He also links adequate vitamin E to a lower risk of Alzheimer's disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, muscular dystrophy, and cystic fibrosis.
claims.verbatim:
in combination with the trace mineral selenium it can reduce the risk of certain
cancers. It slows down the aging process, preserves the length of telomeres and
reduces the risk of Alzheimer's disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, muscular
dystrophy, and cystic fibrosis, etc.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Can you take too much vitamin E?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls vitamin E extremely safe by mouth — most adults have no problem up to 800 mg a day with no signs of toxicity.
claims.answer: Compared with the other fat-soluble vitamins, Wallach considers vitamin E to be extremely safe when taken by mouth. He states that most adults can take up to 800 mg per day without showing any clinical or biochemical signs of toxicity.
claims.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: Compared to the other fat soluble vitamins vitamin E is
extremely safe when taken orally. Most adults have no problems taking up to 800
mg/day, showing no clinical or biochemical signs of toxicity.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Why does Wallach say Alzheimer's disease isn't genetic?
claims.answer_short: Because supplementing with only vitamin E measurably improved advanced Alzheimer's patients — and a vitamin can't change a truly genetic disease.
claims.answer: Wallach argues that Alzheimer's disease cannot be genetic, pointing to 1992 research from the Salk Institute and UCSD showing that supplementation with only vitamin E produced measurable improvement in advanced Alzheimer's patients. His reasoning is that if a simple vitamin can change how the disease manifests, then it cannot be a truly genetically transmitted disease. For Wallach this is evidence that Alzheimer's is fundamentally a nutritional problem rather than an inherited one.
claims.verbatim:
Wallach also noted in DDDL that Alzheimer's disease could not be
genetic because research reported in 1992 by the Salk Institute and UCSD
demonstrated that “supplementation with only vitamin E demonstrated
measureable improvement in advanced Alzheimer's patients.” Wallach
followed this research release with the statement, “Therefore, Alzheimer's
disease could not be genetic, for supplementation with a vitamin cannot
change how a true genetically transmitted disease manifests itself.”

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: How was vitamin E discovered?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin E was recognized in 1922 when female rats were found to need an unknown dietary factor to carry pregnancies to term without miscarrying.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that vitamin E's existence was first recognized in 1922, when researchers realized female rats required a previously unknown dietary factor to maintain their pregnancies. Deficient females could still ovulate and conceive normally, but at some point in the pregnancy they would suffer a spontaneous miscarriage. Lesions in the testes of deficient males were also reported, tying the new factor to fertility in both sexes.
claims.verbatim:
The existence of vitamin E was first recognized in 1922 when it was learned
that female rats required a previously unknown dietary factor to maintain
pregnancies. Deficient females would ovulate and conceive properly; however,
at some point in the pregnancy a spontaneous miscarriage would occur;
additionally, lesions in the male's testes were reported.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Can vitamin E cure muscular dystrophy?
claims.answer_short: In livestock, Wallach says injecting selenium and vitamin E into animals with 'white muscle disease' (muscular dystrophy) cures it within days.
claims.answer: Wallach treats muscular dystrophy as a nutritional disease of selenium and vitamin E deficiency rather than a purely genetic one. He notes that in livestock, injecting a mixture of selenium and vitamin E into calves, lambs, kids, and piglets afflicted with 'white muscle disease' — the animal form of muscular dystrophy — cures the disease within days. He argues the same nutritional approach, combined with strict gluten avoidance and the 90 essential nutrients, can prevent and reverse muscular dystrophy in people.
claims.verbatim:
In livestock, injections of a mixture of selenium
and vitamin E to calves, lambs, kids, and piglets afflicted with “white muscle
disease” (aka muscular dystrophy) cures the disease in days.

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: What is Vitamin K?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin your liver needs to make prothrombin and other blood-clotting proteins and to lay calcium down properly in bone — so it governs both normal clotting and bone strength.
claims.answer: Vitamin K is one of the fat-soluble vitamins in Wallach's essential-nutrient framework. Isolated in 1939, it is required by the liver to produce prothrombin and at least five other proteins (clotting factors VII, IX and X and proteins C and S), so the blood can clot normally. It also drives the proper deposition of calcium into bone — through the vitamin K-dependent protein osteocalcin — which is why Wallach calls it as essential to healthy bone as vitamin D. It comes in two forms: K1 (phylloquinone) from green plants and K2 (menaquinones) made by friendly bacteria in the colon, which supply roughly half of the body's requirement.
claims.verbatim:
This vitamin, isolated in 1939, is a fat soluble vitamin that is required by the liver
for the production of prothrombin and at least five other proteins (factors VII, IX,
and X, and proteins C and S) and other biologically active substances essential
for proper blood clotting and for the proper deposition of calcium in bones.

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: What does vitamin K do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin the liver needs to make prothrombin and other clotting proteins and to deposit calcium properly in bone.
claims.answer: Wallach describes vitamin K, isolated in 1939, as a fat-soluble vitamin the liver requires to produce prothrombin plus at least five other proteins — clotting factors VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S. These are essential for proper blood clotting and for the proper deposition of calcium in the bones. So vitamin K works on two fronts at once: it lets the blood clot normally and it helps build bone.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin K (menaquinone) function:

This vitamin, isolated in 1939, is a fat soluble vitamin that is required by the liver
for the production of prothrombin and at least five other proteins (factors VII, IX,
and X, and proteins C and S) and other biologically active substances essential
for proper blood clotting and for the proper deposition of calcium in bones.

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: Does your body make its own vitamin K?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says roughly half of your vitamin K requirement is produced by probiotic bacteria in the colon.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, you don't get all your vitamin K from food. Approximately 50% of the body's vitamin K requirement is produced by probiotic (friendly) bacteria in the colon. This is the K2 form, made by gram-positive intestinal micro-organisms, which is why the health and balance of your gut flora directly affects your vitamin K status.
claims.verbatim:
Approximately 50% of the requirement for vitamin K is produced by probiotic
bacteria in the colon,

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: What are the different forms of vitamin K and where does it come from?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin K comes in two forms — K1 (phylloquinone) from plants and K2 (menaquinones) made by gut bacteria — and is concentrated in foods like alfalfa and hog liver fat.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that vitamin K occurs in two forms: K1 (phylloquinone), produced by plants, and K2 (menaquinones), synthesized by gram-positive bacteria in the intestines. Early studies found vitamin K concentrated in hog liver fat and in alfalfa — held in the chloroplasts of green plant leaves and in vegetable oils. Because intestinal microorganisms produce it, considerable quantities also appear in the feces of humans and animals.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin K occurs in two forms: (1) K, (phylloquinone) is produced by plants
and (2) K, (menaquinones) is synthesized by gram positive intestinal micro-
organisms and appears as several compounds.

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: Can you take too much vitamin K?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says overdose signs include jaundice in newborns, and that injected phylloquinone or large doses of synthetic menadione can cause serious reactions and even death.
claims.answer: Wallach describes signs of vitamin K overdose: jaundice (kernicterus) in newborn infants, and — with rapid intravenous injection of phylloquinone in adults — flushing, shortness of breath, chest pain, and death. Large doses of the synthetic form menadione (not phylloquinone) given to animals produced hemolytic anemia, polycythemia (too many red blood cells), an enlarged spleen, kidney and liver damage, and death. He draws a clear line between the natural form and the greater toxicity of synthetic menadione.
claims.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: Symptoms include jaundice (kernicterus) in newborn
infants; rapid intravenous injections of phylloquinone in adult humans can
produce flushing, dyspnea, chest pain, and death. Large doses of menadione
(not phylloquinone) administered to animals has produced hemolytic anemia,
polycythemia (too many red blood cells), splenomegaly, kidney and liver damage
(hyperbilirubinemia) and death.

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: Why is it called vitamin K?
claims.answer_short: Dam named it vitamin K after 'Koagulation' (coagulation), because the nutrient resolved bleeding diseases that no other vitamin could cure.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that Dam et al (1935, 1936) showed hemorrhagic diseases which no known vitamin could cure or prevent were quickly resolved by feeding an as-yet-unidentified fat-soluble substance. He named it vitamin K after 'Koagulation' (coagulation) because the nutrient restored the blood's ability to clot.
claims.verbatim:
Dam etal (1935, 1936) showed that hemorrhagic diseases that were not cured
or prevented by any known vitamins could be quickly resolved by feeding an as
yet unidentified fat-soluble substance, which he named vitamin K (Koagulation
vitamin).

claims.subject: biotin
claims.question: What is biotin?
claims.answer_short: Biotin — also called vitamin H or coenzyme R — is a sulfur-containing B vitamin the body needs for glucose metabolism and the production of fatty acids.
claims.answer: Biotin, also known as vitamin H or coenzyme R, is a sulfur-containing B vitamin and one of Wallach's 90 essential nutrients. The body needs it for glucose metabolism and for the production of fatty acids, where it works as an essential part of enzymes that transport carboxyl units and fix carbon dioxide in animal tissue; converting it to its active coenzyme form depends on magnesium and adenosine triphosphate (ATP). A deficiency shows up in the skin and hair — eczema, baldness, and gray or white hair — which is why biotin is so closely tied to hair and skin health.
claims.verbatim:
Biotin is a
sulfur-containing vitamin. Biotin is an important part of enzymes that facilitate
the transport of carboxyl units and fix carbon dioxide in animal tissue.

claims.subject: biotin
claims.question: What does biotin do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Biotin is a sulfur-containing vitamin required for glucose metabolism and the production of fatty acids, working through enzymes that carry carboxyl units and fix carbon dioxide.
claims.answer: Biotin is a sulfur-containing vitamin the body needs for glucose metabolism and for the production of fatty acids. It works as an essential part of enzymes that transport carboxyl units and fix carbon dioxide in animal tissue. Converting biotin into its active coenzyme form depends on magnesium and adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Two of its enzymes, pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, are required for gluconeogenesis and fatty acid synthesis.
claims.verbatim:
It is
required for glucose metabolism and for the production of fatty acids. Biotin is a
sulfur-containing vitamin. Biotin is an important part of enzymes that facilitate
the transport of carboxyl units and fix carbon dioxide in animal tissue.

claims.subject: biotin
claims.question: Can you take too much biotin? Is biotin toxic?
claims.answer_short: No credible toxicity has been reported from large biotin doses, even above 10 mg daily, and its lethal dose is unknown.
claims.answer: Biotin appears remarkably safe even at high intakes. Wallach notes that biotin's LD50 (lethal dose) is unknown and that there have been no credible reports of toxicity from large doses, even at more than 10 mg per day.
claims.verbatim:
Signs of biotin overdose: The LDso is unknown and there have not been any
credible reports of toxicity from large doses of biotin, even with doses greater
than 10 mg daily.

claims.subject: biotin
claims.question: Can large doses of biotin overcome an inborn error of metabolism?
claims.answer_short: Yes; Wallach says multiple carboxylase deficiencies from defective holocarboxylase synthetase can be overcome in an epigenetic fashion with large doses of biotin.
claims.answer: Multiple carboxylase deficiencies are commonly caused by a defective holocarboxylase synthetase, the enzyme needed to convert inactive apocarboxylase into active carboxylase using biotin. Wallach argues this inborn error of metabolism can be overcome in an epigenetic fashion by supplementing large doses of biotin.
claims.verbatim:
Multiple carboxylase deficiencies are
commonly the result of defective holocarboxylase synthetase, which is required
for the conversion of inactive apocarboxylase to form active carboxylase by the
supplementation of biotin.

claims.subject: biotin
claims.question: How was biotin discovered?
claims.answer_short: Biotin was found through the 'egg white syndrome': rats fed egg whites developed skin inflammation, baldness, paralysis, and hemorrhaging, and in 1940 Paul Gyorgy identified biotin (vitamin H) as the cure.
claims.answer: Biotin's discovery traces to what was called the egg white syndrome. In the early 1930s an English investigator at the Lister Institute of Preventative Medicine in London fed laboratory rats on egg whites for several weeks, producing an eczema-type skin inflammation, alopecia, paralysis, and subcutaneous hemorrhaging. In 1940 Paul Gyorgy identified the substance that cured this condition as biotin, or vitamin H.
claims.verbatim:
In the early 1930s, an English investigator from the Lister Institute of
Preventative Medicine in London fed laboratory rats on egg whites for several
weeks, which produced an eczema type of skin inflammation, alopecia, paralysis,
and subcutaneous hemorrhaging.

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: What does choline do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Choline is a structural building block of all cell membranes, plasma lipoproteins and lung surfactants, and part of the nervous system's sphingomyelin and acetylcholine.
claims.answer: Choline is a major structural component of larger molecules. As part of phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) it is essential to the structure of all cell membranes, plasma lipoproteins and pulmonary surfactants. In the central nervous system it forms part of sphingomyelin and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.
claims.verbatim:
Choline is a major structural component of larger molecules; as a component
of phosphatidylcholine (lecithin), it is essential to the structure of all cell
membranes, plasma lipoproteins, and pulmonary surfactants; in the central
nervous system, choline functions as a structural component of sphingomyelin
and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: When was choline discovered?
claims.answer_short: Choline was first discovered and isolated from hog bile in 1862 and has been known in human and mammalian tissue ever since.
claims.answer: Choline was initially discovered and isolated from hog bile in 1862. It has been known to be present in mammalian tissue, including human tissue, ever since that discovery.
claims.verbatim:
Choline has been known to be present in mammalian tissue, including human,
since it was initially discovered and isolated from hog bile in 1862.

claims.subject: inositol
claims.question: What is Inositol?
claims.answer_short: Inositol (myo-inositol) is a cyclic alcohol chemically similar to glucose that Wallach counts among the essential vitamins; in animals it is a major constituent of the phospholipids that build cell membranes.
claims.answer: Wallach describes inositol - also called myo-inositol or 'muscle sugar' - as a cyclic alcohol (cyclohexanehexol) that is chemically similar to glucose. Of its nine isomers, only myo-inositol is of metabolic importance; it occurs in plants as phytic acid and, in animals, forms a major part of the phospholipids in cell biomembranes. He classes it as one of the 16 essential vitamins for humans and non-human vertebrates, its triphosphate form acting as a second messenger that mobilizes intracellular calcium.
claims.verbatim:
Inositol—aka myo-inositol, is a cyclic alcohol (cyclohexanehexol) that is
chemically similar to glucose. There are nine inositol isomers, however, myo-
inositol is the only one of metabolic importance for plant and animal metabolism.
It is found in plants as phytic acid and in animals myo-inositol is a major
constituent of phospholipids in biomembranes.

claims.subject: inositol
claims.question: How does inositol work in the body?
claims.answer_short: Myo-inositol triphosphate acts as a second messenger that mobilizes intracellular calcium in response to hormonal signals, and inositol is a building block of cell membranes.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that myo-inositol is believed to be an essential nutrient because myo-inositol triphosphate is a second messenger for receptor-mediated hormonal stimuli that mobilize intracellular calcium. It also appears to have a lipotrophic (fat-moving) function stemming from its role as a substrate for building phosphatidyl inositol and polyphosphoinositides, which are essential to the structure of cell membranes.
claims.verbatim:
Myo-inositol is believed to be
an essential nutrient because myo-inositol triphosphate is a second messenger
for receptor-mediated hormonal stimuli for mobilizing intracellular calcium.
Additionally, myo-inositol appears to have a lipotrophic function that may
originate from its vital role as a substrate for the biosynthesis of phosphatidyl

inositol and polyphos-hoinositides, which are essential for the structure of
biomembranes.

claims.subject: inositol
claims.question: Can you overdose on inositol?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports that no signs of inositol overdose are known, even with large supplemental doses.
claims.answer: Wallach states that there are no known signs of inositol overdose, even with large supplemental doses. In his account, inositol carries no established toxicity ceiling.
claims.verbatim: Signs of overdose: none are known, even with “large supplemental doses.”

claims.subject: inositol
claims.question: Does Wallach consider inositol a vitamin?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach classifies inositol as one of the 16 essential vitamins for humans and non-human vertebrates.
claims.answer: Wallach lists inositol among "The 16 Essential Vitamins for Humans and Non-human Vertebrates," alongside vitamins A, C, D, K, the B-complex, biotin, choline, flavonoids and folic acid. This reflects his stance that inositol is a required, essential nutrient for both humans and animals.
claims.verbatim:
The 16 Essential Vitamins for Humans and Non-human Vertebrates

Vitamin A

Vitamin 81 (Thiamin)
Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin)
Vitamin B3 (Niacin)

Vitamin B5 (Pantothenic acid)

Vitamin B12 (Cyanocobalamine)
Vitamin C

Vitamin D

Vitamin

Vitamin K

Biotin

Choline

Flavonoids and bioflavonoids
Folic Acid

Inositol

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: What are flavonoids?
claims.answer_short: Flavonoids are biologically active plant pigments — the yellow, red, and blue colors in flowers — that come in three classes and that Wallach argues are essential nutrients.
claims.answer: Flavonoids (also called bioflavonoids) are a diverse group of biologically active carbon compounds, and they are the plant pigments responsible for the yellow, red, and blue colors of flowers, colors that attract pollinating insects. Inside plants they also act as chemical and physiological messengers and as cell-cycle inhibitors. Wallach divides them into three classes — flavonoids (bioflavonoids), isoflavonoids, and neoflavonoids — and holds that there is more than enough evidence to treat them as essential nutrients.
claims.verbatim:
Flavonoids are widely associated with plants. Flavonoids are plant pigments
that are found in flowers as yellow, red and blue petals, these colors are
attractants for pollinating insects and animals indirectly associated with the
annual sexual cycle of plants. In plants, bioflavonoids also act as chemical
messengers, physiological messengers, and cell cycle inhibitors.

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: How do flavonoids help the heart and cardiovascular system?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says flavonoids cut cardiovascular risk by reducing clotting, atherosclerosis, and blood pressure, easing oxidative and inflammatory stress on vessels, and improving endothelial function.
claims.answer: Wallach states it is well documented that flavonoids play a positive role in reducing cardiovascular disease risk. They inhibit coagulation, thrombus formation, and platelet aggregation, reduce the risk of atherosclerosis, and lower arterial blood pressure and hypertension. They also reduce oxidative stress in vascular cells, modify vascular inflammation, improve endothelial and capillary function, adjust blood lipid levels, help regulate carbohydrate and glucose metabolism, and even modify the mechanisms of aging.
claims.verbatim:
It is well documented that flavonoids have a positive role in reducing the risk
of cardiovascular disease by:

1. Inhibiting coagulation, thrombus formation, and platelet aggregation
2. Reducing risk of atherosclerosis

3. Reducing arterial blood pressure and hypertension

4

. Reducing oxidative stress and related signaling pathways of vascular
cells

5. Modifying vascular inflammatory mechanisms
6. Improving endothelial and capillary function

7. Modifying blood lipid levels

8, Regulating carbohydrate and glucose metabolism

9. Modifying the mechanisms of aging

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: Are flavonoids essential nutrients?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says that although flavonoids aren't officially classed as essential, there is more than enough evidence to support a claim for their essentiality.
claims.answer: Flavonoids are a diverse group of biologically active carbon compounds that were first isolated in 1936. Wallach acknowledges they are not generally considered essential nutrients, but argues there is more than enough evidence to support a claim for essentiality. In his framework the evidence favors treating flavonoids as nutrients the body genuinely needs rather than as optional extras.
claims.verbatim:
Bioflavonoids, a diverse group of carbon compounds that are biologically active,
were isolated in 1936. While not generally considered essential nutrients, there
is more than enough evidence to support a claim for essentiality.

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: Why are flavonoids called that, and what is vitamin P?
claims.answer_short: The name comes from the Latin flavus (yellow); flavonoids were originally called vitamin P because they were related to the permeability levels of small blood vessels.
claims.answer: The name flavonoids, or bioflavonoids, comes from the Latin word flavus, meaning the color yellow that is common in flavonoids. Wallach notes they were originally referred to as 'vitamin P' because they were related to the permeability levels of small blood vessels.
claims.verbatim:
The name,
flavonoids or bioflavonoids, was derived from the Latin, flavus, which translates
to the color yellow common in flavonoids. Flavanoids were originally referred
to as vitamin P, as they were related to the permeability levels of small blood
vessels.

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: What are flavonoids good for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says flavonoid supplements reduce or eliminate allergies and inflammation, raise antioxidant activity, fight microbes, improve gut function, and support immunity in cancer patients.
claims.answer: Wallach draws a line between test-tube results and whole-person results, and puts raising ORAC antioxidant activity on the whole-person side. In in-vivo studies he lists flavonoid supplementation as clinically effective for reducing or eliminating allergies, calming vascular and pulmonary inflammation, raising ORAC antioxidant activity, antimicrobial action against bacteria, viruses, yeast and fungus, improving gastrointestinal function, and supporting the immune system in cancer patients. Flavonoids themselves are plant pigments - the yellow, red and blue in flower petals.
claims.verbatim:
In the whole person
(in vivo studies) supplementation with flavonoids have demonstrated clinical
effectiveness for reducing or eliminating allergies, vascular and pulmonary
inflammation, for increasing ORAC antioxidant activity, antimicrobial properties
(eg,, bacteria, viruses, yeast, fungus), improving gastrointestinal function and
supporting the immune system in cancer patients.

claims.subject: vanadium
claims.question: Does vanadium fight cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says vanadium has known anticarcinogenic properties and blocked mammary tumor growth in mice.
claims.answer: Wallach states that vanadium has known anticarcinogenic properties. In animal work, feeding 25 micrograms of vanadium per gram of diet blocked the induction of mouse mammary tumor growth. The vanadium supplement reduced tumor incidence, lowered the average tumor count per animal, and prolonged median cancer-free time without inhibiting the animals' overall growth or health.
claims.verbatim:
Vanadium has known anticarcinogenic properties. Induction of mouse
mammary tumor growth was blocked by feeding 25 ug/gm of diet. The vanadium
supplement reduced tumor incidence, average tumor count per animal and
prolonged median cancer free time without inhibiting overall growth or health of
the animals (sure beats the results and untoward side effects of chemotherapy
and radiation!)

claims.subject: vanadium
claims.question: Is type 2 diabetes really a mineral deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach argues type 2 diabetes is not genetic but a simple deficiency of chromium and vanadium.
claims.answer: Wallach maintains that type 2 diabetes is not a genetically-transmitted disease but a simple mineral deficiency. He says it has been well documented since 1958 that supplementing the 90 essential nutrients along with chromium and vanadium in an otherwise perfect diet will prevent and cure hypoglycemia, reactive hypoglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, and type 2 diabetes. He cites USDA field-services director Walter Mertz, whose research indicated that universally adding chromium to the diet would wipe out an entire medical specialty.
claims.verbatim:
Since 1958 it has been well documented that supplementation of the 90
essential nutrients along with chromium and vanadium to an otherwise perfect
diet will prevent and cure hypoglycemia, reactive hypoglycemia (narcolepsy),
hyperinsulinemia, and type 2 diabetes. Walter Mertz, the director of the U.S.D.A.
field services, published the results of his research in Federation Proceedings
that showed clearly that an entire medical specialty (endocrinology) would be
wiped out by universally adding chromium to an otherwise perfect diet. Type 2
diabetes is not a genetically-transmitted disease—it is in fact a simple mineral
deficiency!

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: What foods and herbs contain germanium?
claims.answer_short: Beans and tuna carry small amounts, while healing herbs like garlic, ginseng, aloe, comfrey, chlorella and Shiitake mushroom concentrate germanium at 100 to 2,000 ppm.
claims.answer: Food plants and animals contain small amounts of germanium -- for example beans at 4.67 ppm and tuna at 2.3 ppm. Healing herbs concentrate far more: garlic, aloe, comfrey, chlorella, ginseng, watercress, Shiitake mushroom, pearl barley, sanzukon, sushi, waternut, boxthorn seed, and wisteria knob contain germanium in amounts ranging from 100 to 2,000 ppm.
claims.verbatim:
Food plants and animals contain small amounts of germanium (e.g., beans at
4.67 ppm; tuna at 2.3 ppm). Healing herbs such as garlic, aloe, comfrey, chlorella,
ginseng, watercress, Shiitake mushroom, pearl barley, sanzukon, sushi, waternut,
boxthorn seed, and wisteria knob contain germanium in amounts ranging from
100 to 2,000 ppm.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: Who discovered germanium and when?
claims.answer_short: Its existence was predicted by Mendeleev's periodic table, and the element was finally isolated in 1886 by a German chemist, Clemens Winkler, who named it germanium.
claims.answer: The existence of germanium was predicted by Mendeleev's periodic table before the element itself had ever been found. It was not until 1886 that a German chemist, Clemens Winkler, isolated the element and gave it the name germanium.
claims.verbatim:
The existence of the element germanium had been predicted by Mendeleev in
his periodic table, however, it was not until 1886 that a German chemist, Clemens
Winkler, isolated this element and named it Germanium

claims.subject: manganese
claims.question: Can a mother's manganese deficiency make a baby deaf?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach reports that infants born deaf are the result of mothers being deficient in manganese during pregnancy.
claims.answer: From his medical work in rural Africa, Wallach observed that nutritional deficiencies caused predictable birth defects. Infants born deaf, he reports, were the result of mothers being deficient in manganese during pregnancy, much as folic acid or zinc deficiencies produced neural tube defects and cleft palates. He treats congenital deafness as a preventable maternal manganese-deficiency problem rather than a genetic accident.
claims.verbatim:
Infants born with neural tube defects (spina
bifida) and cleft palates from folic acid or zinc deficiencies usually did not survive
the primitive environment. Infants born deaf were the result of mothers being
deficient in manganese during pregnancy.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: Why is boron so rare?
claims.answer_short: Boron is produced by cosmic ray spallation rather than by stellar nucleosynthesis, making it a low-abundance element in both the solar system and Earth's crust.
claims.answer: Unlike most elements, boron is not forged inside stars (stellar nucleosynthesis). Instead it is produced by cosmic ray spallation, the breaking apart of larger nuclei by high-energy cosmic rays. Because of this, boron is a low-abundance element in both the solar system and the earth's crust. Wallach classifies it as an elemental chemical rather than a metallic mineral.
claims.verbatim:
B - Boron is an elemental chemical rather than a metallic mineral. It is
produced by cosmic ray spallation and not by stellar nucleosynthesis.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: What is boric acid used for?
claims.answer_short: Boric acid has antiseptic, antifungal, and antiviral properties, and mild solutions are used as wound disinfectants and eye washes.
claims.answer: Boric acid, one of boron's most important compounds, has antiseptic, antifungal, and antiviral properties. Mild solutions of boric acid are used as wound disinfectants and as an eye antiseptic wash. These practical uses illustrate boron's antimicrobial character.
claims.verbatim:
Boric acid has antiseptic, antifungal, and antiviral properties, and mild
solutions of boric acid are used as wound disinfectants and as an eye antiseptic
wash.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: Is boron used to treat cancer?
claims.answer_short: Yes, boron is the active ingredient in Bortezomib, a first-of-its-kind drug used to treat multiple myeloma and certain lymphomas.
claims.answer: Boron is the active ingredient in Bortezomib, described as the first pharmaceutical of its kind, a proteasome inhibitor. It is used to treat multiple myeloma (bone marrow cancer) and certain lymphomas. This makes boron a component of a modern anti-cancer medication.
claims.verbatim:
Boron is an active ingredient in the first of its kind pharmaceutical as
Bortezomib (a proteasome inhibitor) used for the treatment of multiple myeloma
(bone marrow cancer) and certain lymphomas.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: Is boron toxic or safe to take?
claims.answer_short: Borates have low toxicity in mammals, similar to table salt, but are more toxic to insects and so are used as insecticides.
claims.answer: In mammals, borates have low toxicity, which Wallach compares to that of table salt. They are, however, more toxic to arthropods (insects), which is why boron compounds are used as insecticides. Boric acid is also mildly antimicrobial.
claims.verbatim:
In biology, borates have low toxicity in mammals (similar to table salt), but
are more toxic to arthropods (insects) and are used as insecticides. Boric acid is
mildly antimicrobial.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: Is boron essential for all living things?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach states that boron is essential to life for all organisms, including both plants and animals.
claims.answer: Wallach states plainly that boron is essential to life for all organisms, including both plants and animals. This is a strong, unqualified claim of universal biological necessity, extending boron's importance well beyond human nutrition to the entire living world.
claims.verbatim:
Boron is essential to life for all organisms including plants
and animals.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: What is the story behind 20 Mule Team Borax?
claims.answer_short: Large borax deposits were discovered in Death Valley in 1881, and the mined borax was hauled out by the famous 20-mule-team wagons.
claims.answer: Large deposits of borax, sometimes called diamond boron, were discovered in Death Valley in 1881. The deposits were made famous by the 20 mule team wagons that hauled the mined borax out. Each wagon had rear wheels seven feet high, was sixteen feet long, and could carry 24,000 pounds (12 tons) of borax.
claims.verbatim:
Large deposits of borax or “diamond boron” were discovered in Death Valley
in1881. The Death Valley deposits were made famous by the 20 mule team
wagons that hauled out the mined borax. The rear wheels were seven foot high,
each wagon was sixteen foot long and could carry 24,000 pounds (12 tons) of
borax.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: Where does the name boron come from?
claims.answer_short: The name 'boron' comes from the Arabic word 'buraq' and the Persian 'burah,' both names for borax.
claims.answer: The name boron derives from the Arabic word buraq or the Persian word burah, both of which are names for borax. Boron compounds were known thousands of years ago, and borax itself was known from the deserts of western Tibet as tincal, from the Sanskrit. This deep history reflects boron's ancient use long before it was identified as an element.
claims.verbatim:
The name “boron” is derived from the Arabic word “buraq” or the Persian
word “burah,” which are the names for borax. Boron compounds were known
thousands of years ago and borax was known from the deserts of western Tibet
as “tincal” from the Sanskrit.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: How was vitamin B12 discovered?
claims.answer_short: In 1948 two teams (in the UK and US) isolated pure B12, the anti-pernicious-anemia factor, gleaning just 20 mg from a ton of liver.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that Dr. William Castle theorized the liver contained an anti-pernicious-anemia (APA) factor. The hunt was slow because humans store and recycle B12, until a microorganism, Lactobacillus lactis, was found that could be used to test for it. Later in 1948, two independent teams - one in the UK and one in the US - isolated the pure APA factor, vitamin B12, managing to glean only 20 mg from a ton of liver.
claims.verbatim:
Later in 1948, two independent teams (one in the UK and the other in the U.S)
were able to isolate the pure APA factor: vitamin B,>. They were able to glean 20

mg of the B,, from a ton of liver.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: How much salt do you lose when you sweat?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says soldiers sweating in the desert can lose up to 70 to 100 grams of salt per day — enough that sodium loss historically killed troops.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that death of soldiers from sodium loss was historically common during military operations in tropical countries. Men in the desert could lose up to twenty-four pints of water per day as sweat, and that sweat was not just water but a soup carrying the nutrients in their blood, including up to seventy to one hundred grams of salt per day. It illustrates why heavy sweating creates a real, sometimes fatal need to replace salt and not just water.
claims.verbatim:
The death of soldiers from a sodium loss was historically common during
military operations in tropical countries. Soldiers in the desert could lose up to
twenty-four pints of water per day as sweat. And that much sweat was not just
water, it was a soup that contained all the nutrients floating around in their blood
including up to seventy to one hundred grams of salt per day.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: What does sodium do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Sodium is one of the three indispensable electrolytes and, with chloride and potassium, runs the body's water balance, osmotic and acid-base equilibrium, and nerve and muscle function.
claims.answer: Wallach groups sodium, chloride and potassium together as the three indispensable 'electrolytes.' Sodium makes up about two percent of the body's total mineral content, and along with chloride sits mostly outside the cells (extracellular) while potassium works inside them. Together these three minerals carry out at least four vital jobs: maintaining normal water balance and distribution, osmotic equilibrium, acid-base balance, and the muscular irritability and nerve-impulse transmission behind movement and signaling.
claims.verbatim:
Sodium, K and Cl are involved
in at least four important physiological functions in the body:

1. Maintenance of normal water balance and distribution

2, Maintenance of normal osmotic equilibrium

3. Maintenance of normal acid-base balance

4, Maintenance of normal muscular irritability and neurological impulse
and neurological transmission

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Why do I crave salt?
claims.answer_short: Salt hunger is one of the oldest and most basic cravings of living things, and plant-eaters crave it far more than meat-eaters because grains, vegetables and fruit contain little or no natural salt.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, the craving for salt dates back to the very beginning of animals and man and is one of the most basic drives of all living organisms. Carnivores, man or beast, do not show a strong salt craving because meat naturally contains fairly large amounts of sodium chloride. Herbivores and human vegetarians, by contrast, demand large amounts of salt because there is little or no natural NaCl in grains, vegetables and fruit.
claims.verbatim:
“salt hunger” dates back to the very beginning of animals and man and is one
of the very basic cravings of living organisms. Carnivores (man or beast) do not
typically show the great craving for salt because meat contains relatively large
amounts of NaCl, but herbivores and human vegetarians demand large amounts
of NaCl because there is little or no natural NaCl in grains, vegetables and frui

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Can a low-salt diet cause a vitamin B12 deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Yes, too little salt lowers stomach acid, which stops the intrinsic factor from working, so vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed.
claims.answer: Wallach ties low salt directly to B12 status. When a person has hypochlorhydria, low stomach acid usually caused by a NaCl (salt) deficiency, the intrinsic factor needed to absorb vitamin B12 will not work, so the B12 (cobalt) is not absorbed. This, he notes, is why doctors frequently give B12 shots to older people who are on salt-restricted diets.
claims.verbatim:
If a person has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid—usually a NaCl deficiency)
the intrinsic factor will not work, and By, cobalt is not absorbed. This is
why doctors frequently give By, shots to older people on salt-restricted diets.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: How much salt do you actually need each day?
claims.answer_short: Wallach puts the average human salt requirement at about six to ten grams per day — roughly 0.5% of the dry weight of the daily diet.
claims.answer: Wallach states that the average human salt requirement is approximately 0.5 percent of the dry weight of the daily diet, or about six to ten grams per day. He warns that following a doctor's advice to restrict salt to less than one gram per day can increase the risk of a heart attack by as much as six hundred percent.
claims.verbatim:
The average salt requirement for a human is
approximately 0.5% of the dry weight of the daily diet or six to ten grams per day.
If you are very good at following a doctor's advice and restrict salt to less than
one gram per day, you can increase your risk of a heart attack by as much as six
hundred percent.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Can cutting back on salt cause anemia or low iron?
claims.answer_short: Yes, salt-restricted diets lower stomach acid, and that impaired stomach acid is one of Wallach's listed causes of iron deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach lists hypochlorhydria, low stomach acid from salt-restricted diets or from proton pump inhibitors, among the causes of iron deficiency, alongside unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation, chronic infection, chronic bleeding and impaired absorption. Because stomach hydrochloric acid is required for optimal iron absorption, cutting salt can undermine iron status. Iron deficiency in turn can lead to hypochromic microcytic anemia.
claims.verbatim:
Iron deficiency can result from an unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation,
chronic infections, hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid from salt-restricted diets
or use of proton pump inhibitors), chronic diarrhea, chronic bleeding (from illness
from cancer, uncers, parasites, etc.) and impaired absorption (caused by high-fat
diets, high phytate diets, gluten intolerance, etc).

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Can restricting salt cause thyroid problems or goiter?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach says Americans restricting their salt on doctors' orders has driven goiter and hypothyroidism to epidemic levels.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that iodine intake in the human diet is usually low to begin with. He says that since Americans have begun restricting their salt intake at their doctors' instruction, the rate of 'allopath'-caused goiter and hypothyroidism has become epidemic. In his account, cutting dietary salt is what drove this surge in thyroid disease.
claims.verbatim:
lodine intake in the human diet is usually low to begin
with, but since Americans have begun restricting their salt intake at their doctors
instruction, the rate of “allopath” caused goiter and hypothyroidism has become
epidemic.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: What happens if you don't get enough sodium?
