claims.answer_short: Sodium deficiency strikes mainly in heat and heavy sweating, and low-sodium infant formulas have caused fatal 'water intoxication' with brain swelling; the treatment is water and salt.
claims.answer: Wallach says deficiencies of salt (NaCl) occur mainly in hot weather or during heavy work or exercise in the heat, when large volumes of sweat are lost for body cooling. He warns that 'water intoxication' occurred in infants fed low-sodium formulas out of allopathic doctors' fear of sodium; their brains swelled and they died from a simple sodium deficiency. The treatment for sodium deficiency, he notes, is water and salt, taken orally or given intravenously as 0.9% saline.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of NaCl occur primarily in hot weather (the heat wave of July

1993) or heavy work or exercise in a hot environment when large volumes of
sweat are required for body cooling. “Water intoxication” occurred in infants fed
low Na formulas because of the allopathic doctor's paranoia about Na. Their
brains swelled causing death from a simple Na deficiency.

The treatment for Na deficiency is water and salt either orally or IV (saline
0.9%).

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Is salt actually bad for you?
claims.answer_short: No — Wallach teaches that salt is not intrinsically harmful; its only real danger is that it can trick the body into thinking it already has enough minerals.
claims.answer: Wallach rejects the popular belief that salt is inherently dangerous. He argues that salt itself is not intrinsically harmful; the real problem is that eating salt lets the body falsely perceive it is getting sufficient minerals, so a salt-satisfied craving can mask an underlying mineral deficiency. He calls this the mineral equivalent of the 'empty calorie diet' — just as white flour and sugar satisfy hunger while supplying no protein, essential fatty acids, or vitamins, salt intake convinces the body it has adequate minerals when it may not.
claims.verbatim:
Today, contrary to popular belief, salt is not intrinsically harmful as doctors
would have you believe. It does present the problem of allowing our bodies to
falsely perceive that we are getting sufficient minerals when we eat salt. This
is the mineral equivalent of the "empty calorie diet” concept.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Do low-salt diets actually help high blood pressure?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says no — he claims there is not a single double-blind study showing any benefit from a salt-restricted or low-sodium diet.
claims.answer: Wallach is sharply critical of the medical profession's routine advice to cut salt for hypertension and heart disease, calling it a 'paranoia about salt.' He states flatly that there is not a single double-blind study demonstrating any benefit from a salt-restricted or low-sodium diet. In his account of the 1993 heat wave he blames this low-salt advice for putting vulnerable heart and blood-pressure patients at fatal risk.
claims.verbatim:
The human tragedy of the heat wave of '93 was the direct result of the medical
profession's paranoia about salt. They put their human charges on a low-sodium
or low-salt diet for prevention of hypertension and heart disease. There is not a
single double-blind study that will show any benefit of a salt-restricted or low-
sodium diet.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: If salt causes high blood pressure, why don't farm animals get it?
claims.answer_short: Wallach points out that livestock eat all the salt they want from salt blocks yet never develop high blood pressure or stroke.
claims.answer: Farmers and ranchers put out salt blocks made of at least 85 percent sodium chloride to guarantee their animals get essential minerals — anything less than 85 percent salt gets ignored, even by mineral-deficient animals. Wallach notes these salt-consuming animals never get high blood pressure or stroke, even though by design they eat about 0.5 percent of their diet as salt. He uses this as evidence that free salt intake does not cause hypertension.
claims.verbatim:
Farmers and husbandrymen use the salt-hunger behavior to ensure the
consumption of trace minerals in livestock by incorporating trace minerals into
the formulation of salt blocks containing a minimum of eighty-five percent
sodium chloride. Anything less than eighty-five percent sodium chloride would
be ignored by the animals, even if they were to have major mineral deficiencies.
The salt-consuming animals never get high blood pressure or stroke, even though
by design they will consume 0.5 percent of their diet as salt.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Can your body actually know when it needs salt?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites a 1940 case of a boy whose intense salt craving kept his undiagnosed Addison's disease at bay — he died 48 hours after doctors restricted his salt.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts a 1940 case published by psychologist Curt Richter in which a young boy showed a 'morbid craving for salt,' licking it off crackers and eating it from the shaker before age two. At three-and-a-half he was hospitalized to restrict his salt intake and died 48 hours later; his autopsy revealed Addison's disease (adrenal cortical insufficiency). Wallach's point is that the boy's salt cravings — a form of pica — were correct and had kept him alive, and that restricting his salt is what killed him. He uses it to support the 'wisdom of the body' idea that cravings can signal a real physiological need.
claims.verbatim:
Richter published one of his own cases in 1940 in which a young boy
demonstrated a “morbid craving for salt.” The child had begun licking salt off of
soda crackers at the age one year and he then ate salt from the shaker at 18
months old. At age three-and-a-half years, the boy was hospitalized to restrict his
salt intake. Forty-eight hours after being denied salt the boy died (another great
victory for psychology).

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Is salt really the cause of high blood pressure?
claims.answer_short: No, Wallach argues that the 'salt sensitivity' seen in hypertension is actually driven by low calcium and potassium intake, not by salt itself.
claims.answer: Wallach defines 'salt sensitivity' as a rise in blood pressure and a sustained increase in urinary calcium loss in response to eating salt. But he argues that among black and elderly white patients with essential hypertension, it is restricted intakes of calcium and potassium, rather than high salt consumption itself, that is responsible for the salt sensitivity. In his framework the blood-pressure problem traces to mineral deficiencies, not to the salt.
claims.verbatim:
The phenomenon of salt sensitivity consists of a rise in blood pressure and
sustained increase in urinary loss of Ca in response to salt consumption. Among
black and elderly whites with essential hypertension, restricted intakes of Ca
and K, rather than elevated salt consumption itself, is responsible for the “salt
sensitivity.”

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Why was salt so valuable in ancient times?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says salt was so essential a necessity of life that people in salt-poor Africa gave up everything they owned — even their wives and children — to obtain it, and that African tribesmen said, 'He who has salt has war.'
claims.answer: Wallach describes salt as an absolute necessity of life that was fiercely coveted wherever it was scarce. In salt-poor parts of Africa, people drank cattle blood and urine to obtain it, and residents of the Sierra Leone coast gave up everything they owned — including their wives and children — in exchange for salt. Because salt, like other minerals, is not distributed equally around the earth, it was coveted by the have-nots; as African tribesmen put it, 'He who has salt has war.'
claims.verbatim:
In other parts of salt-poor Africa, humans developed the practice of drinking
cattle blood and urine to obtain salt. The residence of the Sierra Leone coast
gave all they possessed, including their wives and children, in exchange for salt—
after all, salt was a necessity of life. Salt, like other elements and minerals, is not
distributed equally around the earth and is therefore coveted by the have-nots. It
is said by African tribesmen that, “He who has salt has war.”

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Why is salt connected to the word 'salary'?
claims.answer_short: Roman soldiers were partly paid in a salt ration called a 'salarium' — the origin of the word 'salary' and the phrase 'worth their salt.'
claims.answer: Wallach traces the word 'salary' to salt: Roman soldiers 'worth their salt' were paid a 'salary,' derived from salarium, a soldier's 'salt ration.' Rome's major highway, the Via Salacia or Salt Road, was used to carry salt up from the Tiber River, where barges brought it from the salt pans of Ostia. The detail underscores how valuable salt was in the ancient world.
claims.verbatim:
Rome's major highway was called Via Salacia or the Salt Road. Soldiers used
the Salt Road to carry salt up from the Tiber River where barges brought salt from
the salt pans of Ostia. Soldiers “worth their salt” were paid a “salary.” The word
salary is derived from salarium, a soldier's “salt ration.”

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: What causes low blood phosphorus?
claims.answer_short: Low blood phosphorus (hypophosphatemia) results from IV glucose or TPN without phosphorus, excessive antacids, hyperparathyroidism, diuretics, sweating from exercise, and alcoholism.
claims.answer: Wallach lists the clinical causes of phosphorus depletion and resulting low blood phosphorus (hypophosphatemia): IV administration of glucose or total parenteral nutrition without phosphorus supplementation, excessive use of antacids, hyperparathyroidism (which he attributes to low-calcium/high-phosphate diets), improper treatment of diabetic acidosis, use of diuretics, sweating during exercise, and alcoholism with and without liver disease.
claims.verbatim:
Clinical P depletion and resultant low blood P (hypophosphatemia) result
from IV administration of glucose or TPN (Total Parenteral Nutrition) without P
supplementation, excessive use of antacids, hyperparathyroidism (low calcium/
high phosphate diets are the cause of this one), improper treatment of diabetic
acidosis, use of diuretics, sweating during exercise, and alcoholism with and
without liver disease.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: Do vegetarians get enough phosphorus?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says vegetarians and vegans who don't supplement with minerals rarely have a phosphorus deficiency (unless they have chronic gluten intolerance from heavy whole-grain consumption), though because of their high phytic-acid intake they always have other mineral deficiencies, such as calcium, copper, chromium, vanadium, lithium and zinc, unless they supplement.
claims.answer: Wallach observes that vegetarians and vegans who do not supplement with minerals rarely have a phosphorus deficiency — unless they have chronic gluten intolerance from heavy whole-grain consumption. However, because of their high phytic-acid intake from raw vegetables, they always have other mineral deficiencies, such as calcium, copper, chromium, vanadium, lithium and zinc, unless they supplement.
claims.verbatim:
Vegetarians and vegans, who do not supplement with minerals, rarely have P
deficiency (unless they have a chronic gluten intolerance from high whole-grain
consumption). However, because of their high phytic acid intake (raw vegetables)
they always have other mineral deficiencies (such as lack of Ca, Cu, Cr, V, Li, Zn,
etc.) unless they supplement.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: How did phosphorus get its name?
claims.answer_short: In 1669 the German alchemist Hennig Brandt heated human urine with beach sand; the glowing white residue he named 'phosphorus', Greek for 'I bear light.'
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in 1669 the German alchemist Hennig Brandt, trying to transmute materials into gold, reasoned that nothing could be more noble than the human body. Brandt combined human urine with common beach sand and heated the mix in an oven; the soft white residue glowed in a dark room, and he named it 'phosphorus,' Greek for 'I bear light.' Robert Boyle later procured a sample and began manufacturing it in large quantities to sell throughout Europe.
claims.verbatim:
Brandt combined human urine with common beach sand, then heated the mix
in an oven. The soft white residue glowed in a dark room and Brandt named it
“phosphorus” (Greek for “I bear light”).

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: What did alchemists believe about sulfur?
claims.answer_short: Alchemists held that all metals were made of sulphur and mercury, and that the proportions of each decided whether a metal became gold, silver, copper, or tin.
claims.answer: In his history of chemistry, Wallach recounts that alchemists believed all metals were alloys containing sulphur and mercury, and that the varying proportions of each determined whether a metal became gold, silver, copper, tin, or another metal. Gold was supposedly a large amount of mercury with little sulphur; copper held equal amounts of each; and tin was an imperfect blend of impure mercury and a large quantity of sulphur.
claims.verbatim:
They
believed that metals were alloys of unrelated substances, yet all metals contained
sulphur and mercury, and it was the varying proportions of each one that
determined whether the metal would become gold, silver, copper, tin, or other
metals.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Why is chlorine put in drinking water?
claims.answer_short: Since a 1918 U.S. decree, chlorine has disinfected public water—Wallach notes it kills E. coli far better than bromine or iodine.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that by 1918 the U.S. Department of the Treasury decreed that all public drinking-water systems must be disinfected with chlorine. He notes chlorine in water is more than three times as effective a disinfectant against E. coli as an equal concentration of bromine, and more than six times as effective as iodine. In the same history he credits chlorine solutions with ending childbed fever after Semmelweis used them to disinfect doctors' hands in 1847.
claims.verbatim:
By 1918 the U.S. department of the Treasury decreed that all public drinking-
water systems must be disinfected by the use of chlorine. Chlorine in water is
more than three times as effective as a disinfectant against Escherichia coli, than
an equivalent concentration of bromine, and is more than six times more effective
than an equivalent concentration of iodine.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Why is chlorine called chlorine, and what does the word mean?
claims.answer_short: Sir Humphry Davy named it in 1810 from the Greek 'chloros,' meaning green-yellow.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in 1810 Sir Humphry Davy concluded chlorine is an element, not a compound, and named it from the Greek word 'chloros,' meaning 'green-yellow.' In the same account he notes the term 'halogen,' meaning 'salt producer,' was introduced in 1811 to describe chlorine before becoming the generic name for the whole family that includes fluorine, bromine, and iodine.
claims.verbatim:
In 1810 Sir Humphry Davy concluded that chlorine is an element not a
compound, and he named the new element chlorine from the Greek word chloros
or “green-yellow.”

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: What is arginine?
claims.answer_short: Arginine is an amino acid Wallach counts among the essentials—required for cell division, wound healing, ammonia excretion, immune support, and the availability of stored hormones.
claims.answer: Arginine is an amino acid that Wallach adds to the classic list of essential amino acids. Mainstream science treats it as non-essential, but Wallach holds that a long-term deficiency drives specific diseases—notably cancer and peripheral arterial disease (PAD). The body can make arginine from citrulline, but only at a steep energy cost, so supplementing it directly frees up cellular fuel (adenosine triphosphate, ATP). Arginine is required for complete and efficient cell division, wound healing, the excretion of ammonia, immune support, and the availability of stored hormones, and it is the raw material for nitric oxide, which lowers blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed vessels.
claims.verbatim:
Arginine is required for complete and efficient cell division, wound healing,
facilitating the biological use of and the excretion of ammonia, immune system
support, and the availability of stored hormones.

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: Why does supplementing with arginine help fuel the cells?
claims.answer_short: Making arginine internally burns ATP, so supplementing it directly frees up more ATP to fuel cell function.
claims.answer: Building arginine from citrulline is energetically expensive: producing each molecule of argininosuccinate requires hydrolyzing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) down to adenosine monophosphate (AMP). By supplementing with arginine directly, the body is spared that cost, leaving more ATP available to provide fuel for cell function.
claims.verbatim:
This process is expensive in terms of energy
since the production of each molecule of argininosuccinate requires hydrolysis
of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to adenosine monophosphate (AMP), and by


supplementing with arginine, more ATP is available to provide cell function fuel.

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: What does arginine do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Arginine is required for cell division, wound healing, ammonia excretion, immune support, and the availability of stored hormones.
claims.answer: Arginine is required for complete and efficient cell division and for wound healing. It also facilitates the biological use and excretion of ammonia, supports the immune system, and helps make stored hormones available to the body.
claims.verbatim:
Arginine is required for complete and efficient cell division, wound healing,
facilitating the biological use of and the excretion of ammonia, immune system
support, and the availability of stored hormones.

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: Does arginine lower blood pressure and improve circulation?
claims.answer_short: Yes—oral arginine is required to synthesize nitric oxide, and it reduces blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels.
claims.answer: Oral supplementation of arginine is required for the synthesis of nitric oxide (NO). It also reduces blood pressure, increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels, shortens healing time following trauma, and is particularly useful for bone trauma.
claims.verbatim:
The oral supplementation of
arginine is required for the synthesis of nitric oxide (NO), the reduction of healing
time following trauma, and is particularly useful for bone trauma; it reduces
blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels.

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: Can arginine help with tooth pain or sensitivity?
claims.answer_short: An 8% arginine toothpaste gives rapid, effective relief from dental pain by rebuilding a dentin-like layer.
claims.answer: Wallach highlights a surprising dental use of the amino acid arginine: a toothpaste containing 8% arginine gives rapid, effective relief from tooth pain and sensitivity. It works by prompting the formation of a dentin-like material — made of calcium and phosphate — that plugs the microscopic dentin tubules and coats the tooth's surface, sealing off the tiny channels that carry pain signals. It is one of several everyday roles he assigns arginine, alongside wound healing and nitric-oxide production.
claims.verbatim:
Arginine (8%) toothpaste produces rapid and effective relief from dental pain
by producing a dentin-like material that is made up of calcium and phosphate
that is deposited in the dentin tubules and on the surface of dentin.

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: When and how was arginine discovered?
claims.answer_short: Arginine was first isolated in 1886 from a lupin seedling by Swiss chemist Ernst Schultze.
claims.answer: Arginine has a tidy origin story Wallach relays: it was first isolated in 1886 from a lupin seedling by the Swiss chemist Ernst Schultze. Biochemically, the body builds arginine from citrulline using two enzymes — argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and argininosuccinate lyase (ASL) — an energy-costly path, which is one reason he favors supplementing arginine directly. And although mainstream science labels it non-essential, Wallach adds arginine to his own list of essential amino acids, because a chronic deficiency drives specific diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Arginine (Arg) was first isolated in 1886 from a lupin seedling by the Swiss
chemist Ernst Schultze and is synthesized from citrulline by the sequential
employment of the cytosolic enzymes argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and

argininosuccinate lyase (ASL).

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: What is taurine?
claims.answer_short: Taurine is an amino acid Wallach counts as essential -- a sulfur-based compound that conjugates bile acids, acts as an antioxidant, and is vital to the heart, muscles, eyes, and nervous system.
claims.answer: Taurine is one of the amino acids Wallach adds to the classic list of essentials, because over the long haul a deficiency drives a specific disease -- macular degeneration. Chemically it is unusual: a sulfonic acid rather than the carboxyl-acid form most biologically occurring acids take, and the body can synthesize it from methionine. Wallach describes taurine as essential to the cardiovascular system, skeletal muscle, the retina, and the central nervous system, where it conjugates bile acids, acts as an antioxidant, stabilizes membranes, and modulates calcium signaling.
claims.verbatim:
Taurine (Ta) has many biological roles including the conjugation of bile acids,
acts as an antioxidant, osmoregulation, membrane stabilization, and modulation
of calcium signaling. Taurine is essential for the functioning of the cardiovascular
system, skeletal muscle, the retina and the central nervous system.

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: How does the body make taurine?
claims.answer_short: Taurine is synthesized from methionine — Wallach lists it among the compounds methionine is an intermediate in producing.
claims.answer: Taurine is one of the compounds the body builds from the amino acid methionine. Wallach describes methionine as an intermediate in the biosynthesis of cysteine, carnitine, taurine, lecithin, phosphatidylcholine, and other phospholipids, meaning the body can produce taurine from methionine.
claims.verbatim:
Methionine is an intermediate
in the biosynthesis of cysteine, carnitine, taurine, lecithin, phosphatidylcholine,
and other phospholipids.

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: Can you take too much taurine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach warns that doses of taurine above 2 grams a day have been shown to contribute to psoriasis.
claims.answer: Taurine is not risk-free at high intakes. Wallach warns that doses of taurine in excess of 2 grams per day have been shown to contribute to the genesis of psoriasis.
claims.verbatim:
Doses of taurine in excess of 2 gm/day have been shown to contribute to the
genesis of psoriasis.

claims.subject: taurine
claims.question: Where does the name taurine come from?
claims.answer_short: Taurine is named after the Latin Taurus, meaning bull or ox, because it was first isolated from ox bile in 1827.
claims.answer: Taurine gets its name from the Latin 'Taurus,' meaning bull or ox — fittingly, since it was first isolated from ox bile in 1827 by the German scientists Friedrich Tiedermann and Leopold Gmelin. Wallach counts it among the amino acids worth adding to the classic essentials, noting its unusual chemistry (it is a sulfonic acid rather than the usual carboxylic kind) and its wide roles in the heart, skeletal muscle, retina, and central nervous system.
claims.verbatim:
Taurine is named after the Latin Taurus, which means bull or ox, as it was first
isolated from ox bile in 1827 by the German scientists Friedrich Tiedermann and
Leopold Gmelin.

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: What is Tryptophan?
claims.answer_short: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid the body must get from dietary protein; it is a building block for the body's structural enzyme proteins and the raw material it uses to make serotonin, melatonin, and niacin.
claims.answer: Tryptophan (Trp) is an essential amino acid — the body cannot synthesize it, so it must come from protein in the diet. It is used to build the body's structural enzyme proteins, and it is the biochemical precursor from which the body makes serotonin (a neurotransmitter), which in turn can become melatonin (a sleep hormone); niacin (vitamin B3) is also synthesized from it. Because its absorption from the intestine is reduced by gluten intolerance, lactose intolerance, and fructose malabsorption, a shortfall lowers blood tryptophan and can produce clinical depression.
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan (Trp) is an essential amino acid encoded in the standard genetic code
as the codon UGG. Only L-tryptophan is used in structural enzyme proteins.

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: What does tryptophan turn into in the body?
claims.answer_short: Tryptophan is a building block of protein and a precursor of serotonin, which the body can convert to melatonin, and it is also used to make niacin.
claims.answer: Beyond serving as a building block for protein biosynthesis, tryptophan is a biochemical precursor of serotonin (a neurotransmitter), which it forms via the enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase. Serotonin can in turn be converted to melatonin (a neurohormone). Tryptophan is also the raw material from which niacin is synthesized, by way of kynurenine and quinolinic acid intermediates. In plants it is even converted into the phytohormone auxin.
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan is employed as a building block of protein
biosynthesis and is a biochemical precursor of serotonin (a neurotransmitter),
synthesized via tryptophan hydroxylase. Serotonin can be converted to melatonin
(a neurohormone); niacin is synthesized from tryptophan via kynurenine and
quinolinic acids as essential biosynthetic intermediates; auxin (a phytohormone)
is produced when sieve tube elements undergo apoptosis (programed cell-death),
tryptophan is converted to auxins.

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: How much tryptophan equals a milligram of niacin?
claims.answer_short: By convention, 60 mg of tryptophan is considered equivalent to 1 mg of niacin, though measurements found the amount ranged from 39 to 86 mg.
claims.answer: The body can make niacin (vitamin B3) from tryptophan, and researchers measured how much is needed. When niacin status was gauged by urinary metabolite levels, the amount of supplementary tryptophan required to give the same response as one milligram of niacin ranged from 39 to 86 mg. By convention, 60 mg of tryptophan is treated as equivalent to one mg of niacin.
claims.verbatim:
When niacin status was gauged by urinary metablyte levels,
the quantities of supplementary tryptophan required to give the same response
as one mg of niacin ranged from 39 to 86 mg. Convention allows that 60 mg of
tryptophan is equivalent to one mg of niacin,

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: Does phenylalanine affect tryptophan and serotonin?
claims.answer_short: Phenylalanine uses the same transport channel as tryptophan to cross into the brain, so large doses of phenylalanine interfere with serotonin production.
claims.answer: Phenylalanine and tryptophan compete for entry into the brain: phenylalanine employs the same active transport channel as tryptophan to cross the blood-brain barrier. As a result, large doses of phenylalanine will interfere with the production of serotonin, the neurotransmitter the brain makes from tryptophan.
claims.verbatim:
Phenylalanine employs the same active transport channel as tryptophan to cross
the blood-brain barrier, in large doses it will interfere with the production of
serotonin.

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: What is 5-HTP used for?
claims.answer_short: 5-HTP, a metabolite of tryptophan, has been suggested as a treatment for seizure disorders and depression; it rapidly crosses into the brain and is converted to serotonin.
claims.answer: A metabolite of tryptophan called 5-HTP (5-hydroxytryptophan) has been suggested as a treatment for seizure disorders and depression. It acts quickly because it rapidly crosses the blood-brain barrier and is then rapidly decarboxylated into serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT).
claims.verbatim:
A metabolite of tryptophan, S-hydroxytryptophan (S-HTP), has been
suggested as a treatment for seizure disorders and depression. It rapidly
crosses the blood brain barrier and is rapidly decarboxylated to serotonin (5-
hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT).

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: Is tryptophan dangerous? What was the 1989 tryptophan outbreak?
claims.answer_short: In 1989 a tryptophan-associated outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) caused at least 1,500 cases of permanent disability and at least 37 deaths, traced to a supply of L-tryptophan from a single Japanese manufacturer (Showa Denko KK).
claims.answer: In 1989 there was a large tryptophan-associated outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) that caused at least 1,500 cases of permanent disability and at least 37 deaths. The problem was traced to a batch of L-tryptophan produced and exported to the United States by the Japanese manufacturer Showa Denko KK. The final explanation offered was that large doses of tryptophan gave rise to metabolites that inhibit the normal degradation of histamine, and that the resulting excess histamine caused EMS.
claims.verbatim:
In 1989 there was a large tryptophan-associated outbreak of eosinophilia-
myalgia syndrome (EMS) which caused at least 1,500 cases of permanent
disability and at least 37 deaths.

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: Who discovered tryptophan and when?
claims.answer_short: Tryptophan was isolated in 1901 by Frederick Hopkins through the hydrolysis of casein, the protein in milk.
claims.answer: Tryptophan was first isolated in 1901 by Frederick Hopkins, who obtained it through the hydrolysis (chemical breakdown) of casein, the main protein found in milk.
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan was isolated in 1901 by Frederick Hopkins via hydrolysis of
casein (milk protein).

claims.subject: methionine
claims.question: Why is methionine the 'start' amino acid in protein synthesis?
claims.answer_short: Methionine's codon, AUG, doubles as the cell's main 'Start' signal for building a protein, so nearly every protein begins with a methionine.
claims.answer: Methionine is encoded by a single codon, AUG — and AUG is also the most common 'Start' signal in eukaryotic cells. When it sits within a Kozak consensus sequence, AUG tells a ribosome to begin translating a protein from messenger RNA (mRNA). Because that start signal is methionine's own codon, protein synthesis characteristically begins with a methionine residue, giving this amino acid a foundational role in assembling the body's proteins.
claims.verbatim:
The AUG codon is the most common eukaryote “Start”
message for a ribosome that signals the initiation of protein translation from
mRNA when the AUG codon is in a Kozak consensus sequence.

claims.subject: methionine
claims.question: Can restricting methionine extend lifespan?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites studies where restricting methionine lengthened lab-animal lifespans; a Nature fruit-fly study found that adding it back restored fertility without cancelling the lifespan gain from calorie restriction.
claims.answer: Wallach points to studies in which restricting dietary methionine increased the lifespan of laboratory animals. He highlights a study published in Nature showing that when fruit flies were kept on lifespan-extending calorie restriction, adding methionine back into their diet restored their fecundity (fertility) — yet did so without shortening the longer lifespans that calorie restriction normally produces. In effect, methionine governed fertility independently of the lifespan benefit.
claims.verbatim:
Some studies have shown that restriction of methionine can increase lifespans
of laboratory animals. A study, published in Nature, demonstrated that adding
methionine to the diets of fruit flies under dietary calorie restriction restored
fecundity without reducing the longer lifespans that are typical of dietary
restriction.

claims.subject: methionine
claims.question: What does methionine do in plants?
claims.answer_short: In plants, methionine is the raw material for making ethylene (a plant hormone), through a pathway called the Yang Cycle — also known as the methionine cycle.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that methionine's role isn't limited to animals: plants use it as the starting material to synthesize ethylene — a plant hormone — through a pathway known as the Yang Cycle, or methionine cycle.
claims.verbatim:
Methionine is employed by plants for the synthesis of ethylene, the process is
known as the Yang Cycle or the methionine cycle.

claims.subject: phenylalanine
claims.question: What is phenylalanine?
claims.answer_short: Phenylalanine is one of the nine classic essential amino acids—a nonpolar protein building block the body can't make and must get from the diet every day.
claims.answer: Phenylalanine (abbreviated Phe) is one of the nine amino acids classically considered essential, meaning the human body cannot manufacture it and has to take it in from the diet. Chemically it is an alpha amino acid classified as nonpolar because of the water-repelling (hydrophobic) benzyl group on its side chain. It is one of the twenty amino acids the body uses to build the proteins encoded by DNA, and in the genetic code it is specified by the codons UUU and UUC. Beyond protein-building, phenylalanine is the raw material the body converts into tyrosine and, through it, several key signaling chemicals and pigments.
claims.verbatim:
Phenylalanine (Phe) is an alpha amino acid that is classified as nonpolar because
of the hydrophobic nature of its benzyl side chain. Phenylalanine is one of twenty
amino acids employed biochemically to synthesize proteins coded for by DNA.
The codons for phenylalanine are UUU and UUC.

claims.subject: phenylalanine
claims.question: Is phenylalanine an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach lists phenylalanine among the nine classic essential amino acids the body cannot make on its own and must be supplied daily from the diet to prevent deficiency and disease.
claims.answer: Yes. Phenylalanine is one of the nine amino acids Wallach lists as classically 'essential': histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. 'Essential' means the human body cannot synthesize these amino acids on its own, so they have to be consumed every day; without them, Wallach warns, deficiencies and their disease consequences follow. He also argues that three more amino acids—arginine, taurine, and tyrosine—should be treated as essential, because their long-term deficiency causes specific diseases too.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.subject: phenylalanine
claims.question: When was phenylalanine discovered and who first isolated it?
claims.answer_short: Phenylalanine was first isolated in 1879 by Schulze and Barbieri from yellow lupine, and first synthesized in the lab in 1882 by Erlenmeyer and Lipp.
claims.answer: Phenylalanine was first reported isolated in 1879 by the scientists Schulze and Barbieri, who obtained it from the yellow lupine plant (Lupinus luteus). A few years later, in 1882, Erlenmeyer and Lipp became the first to synthesize phenylalanine artificially, building it from phenylacetaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide, and ammonia.
claims.verbatim:
The first reports of the isolation of phenylalanine were made in 1879 by
Schulze and Barbieri, who isolated the amino acid from the yellow Lupine (Lupinus
luteus). In 1882, Erlenmeyer and Lipp first synthesized phenylalanine from
phenylacetaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide and ammonia.

claims.subject: phenylalanine
claims.question: Is phenylketonuria (PKU) really a genetic disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls PKU—the inability to metabolize phenylalanine—'falsely believed' to be a genetically transmitted disease, and notes its symptoms are prevented simply by avoiding phenylalanine.
claims.answer: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism in which the body cannot properly break down phenylalanine. Wallach takes the pointed position that PKU is 'falsely believed to be a genetically-transmitted disease.' Whatever its cause, he notes the practical management is the same: avoiding phenylalanine in the diet prevents the symptoms of PKU. This is why phenylalanine-containing products such as the sweetener aspartame carry warnings for people with the condition.
claims.verbatim:
The inborn error of metabolism known as phenylketonuria (PKU), falsely
believed to be a genetically-transmitted disease, is the inability to metabolize
phenylalanine. Avoidance of phenylalanine prevents the symptoms of PKU.

claims.subject: phenylalanine
claims.question: Does aspartame (Equal, NutraSweet) contain phenylalanine?
claims.answer_short: Yes—aspartame, sold as Equal and NutraSweet, breaks down into phenylalanine, which is why aspartame products carry a 'Contains phenylalanine' warning label.
claims.answer: Yes. A major non-food source of phenylalanine is the artificial sweetener aspartame, sold under the brand names Equal and NutraSweet. When aspartame is metabolized it breaks down into several chemical byproducts, and one of them is phenylalanine. Because of this, aspartame-containing products in the United States, Canada, and Australia must be labeled 'Phenylketonurics: Contains phenylalanine'—a warning aimed at people with PKU who must avoid the amino acid.
claims.verbatim:
A non-food source of phenylalanine is the non-sugar sweetener aspartame
marketed as Equal and NutraSweet, both of which are metabolized into several
chemical byproducts including phenylalanine. Thus, all products in Australia, the
United States, and Canada that contain aspartame are labeled “Phenylketonurics:
Contains phenylalanine.”

claims.subject: phenylalanine
claims.question: What is DL-phenylalanine (DLPA) used for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes DL-phenylalanine is sold as a nutritional supplement for three purposes: as a sleep aid, as an anti-depressant, and as an analgesic (pain reliever).
claims.answer: DL-phenylalanine—a supplement form that combines the two mirror-image versions (D and L) of the amino acid—is marketed as a nutritional supplement for three main uses: as a sleep aid, as an anti-depressant, and as an analgesic, meaning a pain reliever. These uses line up with how phenylalanine shows up throughout Wallach's own protocols, where DL-phenylalanine is dosed for conditions ranging from depression and insomnia to nerve and movement disorders.
claims.verbatim:
DL-Phenylalanine is marketed as a nutritional supplement as a sleep aid, an
anti-depressant and as an analgesic (pain reliever).

claims.subject: phenylalanine
claims.question: Can large doses of phenylalanine lower serotonin?
claims.answer_short: Yes—phenylalanine shares the same brain-entry transport channel as tryptophan, so in large doses it can crowd tryptophan out and interfere with serotonin production.
claims.answer: Phenylalanine uses the same active transport channel as tryptophan to cross the blood-brain barrier—the protective filter that controls what enters the brain. Because the two amino acids compete for that same doorway, Wallach notes that phenylalanine in large doses will interfere with the production of serotonin, the mood- and sleep-related brain chemical the body makes from tryptophan. In effect, loading up on phenylalanine can push tryptophan out of the brain and blunt serotonin synthesis.
claims.verbatim:
Phenylalanine employs the same active transport channel as tryptophan to cross
the blood-brain barrier, in large doses it will interfere with the production of
serotonin.

claims.subject: tyrosine
claims.question: What is tyrosine?
claims.answer_short: Tyrosine is one of 22 amino acids the body uses to build proteins; Wallach adds it to the essential list because a deficiency drives goiter, and it is the raw material for thyroid hormone and key neurotransmitters.
claims.answer: Tyrosine (abbreviated Tyr) is one of the 22 amino acids that cells use to build proteins. Although mainstream science treats it as non-essential, Wallach adds tyrosine to the classic list of essential amino acids because a long-term deficiency drives a specific disease -- goiter. Beyond its role as a protein building block, tyrosine has a special chemistry thanks to its phenol group: it takes part in cellular signaling and, combined with the mineral iodine, is manufactured into the thyroid hormone thyroxin. It is also the precursor the body uses to make the neurotransmitters dopamine and norepinephrine, and the starting material for the pigment melanin.
claims.verbatim:
Tyrosine (Tyr ) is one of 22 amino acids that are employed by cells to synthesize
proteins; its codons are UAC and UAU.

claims.subject: tyrosine
claims.question: Where does the word tyrosine come from?
claims.answer_short: The name tyrosine comes from the Greek word for cheese, because the amino acid was first isolated from cheese in 1846 by the German chemist Justus von Liebig.
claims.answer: The word 'tyrosine' comes from the Greek word for cheese. Wallach explains this is because the amino acid was first isolated from cheese, in 1846, by the German chemist Justus von Liebig. The name reflects where scientists first found the molecule rather than any special property of it -- a small piece of history that ties this thyroid- and brain-supporting amino acid back to a wheel of aged cheese.
claims.verbatim:
The origin of the word “tyrosine” is the
Greek word for cheese, as it was first isolated in 1846 from cheese by the German
chemist Justus von Liebig.

claims.subject: tyrosine
claims.question: What does tyrosine do in cell signaling?
claims.answer_short: Tyrosine's phenol group lets it act as a docking point in cell signaling: enzymes called protein kinases attach phosphate groups to it, which switches the activity of the target protein.
claims.answer: Beyond building proteins, tyrosine has a special job thanks to its phenol chemistry: it is a key player in signal transduction, the system cells use to relay messages internally. Tyrosine sits within signaling proteins where it acts as a receiver for phosphate groups, which enzymes called protein kinases transfer onto it. This phosphorylation of tyrosine's hydroxyl group changes the activity of the target protein, turning cellular processes up or down. Wallach notes that tyrosine phosphorylation is believed to be one of the key steps in signal transduction and in regulating enzyme activity.
claims.verbatim:
In addition to being a proteinogenic amino acid, tyrosine has a special function
because of its phenol functionality. Tyrosine is found in proteins that are part of
a signal transduction function. It acts as a receiver of phosphate groups that are
transferred by means of protein kinases. Phosphorylation of the hydroxyl group
alters the activity of the target protein.

claims.subject: tyrosine
claims.question: What role does tyrosine play in plants and photosynthesis?
claims.answer_short: In plants, tyrosine is essential to photosynthesis: inside the chloroplasts it donates an electron to re-charge oxidized chlorophyll during the light reactions.
claims.answer: Tyrosine matters in plants as well as animals. In plants it plays an essential role in photosynthesis: inside the chloroplasts, tyrosine acts as an electron donor that helps reduce, or re-charge, oxidized chlorophyll. In doing so it gives up a proton from its phenolic OH group, and the resulting radical is ultimately reduced back in photosystem II by the four core manganese clusters. It is a striking example of how the same amino acid serves completely different jobs across the living world.
claims.verbatim:
In plants, tyrosine residues play an essential role in photosynthesis. In
chloroplasts, tyrosine acts as an electron donor in the reduction of oxidized
chlorophyll. In this process tyrosine undergoes deprotonation of its phenolic OH-
group. This radical is ultimately reduced in the photosystem II by the four core
manganese clusters.

claims.subject: lysine
claims.question: What is lysine?
claims.answer_short: Lysine is an essential amino acid the body can't make and must get daily from the diet; it drives protein production and, through its derivative allysine, helps build the collagen and elastin that strengthen tissues and blood vessels.
claims.answer: Lysine (abbreviated Lys) is one of the amino acids Wallach counts among the classic essentials: nutrients the human body cannot make on its own and must take in every day to prevent deficiency and disease. Chemically it is a base, like arginine and histidine, it takes part in hydrogen bonding, and it acts as a general base in catalysis; it is also a common site of methylation, producing methyl-, dimethyl-, and trimethyllysine. Its core job is protein production, and through its derivative allysine it is essential for building the collagen and elastin that hold connective tissue and blood vessels together. Lysine is encoded by the DNA codons AAA and AAG.
claims.verbatim:
Lysine (Lys) is an essential amino acid with the codons AAA and AAG. Lysine is
a base, as are arginine and histidine. Lysine participates in hydrogen bonding
and a general base in catalysis. Common post-translational modifications of lysine
include methylation producing methyl-, dimethyl-, and trimethyllysine.

claims.subject: lysine
claims.question: How does the body break down lysine?
claims.answer_short: In mammals, lysine is metabolized into acetyl-CoA, a central fuel molecule, in a process that starts with a transamination reaction with alpha-ketoglutarate.
claims.answer: In mammals, lysine is broken down to produce acetyl-CoA, a key molecule that feeds the body's central energy-generating pathways. Wallach notes that this breakdown begins with an initial transamination, a reaction in which lysine hands off its nitrogen-containing amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate.
claims.verbatim:
Lysine in mammals is metabolized to produce acetyl-CoA through an initial
transamination with alpha ketogluterate.

claims.subject: lysine
claims.question: What is the 'lysine contingency' in Jurassic Park?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts how the film Jurassic Park gave its cloned dinosaurs a 'lysine contingency', engineering them so they couldn't make their own lysine, keeping them dependent on lysine supplements and unable to survive outside the park.
claims.answer: To illustrate how vital an essential amino acid is, Wallach points to the 1993 film Jurassic Park (from Michael Crichton's 1990 novel), in which dinosaurs are recreated by DNA engineering. In the story the dinosaurs are deliberately altered so they cannot produce their own lysine, the so-called 'lysine contingency', which would keep them from surviving outside the park and force them to depend on lysine supplements provided by the park's supplement program. The plot device works precisely because lysine is essential: an animal that cannot make it and is not fed it will not survive.
claims.verbatim:
the dinosaurs were altered so that they could not produce lysine (the “lysine
contingency”) that would prevent the dinosaurs survival outside of the park

claims.subject: lysine
claims.question: Why is lysine considered an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Lysine is one of the nine amino acids Wallach lists as classically essential: the body cannot synthesize them, so they must be eaten every day to prevent deficiencies and disease.
claims.answer: Lysine is one of the nine amino acids that Wallach, following the classic classification, calls 'essential': histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. What makes them essential is that the human body cannot synthesize them on its own, so they must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies and their disease consequences. Wallach further argues that three more amino acids, arginine, taurine, and tyrosine, should be treated as essential too, because long-term shortages of them drive cancer, macular degeneration, and goiter respectively.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.subject: leucine
claims.question: What kind of amino acid is leucine and what proteins is it part of?
claims.answer_short: Leucine is a branched-chain, hydrophobic alpha amino acid encoded by six codons; Wallach says it forms a significant part of the ferritin and astacin protein subunits and a class of 'buffer' proteins.
claims.answer: Leucine (abbreviated Leu) is a branched-chain alpha amino acid that Wallach classifies as hydrophobic, meaning it avoids water and tends to tuck into the interior of proteins. It is unusual in being specified by six different genetic codons (UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, and CUG), more than most amino acids, and it makes up a significant part of the subunits of ferritin and astacin, as well as a class of so-called 'buffer' proteins. That structural profile is part of why leucine is woven throughout the body's core protein machinery rather than serving one narrow role.
claims.verbatim:
Leucine (Leu) is a branched chain alpha amino acid that is classified as a
hydrophobic amino acid. It has six codons (UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, and CUG)
and is a significant part of the subunits of ferritin, astacin, and a class of “buffer”
proteins.

claims.subject: leucine
claims.question: Does leucine help build muscle?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach calls leucine a catalyst for muscle growth and muscle 'insurance,' and says it activates the mTOR kinase, the master switch that regulates cell growth.
claims.answer: Leucine is the amino acid Wallach ties most directly to muscle. He describes it as a catalyst for muscle growth and muscle 'insurance,' and says it activates the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase, the cellular switch that regulates cell growth. Read alongside his point that leucine is solely responsible for the synthesis of muscle proteins, this is why leucine is the branched-chain amino acid most associated with building and protecting muscle tissue.
claims.verbatim:
Leucine is important as a catalysts for muscle growth and muscle “insurance.”
Additionally, leucine activates the mammalian target of rapamycin kinase that
regulates cell growth.

claims.subject: leucine
claims.question: Where in the body does leucine work?
claims.answer_short: Leucine has major functions in the liver, fat (adipose) tissue, and muscle; in muscle and fat it is used to synthesize sterols, and its combined use there is greater than in the liver.
claims.answer: Wallach places leucine's major functions in three tissues: the liver, the adipose (fat) tissue, and muscle. In both muscle and adipose tissue leucine is used to synthesize sterols—the fat-like building blocks that include cholesterol and steroid compounds—and he notes that leucine's combined use across muscle and fat is actually larger than the amount used by the liver. So while the liver is the usual hub of amino-acid metabolism, for leucine the muscle and fat tissues do the heavier work.
claims.verbatim:
Leucine has major functions in the liver, adipose tissue, and muscle. In muscle
and adipose tissue, leucine is employed to synthesize sterols and its combined use
in these tissues is larger than that used by the liver.

claims.subject: leucine
claims.question: Can leucine be toxic?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach warns that leucine toxicity, as in decompensated Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD), produces delirium and neurologic compromise and can be life-threatening.
claims.answer: Leucine is not harmless in excess. Wallach warns that leucine toxicity—seen when Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) becomes decompensated, meaning the body can no longer keep the amino acid in check—produces delirium and neurologic compromise and can be life-threatening. MSUD is the classic picture of what happens when branched-chain amino acids like leucine build up unchecked, and it is why leucine, for all its muscle benefits, carries a genuine upper limit.
claims.verbatim:
Leucine toxicity, manifested as in decompensated Maple Syrup Urine Disease
(MSUD), produces delirium, neurologic compromise and can be life threatening.

claims.subject: leucine
claims.question: Can too much leucine cause pellagra?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says excessive leucine intake can produce a clinical pellagra—the classic 'four D's': diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, too much leucine can produce a clinical pellagra, identified by the classic 'four D's': diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death. Pellagra is normally associated with a shortage of niacin, so it is striking that Wallach flags an excess of leucine—not a shortage of anything—as a cause. It is a pointed caution that with leucine, more is not automatically better and that intake has a real ceiling.
claims.verbatim:
Excessive leucine intake can produce clinical pellagra ("the four D's"), ie.,
diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death.

claims.subject: leucine
claims.question: Is leucine an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach lists leucine among the nine classic essential amino acids the body can't make itself and must get from the diet every day to prevent deficiency and disease.
claims.answer: Leucine is one of the nine amino acids Wallach counts as classically 'essential': histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. 'Essential' here has a precise meaning—the human body cannot synthesize these amino acids on its own, so they must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies and the disease consequences that follow. (Wallach separately argues that arginine, taurine, and tyrosine should be added to this classic list, but leucine sits squarely inside the traditional nine.)
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.subject: valine
claims.question: Is valine an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes. Wallach lists valine among the nine classic essential amino acids—ones the body can't make on its own, so you must get them from the diet every day to avoid deficiency and disease.
claims.answer: Valine is one of the nine amino acids Wallach classifies as classically 'essential': histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. Calling it essential means the human body cannot synthesize (make) valine on its own, so it must be consumed from the diet on a daily basis. Without that steady daily intake, Wallach warns, deficiencies and their disease consequences follow.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.subject: valine
claims.question: Where does the name valine come from, and who discovered it?
claims.answer_short: Valine — a branched-chain amino acid named after the flowering plant valerian — was first isolated in 1901 from casein (the main protein in milk) by the chemist Emil Fischer.
claims.answer: Valine is a branched-chain amino acid, and its name comes from valerian, the flowering plant. It was first isolated in 1901 by the German chemist Emil Fischer, who extracted it from casein — the principal protein in milk.
claims.verbatim:
Valine is a branched chain amino acid that was named for the plant valerian. In
1901 valine was isolated from casein by Emil Fischer.

claims.subject: valine
claims.question: What are the codons for valine?
claims.answer_short: Valine (abbreviated Val) is an alpha amino acid encoded by four genetic codons: GUU, GUC, GUA, and GUG.
claims.answer: At the chemical level, valine—abbreviated 'Val'—is an alpha amino acid, the standard structural form the body uses to build proteins. In the genetic code it is specified by four codons: GUU, GUC, GUA, and GUG, meaning any one of these three-letter genetic sequences directs a cell to add valine to a protein it is building.
claims.verbatim: Valine (Val) is an alpha amino acid with the codons GUU, GUC, GUA, and GUG.

claims.subject: valine
claims.question: What does valine have to do with sickle cell disease?
claims.answer_short: In sickle-cell disease valine takes the place of glutamic acid in hemoglobin; because valine repels water while glutamic acid attracts it, the hemoglobin becomes more likely to clump together.
claims.answer: Wallach points to valine's role in sickle-cell disease as an example of how a single amino-acid substitution changes a protein. In this condition, valine substitutes for glutamic acid within hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells. Because glutamic acid is hydrophilic (water-loving) and valine is hydrophobic (water-repelling), swapping one for the other alters the protein's behavior in water and makes the hemoglobin more likely to aggregate—to clump together.
claims.verbatim:
In sickle-cell disease, valine can substitute for the hydrophilic amino acid
glutamic acid in hemoglobin. Valine is hydrophobic; therefore the hemoglobin is
more likely to aggregate.

claims.subject: histidine
claims.question: Is histidine an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach lists histidine among the nine classic essential amino acids, which the body can't make and must get from the diet every day to avoid deficiency disease.
claims.answer: Wallach counts histidine among the nine amino acids classically considered "essential" -- alongside isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. "Essential" means the body cannot synthesize these on its own, so they must be consumed every day through the diet; without them, Wallach warns, deficiencies and specific disease consequences follow. (He separately argues that arginine, taurine, and tyrosine should be added to this classic list, because their long-term deficiency also produces specific diseases.)
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.subject: histidine
claims.question: Who discovered histidine and when?
claims.answer_short: Histidine was first isolated in 1896 by the German physician Albrecht Kossel, and is one of the 22 amino acids the body uses to build proteins.
claims.answer: According to the Epigenetics account, histidine was first isolated in 1896 by the German physician Albrecht Kossel. It is one of the 22 proteinogenic amino acids -- the building blocks the body strings together to make its proteins.
claims.verbatim:
Histidine was first
isolated in 1896 by the German physician Albrecht Kossel.

claims.subject: histidine
claims.question: How does histidine work in enzymes?
claims.answer_short: Histidine's imidazole side chain binds metals and sits in enzyme catalytic sites, where it pulls a proton off serine, threonine, or cysteine to switch them on as nucleophiles.
claims.answer: Histidine's chemistry comes from its imidazole side chain. That ring makes histidine a coordinating ligand of metalloproteins -- it binds and holds metal atoms -- and places it at the catalytic sites of certain enzymes. In a catalytic triad, the basic nitrogen of histidine abstracts (pulls away) a proton from a nearby serine, threonine, or cysteine, activating that residue as a nucleophile so it can attack and break chemical bonds. The same imidazole also lets histidine act as a proton shuttle, moving hydrogen ions quickly where they are needed.
claims.verbatim:
The imidazole sidechain of histidine is a coordinating ligand of
metalloproteins and is a part of catalytic sites in certain enzymes. In catalytic
triads, the basic nitrogen of histidine is used to abstract a proton from serine,
threonine, or cysteine to activate it as a nucleophile.

claims.subject: isoleucine
claims.question: What is isoleucine?
claims.answer_short: Isoleucine is one of the nine classically essential amino acids—an alpha amino acid with a hydrocarbon side chain that makes it hydrophobic, and the body uses it to build protein.
claims.answer: Isoleucine (abbreviated Ile) is an alpha amino acid and one of the nine amino acids classically considered essential, meaning the human body cannot make it and it must come from the diet every day. Its hydrocarbon side chain makes it a hydrophobic amino acid, and it is carried on the genetic codons AUU, AUC, and AUA. In Wallach's table of essential amino-acid functions, isoleucine's role is protein production.
claims.verbatim:
Isoleucine (Ile) is an alpha amino acid with the codons AUU, AUC, and AUA. As
a result of its hydrocarbon side chain, isoleucine is classed as a hydrophobic
amino acid.

claims.subject: isoleucine
claims.question: Is isoleucine an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes—isoleucine is one of nine classically essential amino acids the human body cannot synthesize, so it must be eaten every day to prevent deficiency and disease.
claims.answer: Isoleucine is one of the nine amino acids classically considered essential, alongside histidine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. Wallach explains that because the human body cannot synthesize these amino acids on its own, they must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies and their disease consequences.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.subject: isoleucine
claims.question: Who discovered isoleucine and when?
claims.answer_short: Isoleucine was isolated in 1903 by Felix Ehrlich, a German chemist, who obtained it from hemoglobin.
claims.answer: Isoleucine was first isolated in 1903 by Felix Ehrlich, a German chemist, who obtained it from hemoglobin—the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells.
claims.verbatim:
In 1903 Felix Ehrlich, a German chemist, isolated isoleucine from
hemoglobin.

claims.subject: threonine
claims.question: Is threonine an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach lists threonine among the nine classic essential amino acids the body can't make itself, so it must be eaten every day to prevent deficiency diseases.
claims.answer: Wallach places threonine on the classic list of nine "essential" amino acids—alongside histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and valine. "Essential" carries a precise meaning here: the human body cannot synthesize these amino acids on its own, so they have to be supplied through the diet every single day. Wallach's point is that falling short of them does not just cause a shortage on paper—it leads to real deficiencies and their disease consequences, which is why he treats the daily intake of threonine and its fellow essentials as non-negotiable.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.subject: threonine
claims.question: How does the body process and metabolize threonine?
claims.answer_short: After it's built into proteins threonine can be tagged by glycosylation and phosphorylation, and it's broken down via threonine dehydrogenase into intermediates like pyruvate, acetyl-CoA, and glycine.
claims.answer: Wallach describes threonine as biochemically busy in two ways. First, once it is part of a protein, the threonine residue is a target for numerous post-translational modifications—chemical tags added by glycosylation and by phosphorylation through the enzyme threonine kinase. Second, threonine is actively broken down for energy: threonine dehydrogenase converts it to pyruvate, and an intermediate in that pathway can react with coenzyme A (thiolysis) to yield acetyl-CoA and glycine. Alternatively, threonine can be converted to alpha-ketobutyrate by serine dehydrogenase, feeding into the succinyl-CoA pathway.
claims.verbatim:
The threonine
residue is susceptible to numerous post-translational modifications; it can undergo
glycosylation and phosphorylation through the action of threonine kinase.
Threonine is converted to pyruvate via threonine dehydrogenase, an

intermediate in this pathway can undergo thiolysis with CoA to produce acetyl-
CoA and glycine; it can also be converted to alpha ketobutyrate via the enzyme
serine dehydrogenase entering the pathway leading to succinyl-CoA.

claims.subject: omega-9
claims.question: What are the omega-3, omega-6, and omega-9 fatty acid groups?
claims.answer_short: Wallach groups the fatty acids into families -- omega-3 (which he lists as DHA and EPA), omega-6, omega-9, and cholesterol -- though elsewhere he counts only omega-3 and omega-6 as classically essential.
claims.answer: In one fatty-acid overview Wallach names the essential fatty acids as linoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic, and says these are further divided into omega-3 (which he lists as DHA and EPA), omega-6, omega-9, and cholesterol. This is the single place he slots omega-9 into the omega grouping alongside the others. It is worth reading against his dominant stance in the same book and elsewhere, where he states that only two fatty acids are classically regarded as essential -- alpha-linolenic acid (an omega-3) and linoleic acid (an omega-6) -- so he does not label omega-9 itself essential.
claims.verbatim:
Essential fatty acids include the linoleic, linolenic and arachadonic fatty acids,
which are further divided into the Omega-3 (DHA and EPA), Omega-6, Omega-9,
and cholesterol.

claims.subject: carbon
claims.question: Why do some minerals have a carbon coating?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's framework carbon forms a protective coating — a chain of about 10 to 12 carbon atoms — around the third and most stable type of naturally occurring organic mineral colloid.
claims.answer: Wallach lays out four types of mineral colloid, and the third is the one he describes as the most stable form found in nature. In it, carbon itself forms the protective coating around the mineral, a molecular chain roughly 10 to 12 carbon atoms long. He notes this carbon-coated colloid also occurs in bacteria, fungi, plants (including some forms of petrified wood), animals and humans. It is this carbon-coated type that he calls the most stable of the naturally occurring organic mineral colloids.
claims.verbatim:
The third type of organic mineral colloid has a protective coating of
carbon with a molecular chain length of 10 to 12 carbon atoms. This
type of colloid is also found in bacteria, fungi, plants (including some
forms of petrified wood), animals and humans and is thought to be the
most stable form of naturally occurring organic mineral colloids.

claims.subject: omega-6
claims.question: Is arachidonic acid an omega-6 fatty acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach classes arachidonic acid and gamma-linolenic acid as omega-6 fatty acids, both in his 'conditionally essential' group.
claims.answer: Beyond the two classically essential fatty acids, Wallach identifies a 'conditionally essential' group of fats. He places three fatty acids in it: arachidonic acid and gamma-linolenic acid, which are both omega-6 fatty acids, and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), which is an omega-3. So two of the three fatty acids Wallach calls conditionally essential are omega-6 forms.
claims.verbatim:
Some fatty acids are classified as “conditionally essential.” This group includes:
arachidonic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid), docosahexaenoic acid (an omega-3 fatty
acid) and gamma-linolenic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid).

claims.subject: omega-6
claims.question: Were essential fatty acids once called vitamin F?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach notes the two essential fatty acids were identified in 1923 and first listed as 'vitamin F' before being reclassified as fats.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that the two essential fatty acids -- omega-3 (linolenic) and omega-6 (linoleic) -- were identified in 1923 and were originally listed as 'vitamin F.' In 1929, laboratory rat studies showed the two fatty acids were more properly classed as fats rather than vitamins, so the vitamin label was dropped. It is a piece of nutritional history explaining why these fats were once grouped with the vitamins.
claims.verbatim:
In 1923 the two essential fatty acids were identified, but they were originally
listed as “vitamin F." In 1929 laboratory rat studies indicated that these two fatty
acids were more properly classed as fats rather than being listed as vitamins.

claims.subject: omega-6
claims.question: Should omega-3 and omega-6 be balanced?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says yes -- the essential fatty acids' functions in the body all require proper ratios between the omega-3 and omega-6 forms.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that in the human body the essential fatty acids serve many functions, and all of them require a proper ratio between the omega-3 and omega-6 forms. So getting enough omega-6 is not the whole story -- it has to be in the right balance with omega-3 for those functions to work correctly. He points to traditional diets, which contained nearly equal amounts of omega-3 and omega-6, as the model of that balance.
claims.verbatim:
In the human body the essential fatty acids serve multiple functions, all of
which require proper ratios between omega-3 and omega-6 forms.

claims.subject: omega-6
claims.question: What does the body make from omega-6 fatty acids?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says omega-6 EFAs are the raw material for lipoxins and other eicosanoid signaling compounds the body produces.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the essential fatty acids are required to produce and maintain a whole family of signaling compounds: eicosanoids, endocannabinoids (which affect mood, behavior and inflammation), lipoxins and resolvins. He specifies that lipoxins -- a class of eicosanoid derivatives made through the lipoxygenase pathway -- come from omega-6 EFAs, while resolvins come from omega-3. So omega-6 is not just a structural fat; it is a starting material the body converts into inflammation- and signaling-regulating molecules.
claims.verbatim:
The fatty acids are required for the production and maintenance of
eicosanoids, endocannabinoids (affecting mood, behavior, and inflammation),
lipoxins (a class of eicosanoid derivatives through the lipoxygenase pathway
from omega-6 EFAs), and resolvins from omega-3 (in the presence of
aspirin, downregulating inflammation)

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: Does gallium act like iron in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says gallium and iron-type (ferric) salts behave so alike in the body that gallium ions often stand in for iron ions in medical treatments.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that gallium and ferric (iron) salts behave similarly in biological systems, so gallium ions frequently mimic iron ions in medical applications. Because of that chemical resemblance, gallium can slip into the same biological pathways the body normally uses for iron. He places gallium in the same chemical family as aluminum, but it is this iron-like behavior that gives the metal a role in medicine.
claims.verbatim:
Because gallium and ferric salts behave similarly
in biological systems, gallium ions often mimic iron ions in medical applications.

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: Is gallium used as a medicine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says gallium maltolate, an orally absorbable form of gallium, is used to treat brain cancer, inflammation, and certain infectious diseases.
claims.answer: Wallach points to gallium maltolate -- an orally absorbable form of the gallium(III) ion -- as a form of the mineral used in real medical treatments. He says it is applied against brain cancer, inflammation, and certain infectious diseases. That therapeutic use backs his broader argument that gallium has a genuine biological role, not merely a place on the periodic table.
claims.verbatim:
Gallium maltolate, an orally
absorbable form of gallium (Ill) ion, is used in medical treatments for brain cancer,
inflammation, and certain infectious diseases.

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: Where is gallium found in nature?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says gallium occurs as trace amounts in bauxite and zinc ores and across rocks, water, plants and animals -- richest in shale (about 19 ppm), scarcest in land animals.
claims.answer: Wallach catalogs where gallium turns up in nature: about 15 ppm in igneous rocks, 19 ppm in shale, 12 ppm in sandstone, and just 4 ppm in limestone, thinning to tiny fractions of a part per million in fresh and sea water. In living things the levels fall further -- roughly 0.5 ppm in marine plants and animals but only 0.06 ppm in land plants and 0.006 ppm in land animals. He adds that gallium occurs in nature only as trace amounts in bauxite and zinc ores.
claims.verbatim:
Ga - Gallium is found in igneous rocks at 15 ppm; shale at 19 ppm; sandstone
at 12 ppm; limestone at 4 ppm; fresh water at 0.001 ppm; sea water at 0.00003
ppm; soils at 0.4 to 6.0 ppm to 30.0 ppm; marine plants at 0.5 ppm; land plants
at 0.06 ppm; marine animals at 0.5 ppm; and land animals at 0.006 ppm.
Gallium (Ill) is found in nature as trace amounts in bauxite and zinc ores.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Is aluminum toxic to humans?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says aluminum is remarkably nontoxic - you'd have to swallow more than a pound of aluminum sulfate in a single day to reach a lethal dose.
claims.answer: Wallach holds that aluminum is remarkably nontoxic, and backs it with hard toxicology: aluminum sulfate has an oral LD50 (the dose that kills half of test animals) of 6207 mg/kg in mice, which for an 80 kg person works out to about 500 grams - more than a pound of it - in a single day. He stresses that aluminum is not nearly as toxic as the true heavy metals, so the trace amounts in ordinary food and water are nowhere near a harmful level.
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum is remarkably nontoxic, aluminum sulfate having an LDSO of 6207
mg/kg (oral/mouse), which would be the equivalent of 500 grams (more than a
pound) for an 80 kg human per day.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Is aluminum cookware and deodorant safe?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says studies show aluminum cookware, deodorants, and antiperspirants are generally safe at directed levels, with no evidence they cause disease.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, studies show that everyday aluminum products - cookware, deodorants, and antiperspirants - are generally safe when used at directed levels, and there is no evidence that aluminum in food or liquid causes any disease, including Alzheimer's. He notes one caveat: a small percentage of people are sensitive to aluminum and have reported contact dermatitis and digestive disorders after ingesting aluminum-containing products. For everyone else, he says the toxicity studies show it simply isn't harmful.
claims.verbatim:
Studies have shown
that aluminum cookware, deodorants, and antiperspirants are generally safe at
directed levels. There is no evidence that exposure to aluminum in food or liquid
causes any diseases, including Alzheimer's disease.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Does aluminum affect calcium absorption or bones?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes aluminum can compete with calcium for absorption, so a high dietary aluminum load can reduce bone mineralization (osteopenia).
claims.answer: Wallach flags one genuine trade-off with aluminum: it can compete with calcium for absorption. When the amount of dietary aluminum climbs, that competition can reduce skeletal mineralization - a thinning or under-mineralization of bone he calls osteopenia. So while he considers aluminum broadly nontoxic, he notes that an elevated dietary aluminum load can still come at the expense of bone.
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum can compete with calcium absorption, and increased amounts of
dietary aluminum can result in reduced skeletal mineralization (osteopenia).

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Where does the name aluminum come from?
claims.answer_short: The English chemist Sir Humphrey Davy named it aluminum, 'the metal of clay.'
claims.answer: Wallach traces the metal's name to Sir Humphrey Davy, the English chemist who dubbed it 'the metal of clay' - aluminum. The clay connection runs through its whole story: European chemists in the early 1700s realized a light-weight metal was locked inside clay, and a particularly rich aluminum-bearing clay found at Las Baux in France gave its ore, 'Bauxite,' its name.
claims.verbatim:
Sir Humphrey Davy, a distinguished English chemist of the 16th century gave
the name “aluminum’ to the metal of clay.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Are rubies and sapphires made of aluminum?
claims.answer_short: Rubies and sapphires are aluminum: Wallach explains aluminum occurs only as the oxide alumina, which becomes those gems when traced with other elements.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that aluminum never shows up as a free metal in nature - it is always bound tightly to oxygen as a hard oxide called alumina. When that alumina picks up traces of other elements it turns into gemstones: rubies and sapphires are essentially colored aluminum oxide.
