Those same gems, he notes, have been used as medicine for thousands of years in Ayurvedic practice.
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum does not occur as a free metal in nature, but is found only in
tight combination with oxygen forming a hard oxide known as alumina, When
contaminated with traces of other elements, alumina becomes a gem, such as
rubies or sapphires, which in addition to being used as jewelry, these gems have
also been used as medicine for thousands of years in the practice of Ayruvedic
medicine.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Where is gold found in nature?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports gold occurs only in tiny traces throughout rocks, water, plants and animals -- concentrating in the horsetail plant and forming a colloid in mammalian livers.
claims.answer: Wallach documents that gold is spread only in tiny traces through the natural world -- roughly 0.004 ppm in igneous and sedimentary rocks, 0.00006 ppm in fresh water, and just 0.000011 ppm in sea water, with even smaller amounts in marine and land plants and animals. Among plants, gold specifically concentrates in the horsetail plant, and in mammalian livers it forms a colloid. The vanishingly small figures show how rare and dilute gold is in living tissue.
claims.verbatim:
Au - Gold is found in igneous and sedimentary rocks at 0.004 ppm; fresh water
at 0.00006 ppm; sea water at 0.000011 ppm; marine plants at 0.012 ppm; land
plants at 0.0005 to 0.002 ppm (gold concentrates in the horse tail plant); marine
animals at 0.0003 to 0.008 ppm; land animals 0.00023 and in mammalian livers
it will form a colloid.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Did alchemists try to turn lead into gold?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says medieval alchemists -- the earliest chemists -- spent most of their effort trying to transmute lead and other base metals into gold, which was seen as a noble cure-all.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in medieval times gold was widely seen as beneficial to human health -- believed to be the most noble of substances and the 'panacea,' a medicine thought to treat all disease. He notes the 'alchemists,' whom he calls the earliest of chemists, spent most of their efforts trying to transmute lead and other base metals into gold. That drive to turn cheap metals into gold shaped much of early chemistry.
claims.verbatim:
In medieval times, gold was often seen as beneficial for human health, with
the belief that it was the most noble of substances and would be the “panacea” or
medicine that would treat all disease. The “alchemists,” the earliest of chemists,
spent most of their efforts in trying to transmute lead and other base metals into
gold.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Did the ancient Chinese believe gold could make you immortal?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the Chinese believed gold was immortal and could confer immortality -- even holding that eating daily from gold-colored alloy plates was enough.
claims.answer: Wallach describes an ancient Chinese belief that gold itself was immortal and that consuming it could make a person immortal as well. A practical obstacle, he explains, was that gold powder could not be absorbed and passed through the intestinal tract unchanged, so alchemists searched for ways to make it usable. The conviction ran so deep that the Chinese held it was enough simply to eat meals each day from plates made of alloys that merely looked like gold in order to gain immortality.
claims.verbatim:
The Chinese believed it was sufficient to eat meals each day from plates made
of alloys that looked like gold to gain immortality.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: What are the side effects of gold treatment for arthritis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists gold-therapy toxic reactions including itching, dermatitis, mouth inflammation, GI upset, protein or blood in the urine, aplastic anemia, low white cells, hepatitis and pneumonitis.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that gold therapies carry a wide range of toxic reactions. Milder ones include pruritus (itching), dermatitis, stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth), and gastrointestinal (GI) discomfort, along with increased albumin or blood in the urine. More serious reactions can involve aplastic anemia, a drop in white blood cell count, hepatitis, and pneumonitis (lung inflammation).
claims.verbatim:
Toxic reactions to gold therapies include pruritus (itching), dermatitis,
stomatitis, Gl discomfort, increase in urine albumin, blood in the urine, aplastic
anemia, reduced WBC, hepatitis, and pneumonitis.

claims.subject: bromine
claims.question: Who discovered bromine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts that bromine was discovered independently by two chemists — Carl Jacob Lowig in 1825 and Antoine Balard in 1826.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that bromine was discovered independently by two chemists: Carl Jacob Lowig in 1825 and Antoine Balard in 1826. Balard isolated it from the ash of seaweed gathered in the salt marshes of Montpellier — seaweed that was being processed to obtain iodine but which also happened to contain bromine. Lowig, working separately, isolated it from a mineral-water spring in his hometown of Bad Kreuznach.
claims.verbatim:
Bromine was discovered independently by two chemists, Carl Jacob Lowig
(1825) and Antoine Balard (1826). Balard isolated bromine from the ash of
seaweed collected from the salt marshes of Montpellier. The seaweed was used
to obtain iodine but it also contained bromine. Lowig isolated bromine from a
mineral water spring from his hometown of Bad Kreuznach.

claims.subject: bromine
claims.question: Is bromine toxic?
claims.answer_short: Wallach warns that toxic reactions from a bromine overdose can resemble acne-like skin eruptions.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that toxic reactions from a bromine overdose can resemble acne-like skin eruptions. He places this alongside bromine's long history as a sedative: compounds such as potassium bromide were used as sedatives through the 19th and 20th centuries, and the FDA later removed over-the-counter sedatives such as Bromo-Seltzer from public sale in 1975.
claims.verbatim: Toxic reactions from an overdose can resemble acne-like skin eruptions.

claims.subject: lanthanum
claims.question: What is lanthanum?
claims.answer_short: Lanthanum (symbol La) is what Wallach calls a 'light' rare earth metal, one of the rare earths he counts among the body's essential minerals.
claims.answer: Lanthanum, chemical symbol La, is what Dr. Wallach calls a 'light' rare earth metal, one of the rare earths he groups with the 'cerium metals' (lanthanum, cerium, praseodymium, neodymium, illinium, samarium). He describes it as widely but extremely thinly spread through nature: roughly 30 ppm in igneous rocks and soil, about 20 ppm in shale, only a trace (0.000012 ppm) in seawater, and around 0.085 ppm in land plants. Despite being classed with the exotic 'rare earths,' Wallach lists it among the essential elements the human body should be getting.
claims.verbatim:
La - Lanthanum is a “light” rare earth metal and is found in igneous rocks at
30 ppm; shale at 20 ppm; sandstone at 7.5 ppm; limestone at 6.2 ppm; sea
water at 0.000012 ppm; soil at 30 ppm; marine plants at 10 ppm; land plants at
0.085 ppm

claims.subject: lanthanum
claims.question: Is lanthanum found in the human body?
claims.answer_short: Yes; Wallach reports lanthanum occurs in animal tissue at trace levels and concentrates in bone (about 0.27 ppm) far more than in soft tissue (0.0001 ppm).
claims.answer: According to Wallach, lanthanum does turn up in living tissue, but only in tiny amounts and unevenly. In land animals he reports just 0.0001 ppm in soft tissue against 0.27 ppm in bone, meaning it concentrates in the skeleton far more than in the rest of the body. He also finds it in marine mammals (about 0.1 ppm), so in his data lanthanum appears across animal life at trace levels and preferentially in bone.
claims.verbatim:
mammals at 0.1 ppm; land animals at 0.0001 ppm in soft tissue and 0.27 ppm in
bone.

claims.subject: cerium
claims.question: What is cerium?
claims.answer_short: Cerium is a Rare Earth element — the most abundant of all the rare earths — named after Ceres, the Roman goddess of agriculture.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework cerium is one of the Rare Earth elements, and he singles it out as the most abundant of all the rare earths. Its name comes from the dwarf planet Ceres, which was itself named after the Roman goddess of agriculture. Wallach lists cerium among the roughly 60 essential elements, metals and minerals he holds the body needs, treating it as a plant-derived trace mineral rather than a useless curiosity.
claims.verbatim:
Cerium was named for the dwarf planet Ceres (which was named after the
Roman goddess of agriculture). Cerium is the most abundant form of the rare
earth elements.

claims.subject: cerium
claims.question: Who discovered cerium and when?
claims.answer_short: Cerium was discovered in 1803 at Bastnas, Sweden by Berzelius and Hisinger, and in Germany by Martin Heinrich Klaproth.
claims.answer: Cerium was first identified in 1803. Wallach records that it was discovered at Bastnas in Sweden by Jons Jakob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger, and also in Germany by Martin Heinrich Klaproth the same year. He describes cerium as the most abundant of the rare-earth elements.
claims.verbatim:
Cerium was discovered in Bastnas in Sweden by Jons Jakob
Berzelius and Wihelm Hisinger and also in Germany by Martin Heinrich Klaproth
in 1803.

claims.subject: cerium
claims.question: What plants is cerium found in?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says cerium is commonly found in tobacco plants, barley, and the wood of beech trees.
claims.answer: Cerium is a plant-derived trace mineral in Wallach's system. He notes it is commonly found in tobacco plants, in barley, and in the wood of beech trees. Land plants can concentrate it strongly — accumulating cerium up to 320 ppm — which is part of why he counts it among the plant-sourced minerals worth getting into the diet.
claims.verbatim:
Cerium can
be commonly found in tobacco plants, barley, and in the wood of beech trees.

claims.subject: beryllium
claims.question: What is beryllium?
claims.answer_short: Beryllium is a rare, light, hard gray-white alkaline-earth metal that Wallach lists among the body's essential minerals and that occurs mainly locked inside gemstones like beryl and emerald.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework beryllium is one of the essential minerals, and his books describe it as a relatively rare element in both the universe and the earth's crust. Chemically it is a divalent metal that never occurs free in nature, showing up only bound into alloys or minerals, and it heads the 'alkaline-earth' family alongside calcium and magnesium. In pure form it is a hard, gray-white metal - one of the lightest metals, yet hard enough to scratch glass - and so reactive that it readily combines with oxygen and other elements. You mostly encounter it inside gemstones such as beryl, emerald, aquamarine and chrysoberyl.
claims.verbatim:
Beryllium is a relatively rare element in the universe and the crust of the earth.
It is a divalent element that occurs naturally only in alloys with other elements
or minerals. Gemstones that contain beryllium include beryl (aquamarine and
emeralds) and chrysoberyl.

claims.subject: beryllium
claims.question: Who discovered beryllium?
claims.answer_short: Beryllium was discovered in 1798 by French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin, who isolated it as a new 'rare earth' from emerald and beryl.
claims.answer: Beryllium was first isolated in 1798 by the French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin, who reported to the Institut de France that he had found a new 'rare earth' by dissolving aluminum hydroxide out of emerald and beryl with an added alkali. Because some of the new substance's compounds tasted sweet, the editors of the journal Annales de Chimie et de Physique named it 'glucine.' In Wallach's telling, beryllium entered chemistry already labeled a rare earth pulled straight out of gemstones.
claims.verbatim:
In a 1798 paper read before the Institut de France, Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin
reported that he had found a new “rare earth” by dissolving aluminum hydroxide
from emerald and beryl in an additional alkali. The editors of the journal Annales
de Chimie et de Physique named the new rare earth “glucine” for the sweet taste
of some of its compounds.

claims.subject: beryllium
claims.question: Where does the name beryllium come from?
claims.answer_short: Beryllium was first called 'glucine' or 'glucinium' for its sweet taste, and only got the name 'beryllium,' coined by Wohler in 1828, much later.
claims.answer: For most of its history the element was not called beryllium at all. Because beryllium and many of its compounds have a distinctly sweet taste, it was first named 'glucine,' and for about 160 years it was known as glucinum or glucinium - from the Greek word for sweet - carrying the chemical symbol Gl. Martin Heinrich Klaproth preferred the name 'beryllina' because the rare earth yttria also formed sweet salts, and the modern term 'beryllium' was first used by Wohler in 1828.
claims.verbatim:
Martin Heinrich Klaproth preferred the name “beryllina” due to the fact that
yttria also formed sweet salts. The term “beryllium” was first used by Wohler in
1828. For about 160 years, beryllium was also known as glucinum, or glucinium
with the chemical symbol of Gl, the naming derived from the Greek word sweet
for the sweet taste of the pure substance.

claims.subject: rubidium
claims.question: What is rubidium?
claims.answer_short: Rubidium is a plant-derived trace mineral that Wallach counts among the 60 essential elements the body needs.
claims.answer: Rubidium (symbol Rb) is a trace mineral that Wallach places among 'The 60 Essential Elements, Metals, Minerals, Trace Minerals and Rare Earths' — the full roster of inorganic nutrients he holds the body requires. He groups it with the essential minerals found in high-quality humic shale, the plant-derived colloidal minerals he recommends to replace minerals stripped from modern food. Although rubidium is not 'classically' considered essential, Wallach argues it meets two or more of the criteria for an essential nutrient, so in his framework it belongs on the list of elements people need rather than being dismissed as a throwaway trace element.
claims.verbatim:
The 60 Essential Elements, Metals, Minerals, Trace Minerals and Rare Earths


Aluminum Gold Rhenium
Arsenic Hafnium Rubidium

claims.subject: rubidium
claims.question: Where is rubidium found in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports rubidium's highest levels in land animals concentrate in the liver and muscle, with the lowest levels in bone.
claims.answer: Wallach documents rubidium throughout the natural world — in igneous rocks, shale, sandstone, soil, fresh and sea water, and in both marine and land plants and animals, with land plants at 20 ppm. In land animals it concentrates most heavily in the liver and muscle, and least of all in bone, a distribution he specifically calls out. That places rubidium in living tissue rather than only in geology, consistent with his view that it belongs among the plant-derived trace minerals the body requires.
claims.verbatim:
Rb - Rubidium is found in igneous rocks at 90 ppm; shale at 140 ppm; sandstone
at 60 ppm; limestone at 3 ppm; fresh water at 0.0015 ppm; sea water at 0.12
ppm; soil at 100 ppm (fixed by clay soils); marine plants at 7.4 ppm; land plants
at 20 ppm; marine animals at 20 ppm; land animals at 17 ppm (highest levels in
liver and muscle; lowest levels in bone).

claims.subject: erbium
claims.question: Is erbium found in the body?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach reports that in land animals erbium settles primarily in bone, while plants take it up strongly, reaching up to 46 ppm in Carya species.
claims.answer: In Wallach's survey of the rare earths, erbium is not confined to rock — it moves into living things. He reports that in land animals erbium is stored primarily in bone, while land plants take it up strongly, reaching as much as 46 parts per million in the hickory tree (Carya species). It also turns up in marine animals at 0.02 to 0.04 ppm, and in igneous rock, shale, sandstone and limestone at progressively lower levels. That plants concentrate erbium so heavily fits Wallach's larger view that trace and rare-earth minerals are meant to reach us through plant-derived sources.
claims.verbatim:
Er - Erbium, a rare earth metal, is found in igneous rock at 2.8 ppm; shale at
1.9 ppm; sandstone at 1 ppm; limestone at 0.36 ppm; land plants up to 46 ppm
in Carya spp.; marine animals at 0.02 to 0.04 ppm and land animals primarily in
bone.

claims.subject: europium
claims.question: Where is europium found in nature and in the body?
claims.answer_short: Europium is a plant-derived rare-earth trace mineral that spreads thinly through rocks, plants and animals -- and in land animals it concentrates in bone far more than in soft tissue.
claims.answer: Wallach describes europium as a 'light' rare-earth metal spread thinly through the environment -- roughly 1 to 2 ppm in igneous rock, about 1.1 ppm in shale, and even less in sandstone and limestone. Living things take it up: land plants hold around 0.021 ppm but can accumulate up to 16 ppm in the hickory tree (Carya spp.), and marine animals carry 0.01 to 0.06 ppm. In land animals europium barely registers in soft tissue (0.00012 ppm) yet concentrates in bone at 0.2 ppm -- the same skeletal pattern Wallach notes for its sister rare earths erbium and dysprosium, which also settle primarily in the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Eu - Europium is a “light” rare earth metal found in igneous rock at 1 to 2 ppm;
shale at 1.1 ppm; sandstone at 0.55 ppm; limestone at 0.2 ppm; land plants at
0.021 ppm (accumulates up to 16 ppm in Carya spp.); marine animals at 0.01 to
0.06 ppm; land animals at 0.00012 ppm in soft tissue and 0.2 ppm in bone.

claims.subject: europium
claims.question: Who discovered europium and how?
claims.answer_short: William Crookes observed the phosphorescent spectra of the rare earths in the late 1880s, but europium's discovery is generally credited to French chemist Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who isolated it in 1901.
claims.answer: The road to isolating europium ran through the study of how rare earths glow. In the late 1880s William Crookes observed the phosphorescent spectra of the rare-earth elements; even so, the discovery of europium is generally credited to the French chemist Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who succeeded in isolating it in 1901. Wallach elsewhere notes that Demarcay named the new element for the continent of Europe.
claims.verbatim:
In the late 1880s William Crookes observed the phosphorescent spectra of the
rare earth elements; however, the discovery of europium is generally credited to
the French chemist Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who isolated europium in 1901.

claims.subject: cesium
claims.question: Is cesium found in the body?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach reports cesium occurs in trace amounts in plants and animals, and in land animals the highest concentrations are found in the muscle.
claims.answer: In Wallach's rundown of where cesium occurs, it is spread thinly across the whole natural world, from igneous rock, shale, sandstone and limestone to fresh and sea water, soils, plants and animals, always at very low trace levels. Marine plants carry about 0.07 ppm and land plants about 0.2 ppm, and it also turns up in living animals: land animals hold roughly 0.064 ppm, with the highest concentrations found in the muscle. The point is that cesium is not just a mineral locked in rock and soil; living plant and animal tissue actually take it up, however faintly.
claims.verbatim:
Cs - Cesium (caesium) is found in igneous rocks at 1 ppm; shale at 5 ppm;
sandstone and limestone at 0.5 ppm; fresh water at 0.0002 ppm; sea water at
0.00005 ppm; soils at 0.3 to 25 ppm; marine plants at 0.07 ppm. Land plants at

0.2 ppm; and land animals at 0.064 ppm (highest concentrations in the muscle).
topics: is cesium found in the body

claims.subject: barium
claims.question: Where does the name barium come from?
claims.answer_short: Barium's name traces to the alchemical term 'baryta,' from the Greek 'barys,' meaning 'heavy.'
claims.answer: Wallach traces barium's name to the old alchemy term 'baryta,' which itself comes from the Greek word 'barys,' meaning 'heavy.' It is a fitting name: barium's two most common naturally occurring minerals are barite (barium sulfate) and witherite (barium carbonate), both insoluble in water, and barium sulfate is such a dense salt that it blocks X-rays and is swallowed to outline the gut in medical imaging.
claims.verbatim:
Barium’s
name is derived from the alchemy “baryta” which comes from the Greek word
barys, which translates as “heavy.”

claims.subject: barium
claims.question: When was barium discovered?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says barium was isolated as an element in 1774 but not classed as a metal until 1808, the year he credits to English chemist Sir Humphry Davy.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, barium was first isolated as an element in 1774, but it was not classed as a metal until 1808. In his other books he credits the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy with barium in 1808. Long before chemists isolated the element, barium was familiar through its ore minerals — barite, a barium sulfate, and witherite, a barium carbonate.
claims.verbatim:
Barium was isolated as an element in 1774;
however, it was not classed as a metal until 1808.

claims.subject: barium
claims.question: Which plants are highest in barium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports barium is highest in marine plants like brown algae, and the fruit of Bertholletia excelea is such a strong barium concentrator it can hold up to 4,000 ppm.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that barium accumulates unevenly across the plant world. Marine plants carry it at around 30 ppm, with the highest levels in brown algae, while typical land plants hold only about 14 ppm. The standout is the fruit of Bertholletia excelea, which he calls a genuine barium concentrator — it can build up to 4,000 ppm, hundreds of times the level of ordinary land plants.
claims.verbatim:
plants at 30 ppm (highest in brown algae); land plants at 14 ppm (the fruit of
Bertholletia excelea is a barium concentrator and can have up to 4,000 ppm);

claims.subject: yttrium
claims.question: Is yttrium found in the human body?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says yttrium turns up in living tissue, accumulating in ferns among plants and settling into mammalian bone, teeth and liver.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that yttrium does not stay locked in rock but genuinely enters living things. Among plants it accumulates in ferns, and in animals it is found in mammalian bone, teeth and liver. This uptake into living tissue is part of his case that rare earths like yttrium belong in the diet rather than being dismissed as inert geology.

claims.subject: arsenic
claims.question: Where does the word arsenic come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach traces 'arsenic' from the Syriac al zarniga and Persian Zarnikh ('yellow pigment') through Greek arsenikos (meaning 'masculine'), then Latin arsenicum and Old French arsenic.
claims.answer: Wallach gives arsenic a colorful word-history. The name was taken from the Syriac word al zarniga and the Persian word Zarnikh, both meaning 'yellow pigment' (a nod to the gold-colored ore orpiment). Rendered into Greek as arsenikos, it carried the sense of 'masculine.' From there it was adopted into Latin as arsenicum and into Old French as arsenic, which is where the English word we use today came from.
claims.verbatim:
The word “arsenic” was taken from the Syriac word al zarniga and the Persian
word Zarnikh, which translates to “yellow pigment," translated into Greek as
arsenikos, and which translates into “masculine.” The word was adopted in Latin
as arsenicum and Old French as arsenic from which the English word “arsenic” was
coined.

claims.subject: arsenic
claims.question: Who discovered arsenic and when?
claims.answer_short: Wallach records that arsenic was first isolated and identified in 1250 by Albertus Magnus.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, arsenic was first isolated and identified in 1250 by Albertus Magnus. The substance itself was known and used far earlier, with a history reaching back to ancient China, the Greeks and the Romans. Separately, he records that the French Academy first identified arsenic in dead human bodies in 1834.
claims.verbatim: Arsenic was first isolated and identified in 1250 by Albertus Magnus

claims.subject: arsenic
claims.question: What has arsenic been used to treat?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says arsenic compounds have long served as medicines — arsphenamine and neosalvarsan for syphilis and trypanosomiasis, and arsenic trioxide for cancer and, from 2000, leukemia.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that through the 18th, 19th and 20th centuries a number of arsenic compounds were used as stimulants and medicines. Arsphenamine (developed by Paul Ehrlich) and arsenic trioxide (associated with Thomas Fowler) were among them, and arsphenamine along with neosalvarsan was indicated for syphilis and trypanosomiasis. He adds that arsenic trioxide has been used in various ways for some 500 years, most commonly against cancer, and that the U.S. FDA approved it in 2000 for acute promyelocytic leukemia — with arsenic also used as 'Fowler's solution' for psoriasis.
claims.verbatim:
During the 18th, 19th and 20th centuries, a number of arsenic compounds
were used as stimulants and medicines, including arsphenamine (Paul Ehrlich)
and arsenic trioxide (Thomas Fowler). Arsphenamine as well as neosalvarsan was
indicated for syphilis and trypanosomiasis.

claims.subject: tin
claims.question: What is tin?
claims.answer_short: Tin (symbol Sn) is a trace mineral Wallach counts among the essential elements; chemically it sits in the fourth main group, resembling carbon, silica, germanium, and lead.
claims.answer: Tin, whose chemical symbol is Sn, is a trace mineral that Wallach places among the essential nutrients the body needs. He notes it belongs to the fourth main chemical group of elements, so it shares many chemical and physical properties with carbon, silica, germanium, and lead. Although tin's presence in body tissue was once written off as environmental contamination, Wallach says careful studies later showed it to be a genuine essential trace element.
claims.verbatim:
As a member of the fourth main chemical group
of elements, Sn has many chemical and physical properties similar to those of
carbon, silica, germanium, and lead.

claims.subject: tin
claims.question: Is tin found in the human body?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach says tin occurs in land animals with the highest levels in the lungs and intestines of vertebrates, and in plants it concentrates most in mosses (bryophytes) and lichens.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that tin is genuinely present in living tissue, not just in the environment. In land animals it runs about 0.15 ppm, with the highest concentrations found in the lungs and intestines of vertebrates; among plants it is highest in bryophytes (mosses) and lichens. This distribution in living organisms is part of why he treats tin as a real, biologically active trace element rather than a stray contaminant.
claims.verbatim:
marine plants at 1 ppm; land
plants at 0.3 ppm (highest in bryophytes and lichens); marine animals at 0.2 to
20 ppm; land animals at 0.15 ppm (highest levels are found in the lungs and
intestines of vertebrates).

claims.subject: tin
claims.question: Why do men lose their hearing faster than women?
claims.answer_short: Wallach points to a 1991 federal study finding men now have poorer hearing at any age, thought to result from tin deficiency, with men over 30 losing hearing more than twice as fast as women.
claims.answer: Wallach links age-related hearing loss in men to tin deficiency. He cites a federal study released in November 1991 which found that men in recent generations have poorer hearing at any given age than men in earlier generations -- a decline he says is generally thought to be the result of tin (Sn) deficiency. He adds that men over the age of 30 lose their hearing more than twice as fast as women of the same age.
claims.verbatim:
A federal study released in November of 1991 showed that men in recent
generations have poorer hearing at any given age than in men in earlier
generations and is generally thought to be the result of a Sn deficiency. Men over
the age of 30 lose their hearing more than twice as fast as women of the same
age.

claims.subject: praseodymium
claims.question: Is praseodymium found in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says praseodymium accumulates in mammalian bone and liver, and land plants concentrate it up to 46 ppm.
claims.answer: Wallach describes praseodymium, a 'light' rare earth, as something found throughout the living world, not only in rock. Land plants can accumulate it up to 46 ppm (Carya spp., the hickory tree), and in animals it accumulates in mammalian bone and liver after ingestion. He uses this to make the point that praseodymium enters and builds up in living tissue — part of why he treats it as a plant-derived mineral the body takes in.
claims.verbatim:
Pr - Praseodymium is a “light” rare earth element that is found in igneous rocks
at 8.2 ppm; shale at 6 ppm; sandstone at 2.8 ppm; limestone at 1.4 ppm; marine
plants at 5 ppm; land plants accumulates up to 46 ppm (Carya spp.); marine
animals at 0.5 ppm; land animals at 1.5 ppm (accumulates in mammalian bone
and liver).

claims.subject: rhenium
claims.question: Does Wallach say rhenium is essential?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists rhenium among the 60 essential elements, metals, minerals, trace minerals and rare earths he holds the body requires.
claims.answer: In Epigenetics, Wallach places rhenium within his list of 'The 60 Essential Elements, Metals, Minerals, Trace Minerals and Rare Earths' — the full set of inorganic nutrients he holds the body needs for good health. In his framework rhenium is treated not as an incidental metal but as one of the plant-derived minerals humans require. He acknowledges that many minerals on the list are not 'classically' considered essential, yet argues each meets two or more of his criteria for an essential nutrient.
claims.verbatim:
The 60 Essential Elements, Metals, Minerals, Trace Minerals and Rare Earths


Aluminum Gold Rhenium

claims.subject: thulium
claims.question: Is thulium found in plants and animals?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports that thulium occurs naturally in land plants and land animals, but only in extraordinarily tiny trace amounts.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, thulium is present in living things only in minute traces, about 0.0015 ppm in land plants and just 0.00004 ppm in land animals, far less even than in the rocks it turns up in. It is a 'heavy' rare earth found across igneous rocks, shale, sandstone, and limestone, yet everywhere in scarce quantities. Wallach's broader point is that rare earths like thulium, once carried to us through mineral-rich soils and plants, are now largely absent from the modern food supply.

claims.subject: samarium
claims.question: What is samarium?
claims.answer_short: Samarium is a 'light' rare earth element that Wallach counts among the trace minerals the body needs.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework samarium (symbol Sm) is a 'light' rare earth element, one of the rare-earth trace minerals he holds the body requires. He notes it occurs naturally at very low concentrations throughout the environment, from igneous rocks and shale down to land plants and living animal tissue. He also lists it among the plant-derived minerals found in high-quality humic shale that a mineral-deficient diet should replace through supplementation.
claims.verbatim: Sm - Samarium is a “light” rare earth element found in igneous rocks at 6 ppm;

claims.subject: samarium
claims.question: Is samarium found in the human body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says samarium is present in living tissue in tiny amounts, in heart muscle, bone and liver, and that plants accumulate it.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that samarium is genuinely present in living tissue, not just in rocks: land animals carry 0.01 ppm in heart muscle and 0.0009 ppm in mammalian bone and liver. He also notes that land plants take it up at 0.0055 ppm and can accumulate it to as much as 23 ppm. This fits his view of samarium as a plant-derived trace mineral that reaches the body through food.
claims.verbatim: land animals at 0.01 ppm in heart muscle and 0.0009 ppm in mammalian bone

claims.subject: ytterbium
claims.question: What is ytterbium?
claims.answer_short: Ytterbium (Yb) is a rare-earth trace element Wallach documents in rocks, soil, plants and animals -- and it concentrates in bone, teeth and liver.
claims.answer: Ytterbium (symbol Yb) is one of the rare-earth elements Wallach catalogues as a naturally occurring trace mineral. He records it thinly scattered through the environment -- roughly 3 ppm in igneous rocks, 1.8 ppm in shale, 1.3 ppm in sandstone and 0.43 ppm in limestone -- and present in living things at far smaller levels, from 0.0015 ppm in land plants down to 0.00012 ppm in land animals. What stands out in his account is that, despite those vanishingly small dietary amounts, ytterbium concentrates once inside the body, building up to as much as 0.3 ppm in bone, teeth and liver.
claims.verbatim:
Yb - Ytterbium is a rare earth element found in igneous rocks at 3 ppm; shale
at 1.8 ppm; sandstone at 1.3 ppm; limestone at 0.43 ppm; land plants at 0.0015
ppm; marine animals at 0.02 ppm; land animals at 0.00012 ppm (accumulates up
to 0.3 ppm in bone, teeth and liver).

claims.subject: citrulline
claims.question: How is citrulline related to arginine?
claims.answer_short: Citrulline is the precursor the body converts into arginine, using the enzymes argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and argininosuccinate lyase (ASL).
claims.answer: Citrulline is the raw material the body uses to make the amino acid arginine. Wallach's Epigenetics explains that arginine is synthesized from citrulline through two cytosolic enzymes — argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and argininosuccinate lyase (ASL). The book notes this conversion is energy-expensive, because producing each molecule of argininosuccinate along the way requires spending ATP (adenosine triphosphate, the cell's energy currency); one reason it gives for supplementing arginine directly is that doing so leaves more ATP available to fuel other cell functions. In short, citrulline sits one step upstream of arginine in the body's biochemistry.
claims.verbatim:
Arginine (Arg) was first isolated in 1886 from a lupin seedling by the Swiss
chemist Ernst Schultze and is synthesized from citrulline by the sequential
employment of the cytosolic enzymes argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and

argininosuccinate lyase (ASL).

claims.subject: nitric-oxide
claims.question: What does nitric oxide do, and how does the body make it?
claims.answer_short: Nitric oxide (NO) is made from the amino acid arginine; producing it lowers blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels.
claims.answer: Nitric oxide (NO) is a compound the body produces from the amino acid arginine. According to Wallach's Epigenetics, oral arginine supplementation is required for nitric oxide synthesis, and it lowers blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed (narrowed or blocked) blood vessels. The same passage also credits oral arginine with reducing healing time after trauma — and being particularly useful for bone trauma — alongside supporting cell division, wound healing, and immune function. In Wallach's framing, nitric oxide is the molecule behind arginine's circulation benefits: easier blood flow and lower blood pressure.
claims.verbatim:
The oral supplementation of
arginine is required for the synthesis of nitric oxide (NO), the reduction of healing
time following trauma, and is particularly useful for bone trauma; it reduces
blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels.

claims.subject: serotonin
claims.question: What is serotonin?
claims.answer_short: A neurotransmitter the body makes from the amino acid tryptophan (via the enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase); it can then be converted onward into melatonin.
claims.answer: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter — a chemical that carries signals in the nervous system. The body builds it from the essential amino acid tryptophan using the enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase, which is why tryptophan is called serotonin's biochemical precursor. Serotonin can then be converted a step further into the neurohormone melatonin. In the same discussion Wallach notes that conditions cutting tryptophan absorption — fructose malabsorption, lactose intolerance, and gluten intolerance — lower blood tryptophan and are tied to clinical depression, and that a tryptophan metabolite (5-HTP) rapidly crosses into the brain where it is converted to serotonin (also called 5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT).
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan is employed as a building block of protein
biosynthesis and is a biochemical precursor of serotonin (a neurotransmitter),
synthesized via tryptophan hydroxylase. Serotonin can be converted to melatonin
(a neurohormone)

claims.subject: melatonin
claims.question: What is melatonin?
claims.answer_short: A neurohormone the body makes from serotonin, which in turn comes from the amino acid tryptophan (tryptophan to serotonin to melatonin).
claims.answer: Melatonin is a neurohormone — a hormone that acts on the nervous system. Wallach describes the body producing it from serotonin, which is itself built from the essential amino acid tryptophan, so the pathway runs tryptophan to serotonin to melatonin. The book covers melatonin only briefly, within its discussion of tryptophan — an amino acid it notes is sold as a sleep aid — rather than as a standalone topic.
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan is employed as a building block of protein
biosynthesis and is a biochemical precursor of serotonin (a neurotransmitter),
synthesized via tryptophan hydroxylase. Serotonin can be converted to melatonin
(a neurohormone)

claims.subject: coenzyme-a
claims.question: What is coenzyme A and what does it do?
claims.answer_short: Coenzyme A is the active form of vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) — it activates and transfers acyl groups, the reactions that release energy from carbohydrates, build and break down fatty acids, and make sterols, steroid hormones, and acetylcholine.
claims.answer: Coenzyme A is the active molecule that vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) becomes part of. It works in acyl-group activation and transfer reactions — the chemistry that hands molecular fragments from one step to the next — and these reactions are essential for releasing energy from carbohydrates, for gluconeogenesis (making new glucose), for both building up and breaking down fatty acids, and for synthesizing important compounds including sterols, steroid hormones, porphyrins, and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.
claims.verbatim:
that serves in acyl-group activation and transfer reactions. These reactions are
essential for the release of energy from carbohydrates; in gluconeogenesis; in
the synthesis and degradation of fatty acids; in the synthesis of such essential
compounds as sterols and steroid hormones, porphyrins, and acetylcholine; and
in acylation reactions.

claims.subject: acetylcholine
claims.question: What is acetylcholine?
claims.answer_short: Acetylcholine is one of the body's most common neurotransmitters — the chemical nerve cells use to signal each other; the body builds it in the nervous system with choline as a structural component.
claims.answer: Acetylcholine is one of the body's most common neurotransmitters — a chemical messenger that carries a signal across the gap between nerve cells. It works by binding to receptors on the receiving cell and altering that membrane's permeability to specific ions, which either fires the cell (depolarizing it) or quiets it (hyperpolarizing it). The body assembles acetylcholine in the central nervous system, drawing on choline as a structural component, and its production also relies on the acyl-transfer reactions run by coenzyme A, the active form of vitamin B5.
claims.verbatim:
in the central
nervous system, choline functions as a structural component of sphingomyelin
and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.

claims.subject: gamma-linolenic-acid
claims.question: Is gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) an essential fatty acid?
claims.answer_short: An omega-6 fatty acid Wallach lists as "conditionally essential" — not strictly essential like linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid, but needed from the diet under certain conditions.
claims.answer: Gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) is an omega-6 fatty acid that Wallach places in the "conditionally essential" group of fats — fatty acids the body can normally make on its own but that must come from the diet under certain conditions. This sets it apart from the two fatty acids he calls strictly essential (alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3, and linoleic acid, an omega-6). Alongside GLA, the conditionally essential group includes arachidonic acid (an omega-6) and docosahexaenoic acid or DHA (an omega-3).
claims.verbatim:
Some fatty acids are classified as “conditionally essential.” This group includes:
arachidonic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid), docosahexaenoic acid (an omega-3 fatty
acid) and gamma-linolenic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid).

claims.subject: docosahexaenoic-acid
claims.question: What is DHA and how is low DHA linked to depression?
claims.answer_short: An omega-3 fatty acid; Wallach says low blood DHA signals low brain 5-HIAA (a serotonin breakdown marker), which is directly tied to higher rates of depression and suicide.
claims.answer: DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) is an omega-3 fatty acid. Wallach explains that DHA together with EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) is required for the enzyme pathways the body uses to process long-chain polyunsaturated fats. He ties DHA directly to mental health: a low level of DHA in the blood is a marker for low brain levels of 5-HIAA (a serotonin breakdown product), and low brain 5-HIAA is directly associated with higher rates of depression and suicide. Elsewhere he places DHA in the "conditionally essential" group of fats and lists DHA and EPA among the nutrients that support memory and cognition.
claims.verbatim:
Omega-3 fatty acids, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid
(EPA) are essential for enzymatic pathways required to metabolize long-chain
polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). Low plasma concentrations of DHA is a
marker for low cerebral spinal fluid levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (S-HIAA).
Low brain concentrations of 5-HIAA is directly associated with increased rates of

depression and suicide.

claims.subject: arsenic-trioxide
claims.question: Can arsenic be used to treat cancer?
claims.answer_short: Once a notorious poison, arsenic trioxide became an FDA-approved cancer drug in 2000; low doses put acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) patients into lasting remission.
claims.answer: Arsenic trioxide — the arsenic compound that 18th-century physician Thomas Fowler turned into a medicine — has been used medicinally for roughly 500 years, most often against cancer. In 2000 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved it to treat acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), an often-fatal cancer of the blood and bone marrow. A 1998 New England Journal of Medicine report from Memorial Sloan-Kettering researchers found that low doses of arsenic trioxide destroyed the cancerous cells in 12 seriously ill APL patients and brought them into remission; Chinese researchers had reported the same result in 1997 (journal Blood), and their survivors were still leukemia-free ten years later. Arsenic is also used, as "Fowler's solution," to treat psoriasis.
claims.verbatim:
The doctors were the first in Western medicine to show that low
doses of arsenic trioxide are effective in destroying such cancerous cells.

claims.subject: korsakoff
claims.question: Why does Wallach call Korsakoff's syndrome 'cerebral beriberi'?
claims.answer_short: Because he classifies it as beriberi — thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency — striking the brain; he groups it with MS, ALS, Alzheimer's and Creutzfeld-Jakob as brain-lesion diseases that share a broad symptom list.
claims.answer: Wallach labels Korsakoff's syndrome 'cerebral beriberi' — beriberi being the classic thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency disease, here affecting the brain. He places it in a family of brain-lesion diseases — multiple sclerosis, ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease), Alzheimer's, Wernicke-Korsakoff's (which he calls 'cerebral beriberi and multiple sclerosis combined'), and Creutzfeld-Jakob disease (mad cow disease) — that he says all share a broad symptom list and brain-lesion pattern with Huntington's disease. The label reinforces his central claim that this 'dementia' is a reversible nutrient-deficiency problem, not permanent damage.
claims.verbatim:
Many individuals diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, ALS (Lou Gehrig's
disease), Alzheimer's disease, Korsakoff’s syndrome (cerebral beriberi), Wernicke-
Korsakoff's syndrome (cerebral beriberi and multiple sclerosis combined), and
Creutzfeld-Jakob disease (BSE, Mad Cow Disease, enzootic ataxia, etc.) share the
broad symptom list and brain lesion list with Huntington's disease.

claims.subject: gmo_foods
claims.question: Does Wallach recommend eating non-GMO food?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists consuming and stockpiling organic, non-GMO, fresh foods among his core principles for maximizing health and longevity.
claims.answer: Wallach recommends avoiding GMO food as part of his core health-and-longevity protocol. Under the first of the "three principals" he says must be practiced to the level of an obsession — eliminating acute and chronic damage and growing as much of your own organic food as possible — he directs the reader to consume as much organic food, non-GMO food, and fresh foods as possible, and to store and keep available as much freeze-dried organic and non-GMO food as possible, including a serving in each meal. He pairs this with drinking clean slightly-alkaline water, avoiding processed and nitrate/nitrite-cured meats, and being as gluten-free as possible.
claims.verbatim:
A. Consume as much organic food, non-GMO food, and fresh foods
as possible.
B, Store and have available as much freeze-dried organic food and
non-GMO food as possible

claims.subject: emory_university
claims.question: Where did Wallach discover cystic fibrosis?
claims.answer_short: At Emory University's Yerkes Primate Research Center, Wallach discovered the first non-human case of cystic fibrosis — in a young rhesus monkey in 1977.
claims.answer: It was at Emory University's Yerkes Primate Research Center in Atlanta, Georgia, that Dr. Wallach made his landmark discovery. In 1977, while working there as a pathologist, he discovered the first non-human case of cystic fibrosis — in a young rhesus monkey. Wallach concluded the disease was not genetic but rather a congenital deficiency of the trace mineral selenium in the embryo or early postnatal life, which suggested that at least some forms of cystic fibrosis could be preventable and reversible.
claims.verbatim:
In 1977, while working as a pathologist at the Yerkes Primate Research Center,
Emory University in Atlanta, Georgia, Wallach discovered the first non-human
case of cystic fibrosis in a young rhesus monkey.

claims.subject: emory_university
claims.question: Was Wallach wrongly fired from Emory University?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- when Wallach announced that cystic fibrosis was not genetic but a congenital selenium deficiency, Emory's Yerkes facility summarily terminated him in April 1978 without any chance to defend his findings. Word of the firing by Emory and the NIH then cost him a new St. Louis University post before he had even moved into his offices.
claims.answer: After Dr. Wallach announced that cystic fibrosis was not a genetic disease but rather a congenital deficiency of the trace mineral selenium, he was summarily terminated in April 1978 from his position at Emory University's Yerkes facility — without the chance to defend his observations that a PhD candidate would have been given. The consequences followed him: also in 1978, St. Louis University hired him to be Director of its Laboratory Animal Research colony in the medical school, but after learning of his termination from the Yerkes facility by Emory University and the NIH, the university terminated him before he even moved into his new offices.
claims.verbatim:
In 1978 Wallach was hired by St. Louis University to be the Director of the
Laboratory Animal Research colony in the medical school. However, after learning
of his termination from the Yerkes facility by Emory University and the NIH, he
was summarily terminated before he even moved into his new offices.

claims.subject: twenty_thousand_autopsies
claims.question: What did Wallach's autopsies of children in China find?
claims.answer_short: In 1,700 child autopsies in Keshan Province, China, 35% of those dying of the selenium-deficiency Keshan Disease had lesions consistent with cystic fibrosis.
claims.answer: In a separate study, Wallach performed 1,700 autopsies on human children under age ten in Keshan Province, China, where Keshan Disease, a selenium-deficiency disease, causes sudden death by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The study demonstrated that 35% of the children dying of Keshan Disease had pancreatic and liver lesions consistent with cystic fibrosis, supporting Wallach's contention that cystic fibrosis is itself a manifestation of selenium deficiency in the embryo or suckling infant rather than a purely genetic disease.
claims.verbatim:
The Wallach Keshan study (1,700 human autopsies) demonstrated
that 35% of those children dying of Keshan Disease (a known selenium
deficiency disease) had pancreatic and liver lesions consistent with cystic
fibrosis

claims.subject: stem_cells
claims.question: Does Wallach believe in stem cell therapy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds that essential nutrients, especially colloidal minerals, will always outperform stem cells and other medical technology for preventing and reversing disease.
claims.answer: Wallach's standing position is that raw nutritional materials beat high-tech medicine. He argues that the raw materials required by biological systems, the 90 essential nutrients and most critically the plant-derived colloidal minerals, will always trump medical technology such as genetically-engineered proteins, stem cells, and organ transplants when it comes to preventing and reversing birth defects and degenerative and chronic disease.
claims.verbatim:
Raw materials
that are required by biological systems will always trump medical technology
of genetically-engineered proteins, stem cells, organ transplants, etc.), when it
comes to preventing and reversing birth defects, and degenerative and chronic
disease.

claims.subject: stem_cells
claims.question: Do stem cell injections cure arthritis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says mainstream medicine offers only stem cell injections and joint replacement for arthritis, while he holds that nutrition can prevent and reverse it.
claims.answer: Writing about arthritis, Wallach notes that many doctors call it a genetically-transmitted disease with no way to regrow cartilage, so the only medical answers they offer are pain-relief medication, injections of genetically engineered stem cells to relieve pain, and ultimately joint replacement. He rejects that outlook: his nutritional 'Pig Arthritis Formula' (updated as the Healthy Bone and Joint Pak) was designed to prevent and reverse arthritis, which he says no conventional medical treatment is designed to do.
claims.verbatim:
the only medical answer is the use of pain-relief medication, injections of
genetically engineered stem cells that will relieve pain, and ultimately, in the end,
joint replacement.

claims.subject: stem_cells
claims.question: What is a stem cell?
claims.answer_short: A stem cell is a self-renewing cell that can divide to make identical copies of itself or daughter cells with different developmental potentials.
claims.answer: In his glossary Wallach defines a stem cell as a self-renewing cell that can divide symmetrically, giving rise to two daughter cells whose developmental potential is identical to the parent, or asymmetrically, generating daughter cells with different developmental potentials. In plain terms it is an undifferentiated cell that can renew itself and become other cell types, which is why he equates 'stem cells' with the fibroblasts (connective-tissue cells) used in cell cultures.
claims.verbatim:
Stem cell A self-renewing cell that can divide symmetrically to give rise to two
daughter cells whose developmental potential is identical to the parental stem
cell or asymmetrically to generate daughter cells with different developmental
potentials.

claims.subject: mediterranean_diet
claims.question: Is 'just follow the Mediterranean diet' good nutrition advice?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls 'just follow the Mediterranean diet' an empty catch phrase reflecting little real understanding of nutrition.
claims.answer: Wallach argues that human nutrition is "bogged down with catch phrases based on little understanding about nutrition," and he names "just follow the Mediterranean diet" (combined with other personal dietary restrictions) as a prime example of such a slogan. In his view these catch phrases reflect diets shaped by cultural, ethnic, and religious tradition and by local growing conditions rather than by any genuine understanding of what the body needs nutritionally.
claims.verbatim:
As a result of the environmental,
social, ethnic, and religious limits, human nutrition is bogged down with catch
phrases based on little understanding about nutrition, such as “just follow the
Mediterranean diet” combined with other personal dietary restrictions.

claims.subject: beef
claims.question: Does Dr. Wallach think beef and red meat are good for you?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls red meat an unequaled source of animal protein and essential lipids, and says the only trick is to cook it no more than medium, since well-done or burnt fat forms heterocyclic amines. He even recommends raw steak tartare.
claims.answer: Wallach calls red meat an unequaled source of animal protein and essential lipids; the only trick is to cook it no more than medium, since well-done or burnt fat forms heterocyclic amines. He even recommends raw steak tartare.
claims.verbatim:
Red meat is an unequaled source of animal protein and essential 
lipids - the secret is to not eat meat cooked well done or eat the fat 
burnt as they become heterocyclic amines. Medium rare and me- 
dium are the safe way to eat beef. Steak Tartar is a half pound of raw, 
freshly ground sirloin, served with chopped onions, pepper corns 
and topped with a raw egg - it doesn’t get any better than this!

claims.subject: beef
claims.question: Is it dangerous to eat beef cooked well done?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites a study of 930 women where eating beef and pork very well done raised breast-cancer risk 462% versus medium-rare; his point is that it is not the fat that harms you but how you cook it, because burnt animal fat becomes heterocyclic amines, powerful carcinogens.
claims.answer: Wallach cites a 930-woman study where eating beef and pork very well done raised breast-cancer risk 462% versus medium-rare; his point is that it is not the fat but the cooking that harms you, because burnt animal fat becomes heterocyclic amines, powerful carcinogens.
claims.verbatim:
On November 18, 1998, Dr. Wei Zheng of the University of South 
Carolina reported that in a study of 930 women, those who ate their 
beef and pork cooked very well done increased their risk of breast 
cancer by 462 percent over those women who ate their meat cooked 
medium rare - it is not the amount of fat in the diet that counts, but 
rather, how you cook the fat that counts. Burnt animal fat is con- 
verted to heterocyclic amines which are extremely powerful carcino- 
gens.

claims.subject: beef
claims.question: How does fattening beef cattle explain human obesity in Wallach's view?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's 'Feedlot Syndrome' analogy: ranchers fatten beef cattle on a steady stream of carbohydrate feed paired with optimal nutrients that drive the animal to eat with endless, fervent hunger, growing a 40-lb calf to 900-1,100 lb in a year. He argues humans are fattened by the same carb-heavy diet — but, unlike the optimally-supplemented cattle, humans eat it while mineral-deficient, which is what leaves them with a ravenous appetite.
claims.answer: Wallach's 'Feedlot Syndrome' analogy: ranchers fatten beef cattle on a steady stream of carbohydrate feed paired with optimal nutrients that drive the animal to eat with endless, fervent hunger, growing a 40-lb calf to 900-1,100 lb in a year. He argues humans are fattened by the same carb-heavy diet — but, unlike the optimally-supplemented cattle, humans eat it while mineral-deficient, which is what leaves them with a ravenous appetite.
claims.verbatim:
Raising prime beef successfully, requires a steady stream of car- 
bohydrate, protein and fat calories in the proper ratios specifically 
designed for fattening. 
The intense weight gain, high carbohydrate diet must be accom- 
panied by optimal mixes of nutrients designed to encourage weight 
gain and drive the animal to eat with an endless and fervent hunger. 
Feed, based on corn or other carbohydrates, is made available in 
a steady stream. Beef cattle will grow from a forty pound calf to 900 
- 1,100 pounds in about a year under optimal feedlot conditions.

claims.subject: pork
claims.question: Does eating a lot of pork cause obesity and diabetes?
claims.answer_short: Not on its own, in Wallach's view. He points to the Old Order Amish, who eat pork, beef, goat and mutton 3 times a day plus heavy whole milk, butter and cheese — by his account consuming more sugar, fat, red meat and dairy than anyone in North America — and yet post an obesity rate of just 4% and a type-II diabetes rate of just 6%, only about a tenth and a half, respectively, of their 'modern' neighbors in the very same county. He credits that gap not to their meat-heavy diet, and not even to their hard farm labor (the horses do most of the work), but to the essential minerals in the wood ashes they spread on their garden soil every single morning.

claims.answer_short: Wallach cites a Scientific American longevity summary: the patients who followed doctors' advice to the letter didn't reach 100, while the 'rebellious' ones who ate salt, eggs, red meat, butter and chicken skin did.

claims.subject: eggs
claims.question: How did eggs help cure pellagra historically?
claims.answer_short: Pellagra turned out to be a dietary deficiency disease — a lack of vitamin B3 (niacin) — and eggs were part of the fix. Wallach recounts how a U.S. Public Health Service researcher noticed that in orphanages and mental asylums the residents came down with pellagra while the staff, who ate a wider variety of food, stayed well. When eggs and milk were simply added to the sufferers' diets, the pellagra disappeared. Wallach lays out the competing theories of the era — the main one blamed the limited corn diet, while some held that pellagra was an insect-borne disease like malaria or yellow fever — and this is his illustration that nutrient-dense foods like eggs can reverse a 'disease' that was really malnutrition.

added to the diet of the affected individuals, pellagra disappeared.

claims.subject: fish
claims.question: Did Wallach have a hand in the official omega-3 / heart-health claim?
claims.answer_short: Yes — and it was more than a footnote. Wallach was a co-petitioner on the FDA petition (Docket No. 03Q-0401, filed 6/23/2003) that won the qualified health claim linking omega-3 fatty acids to reduced coronary heart disease risk, which the FDA allowed on 9/8/2004. It matters because it was one front in Wallach's larger legal war against the FDA — waged with First Amendment attorney Jonathan Emord — to force the agency to let supplement makers state health benefits that were actually proven. The same campaign carried his solo selenium-and-cancer claim (approved 4/28/2003); as he tells it, after losing every battle before the 1994 DSHEA Act, his side won every one that followed. So the official omega-3 heart-health language products can now use is partly his doing.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: How much of the liquid mineral supplement should I take?
claims.answer_short: One ounce of plant-derived colloidal minerals per 100 lb of body weight a day, ideally split — a 100-lb person takes 1 oz (½ oz twice daily), a 200-lb person 2 oz. Raise to 1¼ oz per 100 lb to lose 25+ lb.
claims.answer: Wallach's maintenance dose for the liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals: one ounce per 100 pounds of body weight per day, ideally split. A 100-pound person takes one ounce a day (or half an ounce — one tablespoon — twice daily); a 200-pound person, two ounces; a 300-pound person, three, and so on. He specifies the supplement should carry at least 77 minerals at a concentration of 19,000 mg per quart and cover all 90 essential nutrients. For anyone needing to lose 25 pounds or more, the level can be raised to one and one-quarter ounces per 100 pounds.
claims.verbatim:
These liquid minerals should be taken at the rate of one ounce 
per hundred pounds of body weight as a maintenance dose.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: What can I do about sugar cravings and the munchies?
claims.answer_short: Take one ounce of plant-derived colloidal minerals per 100 lb of body weight — even up to 10× a day early on. Wallach reads cravings and pica as a sure sign of mineral deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach's tactic for sugar cravings and the munchies while quitting sugar: take one ounce of plant-derived colloidal minerals per 100 pounds of body weight — even up to ten times a day at first. He reads cravings and pica as a sure sign of mineral deficiency, so flooding the body with absorbable minerals is meant to switch the urge off.
claims.verbatim:
If during the process of giving up sugar you get the “munchies” 
or feel the need to go on the classic “chocoholic” binge, take one 
ounce of plant derived colloidal minerals per 100 pounds of body 
weight - even if it’s ten times per day at the start (remember - cravings 
or pica are the sure sign of mineral deficiencies!!).

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: How do I re-mineralize distilled or filtered water?
claims.answer_short: Add one ounce of liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals to each gallon of distilled or double-filtered water — distilled is mineral-free and otherwise leaches minerals from the body.
claims.answer: A practical use for the liquid complex: distilled water is mineral-free and over time pulls minerals out of the body, so Wallach suggests re-mineralizing it — add one ounce of liquid colloidal minerals (at 19,000 mg of minerals per quart) to each gallon of distilled or double-filtered water.
claims.verbatim:
A good compromise is to use distilled or double filtered water 
that has been “enriched” with liquid colloidal minerals at the rate of 
one ounce of the liquid colloidal minerals (19,000 mg of minerals 
per quart) per gallon of distilled or double filtered water.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Is there a study showing the minerals help with diabetes or obesity?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites a 2004 pilot study he co-authored among the Nez Perce of Idaho: on a plant-derived colloidal mineral program, participants lost weight, lowered blood pressure, and cut fasting blood sugar 30–50%, most reducing or stopping medication.
claims.answer: Wallach's own outcome evidence for the complex, from a 2004 pilot study he co-authored among the Nez Perce of Idaho (Wallach, MacCoy, Henry, and Schrauzer). On a plant-derived colloidal mineral program — framed as replacing the wood ashes the tribe historically got their minerals from — almost all participants lost weight, significantly lowered their blood pressure, and cut fasting blood sugar by thirty to fifty percent, with everyone able to significantly reduce or come off their medication.

A 2004 pilot supplement study (Wallach, J.D., MacCoy, B., Henry, 
L. and Schrauzer, G.N.) with the Nez Perce Indians of Idaho, has 
shown that almost all participants lost weight, significantly reduced 
blood pressure and reduced fasting blood sugars by thirty to fifty 
percent. All were able to significantly reduce or wean off of their 
medication.

Worth noting that Wallach's books print the name two ways - Absorbance in Immortality, Absorption in Hell's Kitchen.

claims.subject: antioxidants
claims.question: Why do I need more antioxidants when I'm losing weight?
claims.answer_short: Because burning fat generates free radicals - losing weight itself creates the damage antioxidants defend against.
claims.answer: Losing weight itself creates the damage antioxidants defend against. Wallach says the byproducts of burning fat can turn into free radicals that inflame the intima, the lining of the arteries, which then drives arteriosclerosis, cardiovascular disease, cancer and Alzheimer's disease. His instruction is not a single daily pill but flooding yourself with multiple antioxidants at every meal, framed as an insurance policy against the free radicals you will eat without knowing it.
claims.verbatim:
To reduce the risk of the complications 
of weight loss, people need to flood themselves with antioxi- 
dants in order to protect themselves.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Is zinc gluconate a good form of zinc?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's view, no — zinc gluconate is a 'metallic mineral' form, and he says metallic minerals are only 8–12% absorbed, dropping to just 3–5% after age 35–40.
claims.answer: Wallach classes common supplement forms such as zinc gluconate as 'metallic minerals,' which in his framework are poorly absorbed. He states that metallic minerals — sold as gluconates, lactates, sulphates, carbonates and oxides — are only eight to twelve percent biologically available in younger people, and that after age thirty-five to forty their availability plummets to three to five percent. This is the basis for his preference for plant-derived colloidal minerals, which he considers the most efficient form of trace-mineral supplement.
claims.verbatim:
Typically, metallic minerals are found in tablets and powders as 
gluconate (calcium gluconate, zinc gluconate, etc.), lactate, sulphates, 
carbonates and oxides (iron oxide, etc.). 
Metallic minerals, despite wild claims to the contrary are only 
eight to twelve percent biologically available to younger animals and 
humans; after attaining the age of thirty five to forty years, the avail- 
ability of metallic minerals plummets to three to five percent.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Does zinc prevent cancer?
claims.answer_short: Not according to the study Wallach cites: in a five-year Chinese cancer trial, zinc showed no statistically significant protective effect against cancer deaths, while a beta carotene, vitamin E and selenium combination did.
claims.answer: Wallach points to a National Cancer Institute five-year study in Henan Province, China, that tested nutrients against a placebo in about 29,000 people aged forty to sixty-nine. He reports that zinc — along with vitamin C, retinol, riboflavin, molybdenum and niacin — had no statistically significant protective effect on cancer deaths after five years. By contrast, the group taking a combination of beta carotene, vitamin E and selenium saw dramatic results: 13% fewer deaths from all cancers, a 21% reduction in stomach-cancer deaths, and a 9% drop in deaths from all causes. In Wallach's account, zinc was not among the standout cancer-protective nutrients in that trial.
claims.verbatim:
The investigators reported that, “vitamin C, retinol, zinc, ribofla- 
vin, molybdenum and niacin had no statistically significant (protec- 
tive) effect on cancer deaths after five years.” 
The group that took the combination of beta carotene, vitamin E 
and selenium for five years had dramatically positive results: 13 per- 
cent fewer deaths from all cancers, 21 percent reduction in deaths 
from stomach cancer and a 9 percent decrease in deaths from all 
causes.

claims.answer: Wallach points to a November 2003 Tufts University analysis of fatty-acid blood levels from 1,137 Framingham Heart Study patients, followed for about ten years for new dementia including Alzheimer's. He reports the finding that those with diets rich in omega-3 fatty acids had a significant 48 percent reduction in the risk for the onset of dementia.

disease. Those with, “diets rich in Omega-3 fatty acids had a signifi- 
cant 48 percent reduction in the risk for the onset of dementia.”

claims.subject: vitamin-c

claims.answer_short: Linus Pauling recommended taking 10 to 12 grams of vitamin C every day - for colds, and to help prevent cancer and heart disease.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that Dr. Linus Pauling, a double Nobel Prize winner, championed large doses of vitamin C in his book Vitamin C and the Common Cold, both for fighting colds and for preventing cancer and heart disease. Pauling recommended that individuals take 10 to 12 grams of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) each day - far above ordinary intakes.

Pauling recommends that individuals take 10 - 12 
grams of ascorbic acid or vitamin C each day.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: What foods are high in vitamin C?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes that capsicum - cayenne peppers - are rich in vitamin C.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in 1928 the biochemist Albert Szent-Gyorgyi found that capsicum, or cayenne peppers, are rich in vitamin C. This makes peppers one of the concentrated dietary sources of the vitamin.
