In 1928, Albert Szent-Gyorgyi, an American biochemist found 
that capsicum or cayenne peppers are rich in vitamin C.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Can vitamin C help prevent Alzheimer's disease?
claims.answer_short: In a Johns Hopkins study, people taking vitamin C and vitamin E had a 78% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.
claims.answer: Wallach cites a January 2004 Johns Hopkins University study of 4,740 men and women over age 65 which found that those taking vitamin C and vitamin E together had a 78 percent reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease. He groups this with other antioxidant and omega-3 findings, concluding that antioxidant intake can substantially lower the onset of Alzheimer's.
claims.verbatim:
On January 20, 2004, researchers from the Johns Hopkins Uni- 
versity School of Public Health, released the results of a study on 
4,740 men and women over the age of sixty five that showed, those 
taking vitamin C and vitamin E had a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s 
disease by 78 percent.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Does vitamin C prevent cancer?
claims.answer_short: In a large five-year National Cancer Institute study, vitamin C showed no statistically significant protective effect on cancer deaths.
claims.answer: Wallach cites a 1993 National Cancer Institute study of 29,000 people in China's Henan Province, which found that vitamin C - along with retinol, zinc, riboflavin, molybdenum and niacin - had no statistically significant protective effect on cancer deaths after five years. By contrast, the group taking beta carotene, vitamin E and selenium had markedly better results, with fewer cancer deaths. In this trial vitamin C on its own did not lower cancer mortality.
claims.verbatim:
The investigators reported that, “vitamin C, retinol, zinc, ribofla- 
vin, molybdenum and niacin had no statistically significant (protec- 
tive) effect on cancer deaths after five years.”

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Is synthetic vitamin C the same as natural vitamin C?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts that when vitamin C was first synthesized in 1933, the artificial form was identical to the natural one.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in 1933 Tadeus Reichstein became the first person to produce a vitamin synthetically in the laboratory, and that his artificial form of vitamin C was identical to the natural one. In other words, lab-made ascorbic acid is chemically the same molecule as the vitamin C found in food.
claims.verbatim:
In 1933, Tadeus Reichstein has become the first to produce a 
vitamin synthetically in the laboratory, and his “artificial form of vita- 
min C is identical to the natural one.”

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: How did vitamin A get its name, and how is it related to vitamin D?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts that in 1922 the original 'vitamin A' was found to consist of two separate factors: the growth factor kept the name vitamin A, while the anti-rachitic (anti-rickets) factor was designated vitamin D.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in 1922 it was established that the original vitamin A actually consisted of two separate factors. The original growth factor retained the name vitamin A, while the anti-rachitic (anti-rickets) factor was designated vitamin D. Fortification of milk with vitamin D soon followed in the United States.
claims.verbatim:
In 1922, it was established that the original vitamin A consisted 
of two separate factors. The original growth factor retained the name 
vitamin A, while the anti-rachitic factor was designated vitamin D.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Can iron deficiency make you fat?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says a combined iron and phosphorus deficiency can trigger almost psychotic binge eating and soft-drink bingeing that ends in morbid obesity.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework, deficiencies of two or more essential minerals produce significant pica, cravings, and binge eating. He states that iron and phosphorus deficiencies occurring at the same time will result in an almost psychotic binge eating and soft-drink consumption rampage that ends in morbid obesity. The craving, in his view, is the mineral-starved body driving the person to eat — not simple gluttony.
claims.verbatim:
The deficiency of two or more essential minerals will pro- 
duce a significant level of pica, cravings and binge eating. Iron 
and phosphorus deficiencies occurring at the same time will re- 
sult in an almost psychotic binge eating and soft drink consump- 
tion rampage that results in morbid obesity.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Does calcium help with weight loss?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says consuming 1,200 mg of calcium a day cuts your risk of being overweight by 65 percent, and combined with dropping 500 calories a day it doubles the rate of weight loss—without exercise.
claims.answer: In Hell's Kitchen, Wallach frames calcium as a weight-control mineral: consuming 1,200 mg of calcium each day, even if you do nothing else, will reduce your risk of being overweight by sixty-five percent. If you are already overweight, cutting 500 calories a day (about one burger) while taking the 1,200 mg of calcium will double your rate of weight loss—he says, even without the need for exercise.
claims.verbatim:
We know that if you do nothing else, consuming 1,200 mg of ) 
calcium each day will reduce your risk of being overweight by sixty 
five percent! If you are overweight, give up 500 calories each day 
(one burger), and consume the 1,200 mg of calcium per day and you 
will double your rate of weight loss - even without the need for exer- 
cise!

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: Who first described pellagra?
claims.answer_short: Gaspar Casal published the first account of pellagra — a vitamin B3 deficiency — in Spain in 1755, calling it a 'new disease.'
claims.answer: In 1755 the Spanish physician Gaspar Casal (1680-1759) published an account of pellagra — a vitamin B3 deficiency — then considered 'a new disease' in Spain. He described it by the 'Three D's': dermatitis (a horrible dry, scabby crust crossed with cracks), diarrhea, and dementia, plus premature death, and noted the disease flared up each spring.
claims.verbatim:
In 1755, Gaspar Casal (1680-1759), published an account of 
pellagra (a vitamin B3 deficiency), then “a new disease” in Spain. 
Pellagra is characterized by the “Three D’s” including dermatitis (“a 
horrible crust, dry, scabby...crossed with cracks”), diarrhea, demen- 
tia and premature death - this disease flared up each Spring.

claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: What foods are high in vitamin B6?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes that a handful of pistachios provides twenty-five percent of the USDA recommended daily value for vitamin B6.
claims.answer: In his discussion of nuts, Wallach points to pistachios as a source of vitamin B6: a handful supplies twenty-five percent of the USDA recommended daily value. One ounce (50 dry-roasted nuts) contains 160 calories and 13 grams of fat.
claims.verbatim:
Pistachios: a handful of pistachios gives twenty five percent of 
the USDA recommended daily value for vitamin B6.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: Does folic acid help prevent breast cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites research that folic acid supplementation can reduce the risk of breast cancer for nondrinkers and drinkers alike.
claims.answer: Discussing alcohol and breast cancer, Wallach notes that one large study put the lifetime risk of breast cancer at 8.8 percent in nondrinkers and 10.1 percent in women who consume two drinks per day. He adds that research also shows folic acid supplementation can reduce the risk of breast cancer for nondrinkers and drinkers alike. In his framing, folic acid is protective regardless of alcohol intake.
claims.verbatim:
One large study indicates that the lifetime risk of breast cancer is 
8.8 percent in nondrinkers and 10.1 percent in those women who 
consume two drinks per day - research also shows that folic acid 
supplementation can reduce the risk of breast cancer for nondrink- 
ers and drinkers alike.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: What foods are high in folic acid?
claims.answer_short: Wallach points to liver as rich in folic acid (along with iron, copper, selenium, B12, and vitamins A, C, and D), citing Whipple's 1925 experiment where liver-fed dogs rebuilt red blood cells fastest.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in 1925 the pathologist George Hoyt Whipple bled dogs to produce anemia, then fed them varying diets to see which best rebuilt red blood cells. Dogs that ate liver — which is rich in iron, copper, selenium, vitamin B12, vitamins A, C, and D, folic acid, and essential fatty acids — formed red blood cells more quickly than the others. The passage highlights liver as a dense natural source of folic acid and the other blood-building nutrients.
claims.verbatim:
In 1925, Dr. George Hoyt Whipple, an American pathologist took 
large amounts of blood from dogs to produce anemia. Whipple fed 
the dogs varying diets to learn how different diets affect the produc- 
tion of red blood cells. He recorded that dogs that ate liver, which is 
rich in iron (and copper, selenium, vitamin B12, vitamin A, vitamin 
C, vitamin D, folic acid and essential fatty acids), formed red blood 
cells more quickly than those that did not.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: Why did it take so long to add folic acid to food?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the FDA's 1963 restrictions on folic acid stayed in place for thirty-one years; the FDA only ordered folic acid fortification of flour in 1996, and by 1998 the spina bifida rate had dropped twenty percent.
claims.answer: Wallach charges that the FDA's 1963 restrictions on folic acid remained in place for thirty-one years. He notes that by 1998, following the institution of folic acid supplementation, the spina bifida rate had dropped by twenty percent. Only in 1996 did the FDA, in his words 'being dragged, kicking and screaming to the end,' finally order folic acid fortification of flour.
claims.verbatim:
The 1963 restrictions on folic acid remained in place for thirty 
one years - by 1998, and the institution of folic acid supplementa- 
tion, the spina bifida rate had dropped by twenty percent. 
In 1996, the FDA (being dragged, kicking and screaming to the 
end), finally orders folic acid fortification of flour.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: Can a low-salt diet cause a B12 deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Yes — salt is the raw material for stomach acid, and stomach acid is needed to activate the intrinsic factor that absorbs vitamin B12.
claims.answer: Wallach holds that salt is the raw material the body uses to manufacture stomach acid, and that stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) is what digests food, ensures mineral absorption, activates the digestive enzyme pepsin, and activates the 'intrinsic factor.' That intrinsic factor is exactly what is needed to absorb vitamin B12. By this logic, restricting salt undercuts stomach acid and can therefore drive a vitamin B12 deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Salt is the raw material needed to manufacture stomach acid. 
Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid that is necessary to digest food, 
ensure absorption of minerals, activate pepsin (protein digestive en- 
zyme produced by the stomach) and activate the “intrinsic factor”

HELLS KITCHEN 257 
necessary to absorb vitamin B12.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: What is pernicious anemia and how is it related to B12?
claims.answer_short: Pernicious anemia is a fatal anemia, first reported in 1849, caused by missing vitamin B12; absorbing B12 requires both stomach acid and an acid-dependent 'intrinsic factor.'
claims.answer: In 1849 Thomas Addison described a fatal anemia, later named pernicious anemia, marked by a low count of abnormally enlarged red blood cells. Vitamin B12 was eventually identified as the missing nutrient, but the disease had a second twist: the stomach must produce two things, stomach acid and an acid-dependent 'intrinsic factor,' or B12 cannot be absorbed. Wallach notes that B12 injections can cure the disease by bypassing the stomach entirely, and that stomach-acid substitutes like betaine HCl can be used to reactivate intrinsic factor and restore absorption.
claims.verbatim:
In 1849, Thomas Addison reported the existence of a hitherto 
unknown fatal anemia, that was eventually called pernicious anemia 
- it was characterized by a low red blood cell count, but the cells that 
were observed were enlarged red blood cells. Vitamin B12 was even- 
tually identified as the missing essential nutrient, however, there was 
another feature unique to pernicious anemia - the stomach had to 
produce two important substances: 1) stomach acid and 2) an acid 
dependent cofactor known as “intrinsic factor” - without either or 
both vitamin B12 could not be absorbed.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What foods are high in copper?
claims.answer_short: Wallach points to animal organs—heart, liver, kidneys, and brains—as rich stores of copper along with zinc and selenium.
claims.answer: In tracing how early humans got their minerals, Wallach describes animal organs — the heart, livers, kidneys, and brains — as rich in stored minerals such as selenium, zinc, and copper (and vitamins including B12, A, C, and D). He presents organ meats as a dependable dietary source of copper.
claims.verbatim:
The 
animals organs, including the heart, livers, kidneys and brains were 
rich in stored minerals such as selenium, zinc and copper

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: Are cashews a good source of copper?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach notes a handful of cashews supplies about 30 percent of the recommended daily allowance of copper, along with magnesium and iron.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that a handful of cashews contains about 30 percent of the USDA recommended daily allowance of copper, plus 20 percent of magnesium and 10 percent of iron. This makes cashews one of the concrete everyday foods he cites as a copper source.
claims.verbatim:
Cashews: a handful contains 20 percent of the USDA recom- 
mended daily allowance of magnesium, 30 percent of copper, and 
10 percent of iron.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: Did Einstein really die of a copper deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says Einstein died of a simple copper deficiency, the same ruptured-aneurysm problem he had already eliminated in turkeys years earlier just by raising copper in their feed.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that a decade before Einstein's death his team had eliminated ruptured aneurysms in turkeys simply by increasing the copper in their feed pellets. Despite the best doctors money could buy, he says Einstein died of a simple copper deficiency, and that Einstein had shown warning signs of it for decades in the form of grey hair and deep skin wrinkles.
claims.verbatim:
ten years earlier we had eliminated ruptured aneurysms 
in turkey’s (a cause of devastating losses) by simply increasing the 
copper levels in their food pellets. 
We are sure that Einstein had the very best doctors that money 
could buy and that medical science could provide - yet Einstein died 
of a simple copper deficiency - a deficiency that he had warnings of 
(grey hair and deep skin wrinkles) for decades before he died.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: What is chromium?
claims.answer_short: Chromium is an essential trace mineral the body must have for normal glucose metabolism, working hand-in-hand with insulin to control blood sugar.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework chromium is an essential trace element the body must have for normal glucose metabolism, and its function is tied directly to insulin. It is the working core of GTF, the glucose tolerance factor (a complex of chromium III, dinicotinic acid, and glutathione), and only the trivalent form is biologically active. The whole body holds only about 1.5 mg, yet Wallach considers chromium so central to blood-sugar control that he names its deficiency, together with vanadium, a primary cause of diabetes and hypoglycemia. He cites the USDA's Richard Anderson that ninety percent of Americans are deficient in it.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium is required for circulating glucose tolerance factor to 
function properly. Chromium is an essential trace element necessary 
for the normal glucose metabolism, It’s function is directly related to 
the function of insulin.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: What is chromium and what does it do?
claims.answer_short: Chromium is an essential trace mineral required for normal glucose metabolism, and its job is tied directly to how insulin works.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework chromium is an essential trace element the body must have for normal glucose metabolism. Its function is directly tied to insulin, and chromium is required for the glucose tolerance factor to work properly so blood sugar can be managed. Without enough chromium, insulin cannot do its job efficiently.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium is required for circulating glucose tolerance factor to 
function properly. Chromium is an essential trace element necessary 
for the normal glucose metabolism, It’s function is directly related to 
the function of insulin.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Which form of chromium is active in the body?
claims.answer_short: Only trivalent chromium is biologically active, and it does more than manage blood sugar — it also drives amino acid transport and protein synthesis.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that only the trivalent state of chromium is biologically active, working by forming complexes with organic compounds. Chromium's role is not limited to glucose metabolism. Animal studies show it also stimulates amino acid transport and protein synthesis.
claims.verbatim:
Only the trivalent state of chromium is biologically active and it 
works by forming complexes with organic compounds. Insulin-chro- 
mium relationships are not restricted to glucose metabolism. Animal 
studies have shown that chromium stimulates amino acid transport 
and protein synthesis.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: What are the symptoms of chromium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Chromium deficiency shows up as glucose intolerance, poor growth, peripheral neuropathy, muscle and protein loss, and a lowered respiratory quotient.
claims.answer: Wallach characterizes chromium deficiency by glucose intolerance — hypoglycemia, insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and diabetes. It also produces poor growth, peripheral neuropathies, and a negative nitrogen balance, meaning loss of muscle mass or sarcopenia. A decreased respiratory quotient is another sign.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiency of chromium is characterized by glucose intolerance 
(hypoglycemia, insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia and diabetes), 
poor growth, peripheral neuropathies, negative nitrogen balance (loss 
of muscle mass - sarcopenia) and a decreased respiratory quotient.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: What causes intense sugar, carb, and chocolate cravings?
claims.answer_short: According to Wallach, obsessive carb cravings and the 'munchies' — especially for chocolate and sweets — are sure signs of a chromium and vanadium deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach says chromium and vanadium deficiencies show up as a thirst for liquids like soft drinks, juices, and alcohol, with plain water the last choice, plus an obsessive hunger for carbohydrates of all kinds. The 'munchies' and cravings for alcohol and candy, especially chocolate, are in his view sure signs of a chromium and vanadium deficiency. He cites Reagan's craving for jelly beans as an example.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium and vanadium deficiencies are manifested by thirst 
for liquids (soft drinks, juices, alcohol, etc.), with water being the 
last choice and an obsessive hunger for carbohydrates of all types. 
The “munchies,” cravings for alcohol and candy cravings (Regan’s 
cravings for jelly beans), especially chocolate, are sure signs of a chro- 
mium and vanadium deficiency.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Can chromium replace insulin injections?
claims.answer_short: In 1977 K. N. Jeejeebhoy reported that intravenous chromium eliminated the need for medical insulin in human diabetics and reversed their peripheral neuropathy.
claims.answer: Wallach cites K. N. Jeejeebhoy, who by 1977 reported that chromium could eliminate the need for medical insulin in human patients. His intravenous use of chromium in human diabetics eliminated peripheral neuropathies and removed the need for insulin treatments to stabilize blood sugar. Wallach uses this as evidence that chromium addresses the root of the disease.
claims.verbatim:
By 1977, K. N. Jeejeebhoy reported that chromium could elimi- 
nate the need for medical insulin in human patients. His intravenous 
use of chromium in human diabetics eliminated peripheral neuropa- 
thies and well as eliminated the need for insulin treatments to stabi- 
lize blood sugar.

claims.subject: potassium
claims.question: What happens to animals that lack potassium?
claims.answer_short: Potassium-deficient rats turn hyper-alert and hyperactive and lick everything in sight — cage, equipment, each other, even urine.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that potassium-deficient laboratory rats become hyper-alert and hyperactive and start licking everything within reach — their metal cage, lab equipment, each other, and even urine puddles. Even under a severe potassium deficiency, he notes, the rats still show a strong craving for sodium chloride (common salt). He uses these animal observations to show how a mineral shortfall can drive compulsive licking and craving behavior.
claims.verbatim:
Potassium deficient rats are hyper alert, hyper active and tend to 
lick everything including their metal cage, lab equipment, each other 
and urine puddles (beer and urine have a similar taste). It is also 
interesting to note that even with a severe potassium deficiency labo- 
ratory rats have a strong craving for sodium chloride (salt).

claims.subject: potassium
claims.question: Can you actually become deficient in potassium?
claims.answer_short: Naturally it's rare because grains, fruits and vegetables are potassium-rich, but diuretics or a junk-food diet can cause it.
claims.answer: Wallach says a natural potassium deficiency is highly unlikely, because grains, fruits and vegetables all tend to be rich in potassium (the K in NPK fertilizer). Where it does appear, he points to two causes: taking diuretics, and eating a diet where the only 'vegetable' is French fries and ketchup. In his view, genuine deficiency usually comes from drugs or a produce-free diet rather than from ordinary eating.
claims.verbatim:
A natural potassium deficiency is highly unlikely in nature, as all 
grains, fruits and vegetables tend to be rich in potassium (NPK fertil- 
izer) - a potassium deficiency can be found in individuals given di- 
uretics and individuals whose only vegetable intake is French fries 
and ketchup.

claims.subject: iodine
claims.question: Why is table salt iodized?
claims.answer_short: Iodized salt was introduced in 1925 (Morton Salt) specifically to prevent goiter by restoring iodine to the diet.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in April 1925 the Morton Salt Company placed an ad in the Woman's Home Companion to market iodized salt as a new table salt that prevents goiter. The pitch promised that "Nature's iodine restored" would prevent goiter, then described as threatening almost every child, with no change in taste. Adding iodine to salt became a public-health fix once physicians identified insufficient iodine in the thyroid as the cause of goiter.
claims.verbatim:
“Now - a new table salt that prevents goiter. Save children! Nature's 
iodine restored - yet tastes no different.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: What foods are high in vitamin E?
claims.answer_short: When vitamin E was first identified as a fertility factor, it was found abundant in green leafy vegetables and wheat germ.
claims.answer: When vitamin E was first identified as a dietary fertility factor, researchers found it was abundant in green leafy vegetables and wheat germ. These are among the food sources Wallach cites for the vitamin. It was this fat-soluble factor, unrelated to other known vitamins, that came to be called vitamin E.
claims.verbatim: fertility factor was abundant in green leafy vegetables and wheat germ.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Which foods are high in vitamin E?
claims.answer_short: Nuts are a rich source; Wallach notes hazelnuts, almonds and walnuts all supply vitamin E, with 24 hazelnuts giving about 20% of the daily value.
claims.answer: Wallach points to nuts as a good source of vitamin E. He notes that 24 hazelnuts (filberts) provide about twenty percent of the USDA recommended daily value of vitamin E, along with ninety percent of the manganese. Almonds are also rich in vitamin E, and English walnuts supply it too, so a handful of nuts is an easy dietary source.
claims.verbatim:
Hazelnuts (Filberts): 24 nuts provide twenty percent of the 
USDA recommended daily value of vitamin E and ninety percent of 
the manganese.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Does vitamin E help with Alzheimer's disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites studies showing vitamin E can ease memory loss and slow decline in Alzheimer's patients, delaying the need for nursing-home care.
claims.answer: Wallach presents research indicating that vitamin E, a simple antioxidant, can ease memory loss in Alzheimer's patients. He cites a 1992 University of California, San Diego and Salk Institute study to this effect, and an April 1997 UCSD study reporting that vitamin E could slow the devastating decline in some Alzheimer's patients and significantly delay the need for nursing-home care.
claims.verbatim: antioxidant vitamin E can ease memory loss in Alzheimer’ patients.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Does vitamin E help prevent cancer?
claims.answer_short: In a five-year China study Wallach cites, beta carotene, vitamin E and selenium together gave 13% fewer cancer deaths and 21% fewer stomach-cancer deaths.
claims.answer: Wallach points to a large study in Henan Province, China, in which one group took a combination of beta carotene, vitamin E and selenium for five years. That group had dramatically positive results: 13 percent fewer deaths from all cancers, a 21 percent reduction in deaths from stomach cancer, and a 9 percent decrease in deaths from all causes. Other single nutrients tested showed no statistically significant protective effect, which he takes as evidence for this antioxidant trio.
claims.verbatim:
The group that took the combination of beta carotene, vitamin E 
and selenium for five years had dramatically positive results: 13 per- 
cent fewer deaths from all cancers, 21 percent reduction in deaths 
from stomach cancer and a 9 percent decrease in deaths from all 
causes.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Why is it called vitamin E?
claims.answer_short: The newly found fertility factor was fat-soluble but not related to any known vitamin, so it was named vitamin E.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the newly found fertility factor was fat-soluble but not related to any of the vitamins already identified, so it was named vitamin E. Its discovery came out of work by Herbert McLean Evans and Katherine Scott Bishop, who found it abundant in green leafy vegetables and wheat germ.
claims.verbatim:
The fertility factor was fat soluble but not related to any other vita- 
min so it was called vitamin E.

claims.subject: vanadium
claims.question: Can low vanadium cause weight gain?
claims.answer_short: Without enough chromium and vanadium, blood glucose is converted into blood fats and body fat instead of being burned for energy.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that when dietary or supplemental chromium and vanadium are absent or insufficient, blood glucose is converted into blood lipids and body fat rather than being efficiently burned for energy. The concurrent deficiencies of chromium, vanadium, and other minerals produce ravenous hunger, cravings, binge eating, pica, and the munchies. He identifies this combination as a basic root cause of obesity.
claims.verbatim:
The absence of or insufficient levels of dietary or supplemental 
chromium and vanadium, results in blood glucose being converted 
into blood lipids and body fat, rather than efficiently being burned 
for energy. The concurrent deficiencies chromium, vanadium and 
other minerals results in ravenous hunger, cravings, binge eating, 
pica, cribbing and the munchies.

claims.subject: manganese
claims.question: What foods are high in manganese?
claims.answer_short: Hazelnuts (filberts) are a standout, with 24 nuts supplying ninety percent of the daily value for manganese.
claims.answer: Among nuts, hazelnuts (filberts) are an outstanding source of manganese. Wallach notes that 24 hazelnuts provide ninety percent of the USDA recommended daily value of manganese, along with twenty percent of the daily value for vitamin E. A one-ounce serving of 20 nuts carries 180 calories and 17 grams of fat, making hazelnuts an easy whole-food way to boost manganese intake.
claims.verbatim:
Hazelnuts (Filberts): 24 nuts provide twenty percent of the 
USDA recommended daily value of vitamin E and ninety percent of 
the manganese.

claims.subject: molybdenum
claims.question: Is molybdenum essential for plants?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists molybdenum among the micronutrients that plants require for optimal health.
claims.answer: In a table of elements required by plants for optimal health, Wallach classes molybdenum as a micronutrient - one of the trace elements that plants need in small amounts, alongside iron, chlorine, copper, zinc, boron, and manganese. These micronutrients are distinguished from the macronutrients plants need in larger quantities, such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.
claims.verbatim:
Elements Required by Plants for Optimal Health 
Macronutrients 
Nitrogen (N) 
Phosphorus (P) 
Potassium (K) 
Calcium 
Magnesium 
Sulfur 
Micronutrients 
Iron 
Chlorine 
Copper

claims.subject: molybdenum
claims.question: Does molybdenum help prevent cancer?
claims.answer_short: In a large China study Wallach cites, molybdenum had no statistically significant protective effect against cancer deaths, unlike beta carotene, vitamin E, and selenium.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts a National Cancer Institute study in Henan Province, China, in which molybdenum was one of the nutrients tested against cancer. He reports that vitamin C, retinol, zinc, riboflavin, molybdenum, and niacin had no statistically significant protective effect on cancer deaths after five years. By contrast, the group taking beta carotene, vitamin E, and selenium saw dramatically positive results, including 13 percent fewer deaths from all cancers.
claims.verbatim:
The investigators reported that, “vitamin C, retinol, zinc, ribofla- 
vin, molybdenum and niacin had no statistically significant (protec- 
tive) effect on cancer deaths after five years.”

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Why does the body need salt?
claims.answer_short: Salt is the raw material for stomach acid, which digests food, absorbs minerals, and activates pepsin and B12's intrinsic factor.
claims.answer: Wallach frames salt as essential because it is the raw material the body needs to manufacture stomach acid. That stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, which he says is necessary to digest food, ensure the absorption of minerals, activate pepsin (the stomach's protein-digesting enzyme) and activate the intrinsic factor required to absorb vitamin B12. In his view, cutting salt undermines this entire digestive chain.
claims.verbatim:
Salt is the raw material needed to manufacture stomach acid. 
Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid that is necessary to digest food, 
ensure absorption of minerals, activate pepsin (protein digestive en- 
zyme produced by the stomach) and activate the “intrinsic factor”

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: What happens if you don't eat enough salt?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says restricting salt causes heat intolerance, digestive problems like GERD, and low stomach acid that raises disease risk.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, restricting salt backfires badly. He says low salt intake makes you heat intolerant and, over the long term, produces digestive problems including belching, burping, intestinal gas and GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease). The resulting hypochlorhydria, or low stomach acid, then raises the risk of nutritional deficiency diseases he lists as obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, arthritis, osteoporosis, kidney stones, cataracts and fibromyalgia.
claims.verbatim:
Restricted salt intakes will make you heat intolerant and over the 
long term will result in digestive problems including belching, burp- 
ing, intestinal gas and G.E.R.D. (gastro esophageal reflux disease). 
Restricted salt diets with the resultant hypochlorhydria (low stom- 
ach acid) will increase risks of nutritional deficiency diseases includ- 
ing obesity (reduced absorption of minerals increases the munchies), 
diabetes, high blood pressure, arthritis, osteoporosis, kidney stones, 
cataracts, fibromyalgia, etc.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Does salt cause high blood pressure?
claims.answer_short: No — Wallach says salt does not cause high blood pressure, and restricting it actually shortens your life.
claims.answer: Wallach rejects the conventional warning against salt. He states plainly that salt does not cause high blood pressure and that cutting back will not reduce your risk of high blood pressure or add even ten seconds to your life. On the contrary, he argues that restricting salt actually shortens your life and makes it miserable, and he simply tells readers to salt their food to taste.
claims.verbatim:
Salt your food to taste. Salt does not cause high blood pressure 
and restricting salt will not reduce your risk of high blood pressure 
or add ten seconds to your life - in fact restricting salt will shorten 
your life and make your very short life miserable.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Is a low-salt diet actually bad for your heart?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach cites a 1997 Sodium Task Force report that heavy salt-restrictors had 600% more heart attacks.
claims.answer: Wallach turns the anti-salt message on its head with evidence that cutting salt harms the heart. He reports that in April 1997 the Sodium Task Force found that people who restricted their salt intake to one gram per day had a 600 percent higher rate of heart attacks than those who consumed more than two grams of salt per day. He uses this finding to argue that aggressive salt restriction is dangerous rather than protective.
claims.verbatim:
In April 1997, The Sodium Task Force reported that those indi- 
viduals who restricted their salt intake to one gram per day had a 
600 percent higher rate of heart attacks than those who consumed 
more than two grams of salt per day.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Why do the Japanese eat so much salt but have less heart disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes the Japanese ate 15 grams of salt a day yet had 85% less cardiovascular disease and hypertension than Americans.
claims.answer: Wallach uses Japan as a counterexample to the anti-salt orthodoxy. He notes that while American doctors told patients to eat less than one gram of salt per day, the Japanese by contrast consumed about fifteen grams of salt per day. Despite this, he reports, the Japanese had eighty-five percent less cardiovascular disease and hypertension than Americans — evidence he uses to argue that high salt intake is not the cause of heart disease or high blood pressure.
claims.verbatim:
The Japanese consumed an enormous amount of salt each day 
compared to Americans. The Americans were admonished by their 
doctors to eat less then one gram of salt per day. The Japanese by 
contrast consumed fifteen grams of salt per day, yet they had eighty 
five percent less cardiovascular disease and hypertension than did 
the Americans.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: Can mineral deficiency cause binge eating and obesity?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says iron and phosphorus deficiencies occurring together trigger an almost psychotic binge-eating and soft-drink rampage that results in morbid obesity.
claims.answer: In Hell's Kitchen, Wallach argues that a deficiency of two or more essential minerals produces significant pica, cravings and binge eating. He singles out iron and phosphorus deficiencies occurring at the same time as capable of driving an almost psychotic binge-eating and soft-drink consumption rampage that results in morbid obesity. In his framework, obesity is a mineral-deficiency disease, not simply a matter of overeating or too little exercise.
claims.verbatim:
The deficiency of two or more essential minerals will pro- 
duce a significant level of pica, cravings and binge eating. Iron 
and phosphorus deficiencies occurring at the same time will re- 
sult in an almost psychotic binge eating and soft drink consump- 
tion rampage that results in morbid obesity.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Is a low-salt diet actually bad for you?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says salt deficiency is common and is often caused by doctors wrongly telling patients to cut salt—the profession, he says, thinks humans are dumber than cows.
claims.answer: Wallach argues that salt (NaCl) deficiency occurs commonly and is oftentimes caused by ignorant and over-zealous doctors who demand their patients reduce or eliminate salt intake. He mocks the advice, saying the medical profession must think humans are dumber than cows, since the first thing a farmer puts in the pasture is a salt block. Livestock, he points out, are given free-choice access to salt and other minerals in uncontrolled, unlimited amounts.
claims.verbatim:
Salt (NaCl) deficiency occurs commonly, and is oftentimes caused 
by ignorant and over zealous doctors who demand that “their” pa- 
tients reduce or eliminate salt intake. The medical profession must 
think that humans are dumber than cows! The first thing that a farmer 
or rancher puts in the pasture for their livestock is a salt block (and 
they have been doing it for tens of thousands of years) - the animals 
have free choice access to salt and other minerals in uncontrolled 
and unlimited amounts.

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: Can arginine raise growth hormone (HGH)?
claims.answer_short: Yes—L-arginine with ornithine can trigger HGH release from the pituitary gland when supplemented in significant doses.
claims.answer: The amino acids L-arginine and ornithine can cause human growth hormone (HGH) to be released from the pituitary gland when supplemented in significant doses. This matters because, per studies cited from the New England Journal of Medicine, HGH can reverse symptoms of human biological aging.
claims.verbatim:
The amino acids L-arginine and ornithine can cause HGH to be 
released from the pituitary gland if supplemented in significant doses.

claims.subject: omega-9
claims.question: Is oleic acid a monounsaturated fat, and where is it found?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes oleic acid as a monounsaturated fat, the same fat found in olive oil, and says it makes up about 30 percent of cocoa butter (the fat in chocolate).
claims.answer: Wallach identifies oleic acid as a monounsaturated fat -- the same type of fat found in olive oil. He points to it as a major component of cocoa butter, the fat in chocolate: cocoa butter is roughly 34 percent stearic acid, 20 percent palmitic acid, and 30 percent oleic acid. Stearic and palmitic acids are the saturated fats in that mix, while oleic acid is the monounsaturated portion, the fraction he links to olive oil.
claims.verbatim:
The fat in chocolate, cocoa butter, is comprised of stearic acid 
(34 percent), palmitic acid (20 percent) and oleic acid (30 percent). 
Both stearic and palmitic acids are saturated fats; oleic acid is a 
monounsaturated fat that is also found in olive oil.

claims.subject: silica
claims.question: Does beer contain silica?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes that beer — often called 'liquid bread' — contains significant levels of silica, the mineral needed for healthy bones, skin, hair and nails.
claims.answer: Wallach points out that beer, often called 'liquid bread,' contains many nutrients — including significant levels of silica, the mineral he says is required for the optimal health of the bones, skin, hair and nails. He makes the same point about diet more broadly: high-fiber foods contain a lot of silicon, so plant-derived foods and drinks turn up as natural sources of the mineral.
claims.verbatim:
Beer is often referred to as “liquid bread.” Beer contains many 
nutrients including significant levels of silica, a mineral required for 
the optimal health of bones, skin, hair and nails.

claims.subject: cesium
claims.question: Is cesium an essential mineral?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach lists cesium among the essential minerals found in high-quality humic shale, holding that it meets the criteria for an essential nutrient even though it isn't 'classically' considered one.
claims.answer: Wallach counts cesium among the essential minerals found in a high-quality humic shale, the plant-derived colloidal mineral source at the heart of his program. He grants that many of the minerals on that list, cesium included, are not 'classically' regarded as essential, but argues each one meets at least two of the criteria used to declare a nutrient essential. On that reasoning he treats cesium as one of the plant minerals modern diets have lost and should consciously replace, rather than an optional trace element.

claims.subject: titanium
claims.question: Does Wallach say titanium is an essential mineral?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists titanium among the essential minerals in humic shale, holding it meets two or more criteria for an essential nutrient.
claims.answer: Wallach counts titanium among the essential minerals found in high-quality humic shale — the plant-derived colloidal minerals he argues modern diets have lost. He acknowledges that titanium and many of the minerals on that list are not 'classically' considered essential, but holds that they each meet two or more of the criteria for an essential nutrient. claims.subject: tantalum
claims.question: Does Wallach consider tantalum an essential mineral?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach lists tantalum among the essential minerals found in high-quality humic shale, holding that although such minerals aren't classically considered essential, they each meet two or more criteria for an essential nutrient.
claims.answer: Wallach places tantalum on his roster of essential minerals found in a high-quality humic shale -- the plant-derived colloidal minerals he champions. He acknowledges that many of the minerals on that list, tantalum among them, are not 'classically' considered essential by conventional nutrition. His position is that they nonetheless qualify, because each meets two or more of the criteria for an essential nutrient. On that basis Wallach treats tantalum as one of the plant-derived trace minerals the body needs.
claims.verbatim:
* Many of the minerals listed are not “classically” considered to be “es- 
sential,” however, they all meet two or more of the criteria for an essential 
nutrient.

claims.subject: zirconium
claims.question: Is zirconium an essential nutrient?
claims.answer_short: Wallach argues that although zirconium isn't 'classically' considered essential, it -- like the other plant-derived humic-shale minerals -- meets two or more of the criteria used to declare a nutrient essential.
claims.answer: Zirconium doesn't appear on the conventional lists of essential nutrients, and Wallach acknowledges it isn't 'classically' considered one. But he argues that zirconium -- along with the many other minerals and elements found in high-quality humic shale, his plant-derived colloidal mineral source -- meets two or more of the criteria used to declare a substance an essential nutrient. On that basis he includes it among the essential elements the body should be getting.
claims.verbatim:
Many of the minerals listed are not “classically” considered to be “es- 
sential,” however, they all meet two or more of the criteria for an essential 
nutrient.

claims.subject: ornithine
claims.question: Does ornithine boost human growth hormone (HGH)?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says the amino acids L-arginine and ornithine can make the pituitary gland release HGH when supplemented in significant doses.
claims.answer: Ornithine is an amino acid that, taken together with L-arginine in significant doses, can cause the pituitary gland to release human growth hormone (HGH). Wallach raises this in a discussion of age-related HGH decline: he cites the New England Journal of Medicine that HGH can reverse symptoms of human biological aging — restoring muscle mass, thickening skin and reducing wrinkles, restoring lost hair and hair color, and increasing energy, sex drive, memory, immune function, and wound-healing capacity. In that light, supplementing ornithine (with arginine) is presented as a way to stimulate the body's own growth-hormone output.
claims.verbatim:
The amino acids L-arginine and ornithine can cause HGH to be 
released from the pituitary gland if supplemented in significant doses.

claims.subject: meat
claims.question: Does Wallach think red meat is healthy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls red meat an unequaled source of animal protein and essential lipids — with one caveat: don't cook it well-done or burn the fat, which forms cancer-linked heterocyclic amines.
claims.answer: Wallach calls red meat an unequaled source of animal protein and essential lipids. His one caveat is preparation: don't eat it cooked well-done or with the fat burnt, because that forms heterocyclic amines (compounds tied to cancer risk).
claims.verbatim:
Red meat is an unequaled source of animal protein and essential 
lipids - the secret is to not eat meat cooked well done or eat the fat 
burnt as they become heterocyclic amines.

claims.subject: sucralose
claims.question: Is Splenda safe to use?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says that despite public controversy, sugar substitutes like Splenda are “considered” safe when used in moderation and have been used for years, and Splenda can replace sugar teaspoon for teaspoon in baking.
claims.answer: Wallach takes a moderate view of sugar substitutes such as Splenda. He acknowledges there is considerable public controversy over their use, but states that used in moderation they are “considered” safe and have been used for years, and that they let you satisfy a sweet tooth without adding significant calories. Practically, he notes Splenda can be substituted teaspoon for teaspoon for sugar in baking.
claims.verbatim:
used in moderation they are “considered” safe and have been 
used for years. Typically, Splenda can be used teaspoon for teaspoon 
of sugar for baking.

claims.subject: sucralose
claims.question: Is Splenda natural or artificial?
claims.answer_short: Wallach classifies Splenda (Sucralose) as a natural substance extracted from sugar cane, unlike the man-made sweeteners aspartame and saccharin.
claims.answer: Wallach describes Splenda — also known as Sucralose — as a natural substance extracted from sugar cane. He sets it apart from the man-made sweeteners: aspartame (sold as Nutrasweet and Equal), which is created by joining two amino acids, and saccharin (Sweet and Low), a man-made chemical discovered in the 1800s. Stevia, the fourth substitute he lists, is an herb (Stevia rebaudiana).
claims.verbatim:
1. Aspartamine - (also known as Nutrasweet and Equal) 
A man made sweetener created by joining two amino acids. 
2. Splenda - (also known as Sucralose) A natural substance 
extracted from sugar cane.

claims.subject: sucralose
claims.question: When did Splenda become the most popular sweetener?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes that during 2004 Splenda became the number one blended sweetener in the U.S., outselling every other brand of faux and real sugar.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that during 2004 Splenda became the number one blended sweetener in the United States, selling more than all the other brands of “faux” and real sugar. He adds that sugar substitutes have nonetheless failed to fully replace sugar for baking, because sugar does more than sweeten — it helps a cake rise, gives it volume and texture, caramelizes to produce the golden-brown color of quality baked goods, and provides greater shelf life.
claims.verbatim:
During 2004, Splenda became the number one blended sweet- 
ener in the U.S., selling more than all the other brands of “faux” and 
real sugar.

claims.subject: high_fructose_corn_syrup
claims.question: Why is high fructose corn syrup in everything?
claims.answer_short: Because it is cheaper, sweeter, and easier to handle than granulated sugar, so manufacturers put it in nearly every processed food, replacing more nutritious ingredients.
claims.answer: Wallach describes high-fructose corn syrup as a cheap industrial sweetener that has taken over the American food supply. About five percent of U.S. corn is converted into it because it is more economical, sweeter, and easier to handle than granulated sugar. Soft drink and juice manufacturers are encouraged to use the low-priced corn syrup in just about every canned, bottled, frozen, baked, and bagged "food," where it replaced the far more nutritious materials — one of the ways the modern processed diet lost its nutrition.
claims.verbatim:
About fifty seven percent of the American corn that is produced is fed 
to livestock, five percent is converted to high fructose corn syrup, which is 
more economical, sweeter and easier to handle than granulated sugar. 
Soft drink and juice manufacturers are encouraged to use the low priced 
corn syrup in just about every canned, bottled, frozen, baked and bagged 
“food,” in which it replaced the far more nutritious materials.

claims.subject: yogurt
claims.question: Is low-fat or fat-free yogurt healthy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's warning is specifically about LOW-FAT and 98% fat-free yogurt, which he says are 'loaded with sugar' -- not about yogurt itself. Elsewhere he counts whole-milk, live, and Greek yogurt among the staples of the longest-lived peoples (the Hunza and the Greek island of Symi), so full-fat yogurt is fine; it is the sugar-heavy reduced-fat versions he says to avoid.
claims.answer: As part of his program to eliminate sugar from the diet, Wallach warns against low-fat and 98% fat-free yogurt because they are loaded with sugar. He lists them among the sweetened foods to give up — alongside candy, ice cream, pastries, boxed cereals, fruit juices, honey and colas — in order to reduce the risk of obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, the Metabolic Syndrome, dementia and cancer.
claims.verbatim:
No low fat yogurt or 98% fat free yogurt (they are loaded 
with sugar)

claims.subject: microwaving_food
claims.question: How does a microwave oven cook food?
claims.answer_short: Wallach simply describes the mechanism, without judging microwaves good or bad: the oven bombards food with ultra-short microwaves that make its water molecules vibrate millions of times per second, and the friction produces heat that cooks the food 'from the inside out.'
claims.answer: Wallach describes how a microwave oven cooks food: it bombards the food with ultra-short microwaves, and when those microwaves strike the food they make the water molecules inside vibrate millions of times per second. That vibration generates friction, and the friction produces the heat that cooks the food "from the inside out." He notes this in the context of the first home microwave ovens going on sale.
claims.verbatim:
The first home microwave ovens go on sale. The ovens work by 
bombarding food with ultra-short microwaves. When the microwaves 
strike the food, they cause the water molecules inside to vibrate mil- 
lions of times per second which generates friction, which produces 
heat that cooks the food “from the inside out.”

claims.subject: microwaving_food
claims.question: When were microwave ovens first sold?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the first microwave ovens were marketed in the United States in 1947, though early sales were far lower than hoped.
claims.answer: According to Wallach's history of the modern kitchen, the first microwave ovens were marketed in the United States in 1947, but sales were initially far less than had been hoped for. Home microwave ovens did not go on sale until roughly two decades later.
claims.verbatim:
In 1947, the first microwave ovens were marketed in the United 
States, however, sales were initially far less than had been hoped for.

claims.subject: keto_diet
claims.question: What does Dr. Wallach think of the keto or low-carb diet?
claims.answer_short: Wallach favors low-carb, low-glycemic diets and counts his own See Food Diet -- his low-carb plan built around supplementing all 90 essential nutrients to kill cravings -- among them, but insists mineral intake matters far more than the exact ratio of carbs, fat, and protein, because he blames obesity on mineral deficiency, not carbohydrates.
claims.answer: Dr. Wallach considers his own 'See Food Diet' the best of the low-carbohydrate, low-glycemic-index diets. What sets it apart from every other low-carb plan, he says, is that it weights mineral intake far more heavily and treats it as more important than parsing the exact percentages of carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
claims.verbatim:
Dr. Wallach’s See Food Diet is perhaps the best of the best when 
it comes to low carbohydrate, low glycemic index diets. Our low 
carb diet differs from all others in that our concerns for the mineral 
intake is actually more heavily weighted and more important than 
parsing words on the percentages of carbohydrates, fats and pro- 
teins.

claims.subject: low_carb_diet
claims.question: Are low-carb diets the answer to obesity?
claims.answer_short: No -- Wallach grants low-carb diets can speed weight loss, but warns that if cutting carbs is your 'sole consideration ... you are in for a rude awakening': if low-carb were really the answer to obesity, we wouldn't be facing a projected 40% obesity rate. The rude awakening is that obesity's real root cause is mineral deficiency -- the cravings and binge-eating a mineral-starved body drives -- not carbohydrates. So cutting carbs alone can't solve it.
claims.answer: Wallach argues low-carbohydrate diets are not the solution to obesity on their own: if they were, he says, we wouldn't be facing a projection of forty percent of Americans being obese by 2010. He grants that low-carb eating and low glycemic loads can speed up weight loss, but warns that if cutting carbs is your sole consideration you are 'in for a rude awakening' — because obesity's real root is mineral deficiency and the cravings a mineral-starved body drives, not carbohydrates alone.
claims.verbatim:
If low carbohydrate diets were the answer to our obesity problem 
we wouldn't have the projection of forty percent of Americans being 
obese by 2010.

claims.subject: low_carb_diet
claims.question: Are low-carb diets dangerous?
claims.answer_short: Low-carb weight loss can bring pitfalls like heart attacks, kidney stones, osteoporosis and stroke; Wallach says you must guard against mineral deficiencies and the free-radical damage from burning body fat.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that low-carb weight loss is not automatically safe. To lose weight safely and avoid its common pitfalls — heart attacks, liver damage, high blood pressure, Beriberi, arthritis, osteoporosis, periodontal disease, cancer, sudden death, stroke and kidney stones — a dieter must protect against mineral nutritional deficiencies, which he says drive 'psychotic eating,' and against the free-radical damage generated by burning body fat.
claims.verbatim:
To lose weight safely and prevent the 
common pitfalls of weight loss (i.e. - heart attacks, liver damage, 
high blood pressure, Beriberi, arthritis, osteoporosis, periodontal dis- 
ease, cancer, sudden death, stroke, kidney stones, etc.), one has to 
protect themselves from the ravages of mineral nutritional deficien- 
cies that result in psychotic eating and free radical damage generated 
by burning body fat.

claims.subject: low_carb_diet
claims.question: Do low-carb diets create free radicals?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says burning body fat, like burning any fuel, produces free radicals and other harmful byproducts that must be countered with an antioxidant plan.
claims.answer: Wallach cautions that burning body fat for fuel — the goal of a low-carb diet — is not a danger-free process. Like the combustion of any fuel (wood, coal, oil, gasoline, sugar or fat), it produces wastes, pollution and dangerous byproducts including free radicals, which he says must be neutralized with an aggressive, proactive antioxidant plan.
claims.verbatim:
The burning of body fat is not a danger free process. The com- 
bustion of all fuels, including wood, coal, oil, gasoline, sugar and fat, 
produces wastes, pollution and dangerous combustion byproducts 
including free radicals.

claims.subject: low_carb_diet
claims.question: What is a low-carb diet?
claims.answer_short: A low-carb diet limits the amount and type of carbohydrates to steady blood sugar and lower glucose and insulin levels, reducing bouts of ravenous hunger.
claims.answer: In Wallach's shortest description, a low-carb diet is conceived to keep blood sugar levels from having wild fluctuations. Its purpose is to 'steady' blood sugar, which helps reduce episodes of ravenous hunger; the amount and type of carbohydrates are limited to lower the body's glucose and insulin levels and make weight management easier.
claims.verbatim:
In the shortest possible description and purpose of a low carb 
diet, one can say that it is conceived to keep blood sugar levels from 
having wild fluctuations. The purpose is to “steady” blood sugar lev- 
els, which will help reduce episodes of ravenous hunger.

claims.subject: grilled_bbq_meat
claims.question: Does grilled or charred meat cause cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says heterocyclic amines — free radicals formed in well-done meat and burnt animal fat — can raise the risk of breast, prostate, and colon cancer by as much as 462 percent compared with meat cooked medium-rare; it is the burning, not the meat, that harms you.
claims.answer: Wallach identifies heterocyclic amines as free radicals that form in well-done meat and burnt animal fat. He calls them extremely dangerous, warning that they can raise a person's risk of breast, prostate, and colon cancer by as much as 462 percent. It is the reason he tells people never to eat meat cooked well done or with the fat burnt.
claims.verbatim:
Heterocyclic amines are free radicals that are found in well done 
meat and burnt animal fat. They are extremely dangerous and can 
increase one’s risk of breast, prostate and colon cancer by as much as 
462 percent!

claims.subject: dialysis
claims.question: Who invented the dialysis machine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach credits Dr. Willem Kolff, a Dutch physician, with developing the "artificial kidney" or dialysis machine, first employed in the United States, which cleanses metabolic wastes from the blood through a cellulose membrane.
claims.answer: Dr. Joel Wallach recounts that the dialysis machine — the "artificial kidney" — was developed by Dr. Willem Kolff, a Dutch physician, and was first employed in the United States. He describes how it works: blood from a patient's artery is diverted into the machine, which looks like a large rotating cylinder or drum. The blood enters a cellulose membrane wrapped around the drum, and as the drum rotates the cellulose is submerged in a saline solution. The membrane allows metabolic wastes to pass out of the blood while the blood cells are too large to pass through, and the cleansed blood is then pumped back into the patient.
claims.verbatim:
Dr. Willem Kolff, a Dutch physician, developed an “artificial kid- 
ney” or dialysis machine, which was first employed in the United 
States. Blood from a patient's artery is diverted into the dialysis ma- 
chine, which looks like a large rotating cylinder or drum. The blood 
enters a cellulose membrane, which is wrapped around the drum. As 
the drum rotates, the cellulose in submerged in a saline solution. The 
membrane allows metabolic wastes to pass out of the blood. The 
blood cells are too large to pass through the membrane. The cleansed 
blood is then pumped back into the patient.

claims.subject: dialysis
claims.question: What is dialysis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach defines dialysis as a separation process in which inorganic colloids are too large to cross a semi-permeable membrane while dissolved salt, starch and sugar pass through as individual atoms or small molecules.
claims.answer: Dr. Joel Wallach defines dialysis as a separation process: inorganic colloidal material that readily passes through filter paper can be separated from dissolved substances such as starch, sugar or salt by placing the mixture in a parchment shell surrounded by distilled water. The inorganic colloids are "too large" to pass through the semi-permeable membrane, while the molecules of salt, starch and sugar (which separate into individual atoms or very small molecules) pass readily through it. Wallach invokes this principle to explain mineral absorption: during digestion, minerals from food or supplements become inorganic colloids too large to cross the intestinal wall, and only a small percentage — chelated by amino acids into organic "crystalloids" — can be dialyzed through the intestinal membrane into the bloodstream.
claims.verbatim:
Inorganic colloidal material which readily passes through filter 
paper may be separated from dissolved substances, such as starch, 
sugar or salt, by placing the mixture of mineral colloid and non- 
colloid in a parchment shell surrounded by distilled water. The inor- 
ganic colloids are “too large” to pass through the membrane, but the 
molecules of salt, starch and sugar or any other dissolved substance 
pass readily through the semi-permeable membrane (they separate 
into individual atoms or very small molecules). This kind of separa- 
tion process is called dialysis.

claims.subject: noni_juice
claims.question: Is noni an antioxidant?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach lists noni among the fruits that contain antioxidants in substantial quantities.
claims.answer: Dr. Wallach lists noni among the fruits that contain antioxidants in substantial quantities, alongside blueberries, cherries, kiwis, pink grapefruit, oranges, plums, prunes, raisins, raspberries, red grapes, strawberries, boysenberries, pomegranate and mangosteen. He believes antioxidants will be added to the list of essential nutrients, because without them the body cannot protect itself from dietary and environmental free radicals or attain maximum life spans. He stresses this especially for people burning body fat, since burned fat produces free-radical waste products (trans fats, oxidized fats and ceroid lipofuscin).
claims.verbatim:
An- 
tioxidants are found in substantial quantities in: 
Fruit - blueberries, cherries, kiwis, pink grapefruit, oranges, plums, 
prunes, raisins, raspberries, red grapes, strawberries, boysenberries, 
pomegranate, noni and mangostein.

claims.subject: keto_diet
claims.question: How does the keto or low-carb diet work?
claims.answer_short: Carbohydrates are cut to about twenty grams a day, with unlimited meat and fat, to lower glucose and insulin and push the body into ketosis so it burns fat for energy instead of carbohydrates.
claims.answer: A low-carbohydrate (keto) diet limits both the total amount and the type of carbohydrate to lower the body's glucose and insulin levels and make weight loss and weight management easier. In its initial phase the dieter can eat unlimited meat and fat but must keep carbohydrates to twenty grams or less per day, about one slice of bread, and for the first fourteen days eats no fruit, bread, pasta, grains, milk or even ketchup. Its stated purpose, as Wallach describes it, is 'to create a state of ketosis, encouraging your body to burn fat for energy rather than carbohydrates.'
claims.verbatim:
3. Low Carb - The total amount and the type of carbohydrates 
are limited to reduce the body’ glucose and insulin levels in an effort 
to make weight loss and weight management easier. 
In the diet’s initial phase, one can eat unlimited meat and fat, 
however, carbohydrates must be limited to twenty grams of carbo- 
hydrates or less per day (approximately one slice of bread). 
For the first fourteen days, the dieter consumes no fruit, bread, 
pasta, grains, milk or even ketchup. The stated purpose of the low 
carb diet, “is to create a state of ketosis, encouraging your body to 
burn fat for energy rather than carbohydrates.”

claims.subject: keto_diet
claims.question: Is the keto or low-carb diet dangerous?
claims.answer_short: An unsupplemented high-protein low-carb diet forgets the minerals and can increase the risk of kidney stones, which is why Wallach insists on mineral supplementation alongside it.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that popular low-carb, high-protein weight-loss diets have forgotten the minerals: an unsupplemented high-protein diet can increase the risk of kidney stones. This is a central reason his own low-carb approach weights mineral supplementation more heavily than the carbohydrate, fat and protein percentages that other low-carb diets fixate on.
claims.verbatim:
They certainly have forgot- 
ten the minerals and an unsupplemented high protein diet can in- 
crease the risk of kidney stones.

claims.subject: see_food_diet
claims.question: What is Dr. Wallach's See Food Diet?
claims.answer_short: The See Food Diet is Dr. Wallach's own low-carb, low-glycemic weight-loss plan. What sets it apart, he says, is that it targets the real root cause of obesity -- mineral deficiency -- so the cravings, pica, and binge-eating that sink other diets disappear once the body is saturated with the essential minerals. (The name is Wallach's pun on 'see food and eat it.')
claims.answer: The 'See Food Diet' is Dr. Wallach's own weight-loss plan. He argues that other diets fail universally because they don't address what he considers the real root cause of obesity -- mineral deficiency. The See Food Diet's defining difference is that, by correcting that deficiency, it eliminates the pica, cravings, binge-eating, 'munchies,' and 'stand in front of the open refrigerator' syndrome that make other diets fail -- which, he says, is what makes lasting success achievable for everyone.
claims.verbatim:
The basic reasons for the universal failure of “weight loss diets” 
of any ilk, is that they don’t deal with the basic root cause of obesity 
- the mineral deficiencies. Therefore, the primary difference of the 
Dr. Wallach’s See Food Diet, the principal that sets it apart from the 
others is that the pica, cribbing, cravings, binge eating, the munchies 
and the “stand in front of the open refrigerator” syndrome is dealt 
with and eliminated - these basic failure factors having been removed 
will guaranty success for everyone.

claims.subject: osteoporosis
claims.question: How can osteoporosis of the skull cause nerve diseases?
claims.answer_short: Wallach teaches that the common cause of the cranial-nerve and spinal-cord neuropathies behind as many as 25 diseases is osteoporosis of the skull, where nutritional deficiency drives bone matrix to fill and narrow the tunnels the nerves travel through, pinching them — and he holds this is preventable and reversible.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that the single common cause of the cranial-nerve and spinal-cord neuropathies behind as many as 25 different diseases is osteoporosis of the skull (which he also names Paget's Disease or Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia). Nutritional deficiency drives a universal mineral loss and an over-production of bone matrix that fills the bony tunnels the nerves travel through, narrowing them and incarcerating (pinching) the nerve -- and he holds this is preventable and reversible.
claims.verbatim:
It turns out that the common cause
of these neuropathies is osteoporosis of the skull which results in a universal
mineral loss and an increase in bone matrix production. The bone matrix fills up
the tunnels that the cranial nerves and spinal cord travel through, reducing the
inside caliber of the tunnels which then produces an incarceration of the nerve.

claims.subject: pagets_disease
claims.question: What is Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia?
claims.answer_short: Wallach defines 'Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia' as the replacement of normal bone architecture, including the bone-marrow cavity, with connective tissue, which reduces the body's production of platelets, white blood cells, red blood cells, and antibody-making stem cells.
claims.answer: Wallach defines 'Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia' as the replacement of normal bony architecture -- including the bone-marrow cavity -- with connective tissue, which in turn reduces the body's production of platelets, white blood cells, red blood cells, and the stem cells that make antibodies.
claims.verbatim:
The Replacement of normal boney architecture, including the bone
marrow cavity, with connective tissue. Resulting in reduced production
of platelets, white blood cells, red blood cells, and stem cells that make

antibodies.

claims.subject: headache
claims.question: Are chronic headaches, receding gums, and tooth loss caused by osteoporosis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds that headaches, sinus trouble, tooth loss, receding gums, periodontal disease, and jaw pain are not from poor dental care or genetics but are really manifestations of osteoporosis of the skull.
claims.answer: Wallach holds that many common cranial and dental problems -- headaches, sinus trouble, tooth migration and tooth loss, receding gums, periodontal disease, jaw pain (trigeminal neuralgia), and even a change in the shape of the head (Hunter's syndrome) -- are not caused by poor flossing, brushing, or skipped dental visits, nor by autoimmune, familial, or genetic factors, but are in reality manifestations of osteoporosis of the skull.
claims.verbatim:
A wide variety of cranial (head aches, sinus, etc.) and dental issues, including

tooth migration, tooth loss, receding gums, periodontal disease, jaw pain
(trigeminal neuralgia), change in the shape of the head (Hunter's syndrome)

claims.subject: osteoporosis
claims.question: How do you reverse osteoporosis of the skull and spine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says osteoporosis of the skull and spine is preventable and reversible by supplementing the 90 essential nutrients — 60 minerals, 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids, and 3 fatty acids — dosed for bodyweight, and by protecting absorption through avoiding bad foods and gluten.
claims.answer: Wallach's prescribed solution: osteoporosis of the skull and spine (Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia) is preventable and reversible by supplementing the full set of 90 essential nutrients -- 60 minerals, 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids, and 3 fatty acids -- dosed for bodyweight, and by protecting absorption through avoiding 'bad foods' and gluten (wheat, barley, rye, oats).
claims.verbatim:
Osteoporosis of the skull and spine, Wallach’s Fibrous Dysplasia, are
preventable, amenable, and reversible with supplementation with the 90
essential nutrients, 60 minerals, 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids, and 3 fatty acids
appropriate for bodyweight. Absorption is essential and so avoiding the bad
foods AND gluten (wheat, barley, rye, oats) is imperative to get maximum
benefit.

claims.subject: anosmia
claims.question: What causes loss of the sense of smell?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains that osteoporosis of the skull narrows the bony channel of the olfactory nerve, pinching it and reducing or eliminating the sense of smell.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the olfactory (first cranial) nerve carries the sense of smell from the lining of the nose through the cribriform plate of the skull to the brain. When osteoporosis of the skull narrows that bony channel, the nerve is pinched and the sense of smell is reduced or lost entirely (anosmia).
claims.verbatim:
The olfactory nerve originates in the nasal mucosa and travels through the
cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to the olfactory lobe of the brain to
produce the sense of smell. Osteoporosis of the skull will reduce the caliber of
the tunnels resulting in the reduction of or the total loss of the sense of smell.

claims.subject: optic_nerve_atrophy
claims.question: Can skull osteoporosis cause vision loss?
claims.answer_short: Wallach teaches that skull osteoporosis narrows the optic canal and pinches the optic nerve, causing optic nerve atrophy — a gradual vision loss that eyeglasses cannot correct.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that the optic (second cranial) nerve carries vision from the retina through the optic canal of the skull to the brain. Skull osteoporosis narrows that canal and pinches the nerve, causing optic nerve atrophy -- a gradual vision loss that eyeglasses (lens prescriptions) cannot correct.
claims.verbatim:
Osteoporosis of the skull causes a reduction of the internal caliber of the
optic canal resulting in optic nerve atrophy (ONA) which produces a gradual
vision loss that will not benefit from lens prescriptions.

claims.subject: ptosis
claims.question: What causes a drooping eyelid?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says a drooping eyelid and a pupil that won't respond to light come from skull osteoporosis pinching the oculomotor nerve that lifts the eyelid and controls the pupil.
claims.answer: Wallach maps the oculomotor (third cranial) nerve, which controls the pupil's response to light and four of the six eye muscles -- including the elevator palpebrae that lifts the upper eyelid. When skull osteoporosis pinches this nerve (per his disease table) the result is ptosis (a drooping eyelid) and a pupil that no longer responds to light.
claims.verbatim:
This nerve travels through the eye via

the superior orbital fissure to activate the eye muscles elevator palpebrae, superior rectus, medial rectus and inferior rectus motor muscles.

claims.subject: diplopia
claims.question: What causes double vision?
claims.answer_short: Wallach attributes double vision to skull osteoporosis pinching the trochlear (fourth cranial) nerve, the motor nerve controlling downward, outward, and inward eye movement, so the eyes no longer move together.
claims.answer: Wallach describes the trochlear (fourth cranial) nerve as the motor nerve of the superior oblique muscle, which controls downward, outward and inward eye movement. When skull osteoporosis pinches it (per his disease table) the eyes no longer move together, producing double vision (diplopia), palsy, and pain above the eyebrow.
claims.verbatim:
The trochlear nerve is a motor nerve that travels through the superior
orbital fissure. This nerve enervates the somatomotor muscle and the superior
oblique muscle that controls the superior oblique muscle which controls the
downward, outward and inward eye movement.

claims.subject: trigeminal_neuralgia
claims.question: What causes trigeminal neuralgia?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reframes trigeminal neuralgia as a nutritional and structural problem, caused when osteoporosis of the skull pinches the trigeminal nerve.
claims.answer: Wallach identifies the trigeminal (fifth cranial) nerve -- the largest cranial nerve, carrying sensation from the face and motor control of the jaw -- as the source of classic trigeminal neuralgia when osteoporosis of the skull strangles (pinches) it. This reframes trigeminal neuralgia as a nutritional/structural problem rather than an idiopathic one.
claims.verbatim:
Strangulation of the trigeminal nerve is secondary to osteoporosis of the
skull which produces the classic trigeminal neuralgia.

claims.subject: strabismus
claims.question: What causes crossed eyes (strabismus)?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains the sixth cranial (abducens) nerve controls the muscle that turns the eye outward, and when it is squeezed in the superior orbital fissure the eyes cross inward toward the nose.
claims.answer: Wallach explains the abducens (sixth cranial) nerve controls the lateral rectus muscle that turns the eye outward. When it is squeezed in the superior orbital fissure it produces an 'eye palsy' in which the eyes cross inward toward the nose -- strabismus.
claims.verbatim:
This nerve originates in the
pons region of the brain stem then enters the eye socket where it controls the
lateral rectus muscle. When squeezed as it travels through the superior orbital

fissure it produces an “eye palsy” where the eyes cross inward toward the nose.

claims.subject: bells_palsy
claims.question: What causes Bell's palsy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach attributes Bell's palsy to strangulation of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve where it passes through bony tunnels narrowed by skull osteoporosis, which he calls Paget's Disease / Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia.
claims.answer: Wallach attributes Bell's palsy (facial paralysis) to strangulation of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve as it passes through bony tunnels narrowed by skull osteoporosis (Paget's Disease / Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia), which he says produces many forms of neuralgia including the classic Bell's palsy.
claims.verbatim:
Strangulation of the facial nerves as it passes through the obstructed
tunnels (Paget's Disease / Wallach’s Fibrous Dysplasia) produces many forms
of neuralgia including the classic Bell’s palsy.

claims.subject: menieres_disease
claims.question: What causes Meniere's disease, tinnitus, and vertigo?
claims.answer_short: Wallach attributes tinnitus, vertigo, and gradual deafness to the eighth cranial nerve being pinched by skull osteoporosis, renaming the vertigo 'Wallach's Vertigo' and equating it with Meniere's disease as a treatable nerve incarceration.
claims.answer: Wallach maps the vestibulocochlear (eighth cranial) nerve, which carries hearing and balance. When its cochlear branch is incarcerated by skull osteoporosis a tinnitus (ringing tone) is produced and gradual deafness can follow; when its vestibular branch is incarcerated it produces vertigo. Wallach renames this vertigo 'Wallach's Vertigo' and (in his disease table) equates it with Meniere's disease -- recasting Meniere's as a treatable nerve-incarceration rather than an unexplained inner-ear disorder.
claims.verbatim:
When the cochlear branch is incarcerated a “tinnitus” or tone is produced
(gradual deafness can occur); when the vestibular nerve is incarcerated it
produces a vertigo (Wallach’s Vertigo).

claims.subject: dysphagia
claims.question: What nerve problem causes difficulty swallowing and loss of taste?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes the glossopharyngeal (ninth cranial) nerve, which carries taste from the rear of the tongue and throat sensation and drives a swallowing muscle; when skull osteoporosis pinches it, the result is loss of the gag reflex, loss of taste, difficulty swallowing, and voice change.
