claims.answer: Wallach describes the glossopharyngeal (ninth cranial) nerve, which carries taste from the rear of the tongue and sensation from the throat, and drives the stylopharyngeal swallowing muscle. When skull osteoporosis pinches it (per his disease table) the result is loss of the gag reflex, loss of taste, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), and voice change.
claims.verbatim: This nerve sends sensory information from the sinuses, back of the throat, inner ear, and posterior region of the tongue; it records the sense of taste from the rear of the tongue. Through its motor branches it provides voluntary movement of the stylopharyngeal throat muscle

claims.subject: atrial_fibrillation
claims.question: Can a pinched vagus nerve cause A-fib?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says a vagus nerve pinched by skull osteoporosis can produce throat and esophageal problems, gastroparesis, COPD, A-fib, and hiccups.
claims.answer: Wallach ties several major conditions to incarceration of the vagus (tenth cranial) nerve -- the longest cranial nerve, which carries signals to the heart, lungs, and digestive tract. When skull osteoporosis pinches it, he says it produces throat and esophageal problems, gastroparesis (a sluggish, bloated stomach with reflux and diarrhea), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), atrial fibrillation (A-fib, an abnormal heart rhythm), and hiccups when the recurrent branch is involved.
claims.verbatim:
When the vagus nerve is incarcerated it will produce throat and esophageal
issues, gastroparesis (bloating, reflux, diarrhea, etc.) COPD, A-fib, and hiccups
if the recurrent branch is also involved.

claims.subject: cranial-nerves
claims.question: What does the accessory nerve (11th cranial nerve) do?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes the accessory (11th cranial) nerve as the motor nerve driving the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid to rotate, flex and extend the neck and shoulders; skull osteoporosis pinching it at the foramina causes loss of those muscles' function.
claims.answer: Wallach describes the accessory (eleventh cranial) nerve as the motor nerve that rotates, flexes, and extends the neck and shoulders by driving the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. When skull osteoporosis pinches it as it passes through the foramen magnum and jugular foramen (per his disease table) the result is loss of function of those neck and shoulder muscles.
claims.verbatim:
The accessory nerve travels through the foramen magnum into the skull
and then exits quickly through the jugular foramen to innervate the motor
functions of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles.

claims.subject: tongue_atrophy
claims.question: What makes the tongue waste away?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes the twelfth cranial (hypoglossal) nerve as the motor nerve of the tongue; when skull osteoporosis pinches it in the hypoglossal canal, the tongue atrophies and speech malfunctions.
claims.answer: Wallach describes the hypoglossal (twelfth cranial) nerve as the motor nerve of the tongue, supplying all the tongue muscles except the palatoglossus. When skull osteoporosis pinches it in the hypoglossal canal (per his disease table) the tongue wastes away (atrophy) and speech malfunctions.
claims.verbatim:
The hypoglossal nerve is involved with the motor function of the tongue, it originates in the medulla oblongata then travels into the jaw and tongue. The
hypoglossal nerve travels through the hypoglossal canal and provides motor

innervation for all of the tongue muscles except for the palate glossus.

claims.subject: erbs_palsy
claims.question: What conditions does Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia (Erb's palsy) cause?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says spinal-cord impingement where it exits the skull, which he calls Erb's Palsy / Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia, is often misdiagnosed as carpal tunnel syndrome and also manifests as fibromyalgia, atrial fibrillation, lupus, and sciatica.
claims.answer: Wallach extends the same mechanism to the spinal cord: impingement where it exits the skull through the foramen magnum (which he names Erb's Palsy / Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia) produces numerous diseases. He says it is often misdiagnosed as carpal tunnel syndrome (numbness and tingling in the arms, wrist, and hands), behaves like a sciatica of the shoulder girdle, and that fibromyalgia, atrial fibrillation (A-fib), lupus, and sciatica are among its other manifestations.
claims.verbatim:
Fibromyalgia, A-fib, Lupus, and Sciatica are some of the other symptoms of
Erb's Palsy / Wallach’s Fibrous Dysplasia.

claims.subject: essential_nutrients
claims.question: Why do the 90 essential nutrients matter?
claims.answer_short: They're the cofactors enzymes need to work - miss one and the enzyme stalls. Most people never reach optimal levels, a 'subclinical' shortfall felt as fatigue and low mood.
claims.answer: Wallach explains why the 90 essential nutrients matter at the cellular level: vitamins and minerals act as cofactors that enzymes and coenzymes require to do their work, and if an essential cofactor is missing the enzyme cannot perform properly, if at all. He notes that most people never reach optimal levels of all 90 nutrients — a state he calls subclinical (marginal) deficiency — which typically shows up as chronic fatigue, lethargy, depression, and lack of concentration.
claims.verbatim:
The general role of vitamins and minerals is their requirement as cofactors to
implement the activity of enzymes and coenzymes.

claims.subject: essential_nutrients
claims.question: Can you get all your nutrition from food alone?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says no - food itself is depleted (vitamins down 37%, trace minerals 77%), so he calls a full 90-nutrient supplement program a cornerstone of health.
claims.answer: Wallach argues you cannot eat your way to full nutrition because the food supply itself is depleted: vitamin levels in food fell more than 37% (1950 to 1999) and trace minerals 77% (1940 to 1991). He attributes this not to fertilizers or seed types but to two facts — minerals occur in veins rather than spread evenly through the soil and plants cannot manufacture them, and the traditional renewal of farm-soil minerals through wood ashes ended once the Industrialized World switched from wood fuel to electricity, natural gas, and propane after Thomas Edison's first commercial power plant opened in 1882. Even organic and vegetarian diets fall short, so he calls a complete 90-nutrient supplementation program a cornerstone of optimal health.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin levels in food
have decreased by more than 37% between 1950 and 1999, and trace mineral
levels have decreased by 77% between 1940 and 1991.

claims.subject: wallach
claims.question: What are Dr. Wallach's credentials?
claims.answer_short: A 1991 Nobel Prize nomination for linking selenium to cystic fibrosis, two research medals, co-author of the DSHEA supplement law, and credit as an early founder of epigenetics.
claims.answer: Wallach's About-the-Author biography records the recognition his trace-mineral research has received: the 1988 Wooster Beach Gold Medal for a breakthrough in understanding the cause of cystic fibrosis, a 1991 Nobel Prize in Medicine nomination for linking selenium deficiency to cystic fibrosis, and the 2011 Klaus Schwarz Commemorative Medal for discovering the animal model of cystic fibrosis and elucidating its cause in humans. He is also credited as a co-author of the Dietary Supplement and Health Education Act — the law that keeps nutritional supplements legally categorized as food rather than pharmaceuticals. Accepting the Klaus Schwarz Medal, the awards committee wrote: "From a Historical perspective, Wallach is to be regarded as one of the first practitioners, if not founders, of epigenetics, the new research discipline that investigates heritable alterations in gene expression caused by mechanisms other than changes in DNA sequence."
claims.verbatim:
From a
Historical perspective, Wallach is to be regarded as one of the first practitioners, if not
founders, of epigenetics, the new research discipline that investigates heritable alterations
in gene expression caused by mechanisms other than changes in DNA sequence.

claims.subject: cranial-nerves
claims.question: What are the cranial nerves and how do they affect my health?
claims.answer_short: The cranial nerves pass through bony tunnels in the skull; Wallach says skull osteoporosis narrows those tunnels and pinches the nerves, which can drive as many as 25 different diseases.
claims.answer: Wallach's central thesis on the cranial nerves: neuropathies of one or more of them (and the spinal cord) can produce as many as 25 different diseases. He argues the common cause is osteoporosis of the skull — a universal mineral loss that increases bone matrix, filling the bony tunnels the nerves travel through, narrowing them and pinching (incarcerating) the nerve.
claims.verbatim:
Peripheral neuropathies of one or more of the cranial nerves and spinal cord
can produce as many as 25 different diseases. It turns out that the common cause
of these neuropathies is osteoporosis of the skull which results in a universal
mineral loss and an increase in bone matrix production. The bone matrix fills up
the tunnels that the cranial nerves and spinal cord travel through, reducing the
inside caliber of the tunnels which then produces an incarceration of the nerve.

claims.subject: iodine
claims.question: What causes goiter?
claims.answer_short: Goiter is a nutritional deficiency of the thyroid — mainly too little iodine (also copper, molybdenum, and tyrosine) — and can also be triggered by 'goitrogens' like nitrates that suppress the thyroid even when iodine is present.
claims.answer: Wallach frames goiter (an enlarged, or 'colloid,' thyroid) as a straightforward nutritional-deficiency disease rather than a mysterious gland disorder. It is caused by a simple deficiency of the nutrients the thyroid needs — chiefly iodine, but also copper, molybdenum, and the amino acid tyrosine. Goiter can also be driven by 'goitrogens' — substances such as the nitrates in luncheon meats, hot dogs, and fertilizer-contaminated well water, plus vegetables like cabbage, broccoli, and Brussels sprouts — which depress thyroid activity and can produce a goiter even when iodine is present in the diet. Starved of its nutrients, the thyroid gland swells 50 to 100 times its normal size, creating the visible lump at the front of the neck.
claims.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in
communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease
(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

claims.subject: twenty_thousand_autopsies
claims.question: How many autopsies did Dr. Wallach perform?
claims.answer_short: Wallach performed more than 20,000 autopsies: over 17,500 on animals across 454 species, plus 3,000 humans for comparison.
claims.answer: Wallach's health framework is built on an unusually large base of comparative pathology. As a pathologist for a multi-institution research program - The Center for the Biology of Natural Systems, funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) along with several zoos and universities - he performed autopsies on a scale almost no one else has: more than 20,000 of them, spanning over 17,500 captive wild, laboratory, and domestic animals across more than 454 species, plus 3,000 humans for comparison. That vast cross-species record is what led him to his central claim - that creatures dying of so-called "natural causes" were really dying of nutritional deficiency diseases.
claims.verbatim:
As a comparative pathologist, I (Wallach) performed
more than 20,000 autopsies of over 17,500 captive wild
animals, laboratory species and domestic animals, of over 454
species and 3,000 humans for a comparison.

claims.subject: macronutrients
claims.question: Are carbohydrates an essential nutrient?
claims.answer_short: No, says Wallach - the body can make all the carbs and sugar it needs by breaking down and rebuilding fats and proteins, so none has to come from the diet.
claims.answer: Wallach's stance on carbohydrates and sugars: they are not essential nutrients. His reasoning is that the body can make all the carbohydrate and sugar it needs - for energy, upkeep, and structural repair - by breaking down and rebuilding fats and proteins inside the cell, so none has to come from the diet. This runs counter to the popular view of carbohydrates as a required food group.
claims.verbatim:
Contrary to popular belief, carbohydrates and sugars
are not essential nutrients by anybody’s standards, as we
can make all of the carbohydrates and sugars we need for
energy and maintenance and repair of structural components
by breaking down and reconfiguring fats and proteins at the
cellular level.

claims.subject: amino_acids
claims.question: How many essential amino acids are there?
claims.answer_short: Wallach counts 12 the body can't make. Miss any for long and a specific deficiency disease follows.
claims.answer: Wallach counts 12 essential amino acids - the protein building blocks the body cannot make for itself and so must obtain from the diet: valine, tyrosine, tryptophan, lysine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, histidine, phenylalanine, arginine, taurine, and leucine. He warns that if any essential amino acid is missing from the diet for any length of time, a specific - sometimes reversible - disease results. A footnote adds that selenium researcher Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer considered selenomethionine (the selenium analog of methionine) a 13th essential amino acid.
claims.verbatim:
There are 12 amino acids that are required by the body
as protein building blocks, and because the body is unable to
manufacture them, they are termed “essential amino acids.”

claims.subject: wallach
claims.question: How did Wallach beat the FDA over omega-3?
claims.answer_short: After a long legal fight, on Sept 8, 2004 the FDA let his petition stand — allowing the claim that omega-3s cut heart-disease risk, which had been illegal to state for 65 years.
claims.answer: For more than 65 years it was known that omega-3 essential fatty acids were needed to prevent disease - but because the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had ruled the evidence "inconclusive," it was actually illegal to tell people that omega-3 supplements could lower their risk of stroke and sudden cardiac death. Wallach fought this: his company (Wellness Lifestyles, Inc.) petitioned the FDA for a qualified health claim, and after a hard-fought battle, won - on September 8, 2004 the FDA allowed the claim linking omega-3 fatty acids to reduced coronary heart disease risk (Docket No. 03Q-0401).
claims.verbatim:
To make a long story short, Wellness Lifestyles,
Inc (Wallach) filed a petition for an Amended Health
Claim: Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Coronary Heart Disease
(Co-Petitioner); Docket No. 03Q-0401; filed on 6/23/2003;
qualified claim allowed by FDA on 9/8/2004.

claims.subject: cholesterol
claims.question: Is cholesterol bad for you?
claims.answer_short: No — Wallach calls cholesterol an essential nutrient: it builds every cell membrane, all the steroid hormones, and the brain's myelin.
claims.answer: Is cholesterol bad for you? Wallach's answer is no - he calls it an essential nutrient. He points out that cholesterol is a necessary building block of the structural membranes of every cell, of all steroid hormones, and of the brain's myelin (the fatty insulating sheath around nerves) and nerve cells themselves. This counters the popular view of cholesterol as merely something to avoid.
claims.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential nutrient and an essential
component of the structural membranes of all cells, all steroid
hormones and is a major component of brain (myelin) and
nerve cells.

claims.subject: vitamins
claims.question: What happens if you're vitamin-deficient during pregnancy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach warns it can cause catastrophic birth defects - among them neural-tube defects, cleft lip and palate, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis and heart defects.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that vitamin deficiencies during pregnancy can cause catastrophic birth defects - he lists neural tube defects, mental retardation, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft lip, cleft palate, and heart defects among the possible outcomes.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of many vitamins during pregnancy
can result in catastrophic birth defects (neural tube defects,
mental retardation, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft
lip, cleft palate, heart defects, etc.).

claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: Does vitamin B6 help with morning sickness?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the morning sickness of early pregnancy is thought to be due to pyridoxine (B6) deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach attributes the "morning sickness" of early pregnancy to a deficiency of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): he notes it is commonly seen in the first trimester and is thought to be caused by too little B6. This complements his morning-sickness protocol elsewhere, which treats it with B6 plus a B-complex.
claims.verbatim:
“Morning sickness” commonly observed in the first
trimester of pregnancy is thought to be due to pyridoxine
deficiency.

claims.subject: vitamins
claims.question: Does the birth-control pill deplete a vitamin?
claims.answer_short: Yes - Wallach says 15-20% of women on the pill show vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency: malaise, depression, and glucose intolerance (trouble handling blood sugar).
claims.answer: Does the birth-control pill deplete a nutrient? Per Wallach, yes: 15 to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives show symptoms of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency - including malaise, depression, and glucose intolerance (trouble regulating blood sugar).
claims.verbatim:
Fifteen to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives
show the symptoms of pyridoxine deficiency manifested by
malaise, depression and glucose intolerance.

claims.subject: wallach
claims.question: Does Wallach agree with Linus Pauling?
claims.answer_short: Not on minerals — he corrects even the two-time Nobel laureate, who dismissed minerals as secondary and capped selenium at 15 mcg (today's safe limit is 200–1,000 mcg).
claims.answer: Wallach corrects even Linus Pauling - the two-time Nobel laureate - on minerals. Pauling (author of The Nature of the Chemical Bond) treated minerals as secondary to vitamins, recommending only eight to eleven of them at minimal doses. His selenium advice is Wallach's example of how wrong this was: Pauling insisted selenium's safe upper limit was just 15 mcg, whereas today the recommended safe limit is 200 to 1,000 mcg for an adult.
claims.verbatim:
Linus Pauling, two time Nobel laureate, and author of the
great work, The Nature of the Chemical Bond, relegated minerals
to secondary importance to vitamins, recommending only eight
to eleven minerals (calcium, magnesium, phosphorous, iron,
zinc, copper, manganese, chromium, molybdenum, iodine and
selenium) and then only at minimal doses - an example was
selenium for which he insisted the upper safe limit was 15 mcg
(today the recommended safe limit for selenium is 200 to 1,000
mcg for an adult).

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Can selenium deficiency cause prostate cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach links selenium deficiency to prostate cancer, using Linus Pauling — who downplayed minerals and died of prostate cancer at 94 — as his example.
claims.answer: Wallach links selenium deficiency to prostate cancer - and uses Pauling himself as the example: Pauling, who downplayed minerals, died of prostate cancer at age 94, which Wallach attributes to a selenium deficiency (selenium is strongly prostate-protective in his framework).
claims.verbatim:
Pauling died of prostate cancer at age 94 - a
common result of a selenium deficiency.

claims.subject: obesity
claims.question: Why do immigrants gain weight after moving to America?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites a 2004 JAMA study finding the longer immigrants live in the US the more likely they are to be obese (about 10 pounds after 15 years), which he calls the 'Feedlot Syndrome' from the mineral-depleted American diet, reframing obesity as a mineral-deficiency disease, not one of excess.
claims.answer: Wallach reframes obesity as a mineral-deficiency disease - "not a disease of excess." His evidence: a study in the Journal of the American Medical Association (December 15, 2004) found that the longer immigrants live in the US, the more likely they are to be obese, averaging about a 10-pound weight gain after 15 years. He calls this the "Feedlot Syndrome" - people placed on the mineral-depleted American "four food group" diet, having lost their traditional mineral-rich "culinary" and garden ashes, gain weight unless they consciously supplement with plant minerals.
claims.verbatim:
“The longer you live in America,
the more likely you are to be obese.” (Remember - obesity is a
mineral deficiency disease - not a disease of excess)

claims.subject: essential_nutrients
claims.question: How depleted is the food supply?
claims.answer_short: A USDA comparison (1975-2004) shows steep losses - broccoli lost 54% of its calcium, apples 60% of their iron - so Wallach says food alone can't supply enough minerals.
claims.answer: A central Wallach teaching: our food has been massively depleted of vitamins and minerals as farm soils were stripped. A USDA database comparing common foods between 1975 and 2004 shows dramatic losses - for example, broccoli lost 54% of its calcium and 74% of its vitamin A, onions lost 95% of their vitamin A, apples lost 60% of their iron, and kale lost 46% of its calcium. His conclusion: we can no longer get adequate minerals from food alone and must supplement, especially with plant-derived minerals (the "culinary ashes" of traditional diets).
claims.verbatim:
Only when one looks at a USDA data base that
compares the level of vitamins and minerals in certain common
foods between 1975 and 2004, do we truly understand how
depleted our foods have become since we gave up the back
yard gardens and wood ashes (plant minerals).

claims.subject: essential_nutrients
claims.question: What are the 90 essential nutrients?
claims.answer_short: Of 79+ elements found in the body, Wallach counts 60 minerals as essential - plus 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids and 3 essential fatty acids: the '90 essentials.'
claims.answer: How many minerals does the body actually need? Wallach's starting point: more than 79 elements and minerals have been detected in human and animal tissue, and simply being present in the tissue meets the first criterion for calling a substance an 'essential nutrient.' From there, he says thousands of studies support designating 60 of those 79 as truly essential - the mineral backbone of his '90 essential nutrients' framework (60 minerals, 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids, and 3 essential fatty acids).
claims.verbatim:
More than 79 elements and minerals have been detected
in animal and human tissue (i.e. - blood, liver, muscle, brain,
bones, connective tissue, etc.) in the 20th and 21st centuries. Their
presence in human tissue fulfills the first criteria for designating
an element or mineral an “essential nutrient.” Literally thousands
of additional studies provide support for designating 60 of these
79 elemental nutrients to be essential nutrients.

claims.subject: minerals
claims.question: How many diseases can one mineral deficiency cause?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's rule of thumb is that on average about ten deficiency diseases arise from missing any one essential mineral, with calcium the extreme case at as many as 147 diseases.
claims.answer: Wallach's rule of thumb for how much a single missing mineral can cost you: on average about ten different deficiency diseases can arise from the absence of any one essential mineral - and calcium is his extreme case, capable of producing as many as 147 different diseases when the body is short of it.
claims.verbatim:
On the average there are ten deficiency diseases that
can occur in the absence of each essential mineral, others, like
calcium can produce as many as 147 different diseases when
the body is deficient.

claims.subject: pica
claims.question: Are cravings for non-food items a sign of mineral deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes pica and 'the munchies' as the body's earliest warning sign of trace-mineral deficiency, and stresses that at this early stage it is fully reversible — restoring the missing minerals makes the cravings disappear.
claims.answer: Wallach describes cravings - pica (a compulsive craving for non-food items) and 'the munchies' - as the body's earliest warning sign of trace-mineral deficiency, and stresses that at this early stage it is fully reversible: restore the missing minerals and the cravings disappear.
claims.verbatim:
Pica, or the “munchies” appear in a mild form
in this early stage of deficiency. This phase of trace mineral
deficiency returns to normal (including the elimination of
the “munchies”) quickly following the return of an optimal
intake.

claims.subject: essential_nutrients
claims.question: How does a mineral deficiency progress before you notice?
claims.answer_short: In four hidden stages: initial (just 'low energy,' tests normal), compensated (cravings, odd symptoms), decompensated (real disease), then clinical (full disease, even death).
claims.answer: Wallach maps trace-mineral deficiency as a four-stage progression that mostly hides from standard testing until it is advanced. Initial Depletion - the body quietly adjusts and tests still look normal; the only clue is 'lack of energy' plus mild cravings. Compensated Metabolic - specific biochemical functions falter (low blood sugar, irregular heartbeat, loss of hair color, mild weight gain) and cravings intensify into 'chocoholic' or 'cola addict' behavior. Decompensated - serious metabolic, cognitive, emotional, developmental and structural disorders appear. Clinical - full disease and even death; yet orthodox physicians rarely diagnose the mineral cause, and the cure is often simply replacing the specific missing element.
claims.verbatim:
Initial depletion of trace elements in animals and
humans is characterized by changes only in the metabolism
of the element itself in response to a suboptimal intake, the
individual target tissue compensating so that no disturbance
of biological structure or function are detectable by means of
a test. However, the individual usually complains of “lack of

energy.”

claims.subject: adhd
claims.question: Can a mineral deficiency cause mood and behavior problems?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties trace-mineral deficiency to cognitive and emotional problems — learning disabilities, ADD, ADHD, autism, depression, bipolar, anxiety and panic attacks, and at the extreme explosive anger and a 'Jekyll-and-Hyde' temperament from a mineral-starved nervous system.
claims.answer: Wallach ties trace-mineral deficiency to a broad spectrum of cognitive and emotional/behavioral problems - not just physical disease. On the cognitive side he lists learning disabilities, ADD, ADHD and autism; on the emotional side, depression, manic depression/bipolar, anxiety and panic attacks - extending at the extreme to explosive anger and the volatile 'Jekyll-and-Hyde' or 'bad seed' temperament he attributes to a mineral-starved nervous system. His point for the reader: mood and behavior problems many people never connect to nutrition may trace back to a correctable deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
The decompensated phase of trace element deficiency is
characterized by the appearance of serious clinical symptoms
or defects in the metabolic (i.e. - pre-diabetes, significant weight
gain, obesity), cognitive (i.e. - learning disabilities, ADD,
ADHD, autism, etc.), emotional (i.e. - DR. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde,
“Bad Seeds,” depression, manic depression, bipolar

claims.subject: cardiomyopathy
claims.question: What diseases does Wallach blame on trace mineral deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says untreated trace-mineral deficiency finally reaches a clinical stage of full-blown disease and death — including cardiomyopathy, diabetes, aneurysm, arthritis, gum disease, degenerative disc disease, cataracts, goiter, and morbid obesity — that doctors rarely trace to a missing mineral, though the cure is often simply replacing the specific element.
claims.answer: Left uncorrected, Wallach says trace-mineral deficiency finally reaches a 'clinical' stage of full-blown disease and even death - he lists cardiomyopathy (heart-muscle disease), diabetes, aneurysm (a bulging, weakened artery wall), arthritis, periodontal (gum) disease, degenerative disc disease, cataracts, goiter (a swollen thyroid) and morbid obesity among the endpoints. His hopeful counterpoint: orthodox physicians almost never trace these back to a missing mineral, yet the cure is often as simple as replacing the specific trace element.
claims.verbatim:
The clinical phase of trace mineral deficiency is
characterized by the onset of full blown disease states and
even death (i.e. - cardiomyopathy, diabetes, aneurysm,
arthritis, periodontal disease, degenerative disc disease,
cataracts, goiter, morbid obesity, etc.). For most trace
mineral deficiencies in the clinical phase, correct diagnosis
by the “orthodox” physician is almost nonexistent; the cure,
however, is accomplished simply by the replacement of the
specific trace element.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Which form of calcium gives the most elemental calcium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's table for a 1,000 mg tablet shows calcium carbonate delivers the most metallic calcium (400 mg), followed by acetate (230), citrate (210), lactate (140) and gluconate (90), while 1,000 mg of cow's milk gives just 10 mg.
claims.answer: How much real (elemental) calcium a supplement delivers depends heavily on its form. Wallach's table for the metallic calcium in a 1,000mg tablet: calcium gluconate 90mg, calcium carbonate 400mg, calcium acetate 230mg, calcium citrate 210mg, calcium lactate 140mg - and cow's milk (1,000mg of fluid) just 10mg. (These are the milligrams of calcium present; how much you actually absorb is lower still - see his metallic-absorption note.)
claims.verbatim:
Amounts of Metallic Calcium in a 1,000 mg Tablet

Calcium Source Mg Available

Calcium gluconate 90
Calcium carbonate 400
Calcium acetate 230
Calcium citrate 210
Calcium lactate 140
Cow’s milk (1,000 mg fluid) 10

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: What are chelated minerals, and do they absorb better?
claims.answer_short: Chelated minerals wrap an amino acid around each mineral, absorbing ~40–65% — a 400% jump over metallic (8–12%); on a label they read as 'picolinate' or 'amino acid chelate.'
claims.answer: Chelated minerals - where an amino acid, protein, or enzyme is wrapped ('claw,' from the Latin) around each mineral - absorb far better than plain metallic ones: about 40-65%, which Wallach calls a 400% improvement over metallic minerals (8-12%). He notes the form was a 1940s livestock-industry invention (the original chelating agent, calcium EDTA, was a German pre-WWI antidote for arsenic and lead exposure, still used today for intravenous chelation of clogged arteries), and that you can spot chelated forms on a label as selenomethionine, chromium picolinate, or 'amino acid chelate.'
claims.verbatim:
Chelated minerals are approximately 40 to 65%
bioavailable, a 400% increase over the availability of metallic
minerals - certainly, a significant improvement over the


amounts elemental minerals that are absorbed.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: What actually is a 'colloidal' mineral?
claims.answer_short: An ultra-fine particle. Wallach describes a colloidal mineral as a particle so small (~1 billion would fit in 0.01 cubic inch) it can't be seen with the naked eye, and which stays grouped together instead of separating into individual atoms the way salt does in water — kept within the 1–100 nanometer range he calls 'nano-technology.'
claims.answer: What is a colloidal mineral - and what does 'nano-technology' have to do with it? Wallach describes a colloid as a substance existing as ultra-fine particles suspended in a medium of different matter - so small (about one billion would fit into 0.01 cubic inch) that they cannot be seen with the naked eye. In the colloidal state, he says, the particles remain grouped together instead of separating into individual atoms the way salt does in a true solution. He notes colloids remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble as long as a larger number of the particles, if not all, stay within the colloidal size range of 1nm to 100nm - a range, he points out, known as 'nano-technology.'
claims.verbatim:
The interesting
thing about colloids is that they remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble at different concentrations as long as a
larger number if not all of the particles are within a range of
sizes of colloids (1nm to 100nm) known as “nano-technology.”

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Why can't you just swallow ground-up rock minerals?
claims.answer_short: Inorganic mineral particles are too large to cross the gut wall; only when amino acids convert them into absorbable 'crystalloids' can the intestine take them up.
claims.answer: Why can't you just swallow ground-up rock minerals? Wallach's answer: inorganic mineral colloids are 'too large' to pass through the gut wall or cell walls into the bloodstream. But in the presence of amino acids (from protein-containing food), a small percentage of them get converted into chelated minerals and organic colloids that CAN be absorbed through the intestinal membranes - this absorbable state he calls a 'crystalloid.' He adds that almost all nutrients are actually taken up by 'active transport' (the intestinal cell reaching out with a pseudopodium, a finger-like projection, to engulf the particle), not by passively drifting through a membrane.
claims.verbatim:
In the presence of amino acids, a small
percentage of the inorganic colloids form chelated minerals
and organic colloids which are able to be dialyzed through the
mucus membranes of the intestinal walls into the blood stream
- this bio-available mineral state is known as a “crystalloid.”

Crystalloids or organic colloids readily pass
through cell walls, while inorganic colloids are “too large.”

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Which form of colloidal mineral is best?
claims.answer_short: The plant-derived, living organic colloid — coated in a water-loving protein, up to 98% bioavailable — is the form Wallach favors over bare 'rock flour' or industrial versions.
claims.answer: Wallach classifies colloidal minerals into four forms that differ wildly in usability: (1) unprotected 'rock flour' - bare inorganic colloids from sea beds, clays and 'glacial milk,' which are really just metallic minerals and only feed plants (and only in healthy, microbe-rich soil); (2) organic mineral colloids from living systems (bacteria, fungi, green food crops, animals, humans) coated in a water-loving substance like gelatin, albumin or collagen - a 'crystalloid' with bioavailability up to 98%; (3) a carbon-coated form (a 10-12 carbon chain), thought to be the most stable natural type; and (4) an industrial form not found in nature, made by coating metallic colloids with sulfated castor oil. The second - the plant/living organic colloid - is the highly absorbable form his framework favors.
claims.verbatim:
The second type of mineral colloid is found in living
systems of bacteria, fungi, green plants (food crops), animals
and humans and is coated with a water-loving (hydrophilic)
substance such as gelatin, albuminoids or collagen. This
coating protects the now “organic mineral colloid” and allows
it to be a crystalloid for absorption, storage and physiological
uses and thus maximizing its bioavailability up to 98%.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: What is silver?
claims.answer_short: Silver is a mineral Wallach counts as essential -- not because an enzyme requires it, but because it works as a systemic disinfectant and immune-system stimulator, so a silver deficiency leaves the immune system impaired.
claims.answer: Wallach counts silver as an essential mineral - not because an enzyme requires it, but because it works as a systemic disinfectant and immune-system stimulator. A silver deficiency, he says, leaves the immune system impaired (a link Dr. Robert Becker documented in The Body Electric, tying low tissue and dietary silver to higher illness rates). He puts the safe intake at up to 400 mcg of silver per day.
claims.verbatim:
Humans can consume 400 mcg of silver per day. A
silver “deficiency” results in an impaired immune system.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: How does silver kill bacteria and viruses?
claims.answer_short: Per Wallach, silver is an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal 'anti-metabolite' that disables the specific enzymes microorganisms use to breathe (respire) -- so efficient that our great-grandmothers dropped silver dollars into milk to keep it from spoiling.
claims.answer: How does silver fight germs? Per Wallach, it acts as an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal 'anti-metabolite' - it disables the specific enzymes microbes need to breathe (respire). He notes it is such an efficient bactericide (bacteria-killer) that our great-grandmothers dropped silver dollars into fresh milk to keep it from spoiling at room temperature.
claims.verbatim:
Silver is an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-metabolite that disables specific enzymes that microorganisms
use for respiration. Silver is such an efficient bactericide that
our great-grandmothers put silver dollars into fresh milk to
keep bacterial counts down and to keep it from spoiling at
room temperature.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: Does silver help wounds heal?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says silver drives tissue repair by stimulating fibroblast stem cells to multiply, generating primitive embryonic-like cells that can become whatever cell types are needed to heal a wound or rebuild lost tissue.
claims.answer: Beyond killing germs, Wallach says silver actively drives tissue repair: it stimulates fibroblast (stem) cells to multiply faster, generating primitive, embryonic-like cells in wounds that can then differentiate into whatever cell types are needed to heal the wound or rebuild lost tissue.
claims.verbatim:
Human fibroblast (stem) cells were able to multiply at a
greater rate, producing large numbers of primitive, embryonic
cells in wounds. These stem cells are able to differentiate into
whatever cell types that are necessary to heal the wound or
replace tissue mass.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: Can taking too much silver turn your skin blue-gray?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says silver is absolutely non-toxic at standard intake, but chronic overdosing can cause argyria -- a permanent, whole-body dusky blue-gray discoloration of the skin.
claims.answer: Is silver dangerous? Wallach's answer: at standard intake it is absolutely non-toxic - but chronic overdosing carries one distinctive risk, argyria: a permanent, whole-body dusky blue-gray discoloration of the skin (a 'tattoo' that does not fade).
claims.verbatim:
Silver is absolutely non-toxic to humans at standard rates of consumption. CAUTION:
chronic overdoses can cause a whole body tattoo that produces
a permanent dusky blue discoloration of the skin.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: What was colloidal silver used for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach relays older medical reports (not his own protocol): in 1917-18 colloidal silver was described as soothing inflammation and helping prostate/bladder irritation, itching, catarrh, even a post-childbirth blood infection. Silver sulfadiazine is still used in ~70% of U.S. burn centers.
claims.answer: Silver has a long clinical track record that Wallach relays from the older medical literature (presented for reference, not as his own protocol). Colloidal silver was reported in the British Medical Journal (Sir Malcolm Morris, 1917) as soothing rather than irritating - subduing inflammation and promoting healing - and used for enlarged prostate with bladder irritation, pruritus (itching) of the anus, perineal eczema, and hemorrhoids; J. Mark Hovell (1917) reported benefit for the Eustachian tubes, nasal-and-throat congestion (catarrh), and mouth, throat and ear infections; and T.H. Anderson Wells (Lancet, 1918) used it intravenously for a post-childbirth blood infection. Silver sulfadiazine (Silvadene) is used in about 70% of U.S. burn centers and stops the herpes simplex virus behind cold sores.
claims.verbatim:
colloidal silver is free from the drawbacks of
other preparations of silver, viz. pain caused and discoloration
of the skin. Instead of producing irritation, it has a distinctly
soothing effect. It rapidly subdues inflammation and promotes
healing of the lesions. It can be used with remarkable results
in enlarged prostate with irritation of the bladder, in pruritus
ani and perineal eczema, and in hemorrhoids.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Is aluminum an essential nutrient?
claims.answer_short: Yes - Wallach classifies the organically-bound colloidal aluminum in soil-grown plants as an essential, nontoxic nutrient, and lab-diet aluminum deficiency caused congenital limb defects.
claims.answer: Surprisingly, Wallach classifies aluminum as an essential nutrient - specifically the organically-bound colloidal aluminum found in all soil-grown plants, which he considers nontoxic. Its biological job: activating the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase. In animal studies, an aluminum-deficient diet produced congenital limb defects (non-genetic birth defects) in the young and liver cirrhosis (scarring) in adults, while supplementing it raised newborn survival - leading chemistry professor Gerhard Schrauzer to call it 'probably an essential mineral for human nutrition.'
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum’s known biological function is to activate
the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase. Deficiencies of aluminum
created in laboratory diets results in congenital limb defects
(non-genetic birth defects) in laboratory animals and cirrhosis
of the liver in mature animals.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Is aluminum in our food, and is that dangerous?
claims.answer_short: Unavoidable but normal, Wallach says: aluminum is Earth's most abundant metal (~12% of crust) and every plant takes it up - so no food or natural water is free of it.
claims.answer: Aluminum is everywhere in the food supply, and Wallach frames that as normal, not alarming: it is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust (12%) and is taken up by every plant grown in soil - so you cannot eat any grain, vegetable, fruit or nut, or drink any natural water, without ingesting it. He notes it is especially high in plankton and red algae and concentrates in mammals' hair and lungs.
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum represents 12%
of the earth’s crust and is the third most abundant element in the
earth’s crust and the most abundant metal in the earth’s crust.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Does aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says no - he calls it a myth from 'a single faulty study,' citing later work (Oxford 1992, a 2007 German assessment) that found no proven dietary-aluminum link.
claims.answer: Does aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease? Wallach says no - and calls the scare a myth built on 'a single faulty study.' He cites the follow-up work: a 1992 study in Nature by Frank Watt and colleagues at Oxford, using a highly accurate technique, found the same aluminum levels in the brains of non-Alzheimer's controls as in Alzheimer's patients; a 1997 Berkeley newsletter and a 2007 German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment opinion both concluded there is no proven link between dietary aluminum and Alzheimer's.
claims.verbatim:
A single faulty study over 35 years ago suggested a link
between chronic aluminum exposure and Alzheimer’s disease.

claims.subject: obscure_elements
claims.question: What is actinium?
claims.answer_short: A naturally radioactive metal that glows in the dark like radium (its name is Greek for 'ray'). Wallach lists it among elements found in living tissue -- it gathers in bone and liver, where he speculates it may have a metabolic role, though he assigns it no health use.
claims.answer: Actinium is a naturally occurring (and radioactive) element that Wallach includes among those detected in living tissue. Beyond the physics - it is a metal that, like radium, glows in the dark, and its name comes from the Greek aktinos ('ray') - his biological note is speculative but intriguing: actinium accumulates in the bones and liver, where he suggests it may have some metabolic function. He also observes that plant roots readily absorb it, though little travels up into the plant. Presented for the curious; Wallach assigns it no specific health role.
claims.verbatim:
Actinium accumulates in and presumably has metabolic
functions in the bones and liver.

claims.subject: arsenic
claims.question: Is arsenic an essential nutrient?
claims.answer_short: Wallach records that arsenic was determined to be an essential nutrient in 1947, notes typical human blood levels, that minute traces stimulate red-blood-cell production and promote growth, and that arsenic combined with choline prevents 100% of perosis in poultry.
claims.answer: Arsenic is an essential nutrient in Wallach's framework, determined to be one in 1947 - though he notes some soil regions in Argentina and New Zealand carry toxic levels of it. He records that arsenic normally appears in human female blood at 0.64 ppm, rising to 0.93 ppm during menstruation and 2.20 ppm during months five and six of pregnancy; that minute traces stimulate the production of red blood cells; that at 90 to 120 ppm it promotes and enhances the growth rate of chicks, and that arsenic likewise speeds the growth and metamorphosis of tadpoles; and that arsenic combined with the B-vitamin choline prevents 100% of perosis ("slipped tendon") in poultry.
claims.verbatim:
Arsenic was determined to be an essential nutrient
in 1947; the French Academy first identified arsenic in
dead human bodies in 1834.

claims.subject: arsenic
claims.question: Can too little arsenic cause carpal tunnel syndrome?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach holds that arsenic deficiency in humans shows up as carpal tunnel syndrome, TMJ and other repetitive-motion degenerative joint diseases.
claims.answer: A surprising deficiency link from Wallach: too little arsenic can surface as carpal tunnel syndrome, TMJ (temporomandibular joint, or jaw-joint, disorder), and other 'repetitive motion' type degenerative joint diseases. He adds that trace amounts stimulate red-blood-cell production.
claims.verbatim:
Arsenic
deficiency in humans results in a “carpal tunnel syndrome,”
“TMJ,” and other “repetitive motion” type degenerative joint
diseases and minute traces stimulate the production of red
blood cells.

claims.subject: arsenic
claims.question: Can arsenic treat leukemia?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center that arsenic infusions work better than any other drug for certain types of leukemia.
claims.answer: Arsenic isn't merely tolerated by the body - Wallach cites it as a leukemia treatment. Per the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, arsenic infusions work better than any other drug for certain leukemias; in a study of 12 gravely ill patients with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), 11 went into remission within 12-39 days, and 8 were still in remission ten years later - results the lead researcher said appeared to exceed any single drug for APL.
claims.verbatim:
According to the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer
Center in New York, “infusions of arsenic works better than
any other drug for the treatment of certain types of leukemia.”
Their study involved 12 seriously ill patients suffering from
acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL).

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Does gold treat arthritis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach is cautious - doctors add gold to aspirin for arthritis, but he stresses it only helps ACTIVE joint inflammation, not advanced, destructive rheumatoid arthritis.
claims.answer: Does gold treat arthritis? Wallach reports that orthodox physicians frequently give gold compounds (gold sodium thiomalate, aurothioglucose) as an add-on to aspirin (salicylates) for arthritis when added pain relief is required, and he notes their reported limitation: gold has been reported effective ONLY against active joint inflammation, and is not usually helpful for advanced, destructive rheumatoid arthritis. He is describing and bounding an existing orthodox therapy, not putting gold forward as a broad arthritis cure.
claims.verbatim:
Gold compounds (gold sodium thiomalate, gold
thioglucose also known as aurothioglucose) are frequently
administered by orthodox physicians as an add-on therapy
with salicylates (aspirin) for arthritis when added pain relief
is required. Gold has been reported only to be effective
against active joint inflammation and is not usually helpful
for treating advanced destructive rheumatoid arthritis.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Is gold used to treat cancer?
claims.answer_short: One form is: gold-198, a short-lived radioactive isotope (2.7-day half-life), is used as radiation therapy for some cancers - a medical use Wallach notes, not nutrition.
claims.answer: Separate from gold's nutritional role, Wallach notes a purely medical use of a radioactive form of gold: gold-198, a short-lived isotope (half-life 2.7 days, made by bombarding natural gold with neutrons in a reactor), is used to treat some forms of cancer. This is radiation therapy, not nutrition - included for reference.
claims.verbatim:
A radioactive isotope of gold
with a short half-life of 2.7 days is used to treat some forms of
cancer. Known as gold-198, it is easily produced by exposing
natural gold to a beam of neutrons in a nuclear reactor.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: What is boron and what does it do?
claims.answer_short: Boron is one of Wallach's essential minerals — accepted as essential for humans only in 1990 — and its core job is bone metabolism, helping the body use calcium and magnesium and keeping the ovaries, testes and adrenals working properly.
claims.answer: Boron is one of the 60 minerals Wallach counts as essential - though mainstream science was slow to agree, accepting it as an essential nutrient for humans only in 1990 (it had been shown essential for growing chicks about a decade earlier). Its core job, per Wallach, is in bone metabolism: it helps the body use calcium and magnesium efficiently and keeps the endocrine glands - the hormone-producing ovaries, testes and adrenals - working properly.
claims.verbatim:
Boron is essential for bone metabolism including the
efficient use of calcium and magnesium and proper function
of endocrine glands (i.e. - ovaries, testes and adrenals).

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: Does boron raise testosterone and estrogen?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports that boron supplementation doubles blood levels of both estrogen (estradiol) and testosterone in men and women.
claims.answer: Wallach points to boron's bone-protective and hormonal effects. He says it is needed both to maintain bone density and to keep normal blood levels of estrogen and testosterone. He cites a supplementation finding: within eight days of taking boron, women held on to far more of their minerals - excreting 40% less calcium, 33% less magnesium, and less phosphorus in their urine - while their level of 17-beta estradiol (the main, most active form of estrogen) doubled to what is seen in women on estrogen-replacement therapy, and testosterone doubled in both men and women.
claims.verbatim:
Boron is required for the maintenance of bone density
and normal blood levels of estrogen and testosterone. Within
eight days of supplementing boron, women lost 40% less
calcium, 33% less magnesium, and less phosphorus through
their urine. Women receiving boron supplements had blood
levels of estradiol 17B doubled to “levels found in women
on estrogen replacement therapy.” Levels of testosterone
also double in both men and women following boron
supplementation.

claims.subject: barium
claims.question: What is barium?
claims.answer_short: Barium is a mineral Wallach counts among the body's essential nutrients, though most people know it from the 'barium meal' that lights up the gut on an X-ray.
claims.answer: Barium is one of the 60 minerals Wallach counts as essential (recognized as essential for mammals in 1949). To most people, though, barium is familiar from medicine: because barium sulfate is a very dense salt that blocks X-rays, radiologists have a patient drink it (a 'barium swallow') or receive it as an enema so the hollow organs of the digestive tract show up clearly, outlined in white, on the film.
claims.verbatim:
As the barium
sulfate absorbs X-rays and blocks their transmission, the
gastrointestinal organs will be clearly outlined in white in an
X-ray film.

Barium was considered essential for mammals in 1949.

claims.subject: beryllium
claims.question: What is berylliosis?
claims.answer_short: Berylliosis is a painful, sometimes fatal lung disease Wallach says comes from inhaling beryllium oxide dust from mining and industry.
claims.answer: Beryllium is on Wallach's list of essential minerals, but it is one of the thin ones - in this book he assigns it no specific positive role in the body, offering mostly geology and history (it heads the 'alkaline-earth' metal family, alongside calcium and magnesium). What he does flag is a hazard: breathing beryllium-oxide dust, a mining and industrial contaminant, can cause berylliosis, a painful and sometimes fatal lung disease.
claims.verbatim:
Inhalation of beryllium oxide dust (mining and
industrial contaminants) can lead to “berylliosis,” a painful
and sometimes fatal lung disease.

claims.subject: bismuth
claims.question: What is bismuth used for, and did stress really cause ulcers?
claims.answer_short: Bismuth is the pink in Pepto-Bismol, used for stomach ulcers and gut infections for millennia. Wallach's myth-buster: ulcers were blamed on stress historically, but the real cause is Helicobacter pylori bacteria (Marshall & Warren, 1983) -- treated with antibiotics, antacids and bismuth.
claims.answer: Bismuth is not one of Wallach's essential nutrients, but he gives it a memorable entry. Chinese alchemists used it to treat gastric ulcers and gastroenteritis (stomach and intestinal inflammation) for more than 8,000 years, and today it is the pink liquid in over-the-counter gastrointestinal remedies like Pepto-Bismol. His larger point is a myth-buster: stress has historically been blamed as the cause of gastric, peptic and duodenal ulcers, but the true cause turned out to be infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori - a link Australians Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proposed in 1983 (and one already known in pigs back in 1952). His treatment of choice is a two-to-four-week course of tetracycline antibiotics, antacids and bismuth subsalicylate.
claims.verbatim:
Stress has historically been blamed as the boogy-man
as the cause of gastric, peptic, and duodenal ulcers. Animal
and human studies have in fact demonstrated that the true
cause of ulcers is an infection with a bacterium known as
Helicobacter pylori.

Australian gastroenterologist Barry Marshall, M.D.
and pathologist J. Robin Warren proposed their theory for the
bacterial cause of gastric ulcers in 1983. The bacterial cause
(H. pylori) for gastric ulcers was known in pigs in 1952.

claims.subject: bromine
claims.question: What is bromine?
claims.answer_short: Bromine is a halogen in the same chemical family as iodine that Wallach counts among the essential minerals, working in the body in its active form as brominated amino acids.
claims.answer: Bromine is a canon essential mineral in Wallach's framework and a halogen - the same chemical family as iodine. He says it works in the body in its active form as brominated amino acids, and that there is strong evidence for its essentiality in both mammals and humans.
claims.verbatim:
There is strong evidence for Bromine’s essentiality in
mammals and humans.

claims.subject: obscure_elements
claims.question: Where does the word 'bromide' come from?
claims.answer_short: From medicine: sodium bromide, a bromine salt, was a common mild sedative in the late 1800s used to calm the nerves -- which is why we still speak of taking a 'bromide' to settle down.
claims.answer: A bit of history on bromine: sodium bromide (a bromine salt) was a common mild sedative in the late 1800s and early 1900s. That is where the old expression comes from - people still talk about taking a 'bromide' to settle down and ease stress and tension.
claims.verbatim:
Sodium bromide, a salt of bromine, is a mild sedative
that was commonly used in the late 19th and early 20th
centuries. People still speak of taking a “bromide” to calm
down and ease stress and tension.

claims.subject: carbon
claims.question: What is carbon?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls carbon the element most essential for life on Earth — the structural backbone of every organic molecule, from carbohydrates, fats and amino acids to vitamins and enzymes.
claims.answer: Carbon is the element most essential for life on Earth - Wallach calls it the center of the 'organic' world. Because carbon atoms link into long chains that form the backbone (spine) of almost every biological molecule, virtually all of the body's building blocks are carbon-based: carbohydrates, fats, amino acids, vitamins and enzymes. DNA itself is one such long carbon-chain molecule.
claims.verbatim:
Carbon functions as an essential structural element for
all living organisms and organic molecules (i.e.- carbohydrates,
fats, amino acids, vitamins, enzymes, etc.).

claims.subject: carbon
claims.question: What is Wallach's view on global warming?
claims.answer_short: Off nutrition, he is skeptical of blaming humans -- calling our share of Earth's biomass 'pitifully small' and noting Ice Ages and warm spells have always cycled naturally. His fix is simply to plant more trees, which pull carbon dioxide from the air. (His personal stance on a debated topic.)
claims.answer: Outside of nutrition, Wallach shares his personal view on climate. He is skeptical of blaming human activity for global warming - he calls humanity's share of the planet's biomass 'pitifully small' and argues that Ice Ages and warm periods have cycled naturally throughout Earth's history, so today's warming is part of that long-running cycle. His proposed remedy is simply to plant more trees, which pull carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen and water.
claims.verbatim:
While many individuals and organizations, want to
blame man’s activities and pitifully small biomass for “global
warming,” we must look to the past for the cycles of Ice Ages and
“global warming” that have taken place over and over through
the millennia to understand the cyclic nature of these events.

claims.subject: macronutrients
claims.question: What are carbohydrates?
claims.answer_short: The body's convenient fuel (but not essential) - plants build them from CO2 and water by photosynthesis. Sized as single sugars, double sugars, and long chains like starch and fiber.
claims.answer: What are carbohydrates? Wallach explains that carbs and sugars are the body's convenient everyday fuel, but - importantly - they are NOT essential nutrients: the body can make all the carbohydrate it needs by reconfiguring proteins and fats. Plants build carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight (photosynthesis, which runs on chlorophyll, a magnesium/carbon ring). Carbohydrates are classified by size: single sugars (monosaccharides like glucose and fructose), double sugars (disaccharides like sucrose, maltose and lactose), and large chains (polysaccharides like starch, cellulose, fiber and glycogen).
claims.verbatim:
While
carbohydrates and sugars are convenient sources of fuel for
energy, they are not essential nutrients as all living organisms
can make them by reconfiguring proteins and fats.

claims.subject: macronutrients
claims.question: What are fats?
claims.answer_short: Water-repelling molecules packing ~9 calories a gram (vs 4.5); mostly triglycerides (glycerol + fatty acids). Fatty acids differ by chain length, saturation, and 'omega' number.
claims.answer: A primer on fats: like carbohydrates, fats (lipids) are built from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but they don't dissolve in water and pack more energy - about 9 calories per gram versus 4.5 for carbohydrate or protein. The main form of fat is the triglyceride: a molecule of glycerol joined to fatty acids. Fatty acids are described three ways - chain length (short, medium or long, by the number of carbons), how 'saturated' they are with hydrogen (no double bonds = saturated; one = monounsaturated; several = polyunsaturated), and where the first double bond sits counting from the tail (the 'omega' number, e.g. omega-3, omega-6).
claims.verbatim:
Triglycerides (the primary component of fats and oils)
are composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Structurally,
they are esters of a trihydric alcohol (glycerol) and fatty acids.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Why do babies and children need omega-3?
claims.answer_short: Wallach warns that EFA deficiency in infants causes poor growth, lowered IQ, seizures, learning disabilities, eczema, asthma, and weaker immunity.
claims.answer: Essential fatty acids (EFA) are the fats the body cannot make for itself and so must get from the diet. Wallach names three polyunsaturated ones - linoleic, linolenic and arachidonic acid - and notes only two (linoleic and linolenic) are strictly essential, since the body can build arachidonic acid from linolenic; 3% of daily calories must come from EFAs. They do vitamin-like jobs: carrying and processing fat, keeping cell membranes intact, lowering blood cholesterol, and serving as the raw material for prostaglandins that help regulate blood pressure, heart rate, blood-vessel and airway width, blood clotting, and brain and spinal-cord function. A shortage is especially damaging in infants.
claims.verbatim:
EFA deficiency in human infants results in a poor growth rate,
lowered IQ, seizures, learning disabilities, eczema, asthma,
and a lowered resistance to infectious diseases.

claims.subject: cholesterol
claims.question: What does cholesterol actually do in the body?
claims.answer_short: It's the raw material for vitamin D, bile acids, and the adrenal stress and sex hormones — so a cholesterol deficiency can worsen menopause and flatten libido.
claims.answer: Is cholesterol bad for you? Wallach's answer is emphatically no - it is essential. It is a structural part of every cell membrane and of the myelin that insulates the brain and spinal cord, and it is the raw material the body uses to make vitamin D, bile acids (which digest fat), the adrenal stress hormones, and the sex hormones estrogen, progesterone and testosterone. Because of that hormone role, he warns that a cholesterol deficiency can make menopause miserable for women and can flatten a man's sex drive.
claims.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential part of the structure of cell walls,
brain and spinal cord (myelin), the raw material for the
production of vitamin D in the human body, bile acids, adrenal
cortical hormones, estrogens (a cholesterol deficiency makes
menopause a living hell), progesterone, and testosterone (a
cholesterol deficiency will turn hubby into a TV watching
steer who is totally disinterested in sex).

claims.subject: macronutrients
claims.question: What are proteins?
claims.answer_short: The body's most abundant carbon compound - the main stuff of muscle and every cell, and enzymes are proteins too. Built from amino acids linked by peptide bonds; they add nitrogen.
claims.answer: What are proteins? Like carbohydrates and fats they contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but proteins add nitrogen (about 16%, the 'amine' group), sometimes with phosphorus, iron, sulfur or cobalt. Their basic building block is the amino acid; amino acids link by 'peptide bonds' into long chains, and digestion breaks those bonds to free the individual amino acids again. Proteins are the most abundant carbon-based compound in the body - the main stuff of muscle and every cell - and enzymes (the workers that speed up the body's chemical reactions) are themselves proteins.
claims.verbatim:
Proteins are the fundamental structural components
of the living cell (cytoplasm). They are essential parts of the
cell nucleus and protoplasm. Proteins are the most abundant
of all carbon containing organic compounds in the human
body.

claims.subject: macronutrients
claims.question: Can you eat too much protein?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's view: a healthy person can eat even 300 g of protein a day (nearly 3/4 lb of meat) with no harm - as long as they have no kidney or liver disease and supplement properly.
claims.answer: Can you eat too much protein? Wallach's view: a healthy person can consume even 300 grams of protein a day - nearly three-quarters of a pound of meat - with no ill effects, as long as they do not have kidney or liver disease and they supplement properly with vitamins and minerals.
claims.verbatim:
An individual consuming protein at even 300 gm per
day (almost 3/4 of a pound of meat a day) will have no adverse
effects as long as they do not have kidney or liver disease and
supplement properly with vitamins and minerals.

claims.subject: amino_acids
claims.question: What does each amino acid do?
claims.answer_short: Many build protein (valine, lysine, leucine...); tryptophan makes niacin and serotonin; phenylalanine makes thyroid hormone and adrenaline; methionine makes choline and creatine.
claims.answer: Wallach's essential amino acids and what each does. Classically there are nine that must come from the diet because the body cannot make them, and Wallach would add three more - arginine, taurine and tyrosine. Their roles: valine, lysine, threonine, leucine and isoleucine build protein; tryptophan is the precursor of niacin (vitamin B3) and serotonin; phenylalanine makes thyroxine (a thyroid hormone) and epinephrine (adrenaline); methionine makes choline and creatine phosphate; histidine makes histamine; and the added three help prevent specific diseases (arginine, taurine, tyrosine - see the related claim).
claims.verbatim:
Classically there are nine essential amino acids that are
required in the daily diet as they cannot be manufactured by
the human body.

claims.subject: arginine
claims.question: Does Wallach consider arginine an essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Yes—Wallach adds arginine to the classic essential amino acids, tying its long-term deficiency to cancer and PAD.
claims.answer: Beyond the classic list, Wallach singles out three amino acids that, over the long haul, help prevent specific diseases: arginine guards against cancer and PAD (peripheral arterial disease, clogged arteries in the limbs), taurine against macular degeneration (an eye disease that erodes central vision), and tyrosine against goiter (a swollen thyroid).
claims.verbatim:
To the classic list of essential amino acids, we would
add arginine, taurine, and tyrosine. Over the long haul, these
three amino acids help prevent certain specific diseases,
respectively, these diseases are cancer and PAD, macular
degeneration and goiter.

claims.subject: vitamins
claims.question: What are vitamins?
claims.answer_short: Organic compounds the body needs in tiny daily amounts but can't make itself; they work mostly as coenzymes (switching enzymes on) and supply no calories and no body mass.
claims.answer: What are vitamins? Wallach defines them as a group of unrelated, carbon-based organic compounds the body needs in tiny daily amounts for specific chemical reactions - essential for normal growth, development, maintenance, health, longevity and life itself. They work mainly as coenzymes (helper molecules that switch enzymes on) and cannot be manufactured by the human body, yet they supply no calories and add no body mass. Getting optimal vitamins, he says, goes a long way toward preventing birth defects and many debilitating degenerative diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamins are essential nutrients in that, they can not
be manufactured by humans; they do not supply calories or
contribute to body mass.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What is calcium and why is it important?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says calcium is essential to all living organisms — forming plant cell walls and mammalian bones and teeth — and also regulates electrochemical functions in cells and activates several enzymes; it is the fifth most abundant mineral in the earth's crust.
claims.answer: Calcium is essential for all living organisms — it forms the cell walls of plants, all calcareous tissues, and mammalian bones and teeth. Beyond that structural role, it also helps regulate the electrochemical functions inside cells and is a required cofactor that activates several enzymes. It is the fifth most abundant mineral element in the earth's crust and biosphere.
claims.verbatim:
Calcium is essential for all living organisms and is
found in the cell walls of plants, in all calcareous tissues, and
mammalian bones and teeth. Calcium also helps to regulate
electrochemical functions in cells and is a required cofactor
necessary to activate several enzymes.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How much calcium are humans designed to eat?
claims.answer_short: Wallach argues we're built for Stone-Age intakes of 1,600–3,000 mg a day; modern Americans get a fraction — as little as 300 mg.
claims.answer: Wallach argues humans are biologically designed to eat high-calcium diets. In the late Paleolithic (35,000–10,000 years ago), wild plant foods and game supplied about 1,600 mg of calcium a day at rest and 2,000–3,000 mg at the activity levels of hunting and labor. The agricultural revolution ~10,000 years ago narrowed the variety of foods and permanently lowered mineral intake — by the 20th century American adults took in only one-fifth to one-third as much, a median of 300–508 mg/day for women and 680 mg/day for men (National Health & Nutrition Examination Survey II).
claims.verbatim:
The
uncultivated food plants and wild game commonly available
to Stone Age humans would supply 1600 mg of calcium at
basal energy intakes and between 2,000 and 3,000 mg of
calcium at the energy levels required to support hunting and
work.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What diseases are caused by calcium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's Common Calcium Deficiency Diseases table lists bone-loss disorders (osteoporosis, osteopenia), spinal curvatures and fractures, receding gums and periodontal disease, osteomalacia and arthritis, plus high blood pressure, insomnia and kidney stones.
claims.answer: Wallach's Immortality book prints a long table titled "Common Calcium Deficiency Diseases" — the conditions he attributes to a chronic shortage of calcium. This is the first half. It gathers the many forms of bone loss (osteoporosis and its milder early stage, osteopenia), the spinal curvatures and collapse (kyphosis and dowager's hump = a hunched upper back, lordosis = swayback, plus compression and spontaneous fractures), the childhood hip disease Legg-Perthes, receding gums and periodontal (gum) disease, the softening and wearing of bone and joints (osteomalacia = soft bones, osteoarthritis, degenerative arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis = a spine-fusing arthritis), and then high blood pressure (with glaucoma), insomnia and kidney stones.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What symptoms come from low calcium?
claims.answer_short: The second half of Wallach's calcium-deficiency table lists bone and heel spurs, calcium deposits, cramps and twitches, PMS, sciatica and low-back pain, Bell's palsy, tinnitus, Ménière's disease, trigeminal neuralgia, tetany, panic attacks, anemia and restless leg syndrome.

It continues from bony overgrowths and deposits (bone and heel spurs, calcium deposits) through muscle cramps and twitches, PMS (premenstrual syndrome), sciatica and low back pain, the facial-nerve palsy (Bell's palsy), ringing in the ears (tinnitus), and the vertigo he calls "Wallach's vertigo" (Ménière's disease); then trigeminal neuralgia (stabbing facial-nerve pain) and spinal stenosis, the parathyroid disorder a raging calcium deficiency drives (nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, which pushes blood calcium too high — hypercalcemia), the bone-and-marrow scarring diseases (osteofibrosis, myelofibrosis), tetany (calcium-starved muscle spasm) and panic attacks, anemia, prolonged clotting time, and restless leg syndrome.
