claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How much calcium is in your body, and where?
claims.answer_short: Calcium is the body's most abundant mineral (~1–1.2 kg); 99% sits in the bones and teeth, and the last 1% works in blood and cells.
claims.answer: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body. The average man holds 1,200 grams and the average woman 1,000 grams — 2% of adult body weight, and up to 39% of the body's total mineral reserves (the ash left after cremation). Ninety-nine percent of it sits in the bones and teeth; the remaining 1% circulates in blood, extracellular fluid and inside cells, where it acts as a cofactor and activator for numerous enzyme systems.
claims.verbatim:
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human
body. The average male has 1,200 grams and the average
female has 1,000 grams. Calcium makes up two percent of the
adult body weight (water makes up 65 to 75%). Calcium also
composes up to 39% of the total mineral reserves (ash after
cremation). Ninety-nine percent of body calcium is found in
bones and teeth. The other one percent is found in the blood,
extracellular fluids, and within cells where it is a cofactor and
activator for numerous enzyme systems.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How is calcium stored in your bones?
claims.answer_short: As hydroxyapatite crystals on a protein 'bone matrix' — soak a bone in vinegar two weeks and the calcium leaches out, leaving the bendy scaffold.
claims.answer: In bone, calcium is stored as hydroxyapatite salts (calcium phosphate plus calcium carbonate) laid down in a crystal lattice bound to a protein scaffold called the "bone matrix." Wallach offers a simple demonstration of that matrix: put a chicken "drumstick" bone in a quart of vinegar for two weeks and the calcium is leached out of the bone, leaving the protein matrix behind.
claims.verbatim:
in a classic crystal structure bound to a protein framework
called “bone matrix.”

To extract the calcium from a bone and reveal the
protein matrix, put a chicken “drumstick” bone in a quart of
vinegar for two weeks and the calcium will be leached out of
the bone leaving the protein matrix.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What does calcium do besides build bone?
claims.answer_short: It's a working cofactor: it releases ATP energy for muscle, drives blood clotting, moves signals across membranes, fires nerves and paces the heartbeat.
claims.answer: Beyond its structural role, calcium is a working cofactor throughout the body. It is required to release energy from ATP (adenosine triphosphate) for muscle contraction, and it is a required cofactor in blood clotting: ionized calcium stimulates platelets to release thromboplastin and converts prothrombin to thrombin, which helps convert fibrinogen into fibrin — the protein web that traps red blood cells to form a clot. Calcium also mediates transport across cell and organelle membranes, affects the release of neurotransmitters at synapses, mediates the synthesis, secretion and metabolic effects of hormones and enzymes, and helps regulate the rate and strength of the heartbeat, muscle tone and how receptive muscle is to nerve stimulation.
claims.verbatim:
In addition to being a major structural mineral, Ca is also
required as a cofactor for the release of energy from ATP for
muscular contraction, and blood clotting. In the blood clotting
process, ionized Ca stimulates the release of thromboplastin
from platelets and converts prothrombin to thrombin. Thrombin
helps to convert fibrinogen to fibrin, and fibrin is the protein
web that traps red blood cells to create blood clots.

claims.subject: absorption
claims.question: What blocks calcium from being absorbed?
claims.answer_short: It depends on the form and the gut: a metallic calcium pill may be only 1–3% absorbed, and phytates in grains, low stomach acid, celiac damage, sugar and carbonation all drive it lower.
claims.answer: How well calcium is absorbed depends heavily on its form and the gut environment. It is taken up mainly in the duodenum while the contents are still acidic; once the intestine turns alkaline, absorption falls off. Plain metallic calcium may be only 1-3% absorbed, whereas an organically bound, plant-derived colloidal or water-soluble chelated form can reach up to 98%. Wallach lists the causes of a calcium deficiency as: too little vitamin D; low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, which can follow a salt-restricted diet); lactose intolerance; celiac disease; a high-fat or low-protein diet; and heavy fiber and phytate intake. Phytic acid (in grain bran, oatmeal, whole wheat) and oxalic acid (in rhubarb, spinach, chard, mustard greens) each bind calcium into insoluble, unabsorbable salts, and excess sugar, carbonation and caffeine leach stored calcium from the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Causes of a calcium deficiency can include, a
deficiency or lack of vitamin D; the lack of stomach acid
or hypochlorhydria can result from a restricted NaCl (salt)
intake; lactose intolerance; celiac disease; high fat diet; low
protein diet; and a high fiber and phytate consumption.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How does the body keep blood calcium steady?
claims.answer_short: Two hormones — parathormone and calcitonin — hold serum calcium at 8.5–10.5 mg/dL, mostly by borrowing it from and returning it to bone.
claims.answer: The body holds blood calcium within a tight range using two hormones. Parathormone (from the parathyroid glands) and calcitonin (from the thyroid) keep serum calcium at 8.5-10.5 mg/dL, largely by drawing on the calcium reserves in bone. Parathormone raises blood calcium — pulling it from bone, making the kidney retain more, and making the gut absorb more efficiently; when blood calcium climbs above 10.5 mg/dL from too much parathyroid activity, calcitonin reduces how much calcium is released from the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Under optimal conditions, parathormone secreted by
the parathyroid gland and calcitonin secreted by the thyroid
gland, maintain a serum calcium of 8.5 to 10.5 mg% by drawing
on calcium reserves from the bones.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What in the modern diet drains your calcium?
claims.answer_short: Fiber, salt and soft-drink phosphate force calcium out of the body — the modern diet's calcium-to-phosphorus ratio simply can't be met by eating alone.
claims.answer: Several common features of the modern diet quietly raise the body's calcium requirement — an increased calcium "cost." Overloading on fiber, salt and phosphates (soft drinks) all force more calcium out: urinary calcium loss rose from 96 mg to 148 mg per day when food was heavily salted, and doubling phosphate intake raised urinary calcium output by 50%. Wallach argues the industrialized diet is chronically calcium-poor and phosphorus-rich, so the ideal calcium-to-phosphorus (Ca:P) ratio of 2:1 is impossible to hit by eating alone (you would have to eat 25 pounds of broccoli for every 16 oz T-bone steak); the only practical route is to avoid high-phosphorus foods and supplement with plant-derived colloidal and chelated calcium.
claims.verbatim:
Other nutrients that are commonly found in the
American diet can aggravate the national calcium deficiency
crisis. Diets rich with an overabundance of fiber, salt and
phosphates (soft drinks) result in an increased calcium “cost.”
In effect, these foods increase the dietary requirements for
calcium. Urinary calcium loss increased from 96 mg per day
to 148 mg per day when food was excessively salted. As


 

phosphate intake is doubled, the output of urinary calcium
increases by 50%.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Can calcium deficiency cause high blood pressure?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach cites research linking chronic calcium deficiency to hypertension, with more than 30 studies supporting it and lower ionized calcium found in untreated hypertensives.
claims.answer: Wallach ties chronic calcium deficiency to high blood pressure. In 1980 McCarron and colleagues theorized that chronic calcium deficiency leads to hypertension, and more than 30 later studies supported it; serum ionized calcium runs consistently lower in people with untreated hypertension. The link is clearest in people taking in less than 500 mg of calcium a day. In salt-sensitive hypertension, a rise in blood pressure tracks with urinary calcium loss from excess salt on top of an existing calcium deficiency — and among Black and elderly white people with essential hypertension, low calcium and potassium (rather than high salt) drive the "salt sensitivity." In a four-year study of 58,218 nurses, hypertension was more likely in women taking in less than 800 mg of calcium per day.
claims.verbatim:
In 1980, McCarron et al theorized that chronic calcium
deficiency probably led to hypertension. More than 30
subsequent studies supported the original theory of calcium
deficiency as the cause of hypertension. In addition, recent
studies have shown that serum ionized calcium is consistently
lower in humans with untreated hypertension.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Do you need surgery for an enlarged parathyroid gland?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says no — an enlarged parathyroid from calcium deficiency is often mislabeled a 'tumor,' but supplementing usable calcium resolves it, so don't get surgery.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism — driven by a raging calcium deficiency — raises blood calcium and makes the parathyroid glands enlarge as they strain to pull more calcium from the gut. Surgeons almost always mistake the enlarged (hypertrophied) glands for a "tumor" and recommend surgery; Wallach says supplementing with the right amounts of usable calcium resolves the problem rapidly and completely, and bluntly advises: DO NOT GET SURGERY.
claims.verbatim:
Nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, resulting
from a raging calcium deficiency, produces a significant
elevation in blood calcium levels. The parathyroid glands
will attempt to compensate and will enlarge in an attempt
to absorb more calcium from the gut. This scenario will
almost always result in the surgeon calling the enlarged or
hypertrophied parathyroid glands a “tumor” and they will
recommend surgery. Supplementation with the appropriate
amounts of usable calcium will result in a rapid and complete
resolution of the problem - DO NOT GET SURGERY!

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How many diseases does Wallach tie to calcium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: 147 — Wallach links no fewer than 147 diseases to calcium deficiency or imbalance, and says U.S. diets are so deficient that only supplements fix it.
claims.answer: Wallach holds that there are no fewer than 147 deficiency diseases attributable to calcium deficiencies or imbalances, and that American diets across the board are critically deficient in calcium — so the only practical way to get enough is supplementation. He jabs at the researchers who studied the problem: instead of recommending effective calcium supplementation, they told people to eat five cups of broccoli a day ("Try and get a kid to eat five cups of broccoli each day").
claims.verbatim:
There are no less than 147 deficiency diseases that can
be attributed to calcium deficiencies or imbalances. The most
recent clinical research clearly points out that the entire scope
of American diets are critically deficient in calcium. The only
practical way to obtain enough sufficient amounts of calcium
is through supplementation.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Which famous people did Wallach say had calcium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: He points to Pope John Paul II, Elizabeth Taylor, 'Bo' Jackson and vegan NBA star Bill Walton — all, he says, with osteoporosis or fractures.
claims.answer: To make the point that calcium deficiency reaches even the famous and well-fed, Wallach lists public figures he says suffered an advanced degree of it: Pope John Paul II (fractured hip / osteoporosis), Elizabeth Taylor (osteoporosis / multiple hip-replacement surgeries), "Bo" Jackson (fractured hip / osteoporosis), and Bill Walton, a vegan of professional-basketball fame (osteoporosis, arthritis, fractures).
claims.verbatim:
Famous people who have suffered from an advanced
degree of calcium deficiency include Pope John Paul II
(fractured hip/ osteoporosis), Elizabeth Taylor (osteoporosis/
multiple hip replacement surgeries), “Bo” Jackson (fractured
hip/osteoporosis), Bill Walton, a vegan of professional
basketball fame (osteoporosis, arthritis, fractures), etc.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: What are the most common signs of calcium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the most common calcium-deficiency diseases are easy to spot — from poor blood-clotting time (noticed when you nick yourself shaving) through arthritis to the dozens of variations of osteoporosis.
claims.answer: Wallach says the most common calcium-deficiency diseases are easy to recognize, ranging from poor clotting time of the blood — noticed when you nick yourself shaving, because calcium is a cofactor in the clotting mechanism — through arthritis (which physicians treat with painkillers, anti-inflammatory drugs and surgery), to the dozens of variations of osteoporosis.
claims.verbatim:
The most common calcium deficiency diseases are
easy to recognize and range from poor clotting time of the
blood when you nick yourself shaving (calcium is a cofactor
in the clotting mechanism), arthritis (which physicians treat
with pain killers, anti-inflammatory drugs and surgery), to
the dozens of variations of osteoporosis.

claims.subject: digestion
claims.question: What does stomach acid actually do?
claims.answer_short: Salt (sodium chloride) is the raw material your stomach uses to make hydrochloric acid — and that acid is what activates pepsin to digest protein, activates intrinsic factor to absorb B12, and lets you absorb minerals.
claims.answer: Chlorine (as chloride) is essential to every living species. Wallach says it powers electrochemical and catalytic functions, activates numerous enzymes, and is the basic raw material the stomach uses to make stomach acid (hydrochloric acid, HCl) — which is required to activate protein digestion by the enzyme pepsin, to absorb vitamin B12 (by activating intrinsic factor), and to absorb minerals. Ordinary salt (sodium chloride, NaCl) is the universal source of chloride ions for all living things.
claims.verbatim:
Chlorine


 

is essential for all living species’ electrochemical and catalytic
functions, activates numerous enzymes, and is the basic
raw material for our stomachs to make stomach acid (HCl)
required to activate protein digestion by the enzyme pepsin,
B12 absorption (intrinsic factor activation), and for absorption
of minerals.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: What does cobalt do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Cobalt is essential for all forms of life; it activates enzymes, helps fix nitrogen, and sits at the very center of vitamin B12.
claims.answer: Cobalt is essential to every form of life — from blue-green algae, bacteria and fungi to plants, insects, and all the vertebrates including humans. It works as an enzyme cofactor and activator, helps "fix" nitrogen during amino-acid production, and — most importantly — a single cobalt atom sits at the center of vitamin B12, which is itself a cofactor and activator (the cobamide coenzymes) for several essential enzymes.
claims.verbatim:
Cobalt is essential for all forms of life including blue-green algae, some bacteria and fungi, some plants, insects,
birds, reptiles, amphibians and mammals including man.
Cobalt functions as a cofactor and an activator for enzymes,
“fixes” nitrogen during amino acid production, and a single
cobalt atom is the central metal component of vitamin B12,
which itself is a cofactor and activator (cobamide coenzymes)
for several essential enzymes.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: What does vitamin B12 do in the body?
claims.answer_short: B12 helps build DNA and RNA, forms the myelin that insulates nerves, and is required to make red blood cells.
claims.answer: Vitamin B12 (and its cobalt) does some of the body's most fundamental work. Together with folic acid, choline and the amino acid methionine, it transfers single-carbon (methyl) groups used to build RNA and to make DNA from RNA — so it sits at the heart of gene function, which is why Wallach ties preconception nutrition to preventing birth defects. Growth, the formation of myelin (the insulating sheath — made by converting cholesterol — around nerves in the brain, spinal cord and large nerve trunks), and red-blood-cell production all depend on B12. Cobalt is also a required cofactor for making the thyroid hormone thyroxine.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12/cobalt joins with folic acid, choline, and
the amino acid methionine to transfer single carbon groups
(methyl groups) in the synthesis of the raw material to make
RNA and the synthesis of DNA from RNA. DNA and RNA
are directly involved in gene function; remember the concept
of preconception nutrition to prevent birth defects. Growth,
myelin formation (converts cholesterol into the insulating
material myelin found around nerves in the brain, spinal
cord, and large nerve trunks), and red blood cell synthesis are
dependent on B12.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: Why can’t I absorb vitamin B12?
claims.answer_short: Because B12 uptake depends on stomach acid. Wallach explains that intrinsic factor only works when the stomach is acid enough; with hypochlorhydria it fails and B12 is not absorbed — which is why doctors give B12 shots to older people on salt-restricted diets.
claims.answer: How well cobalt/B12 is absorbed depends on stomach acid and intrinsic factor. Metallic cobalt is absorbed at 20–26.2% only if intrinsic factor (Castle's factor, a mucoprotein in normal stomach secretions) is present and the stomach pH is 2.0 or lower. If a person has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid — usually from a salt/NaCl deficiency), intrinsic factor fails and B12/cobalt isn't absorbed — which is why doctors often give B12 shots to older people on salt-restricted diets (sublingual and oral-spray B12 are alternatives). Plant-derived cobalt is highly bioavailable, but because of low-salt diets and cobalt-depleted soils, vegetarians frequently run B12 deficiencies.
claims.verbatim:
If a person
has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid- usually a NaCl
deficiency) the intrinsic factor will not work and B12 cobalt is
not absorbed - this is why doctors frequently give B12 shots
to older people on salt restricted diets. Sublingual (under the
tongue) and oral spray B12 is available. Plant derived cobalt is
very bioavailable; however, because of low salt diets and cobalt
depleted soils, vegetarians frequently have B12 deficiencies.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: How was cobalt discovered to be essential?
claims.answer_short: It came from 'bush sickness,' a fatal wasting disease of cattle and sheep in Australia and New Zealand that was cured and prevented by cobalt.
claims.answer: Cobalt's essentiality was discovered through "bush sickness," a fatal disease of cattle and sheep in Australia and New Zealand that could be successfully treated and prevented with cobalt supplements. Bush sickness was marked by emaciation (Wallach likens it to unsupplemented vegans), a dull stare, a listless and starved look, pale mucous membranes, anorexia (loss of appetite), and pernicious anemia (a macrocytic/hypochromic anemia — large, pale red cells).
claims.verbatim:
The discovery of the essentiality of cobalt came from
observing a fatal disease (“bush sickness”) in cattle and
sheep from Australia and New Zealand. It was observed that
“bush sickness” could be successfully treated and prevented
by cobalt supplements. Bush sickness was characterized by
emaciation (unsupplemented vegans), dull stare, listless
and starved look, pale mucus membranes, anorexia, and
pernicious anemia (macrocytic/hypochromic).

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: What diseases does a cobalt or vitamin B12 deficiency cause?
claims.answer_short: Failing to absorb B12/cobalt causes pernicious anemia and demyelination of the spinal cord and large nerve trunks.
claims.answer: In humans, failing to absorb B12/cobalt causes a deficiency disease. It can follow surgical removal of part of the stomach (which wipes out the zones that make intrinsic factor) or of the ileum, small-intestinal pouches (diverticulae), parasites (tapeworm), celiac disease (gluten/grain and cow's-milk-albumen allergy), and other malabsorption disorders. The classic results are pernicious anemia and demyelination — stripping of the myelin insulation — of the spinal cord and the large nerve trunks.
claims.verbatim:
In humans, a failure to absorb B12/cobalt results in a
deficiency disease. This can result from a surgical removal
of parts of the stomach (eliminates zones of intrinsic factor
production), or surgical removal of the ileum portion of
the small bowel, small intestinal diverticulae, parasites
(tapeworm), celiac disease (allergies to wheat gluten, barley,
rye, oats and cows milk albumen), and other malabsorption
diseases. Pernicious anemia and demyelination of the spinal
cord and large nerve trunks are classic diseases that are the
result of B12/cobalt deficiency.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: How much cobalt or vitamin B12 should I take a day?
claims.answer_short: The RDA is only 3–4 mcg a day, but Wallach prefers 250 to 400 mcg for a real safety margin, especially before and during pregnancy and nursing.
claims.answer: Wallach gives the quantitative picture for cobalt/B12. In the soil, less than 0.07 ppm cobalt leaves crops (and the animals and people who eat them) deficient, while 0.11 ppm prevents and cures the deficiency. The official RDA for B12/cobalt is just 3–4 mcg per day, but Wallach recommends 250–400 mcg for a respectable safety margin, and urges pregnant and nursing mothers especially to supplement (a baby nursed by a deficient mother carries the congenital deficiency longer, risking serious, permanent nerve damage). At the other extreme, a cobalt excess in humans (20–30 mg/day) can over-stimulate red-blood-cell production (erythropoiesis) by raising the kidney hormone erythropoietin.
claims.verbatim:
The human RDA for B12/cobalt is 3 to 4 mcg per day,
however 250 to 400 mcg gives a respectable safety margin.
Pregnant and nursing mothers should especially take care
to supplement with the optimum levels of B12.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: What does cobalt have to do with vitamin B12?
claims.answer_short: Cobalt is the heart of vitamin B12 -- it sits in a ring related to the ones holding iron in hemoglobin and magnesium in chlorophyll, and gives B12 its red color. 'Cyanocobalamine' was named for a cyanide group on the first B12 isolated (1948).
claims.answer: Some biochemistry of vitamin B12: its cobalt sits chelated in a large tetrapyrrole ring — the same ring family as the porphyrin ring that holds iron in hemoglobin and magnesium in chlorophyll. The first B12 molecule isolated in the lab carried a cyanide group, hence the name cyanocobalamine; several cobalamine forms have B12 activity, with cyanocobalamine and hydroxycobalamine the most active. B12 is a red, water-soluble crystalline substance (the red comes from the cobalt atom), slowly destroyed by acid, alkali, light and oxidizing/reducing agents — and about 30% of its activity is lost in cooking. It was isolated from liver extracts in 1948 and shown to have anti-pernicious-anemia activity.
claims.verbatim:
B12 cobalt is chelated in a large tetrapyrrole ring
similar to the porphyrin ring found in hemoglobin (iron) and
chlorophyll (magnesium).

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: How do animals get vitamin B12 from cobalt?
claims.answer_short: Microbes do the work: gut bacteria in a cow's rumen turn elemental cobalt into B12, which the animal absorbs. Carnivores get it secondhand from prey, and rabbits and rodents eat their own night feces (coprophagy) to recover it.
claims.answer: Wallach explains how animals actually get their B12 from elemental cobalt — a job done by microbes, not the animal itself. Ruminants (cows, sheep, goats, deer, antelope, buffalo, giraffe) rely on the microbes fermenting plant material in their first stomach (the rumen) to convert elemental cobalt into vitamin B12, which the animal then absorbs. Carnivores get their B12 secondhand by eating the stomach contents, liver, bone and muscle of their ruminant prey. And poultry, lagomorphs (rabbits and hares) and rodents eat feces at night (coprophagy) to recover the B12 their own gut microbes manufactured.
claims.verbatim:
Ruminants (i.e. cows, sheep, goats, deer, antelope,
buffalo, giraffe, etc.) can use elemental cobalt because the
microbes fermenting and digesting plant material in their first
stomach (rumen) convert elemental cobalt into vitamin B12,
which the animal then uses.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: What is chromium and what does it do?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes chromium as a trace mineral that activates phosphoglucomutase and is the working core of glucose tolerance factor (GTF) — a complex of chromium III, dinicotinic acid and glutathione — with the body holding only about 1.5 mg, best read by hair analysis.
claims.answer: Chromium is a small but metabolically busy trace mineral. Wallach says it activates the enzyme phosphoglucomutase and others, and — most importantly — it is the working core of glucose tolerance factor (GTF), the compound that lets insulin do its job of controlling blood sugar. GTF is a complex of chromium in its trivalent (chromium-III) form, dinicotinic acid (a niacin / vitamin-B3 derivative), and glutathione (the body's main built-in antioxidant). The whole body holds only about 1.5 mg of chromium, and because hair concentrates it roughly ten times higher than blood does, hair analysis gives a more accurate read on tissue stores than a blood test.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium activates phosphoglucomutase and other
enzymes and is closely associated with glucose tolerance factor
(GTF). Glucose tolerance factor is a combination of chromium
III, dinicotinic acid and glutathione.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: What are the diseases and symptoms of chromium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's Immortality table of chromium-deficiency diseases runs from low blood sugar, pre-diabetes and type-2 diabetes to hyperactivity, ADD/ADHD, autism, depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety and panic attacks, plus impaired growth, high cholesterol, heart-vessel disease, infertility, obesity and a shortened life span.
claims.answer: Wallach's Immortality prints a table titled "Diseases and Symptoms of Chromium Deficiency" — the conditions and symptoms he attributes to a chronic shortage of chromium. Because chromium governs blood-sugar control (through glucose tolerance factor and insulin), most of the list is metabolic or neuro-behavioral: low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), prediabetes and adult-onset (type II) diabetes, excess insulin (hyperinsulinemia, which he links to narcolepsy), hyperactivity, learning disabilities, attention-deficit disorder (ADD/ADHD), autism, extreme irritability, depression, manic depression / bipolar disease, and anxiety and panic attacks — up to violent 'Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde' rages. The rest are bodily: impaired growth, peripheral neuropathy (nerve damage), negative nitrogen balance (net loss of body protein), elevated triglycerides and cholesterol, coronary blood-vessel disease and aortic cholesterol plaque, infertility and decreased sperm count, obesity, and a shortened life span.

claims.subject: diabetes
claims.question: How does chromium deficiency lead to diabetes?
claims.answer_short: Chromium runs the body's blood-sugar handling; deficiency wrecks glucose tolerance (77% of 'normal' over-70s) — and Wallach cites the USDA that 90% of Americans are chromium-deficient.
claims.answer: Wallach ties chromium deficiency straight to the body's handling of blood sugar. Pregnant women run lower fasting plasma chromium than non-pregnant women, and the well-documented worsening of glucose tolerance during a 'normal' pregnancy reflects that deficiency — which, he says, often tips over into pregnancy-onset (gestational) diabetes. He frames it as widespread and worsening with age: one study found abnormal glucose tolerance in 77% of clinically 'normal' adults over 70, and he cites the USDA's Richard Anderson that 90% of all Americans are chromium-deficient.
claims.verbatim:
The fasting level of plasma chromium is lower in
pregnant women than in non-pregnant women. Increasing
impairment of glucose tolerance in “normal” pregnancy is
well documented and reflects a chromium deficiency that
oftentimes results in pregnancy onset diabetes. One study
demonstrated abnormal glucose tolerance in 77% of clinically
“normal” adults over the age of 70. According to Richard
Anderson of the USDA, “Ninety percent of all Americans are
deficient in chromium.”

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Can chromium help you live longer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites Gary Evans's finding that chromium supplementation increased the lifespan of laboratory animals by 33.3 percent, challenging the prior view that only severe calorie restriction could extend life.
claims.answer: Gary Evans of Bemidji State University (Minnesota) showed that simply supplementing chromium increased the lifespan of laboratory animals by 33.3% — a striking result, because until then the gerontologist Dr. Roy Walford and colleagues believed calorie restriction was the only proven way to extend life past the average. Wallach adds that chromium deficiency in humans brings a wide range of clinical diseases plus a shortened life expectancy, and that these are made worse by a simultaneous vanadium deficiency and by high sugar or alcohol intake.
claims.verbatim:
Gary Evans, Bemidji State University, Minnesota, very
clearly showed an increased lifespan in laboratory animals
by 33.3%, when they were supplemented, with chromium.
Prior to this study, gerontologist, led by Dr. Roy Walford,
felt a Calorie Restricted diet was the only way to extend life
past the expected average age. Deficiencies of chromium in
humans are characterized by a wide variety of clinical diseases
as well as a shortened life expectancy. The clinical diseases of
chromium deficiency are aggravated by concurrent vanadium
deficiencies and increased sugar or alcohol intakes.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Why is chromium so easy to lose and hard to absorb?
claims.answer_short: Sugar flushes chromium out in urine (up 300% for 12 hrs) and food chromium is barely retained; form decides - ~25% of chelated vs up to 98% of colloidal is absorbed.
claims.answer: Wallach explains why chromium is both easy to lose and hard to absorb — his argument for supplementing it in a highly-absorbable form. Eating sugar (colas, fruit juices, honey, candy, table sugar, fructose) raises the rate at which chromium is flushed out in the urine by 300% for 12 hours. And ordinary inorganic chromium from food and water is poorly used: a typical 50-100 microgram (mcg) intake yields only 0.25-5 mcg the body can actually retain. Form is decisive — 25% of chelated chromium is absorbed, versus up to 98% of colloidal chromium. He notes the chromium RDA (the government's Recommended Daily Allowance) is 50-200 mcg of usable chromium per day for adults.
claims.verbatim:
Dietary sugar
loads (i.e. colas, apple juice, grape juice, honey, candy, table
sugar, fructose, etc.) increase the natural rate of urinary Cr loss
by 300% for 12 hours. The average intake of 50 to 100 ug of
inorganic chromium from food and water supplies only 0.25
to 5 ug of usable and retainable chromium. By contrast, 25%
of chelated chromium is absorbed and up to 98% of colloidal


 

chromium is absorbed. The chromium RDA for humans is a
range of 50 to 200 ug of usable chromium per day for adults.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Has Americans' chromium level been falling?
claims.answer_short: Yes - the young hold more chromium than the old, unsupplemented tissue steadily drops with age, and Wallach charts a steep fall in average American blood chromium since 1948.
claims.answer: A recurring worry in the book: Americans' chromium status has been sliding for decades. Newborn animals and people carry more chromium per pound of body weight than older ones, and in anyone who doesn't supplement, tissue chromium steadily falls with age. Wallach flags a population-wide drop in average American blood chromium since 1948, tabulating mean levels in micrograms per liter (mcg/L) by year: 28 in cities and 1000 in rural areas in 1948, 13 in 1971, 10 in 1972, 4.7-5.1 in 1973, 0.73-1.6 in 1974, 0.16 in 1978, 0.43 in 1980, and 0.13 by 1985.
claims.verbatim:
The concentration of chromium found in newborn
animals and humans is higher per pound of body weight
than it is in older individuals. In fact, the chromium levels of
unsupplemented human tissue, steadily decreases throughout
life. Of greater concern has been the steady decline in the
average American serum chromium since 1948.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: How was chromium discovered, and why does it color gemstones?
claims.answer_short: Found in 1797 by Vauquelin and named from Greek 'chroma' (color) for its vivid compounds - trace chromium makes rubies red, emeralds green, and alexandrite shift color.
claims.answer: The element's backstory — and why it colors gemstones. Chromium was discovered by the French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797 and named from the Greek chroma, 'color,' because all its compounds display a color (the pure metal itself, though, is a hard, brittle, silver-white). Added to steel at 18% it makes stainless steel, and its almost-invisible oxide layer makes it extremely resistant to corrosion — the decorative, protective plating on bathroom fixtures, jewelry and car bumpers. Trace chromium is what tints many gems: it makes rubies red (in corundum), emeralds green (in beryl), and gives alexandrite (in chrysoberyl) its color-shift — red in firelight, blue in daylight.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium was discovered by French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797 and named from the Greek word
chroma, which translates to “color.”

claims.subject: ph
claims.question: What is cesium?
claims.answer_short: An alkali metal that behaves chemically like sodium, potassium and rubidium. Wallach says cesium and potassium pair up inside the cell, which is also why taking extra potassium makes you lose cesium faster.
claims.answer: Cesium is an alkali (alkaline) metal, so chemically it behaves much like sodium, potassium and rubidium. Wallach describes cesium and potassium forming a 'solute complex' inside the cell that takes part in ion antagonism (the balancing push-pull between minerals), osmosis, regulating what crosses the cell membrane (permeability), and keeping the cell's interior in its proper gel-like 'colloidal' state. Because the two minerals trade places, taking extra potassium speeds up how fast the body excretes and loses cesium.
claims.verbatim:
As an alkaline mineral, cesium behaves chemically in a
similar manner as sodium, potassium and rubidium. Cesium
and potassium enter into a solute complex, which participates
in ion antagonism, osmosis, permeability regulation, and
maintenance of the colloidal state in the living cell. The increase
in supplemental potassium increases the rate of excretion or
loss of cesium.

claims.subject: obscure_elements
claims.question: How was cesium discovered?
claims.answer_short: In 1860 the German chemists Bunsen and Kirchhoff identified cesium by its spectral 'fingerprint' -- the colors of light it emits when heated. Its lines were sky-blue, so they named it from the Latin caesius, 'sky blue.'
claims.answer: The element's discovery story. Cesium was discovered in 1860 by the German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, who isolated it by observing its spectral 'fingerprint' — the specific colors of light (spectral emission lines) it emits when heated. Those lines were bright blue, which is why they named it cesium, from the Latin caesius ('sky blue').
claims.verbatim:
Cesium was discovered in 1860 by the German chemists
Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff. They isolated cesium by
observing colors or spectral emission lines, that cesium emits
when it is heated. The color lines were bright blue, which
prompted them to name the element cesium after the Latin
coesius (“sky blue”).

claims.subject: ph
claims.question: Can making the body alkaline treat cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach presents cesium chloride as “high-pH therapy” — cesium enters the cancer cell and makes its interior alkaline. He says it has been recommended for all cancers, including sarcomas, bronchiogenic carcinoma and colon cancer.
claims.answer: Wallach presents cesium chloride as a cancer therapy — the basis of what's called 'high-pH therapy.' The idea: cesium enters the cancer cell and makes its interior alkaline (raises its pH), an environment hostile to the cancer. He says it has been recommended for all cancers, including sarcomas (cancers of connective or soft tissue), bronchiogenic carcinoma (lung cancer arising in the bronchi), and colon cancer.
claims.verbatim:
Cesium chloride is used as part of alternative cancer
therapy programs. Cesium provides “high pH therapy” for
cancer by entering the cancer cell and producing an alkaline
environment. It has been recommended for all cancers including
sarcomas, bronchiogenic carcinoma and colon cancer.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What is copper, and where does its name come from?
claims.answer_short: A soft reddish metal - only 0.007% of Earth's crust. Its name is Latin 'cuprum' ('from Cyprus,' where Rome mined it), and it was one of humanity's first metals.
claims.answer: The element's name and history. Copper makes up only 0.007% of the earth's crust. Its name comes from the Latin cuprum, meaning 'from Cyprus' — the Romans mined their copper on the island of Cyprus. Copper was one of the first metals humanity used: copper jewelry dating back to 9000 B.C. has been found in Iraq. Because pure copper is soft, ancient peoples alloyed it with tin to make bronze, zinc to make brass, and nickel to make monel, producing harder metals for tools and weapons.
claims.verbatim:
Despite the common use of copper, it makes up only
0.007% of the earth’s crust. Copper gets its name from the
Latin word, cuprum, which translates to “from Cyprus,” a
reference to the fact that the Romans mined their copper from
the island of Cyprus.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What is copper and why is it essential?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls copper a genuine essential nutrient for all living things — a cofactor for hundreds of metalloenzymes — and says copper deficiency is widespread and common.
claims.answer: Copper is a genuine essential nutrient for every living thing. Wallach frames it as a universally important cofactor — a helper the body's enzymes need to work — for many hundreds of metalloenzymes (enzymes built around a metal atom). He stresses that copper deficiency is widespread and common, and that copper-deficiency diseases have a real impact on human populations.
claims.verbatim:
Copper is an essential nutrient for all living organisms
and is a universally important cofactor for many hundreds
of metalloenzymes. Copper deficiency is widespread and
common and copper deficiency diseases have an important
impact on human populations.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What are the signs of copper deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists white, grey and silver hair, loss of skin pigment (vitiligo), and dry brittle hair among the first signs, alongside aneurysms, varicose veins, anemia and arthritis.
claims.answer: Wallach prints a long table of the conditions he attributes to copper deficiency — many tied to copper's role in pigment, connective tissue and blood vessels. Hair and skin: white/grey/'silver' hair, vitiligo (loss of skin pigment), dry brittle hair. Sagging and weakened tissue: ptosis (drooping eyelids, 'crow's feet,' sagging skin/breasts/belly), hernias, varicose veins, hemorrhoids, spider veins, and aneurysms (rupture-prone weak spots in artery walls) — including Kawasaki disease (congenital aneurysms with streptococcal infections). Also anemia, hypo- and hyperthyroid dysfunction, arthritis, disc disease and liver cirrhosis. Neuro-behavioral: violent behavior / blind rage / 'criminal' behavior, learning disabilities (ADD, ADHD, some autism), cerebral palsy, and aplasia/hypoplasia (underdevelopment) of the cerebellum. Copper-deficiency brain diseases across species: enzootic ataxia in sheep, Mad Cow Disease in cattle, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans. Plus elevated blood cholesterol (above 350), iron storage disease (hemosiderosis), reduced carbohydrate tolerance, and neutropenia (low neutrophil count).

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What does copper do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Copper is needed for RNA and DNA, lysyl oxidase and elastic fibers, melanin (skin and hair color), and the electron transport that powers cellular respiration.
claims.answer: Wallach lists the many jobs copper does inside cells and tissues. It's needed for RNA and DNA; for lysyl oxidase, the cofactor behind elastic fibers; for making melanin (the pigment of skin and hair); and for electron transport in the cell's respiration. Through those elastic fibers copper gives tensile strength to skin, hair, wool (poor copper makes 'steely wool' in sheep), cartilage, tendons, ligaments, the vertebral discs and blood vessels.

physiological functions: RNA, DNA, Lysyl oxidase (elastic
fiber cofactor), melanin production (skin and hair), electron

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: How was copper deficiency first shown to cause neurological disease?
claims.answer_short: In 1937, enzootic ataxia (sway back) in newborn lambs was recognized as a copper deficiency in pregnant sheep — copper supplements prevented it — an early proof that copper deficiency causes neurological disease marked by demyelination of the cerebellum and spinal cord.
claims.answer: One of the earliest proofs that copper deficiency causes neurological disease. In 1937, 'enzootic ataxia' in newborn lambs — also called sway back or lamkruis, a loss of muscle coordination — was recognized as a copper deficiency in pregnant sheep. Giving the ewes copper supplements prevented it. The disease was marked by demyelination (loss of the protective myelin sheath around nerves) in the cerebellum (the brain's coordination center) and the spinal cord.
claims.verbatim:
Neonatal “enzootic ataxia” (sway back, lamkruis) was
recognized as a clinical and disease entity in 1937 as a copper
deficiency in pregnant sheep. Copper supplements prevented
the syndrome, which was characterized by demyelination of
the cerebellum and spinal cord.

claims.subject: mad_cow_disease
claims.question: Is mad cow disease caused by copper deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach classifies Mad Cow Disease (BSE) and its human counterpart Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease as copper-deficiency diseases, because their brain lesions resemble those of enzootic ataxia, a known copper deficiency in sheep.
claims.answer: Wallach classifies Mad Cow Disease — technically Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) — and its human counterpart, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, as copper-deficiency diseases. His evidence is the brain damage itself: the lesions of BSE closely resemble those of enzootic ataxia in sheep, a long-established copper-deficiency disease.
claims.verbatim:
The brain lesions of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy
(BSE) appear to be similar to those of Enzootic Ataxia in sheep
- a copper deficiency.

claims.subject: cerebral_palsy
claims.question: What does Wallach say causes cerebral palsy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach argues cerebral palsy is a copper deficiency, saying the brain lesions of copper-deficient sheep — white-matter damage, nerve-cell death and myelin failing to form — are identical to the classic brain changes of human cerebral palsy.
claims.answer: Wallach extends the copper-deficiency argument to cerebral palsy. In sheep, copper deficiency produces a set of brain lesions — cavities or jelly-like damage in the cerebral white matter, chromatolysis (breakdown of nerve-cell structures), nerve-cell death, and myelin aplasia (myelin failing to form during fetal development). He says these congenital lesions are identical to the classic brain changes of human cerebral palsy.

Cavitation or gelatinous lesions of the cerebral white
matter, chromatolysis, nerve cell death and myelin aplasia
(failure to form during embryonic development) were also
identified as a copper deficiency disease in sheep - these
congenital lesions are identical to those of the classical changes
of human cerebral palsy.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: How common are aneurysms from copper deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says 4 to 6 of every 100 Americans autopsied died of a ruptured aneurysm, and names Einstein, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Paavo Airola, Conway Twitty and John Ritter as copper-deficiency aneurysm deaths.
claims.answer: To dramatize how common copper deficiency is, Wallach names famous people he says show its signs — mostly fatal aneurysms (weak arterial walls that balloon and burst, an elastin failure copper is meant to prevent): Albert Einstein (ruptured aortic aneurysm), Franklin D. Roosevelt (ruptured cerebral aneurysm), the nutritionist Paavo Airola (ruptured cerebral aneurysm), Conway Twitty and John Ritter (ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysms), and George and Barbara Bush (thyroid disease and white hair). He adds a striking autopsy statistic: 4 to 6 of every 100 Americans autopsied died of a ruptured aneurysm, and another 40% had aneurysms that had not yet ruptured.

Franklin D. Roosevelt (ruptured cerebral aneurysm), Paavo

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: How much copper is in the body and how much do you need daily?
claims.answer_short: A well-nourished adult holds about 80–120 mg of copper, concentrated in the brain, liver, heart and kidneys; the daily need is highest in newborns (0.08 mg/kg), dropping to 0.04 mg/kg in toddlers and 0.03 mg/kg in adults.
claims.answer: Wallach gives the body's copper content and daily needs. A well-nourished adult holds about 80–120 mg of copper total, concentrated in the brain, liver, heart and kidneys; bone and muscle hold lower percentages but, by sheer mass, store about half the body's copper. Newborns carry the highest concentrations. The daily copper requirement is highest per unit of body weight in the newborn — 0.08 mg per kilogram (mg/kg) — dropping to 0.04 mg/kg for toddlers and just 0.03 mg/kg for adults.
claims.verbatim:
The daily copper requirement for the newborn is 0.08
mg/kg; toddlers require 0.04 mg/kg; and adults only 0.03
mg/kg.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What are normal copper levels in the blood?
claims.answer_short: Average plasma copper is about 87-153 (women) and 89-137 (men) micrograms per deciliter, and ~90% of it rides on a carrier protein called ceruloplasmin.
claims.answer: Typical copper levels in the blood. Wallach gives average plasma copper as 87–153 mg/dl (women) and 89–137 mg/dl (men). About 90% of the copper in plasma travels bound to a carrier protein called ceruloplasmin.
claims.verbatim:
The average plasma copper levels of women ranges
from 87 to 153 mg/dl; for men the range is 89 to 137 mg/dl.
About 90% of the plasma copper is bound in a protein called
ceruloplasmin.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: How does copper keep arteries and veins strong?
claims.answer_short: Copper runs the enzyme lysyl oxidase that turns proelastin into elastin, so a deficiency weakens vessel walls and produces spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids and aneurysms.
claims.answer: The mechanism behind copper's cardiovascular effects. Copper activates numerous 'cupro-enzymes' (copper-dependent enzymes) that build and maintain the heart and blood vessels. In a copper-deficient pregnancy this causes congenital defects of the heart and vessels (Kawasaki disease) and of the brain (cerebral palsy, plus atresia — failure to form — and hypoplasia, or underdevelopment, of the cerebellum). Copper deficiency also lowers the activity of lysyl oxidase, the enzyme that converts proelastin into elastin; with less elastin, the walls of veins and arteries lose tensile strength — producing spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids and aneurysms.
claims.verbatim:
Copper functions as a cofactor and activator of numerous
cupro-enzymes that are involved with the development and
maintenance of the cardiovascular system. Deficiency of
copper in the pregnant female results in congenital defects of
the heart and vascular system (Kawasaki disease) and brain
(cerebral palsy, atresia and hypoplasia of the cerebellum).
Deficiency of copper also results in reduced lysyl oxidase
activity causing a reduction in conversion of proelastin to
elastin causing a decrease in the tensile strength of venous
and arterial walls (spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids
and aneurysms).

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: Can copper deficiency cause arthritis in children?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says copper deficiency weakens bone, connective tissue and muscle, and can produce a specific childhood arthritis that forms bone spurs in the growth plates.
claims.answer: Copper deficiency also weakens the body's structural framework — bone, connective tissue and muscle. Wallach says this can produce a specific childhood arthritis that forms bone spurs (bony overgrowths) in the growth plates, the zones of developing cartilage at the ends of a child's bones.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiency of copper also results in a reduced skeletal,
connective tissue and muscular integrity which can produce
a specific type of arthritis in children that forms bone spurs in
the bone growth plates.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What are the early signs of copper deficiency in babies?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the earliest signs of copper deficiency in an infant are neutropenia and leukopenia (low white blood cells), with copper lack also causing myelin defects, anemia, poorly formed hair and loss of hair color — and cow's-milk-fed infants often develop copper-deficiency anemia.
claims.answer: The earliest signs of copper deficiency, especially in infants. Lack of copper can result in myelin defects (poor nerve insulation), anemia, poor hair keratinization (poorly formed hair), and loss of hair color. In a baby, the earliest indications are neutropenia (too few neutrophils, a type of white blood cell) and leukopenia (a low total white-cell count). Infants whose diets are primarily cow's milk frequently develop copper-deficiency anemia and/or iron storage disease.
claims.verbatim:
Lack of copper can result in myelin defects, anemia,
poor hair keratinization and loss of hair color. Neutropenia
(reduced numbers of neutrophilic WBCs or white blood cells)
and leucopenia (reduced total WBC count) are the earliest
indications of a copper deficiency in an infant. Infants whose
diets are primarily cow’s milk frequently develop copper
deficiency anemia and/or iron storage disease.

claims.subject: menkes_syndrome
claims.question: What is Menkes Kinky Hair Syndrome?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes Menkes' Kinky Hair Syndrome as a sex-linked recessive genetic defect of copper absorption, causing kinky depigmented hair, stunted growth, aneurysms, growth-plate arthritis and progressive mental deterioration; he says copper and liver injections plus a celiac-type diet are useful.
claims.answer: Menkes' Kinky Hair Syndrome is the genetic disorder Wallach ties most directly to copper. He says it is thought to be a sex-linked recessive genetic defect of copper absorption. Affected infants show stunted growth, defective keratin in the hair (the 'kinky' hair), loss of hair pigment, low body temperature (low thyroid function, anemia), degeneration and fractures of the aortic elastin (aneurysms), arthritis in the growth plates of the long bones, and progressive mental deterioration — the last because the brain is left totally devoid of cytochrome oxidase, an essential copper-dependent enzyme. Because of the copper absorption problem, Wallach says injections of copper and liver extracts plus a diet program designed for celiac patients will be useful for these children.
claims.verbatim:
Menkes’ Kinky Hair Syndrome is thought to be a sex-linked recessive genetic defect of copper absorption. The affected
infants exhibit retarded growth, defective keratin formation
of the hair, loss of hair pigment, low body temperature (low
thyroid function, anemia), degeneration and fractures of aortic
elastin (aneurysms), arthritis in the growth plates of long bones,
and a progressive mental deterioration. Mental deterioration
results from brain tissue being totally devoid of the essential
copper dependent enzyme cytochrome oxidase.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What raises blood copper, and what is copper overload?
claims.answer_short: Copper roughly doubles in pregnancy and on the pill, and rises with infection, liver disease and pellagra; overload shows as copper Kayser-Fleischer rings in the eye.
claims.answer: Some situations that raise blood copper. Serum and plasma copper roughly double (increase 100%) in pregnant women and in women taking oral contraceptives (the pill), and rise during acute infections, liver disease, and pellagra (the disease of niacin / vitamin-B3 deficiency). When copper accumulates in the cornea of the eye it forms visible Kayser-Fleischer rings — a classic sign of copper overload.
claims.verbatim:
Serum and plasma copper increases 100% in pregnant
women and women using oral contraceptives. Serum copper
levels are also elevated during acute infections, liver disease,
and pellagra (niacin deficiency).

Accumulations of copper in the cornea form Kayser-Fleischer Rings.

claims.subject: rare_earth_elements
claims.question: What is dysprosium?
claims.answer_short: A soft, silvery rare-earth metal -- the 9th most abundant of the rare earths -- discovered in 1886 and named from the Greek for 'hard to get at.' Its magnetic alloys help CDs work, and in the body it collects in bone.
claims.answer: Dysprosium is a rare earth element and, Wallach notes, the ninth most abundant of the rare earths. It was discovered in 1886 by the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran while working with a sample of erbium oxide, and named from the Greek dysprositos — 'hard to get at.' It's a soft, shiny, silvery metal (soft enough to cut with a knife) that is fairly stable in air, and its magnetic alloys are used to help compact discs (CDs) work efficiently. In the body it accumulates in the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Of the rare earths, dysprosium is a metal that ranks
ninth in abundance. It was discovered in 1886 by the French
chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran who was working
with a sample of erbium oxide. It was named for the Greek
word dysprositos, which translates to “hard to get at.”

claims.subject: rare_earth_elements
claims.question: What is erbium used for?
claims.answer_short: A scarce rare-earth metal (found 1843), alloyed with vanadium to improve workability; its most memorable use is tinting glass and enamel pink -- the pink glass of sunglasses and costume jewelry. In the body it settles in bone.
claims.answer: Erbium is a scarce rare earth metal, discovered in 1843 by the Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander; in its ores it occurs as an impurity among the other rare earths. Industrially, erbium is alloyed with metals like vanadium to improve their workability, and — its most memorable use — it is added to glass and enamel to tint them pink, the pink glass being used for sunglasses and costume jewelry. In the body it concentrates mainly in bone.
claims.verbatim:
Erbium is employed in special alloys with metals such
as vanadium to improve their workability characteristics.
Erbium is frequently added to glass and enamel to tint them
pink, this glass is commonly used for sunglasses and costume
jewelry.

claims.subject: rare_earth_elements
claims.question: What is europium?
claims.answer_short: One of the rarest rare earths, isolated in 1901 and named for Europe; it is the softest of them and so reactive it bursts into flame in air above 150C. It is mined from the ores monazite and bastnasite.
claims.answer: Europium is a 'light' rare earth and one of the rarest of all the rare earth elements. It was isolated in 1901 by the French chemist Eugène-Anatole Demarçay, who named it for the continent of Europe. It is the softest of the rare earths and ignites spontaneously in air above 150°C. It occurs in the ores monazite and bastnäsite — monazite (found in the river sands of India and Brazil and in Florida beach sand) carries all the rare earths plus thorium and calcium, and large bastnäsite deposits sit in Southern California.
claims.verbatim:
Europium is one of the most-rare of the rare earth
elements. It was isolated in 1901 by the French chemist
Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who named the new element for
the continent of Europe.

claims.subject: europium
claims.question: Is europium found in breast milk?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach reports europium occurs in higher concentrations in the breast milk of women in third-world countries than in American women.
claims.answer: Wallach reports two observations about europium, a rare-earth element: europium supplementation extended the life expectancy of laboratory species by 100% over their expected lifespan; and europium is found in higher concentrations in the breast milk of women in third-world countries than in American women.
claims.verbatim:
Europium supplementation has extended the life
expectancy of laboratory species over their expected lifespan
by 100%. Europium is found in higher concentrations in breast
milk from women in third world countries than in American
women.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: What is fluorine?
claims.answer_short: The smallest, lightest and most reactive halogen ('salt former') - a pale-yellow gas so reactive it never occurs free, locked instead in minerals like fluorite.
claims.answer: Fluorine is a halogen — the family Wallach calls the 'salt formers,' which also includes chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. These elements react by grabbing electrons from other atoms and readily combine with metals to make salts. Fluorine is the smallest, lightest and most reactive of the whole family — a pale-yellow gas whose molecules pair up into two atoms (diatomic), and so reactive it never occurs free in nature; it's found instead locked in minerals like fluorite (calcium fluoride, also called fluorspar).
claims.verbatim:
Fluorine is a member of the halogen family or “salt
formers.” The other members are chlorine, bromine, iodine
and astatine. All halogen atoms react chemically by accepting
electrons from other atoms and easily combine with metals
to form compounds known as salts. Fluorine is the smallest,
lightest and most reactive member of the halogen family.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: Who discovered fluorine, and what does its name mean?
claims.answer_short: Henri Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize for first isolating pure fluorine (1886), after 75 years of effort; the name is Latin 'fluere,' to flow.
claims.answer: The element's discovery. The French chemist Henri Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize for being the first to produce fluorine in its pure elemental form — the culmination of 75 years of effort by many chemists, with Moissan finally isolating it in 1886. The name comes from the Latin fluere, 'to flow.'
claims.verbatim:
The French chemist Henri Moissan won the Nobel
Prize in 1906 for being the first to produce fluorine in its pure
elemental form. The name fluorine is derived from the Latin
word fluere, which translates to “to flow.”

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: Is fluoride an essential nutrient?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says yes in trace amounts - before 1972 it was only 'considered' essential for tooth enamel, then Schwarz proved it essential for animals and humans.
claims.answer: Wallach's stance on fluoride's essentiality. Before 1972 fluoride was only 'considered' essential in animals, based on its apparent benefit to tooth enamel in warding off cavities. Then in 1972, Schwarz proved that fluoride was in fact an essential mineral for both animals and humans. (Note: despite this, fluoride is not carried in this system's operational list of Wallach/Youngevity supplement essentials — see the full fluoride stance for why the picture is two-sided.)
claims.verbatim:
Prior to 1972, fluoride was considered essential in
animals because of its apparent benefit for tooth enamel in
warding off dental caries (“cavities”). In 1972, Schwarz proved
that fluoride was in fact an essential mineral for animals and
humans.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: How does fluoride protect teeth?
claims.answer_short: Fluoride lets the enamel-rebuilding process form fluorapatite, a version of enamel far more resistant to the acid that causes decay — which is why it's added to toothpaste.
claims.answer: How fluoride protects teeth — the mechanism behind fluoride toothpaste. Tooth enamel is made of a hard mineral, hydroxyapatite. Acids that mouth bacteria produce from sugary food and drink slowly dissolve it, and that loss of enamel starts tooth decay ('caries'). The body constantly fights back by rebuilding enamel (remineralization). When sodium fluoride is present, the rebuilt enamel forms as fluorapatite — a version considerably more resistant to acid damage than natural enamel. That acid-resistance is exactly why manufacturers add sodium fluoride to toothpaste.
claims.verbatim:
The resulting loss of the hydroxyapatite enamel


promotes the initiation of tooth decay or “caries.” One of the
body’s defenses against the breakdown of hydroxyapatite is
to generate new enamel continuously (remineralization).

In the presence of sodium fluoride, the remineralization
process manufactures a form of enamel referred to as
fluorapatite. Fluorapatite is considerably more resistant to
damage from acid than the natural enamel.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: How much fluoride is in and around us?
claims.answer_short: An adult skeleton can bank up to 2.6 g of fluoride, and the average American takes in ~4.4 mg a day from food, water, toothpaste and supplements combined.
claims.answer: How much fluoride is in and around us. The skeleton of an adult man can hold up to 2.6 grams (2,600 mg) of fluoride in reserve, and the average American takes in 4.4 mg per day from the combination of food, water, toothpaste and nutritional supplements.
claims.verbatim:
The skeletal reserves of fluoride in an adult man can
reach 2.6 gm (2,600 mg); the average daily intake by Americans
is 4.4 mg from combined sources of food, water, toothpaste
and nutritional supplements.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: At what levels does fluoride become toxic?
claims.answer_short: Wallach gives fluoride's toxicity by concentration: dental fluorosis (mottled, discolored teeth) at 2-7 ppm, osteosclerosis (abnormal bone hardening) at 8-20 ppm, and chronic whole-body toxicity when daily intake stays above 20-80 ppm for several years.
claims.answer: Fluoride's toxicity thresholds — the other side of the mineral. Wallach lays out where fluoride becomes harmful by concentration: dental fluorosis (mottled, discolored teeth) appears at fluoride concentrations of 2 to 7 ppm; osteosclerosis (an abnormal hardening/thickening of bone) at 8 to 20 ppm; and chronic whole-body (systemic) toxicity when daily fluoride intake stays above 20 to 80 ppm for several years.
claims.verbatim:
Clinical toxicity
is observed as dental fluorosis at fluoride concentrations of 2
to 7 ppm and osteosclerosis at 8 to 20 ppm. Chronic systemic
toxicity appears when the daily fluoride intake levels are
above 20 to 80 ppm over several years.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: How widespread is water fluoridation?
claims.answer_short: About 10,000 U.S. towns fluoridate water at 1 mg/L for 100 million people, reportedly cutting cavities 60-70% - but naturally high levels mottle children's teeth.
claims.answer: The scale of U.S. water fluoridation and its trade-off. About 10,000 American towns and cities — serving 100 million people — add fluoride to municipal drinking water at 1 mg/L (one part per million), which has reportedly cut dental cavities by 60 to 70%. But in certain western U.S. states there is an excess of fluoride — 10 to 45 ppm — with the visible result of mottled (fluorosis-stained) teeth in children.
claims.verbatim:
Approximately 10,000 American towns and cities
serving a total of 100 million people have added fluoride to
their municipal drinking water at the rate of 1 mg/L, which
has reportedly reduced dental caries by 60 to 70%. In certain
western states in the U.S., there is an excess of fluoride,
reaching levels of 10 to 45 ppm with a resultant mottling of
teeth in children.

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: Does fluoride cause cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites 1990 National Toxicology Program animal results in which fluoride raised precancerous oral-mucosa lesions, oral squamous-cell carcinoma, a rare osteosarcoma at double the rate in males, and thyroid and liver cancers, after Yiamouyiannis and Burk's 1977 charge of 10,000 excess cancer deaths from fluoridation.
claims.answer: The fluoride-cancer studies Wallach cites. Epidemiological work by Yiamouyiannis and Burk in 1977 led to full-scale U.S. congressional hearings over the charge that fluoridation of public water systems had caused 10,000 excess cancer deaths. The hearings ordered the U.S. National Toxicology Program to run animal studies focused on oral, liver and skeletal cancers. In 1990 those results showed, in rats, an increase in precancerous lesions of mucous-membrane cells; an increase in cancers of the oral mucous membranes (squamous cell carcinoma); a rare osteosarcoma (bone cancer) appearing at double the rate in males as in females; and increases in thyroid follicular-cell tumors and in liver cancer (hepatocholangiocarcinoma).
claims.verbatim:
In 1990, the results of the fluoride study showed an
increase in rat precancerous lesions in mucus membrane cells.
There was an increase in cancers of the oral mucus membranes
(squamous cell carcinoma). A rare form of osteosarcoma
appeared at double the rate in males as females, and there was
an increase in thyroid follicular cell tumors and liver cancer
(hepatocholangiocarcinoma).

claims.subject: fluoride
claims.question: Is fluoridated water safe?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls it 'still highly controversial' - laying out both the cavity benefit and the fluorosis, bone-fracture and cancer concerns without a flat verdict.
claims.answer: Wallach's full stance on fluoride — why it sounds both essential and dangerous, made clear. WHAT IT IS: fluoride is the most reactive halogen and, per a 1972 study by Schwarz, a nutritionally essential trace mineral for animals and humans. ITS REAL BENEFIT: fluoride hardens tooth enamel — teeth rebuild it as acid-resistant fluorapatite, which fights the cavities caused by sugar-fed mouth bacteria; that is why it's in toothpaste, and water fluoridation (~1 mg/L) has reportedly cut cavities 60–70%. ITS REAL HARMS: fluoride is also toxic above trace levels — dental fluorosis (mottled teeth) at 2–7 ppm, osteosclerosis (abnormal bone hardening) at 8–20 ppm, and chronic systemic toxicity above 20–80 ppm/day over years — and Wallach cites studies (Yiamouyiannis & Burk 1977; the U.S. National Toxicology Program's 1990 rat study) tying fluoridation to excess cancer deaths and to oral, bone (osteosarcoma), thyroid and liver tumors. HOW IT'S BOTH — the reconciliation: the dose makes the poison. Fluoride is essential only in tiny amounts (skeletal reserves in an adult man can reach 2.6 g; the average daily intake by Americans is 4.4 mg), while the harms appear at higher, sustained exposure — so 'essential in trace' and 'toxic in excess' are the same mineral at different doses, not a contradiction. ON WATER FLUORIDATION: Wallach calls it 'still highly controversial' and presents both sides — the cavity benefit versus the fluorosis, bone and cancer concerns, even noting that studies disagree on whether fluoridated water reduces or increases bone fractures. In this passage he lays out the debate and flags the toxicity/cancer evidence rather than issuing a flat yes-or-no verdict on whether you should drink it.
claims.verbatim:
The universal fluoridation of drinking water is still
highly controversial. Some studies show that fluoridated
water helps reduce fractures from osteoporosis, while other
studies showed an increase in hip fractures.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What is iron, and where does it come from?
claims.answer_short: Iron is the 4th most abundant element in Earth's crust — its ores opened the Iron Age (~1100 B.C.), and Earth's molten core is thought to be magnetized iron.
claims.answer: How abundant iron is, and its place in human history. Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust and the second most abundant metal (after aluminum); its content is responsible for most soil color, and the planet's molten core is thought to be magnetized iron. Learning to smelt iron from its red-brown ores (mainly hematite and magnetite) was a milestone that opened the Iron Age (~1100 B.C.), giving humanity tools and weapons harder than those of the earlier Bronze Age; today iron makes up about 90% of all metal extracted from ore.
claims.verbatim:
Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the earth’s
crust and is second only to aluminum as the most abundant
metal. The “core” or interior of the earth is theorized to be
made up of magnetized, molten iron.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Why does the body need iron?
claims.answer_short: Iron sits at the center of hemoglobin, where its atoms bind oxygen in the lungs and carry it to every cell.
claims.answer: Why iron is essential — it is what lets your blood carry oxygen. Iron is an essential nutrient for all land animals. Each hemoglobin molecule (the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells) is built around four iron atoms; oxygen chemically bonds to those iron atoms in the tiny blood vessels of the lungs (capillaries) and is then carried through the circulation to cells throughout the body. Iron was first recognized as an essential animal nutrient by Boussingault in the 1860s.
claims.verbatim:
Iron is an essential nutrient for all terrestrial species
of animals. It is the four iron atoms in each hemoglobin
molecule that are central to its structure and physiological
function. Oxygen actually bonds to the iron atoms in the lung
capillaries, and then are transported via the circulation to
distant cells.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Why is carbon monoxide so deadly?
claims.answer_short: Carbon monoxide binds the iron in hemoglobin ~200x more tightly than oxygen — crowding oxygen out of the blood, which is what makes it poisonous.
claims.answer: Why carbon monoxide is so deadly — it hijacks iron's oxygen seat. Carbon monoxide, a gas produced by incomplete burning of fuel, binds to the iron in hemoglobin 200 times more tightly than oxygen does. Because it clings so hard, it crowds oxygen out of the blood — which is what makes carbon monoxide poisoning dangerous.
claims.verbatim:
Carbon monoxide, a byproduct of imperfect
combustion, is bound to the hemoglobin iron 200 times more
tightly than oxygen - this phenomenon can lead to “carbon
monoxide poisoning!”

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: How much iron is in your body, and where?
claims.answer_short: A healthy adult carries 3-5 g of iron; ~60-70% is 'functional' (in hemoglobin, muscle and enzymes) and 30-40% is stored in marrow and liver.
claims.answer: How much iron your body holds, and where it sits. A healthy adult carries about 3 to 5 grams of iron, and a newborn has nearly twice as much per kilogram of body weight as an adult. Roughly 60 to 70% is 'functional' iron doing active work — in hemoglobin, in muscle's oxygen-storing pigment myoglobin, and in the cell's respiratory enzymes — while 30 to 40% is held in reserve as storage iron (as ferritin and hemosiderin in the bone marrow and liver).
claims.verbatim:
In a healthy adult human there is three to five grams
of iron, the newborn infant has nearly double the amount of
iron per kg than adults. Sixty to 70% of tissue iron is used as
essential or functional iron, and 30 to 40% as storage iron.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Is eating ice or dirt a sign of iron deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says pica (craving ice, dirt, paint, or excess food) is a specific sign of iron deficiency.
claims.answer: Pica — abnormal eating cravings — is a specific sign of iron deficiency. Wallach says the experimental evidence shows very clearly that 'pica' points specifically to a lack of iron. The pica drive can push children and adults to eat ice (pagophagia), dirt (geophagia), lead paint, excess food ('the munchies,' leading to obesity), alcohol (alcoholism), and sugar (a 'sweet tooth').
claims.verbatim:
Experimental evidence shows very clearly that
“pica” is a specific sign of iron deficiency. The pica behavior
can drive children and adults to eat ice (pagophagia), dirt
(geophagia), lead paint, excess food (“munchies,” obesity),
alcohol (alcoholism) and sugar (sweet tooth).

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What causes iron deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's list: unsupplemented pregnancy, heavy periods, chronic infection or bleeding, low stomach acid, diarrhea, and poor absorption from high-fiber diets.
claims.answer: What causes iron deficiency in the first place. Wallach lists the drivers: an unsupplemented pregnancy; painful menstruation (dysmenorrhea); chronic infections; low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, e.g. from a salt-restricted diet); chronic diarrhea; ongoing blood loss (from cancer, ulcers, parasites, blood-thinning drugs, or other nutritional deficiencies); and poor absorption (from high-fat or high-fiber diets, or celiac disease).
claims.verbatim:
Iron deficiency can be the result of unsupplemented
pregnancy, dysmenorrhea, chronic infections, hypochlorhydria
(low stomach acid from a salt-restricted diet), chronic diarrhea,
chronic bleeding (i.e. cancer, ulcers, parasites, blood thinners,
nutritional deficiencies, etc.) and impaired absorption (i.e.
high fat diets, high fiber diets, celiac disease, etc.).

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What are the symptoms of iron deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Iron deficiency brings fatigue, listlessness, palpitations on exertion, poor memory and concentration, a sore tongue, and microcytic anemia.
claims.answer: The symptoms of iron deficiency. They include listlessness and fatigue, heart palpitations on exertion, reduced thinking ability (cognition) and memory deficits, a sore tongue, cracks at the corners of the mouth (angular stomatitis), difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) with poor appetite and pica, obesity, and hypochromic microcytic anemia — the classic 'small, pale red-blood-cell' anemia of iron lack.
claims.verbatim:
Symptoms of iron deficiency include listlessness,
fatigue, heart palpitations on exertion, reduced cognition,
memory deficits, sore tongue, angular stomatitis, dysphagia
(poor appetite, pica, etc.), obesity and hypochromic microcytic
anemia.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What helps or blocks iron absorption?
claims.answer_short: Stomach acid and vitamin C boost iron absorption; fiber and phytates block it — so Wallach says the 18 mg RDA is too low for vegans and high-fiber diets.
claims.answer: What helps and hinders iron absorption — and why the standard allowance can fall short. Stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) is needed to absorb iron well, and vitamin C (ascorbic acid) increases absorption; clays and dietary fiber (phytates) reduce it. Because of that, Wallach argues the official RDA (Recommended Dietary Allowance) of 18 mg per day of metallic iron is too low for people eating high-fiber, high-phytate diets, such as vegans and vegetarians.
claims.verbatim:
Stomach hydrochloric acid is required for optimal
absorption of iron. Ascorbic acid increases the absorption of
iron; clays and dietary fiber (phytates) decrease the absorption
of iron. The RDA of 18 mg per day as metallic iron is too low
for those individuals consuming high fiber, high phytate diets
(vegans, vegetarians, etc.).

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Can you get too much iron?
claims.answer_short: Yes — excess iron can lead to liver cirrhosis, pancreatic fibrosis, diabetes and heart failure, largely by driving up the body's need for other minerals.
claims.answer: Too much iron can harm you — but Wallach says not by direct poisoning. Excess iron can lead to cirrhosis of the liver, fibrosis (scarring) of the pancreas, diabetes, and heart failure. His key point: these are not caused by iron being directly toxic — instead, the extra iron drives up the body's need for other minerals (selenium, chromium, vanadium, copper, zinc), and it is that induced shortfall that does the damage.
claims.verbatim:
Excesses of iron can result in cirrhosis of the liver,
fibrosis of the pancreas, diabetes and heart failure. These
diseases are not the direct result of toxic effects of iron, but
rather, the increased iron consumption produces an increased
need for selenium, chromium, vanadium, copper, zinc, etc.

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: What is gallium - the metal that melts in your hand?
claims.answer_short: A soft, aluminum-like metal so low-melting it liquefies from your body heat, yet has the widest liquid range of any metal; named for Gallia (the Latin name for France).
claims.answer: Gallium — the metal that melts in your hand. Gallium is in the same chemical family as aluminum and behaves much like it. It is so soft you can cut it with a knife, and its melting point is so low (29.8 degrees C, about 86 degrees F) that it turns liquid from the warmth of your hand; yet it does not boil until 2,403 degrees C, giving it the widest liquid range of any known metal. Its existence was predicted by Mendeleyev's periodic table in 1871, and Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran identified it in 1875, naming it for Gallia (the Latin name for France).
claims.verbatim:
It is an extremely soft metal that can easily be cut with a knife.
It also has an extremely low melting point of 29.8 degrees C,
allowing gallium to liquefy when it is held in the hand. Gallium
has an extremely high boiling point of 2,403 degrees C, allowing
gallium to be in its liquid form in a range greater than that of
any known metal.

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: Does gallium help protect against brain cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says gallium has specific metalloenzyme activity in the human brain and has been reported to specifically reduce the rate of brain cancer in laboratory animals.
claims.answer: Gallium and the brain — a possible guard against brain cancer. Gallium was claimed to be an essential element in 1938 and again in 1958.
