claims.question: What diseases does magnesium deficiency cause?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists magnesium deficiency diseases including asthma, anorexia, menstrual migraines, growth failure, ECG changes, neuromuscular problems, tetany, depression, muscular weakness, tremors, vertigo, and calcification of the arteries and soft tissue.
claims.answer: Magnesium deficiency diseases. Wallach lists the conditions that flow from a magnesium deficiency: asthma, anorexia, menstrual migraines, growth failure, ECG (electrocardiogram, a heart tracing) changes, neuromuscular problems, tetany (convulsions with muscle cramping), depression, muscular weakness, tremors, and vertigo -- plus calcification of the arterial wall and 'malignant calcification' of soft tissue.
claims.verbatim:
Magnesium Deficiency Diseases

Asthma
Anorexia

Menstrual migraines


 

Growth failure

ECG changes

Neuromuscular problems

Tetany (convulsions with muscle cramping)
Depression

Muscular weakness

Muscle “ties”

Tremors

Vertigo

Calcification of arterial media

“Malignant calcification” of soft tissue

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Is cholesterol really what hardens your arteries?
claims.answer_short: No — Wallach argues the real driver of arterial hardening is magnesium deficiency, not cholesterol; a lack of magnesium lets calcium deposit into the artery walls in what he calls 'malignant calcification.'
claims.answer: Magnesium deficiency, not cholesterol, as the root of arterial calcification. Wallach calls 'malignant calcification' -- calcium deposits in soft tissue, especially the middle layer (media) of the artery wall -- perhaps the most important manifestation of magnesium deficiency today. He argues magnesium deficiency, not elevated cholesterol or triglycerides, is the basic root cause of the calcium deposits that harden the arteries.
claims.verbatim:
Perhaps the most important manifestation of
magnesium deficiency in modern times is “malignant
calcification.” Malignant calcification appears as calcium
deposits in soft tissue, especially the media or middle layer of
arterial walls. Magnesium deficiency appears to be the basic
root cause of arteriosclerotic calcium deposits, not elevated
blood cholesterol or triglycerides!

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Can too much calcium cause a magnesium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains calcium and magnesium play antagonistic roles in muscle contraction — calcium the stimulator, magnesium the relaxer — and warns that an excessive amount of calcium can itself induce signs of a magnesium deficiency.
claims.answer: Calcium and magnesium balance each other. In normal muscle contraction they play antagonistic roles -- calcium the stimulator, magnesium the 'relaxer.' Wallach warns that an excessive amount of calcium can itself induce the signs of a magnesium deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Calcium and magnesium have antagonistic roles in
normal muscle contraction, calcium acting as the stimulator
and magnesium as the “relaxer.” An excessive amount of
calcium can induce signs of magnesium deficiency.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: What does magnesium actually do in the body?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's framework magnesium is required to produce and transfer energy, build proteins, contract your muscles, and fire your nerves — while too much of it can actually inhibit bone from calcifying.
claims.answer: What magnesium does -- and what too much does. Magnesium is required for producing and transferring energy, for protein synthesis, for muscle contractility and nerve excitability, and as a cofactor in a myriad of enzyme systems. Wallach also warns (his emphasis) that an excess of magnesium will cause diarrhea and inhibit bone calcification.
claims.verbatim:
Magnesium is required for the production and transfer
of energy for protein synthesis, for contractility of muscle and
excitability of nerves, and as a cofactor in a myriad of enzyme
systems. AN EXCESS OF MAGNESIUM WILL CAUSE
DIARRHEA AND INHIBIT BONE CALCIFICATION.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Why is magnesium called the source of all biological energy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach points out that magnesium is the metal atom at the heart of chlorophyll in every green plant — making it, in his words, the ultimate source of all biological energy.
claims.answer: Magnesium as the 'ultimate source of all biological energy.' Magnesium is the metal atom found in the chlorophyll of every green plant, driving photosynthesis -- the process that stores the sun's energy as the chemical 'solar currency' feeding all plants, animals, and humans. Wallach calls magnesium, the source of the deep green of plants, the ultimate source of all biological energy.
claims.verbatim:
It is also the metallic atom found in
chlorophyll of all green plants, which plays an essential role
in photosynthesis, the photochemical process that converts the
sun’s solar energy into a stored “solar currency” for a source
of chemical energy for all plants and all animals and humans.
Magnesium, the source of the deep green color of plants, is the
ultimate source of all biological energy!

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: What's the most absorbable form of magnesium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says magnesium absorption ranges from just 24% up to 85% — metallic (rock/mineral) forms are absorbed the least, while plant-derived magnesium is absorbed the best.
claims.answer: How well magnesium is absorbed. Absorption ranges from 24% to 85%: metallic sources of magnesium are absorbed least, and plant-derived colloidal mineral sources most. Vitamin D has no effect on magnesium absorption; dietary fat, phytates, and calcium reduce it; and high-performance athletes lose a considerable amount of magnesium in sweat.
claims.verbatim:
The rate of absorption of magnesium ranges from 24
to 85%. The lesser absorption rate is for metallic sources of
Mg, the higher rates of absorption are associated with plant
derived colloidal mineral sources. Vitamin D has no effect
on Mg absorption. The presence of dietary fat, phytates, and
calcium reduces the efficiency of absorption. High performance
athletes lose a considerable amount of Mg in sweat.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Can you take too much magnesium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites the magnesium RDA (350 mg/day for men, 300 for women, 450 for pregnant and lactating women) and notes that, with healthy kidneys, there is no evidence of toxicity even at supplemental doses up to 6,000 mg/day.
claims.answer: Magnesium's reference intake and safety ceiling. Wallach cites the RDA (Recommended Dietary Allowance) -- 350 mg/day for adult men, 300 mg/day for women, and 450 mg/day for pregnant and lactating women -- and notes that, with healthy kidneys, there is no evidence of toxicity even at supplemental doses up to 6,000 mg/day.
claims.verbatim:
The RDA for Mg is 350 mg/day for adult males, 300
mg/day for adult females, and 450 mg/day for pregnant and
lactating females. If the kidneys are healthy, there is no evidence
of toxicity at supplemental doses of up to 6,000 mg/day.

claims.subject: keshan_disease
claims.question: What causes Keshan disease?
claims.answer_short: A selenium deficiency. Endemic to selenium-poor Keshan Province, China, it is a heart-muscle disease (cardiomyopathy) that selenium supplementation was shown to prevent.
claims.answer: Wallach attributes Keshan disease (KSD) to a selenium deficiency. Named for Keshan Province, China, where selenium-poor soil made it endemic, the disease is a cardiomyopathy — a degeneration of the heart muscle that Wallach classes as a form of muscular dystrophy of the heart (also called 'mulberry heart disease'). He notes the World Health Organization tied the Chinese cardiomyopathy to the selenium deficiency of the local soil, and that large-scale double-blind supplementation trials confirmed selenium deficiency as the cause — supplementing children with selenium sharply cut the disease rate.
claims.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in
communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease
(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

claims.subject: cardiomyopathy
claims.question: What causes cardiomyopathy?
claims.answer_short: A selenium deficiency. Wallach calls cardiomyopathy the same disease as Keshan / 'mulberry heart' disease, and says cheap selenium can prevent it and even cure it early.
claims.answer: Wallach identifies cardiomyopathy — degeneration of the heart muscle — as a selenium deficiency disease. He equates it with Keshan disease and 'mulberry heart disease' (a heart muscular dystrophy), and points to the WHO's finding that the cardiomyopathy of Chinese children in Keshan Province was caused by the selenium deficiency of the local soil. In his view the same deficiency underlies cardiomyopathy generally — he cites it as what killed running author Jim Fixx ('a simple selenium deficiency disease') — and he holds that inexpensive selenium supplementation can prevent it and, in its early phases, even clinically cure it.
claims.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in
communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease
(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: What causes pica?
claims.answer_short: Mineral deficiency. Wallach frames pica — the craving and chewing or eating of odd non-food substances — as the body hunting for the minerals it lacks, not a vitamin, protein, or calorie shortfall; the phosphate-deficiency form he places in South Africa.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that pica is fundamentally a mineral-deficiency behavior. He describes it as a seeking or craving — with licking, chewing, and the eating of bizarre non-food substances — that has its genesis in mineral deficiencies, and he is emphatic that neither vitamin, protein, nor calorie deficiency triggers it, and that eating sugar, carbohydrate, fat, or protein will not quench it. The body is hunting for the minerals it lacks. In his survey of regional mineral-deficiency diseases, Wallach attributes the phosphate (phosphorus) deficiency form of pica specifically to South Africa.
claims.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in
communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease
(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: Where was copper deficiency common?
claims.answer_short: In Australia. Wallach notes enzootic ataxia — a copper-deficiency disease of lambs and sheep marked by poor coordination and spinal-cord lesions — was common across Western Australia, South Australia, and Victoria.
claims.answer: Wallach points to Australia as the classic home of copper-deficiency disease. Enzootic ataxia — a copper deficiency — was a common disease of Australian lambs and adult sheep from the late 19th century; it was first scientifically described in the Australian veterinary journals in 1932 and reported across Western Australia, South Australia, and Victoria. The disease is characterized by poor coordination, weakness, and demyelinating lesions in the spinal cord.
claims.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in
communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease
(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

claims.subject: phytates
claims.question: What are phytates, and which minerals do they block?
claims.answer_short: Phytic acid (inositol hexaphosphate) in whole grains and raw vegetables interferes with absorbing calcium, iron, zinc and other nutrients.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that phytates are phytic acid — chemically inositol hexaphosphate — found abundantly in whole grains and raw vegetables, and that this same compound interferes with the absorption of calcium, iron, zinc and other nutrients, making it a required nutrient on one hand and a dietary negative on the other.
claims.verbatim:
It
occurs abundantly in diets containing whole grains and
raw vegetables as inositol phospholipids and as phytic acid
(inositol hexaphosphate or “phytates”).


 

Phytic acid interferes with the absorption of calcium,
iron, zinc and other nutrients - on one hand a required nutrient
and on the other a negative in the diet.

claims.subject: phytates
claims.question: How does Wallach say to get enough calcium despite phytates?
claims.answer_short: Avoid high-phosphorus/phytate foods (raw vegetables, colas) as much as possible and supplement with plant-derived colloidal and chelated calcium.
claims.answer: Because phytate/high-phosphorus foods block calcium and make the ideal 2:1 calcium-to-phosphorus ratio unreachable from food alone, Wallach's practical answer is to avoid high-phosphorus foods such as raw vegetables (phytates) and colas as much as possible, and supplement instead with highly absorbable plant-derived colloidal and chelated calcium.
claims.verbatim:
The only
possible way to approach the 2:1 ideal is to avoid as much as
possible the food items containing high levels of phosphorous
(i.e. - raw vegetables (phytates), colas, etc.) and supplement
with plant derived colloidal and chelated calcium.

claims.subject: sugar
claims.question: Does sugar, soda, and caffeine affect my calcium and bones?
claims.answer_short: Excess sugar, carbonation and caffeine both cut calcium absorption and leach stored calcium out of the bones.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that heavy intake of sugar, carbonation, and caffeine (from coffee, tea, colas) works against calcium two ways at once: it lowers how efficiently calcium is absorbed AND pulls stored calcium back out of the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Excesses of sugar, carbonation and
caffeine from coffee, tea, colas, etc. will reduce the efficiency
of absorption and will leach stored calcium from the bones.

claims.subject: eggs
claims.question: Why does Wallach warn against eating raw egg whites?
claims.answer_short: Raw egg white contains avidin, which binds biotin in the gut; 24 raw whites can cause a biotin deficiency (cooking denatures it).
claims.answer: Wallach explains that raw egg whites contain avidin, which binds biotin in the gut and blocks its absorption -- it takes 24 raw egg whites to create a biotin deficiency, which is an argument for cooking eggs rather than eating whites raw.
claims.verbatim:
Originally biotin deficiency was
observed in chicks and rats that were fed raw egg whites, which
it was learned later, contained an “egg-white-injury” factor.

Avidin, a material found in egg white, combines with
biotin in the intestine making it unavailable for absorption.
It takes 24 raw egg whites to contribute enough avidin to
create a biotin deficiency in humans.

claims.subject: dairy
claims.question: What are Wallach's best food sources of vitamin B12, and is pasteurized milk as good?
claims.answer_short: Fresh whole milk, eggs, cheese, muscle meats, liver and kidney; pasteurized and evaporated milk lose 40-90% of their B12.
claims.answer: Wallach lists fresh whole milk, eggs, cheese and muscle meats (along with liver and kidney) as rich sources of vitamin B12, and warns that pasteurized and evaporated milk have lost 40 to 90 percent of their B12.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B,, is found in liver, kidney, fresh whole milk,
eggs, cheese and muscle meats are rich sources. Pasteurized
and evaporated milk have lost 40 to 90% of vitamin B,,.

claims.subject: butter
claims.question: Is butter or margarine better for your heart?
claims.answer_short: Wallach flips the conventional wisdom: the hydrogenated and partially-hydrogenated vegetable oils (margarine) sold as the safe substitute for butter to prevent arteriosclerosis, atherosclerosis and stroke are now known to be a direct cause of those very diseases — vindicating real butter over its processed replacement.
claims.answer: Wallach flips the conventional wisdom: the hydrogenated and partially-hydrogenated vegetable oils (margarine) once sold as the safe substitute for butter to prevent arteriosclerosis, atherosclerosis and stroke are now known to directly CAUSE those very diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated vegetable
oils, once touted by the medical trade as a safe substitute for
butter in the prevention of arteriosclerosis, atherosclerosis and
stroke, are now known to be the direct cause of these diseases.

claims.subject: butter
claims.question: How much vitamin A is actually in butter?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists butter as having 165 IU Vitamin A per teaspoon. In the same table (a USDA vitamin-A food table) margarine is listed as having the same amount when fortified, but Wallach's stance is clear: Partially hydrogenated and hydrogenated vegetable oils such as margarine (once sold as the safe substitute for butter to prevent arteriosclerosis, atherosclerosis and stroke) are in fact a direct cause of those diseases, and he tells readers to cook with butter, ghee or mutton fat instead.
claims.answer: Wallach lists butter as having 165 IU Vitamin A per teaspoon. claims.subject: beef
claims.question: Does Wallach think red meat like beef is healthy, or should I avoid it like the vegans say?
claims.answer_short: Wallach flatly rejects the vegan line — he says red meat is healthy and that every long-lived population on earth eats it. In his words, all long-lived peoples eat red meat (pork, beef, goat, lamb), plus poultry, fish, eggs and dairy, and vegans 'lie to themselves' when they insist the world's healthiest people avoid animal products. His warning is concrete: strict vegans who don't supplement minerals correctly tend, within 5 years, to develop grey hair, receding gums, periodontal disease, arthritis, osteoporosis, anemia, hypertension, chronic fatigue, even cancer and liver cirrhosis — because an unsupplemented plant diet leaves them 51 to 57 of the body's essential minerals short (plants can't manufacture minerals).
claims.answer: Wallach flatly rejects the vegan line — he says red meat is healthy and that every long-lived population on earth eats it. In his words, all long-lived peoples eat red meat (pork, beef, goat, lamb), plus poultry, fish, eggs and dairy, and vegans 'lie to themselves' when they insist the world's healthiest people avoid animal products. His warning is concrete: strict vegans who don't supplement minerals correctly tend, within 5 years, to develop grey hair, receding gums, periodontal disease, arthritis, osteoporosis, anemia, hypertension, chronic fatigue, even cancer and liver cirrhosis — because an unsupplemented plant diet leaves them 51 to 57 of the body's essential minerals short (plants can't manufacture minerals).
claims.verbatim:
Vegans as a group tend to lie to themselves and
convince themselves (and try to convince others) that all of
the long-lived people on earth do not eat animal products. In
fact all long lived peoples on earth eat red meat (including
pork, beef, goat, lamb, etc.), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy.

claims.subject: chicken
claims.question: Does Wallach think chicken and other poultry belong in a healthy diet, or should we go vegan?
claims.answer_short: Wallach is firmly against going vegan and puts chicken squarely inside a healthy, long-life diet. His core claim: every long-lived population on earth eats animal foods — red meat (pork, beef, goat, lamb), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy — and no vegan, he says, has ever lived to 100 or raised a thriving colony of healthy kids on the diet. Unsupplemented strict vegans, he warns, tend to develop grey hair, receding gums, osteoporosis, anemia, arthritis and even cancer within 5 years, and he points to vegan crusader Linda McCartney, who died at 56 of breast cancer. So poultry isn't something to avoid — it's part of what he sees as a longevity diet, not a food to apologize for.
claims.answer: Wallach is firmly against going vegan and puts chicken squarely inside a healthy, long-life diet. His core claim: every long-lived population on earth eats animal foods — red meat (pork, beef, goat, lamb), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy — and no vegan, he says, has ever lived to 100 or raised a thriving colony of healthy kids on the diet. Unsupplemented strict vegans, he warns, tend to develop grey hair, receding gums, osteoporosis, anemia, arthritis and even cancer within 5 years, and he points to vegan crusader Linda McCartney, who died at 56 of breast cancer.
claims.verbatim:
Vegans as a group tend to lie to themselves and
convince themselves (and try to convince others) that all of
the long-lived people on earth do not eat animal products. In
fact all long lived peoples on earth eat red meat (including
pork, beef, goat, lamb, etc.), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy.

claims.subject: chicken
claims.question: Is fried chicken okay to eat?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lumps commercial fried chicken in with French fries, fried seafood, high-fructose corn syrup, soft drinks and white flour as things the world's longest-lived ('Blue Zone') peoples have no access to — the frying and processing is the problem, framing fried chicken as a food of ill health.
claims.answer: Wallach groups commercial FRIED chicken with French fries, fried seafood, high-fructose corn syrup, soft drinks and white flour as things the world's longest-lived Blue Zone peoples simply have no access to — framing the frying and processing, not the chicken itself, as the food of ill health.
claims.verbatim:
One of the unintended benefits of the Blues Zones is
that they are remote and have little or no access to doctors,
pharmaceuticals, commercial French fries, fried chicken, fried
fish, fried shrimp, fried clams, high fructose corn syrup, soft
drinks, white flour, etc.

claims.subject: chicken
claims.question: How can I actually see that bone is made of both calcium and protein?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's kitchen demonstration: soak a chicken drumstick bone in a quart of vinegar for 2 weeks and the acid leaches out the calcium, leaving behind the rubbery protein matrix — showing bone is a protein framework mineralized with calcium, not solid rock.
claims.answer: Wallach offers a kitchen demonstration that bone's calcium sits in a crystal structure bound to a protein framework: put a chicken drumstick bone in a quart of vinegar for 2 weeks and the calcium is leached out, leaving the protein matrix behind.
claims.verbatim:
To extract the calcium from a bone and reveal the
protein matrix, put a chicken “drumstick” bone in a quart of
vinegar for two weeks and the calcium will be leached out of
the bone leaving the protein matrix.

claims.subject: chicken
claims.question: What can chickens teach us about human joint disease like carpal tunnel?
claims.answer_short: Wallach uses poultry as the model: arsenic plus the B-vitamin choline prevents 100% of perosis ('slipped tendon') in chickens, and the same arsenic deficiency in humans shows up as carpal tunnel syndrome, TMJ and other repetitive-motion joint diseases.
claims.answer: Wallach uses poultry as the model: arsenic plus the B-vitamin choline prevents 100% of perosis ('slipped tendon') in chickens, and the same arsenic deficiency in humans shows up as carpal tunnel syndrome, temporomandibular jaw-joint pain (TMJ) and other repetitive-motion joint diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Arsenic in combination with the B-vitamin choline
prevents 100% of perosis (“slipped tendon”) in poultry. Arsenic
deficiency in humans results in a “carpal tunnel syndrome,”
“TMJ,” and other “repetitive motion” type degenerative joint
diseases and minute traces stimulate the production of red
blood cells.

claims.subject: chicken
claims.question: How has chicken been viewed in traditional healing systems?
claims.answer_short: Relaying Taoist Chinese tradition, Wallach notes poultry (with vegetables and fish) is held to nourish the heart, lungs and kidneys, which the Tao relates to fire, metal and water respectively.
claims.answer: Relaying Taoist Chinese tradition, Wallach notes that under the Tao the heart is related to fire, the lungs to metal and the kidneys to water, and that poultry, vegetables and fish are held to nourish these organs.
claims.verbatim:
According to the Tao, the heart is related to
fire, the lungs to metal, the kidneys to water and foods that
nourish these organs include poultry, vegetables and fish.

claims.subject: chicken
claims.question: What is a pollo-vegetarian?
claims.answer_short: Wallach defines a 'pollo-vegetarian' as really an omnivore who eats poultry on top of grains, vegetables, fruit and nuts — part of his point that most self-described vegetarians actually eat animal foods.
claims.answer: Wallach defines a 'pollo-vegetarian' as really an omnivore who eats poultry on top of grains, vegetables, fruit and nuts — part of his point that most self-described vegetarians actually eat animal foods.
claims.verbatim:
Pollo-vegetarians - omnivores, who, eat poultry in
addition to grains vegetables, fruit and nuts.

claims.subject: pork
claims.question: Does Wallach think pork is healthy, or should it be avoided?
claims.answer_short: Wallach counts pork as a legitimate red meat — he points out that every long-lived people on earth eats it, so it is sound animal protein, not a food to shun.
claims.answer: Wallach classes pork as a red meat and notes that every long-lived people on earth eats it, so pork counts as legitimate animal protein rather than something to shun.
claims.verbatim:
In
fact all long lived peoples on earth eat red meat (including
pork, beef, goat, lamb, etc.), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy.

claims.subject: pork
claims.question: Why does Wallach warn against ham, bacon, and sausage?
claims.answer_short: The nitrates and nitrites cured into processed meats such as ham, bacon, and sausage act as goitrogens, interfering with normal thyroid metabolism and capable of producing thyroid disease.
claims.answer: The nitrates and nitrites in cured and processed meats such as ham, bacon, sausage, salami, pastrami and deli-meats act as goitrogens, interfering with normal thyroid metabolism and capable of producing thyroid disease.

claims.subject: pork
claims.question: Do any famously long-lived people eat pork?
claims.answer_short: Yes — and they may be the best example there is. Wallach points to the Okinawans, whom the World Health Organization ranked in 1996 as the longest-lived people in the entire industrialized world, and boiled pork is a staple of their 1,500-calorie daily diet. He puts their life expectancy at 78 years for men and 86 for women, with a documented centenarian rate of 5 per 10,000 people — and, citing the 25-year Okinawa Centenarian Study, he credits their lifestyle and mineral-rich diet, not their genes, for that longevity. Their table alongside the pork includes chicken, eggs, dried minnows, miso and fish soup, tofu, sea and garden vegetables, kelp, garlic, purple sweet potatoes and bitter melon.
claims.answer: Yes — and they may be the best example there is. Wallach points to the Okinawans, whom the World Health Organization ranked in 1996 as the longest-lived people in the entire industrialized world, and boiled pork is a staple of their 1,500-calorie daily diet. He puts their life expectancy at 78 years for men and 86 for women, with a documented centenarian rate of 5 per 10,000 people — and, citing the 25-year Okinawa Centenarian Study, he credits their lifestyle and mineral-rich diet, not their genes, for that longevity. Their table alongside the pork includes chicken, eggs, dried minnows, miso and fish soup, tofu, sea and garden vegetables, kelp, garlic, purple sweet potatoes and bitter melon.

The Okinawan diet contains an average of 1,500 calories and

claims.subject: eggs
claims.question: Are eggs a good source of vitamin B12?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists eggs among the rich dietary sources of vitamin B12, alongside liver, kidney, whole milk, cheese, and muscle meats, relevant because vegans risk B12 deficiency without it.
claims.answer: Wallach lists eggs among the rich dietary sources of vitamin B12, alongside liver, kidney, whole milk, cheese, and muscle meats, which matters because vegans risk B12 deficiency without such foods.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B,, is found in liver, kidney, fresh whole milk,
eggs, cheese and muscle meats are rich sources.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: Does the body need cobalt or vitamin B12?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says cobalt's essentiality is unusual — the body needs not cobalt itself but the cobalt complex cyanocobalamine, vitamin B12 — and a pure cobalt requirement is found only in some bacteria and algae.
claims.answer: Wallach calls cobalt's essentiality unusual: what the body requires is not cobalt on its own but a cobalt COMPLEX — the molecule cyanocobalamine, better known as vitamin B12. A requirement for pure cobalt, he says, is found only in some bacteria and algae. The need for B12 cobalt, he notes, is thought by some to represent a symbiosis: microbes build B12 out of elemental cobalt, and vertebrates — us — require the finished B12.
claims.verbatim:
The essentiality
of cobalt is unusual in that the requirement is for a cobalt

complex known as cyanocobalamine or vitamin B12. A pure
cobalt requirement is only found in some bacteria and algae
and the need for B12 cobalt is thought by some to represent a
symbiotic relationship between microbes which generate and
manufacture B12 from elemental cobalt and vertebrates that
require B12.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Has any public figure used the liquid mineral supplement?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites Nelson Mandela — sharp and animated at his 90th birthday after 27 years imprisoned — taking a liquid plant-derived mineral supplement sent from Atlanta by former UN Ambassador Andrew Young.
claims.answer: A public figure Wallach points to for the liquid supplement. Nelson Mandela was mentally sharp and physically animated at his 90th birthday in 2008 — remarkable, Wallach notes, after 27 years in a South African prison on a very low-calorie, protein-restricted diet. On his release, Mandela began drinking South African wine for its antioxidants and taking a liquid form of plant-derived minerals, sent to him from Atlanta by former UN Ambassador Andrew Young.
claims.verbatim:
Immediately upon release from prison Mandela began
to drink South African wine (a significant source of resveratrol
and polyphenols - antioxidants) and supplement with a liquid
form of plant derived minerals shipped to him from Atlanta,
Georgia by former UN Ambassador Andrew Young.

claims.subject: orac
claims.question: What is an ORAC score?
claims.answer_short: A single number rating a food's antioxidant power - the higher the score, the more free-radical damage it can absorb.
claims.answer: ORAC stands for Oxygen Radical Absorbance Capacity. Wallach calls it the universally agreed method of predicting the antioxidant power and free-radical neutralising value of foods, drink and supplements. Because it puts all three on one scale, he can set a daily point target rather than simply telling people to eat more vegetables.
claims.verbatim: ORAC is a method of measuring antioxidant capacities of various foods.

claims.subject: orac
claims.question: Who invented the ORAC test?
claims.answer_short: Scientists at the National Institute on Aging - a division of the NIH in Baltimore - working with Tufts University in Boston.
claims.answer: The ORAC test is a government-developed metric, not a supplement-industry one. It was created by scientists at the National Institute on Aging, a division of the NIH in Baltimore, working with Tufts University in Boston. The USDA went on to publish ORAC values for 277 commonly eaten foods in 2007 and a full database in 2008.
claims.verbatim:
It was developed
by scientists at the National Institute on Aging, a division of the National Institute
of Health (NIH) in Baltimore, Maryland and Tufts University, Boston, Massachusetts.

claims.subject: orac
claims.question: How does the ORAC test actually work?
claims.answer_short: A fluorescent dye is put in a tube with peroxyl radicals that destroy it; how well the food protects that dye becomes its score.
claims.answer: The ORAC assay puts a fluorescent dye in a tube with peroxyl radicals that destroy it, and scores how well a food protects that dye. The peroxyl radical is chosen deliberately: it is one of the most common reactive oxygen species found in the human body, so the test measures defence against damage that actually happens in you rather than an abstract laboratory reaction.
claims.verbatim:
The ORAC analysis, which utilizes Florescein as the florescent probe, provides a
measure of the scavenging capacity of antioxidants against the peroxyl radical, which
is one of the most common reactive oxygen species (ROS) found in the body.

claims.subject: orac
claims.question: How many ORAC points should I get a day?
claims.answer_short: 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points a day - the intake Wallach says is optimal for reaching 100.
claims.answer: Wallach's daily target is 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points, which he gives as the optimal intake for reaching the age of 100. It is a maintenance figure, not a cure, and he never presents it alone: in the same book he pairs it with cutting free-radical foods such as fried food, trans fats, burnt fat, nitrites, alcohol and sugar, taking every essential nutrient with a special focus on minerals, and a calorie-restricted diet. He is also explicit that antioxidants by themselves raise a population's average lifespan but not its maximum.
claims.verbatim:
A universally agreed upon method of predicting the antioxidant power and free radical
neutralizing value of foods, drink and supplements is the Oxygen Radical Absorbance
Capacity or ORAC value - based on current studies, we believe that the optimal total
daily intake of ORAC points to reach the age of 100 years is 20,000 to 25,000 per day.

claims.subject: orac
claims.question: Where do ORAC numbers come from?
claims.answer_short: The USDA published ORAC values for 277 commonly eaten American foods in 2007, then a full database in 2008.
claims.answer: The published ORAC numbers come from the USDA, which released an updated list of values for 277 commonly consumed American foods in 2007 and a full database in 2008. The list spans fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, spices, grains and drinks. What interests Wallach is the pattern it exposed: the correlation between high-antioxidant fruits and vegetables and better health outcomes is what ties the metric back to the free-radical theory of aging.
claims.verbatim:
In 2007, scientists with the USDA published an updated list of ORAC values for 277
foods commonly consumed by the U.S. population (fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds,
spices, grains, drinks, etc.).

claims.subject: antioxidants
claims.question: Which foods have the highest ORAC score?
claims.answer_short: Ground cloves at 314,446 and cinnamon at 267,536 - spices outscore every fruit by more than tenfold.
claims.answer: Spices dominate Wallach's ORAC table by more than tenfold over any fruit: ground cloves score 314,446 and cinnamon 267,536 per serving. Below them come black sorghum at 100,800, then the dark berries and beans that make up realistic daily intake - aronia chokeberry 16,062, small red bean 13,727, wild blueberry 13,427, peppermint 13,978, red kidney bean 13,259, pinto bean 11,864, cranberry 8,983 and artichoke hearts 7,904.

claims.subject: orac
claims.question: Is red wine actually good for you?
claims.answer_short: By ORAC, red beats white by roughly thirteen to one - Cabernet Sauvignon 5,034 against white wine's 392.
claims.answer: Wallach's ORAC table scores wine by type, and the gap is large: Cabernet Sauvignon reaches 5,034 per serving and Merlot 3,873, while rose falls to 1,005 and white wine to just 392 - roughly a thirteenfold spread between red and white. Elsewhere he explains why, describing resveratrol as a fat-soluble polyphenol antioxidant found in far greater amounts in red wine than white, and notes a sixteen-year Danish study of 13,000 people in which a daily glass of red wine was associated with a 32 percent lower risk of thrombotic stroke.
claims.verbatim:
Wine, red (Merlot) 3,873
Wine, red (Cabernet Suavignon) 5,034
Wine, rose 1,005
Wine, white 392

claims.subject: orac
claims.question: How do you pick a good chocolate?
claims.answer_short: Four ways: the percentage of chocolate, the country of origin, the ORAC value, and taste.
claims.answer: Wallach gives four ways to judge a chocolate: the percentage of chocolate in the product, the country of origin, the ORAC value, and taste. He treats dark chocolate as a genuine antioxidant food on two lines of evidence. The Kuna studies found high cocoa consumption tracked with better cardiovascular health, that urban Kuna eating less cocoa lost the advantage, and that risk factors fell again when consumption rose. And in the Engler trial, 21 people ate either high- or low-flavanoid dark chocolate daily for two weeks, with the high-flavanoid group showing significantly better function in the endothelial lining of their blood vessels.

claims.subject: free_radicals
claims.question: What do free radicals actually do to your body?
claims.answer_short: They attack your cells, cell walls and mitochondria - raising the risk of heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer's, cataracts and diabetes, and speeding aging itself.
claims.answer: Free radicals are molecules carrying an extra unpaired electron, and Wallach quotes Dr. Roy Walford calling them the great white sharks in the biochemical sea. The damage runs in steps: they attack polyunsaturated fats and cholesterol in cell membranes, producing lipid peroxides, which decompose into aldehydes that cross-link proteins, lipids and DNA. The result is membranes that stiffen, so nutrients and oxygen cannot get in and wastes cannot get out. They reach us through skin, breath, food and drink, and are also produced internally during normal metabolism.
claims.verbatim:
quench or neutralize free radicals that attack our cells, cell walls, mitochondria and
physiological processes and increase our risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer,
Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, cataracts, diabetes and aggressively speed up
the process and damage of aging itself.

claims.subject: free_radicals
claims.question: What causes age spots and liver spots?
claims.answer_short: They're ceroid lipofuscin, the pigment left behind by free-radical damage - and if you have one on the outside, Wallach says you have millions on the inside.
claims.answer: Age spots and liver spots are ceroid lipofuscin, the pigment left behind by free-radical damage - and Wallach's point is that the ones you can see are the readable surface of an accumulation happening throughout the body. It is the end byproduct of malondialdehyde attacking oxidised cell-wall and mitochondrial fats, and it builds up inside the cell's cytoplasm over a lifetime. He cites measurements of how much of a human brain cell's interior it occupies with age: roughly 35 percent at 30 to 40 years, 41 percent at 50 to 60, 55 percent at 70 to 80, and 78 percent at 90 to 100.
claims.verbatim:
Ceroid lipofuscin shows up in humans as “age spots”
or “liver spots” on the skin of the hands or face. If you have
one liver spot or age spot on the outside you have millions of
them on the inside!

claims.subject: free_radicals
claims.question: Are age spots a warning sign of something worse?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says yes - how many you have and how dark they are tracks your free-radical damage, and forecasts cataracts, heart disease, diabetes and dementia.
claims.answer: Wallach treats age spots as a readable gauge of internal damage: how many you have and how dark they are tracks your level of free-radical damage directly. He calls them a predictive barometer for cataracts, macular degeneration, coronary artery disease, diabetes, senile dementia, Alzheimer's disease and cancer. The reasoning follows from what the pigment is - the same ceroid lipofuscin is accumulating in the brain, heart, liver, lungs, bone marrow and eyes, where it cannot be seen.
claims.verbatim:
The number and intensity of pigment levels in age
spots are directly related to the level of free radical damage
and can be a predictive barometer of sinister things to come -
i.e. - cataracts, macular degeneration, coronary artery disease,
diabetes, senile dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, cancer, etc.

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: Is aging reversible?
claims.answer_short: On the aging pigment specifically Wallach says yes - and calls the belief that it can't be undone a medical dogma that is simply wrong.
claims.answer: On the aging pigment specifically, Wallach says reversal is possible, and he calls the opposite view a medical dogma that is simply wrong. His charge is that doctors and most gerontologists falsely believe accumulated ceroid lipofuscin is not preventable, removable or reversible, and he points to cell-culture, animal and human studies showing otherwise. He draws a real limit in the same chapter, though: raising antioxidant intake alone increases a population's mean lifespan, not its maximum. Clearing the pigment is not the same as extending the human ceiling.
claims.verbatim:
Fortunately, the accumulation of ceroid lipofuscin
in the brain, heart, liver, lungs, bone marrow, eyes, etc. can
easily be prevented and quickly reversed.

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: How do you reverse the aging pigment?
claims.answer_short: Cut free-radical foods hard, take every essential nutrient, and push antioxidants to 20,000-25,000 ORAC points a day.
claims.answer: Wallach's method for reversing the aging pigment has three parts: cut free-radical foods hard, take every known essential nutrient, and push antioxidants to 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points a day. The foods he names to cut are fried foods, trans fats, burnt fats, heterocyclic amines, super-heated carbohydrates, acrylamides, nitrites, alcohol and sugar. He frames the whole thing inside Clive McKay's equation - a calorie-restricted diet without malnutrition yielding a 30 to 100 percent longevity increase - where without malnutrition means every known essential nutrient at optimal levels well above the RDI, with a special focus on minerals.
claims.verbatim:
Preventing and reversing the accumulation of ceroid
lipofuscin pigments is well documented in many animal
species and humans - to accomplish this “antiaging” feat
requires a significant reduction of the intake of free radicals
(fried foods, trans fats, burnt fats, heterocyclic amines, super-heated carbohydrates, acrylamides, nitrites, alcohol, sugar,
etc.) and a significant increase in the intake of all known
essential nutrients and an extraordinary increased intake of
antioxidants (20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points/ day).

claims.subject: antioxidants
claims.question: Do antioxidants really help you live longer?
claims.answer_short: Yes for average lifespan, no for the maximum - and only in combination, never one at a time.
claims.answer: Wallach is more careful here than he is often given credit for. He says antioxidant intake alone raises a population's mean lifespan but not its maximum. What moves the 50 percent survival rate is combinations - vitamins A, C and E, selenium, the sulphur-bearing amino acids methionine, cysteine and cystine, plus catechins, resveratrol, proanthocyanins, leutines, lycopenes, flavonols and polyphenols. His clearest evidence is a fruit-fly study: engineering the flies to overexpress SOD alone, or catalase alone, changed longevity little or not at all, while doing both together raised mean and maximum lifespan by as much as 40 percent.
claims.verbatim:
Daily consumption of antioxidant rich food and drink is a universal feature of those
living in Blue Zones and in particular centenarians.

claims.subject: antioxidants
claims.question: What do the world's longest-lived people actually eat?
claims.answer_short: Dark fruits and berries, yellow and red vegetables, cocoa, red wine, green tea and coffee - every day, not occasionally.
claims.answer: The world's longest-lived people eat dark fruits and berries, yellow and red vegetables, cocoa, red wine, green tea and coffee - every day rather than occasionally. Wallach maps compound to source: lycopenes from tomatoes, leutines from green leafy vegetables, proanthocyanins from red grape skins and seeds, resveratrol from red wine, red grape juice and giant Japanese knotweed, and flavonols and polyphenols from dark chocolate, red wine and green tea. What he stresses is the constancy - seasonal variety changes with the growing season, but daily consumption of multiple antioxidant sources does not.
claims.verbatim:
In the "Blue Zones" of the world, large quantities of vitamin C, Beta carotene,
flavanols, lycopenes, leutenes, proanthocyanins, resveratrols, catechens (EGCGs) and
polyphenols are found in dark fruits and berries, yellow and red vegetables, cocoa, red
wine, green tea or coffee - these are the antioxidants that have universally been found
to be consumed daily in the Blue Zones and are known to protect the centenarians.

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: What are the four things that get you to 100?
claims.answer_short: Antioxidants, a calorie-restricted diet, mineral-rich food, and avoiding the land mines - leave any one out and Wallach says the whole thing fails.
claims.answer: Wallach's anti-aging framework has exactly four parts, and he is blunt that leaving any one out causes total failure. The four longevity pieces are the section headings of his own chapter: ANTIOXIDANTS (20,000-25,000 ORAC points a day), CALORIE RESTRICTED DIETS (1,250 to 1,800 calories, without malnutrition), MINERAL-RICH DIETS (an absolute requirement, and the piece he says a low-vitamin diet can survive but a low-mineral diet cannot), and avoiding the LAND MINES (smoking, excess alcohol, street or prescription drugs, fried foods, burnt meat, sugar). ORAC is one quarter of the answer, not the whole of it.
claims.verbatim:
The omission of any one or any part of the four longevity pieces will result in
catastrophic failure:

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: Can I actually live past 100?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says every human already has the genetic equipment for it - the reasons people don't get there are things they're doing, not things they inherited.
claims.answer: Wallach's position is that living past 100 is standard human equipment, not a lottery win. Every human, he says, has the genetic potential, the genetic equipment and the genetic capacity to live well beyond 100 - and the only reasons people do not get there are that they leave pieces of the anti-aging circuitry out of their daily lives, or they knowingly step on the land mines. He accepts there is a genetic upper limit; his argument is that almost nobody is anywhere near it.
claims.verbatim:
While there are genetic upper limits to human longevity, all humans certainly and
predictably have the genetic potential, the genetic equipment and the genetic capacity
to live well beyond 100!

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: Do I even want to live to 100?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's target isn't extra years in decline - it's reaching past 100 in a beautiful, healthful and functional way.
claims.answer: The goal Wallach states is not extra years in decline - it is reaching beyond 100 in a beautiful, healthful and functional way. That phrasing is the whole answer to the objection that a longer life just means a longer old age: the same accumulated knowledge that adds the years is what prevents the deterioration people are picturing when they say they would not want them. He frames aging as something that starts at conception and runs at a rate you influence daily, not a switch that flips at 70.
claims.verbatim:
There is an accumulated knowledge, however, that will allow each of us to prevent and
slow the aging process so that we can successfully reach beyond 100 years of age in a
beautiful, healthful and functional way.

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: Do I need good genes to live to 100?
claims.answer_short: No - and good genes won't save you either. Wallach says even if everyone in your family died at 35, you can still make it healthfully to 100.
claims.answer: Wallach dismisses both halves of the genetics excuse. Good genes will not carry you to 100 if you ignore the physiological requirements - and bad family history will not stop you if you meet them. His example is deliberately extreme: even if everyone in your family died at 35, fulfilling the requirements and avoiding the land mines can still get you healthfully to 100. He calls these physiological laws as unforgiving and predictable as gravity, and compares ignoring them to stepping off a third-storey roof without a ladder.
claims.verbatim:
On the other hand, if everyone in your family died at 35 years of age and you accurately
fulfill your physiological requirements for longevity and you avoid the land mines, you
can easily make it healthfully to 100.

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: How many years are we losing?
claims.answer_short: 20 to 25. Wallach says the industrialized world should average 95-100 years and instead averages about 75 - with America falling from 17th in the world to 48th.
claims.answer: Wallach's measure of the gap is stark: the industrialized world should be averaging 95 to 100 years, and instead averages about 75 - some 20 to 25 years short of our genetic potential. He tracks the American slide with CDC and WHO rankings: 17th in the world for longevity in 1990, down to 24th by 2000, down to a pitiful 46th by 2005, and 48th by 2008.
claims.verbatim:
the
average age of peoples in the industrialized world should
be somewhere between 95 and 100 years of age. However,
the average age of those living in the industrialized world
is somewhere around 75 years of age (give or take five
years), in fact 20 to 25 years short of our genetic potential for
longevity.

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: How many calories should I eat to live longer?
claims.answer_short: 1,250 to 1,800 a day - but only WITHOUT malnutrition, meaning every essential nutrient at optimal levels inside those calories.
claims.answer: The second longevity piece is a calorie-restricted diet WITHOUT malnutrition - a distinction Wallach says most practitioners of calorie restriction miss entirely. It is universally known to extend the life span of laboratory, pet and farm animals, and it is a common thread among centenarians both historically and in every Blue Zone today. The levels he cites are 1,250 to 1,800 calories a day, with those doing heavier physical labour at the upper end. The 'without malnutrition' half means every known essential nutrient at optimal levels, well above the RDI, in fewer calories - which is why the mineral piece and the calorie piece are inseparable.
claims.verbatim:
In most cases the caloric levels fall between 1,250 and
1,800 calories per day, with those performing more physical
labor consuming the higher calorie levels.

claims.subject: low_carb_diet
claims.question: Do low-carb high-protein diets need more minerals?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says a high-protein, low-carb diet is relatively forgiving of low vitamins but unforgiving of a low-mineral diet.
claims.answer: This is Wallach's sharpest line on why minerals outrank vitamins, and it is the third longevity piece. Mineral-rich diets are found universally across every Blue Zone and he calls them an absolute requirement to reach the centenarian club - in every case those populations have multiple sources rich in a wide spectrum of minerals. His rule of thumb: a high protein, low carbohydrate diet is relatively forgiving of a low vitamin intake, but unforgiving of a low mineral diet. Antioxidants raise your average; this is the piece that gets you to the ceiling.
claims.verbatim:
A high protein, low carbohydrate diet is relatively
forgiving of a low vitamin intake, but unforgiving of a low
mineral diet.

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: Where did the world's longest-lived people get their minerals?
claims.answer_short: Glacial milk, river silt, rock dust and wood ashes - not a supplement aisle. The ground they ate from still had the minerals in it.
claims.answer: Where the world's longest-lived populations actually got their minerals, in Wallach's list: glacial milk, river silt, rock dust, wood ashes (which he marks as universal across all Blue Zones), kelp ashes, seaweed ashes, rice straw ashes, peat moss ashes and manure ashes. None of it is a supplement aisle - it is dust, ash and silt entering the food and water supply. It is the same argument behind plant-derived minerals: the minerals reached people because the ground they ate from still had them.
claims.verbatim:
Mineral rich diets, found universally in all Blue Zones,
are an absolute requirement to reach the centenarian club. In
all cases, the Blue Zones have multiple sources rich in a wide
spectrum of minerals.

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: What will stop me reaching 100 no matter what else I do?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's land mines: smoking, excess alcohol, street or prescription drugs, fried foods, burnt meat, sugar and super-heated carbs.
claims.answer: The fourth longevity piece is subtractive - the things that will stop you reaching 100 no matter what else you do right. Wallach's land mines are smoking, drinking excess alcohol, using street or prescription drugs, not getting second medical opinions, eating fried foods (trans fatty acids), eating burnt or well-done meats (heterocyclic amines), consuming sugar and large quantities of super-heated carbohydrates (acrylamides), and indulging in high-risk behaviour. He notes an unintended advantage of the Blue Zones: they are remote enough to have little or no access to doctors, pharmaceuticals, commercial fried food, high fructose corn syrup, soft drinks or white flour.
claims.verbatim:
Land mines that will certainly prevent you from reaching
100 years of age include smoking, drinking excess alcohol,
using street or prescription drugs, not getting second medical
opinions, eating fried foods (trans fatty acids), eating burnt or
well-done meats (heterocyclic amines), consuming sugar and
large quantities of super-heated carbohydrates (acrylamides),

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: How many more years can I actually add?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calculates 25 to 50 additional HEALTHFUL years for a 150-175 lb person - and says it saves money, because cheaper food offsets the supplements.
claims.answer: Wallach puts a number on the payoff and ties it straight to cost. He calculates that a 150 to 175 pound person can add 25 to 50 additional HEALTHFUL years to their life - not years of decline - by practicing a calorie-restricted diet and faithfully following a supplement program. And it saves money rather than costing it: the reduced cost of food more than compensates for the cost of the supplements. It is the same prevent-don't-cure logic that runs through his work, and the direct rebuttal to 'I don't want to live to 150' - the years he is offering are healthful ones, and the bill is lower, not higher.
claims.verbatim:
We calculate that a 150 - 175 pound person can add
25 to 50 additional healthful years to their life with a net
savings in their cost of living by practicing a CR diet and by
faithfully employing a modified supplement program

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: How long can a person actually live?
claims.answer_short: Wallach: "who is to say we can't live to be 150, 175 or 200 - we believe we can!" He lists the four-minute mile and the moon landing as things the experts also called impossible.
claims.answer: This is Wallach's boldest statement of the ceiling. He lines up a history of things the experts swore were impossible - that our hearts would explode if we drove cars at 50 mph, that no one could break the four-minute mile (then 300 runners did within a year), that the sound barrier could not be broken, that a man would never reach the moon and return - and then asks: who is to say we can't live to be 150, 175 or 200? We believe we can. It is the direct answer to the ceiling question: antioxidants raise your average, the full program raises the maximum, and Wallach puts that maximum far past 100.
claims.verbatim:
it was believed that we would never
get a man to land on the moon and return to earth and so on - who is to say we can’t live
to be 150, 175 or 200 - we believe we can!

claims.subject: free_radicals
claims.question: How much of a brain cell fills with aging pigment as you get older?
claims.answer_short: By Adelman's data Wallach cites, ceroid lipofuscin fills about 35% of a brain cell at age 30-40, 41% by 50-60, 55% by 70-80, and 78% by 90-100.
claims.answer: Wallach cites Adelman's data on how the aging pigment ceroid lipofuscin accumulates in human brain cells with age: it fills about 35% of a cell at 30-40 years, 41% by 50-60, 55% by 70-80, and 78% by 90-100.

30 - 40  35

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: How far has American longevity fallen in the world rankings?
claims.answer_short: By CDC/WHO surveys, the US fell from 17th in the world in 1990 to 24th by 2000, 46th by 2005, and 48th by 2008.
claims.answer: Wallach tracks the US decline in world longevity rankings from CDC and WHO surveys: Americans ranked 17th in 1990, fell to 24th by 2000, 46th by 2005, and 48th by 2008.
claims.verbatim:
In a CDC (Atlanta, GA) and WHO survey in 1990,
Americans ranked 17th in the world in longevity; in the year
2000 Americans dropped in ranking to 24th in longevity; and
in 2005, Americans dropped in ranking again to a pitiful 46th,
and in 2008 Americans again dropped to 48th in the world
when it comes to health and longevity.

claims.subject: orac
claims.question: Which foods have the highest ORAC antioxidant score?
claims.answer_short: On Wallach's centenarian-foods ORAC table the pecan tops all nuts at 17,940, ahead of raspberry 6,058, strawberry 5,938 and Red Delicious apple 5,900.
claims.answer: Continuing Wallach's per-serving ORAC table of centenarian foods, the pecan stands out at 17,940 — the highest-scoring nut on his list — among a run of berries and fruits: raspberry 6,058, strawberry 5,938, Red Delicious apple 5,900, Granny Smith apple 5,381, sweet cherry 4,873, black plum 4,844, plum 4,118, gala apple 3,903 and acai 1,842. The same block also lists russet potato 4,649, black bean 4,181, and four commercial baby foods (peaches 6,257, apple-blueberry 4,822, strained applesauce 4,123 and bananas 2,658).

claims.answer_short: On Wallach's ORAC table blueberry juice leads the juices at 9,019 with prune juice at 7,291; hazelnuts reach 9,275 among nuts and raw lentils score 7,282.

claims.subject: detox
claims.question: Does selenium protect against mercury and heavy-metal poisoning?
claims.answer_short: Selenium is a direct antagonist of mercury; Wallach tells anyone exposed to it — dental amalgams, industrial pollution — to supplement selenium before, during, and after any detox.
claims.answer: Wallach singles out selenium as an antagonist of mercury: the two compete in the body, so keeping selenium up blunts mercury's toxicity. He names dental amalgams and industrial pollution as the common chronic-exposure routes, and gives a practical rule — anyone at risk should supplement selenium before, during, and after a detox, so mercury freed during the process does not do damage on its way out. It sits inside his broader case for selenium as a cornerstone mineral; he links its deficiency to conditions ranging from cardiomyopathy and muscle weakness to a raised risk of cancer.
claims.verbatim:
Selenium acts as an antagonist of mercury. Those at
risk for chronic mercury toxicity (dental amalgams, industrial
pollution, etc.) supplement with
selenium prior to, during and after detoxification activities.

claims.subject: detox
claims.question: What is EDTA chelation and where did it come from?
claims.answer_short: Calcium EDTA was invented in Germany just before WWI to antidote arsenic and lead from chemical warfare; the same agent now does IV chelation to clear obstructed arteries.
claims.answer: EDTA has a striking origin: calcium EDTA was a man-made amino acid the Germans engineered just before World War I to antidote the arsenic and lead of chemical-warfare exposure — it was born as a heavy-metal antidote. That same claw-like binding ('chelate' is Latin for claw) is why it is used today for intravenous chelation therapy to open obstructed arteries, and Wallach folds IV EDTA chelation into his programs for cardiovascular problems — poor circulation, arteriosclerosis, stroke. Do not confuse it with the 'chelated minerals' on a supplement label (a livestock-industry invention for better absorption) or with plant-derived colloidal minerals — EDTA is the therapeutic chelator that grabs metals and pulls them out.
claims.verbatim:
The original chelating agent use was calcium EDTA, a
man-made amino acid that was created by the Germans just
prior to WWI to antidote arsenic and lead exposure in chemical
warfare attacks (calcium EDTA is used today for intravenous
chelation therapy to open up obstructed arteries).

claims.subject: free_radicals
claims.question: What are free radicals and why are they dangerous?
claims.answer_short: The gerontologist Roy Walford called free radicals 'the great white sharks in the biochemical sea' — short-lived but voracious molecules that oxidize and damage tissue, especially cell and mitochondrial membranes.
claims.answer: The gerontologist Roy Walford — cited throughout Wallach's longevity work — called free radicals 'the great white sharks in the biochemical sea': short-lived but voracious molecules that oxidize and damage tissue, hitting cell membranes and mitochondrial membranes hardest. Most free radicals the body meets are oxidants — a loose electron whirling around a super-activated oxygen atom — and their 'shark attacks' on the polyunsaturated fats in those membranes produce lipid peroxides that go on to cross-link proteins, lipids and DNA. It is the vivid image behind why Wallach treats antioxidants, and the ORAC score that measures them, as essential defense.
claims.verbatim:
Dr. Roy Walford referred to free radicals as the “Great
white sharks in the biochemical sea” - these short-lived but
voracious chemicals oxidize and damage tissue, particularly
cell membranes and mitochondrial membranes.

claims.subject: antioxidants
claims.question: What are antioxidants?
claims.answer_short: Antioxidants are the body's defense against free radicals — but Wallach's key point is they can't work without minerals: your antioxidant enzymes need cofactors like selenium (for glutathione) to run at full strength.
claims.answer: Antioxidants are the body's defense against free radicals — the reactive molecules that oxidize and damage your cells, cell walls and mitochondria. Wallach's signature point is that they don't work alone: the antioxidant enzyme systems present in every healthy cell need raw materials and mineral cofactors to run at full capacity — glutathione, for example, requires selenium. So in his framework, getting the benefit of antioxidants is inseparable from getting the minerals that power them, and he measures the antioxidant strength of foods by their ORAC score.
claims.verbatim:
Antioxidant enzyme systems are normally present in all
healthy aerobic cells - remember, antioxidants also need raw
materials and mineral cofactors to operate at their optimum
capacity (glutathione requires selenium, etc.).

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Does selenium protect against mercury poisoning?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach describes selenium as mercury's natural antidote. The two minerals are mutually antagonistic, so selenium supplements protect against mercury poisoning, shielding both the kidneys and the developing fetus.
claims.answer: Wallach explains a mutual “metabolic antagonism” between mercury and selenium — each blunts the other's toxicity. In practice that means selenium supplements protect against mercury poisoning two specific ways: they guard the human kidney against the tissue death (necrosis) mercury causes, and they block mercury from crossing the placenta into the fetus — a real concern in his view, since mercury vapor off-gasses continuously from “silver” dental amalgam fillings. The antagonism runs both directions (mercury, in turn, protects against selenium overdose), but the practical upshot is that he treats adequate selenium as a frontline defense for anyone carrying mercury fillings or exposed to environmental mercury.
claims.verbatim:
Because a mutual antagonism between
Hg and Se exists, Se protects the human kidney from necrosis
(tissue death) by mercury poisoning and the placental transfer
of mercury.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Why do some people crave eating dirt, ice, or other non-food things?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties pica — the urge to eat dirt, ice, paint, hair, or wool — to zinc deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach explains pica and 'cribbing' — the compulsion to eat non-food items — as a sign of zinc deficiency. The behaviors he lists include geophagia (dirt eating), pagophagia (ice eating), and the eating of wool, hair, and paint. Rather than treating these cravings as purely psychological, he reads them as the body signaling a mineral shortfall, one that also shows up in unsupplemented athletes who lose heavy zinc in sweat.
claims.verbatim:
Pica/Cribbing (geophagia, pagophagia, wool eating,
hair eating, dirt eating, paint eating, etc.)

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: What is magnesium?
claims.answer_short: Magnesium is a mineral no living thing can do without. In Wallach's framework it switches on a vast number of the body's enzymes, carries out electro-chemical, catalytic and structural jobs, and is the metal atom at the center of the chlorophyll in every green plant.
claims.answer: In Wallach's account magnesium is a white, silvery, very lightweight metal that is essential to all living organisms. It works as a cofactor with electro-chemical, catalytic and structural roles, activating numerous enzymes throughout the body, and it is a constituent of every chlorophyll molecule -- which is why Wallach calls it the ultimate source of all biological energy. An adult body holds 20 to 28 grams of magnesium, most of it locked in bone and skeletal muscle. Wallach treats magnesium as the calcium 'relaxer' and blames a shortage for problems ranging from muscle cramps, migraines and heart palpitations to the arterial 'malignant calcification' he pins on magnesium deficiency rather than on cholesterol.
claims.verbatim:
Magnesium, as a mineral is essential to all living
organisms and has cofactor, electro-chemical, catalytic, and
structural functions. It activates numerous enzymes and is a
constituent of all chlorophylls.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: How much magnesium is in the human body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach puts total body magnesium at 20 to 28 grams in an adult, with about 60% locked in the bones and roughly a quarter in skeletal muscle.
claims.answer: Wallach states that an adult human carries 20 to 28 grams of magnesium in total, with roughly 60% stored in bone and about 26% in skeletal muscle; the rest is spread across organs and body fluids. In the blood, magnesium runs 1.5 to 2.1 mEq/L and is second only to potassium as an intracellular cation. About half of the body's magnesium — most of it bound in bone — is not exchangeable, meaning it can't be readily called on when you run short.
claims.verbatim:
The adult human contains 20 to 28 grams of total body
Mg. Approximately 60% is found in bone. Twenty-six percent
is associated with skeletal muscle and the balance is distributed
between various organs and body fluids. Serum levels of Mg
range from 1.5 to 2.1 mEq/L (a measure of electrolytes) and is
second to potassium as an intracellular cation. Half of the Mg,
including most that is bound in bone, is not exchangeable.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Why do magnesium supplements taste so bad?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says magnesium tastes so unpleasant that deficient animals crave salt instead, and will actually die of deficiency-driven seizures rather than eat a pure magnesium supplement.
claims.answer: Unlike some deficiencies, a magnesium shortfall doesn't produce a specific pica craving for magnesium itself, Wallach notes — magnesium-deficient animals instead crave and eat common salt. In fact magnesium tastes bad enough that animals will die of magnesium-deficiency-initiated seizures rather than consume a pure magnesium supplement. He adds that recovery from the deficiency can be so unpleasant that the bad taste of the needed supplement outweighs the misery of the deficiency itself.
claims.verbatim:
There is no evidence of a specific pica behavior unique
to a magnesium deficiency. Magnesium deficient animals will
crave and eat common salt. Magnesium tastes bad enough that
animals will die of magnesium deficiency initiated seizures
rather than consume a pure magnesium supplement.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: What is milk of magnesia, and what are Epsom salts?
claims.answer_short: Both are everyday magnesium remedies: milk of magnesia is magnesium hydroxide used as an OTC laxative, and Epsom salts are magnesium sulfate used as a wound disinfectant and to ease the swelling of bruises, strains and sprains.
claims.answer: Wallach points to two familiar over-the-counter products built on magnesium. Milk of magnesia is a suspension of magnesium hydroxide in water, used as an everyday laxative. Epsom salts are a hydrated form of magnesium sulfate — first found in the well water of Epsom, England in the mid-1600s — and are still used today as a wound disinfectant and to reduce the swelling and inflammation of bruises, strains and sprains.
claims.verbatim:
Milk of magnesia is a suspension of magnesium
hydroxide, Mg(OH),, in water, it is used as an everyday OTC
laxative. Another OTC remedy containing magnesium is
Epsom salts. These salts are a hydrated form of magnesium
sulfate; it was first discovered in well water from Epsom,
England in the mid 17th century. Epsom salts are still used
today as a wound disinfectant and for reducing the swelling
and inflammation of bruises, strains and sprains.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Is there magnesium in drinking water?
claims.answer_short: It can be very high: Wallach describes the Nicoyans' water in Costa Rica, filtered up through limestone bedrock, as so rich in calcium and magnesium it reportedly had to be diluted 50% just to be tested.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that water itself can be a real source of magnesium. He points to the Nicoyan water supply in Costa Rica, which percolates up through limestone bedrock and carries high levels of calcium, magnesium and other minerals. It was reportedly so hard — so loaded with calcium and magnesium — that it had to be diluted 50% with distilled water before it could even be tested.
claims.verbatim:
The Nicoyan water supply percolated up through the
Nicoya limestone bedrock and contains high levels of calcium,
magnesium and other minerals.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Where does magnesium get its name?
claims.answer_short: Magnesium is named after Magnesia, a district in ancient Greece, where its ore magnesite (largely magnesium carbonate) is believed to have first been mined.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that magnesium — a white, silvery, very lightweight metal — takes its name from its ore, magnesite (dolomite), which is primarily magnesium carbonate. That ore is believed to have first been mined in Magnesia, a district in ancient Greece. The element itself was later identified as a separate element by the British chemist Sir Humphry Davy in 1808, who used electrolysis to extract it from magnesium oxide.
claims.verbatim:
Magnesium is a white silvery metal that is very light
weight, its name is derived from the ore magnesite (dolomite)
which is primarily magnesium carbonate. Magnesite is
believed to have been originally mined in Magnesia, a district
in ancient Greece.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: How much omega-3 do I need each day?
claims.answer_short: Wallach sets the daily essential fatty acid requirement at two to three percent of calories — about five grams on a 1,500-calorie diet.
claims.answer: Wallach puts the daily requirement for essential fatty acids, which include omega-3, at two to three percent of total calories consumed. He works the example that a 1,500-calorie daily diet would call for 45 calories, or about five grams, of EFA.
claims.verbatim:
The daily requirement for the essential fatty acids is
two to three percent of the total calories consumed. A daily
diet containing 1,500 calories would dictate an essential fatty
acid requirement of 45 calories or five grams of EFA.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: How can I absorb omega-3 if my gallbladder was removed?
claims.answer_short: Wallach advises supplementing ox bile after gallbladder removal so bile salts can absorb essential fatty acids and other good fats.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that bile salts are required to absorb essential fatty acids, good fats such as triglycerides and cholesterol, and the fat-soluble vitamins. He advises that people who have had their gallbladders removed should supplement with ox bile to restore the bile salts needed for efficient absorption of these fats.
claims.verbatim:
People who have
their gall bladders removed should supplement with ox bile
to increase the availability of bile salts which are required
for the efficient absorption of essential fatty acids, good fats
(triglycerides, cholesterol, etc.) and fat soluble vitamins.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Can omega-3 prevent stroke and sudden heart death?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says supplementing omega-3 essential fatty acids reduces the risk of stroke and coronary-thrombosis sudden death — a claim the FDA long forbade sharing.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that for years the FDA ruled the evidence 'inconclusive' and made it illegal to tell people they could reduce their risk of stroke and coronary-thrombosis sudden death by supplementing with omega-3 essential fatty acids. He holds that omega-3 supplementation does lower those cardiovascular risks, and fought to win the right to say so.
claims.verbatim:
because the FDA ruled that the information was “inconclusive”
it was deemed illegal to inform people that they could reduce
their risk of stroke and coronary thrombosis sudden death by
supplementing with omega-3 essential fatty acids.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Does vitamin C help with colds?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin C has been shown to cut the rate, severity and duration of a cold by about 20% on average.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that, after much fanfare, vitamin C supplementation has been shown to reduce the rate, severity and duration of a cold on the average by 20%. So while it is not a cure, taking vitamin C can meaningfully cut how often, how badly and how long a cold hits you.
claims.verbatim:
After much fanfare, vitamin C supplementation has
been shown to reduce the rate, severity and duration of a cold
on the average by 20%.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Do smokers need more vitamin C?
claims.answer_short: Yes - cigarette smoking roughly doubles the body's need for vitamin C.
claims.answer: Wallach states that cigarette smoking increases the need for ascorbic acid (vitamin C) to about twice the normal requirement. Smokers therefore need to take in roughly double the vitamin C of a non-smoker to meet their body's demand.
claims.verbatim:
Cigarette smoking increases the need for ascorbic acid
to about twice the normal requirement.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Who discovered vitamin C and when was it isolated?
claims.answer_short: Pure ascorbic acid was isolated in 1928 by Albert Szent-Gyorgyi; in 1932 C. Glenn King reisolated it from lemons and identified it as vitamin C.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that pure ascorbic acid was first isolated in 1928 by Albert Szent-Gyorgyi, who found it in adrenal tissue, orange and cabbage and called it hexuronic acid. It was not until 1932 that C. Glenn King, at the University of Pittsburgh, reisolated ascorbic acid from lemons and identified it as vitamin C, showing it had the properties of preventing and curing scurvy in guinea pigs.
claims.verbatim:
Pure ascorbic acid was isolated in 1928 by Albert
Szent-Gyorgyi, who discovered it in adrenal tissue, orange
and cabbage and identified it as hexuronic acid. It was not
until 1932 that C. Glenn King at the University of Pittsburgh
reisolated ascorbic acid from lemons that it was identified as
vitamin C and had the properties of preventing and curing
scurvy in guinea pigs.

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Why were British sailors called limeys?
claims.answer_short: British sailors were nicknamed 'limeys' because they carried lemons on their ships to prevent and cure scurvy.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, British sailors were often called 'limeys' because they carried lemons - not limes - on their ships to prevent and cure scurvy, the vitamin C deficiency disease. The vitamin C in the citrus kept crews from developing scurvy on long voyages.
claims.verbatim:
British sailors
were oftentimes referred to as “limeys” because they carried
lemons (not limes) on their ships to prevent and cure scurvy.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: Why can't I absorb vitamin A even when I eat enough?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin A is fat-soluble, so it is absorbed with dietary fats — anything that blocks fat absorption (antibiotics, gallbladder disease, celiac disease, high-fiber diets, mineral oil) blocks vitamin A too.
claims.answer: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin, absorbed along with the ordinary dietary fats in a meal and stored mainly in the body's fat. Because of this, any health problem or habit that interferes with fat absorption also interferes with vitamin A absorption and function — Wallach names antibiotic use, gallbladder disease, celiac disease, dietary fat deficiencies, high-fiber diets, and taking mineral oil with meals.
claims.verbatim:
The fat soluble vitamins are absorbed along with other
common and essential dietary lipids and any health challenge
or health practice that interferes with the absorption of fats
(antibiotic use, gall bladder disease, celiac disease, dietary
fat deficiencies, high fiber diets, mineral oil
consumption during meals and overt deficiencies) interferes
with fat soluble vitamin absorption and function.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: What foods are highest in vitamin A?
claims.answer_short: Beef liver is by far the richest source, followed by carrots, sweet potato, spinach, and dried apricots; plants carry vitamin A as carotenoids in yellow, red, and orange pigments.
