claims.answer: Vitamin A comes both preformed in animal foods and as carotenoids in plants. The book's food table lists beef liver highest by far (about 43,900 units per 100 g), then raw carrots (11,000), baked sweet potato (8,100), cooked spinach (7,300), and dried apricots (5,500). Wallach notes vegetables carry vitamin A activity in proportion to their carotenoid content — carotene, cryptoxanthin, and other yellow, red, or orange pigments that are often hidden by the green pigment of chlorophyll.
claims.verbatim:
Vegetables were later found to contain vitamin A
activity in relation to their carotenoid content - carotene,
cryptoxanthin and other yellow, red or orange pigments that
were oftentimes hidden by the green pigment of chlorophyll.

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: How did they figure out vitamin A cures eye disease?
claims.answer_short: Animals on fat-free diets developed eye inflammation and infections that reversed with butter or cod liver oil, and in 1924 Bloch showed childhood xerophthalmia was the same disease.
claims.answer: Investigators noticed that animals kept longer on fat-free diets developed inflammation and infections of the eyes — problems that were quickly reversed when fats from butter or cod liver oil were added to the diet. In 1924 the Danish investigator Bloch showed that xerophthalmia (dry, damaged eyes) in children was the same disease described in laboratory rats in 1913, and that it could be prevented or cured by adding liver, butter, or cod liver oil to the diet.
claims.verbatim:
Investigators also noted that those animals that lived
longer on fat free diets developed inflammation and infections
of the eyes - these conditions were quickly rever sed when fats
from butter or cod liver oil were added to the diet.

In 1924, Bloch, showed that
xerophthalmia in children was the same disease described in
1913 in laboratory rats, and that the disease could be prevented
or cured by adding liver, butter or cod liver oil to their diet.

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: What does vitamin D do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin D drives intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate and, with parathyroid hormone, mobilizes calcium from bone to keep blood levels normal; it also mobilizes phosphate from bone and helps the kidney reabsorb calcium from urine.
claims.answer: Wallach lists vitamin D's core functions as stimulating the active, energy-requiring intestinal absorption of calcium and the active phosphate-transport system in the intestine. Working with parathyroid hormone, it mobilizes calcium from bone to maintain normal blood calcium levels, and it mobilizes phosphate from bone to maintain proper serum phosphate levels. It also supports the kidney's reabsorption of calcium from urine. In short, vitamin D governs how the body handles calcium and phosphorus.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin D Functions:

Stimulates the active, intestinal

absorption of calcium.

energy requiring

Stimulates the active phosphate-transport system in
the intestine.

With the parathyroid hormone, it mobilizes calcium
from bone to maintain normal blood levels of calcium.

It mobilizes phosphate from the bone to maintain
proper serum phosphate levels.

It supports reabsorption of calcium from urine by the
kidney.

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: How does the body make vitamin D from sunlight?
claims.answer_short: In the skin, sunlight or UV light drives the conversion of cholesterol into 7-dehydrocholesterol, the provitamin of vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol); UV light also converts the yeast sterol ergosterol into vitamin D2.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that cholesterol is converted by the intestinal mucosa into 7-dehydrocholesterol, the provitamin of vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol), and that the skin and other tissues also carry out this process when exposed to ultraviolet light and sunlight. Separately, ergosterol, a yeast sterol, is converted into vitamin D2 on exposure to sunlight or UV light. This is why sun exposure is a primary source of vitamin D and why cholesterol is its raw material.
claims.verbatim:
Ergosterol, a yeast
sterol, is converted to vitamin D2 when exposed to ultraviolet
light. Cholesterol is converted by the intestinal mucosa
to 7-dehydrocholesterol, the provitamin of vitamin D3,
cholecalciferol. This process is also carried out by the skin and
other tissues, when exposed to ultraviolet light and sunlight.

claims.subject: vitamin-d
claims.question: Can vitamin D prevent cancer and chronic disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites research that vitamin D deficiency raises the risk of heart attacks, breast and colon cancer mortality, and childhood type II diabetes, while adequate vitamin D may help prevent many serious chronic diseases.
claims.answer: Wallach cites Dr. Michael Holick of Boston University, who said the bottom line is that vitamin D is important for the health of both children and adults and may help prevent many serious chronic diseases. He reports Holick's finding that vitamin D deficiency in adults increases the risk of heart attacks, increases mortality in breast and colon cancer victims, raises mortality in dialysis patients, and increases the risk of type II diabetes in children. This positions vitamin D as protective against major chronic diseases, not just rickets.
claims.verbatim:
In 2006 Dr. Michael Holick, a professor of medicine,
physiology and biophysics at Boston University said, “The
bottom line is, we now recognize that vitamin D, is important
for health for both children and adults and may help prevent
many serious chronic diseases.”
Holick’s studies have shown that deficiencies of
vitamin D, in adults results in an increase in risk of heart

attacks, increased mortality in breast and colon cancer


 

victims, increased risk of mortality in dialysis patients and an
increased risk of developing type II diabetes in children.

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: Is iron from plants as good as iron from meat?
claims.answer_short: No — heme iron from meat is 10% absorbable, while iron from fresh plants is only 1% absorbable because of the plant's phytates.
claims.answer: Not all dietary iron is equal, Wallach explains: heme iron from meat is about 10% absorbable, while iron from fresh plant sources is only about 1% available, because the plants' own phytates lock it up. Absorption happens mainly in the duodenum — the first stretch of the small intestine, where the contents are still acidic — which is one reason low stomach acid worsens iron status. It underlies his caution that vegetarians are especially prone to iron deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Iron is stored in bone marrow and liver (i.e. hemosiderin
and ferritin). Heme iron from meat is 10% available for
absorption, while iron from fresh plant sources are only one
percent available because of the endogenous phytates in the
plant. Iron absorption takes place primarily in the duodenum
where the intestinal environment is still acid.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: How is calcium absorbed in the body?
claims.answer_short: Calcium is absorbed mainly in the acidic duodenum, and absorption drops as the gut turns alkaline; metallic forms may yield only 1-3%, while colloidal or chelated forms reach up to 98%.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that calcium is primarily absorbed in the duodenum while the environment is still acid, and the absorption rate falls once the intestinal contents turn alkaline. It is taken up by active cellular transport and simple diffusion, but metallic calcium absorption may be limited to one to three percent or less and is easily disrupted by other substances in the gut. Under ideal conditions calcium is highly absorbable — up to 98% in the organically bound, plant-derived colloidal and water-soluble chelated forms.
claims.verbatim:
Calcium is primarily absorbed in the duodenum, where
the environment is still acid. Once the food in the intestine
converts to an alkaline pH, the absorption rate of calcium will
decline. Calcium is absorbed from the small intestine by active
cellular transport and by simple diffusion. Metallic calcium
absorption may be limited to one to three percent or less and
can be affected by many substances in the gut. Under ideal
circumstances calcium is highly absorbable, up to 98% in the
organically bound plant derived colloidal mineral and water
soluble chelated form.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Why doesn't calcium carbonate work well as a supplement?
claims.answer_short: Calcium carbonate is a metallic mineral that is barely absorbed — you'd have to take about 25 capsules a day to actually net 2,000 mg of usable calcium.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that a 1,000 mg calcium carbonate tablet only contains 400 mg of metallic (elemental) calcium, and metallic minerals are only about 8 to 12% absorbable in the young and as little as 3 to 5% after age 35 to 40. So two 1,000 mg calcium carbonate capsules do not deliver 2,000 mg of calcium — they supply 800 mg of elemental calcium, of which roughly 80 mg is actually absorbed. To get 2,000 mg of usable calcium from calcium carbonate, he calculates you would have to take 25 capsules a day, meaning a 100-capsule bottle would last only four days.
claims.verbatim:
A typical metallic mineral supplement, either alone or
part of a multiple is calcium carbonate. Calcium carbonate can
be purchased in 1,000 mg tablets or capsules, which breaks
down to 400 mg of metallic calcium and 600 mg of carbonate.
Two 1,000 mg calcium carbonate capsules or tablets do not
give you 2,000 mg of calcium - they only supply 800 mg of
elemental calcium and at a 10% availability rate you will net
only 80 mg of available calcium. Therefore, to get 2,000 mg of
usable calcium from a 1,000 mg capsule or tablet of calcium
carbonate, you would have to take 25 capsules each day! A
100 capsule bottle of calcium carbonate will therefore only
last 4 days.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Where does the word calcium come from and who discovered it?
claims.answer_short: The name comes from the Latin 'calx' (lime), used by the Romans in the 1st century, and the metal was isolated in 1808 by Sir Humphry Davy.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that in the 1st century the Romans used a calcium compound they called calx, the Latin word for lime -- the root of the modern name. The pure metal itself was first isolated in 1808 by Sir Humphry Davy. Calcium is an extremely reactive element that is never found in pure form in nature.
claims.verbatim:
In the 1st century, the Romans used a compound of
calcium they called calx (lime) in Latin.

claims.subject: vitamin-b1
claims.question: What are the symptoms of vitamin B1 deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Mild thiamine deficiency causes mental confusion, muscle weakness, fatigue and appetite loss; chronic deficiency progresses to polyneuritis and congestive heart failure.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, mild vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency produces mental confusion, muscular weakness, peripheral paralysis, calf muscle tenderness, muscle fatigue, emotional instability, loss of appetite, loss of interest in daily tasks and general lethargy. Chronic deficiency advances to a polyneuritis and congestive heart failure with edema and life-threatening pulmonary edema. The signs therefore span both the nervous system and the cardiovascular system.
claims.verbatim:
Mild deficiencies produce mental confusion, muscular
weakness, peripheral paralysis, calf muscle tenderness,
muscle fatigue, emotional instability, loss of appetite, loss of
interest in daily tasks and general lethargy.

Chronic deficiencies of thiamine result in a polyneuritis
and congestive heart failure with edema and life-threatening
pulmonary edema.

claims.subject: vitamin-b1
claims.question: Does eating sugar and carbs use up vitamin B1?
claims.answer_short: Yes — metabolizing carbohydrates requires thiamine, while fats can be burned for energy without it, so fats 'spare' thiamine and a high-carb diet raises the need for it.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that fats spare thiamine because they can be metabolized for energy without the need for it, whereas the metabolism of carbohydrate requires thiamine. In practical terms, a diet high in sugar and refined carbohydrate increases the body's demand for vitamin B1. Fats also aid in the transport and absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
claims.verbatim:
Fats aid in the transport and absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Fats spare thiamin since they
can be metabolized for energy without the need for thiamin,
whereas, the metabolism of carbohydrate requires thiamine.

claims.subject: vitamin-b2
claims.question: What foods are high in vitamin B2 (riboflavin)?
claims.answer_short: Riboflavin is found in milk, cheddar and cottage cheese, organ meats, eggs, and green leafy vegetables.
claims.answer: Where to get riboflavin (vitamin B2): Wallach lists milk, cheddar and cottage cheese, organ meats such as liver, heart, and kidney, eggs, and green leafy vegetables — but only in small amounts, so variety matters. He adds that B2 was first spotted in 1879 as the yellow-green fluorescent pigment in milk whey, and that a shortage shows up first as soreness and burning of the lips, mouth, and tongue, along with light-sensitive, itchy eyes.
claims.verbatim:
Riboflavin is present in small amounts in milk, cheddar
and cottage cheese, organ meats (liver, heart, kidney, etc.),
eggs and green leafy vegetables.

claims.subject: vitamin-b2
claims.question: How was vitamin B2 (riboflavin) discovered?
claims.answer_short: Riboflavin was first seen in 1879 as a yellow-green pigment in milk whey, isolated in 1932, then synthesized and named in 1935 by Kuhn.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that riboflavin (vitamin B2) was recognized in 1879 as a yellow-green fluorescent pigment in milk whey, but its biological significance was not understood until 1932, when a team of German investigators isolated 'Warburg's yellow enzyme' from yeast and demonstrated that the substance was necessary for an intracellular enzyme to function. The substance was synthesized in 1935 by Kuhn, who gave it the name riboflavin.
claims.verbatim:
Riboflavin or vitamin B, was recognized in 1879 as a
yellow-green fluorescent pigment in milk whey. The biological
significance of this yellow pigment was not understood
until 1932 when a team of German investigators isolated
“Warburg’s yellow enzyme” from yeast and demonstrated
that the substance was necessary for the functioning of an
intracellular enzyme. The substance was synthesized in 1935
by Kuhn and named riboflavin.

claims.subject: vitamin-b3
claims.question: What are the symptoms of vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Early niacin deficiency brings muscle weakness, poor appetite, indigestion, and skin eruptions; severe deficiency becomes pellagra.
claims.answer: The early stages of niacin deficiency show up as muscular weakness, anorexia (loss of appetite), indigestion, and skin eruptions. Severe niacin deficiency produces classic pellagra, characterized by the '3 D's' — dermatitis, dementia, and diarrhea — along with tremors and a sore tongue ('beef tongue').
claims.verbatim:
The early stages of niacin deficiency show up as
muscular weakness, anorexia, indigestion and skin eruptions.
Severe deficiency of niacin produces classic pellagra which is
characterized by the “3 D’s” of pellagra (dermatitis, dementia
and diarrhea), tremors and sore tongue or “ beef tongue.”

claims.subject: vitamin-b5
claims.question: What is Vitamin B5?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin B5, or pantothenic acid, is a water-soluble B-complex vitamin and the core building block of coenzyme A - the molecule the body uses to turn carbohydrates, fats, and proteins into energy.
claims.answer: Vitamin B5, also called pantothenic acid, is one of the essential B-complex vitamins. In Wallach's framework it is indispensable because it forms part of coenzyme A, the molecule that runs two-carbon unit metabolism. Through coenzyme A the body requires B5 to metabolize all three major food groups - carbohydrates, lipids (fats), and proteins - which places it at the center of energy production and the manufacture of fatty acids, steroid hormones, and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Because it is water-soluble and continuously used up, it must be supplied through diet and daily supplementation; a shortfall shows up as burning feet, dermatitis, fatigue, depression, and a racing heartbeat.
claims.verbatim:
Pantothenic acid or vitamin B. is part of coenzyme A,
which functions in two-carbon unit metabolism. Pantothenic
acid is required for the metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids
and proteins.

claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: Does vitamin B6 help children with seizures or convulsions?
claims.answer_short: Some children have convulsions from an inborn error of B6 metabolism and need large daily B6 doses to make GABA and prevent permanent retardation.
claims.answer: Wallach describes a pyridoxine deficiency syndrome in mentally retarded children who also have convulsions caused by an inborn error of B6 metabolism. These children are thought to be unable to synthesize GABA, and correcting the syndrome requires daily ingestion of large amounts of B6 to prevent permanent retardation. He adds that children with cryptogenic epilepsy appearing at several years of age likewise need large oral doses of B6 to improve the EEG and control seizures.
claims.verbatim:
A deficiency syndrome for pyridoxine has been
identified in mentally retarded children that also have
convulsions due to an inborn error of B, metabolism. It is
thought that these children are unable to synthesize GABA;
correction of this syndrome requires daily ingestion of large
amounts of B, to prevent permanent retardation.

claims.subject: vitamin-b6
claims.question: When was vitamin B6 discovered?
claims.answer_short: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) was identified in 1938 as a distinct part of the B-complex, and is really a family of three related compounds.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that pyridoxine, or vitamin B6, was identified in 1938 as a separate entity within the vitamin 'B-complex.' Rather than a single molecule, B6 is a functional complex of three closely related chemical compounds: pyridoxine, pyridoxamine, and pyridoxal. Together these forms carry out the vitamin's roles in the body.
claims.verbatim:
Pyridoxine or vitamin B, was identified in 1938 as a
fraction or separate entity of the vitamin “B-complex.” Vitamin
B, is a functional complex of three closely related chemical
compounds - pyridoxine, pyridoxamine and pyridoxal.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: Why can taking folic acid be risky if you have a B12 deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Folic acid can mask a B12 deficiency — it corrects the anemia while the nerve damage silently keeps getting worse.
claims.answer: In pernicious anemia, which is caused by a vitamin B12 deficiency, folic acid will produce a marked improvement in the anemia. However, the gastrointestinal symptoms and the neurologic lesions continue to progress unchecked. Wallach calls this the 'masking effect' of folic acid, because the corrected blood picture hides the ongoing B12-related nerve and gut damage.
claims.verbatim:
In pernicious anemia (B,, deficiency), folic acid will
produce a marked improvement in the anemia, however,
the gastrointestinal symptoms and neurologic lesions will
continue to progress - this is referred to as the “masking
effect” of folic acid.

claims.subject: vitamin-b9
claims.question: How common is folic acid deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says folic acid deficiency may be the most common vitamin deficiency in humans.
claims.answer: Folacin, or folic acid, was first identified as one of many growth factors in bacteria and laboratory animals and in the prevention and treatment of anemia; it was synthesized in 1946 and quickly established as an essential nutrient for humans. Wallach states that folic acid deficiencies may be the most common vitamin deficiency in humans. The deficiency produces poor growth, megaloblastic anemia, multiple blood disorders, glossitis, and gastrointestinal tract disturbances.
claims.verbatim:
Folacin or folic acid was identified as one of many
growth factors in bacteria and laboratory animals and in
the prevention and treatment of anemia. It was synthesized
in 1946 and quickly established as an essential nutrient for
humans.

Folic acid deficiencies may be the most common

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: What is Vitamin B12?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is a red, water-soluble vitamin whose color and biological activity both come from a single cobalt atom at the center of its molecule.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework, vitamin B12 -- also called cobalamin -- is a red, water-soluble vitamin, and both its color and its function trace to a single cobalt atom held at the center of the molecule, which makes B12 the body's main way of using the essential mineral cobalt. It is a fragile compound, slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances, and about 30% of its activity is destroyed during cooking. B12 works together with folic acid to build DNA and RNA, supports the bone marrow in making red blood cells, and is needed to form the myelin that insulates nerves -- so a deficiency shows up as pernicious anemia and progressive nerve damage. Because only bacteria, fungi, and algae can actually manufacture it, B12 reaches people mainly through animal foods and supplements, and absorbing it depends on adequate stomach acid plus an acid-dependent 'intrinsic factor.'
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline substance that is water
soluble. The red color is due to the cobalt atom in the molecule.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: What is vitamin B12?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin B12 is a red, water-soluble vitamin whose color and function come from a single cobalt atom at its center.
claims.answer: Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline, water-soluble vitamin, and its red color comes directly from the cobalt atom held inside the molecule. It is a fragile compound, slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances. Because of this fragility, roughly 30% of B12's activity is destroyed during cooking, whether by electric, gas, microwave, wood, or charcoal heat.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline substance that is water
soluble. The red color is due to the cobalt atom in the molecule.
Vitamin B12 is slowly deactivated by exposure to acid, alkali,
light, and oxidizing or reducing substances. About 30% of
B12 activity is lost during cooking (electric, gas, microwave,
wood, charcoal, etc.).

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: Why do older people need vitamin B12 shots?
claims.answer_short: B12 needs an intrinsic factor plus stomach acid (pH 2.0 or less) to be absorbed, so people with low stomach acid — often from salt-restricted diets — cannot absorb it and are given B12 shots instead.
claims.answer: For vitamin B12 to be absorbed, the intrinsic factor must be present and the stomach must be acidic, at a pH of 2.0 or less. Intrinsic factor is a mucoprotein enzyme (Castle's intrinsic factor) that is part of normal stomach secretions. When a person has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid, usually from a salt/NaCl deficiency), the intrinsic factor stops working and B12 cannot be absorbed, which is why doctors frequently give B12 shots to older people on salt-restricted diets.
claims.verbatim:
Metallic cobalt itself is absorbed at the rate of 20 to
26.2% by mice and in humans if intrinsic factor is present
in the stomach and the stomach pH is 2.0 or less. Intrinsic
factor is a mucoprotein enzyme known as Castle’s intrinsic
factor and is part of normal stomach secretions. If a person
has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid- usually a NaCl
deficiency) the intrinsic factor will not work and B12 cobalt is
not absorbed - this is why doctors frequently give B12 shots
to older people on salt restricted diets.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: Can folic acid hide a vitamin B12 deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Yes — in pernicious anemia, folic acid improves the anemia but lets the nerve and gut damage keep progressing, an effect Wallach calls the 'masking effect.'
claims.answer: In pernicious anemia, which is a B12 deficiency, taking folic acid will produce a marked improvement in the anemia itself. However, the gastrointestinal symptoms and the neurologic lesions continue to progress unchecked. Wallach calls this the 'masking effect' of folic acid, because the visible improvement in the blood hides the ongoing nerve and gastrointestinal damage of untreated B12 deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
In pernicious anemia (B,, deficiency), folic acid will
produce a marked improvement in the anemia, however,
the gastrointestinal symptoms and neurologic lesions will
continue to progress - this is referred to as the “masking
effect” of folic acid.

claims.subject: vitamin-b12
claims.question: Why is vitamin B12 called cyanocobalamin?
claims.answer_short: The first B12 molecule isolated in the lab contained a cyanide group, which gave it the name cyanocobalamin.
claims.answer: The very first vitamin B12 molecule isolated in the laboratory happened to contain a cyanide group, and that is how it got the name cyanocobalamine. Several different cobalamine compounds carry vitamin B12 activity, but cyanocobalamine and hydroxycobalamine are the most active.
claims.verbatim:
The original B12 molecule isolated
in the laboratory contained a cyanide group, thus the name
cyanocobalamine. There are several different cobalamine
compounds that have B12 activity, with cyanocobalamine and
hydroxycobalamine being the most active.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: What is copper?
claims.answer_short: Copper is an essential nutrient for every living organism and a cofactor for many hundreds of enzymes; Wallach considers copper deficiency widespread, common, and behind many everyday diseases.
claims.answer: Copper is a genuine essential nutrient -- every living organism needs it. Wallach frames it as a universally important cofactor, the helper mineral that many hundreds of the body's metalloenzymes (enzymes built around a metal atom) depend on to work. Through those enzymes copper builds the pigment in hair and skin, forms the elastic fibers that give tensile strength to blood vessels, skin and vertebral discs, and helps cells use oxygen. He stresses that copper deficiency is widespread and common, and that copper-deficiency diseases have a real, under-recognized impact on human populations -- which is why he ties so many conditions, from gray hair to aneurysms, back to too little copper.
claims.verbatim:
Copper is an essential nutrient for all living organisms
and is a universally important cofactor for many hundreds
of metalloenzymes. Copper deficiency is widespread and
common and copper deficiency diseases have an important
impact on human populations.

claims.subject: copper
claims.question: Is copper oxide a good source of copper?
claims.answer_short: No, Wallach classes copper oxide as a metallic mineral that is only 8 to 12 percent absorbable, dropping to 3 to 5 percent after age 35 to 40.
claims.answer: Wallach groups copper oxide with the metallic minerals such as calcium carbonate, oyster shell and iron oxide. He says metallic minerals, despite wild claims to the contrary, are only 8 to 12 percent biologically available to younger people and drop to just 3 to 5 percent after age 35 to 40, so he treats copper oxide as a poor form of copper compared with plant-derived colloidal minerals.
claims.verbatim:
Metallic minerals, despite wild claims to the contrary
are only 8 to 12% biologically available to younger animals
and humans; after attaining the age of 35 to 40 years, the
availability of metallic minerals for humans plummets to 3 to
5%.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: What gives rubies and emeralds their color?
claims.answer_short: The radiant colors of many gems come from trace chromium — it makes rubies red and emeralds green.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, the radiant colors of many precious gems come from trace amounts of chromium. Small amounts of chromium in the form of corundum give rubies their red color, while the chromium-bearing mineral beryl produces the characteristic green of emeralds.
claims.verbatim:
The beautiful and radiant colors, of many precious gems,
are also due to the presence of trace amounts of chromium.
The red color of rubies is produced by small amounts of
chromium in the form of corundum. The characteristic green
color of emeralds is produced by the presence of the chromium
bearing mineral beryl.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Where is chromium found in nature?
claims.answer_short: Chromium occurs from about 100 ppm in igneous rocks down to trace levels in water, and in the body it accumulates in RNA and insulin.
claims.answer: Wallach describes where chromium occurs in nature, from about 100 ppm in igneous rocks and 90 ppm in shale down to trace levels in fresh and sea water, with soils ranging from 5 to 3,000 ppm (highest in soils derived from basalt and serpentine). In living tissue, he notes, chromium accumulates in RNA and insulin.
claims.verbatim:
Cr-Chromium is found in igneous rocks at 100 ppm,
shale at 90 ppm, sandstone at 35 ppm, limestone at 11 ppm,
fresh water at 0.00018 ppm, sea water at 0.00005 ppm, soils
at 5 to 3,000 ppm (highest in soils derived from basalt and
serpentine), marine plants at 1 ppm, terrestrial plants at 0.23
ppm, marine animals at 0.2 to 1.0 ppmand in terrestrial animals
at 0.075 ppm, where it accumulates in RNA and insulin.

claims.subject: chromium
claims.question: Are Americans getting less chromium than they used to?
claims.answer_short: Average American serum chromium has fallen steadily since 1948, from 28-1000 down to about 0.13 by 1985.
claims.answer: Wallach highlights a steady decline in the average American serum chromium since 1948. His figures fall from 28 (city) and 1000 (rural) in 1948 to roughly 13 in 1971, down through the 1970s, and to just 0.13 by 1985 — a dramatic collapse in the population's chromium status over a few decades.
claims.verbatim:
Of greater concern has been the steady decline in the
average American serum chromium since 1948.

Mean Chromium Blood Levels (ug/l) Year
28 (city) 1000 (rural) 1948
13 1971
10 1972
4.7-5.1 1973
0.73 - 1.6 1974
0.16 1978
0.43 1980
0.13 1985

claims.subject: potassium
claims.question: How does the body regulate potassium levels?
claims.answer_short: Adrenal-cortex hormones and the pituitary control sodium, potassium and chloride balance; adrenal failure (Addison's disease) causes potassium loss.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the balance of sodium, potassium and chloride is regulated by hormones from the adrenal cortex together with the anterior pituitary gland. In Addison's disease — a loss of adrenal-cortex function — the body can no longer retain sodium and potassium properly, producing general weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss and a marked 'salt hunger.' He notes these symptoms can be relieved by supplementing salt (NaCl) or by giving adrenal cortical hormones.
claims.verbatim:
Hormonal control of Na, K and Cl balance is regulated
by the adrenal cortex hormones as well as by the anterior
pituitary gland. Addison’s Disease, a loss of function of the
adrenal cortex, results in the loss of Na and K retention with
clinical signs of general weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss,
and a marked “salt hunger.” The symptoms can be relieved
with the supplementation of NaCl or by administering adrenal
cortical hormones (steroids).

claims.subject: potassium
claims.question: Who discovered potassium?
claims.answer_short: Sir Humphrey Davy first isolated elemental potassium in 1807 using electrolysis.
claims.answer: Potassium was first isolated in 1807 by the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy, Wallach records, who pried the highly reactive metal from its compounds using electrolysis — passing an electric current through them. He adds context that makes the element feel less abstract: the human body holds roughly 140 grams of potassium, and because a small fraction is the naturally radioactive isotope potassium-40, each of us carries a lifelong trace of internal background radiation.
claims.verbatim:
Potassium was first isolated by Sir Humphrey Davy
in 1807 using electrolysis as a means of separating elemental
potassium from its compounds.

claims.subject: iodine
claims.question: What is iodine?
claims.answer_short: Iodine is a violet-black halogen element the body needs to build thyroid hormone; run short of it and the thyroid swells into a goiter.
claims.answer: Iodine is a violet-black solid element, the heaviest and one of the most reactive members of the halogen family, found in seaweed, brine wells, and the sea. In Wallach's framework it is an essential nutrient for all vertebrates: the body combines it with the amino acid (protein building block) tyrosine to manufacture thyroxin, the main thyroid hormone that regulates metabolism, heart rate, and body temperature. When iodine runs short -- which Wallach says is common, especially since many Americans cut back on salt on their doctors' advice -- the thyroid gland enlarges into a goiter and the body slows into hypothyroidism.
claims.verbatim:
Iodine is a violet-black solid that vaporizes to give a
violet gas. It is found in sea weed and brine wells, in the sea,
in the form of inorganic salts and organic iodides. It is the
heaviest element in the halogen family and is highly reactive.

claims.subject: iodine
claims.question: Does the body absorb iodine well?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach says the metallic form of iodine is absorbed at almost a 1:1 ratio, far better than iron (1:10) or chromium (1:100).
claims.answer: Trace minerals differ widely in how well the gut absorbs them, and iodine is among the best. Wallach states that the metallic form of iodine is absorbed at a ratio of almost 1:1, compared with about 1:10 for iron and just 1:100 for chromium. He uses this to argue for taking the most efficient, absorbable form of trace-mineral supplement.
claims.verbatim:
For the metallic form of iodine the ratio of absorption
is almost 1:1; for iron its 1:10 and for chromium its 1:100.

claims.subject: iodine
claims.question: Where does the name iodine come from?
claims.answer_short: Iodine's name comes from the Greek word iodes, meaning "violet-colored," after the violet gas it forms.
claims.answer: Iodine takes its name from the Greek word iodes, meaning "violet-colored," a reference to the striking violet gas it gives off. It was discovered in 1811 by Bernard Courtois, who noticed a purple vapor rising from a sample of kelp to which he had added sulfuric acid. A drop of iodine will also turn starch, as in potato or flour, a deep blue.
claims.verbatim:
The color of the gas
determined its name, translated from the Greek word iodes,
meaning “violet-colored.” A drop of iodine will turn starch a
deep blue (potato, flour, etc.).

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Can a lack of vitamin E cause infertility or miscarriage?
claims.answer_short: Yes; Wallach lists miscarriage, fetal reabsorption, testicular atrophy and birth defects among the effects of vitamin E deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that vitamin E deficiency can directly harm reproduction. Its effects include miscarriage, fetal reabsorption, testicular atrophy and birth defects. Deficiency can also produce muscular dystrophy, hemolytic anemia, degeneration of the heart muscle (myocardial degeneration), softening of the brain (encephalomalacia) and liver necrosis. This reproductive link echoes vitamin E's discovery, which came from reversing infertility in rats.
claims.verbatim:
Additional symptoms of vitamin E deficiency include
miscarriage, fetal reabsorption, testicular atrophy, birth
defects, muscular dystrophy, hemolytic anemia, myocardial
degeneration, encephalomalacia and liver necrosis.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: How does vitamin E slow aging?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin E protects the fatty membranes of your cells from peroxidation (free-radical damage), and that protection is tied to its anti-aging effect.
claims.answer: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant that shields the lipids in cell membranes from peroxidation, a form of free-radical damage. Wallach explains that this ability to protect membrane fats from oxidation is directly related to vitamin E's anti-aging properties. In the same role it prevents oxidation damage to polyunsaturated fatty acids and protects cellular and mitochondrial membranes, helping keep cells from breaking down over time.
claims.verbatim:
The ability of vitamin E to protect membrane lipids from
peroxidation has been related to its anti-aging properties.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Do vitamin E and selenium work together?
claims.answer_short: Yes; vitamin E and selenium partner in the cell membrane, with selenium activating glutathione peroxidase to destroy peroxides before they cause damage.
claims.answer: Wallach describes a clearly demonstrated relationship between vitamin E, selenium, glutathione peroxidase, the amino acid cystine and the polyunsaturated fats in the cell membrane. Selenium activates glutathione peroxidase, which destroys peroxides after they form but before they can cause cell membrane damage. Vitamin E and selenium therefore act as partners in protecting cells from oxidative damage.
claims.verbatim:
A relationship between vitamin E, selenium,
glutathione peroxidase, cystine and polyunsaturated fats in
the cell membrane has been clearly demonstrated.

Selenium, which activates glutathione peroxidase, destroys
peroxides after they are produced but before they can cause
cell membrane damage.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Who discovered vitamin E?
claims.answer_short: Vitamin E was first identified by Evans and Bishop in 1922, when they found that infertility in rats fed vegetable-oil extracts could be reversed.
claims.answer: Vitamin E, also called tocopherol, was first identified by Evans and Bishop in 1922. They observed that infertility in rats could be reversed when the animals were fed a substance isolated from vegetable oils. The vitamin was later chemically identified in 1938. Its origin in fertility research is reflected in its very name.
claims.verbatim:
Tocopherol or vitamin E was first identified by Evans
and Bishop in 1922, when they observed infertility in rats
could be reversed when they were fed a substance isolated
from vegetable oils.

claims.subject: vitamin-e
claims.question: Why is vitamin E called tocopherol?
claims.answer_short: Tocopherol comes from the Greek 'tokos,' meaning 'offspring,' reflecting vitamin E's link to fertility and reproduction.
claims.answer: Vitamin E was chemically identified in 1938 and given the name tocopherol. The word is built from the Greek 'tokos,' which translates to 'offspring.' The name reflects vitamin E's early association with fertility and successful reproduction. This ties back to its discovery through experiments on infertility in rats.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin E was chemically identified in
1938 and named tocopherol after tokos from the Greek which
translates to “offspring.”

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: Is vitamin K important for your bones?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says vitamin K is as essential to healthy bone maintenance as vitamin D, because the vitamin K-dependent protein osteocalcin directs calcium into bone.
claims.answer: Wallach highlights osteocalcin, a vitamin K-dependent protein now known to modulate the deposition of calcium into the bone matrix. Because of this role, he states that vitamin K is as essential to healthy bone maintenance as vitamin D. In other words, calcium needs vitamin K — not just vitamin D — to be laid down properly in bone.
claims.verbatim:
The vitamin K-dependent Gla-containing protein called
“osteocalcin” is now known to modulate calcium deposition
into bone matrix - vitamin K is as essential to healthy bone
maintenance as vitamin D.

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: Do blood thinners like warfarin affect vitamin K?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says the coumarin blood thinners warfarin and dicumarol work by antagonizing (blocking) the action of vitamin K.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, the coumarin anticoagulant drugs warfarin and dicumarol prevent the blood from coagulating specifically by antagonizing the action of vitamin K. Since vitamin K is required to make the clotting proteins, blocking it thins the blood. This is why these drugs and vitamin K work in direct opposition to each other.
claims.verbatim:
The coumarin anticoagulant drugs (warfarin and
dicumarol) act to prevent coagulation by antagonizing the
action of vitamin K.

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: Is vitamin K deficiency common?
claims.answer_short: No — Wallach says vitamin K deficiency is uncommon, except with a diet low in green leafy vegetables, antibiotic-suppressed gut flora, or a fat-absorption problem.
claims.answer: Wallach considers vitamin K deficiency uncommon. It tends to occur only when the diet is low in green leafy vegetables, when the growth of intestinal flora has been inhibited by antibiotics, or when there is a fat-absorption problem. Because gut bacteria make much of our vitamin K and the vitamin is fat-soluble, both antibiotics and poor fat absorption can quietly cause a shortage.
claims.verbatim:
The deficiency of vitamin K is uncommon except when
an individuals diet is low in green leafy vegetables

claims.subject: vitamin-k
claims.question: How was vitamin K discovered?
claims.answer_short: In 1935 the researcher Dam observed a fatal bleeding disease in chicks on a complete diet that was cured when hog liver fat or alfalfa was added, revealing the missing clotting nutrient.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in 1935, Dam in Copenhagen observed a fatal hemorrhagic (bleeding) disease in newly hatched chickens fed a laboratory diet that contained all of the then-known essential nutrients. When hog liver fat extract or alfalfa was added to the diet, normal clotting time was restored. This revealed a previously unrecognized fat-soluble nutrient — vitamin K — that blood needs in order to clot.
claims.verbatim:
In 1935, Dam in Copenhagen observed a fatal hemorrhagic
disease in newly hatched chickens fed a laboratory diet that
contained all of the known essential nutrients. When hog liver
fat extract or alfalfa was added to the diet normal clotting time
was restored.

claims.subject: biotin
claims.question: Can low biotin cause hair loss and gray hair?
claims.answer_short: Yes; biotin deficiency causes a progressive loss of both hair and hair color, along with skin lesions and nerve symptoms.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework a biotin deficiency in humans produces a progressive loss of both hair and hair color. Alongside the hair changes he describes skin lesions over the nose and mouth, depression, hyperesthesia and paresthesia (especially in the extremities), muscle pain, conjunctivitis, and blepharitis.
claims.verbatim:
Symptoms of biotin deficiency in humans include skin
lesions over the nose and mouth, depression, hyperesthesia
and _ paresthesia particularly over the extremities, muscle
pain, conjunctivitis, blepharitis and a progressive loss of hair

and hair color.

claims.subject: biotin
claims.question: When was biotin discovered, and what else is it called?
claims.answer_short: Biotin - also called vitamin H or coenzyme R - was first isolated in 1936 and synthesized in 1943.
claims.answer: Biotin, also known as vitamin H or coenzyme R, was first isolated in 1936 and synthesized in 1943. Its deficiency was originally observed in chicks and rats fed raw egg whites, which were later found to contain an egg-white-injury factor.
claims.verbatim:
Biotin or vitamin H (coenzyme R) was first isolated in
1936 and synthesized in 1943.

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: What is choline?
claims.answer_short: Choline is an essential, vitamin-like nutrient the body cannot make in sufficient amounts on its own, needed to build cell membranes, carry fat out of the liver, and form the nerve-signal acetylcholine.
claims.answer: Choline is an essential nutrient with a vitamin-like coenzyme function that Wallach groups among the water-soluble vitamins. It has been recognized as essential for more than a hundred years. Choline serves as a structural building block of all cell membranes, plasma lipoproteins and lung surfactant, and in the nervous system it forms sphingomyelin and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. It also carries fat out of the liver, so a shortage leads to a fatty liver. The body can make some choline from the amino acids methionine or serine with vitamin B12 and folate, but not enough to meet daily needs, which is why it must be supplied through diet or supplements.
claims.verbatim:
Choline has been known for more than 100 years as
being essential and it has a vitamin-like coenzyme function.

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: What is choline?
claims.answer_short: Choline is an essential nutrient with a vitamin-like coenzyme function that has been recognized as essential for over a hundred years.
claims.answer: Choline is an essential nutrient that has been known to be essential for more than a hundred years, and it acts with a vitamin-like coenzyme function. Wallach counts it among the nutrients the body must obtain because, although the body can make some of it internally, it cannot make enough to meet daily needs.
claims.verbatim:
Choline has been known for more than 100 years as
being essential and it has a vitamin-like coenzyme function.

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: Is choline a vitamin?
claims.answer_short: Wallach groups choline with the water-soluble vitamins, alongside the B-complex, biotin and vitamin C.
claims.answer: Wallach classifies choline as a water-soluble vitamin, placing it in the same group as the B-complex vitamins, biotin and vitamin C. He describes water-soluble vitamins as essential nutrients that function in the metabolic processes of all living cells.
claims.verbatim:
2) Water soluble - B-complex, biotin, choline and
vitamin C - Water soluble vitamins consists of 10 separate
water soluble B vitamins and vitamin C.

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: How does choline help the brain and nerves?
claims.answer_short: Choline builds sphingomyelin in the brain and peripheral nerves and is the precursor for acetylcholine, so it is involved in transmitting nerve impulses.
claims.answer: Choline is a component of the phospholipid sphingomyelin, an important part of the brain and peripheral nerves. Because it is a precursor for the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, choline is directly involved in the transmission of nerve impulses.
claims.verbatim:
Choline is also a component of another phospholipid,
sphingomyelin, which is an important component of the
brain and peripheral nerves. As a precursor for acetylcholine,
choline is involved in the transmission of nerve impulses.

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: Does choline affect the liver?
claims.answer_short: Choline transports fat out of the liver, so a deficiency lets fat build up as a fatty liver that in severe cases can require a liver transplant.
claims.answer: Choline is part of fat metabolism and the transport of fat out of the liver, so a deficiency can result in a fatty liver. Working through phospholipids, it carries triglycerides and forms lecithin in the liver, a process that removes fatty acids from the liver's glycerides and lowers the triglyceride level. Wallach warns that in a severe form, choline-deficient fatty liver can land a person on a liver transplant list.
claims.verbatim:
The function of choline in humans is part of the
metabolism of and in the transport of fat from the liver. A
deficiency of choline can result ina fatty liver. Asa component
of phospholipids, choline functions in triglyceride transport
and in cell membrane structure. In the liver, choline forms
lecithin (phosphatidyl choline). During this process, fatty
acids are removed from the glycerides of the liver, thus
reducing the triglyceride level.

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: Can the body make its own choline?
claims.answer_short: The body can make some choline from methionine or serine with vitamin B12 and folate, but not enough to meet daily needs, so it must come from the diet.
claims.answer: The body can synthesize choline from the amino acids methionine or serine, a process that requires vitamin B12 and folacin (folate). However, the rate of that internal synthesis is too slow to meet daily requirements, which is exactly why Wallach counts choline as an essential nutrient that must be supplied.
claims.verbatim:
Man can synthesize choline from the amino acids methionine
or serine in the presence of vitamin B,, and folacin. The rate at
which choline can be synthesized is insufficient to meet daily
requirements and for this reason it is considered an essential
nutrient.

claims.subject: choline
claims.question: Can choline help tardive dyskinesia or Huntington's disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says large doses of choline have proved beneficial for managing and easing the symptoms of tardive dyskinesia and Huntington's disease in humans.
claims.answer: Because choline is a raw material for acetylcholine — a key nerve-signaling chemical — and a building block of the brain's and nerves' insulating sphingomyelin, Wallach reports it has real value in movement disorders. Large doses of choline, he says, have proven beneficial for managing and easing the symptoms of tardive dyskinesia (the involuntary movements that can follow long-term drug use) and of Huntington's disease in people. He notes, too, that a choline shortage produces a 'fatty liver.'
claims.verbatim:
Large
doses of choline have proved to be beneficial for managing
and alleviating the symptoms of tardive dyskinesia and
Huntington’s disease in humans.

claims.subject: inositol
claims.question: Where is inositol found in the body and why is it called muscle sugar?
claims.answer_short: Myoinositol, nicknamed "muscle sugar," resembles glucose and is concentrated in the brain, cerebrospinal fluid, muscle, heart, and especially the male reproductive organs and semen.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that myoinositol — nicknamed "muscle sugar" — has a chemical structure resembling glucose and is concentrated in the brain, cerebrospinal fluid, skeletal muscle, heart muscle and other tissues. Free inositol reaches especially high levels in the organs of the male reproductive tract, particularly in semen.
claims.verbatim:
Myoinositol, “muscle sugar,” has a chemical structure
that resembles glucose and is concentrated in the brain,
cerebrospinal fluid, skeletal muscle, heart muscle and other
tissues. Free inositol is found in especially high levels in the
organs of the male reproductive tract, particularly in semen.

claims.subject: inositol
claims.question: What foods are high in inositol?
claims.answer_short: Inositol occurs abundantly in whole grains and raw vegetables, present as inositol phospholipids and phytic acid.
claims.answer: Inositol — recognized as a vitamin in 1940 — is plentiful in whole grains and raw vegetables, Wallach notes, where it occurs both as inositol phospholipids and as phytic acid (inositol hexaphosphate, the 'phytates'). He flags the double edge: the very phytic acid that carries inositol also binds calcium, iron, and zinc in the gut and blocks their absorption, so what is a nutrient in one sense is an anti-nutrient in another.
claims.verbatim:
Inositol was identified as a vitamin in 1940. It
occurs abundantly in diets containing whole grains and
raw vegetables as inositol phospholipids and as phytic acid
(inositol hexaphosphate or “phytates”).

claims.subject: inositol
claims.question: Can inositol help diabetic neuropathy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says inositol has been shown to have a therapeutic role in diabetic neuropathy.
claims.answer: Wallach states that inositol has been shown to have a therapeutic role in diabetic neuropathy — the nerve damage that develops in diabetics. He also notes that a deficiency of inositol will produce pathological fatty liver disease.
claims.verbatim:
Inositol has been shown to have a therapeutic role in
diabetic neuropathy.

Deficiencies of inositol will produce pathological fatty
liver disease.

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: How do flavonoids improve blood flow?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says flavanols in dark chocolate strengthen capillaries and boost nitric oxide, which relaxes blood-vessel muscle to lower blood pressure and improve blood flow.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that flavanols found in dark chocolate help maintain the strength of capillaries, lower blood pressure, and improve blood flow by increasing production of nitric oxide — a molecule the vascular endothelium uses to signal the surrounding muscle to relax. He adds that these flavanols also carry vitamin C-like functions in the body.
claims.verbatim:
Flavanols found in dark chocolate, participate in
maintaining the strength of capillaries, lower blood pressure,
improve blood flow via increased production of nitric oxide
(a molecule used by the vascular endothelium to signal
the surrounding muscle to relax) and have vitamin C-like
functions.

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: Are flavonoids a vitamin?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says flavonoids — vitamin P, found in cocoa, tea, and wine — are now recognized as a third category of vitamins alongside the fat- and water-soluble groups.
claims.answer: Flavonoids, also known as vitamin P and commonly found in cocoa, tea, and wine, are now considered a third category of vitamins, according to Wallach. He states they have been officially added to the water-soluble and fat-soluble vitamin groups by Harvard Medical School. This places flavonoids alongside the traditional vitamins as a distinct class the body requires.
claims.verbatim:
Flavonoids or vitamin P commonly found in cocoa,
tea and wine are now considered to be the third category of
vitamins and are officially added to the water soluble and fat
soluble groups by Harvard Medical School.

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: Do the flavonoids in cocoa really prevent disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites Harvard's Norman Hollenberg, who found the cocoa-drinking Kuna people have a 10% lower risk of four of the five most common killer diseases.
claims.answer: Wallach cites Norman Hollenberg of Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women's Hospital, who reported that the island-dwelling Kuna people, who drink flavanol-rich cocoa, have a 10% lower risk of four of the five most common killer diseases: stroke, heart failure, cancer, and diabetes. Hollenberg regarded the finding as so striking that, if these observations predict the future, they may be among the most important observations in the history of medicine.
claims.verbatim:
Norman Hollenberg from Harvard Medical School
and Brigham and Women’s Hospital reports, “that the island-dwelling Kuna people who drink the flavanol-rich cocoa,
have a 10% lower risk of four of the five most common killer
diseases: stroke, heart failure, cancer and diabetes.”

“If these observations predict the future, then we can
say without blushing that they are among the most important
observations in the history of medicine,” said Hollenberg.

claims.subject: flavonoids
claims.question: Who first discovered flavonoids and what were they first used to treat?
claims.answer_short: Flavonoids were first used clinically in 1936 by Szent-Gyorgyi to treat patients with capillary fragility and hemorrhages.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that flavonoids were first used clinically in 1936 by Szent-Gyorgyi, who treated patients whose diseases were marked by increased permeability and fragility of the capillary wall that resulted in hemorrhages.
claims.verbatim:
Flavonoids were first used clinically in 1936 by Szent-Gyorgyi to treat patients with diseases characterized by
increased permeability and fragility of the capillary wall that
resulted in hemorrhages.

claims.subject: vanadium
claims.question: What are the signs of a vanadium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says carbohydrate and candy cravings, the 'munchies,' and a strong thirst for sweet drinks are sure signs of chromium and vanadium deficiency.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, chromium and vanadium deficiencies show up as an intense thirst for liquids, with sugary soft drinks usually the first choice and water the last, plus a hunger for carbohydrates like soft drinks, sweetened coffee and tea, alcohol, pasta, desserts, and bread. The 'munchies,' cravings for alcohol, and candy cravings, especially for chocolate, are sure signs of a chromium and vanadium deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium and vanadium deficiencies are manifested
by an intense thirst for liquid (high fructose corn syrup laden
soft drinks being the usual first choice and water the last for
minerally deficient humans) and hunger for carbohydrates
(i.e. - soft drinks, coffee and tea with added sugar, alcohol,
pasta, deserts, bread, etc.).

The “munchies,” cravings for alcohol and “candy
cravings” (especially chocolate) are sure signs of chromium
and vanadium deficiencies.

claims.subject: vanadium
claims.question: How did vanadium get its name?
claims.answer_short: Vanadium was named for the Scandinavian goddess Vanadis because of its many beautifully colored compounds.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that vanadium was discovered in 1801 by a Mexican professor of mineralogy, Andres Manuel del Rio. It was later named for the Scandinavian goddess Vanadis because of its many beautifully colored compounds. Vanadium makes up 0.02% of the earth's crust and is present in trace amounts in more than 60 different ores, with vanadinite as its predominant source.
claims.verbatim:
Vanadium makes up 0.02% of the earth’s crust, and is
present in trace amounts in more than 60 different ores. The
predominant source of vanadium is vanadinite. A Mexican
professor of mineralogy, Andres Manuel del Rio, discovered
vanadium in 1801. It was later named for the Scandinavian
goddess Vanadis because of its many beautifully colored
compounds.

claims.subject: germanium
claims.question: Is germanium used in electronics or computers?
claims.answer_short: Germanium is a poor conductor classed as a semiconductor, and when 'doped' with trace elements it is used to make transistors and microcomputers.
claims.answer: Germanium is a poor conductor of electricity, which places it in semiconductor status. Adding tiny amounts of other elements such as arsenic, gallium, or antimony -- a process called 'doping' -- greatly increases its ability to conduct electricity. Doped germanium is used to manufacture transistors, which essentially become micro-computers.
claims.verbatim:
Germanium is a poor conductor of electricity
and therefore is relegated to a semi-conductor status.

The addition of small amounts of other elements such
as arsenic, gallium, or antimony is called “doping” - this
process greatly increases its ability to conduct electricity.
Doped germanium is used to manufacture transistors, which
essentially become micro-computers.

claims.subject: manganese
claims.question: What does manganese do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Manganese activates many enzyme systems, including those for glucose metabolism, energy production, and the antioxidant SOD, and is built into metalloenzymes, hormones, and proteins.
claims.answer: Even though the total body content of manganese in humans is only 10 to 20 mg, it is essential to all living organisms. It activates numerous enzyme systems, including those involved in glucose metabolism, energy production, and the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase (SOD). Manganese is also a major constituent of several metalloenzymes, hormones, and proteins essential to all vertebrates and humans.
claims.verbatim:
The total body content of manganese in humans
is only 10 to 20 mg. Manganese is known to be essential
for all living organisms. Manganese activates numerous
enzyme systems including those involved with glucose
metabolism, energy production and antioxidant properties
of superoxide dismutase (SOD). It is a major constituent of
several metalloenzymes, hormones, and proteins essential to
all vertebrates and humans.

claims.subject: manganese
claims.question: Does manganese help build bones and cartilage?
claims.answer_short: Yes, manganese is essential to forming the three tiny bones of the ear and to the structure of joint cartilage.
claims.answer: Manganese is an essential part of the developmental process and the physical structure of the three fragile ear bones and joint cartilage. Because of this role, a shortage of manganese shows up as defects in cartilage and in the ear's bony structure. This is why Wallach links manganese deficiency to both joint problems and hearing loss.
claims.verbatim:
Manganese is an essential part of the developmental
process and the physical structure of the three fragile ear
bones and joint cartilage.

claims.subject: manganese
claims.question: Does manganese deficiency affect fertility and libido?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach lists infertility (failure to ovulate, testicular atrophy), miscarriages, and loss of libido in both sexes among manganese-deficiency diseases.
claims.answer: Among the deficiency diseases of manganese, Wallach lists infertility, meaning failure to ovulate in women and testicular atrophy in men, as well as still births and spontaneous abortions (miscarriages). He also names loss of libido in both males and females. In his framework, reproductive failure and low sex drive can be signs that the body is short of manganese.
claims.verbatim:
Infertility (failure to ovulate, testicular atrophy)
Still births/ spontaneous abortions (miscarriages)
Loss of libido in both males and females

claims.subject: manganese
claims.question: Where does the name manganese come from?
claims.answer_short: Manganese was identified in 1774 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele, who named it from the Latin magnes ('magnet') for the magnetic properties of its ore.
claims.answer: Manganese was identified in 1774 by the chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele. He named it from the Latin word magnes, meaning 'magnet,' a nod to the magnetic properties of pyrolusite, the manganese ore. The nutrient's name thus ties it directly to the magnetic mineral it was first drawn from.
claims.verbatim:
Manganese was identified in 1774 by Carl Wilhelm
Scheele who named it from the Latin word magnes, which
translates to “magnet,” referring to the magnetic properties
of pyrolusite.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: What is boron?
claims.answer_short: Boron is a scarce trace mineral Wallach counts among the nutrients essential for human health, needed for bone metabolism, the efficient use of calcium and magnesium, and normal sex-hormone levels.
claims.answer: Boron is a scarce, non-metallic trace mineral that never occurs pure in nature, turning up instead in combined compounds such as borax and boric acid. Wallach counts it among the nutrients essential for human health. In his framework boron is required for bone metabolism and the efficient use of calcium and magnesium, for the proper function of the endocrine glands (the ovaries, testes, and adrenals), and for maintaining normal blood levels of estrogen and testosterone. Although it was accepted as a human essential only in 1990, it now sits firmly among the minerals Wallach says the body must have.
claims.verbatim:
Boron is essential for bone metabolism including the
efficient use of calcium and magnesium and proper function
of endocrine glands (i.e. - ovaries, testes and adrenals).

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: Where is boron found in nature?
claims.answer_short: Boron concentrates in plants, especially brown algae and land plants, at far higher levels than in animals.
claims.answer: Boron is far more concentrated in plants than in animals. Marine plants carry 120 ppm (highest in brown algae) and land plants 150 ppm, while marine animals hold 20 to 50 ppm and land animals only 0.5 ppm. Wallach notes that the plant families Chenopodiaceae and Plumbaginaceae are indicator plant families for boron. The pattern shows that plants take up and hold far more boron than animals do.
claims.verbatim:
marine plants 120 ppm (highest levels found in brown
algae), terrestrial plants at 150 ppm (chenopodiaceae and
plumboginaceae are indicator plant families), marine animals
at 20 to 50 ppm, and terrestrial animals at 0.5 ppm.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: When was boron recognized as an essential nutrient?
claims.answer_short: Boron was not considered essential before 1981; it was first shown essential in growing chicks, and was not accepted as essential for humans until 1990.
claims.answer: Prior to 1981, boron was not considered an essential nutrient at all. It was first shown to be an essential mineral for growing chicks, and it was not until 1990 that boron was accepted as an essential nutrient for humans. Boron's recognized status as a human essential is therefore a relatively recent development.
claims.verbatim:
Prior to 1981, boron was not considered an essential
nutrient. Boron was first shown to be an essential mineral for
growing chicks. It was not until 1990 that boron was accepted
as an essential nutrient for humans.

claims.subject: boron
claims.question: Who discovered boron?
claims.answer_short: Boron was first isolated in 1808 by English chemist Sir Humphry Davy together with French chemists Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis-Jacques Thenard.
claims.answer: Boron was first isolated in 1808 by the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy, working alongside two French chemists, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis-Jacques Thenard. Before this, boron existed only in its combined mineral forms, since it is never found pure in nature.
claims.verbatim:
English chemist Sir Humphry Davy and two French chemists,
Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis-Jacques Thenard.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: What is cobalt?
claims.answer_short: Cobalt is a rare trace mineral that's essential to all life — a single cobalt atom sits at the center of vitamin B12, so needing cobalt really means needing B12 (for blood, DNA, nerve myelin and thyroid hormone).
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework, cobalt is an essential trace mineral required by every form of life, from blue-green algae, bacteria and fungi to plants, insects and all the vertebrates including humans. It works as a cofactor and activator for enzymes and helps "fix" nitrogen during amino-acid production, but its defining role is nutritional: a single cobalt atom sits at the very center of vitamin B12 (the cobamide coenzymes). Because of that, the body's cobalt requirement is really a requirement for the finished B12 molecule — cobalt/B12 is needed to build DNA and RNA, form red blood cells, make the myelin that insulates nerves, and produce the thyroid hormone thyroxine. Cobalt is a rare element, making up only about 0.003% of the earth's crust, and where soils are cobalt-depleted the crops, animals and people that depend on them fall deficient.
claims.verbatim:
Cobalt is essential for all forms of life including blue-green algae, some bacteria and fungi, some plants, insects,
birds, reptiles, amphibians and mammals including man.
Cobalt functions as a cofactor and an activator for enzymes,
“fixes” nitrogen during amino acid production, and a single
cobalt atom is the central metal component of vitamin B12,
which itself is a cofactor and activator (cobamide coenzymes)
for several essential enzymes.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: Why is vitamin B12 red?
claims.answer_short: B12's red color comes from the cobalt atom in the molecule, and about 30% of its activity is lost during cooking.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that vitamin B12 is a water-soluble red crystalline substance, and its red color is due to the cobalt atom in the molecule. B12 is slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances. About 30% of B12 activity is lost during cooking, whether by electric, gas, microwave, wood, or charcoal.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline substance that is water
soluble. The red color is due to the cobalt atom in the molecule.
Vitamin B12 is slowly deactivated by exposure to acid, alkali,
light, and oxidizing or reducing substances. About 30% of
B12 activity is lost during cooking (electric, gas, microwave,
wood, charcoal, etc.).

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: What happens to extra vitamin B12 in the body?
claims.answer_short: The body stores a maximum of 2 mg of B12, releasing it slowly to the bone marrow; any excess is simply shed in the urine ('expensive urine').
claims.answer: Wallach explains why megadosing vitamin B12 has limits: the body can store at most about 2 mg of B12, which it releases slowly to the bone marrow as needed, and any intake beyond that storage ceiling is simply flushed out in the urine — what he memorably calls 'expensive urine.' He adds the body recycles B12 through the liver and bile so efficiently that a vegan's deficiency may not surface for five to ten years after giving up meat.
claims.verbatim:
The maximum storage level of B12 is 2 mg which is slowly
released to the bone marrow as needed. Excess intake of B12
above the body’s storage capacity is shed in the urine (expensive
urine).

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: Why do older people often need B12 shots?
claims.answer_short: Cobalt/B12 only absorbs when intrinsic factor is present and stomach pH is 2.0 or less; low stomach acid (often from too little salt) blocks it, so doctors give shots.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that metallic cobalt is absorbed at only 20 to 26.2%, and only if intrinsic factor is present and the stomach pH is 2.0 or less. Intrinsic factor is a mucoprotein enzyme (Castle's intrinsic factor) that is part of normal stomach secretions. When a person has hypochlorhydria - low stomach acid, usually from a NaCl (salt) deficiency - the intrinsic factor won't work and B12/cobalt is not absorbed, which is why doctors frequently give B12 shots to older people on salt-restricted diets.
claims.verbatim:
Metallic cobalt itself is absorbed at the rate of 20 to
26.2% by mice and in humans if intrinsic factor is present
in the stomach and the stomach pH is 2.0 or less. Intrinsic
factor is a mucoprotein enzyme known as Castle’s intrinsic
factor and is part of normal stomach secretions. If a person
has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid- usually a NaCl
deficiency) the intrinsic factor will not work and B12 cobalt is
not absorbed - this is why doctors frequently give B12 shots
to older people on salt restricted diets.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: Can you get too much cobalt?
claims.answer_short: Yes—cobalt excess of 20 to 30 mg a day can drive up red blood cell production by stimulating the kidney hormone erythropoietin.
claims.answer: Too much cobalt has a specific effect Wallach flags: in humans, an excess of about 20 to 30 mg a day can drive accelerated erythropoiesis — an over-production of red blood cells — by stimulating the kidney to release more erythropoietin, the hormone that signals the marrow to make red cells. He stresses that the body's real cobalt need is tiny, since it is required mainly as the cobalt atom at the center of vitamin B12 (an RDA of just 3 to 4 mcg a day).
claims.verbatim:
Cobalt excess in man (20 to 30 mg/day) may create an
accelerated erythropoiesis (RBC -red blood cell- production)
by stimulating an increased production of the kidney hormone
erythropoietin.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: Can cobalt-poor soil cause deficiency in people?
claims.answer_short: Yes—less than 0.07 ppm cobalt in soil causes deficiency in the animals and people who eat crops from it, while 0.11 ppm prevents and cures it.
claims.answer: Cobalt puts Wallach's soil-to-people thesis in sharp numbers: when farmland holds less than 0.07 ppm of cobalt, the animals — and the people — that live on crops grown there develop cobalt deficiency, while just 0.11 ppm in the soil is enough to prevent and cure it. Because the body needs cobalt mainly as the core of vitamin B12, he links this shortfall to pernicious anemia and to demyelination of the spinal cord and major nerves — serious, sometimes permanent nerve damage.
claims.verbatim:
Less than 0.07 ppm Co in the soil results in cobalt
deficiency in animals and people who eat crops grown from
those soils; 0.11 ppm Co in the soil prevents and cures Co
deficiency.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: How rare is cobalt and when was it discovered?
claims.answer_short: Cobalt is a rare element, only 0.003% of the earth's crust, and was first isolated as a metal by Swedish chemist Georg Brandt in 1739.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that cobalt is a rare element, making up only 0.003 percent of the earth's crust, with cobalite - a compound of cobalt, arsenic and sulfur - as one of its common ores. The pure metal has a characteristic bright bluish-white color and is obtained by roasting the ore in air. Cobalt metal was first isolated by the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt in 1739.
claims.verbatim:
Cobalt is a rare element, making up only 0.003 percent
of the earth’s crust. Cobalite is one of its common ores, a
compound made up of cobalt, arsenic and sulfur. The pure
metal, which has a characteristic bright bluish-white color,
is obtained by roasting this ore in air. Cobalt metal was first
isolated by the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt in 1739.

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: Is cobalt magnetic and what is it used for?
claims.answer_short: Cobalt is easily magnetized and holds its magnetism at high temperatures; about a quarter of world production goes into 'alnico,' a super-magnetic alloy.
claims.answer: Wallach describes cobalt as well known for its ability to be magnetized - it is easily magnetized and retains its magnetism at temperatures far higher than those that demagnetize iron. Twenty-five percent of all the cobalt produced in the world is used to make a super-magnetic substance called 'alnico,' an alloy of aluminum, nickel and cobalt used for making industrial magnets.
claims.verbatim:
Cobalt is well known for its ability to be magnetized. It
is easily magnetized and retains its magnetism at temperatures
far higher than those that demagnetize iron. Twenty five
percent of all of the cobalt produced in the world is used to
make a super magnetic substance called “alnico.” Alnico is an
alloy of aluminum, nickel and cobalt and is used for making
industrial magnets.

claims.subject: lithium
claims.question: What is lithium?
claims.answer_short: Lithium is the lightest of all metals and an essential trace mineral Wallach ties directly to mood and behavior — he treats depression, bipolar disorder, and aggression as hallmarks of a lithium deficiency.
claims.answer: Lithium is an alkali metal so light it can actually float on water, and in Wallach's framework it is one of the essential trace minerals the body must have — not merely a psychiatric drug. He treats it as a nutrient central to mental and emotional health: he holds that depression, manic-depression (bipolar disorder), hyperactivity, ADD/ADHD, certain forms of autism, and even rage and violent behavior are, at root, hallmarks of a lithium deficiency aggravated by high sugar and alcohol intake. He points to conventional medicine's own use of lithium for bipolar disorder, and to research linking higher lithium in drinking water to lower rates of crime and suicide, as evidence of how essential this mineral is — and calls for lithium, not fluoride, to be added to public water.
claims.verbatim:
Lithium’s density is so low
that a small piece can actually float on water.

claims.subject: lithium
claims.question: What kind of metal is lithium?
claims.answer_short: Lithium is an extremely reactive metal so light a small piece can float on water, and so reactive it must be stored in oil or kerosene.
claims.answer: Wallach describes lithium as an extremely reactive metal whose density is so low that a small piece can actually float on water. It reacts vigorously with water to produce hydrogen gas and with oxygen to form lithium oxide, so free lithium is usually stored in oil or kerosene to keep these reactions from occurring.
claims.verbatim:
Lithiumisanextremely reactive metal. Itreacts vigorously
with water, to produce hydrogen gas, and with oxygen to form
lithium oxide (Li,O). To prevent these reactions from occurring,
free lithium is usually stored in oil or kerosene.

claims.subject: lithium
claims.question: Why is lithium used to treat bipolar disorder?
claims.answer_short: Lithium carbonate is routinely prescribed for severe bipolar disorder — over 3 million prescriptions a year — with its effect thought to involve how brain cells respond to certain hormones and neurotransmitters.
claims.answer: Wallach points out that mainstream medicine already treats severe bipolar disorder with a trace mineral: lithium, given as lithium carbonate, with more than 3 million prescriptions filled a year. Its exact mechanism, he notes, is thought to involve how brain cells respond to certain hormones and neurotransmitters. He turns this into a larger argument — that if a mineral can steady the most severe mood disorder, everyday depression and irritability may likewise reflect a simple lithium shortage.
claims.verbatim:
Lithium carbonate is regularly used to treat patients
with the severe form of bipolar disorder. More than 3 million
prescriptions for this trace mineral are filled yearly. The role of
lithium is thought to be related to the role the brain cells play
and respond to certain hormones and neurotransmitters.

claims.subject: lithium
claims.question: Is depression caused by a lithium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds that depression and manic depression are simply a lithium deficiency aggravated by high sugar consumption.
claims.answer: While psychiatrists attribute depression and manic depression to feelings of being out of control, negative thinking and self-recrimination, Wallach points out that they nonetheless treat it successfully with the trace mineral lithium. In his framework, depression and manic depression with all that the diagnosis implies are simply a lithium deficiency aggravated by a high consumption of sugar.
claims.verbatim:
While the professional psychiatrist says that depression
and manic depression are due to feelings that “we are out of
control of our lives,” negative thinking, and self recrimination
(‘I'm a loser”), they treat depression successfully with the
trace mineral lithium. Depression and manic depression with
all that implies, are simply a lithium deficiency aggravated by
a high consumption of sugar.

claims.subject: lithium
claims.question: How did lithium get its name?
claims.answer_short: Lithium was discovered in 1817 by Swedish chemist Johan August Arfvedson and named after the Greek word 'lithos,' meaning 'stone.'
claims.answer: Lithium was discovered in 1817 by the Swedish chemist Johan August Arfvedson while assaying ore from a Swedish mine, Wallach recounts, and was named from the Greek word 'lithos,' meaning 'stone.'
