He adds a memorable quirk of the metal: it is so light that a small piece will actually float on water, and so reactive that pure lithium must be stored under oil or kerosene to keep it from reacting with air and moisture.
claims.verbatim:
Lithium was discovered in 1817 by the Swedish chemist
Johan August Arfvedson during a routine chemical assay of
ore from a mine in Sweden. It was named for the Greek word
lithos, which translates to “stone.”

claims.subject: molybdenum
claims.question: What is molybdenum?
claims.answer_short: Molybdenum is an essential trace mineral in Wallach's framework — a hard, silvery metal mined from the ore molybdenite — that every living organism needs as a building block of several key enzymes.
claims.answer: Wallach classes molybdenum as one of the essential trace minerals every living organism requires, even though it is technically a hard, silvery metal. It is extracted from an ore called molybdenite, with large deposits in Colorado, and was identified as a distinct element in 1778. In the body it works as a constituent of numerous metalloenzymes — Wallach names it an integral part of at least three: xanthine oxidase, aldehyde oxidase, and sulfite oxidase. He cites an RDA of 250 mcg per day but recommends far more as a supplement, and warns that a molybdenum deficiency is among the causes of goiter.
claims.verbatim:
Molybdenum is a hard, silvery metal that is extracted
from an ore called molybdenite (MoS,). There are large
deposits of “Moly” molybdenite in Colorado.

claims.subject: molybdenum
claims.question: Can you take too much molybdenum? Is it toxic?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says molybdenum toxicity occurs at 10 mg per day, showing up as a gout-like disease and as interference with copper metabolism.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, molybdenum toxicity occurs at an intake of 10 mg per day. The clinical signs of toxicity appear as a gout-like disease and as interference with copper metabolism. This 10 mg toxic threshold is many times higher than the 250 mcg RDA he cites in the same passage.
claims.verbatim:
Toxicity occurs at 10 mg per day; clinical signs
of toxicity appear as a gout-like disease and interference with
copper metabolism.

claims.subject: molybdenum
claims.question: Can too much molybdenum in soil poison animals?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says a few soils worldwide are rich enough in molybdenum to poison animals grazing on the plants, while numerous other soils are molybdenum-deficient.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that molybdenum in soil is strongly concentrated by humus, especially in alkaline soils, and that a few soils worldwide hold enough of it to cause molybdenum poisoning in animals that consume the local plants. At the same time, he says numerous soils are known to be molybdenum-deficient. He gives a typical soil concentration of about 2 ppm.
claims.verbatim:
soil at 2.0
ppm (strongly concentrated by humus, especially in alkaline
soils; a few soils worldwide are rich enough in molybdenum
to cause molybdenum poisoning in animals consuming
the plants). Numerous soils are known to be molybdenum
deficient.

claims.subject: molybdenum
claims.question: Who discovered molybdenum and when?
claims.answer_short: Molybdenum was first extracted from molybdenite and identified as a new element in 1778 by a Swedish chemist named Scheele.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, molybdenum was originally extracted from the ore molybdenite and identified as a new element in 1778 by a Swedish chemist named Scheele. It was recognized as a distinct new element at that time.
claims.verbatim:
In 1778, molybdenum was originally extracted from
molybdenite and identified as a new element by the Swedish
chemist Carl Eilhelm Scheele who identified it as a new
element.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: What is sodium?
claims.answer_short: Sodium is a soft, highly reactive silvery metal and the sixth most abundant element in the earth's crust, known best as sodium chloride — common table salt. Wallach treats it as an essential macro-mineral and one of the body's three indispensable electrolytes.
claims.answer: In Wallach's mineral encyclopedia, sodium is a highly reactive, bright, silvery metal — light enough to float on water and soft enough to cut with a knife — and the sixth most abundant element in the earth's crust. People know it best as sodium chloride, ordinary table salt. Wallach classes it as an essential macro-mineral and one of three indispensable electrolytes (with chloride and potassium) that maintain the body's water balance, osmotic and acid-base equilibrium, and nerve and muscle function. Far from being the villain conventional medicine makes it out to be, in his framework salt is vital to life — it is the raw material the stomach uses to make hydrochloric acid — and the real danger lies in restricting it, not in eating it.
claims.verbatim:
Sodium is a highly reactive, bright, silvery metal, light
enough to float on water and soft enough to cut witha knife. It
is the sixth most abundant element in the crust of the earth.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: What is sodium?
claims.answer_short: Sodium is a highly reactive, soft silvery metal, light enough to float on water and the sixth most abundant element in the earth's crust.
claims.answer: In his mineral encyclopedia, Wallach describes sodium as a highly reactive, bright, silvery metal that is light enough to float on water and soft enough to cut with a knife. He notes it is the sixth most abundant element in the crust of the earth. It is most familiar to people in the form of sodium chloride, common table salt.
claims.verbatim:
Sodium is a highly reactive, bright, silvery metal, light
enough to float on water and soft enough to cut witha knife. It
is the sixth most abundant element in the crust of the earth.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Why do animals crave salt and need salt licks?
claims.answer_short: Animals have an instinctive salt hunger, so farmers use salt blocks (at least 85% sodium chloride) to make them consume trace minerals.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that farmers and husbandrymen exploit animals' instinctive salt hunger to ensure they eat trace minerals, by blending those minerals into salt blocks that are 85% salt. Anything less than 85% sodium chloride in a salt block will be ignored by the animals — even when they have major mineral deficiencies.
claims.verbatim:
Farmers and husbandrymen use the salt hunger of
animals to ensure the consumption of trace minerals by
incorporating trace minerals into salt blocks containing 85%
salt - anything less than 85% sodium chloride in a salt block
will be ignored by the animals even if they have major mineral
deficiencies!

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Where does table salt come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says table salt (sodium chloride) is mined from ancient salt mines on every continent, and seawater holds a quarter pound of salt per gallon.
claims.answer: Sodium chloride — the chemical name for ordinary table salt — is mined in vast quantities from ancient salt mines on every continent, Wallach notes, and can also be drawn from the sea, where every gallon of seawater holds about a quarter-pound of salt. He frames salt as one of humanity's oldest essentials: prized as a nutrient, preservative, and flavoring since before Roman times, when soldiers were paid an allowance in salt — the very origin of the word 'salary.'
claims.verbatim:
Sodium chloride, the chemical name for common table
salt, is mined in large quantities from ancient salt mines on
every continent on earth. Sea water is another common source
of salt, every gallon of sea water contains a quarter pound of
salt.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Is processed table salt as good as natural salt?
claims.answer_short: No — unprocessed salt once carried trace minerals and rare earths, while modern processed salt fools the body into thinking it is getting minerals.
claims.answer: Wallach says that historically, eating salt to satisfy a pica craving had real value because unprocessed salt often contained trace minerals and rare earths. He argues salt consumption today is not, in and of itself, harmful — but processed salt creates the problem of letting the body think it is getting minerals, the equivalent of an "empty calorie" diet of processed-food calories without vitamins.
claims.verbatim:
Historically, the consumption of salt to satisfy a pica
behavior was of value because salt was not processed and did
often times contain trace minerals and rare earths.

Today, salt consumption, although contrary to popular
belief, is notin and of itself harmful; it does present the problem
of allowing our bodies to think we are getting minerals (the
equivalent of the “empty calorie diets,” i.e. - processed food
calories without vitamins).

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: Who discovered sodium and where does its name come from?
claims.answer_short: Sir Humphry Davy isolated sodium in 1807; the name comes from 'soda,' from the Latin 'sodanum,' an ancient Roman headache remedy.
claims.answer: Sodium was first isolated in 1807 by the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy, Wallach recounts, who separated the reactive, silvery metal from molten sodium hydroxide. Its name carries an old-medicine root: 'sodium' comes from 'soda,' which traces back to the Latin 'sodanum,' a common headache remedy in ancient Rome. He adds that the pure metal is light enough to float on water and soft enough to cut with a knife.
claims.verbatim:
The English chemist, Sir Humphry Davy first isolated and
identified sodium as a new element in 1807 by separating it from
molten sodium hydroxide. The name, sodium is taken from the
English word soda, which itself is derived from the Latin word
sodanum, a common headache remedy of ancient Rome.

claims.subject: phosphorus
claims.question: Who discovered phosphorus?
claims.answer_short: The German physician Hennig Brand discovered phosphorus in 1669 by distilling boiled-down urine, producing a substance that glowed in the dark.
claims.answer: Phosphorus is a nonmetal element discovered by the German physician Hennig Brand in 1669. Working in the tradition of the ancient alchemists, Brand distilled the residue from boiled-down urine and obtained a new element that glowed in the dark and burst into flames when exposed to warm air. He had discovered white phosphorus, a waxy white solid that melts at 44 degrees C.
claims.verbatim:
Phosphorus is a nonmetal element that was discovered
by the German physician Hennig Brand in 1669. Brand carried
out experiments in the fashion of the ancient alchemists. He
distilled the residue from boiled-down urine and obtained a
new element that glowed in the dark and burst into flames
when exposed to warm air.

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: What is sulfur?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's framework sulfur is one of the 60 essential minerals — a structural atom built into most proteins through the sulfur amino acids cystine, cysteine, and methionine.
claims.answer: In Dr. Wallach's framework, sulfur (which he usually spells 'sulphur') is one of the 60 essential elements, metals and minerals the body must obtain. He describes it as an important structural atom in most proteins, carried in through the sulfur-bearing amino acids cystine, cysteine, and methionine, and into small organic molecules. The -SH and -S-S- bonds sulfur forms are what hold many structural proteins in shape and let enzymes do their work, and it is essential to glutathione. Sulfur concentrates in cartilage, tendons, keratin, skin, hair, and nails — the connective tissue and structural proteins that depend on it — and its loss shows up as degenerative arthritis and other collagen diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Sulfur is an important structural atom in most proteins as
sulfur amino acids (cystine, cysteine and methionine) and small
organic molecules.

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: What does sulfur do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Sulfur is a structural atom in most proteins, carried by the sulfur amino acids cystine, cysteine, and methionine, and it is essential to glutathione.
claims.answer: Wallach describes sulfur as an important structural atom in most proteins, built in through the sulfur-bearing amino acids cystine, cysteine, and methionine. Glutathione, a cysteine-containing tripeptide, depends on these sulfur amino acids for the cellular reactions it drives. Sulfur exists in a reduced form (-SH) in cysteine and in an oxidized form (-S-S-) as the double molecule cystine, and these bonds are what give many proteins their working structure.
claims.verbatim:
Sulfur is an important structural atom in most proteins as
sulfur amino acids (cystine, cysteine and methionine) and small
organic molecules. Glutathione, a tripeptide containing cysteine,
is essential to normal cellular reactions involving sulfur amino
acids in proteins. Sulfur is found in a reduced form (-SH) in
cysteine and in an oxidized form (-S-S-) as the double molecule
cystine.

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: Where is sulfur stored in the body?
claims.answer_short: Sulfur concentrates in cartilage, tendons, keratin, skin, intervertebral discs, hair, and nails, and is lowest in the bones.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that in land animals sulfur runs 5,000 ppm, with the highest levels in cartilage, tendons, keratin, skin, intervertebral discs, hair, and nails, and its lowest concentrations in the bones.
claims.verbatim:
S-Sulfur is found in igneous rocks at 260 ppm, shale
at 2,400 ppm, sandstone at 240 ppm, limestone at 1,200
ppm, freshwater at 3.7 ppm, sea water at 885 ppm, soils at
700 ppm, marine animals at 5,000 to 19,000 ppm (highest
in coelenterates and molluscs) and in terrestrial animals at
5,000 ppm (highest levels in cartilage, tendons, keratin, skin,
intervertebral discs, hair and nails). Its lowest concentrations
are in bones.

claims.subject: sulfur
claims.question: Do sulfur amino acids help you live longer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach counts the sulfur-bearing amino acids among the antioxidants shown to significantly extend the average lifespan of a population.
claims.answer: In Immortality, Wallach cites considerable evidence that a population's 50 percent survival rate can be extended significantly by consuming combinations of antioxidants, including vitamins A, C, and E, selenium, the sulfur-bearing amino acids methionine, cysteine, and cystine, and plant phytochemicals. Elsewhere he notes that raising antioxidant intake alone increases the mean life span of a population but not the maximum human life span.
claims.verbatim:
Considerable evidence has been collected to support
the idea that the 50% survival rate of a population can be
extended significantly by the consumption of combinations
of antioxidants, including vitamins A, C, E, selenium, sulfur
bearing amino acids (methionine, cysteine, cystine, etc.) and
phytochemicals such as catechens (green tea, coffee, red wine,
dark berries, exotic fruit, etc.)

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: Why do corn-based diets cause pellagra?
claims.answer_short: Corn has very little niacin and its tryptophan is unavailable and can't be absorbed from the intestine, so there is no tryptophan to convert into niacin, causing pellagra.
claims.answer: Pellagra is common in corn-based diets because corn contains very little niacin, and the tryptophan present in corn is unavailable and cannot be absorbed from the intestine. With no absorbable tryptophan to be converted into niacin, and little niacin in the corn itself, the body is left deficient and pellagra results.
claims.verbatim:
There is very little niacin in corn
and the tryptophan in the corn is unavailable and can’t be
absorbed from the intestine, as a result there is no available
tryptophan to be converted into niacin.

claims.subject: tryptophan
claims.question: Why does soaking corn in lye prevent pellagra?
claims.answer_short: Soaking corn in lye and wood ashes overnight lets the alkali free the tryptophan so it can be absorbed, which is why pellagra is rare where corn is prepared this way.
claims.answer: In corn-consuming societies that soak their corn in lye and wood ashes overnight before eating it, pellagra is rare. The alkali in the lye and wood ashes makes the corn's tryptophan absorbable, so the body can take it up and convert it into niacin, preventing the deficiency disease pellagra.
claims.verbatim:
soaked in lye and wood ashes overnight before it is consumed
- the alkali in the lye and wood ashes allows the tryptophan
to be absorbed and pellagra is rare

claims.subject: cobalt
claims.question: Where does the name cobalt come from?
claims.answer_short: From the German 'kobald,' an evil gnome or spirit that miners blamed for their mining accidents.
claims.answer: Cobalt's name carries an old superstition. Wallach relates that it derives from the 18th-century German word 'kobald,' meaning an evil gnome or spirit — miners of the day commonly blamed their accidents on the malicious 'kobald' hiding in the ore. He adds the metal was first isolated by the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt in 1739, though the ancient Egyptians had already used traces of cobalt to make blue glass thousands of years before.
claims.verbatim:
The name cobalt was derived in the 18th century
from the German word “kobald” that refers to an evil gnome
or spirit. Cobalt miners commonly blamed mining accidents
on the evil “kobald” or cobalt.

claims.subject: methionine
claims.question: Why is selenomethionine called the 13th essential amino acid?
claims.answer_short: Selenium researcher Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer called selenomethionine — methionine with a selenium atom in place of its sulfur — the '13th essential amino acid,' Wallach notes.
claims.answer: Wallach relays that the selenium researcher Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer considered selenomethionine — the form of methionine in which a selenium atom replaces the sulfur — to be the '13th essential amino acid.' Selenomethionine is the compound that carries selenium on the methionine backbone, which is why it appears on supplement labels as a chelated, well-absorbed source of the mineral Wallach regards as one of the body's most important antioxidants.
claims.verbatim:
Selenium researcher, Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer, considers selenomethionine,
the selenium analog of methionine the 13th essential amino acid.

claims.subject: leucine
claims.question: Why do people who eat mostly sorghum or millet get pellagra?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes that in India, where sorghum or millet is a staple, the diet delivers high levels of leucine—and he separately warns that excessive leucine can itself produce pellagra.
claims.answer: Wallach links the grain a population eats to its pellagra risk. In corn-eating societies of Mexico, Central and South America, the corn is soaked in lye and wood ashes overnight, which frees its tryptophan for absorption so pellagra stays rare. By contrast, in India, where sorghum or millet is a common staple food, the diet carries high levels of leucine—and elsewhere Wallach warns that excessive leucine intake can itself produce a clinical pellagra. Together these are part of his explanation for why some grain-based diets breed the disease while others do not.
claims.verbatim:
in India where sorghum
or millet is a common food, high levels of leucine in the

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: Where does the name gallium come from?
claims.answer_short: Gallium was named for Gallia, the Latin word for France, and was identified in 1875 by the chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran.
claims.answer: Gallium's name traces to Gallia, the Latin word for France. Wallach calls the element's history unique because its existence was predicted by Mendeleyev, creator of the periodic chart, back in 1871 -- where, from its position on the table, it was given the placeholder name 'eka-aluminum.' Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran then actually identified gallium in 1875 and named it for Gallia. So gallium is one of the rare elements science expected to find before anyone had ever isolated it.
claims.verbatim:
The history of gallium is unique as it is one of the
elements that was predicted to exist by Mendeleyev (creator of
the periodic chart) in 1871. Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran
identified gallium in 1875 and named it for Gallia, the Latin
word for France.

claims.subject: gallium
claims.question: Can taking gallium during pregnancy lower a child's risk of brain cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites British research finding that pregnant women whose diets are supplemented with gallium have significantly lower rates of brain cancer in their children.
claims.answer: Wallach reports British research showing that when pregnant women's diets are supplemented with gallium, the rate of brain cancer in their children drops significantly. He connects this to gallium's specific metalloenzyme activity in the human brain and to laboratory findings that gallium reduces brain cancer in animals. For Wallach it is one more reason gallium belongs among the essential nutrients rather than being written off as a non-essential trace metal.
claims.verbatim:
British
research has shown that diets, of pregnant women that are
supplemented with gallium, significantly reduces the rate of
brain cancer in children.

claims.subject: hydrogen
claims.question: Where does the name hydrogen come from?
claims.answer_short: Hydrogen means 'water-creator' in Greek, because burning it in oxygen produces water.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that hydrogen is named for what happens when it burns: in air it reacts violently with oxygen, giving off large amounts of heat and forming water. That water-making reaction is the origin of its name, taken from the Greek words hydro, meaning water, and genes, meaning creator. So the word 'hydrogen' literally means 'water-creator.'
claims.verbatim:
When hydrogen burns in air, it reacts violently with
oxygen to form large amounts of heat and water. It is this
reaction with oxygen that gave hydrogen its name, which
is translated from the Greek words hydro (water) and genes
(creator).

claims.subject: hydrogen
claims.question: Is hydrogen gas flammable?
claims.answer_short: Yes, Wallach describes hydrogen as a colorless, odorless, tasteless but extremely flammable diatomic gas.
claims.answer: Wallach describes hydrogen gas as normally existing as a diatomic molecule, meaning each molecule is two hydrogen atoms bonded together (H2). The gas itself is colorless, odorless and tasteless, so it cannot be seen or smelled. Its defining hazard is that it is extremely flammable: when it burns in air it reacts violently with oxygen, releasing large amounts of heat and forming water.
claims.verbatim:
Hydrogen gas is typically a diatomic molecule, meaning
that a hydrogen molecule is made up of two hydrogen atoms
(H2). Hydrogen gas is colorless, odorless and tasteless;
however, hydrogen is extremely flammable.

claims.subject: hydrogen
claims.question: Where is hydrogen found in nature?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports hydrogen is most concentrated in water, about 111,000 ppm in fresh water and 108,000 ppm in seawater, with smaller amounts in rocks and living tissue.
claims.answer: Wallach reports hydrogen's abundance across the natural world: roughly 1,000 ppm in igneous rocks, 5,600 ppm in shale, 1,800 ppm in sandstone and 860 ppm in limestone, but far more in water, at about 111,000 ppm in fresh water and 108,000 ppm in seawater. It is also plentiful in living things, reaching around 70,000 ppm in land animals. This pattern reflects his point that most of the hydrogen on earth is bound up in the water of oceans and lakes rather than existing as free gas.
claims.verbatim:
H-Hydrogen is found in igneous rocks at 1,000 ppm,
shale at 5,600 ppm, sandstone at 1,800 ppm, limestone at 860
ppm, fresh water at 111,000 ppm, sea water at 108,000 ppm,

claims.subject: nitrogen
claims.question: Are the nitrates and nitrites in processed meat bad for you?
claims.answer_short: Wallach warns that nitrates and nitrites in cured and canned foods turn into nitrosamines in the stomach -- potential carcinogens that can also suppress the thyroid.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that nitrates and nitrites are added to canned foods and preserved meats to prevent bacterial growth and keep meat red. In the acid environment of the stomach they are converted to nitrosamines, and those compounds can in turn become cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens). He adds that they can also suppress thyroid function.
claims.verbatim:
Nitrates and nitrites are converted to nitrosamines in
the acid environment of the stomach; these compounds can
be converted to cancer causing chemicals (carcinogens) and
can suppress thyroid function.

claims.subject: oxygen
claims.question: Why do I need minerals to use oxygen?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says even oxygen and water are useless to your cells without mineral cofactors — no nutrient works physiologically without minerals.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework minerals are the master key: you cannot physiologically use any nutrient, phytonutrient, or raw material without mineral cofactors. He pushes this to its limit, arguing that even oxygen and water — the most basic inputs of life — are unavailable to you at the cellular level without those mineral cofactors. He makes the point while criticizing an anti-aging position paper that dismissed all interventions, noting it left out both calorie-restricted diets and plant minerals. The takeaway: breathing and drinking are not enough if the minerals that let cells actually use oxygen and water are missing.
claims.verbatim:
You cannot effectively use any nutrients,
phytonutrients or raw materials physiologically without
mineral cofactors - even oxygen and water are unavailable to
you at the cellular level without mineral cofactors!

claims.subject: oxygen
claims.question: Is oxygen poisonous?
claims.answer_short: Wallach approvingly cites Dr. Roy Walford's point that the oxygen in our atmosphere is actually a highly poisonous gas — one we both require and are damaged by.
claims.answer: Wallach approvingly quotes Dr. Roy Walford, who he says described oxygen-based free radicals 'very well.' Walford's point is that the oxygen of our atmosphere is a highly poisonous gas: alien entities arriving from a methane planet would choke and die on the stuff we breathe so casually. The same oxygen rusts iron, drives the decay and crumbling of granite boulders, and participates in every fire in town — yet we live in it, require it, and love it. Wallach uses the paradox to frame oxygen's double edge: essential for respiration, yet also the source of oxidative free-radical damage to cells and membranes.
claims.verbatim:
Not everybody realizes that the oxygen of our
atmosphere is a highly poisonous gas. Alien entities arriving
from a methane planet would choke and die on the stuff we
breathe so casually. It rusts iron, is involved in the decay and
crumbling of granite boulders, and participates in every fire
in town...

claims.subject: oxygen
claims.question: Do cancer cells die in the presence of oxygen?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites Otto Warburg's Nobel-winning finding that cancer cells ferment sugar anaerobically and die in the presence of oxygen, while normal cells run on aerobic metabolism.
claims.answer: Wallach points to Dr. Otto Warburg of the Max Planck Institute, a two-time unshared Nobel laureate, one of whose prizes was for discovering that the cancer cell's metabolism is fermentative and anaerobic while the normal, noncancerous cell's metabolism is aerobic. During the 1950s Warburg demonstrated clearly that cancer cells ferment sugar under anaerobic conditions and die in the presence of oxygen. This is the mechanistic backbone of Wallach's recurring theme that cancer cells do not like high levels of oxygen. It is why he favors oxygen-raising measures such as germanium (which increases oxygen flow into cells) and hydrogen peroxide in his cancer programs.
claims.verbatim:
the second for discovering that the metabolism of the cancer
cell is fermentative and anaerobic while the metabolism of
the normal noncancerous cell is aerobic. During the 1950s,
Warburg was able to demonstrate clearly that cancer cells
ferment sugar under anaerobic conditions and die in the

presence of oxygen.

claims.subject: oxygen
claims.question: What is hyperbaric oxygen therapy used for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says exposing patients to several atmospheres of oxygen in a hyperbaric chamber can reactivate 'sleeping beauty' cells around a stroke and speed the healing of athletic injuries.
claims.answer: Wallach describes hyperbaric oxygen therapy as putting a patient into a chamber pressurized to several atmospheres of oxygen. In stroke, the tissue surrounding the stroke site contains inactive-but-living 'sleeping beauty' cells that can be reactivated or jump-started when exposed to that high-pressure oxygen. He says the same approach treats athletic injuries: an injured athlete placed in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber heals so much faster that they can return to play in weeks instead of months. It is one of several ways Wallach uses concentrated oxygen therapeutically.
claims.verbatim:
that can be reactivated or jump started when they are exposed
to several atmospheres of oxygen in hyperbaric chambers.
Athletic injuries can also be treated by putting the injured
athlete into a hyperbaric oxygen chamber. The healing time
is shortened significantly so the athlete can return to play in
weeks instead of months.

claims.subject: oxygen
claims.question: How long has oxygen therapy been used in medicine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says oxygen in the form of hydrogen peroxide has been used topically, intravenously, and orally since the Civil War, and widely in Europe for over 50 years.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, oxygen delivered as hydrogen peroxide has a long medical history: it has been used topically, intravenously, and orally since the Civil War. In Europe it has been used for more than 50 years for alternative cancer therapies, circulatory disease, arteriosclerosis, emphysema, asthma, and gangrene, and more recently as a therapy for stroke patients. He frames hydrogen peroxide as essentially a carrier of oxygen, since the body's catalase enzyme rapidly breaks it down into water and a singlet oxygen atom. That is why he counts hydrogen peroxide among his oxygen-based treatments.
claims.verbatim:
Oxygen in the form of hydrogen peroxide has been used
topically, intravenously and orally since the Civil War. It has been
used widely in Europe for over 50 years for alternative cancer
therapies, circulatory disease, arteriosclerosis, emphysema,
asthma, gangrene and more recently as a therapy for stroke
patients.

claims.subject: silica
claims.question: What is silica?
claims.answer_short: Silica is silicon dioxide (SiO2), the most important compound of silicon — the second most abundant element in the earth's crust after oxygen — and Wallach counts it among the body's essential minerals.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework, silica is silicon dioxide (SiO2), the most important compound of the element silicon. Silicon is the second most abundant element in the earth's crust, exceeded only by oxygen, and its oxygen-bonded compounds make up most of the world's sand, rock and soil. Silica occurs in two familiar natural forms — a crystalline form called quartz, the tiny chips of which are the grains in sand, and a noncrystalline form called flint — while gems such as amethyst, opal, agate and jasper are simply quartz crystals carrying colored impurities. Wallach treats silica as an essential mineral, one needed for the optimal health of the bones, skin, hair and nails.
claims.verbatim:
The most important silicon compound is silica, or
silicon dioxide (SiO,). It exists in two familiar forms in nature:
a crystalline form called quartz, small chips of which are
found in sand, a a noncrystalline form called flint. Small gems
and semiprecious stones such as amethyst, opal, agate and
jasper are crystals of quartz with colored impurities.

claims.subject: silica
claims.question: Is silica the same as sand and glass?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains that silica is the main material of sand, and that sand melted with soda ash and limestone becomes glass — of which there are more than a thousand forms.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that silica and everyday sand are the same material: silica as sand can be mixed with soda ash (sodium carbonate) and limestone (calcium carbonate) and then melted to become glass — of which he notes there are more than a thousand forms. Silica's crystalline form is quartz, the chips of which make up ordinary sand, and its noncrystalline form is flint. So the same mineral the body needs for bones, skin, hair and nails is also the raw material of sand and glass.
claims.verbatim:
Silica as sand can be mixed with soda ash (sodium
carbonate) and limestone (calcium carbonate) and when the
mixture is melted it becomes glass - there are more than 1,000
forms of glass.

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Is there aluminum in baby formula?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites a survey putting aluminum in infant formula at about 0.9 mg/kg body weight per week (milk-based) and 1.1 mg (soy-based).
claims.answer: Aluminum turns up even in baby food. Wallach cites a European survey - which was rerunning an earlier WHO report - that measured the aluminum in infant formula at an average of 0.9 mg per kg of body weight per week for milk-based formulas and 1.1 mg for soy-based ones. Some soy-based formulas ran about four times the average level found in that survey.
claims.verbatim:
The amount of aluminum in infant
formulas averages 0.9 mg/kg of body weight per week for
milk based formulas and 1.1 mg/kg of body weight per
week for soy-based infant formulas.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: What is gold?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes gold as the most precious and one of the most beautiful of all metals -- a corrosion-resistant, bright-yellow element prized since ancient times.
claims.answer: In Wallach's account, gold is considered the most precious of all metals and, in its pure state, one of the most beautiful of the elements -- valued for its bright yellow color and its resistance to corrosion. It has been highly prized since ancient times, and was used in conjunction with silver and mercury by ancient Chinese alchemists as far back as 8,000 B.C. in their pursuit of 'immortality.'
claims.verbatim:
Gold is considered the most precious of all metals and
was used in conjunction with silver and mercury by the ancient
Chinese alchemist 8,000 B.C. to provide “immortality”. In its
pure state, gold is one of the most beautiful of elements. With
its bright yellow color and its resistance to corrosion, it has
been highly prized since ancient times.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Where does the name gold and its symbol Au come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says gold's symbol Au comes from the Latin aurum ('shining dawn'), with older roots in the Sanskrit jval and the Anglo-Saxon gold.
claims.answer: Wallach traces gold's naming to its chemical symbol Au, which comes from the Latin word aurum, meaning 'shining dawn.' The name has even older roots, descending from the Sanskrit word jval and the Anglo-Saxon word gold, both of which simply mean 'gold.' That sense of a 'shining dawn' suits a metal he calls the most precious and beautiful of all, prized for its bright yellow color since ancient times.
claims.verbatim:
Its chemical symbol,
Au, comes from the Latin word aurum, which translates to
“shining dawn.” It has even older origins, coming from the
Sanskrit word jval and the Anglo-Saxon word gold, both

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Is gold used in dental fillings?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes gold dissolves in mercury to form an amalgam, and this gold-mercury amalgam is used by dentists to fill teeth.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that gold dissolves in mercury to form an amalgam -- an alloy of mercury and gold -- and that this gold-mercury amalgam is used by dentists to fill teeth. It is one of the practical, non-nutritional uses he lists for the metal, separate from any role it might play inside the body.
claims.verbatim:
Gold dissolves in mercury to form an amalgam, or
alloy of mercury and gold - this gold-mercury amalgam is
used by dentist to fill teeth.

claims.subject: strontium
claims.question: Where does the name strontium come from?
claims.answer_short: Strontium was named in 1789 after the Scottish village of Strontian, where Dr. Adair Crawford first identified the element.
claims.answer: Strontium takes its name from Strontian, a village in Scotland where the English scientist Dr. Adair Crawford first identified the element; both the metal and the mineral strontianite were named in 1789. Wallach describes its natural sources as the mineral ores celestite, a form of strontium sulfate, and strontianite, a strontium carbonate.
claims.verbatim:
Natural sources of strontium are the mineral ores
celestite, which is a form of strontium sulfate, and strontianite,
a strontium carbonate. Both strontium and the mineral
strontianite were named in 1789 by the English scientist
Dr. Adair Crawford, who first identified the element in the
Scottish village of Strontian.

claims.subject: bromine
claims.question: Is bromine a liquid?
claims.answer_short: In its pure form bromine is a reddish liquid, and Wallach notes it and mercury are the only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
claims.answer: In its pure form bromine is a reddish liquid built from diatomic molecules — pairs of bromine atoms bonded together. Wallach highlights an unusual fact: bromine and mercury are the only two chemical elements that stay liquid at ordinary room temperature. In the body, though, it does not remain in that raw elemental form — it works in its active form as brominated amino acids.
claims.verbatim:
In its pure form, bromine is a diatomic molecule
(two bromine atoms) that is a reddish liquid. Bromine and
mercury are the only two elements that are liquids at room
temperature.

claims.subject: bromine
claims.question: What does the name bromine mean?
claims.answer_short: Wallach explains the element was named bromine from the Greek word 'bromos,' which means 'stench.'
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that when the young French student Antoine-Jerome Balard added chlorinated water to the brackish salt-marsh water near Montpellier, it turned brownish — and that color change turned out to be caused by a new element. The French Academy named the element bromine, taken from the Greek word 'bromos,' which translates to 'stench.' In other words, the element's very name comes from a Greek word for a bad smell.
claims.verbatim:
The addition of the chlorine turned the water brownish. The
cause of the color change was found to be a new element that
the French Academy named bromine, taken from the Greek
word bromos, which translates to “stench.”

claims.subject: terbium
claims.question: What is terbium?
claims.answer_short: Terbium is a rare-earth metal that Wallach counts among the essential trace minerals -- one of the least abundant of the rare earths, silvery-white and soft enough to be cut with a knife.
claims.answer: Terbium is a rare-earth metal -- by Wallach's account one of the least abundant of all the rare earth elements. In its pure metallic form it is silvery-white and soft enough to be cut with a knife. Wallach catalogs terbium among the plant-derived rare earths and trace minerals he counts as part of the body's full essential-mineral complement, not as a mere geological oddity.
claims.verbatim:
In its pure metallic form, terbium is silvery-white and
is soft enough to be cut with a knife.

claims.subject: terbium
claims.question: Who discovered terbium and when?
claims.answer_short: Wallach records that terbium was discovered in 1843 by Carl Gustaf Mosander, who isolated its oxide from the mineral yttria.
claims.answer: Wallach records that terbium was discovered in 1843 by Carl Gustaf Mosander, who isolated its oxide from the mineral yttria. Terbium is one of the least abundant of all the rare earth elements. It is also recovered commercially from monazite, but its original identification traced to Mosander's work separating its oxide out of yttria.
claims.verbatim:
Terbium is one of the least abundant of the rare earth
elements. Carl Gustaf Mosander discovered the element in
1843 by isolating its oxide from the mineral yttria.

claims.subject: terbium
claims.question: Where does terbium come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says terbium is recovered commercially from monazite -- a mix of rare earths, thorium and calcium -- found in river sands from India and Brazil and beach sand from Florida.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that terbium is recovered commercially from monazite -- described as a mixture of rare earth elements combined with thorium and calcium. That mineral turns up in river sands from India and Brazil and in beach sand from Florida. Because monazite is itself a blend of the rare earths, terbium is extracted alongside the rest of the family rather than from an ore that is uniquely its own.
claims.verbatim:
Terbium is recovered commercially from the mineral
monazite, a mixture of rare earth elements combined with
thorium and calcium. It is found in river sands from India
and Brazil and in beach sand from Florida.

claims.subject: rubidium
claims.question: Who discovered rubidium?
claims.answer_short: Rubidium was discovered in 1861 by German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, who spotted it by its deep-red spectral line.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that rubidium was discovered in 1861 by the German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, who found it as an impurity mixed in with the alkali metals they were investigating. They identified it as a brand-new element from the spectral lines it emitted — one of which was a distinctive deep-red color. It was the same pair of chemists who, a year earlier in 1860, had isolated cesium using the then-new technique of flame spectroscopy.
claims.verbatim:
In 1861, the German chemists Robert Bunsen and
Gustav Kirchhoff discovered rubidium. They identified
it as an impurity mixed with the alkali metals they were
investigating; they identified rubidium as a new element from
the spectral lines it emitted, one of which is a deep red color.

claims.subject: rubidium
claims.question: Where does the name rubidium come from?
claims.answer_short: The name rubidium comes from the Latin rubidus, meaning 'deep red,' after the red spectral line by which it was identified.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the name rubidium comes from the Latin word rubidus, meaning 'deep red.' The element earned that name from the deep-red spectral line that Bunsen and Kirchhoff saw when they identified it in 1861 — the color that gave the new element away. The name is therefore a direct nod to how rubidium was first recognized: by the distinctive red light it emits.
claims.verbatim:
The name rubidium is taken from the Latin word rubidus,
which translates to “deep red.”

claims.subject: nickel
claims.question: What is nickel?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes nickel as a silvery metal and a rare element, making up only one one-hundredth of one percent of the earth's crust.
claims.answer: Wallach describes nickel as a silvery metal that comes from an ore called millerite, a compound of nickel and sulfur. He classes it as a rare element, since only one one-hundredth of one percent of the earth's crust is nickel. Even so, he says the earth's molten core is thought to be made up primarily of iron and nickel, and that nickel is also a common element found in meteorites.
claims.verbatim:
Nickel is a silvery metal found in an ore called
millerite, which is a compound of nickel and sulfur. Nickel is
considered a rare element because only one one-hundredth of
one percent of the earth’s crust is nickel. The molten core of
the earth is thought to be primarily iron and nickel. Nickel is
a common element found in meteorites.

claims.subject: nickel
claims.question: Where does the name nickel come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says nickel is a German word for Satan, from Kupfernickel, meaning 'Satan's copper.'
claims.answer: Wallach says the name nickel comes from German and actually means Satan: the element is thought to be named after the German word Kupfernickel, which he translates as 'Satan's copper.' He adds that, much like cobalt, nickel was used in the ancient world to color glass — nickel turns glass green.
claims.verbatim:
Nickel is a German
word for Satan, and the element is thought to be named for the
German Kupfernickel, or “Satan's copper.” Like cobalt, nickel
was known in the ancient world as a method for coloring glass
- nickel turns glass green.

claims.subject: nickel
claims.question: Who discovered nickel?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says nickel's pure metal was first identified in 1751 by Swedish chemist Axel Fredrik Cronstedt.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that although nickel compounds were known since ancient times, the pure metal itself was not identified until 1751, by a Swedish chemist named Axel Fredrik Cronstedt. He notes people had already put nickel to use in antiquity — for instance to color glass green — long before anyone recognized it as a distinct element.
claims.verbatim:
While nickel compounds were known since ancient
times, the pure metal was only identified in 1751 by a Swedish
chemist named Axel Fredrik Cronstedt.

claims.subject: nickel
claims.question: What is nickel used for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says nickel is used in the US five-cent coin, in powerful alnico magnets, and in nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cad) batteries.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the U.S. five-cent coin — the 'nickel' — is really an alloy of copper and nickel, with nickel making up 25 percent of it. He notes that, like iron, nickel can be made magnetic: it is part of alnico, an alloy of aluminum, nickel and cobalt used to make some of the most powerful magnets. Another important use he points to is the nickel-cadmium, or Ni-Cad, battery.
claims.verbatim:
The “nickel” or the five cent U.S. coin is made of copper
and nickel, with nickel being 25% of the alloy.

Like iron, nickel can be made magnetic; the alloy
named alnico, formed from aluminum, nickel and cobalt, is
used to produce some of the most powerful magnets.

An important use of nickel is the nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cad) battery.

claims.subject: barium
claims.question: Is barium a rare element?
claims.answer_short: No — despite being grouped with the rare earths, Wallach calls barium an abundant element, ranking sixth among all the elements in the earth's crust.
claims.answer: Although barium sits among the trace minerals and rare earths in Wallach's essential-nutrient lists, he points out that it is actually an abundant element — ranking sixth in abundance among all the elements that make up the earth's crust. In nature it occurs mainly as two ore minerals: witherite, a barium carbonate, and barite, a barium sulfate. So while the body needs it only in trace amounts, barium itself is far from scarce in the ground.
claims.verbatim:
Barium is an abundant element, ranking sixth in
abundance of the elements making up the earth’s crust. It is
found in the minerals witherite, a barium carbonate (BaCO.,),
and barite, a barium sulfate (BaSO,).

claims.subject: neodymium
claims.question: Who discovered neodymium and when?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's book recounts that neodymium was discovered in 1885 by Austrian amateur mineralogist Baron Carl Auer von Welsbach, who split the mineral didymium into two new elements.
claims.answer: According to Wallach's account, neodymium was discovered in 1885 by Baron Carl Auer von Welsbach, an Austrian amateur mineralogist. Welsbach took a mineral then known as didymium and divided it into two new and distinct elemental salts, one of which contained neodymium. A companion passage in the same book notes the other element that came out of that same didymium split was praseodymium, so the two 'twin' elements were separated from a single ore in the same year.
claims.verbatim:
Neodymium was discovered in 1885 by an Austrian
amateur mineralogist, Baron Carl Auer von Welsbach. He
divided a mineral called didymium into two new and distinct
elemental salts, one of which contained neodymium.

claims.subject: neodymium
claims.question: Where does the name neodymium come from?
claims.answer_short: Welsbach coined 'neodymium' from two Greek words, neos ('new') and didymos ('twin'), after splitting the mineral didymium.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that the name 'neodymium' was created by its discoverer, Baron Carl Auer von Welsbach, from two Greek words: neos, meaning 'new,' and didymos, meaning 'twin.' The name records how the element was found, because Welsbach had split the mineral didymium, itself the 'twin,' into two new elements, and neodymium was the 'new twin' that emerged from it.
claims.verbatim:
Welsbach
created the name for this new element from two Greek words,
neos, which translates to “new” and didymos, which translates
to “twin.”

claims.subject: neodymium
claims.question: What is neodymium used for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's book notes neodymium is used to make the most powerful magnets on earth, plus colored glass for welder's goggles and the synthetic 'ruby' in powerful lasers.
claims.answer: Beyond nutrition, Wallach's book describes neodymium's industrial uses. He says it is a magnetic substance used to create the most powerful magnets on earth, with disc magnets strong enough to sense the magnetic printing ink in paper money, which lets them detect counterfeit bills. Wallach adds that neodymium and its rose-colored oxides are also used to make colored glass for welder's goggles and the synthetic 'ruby' used in powerful lasers.
claims.verbatim:
Neodymium is a magnetic substance and is used to
create the most powerful magnets on earth. Disc magnets
made from neodymium are powerful enough to recognize
the magnetic materials in the printing ink used to print paper
money and are used to detect counterfeit paper money.

claims.subject: yttrium
claims.question: What is yttrium?
claims.answer_short: Yttrium is a 'heavy' rare earth element — a silver-gray metal Wallach counts among the plant-derived trace minerals the body needs.
claims.answer: Wallach describes yttrium as a 'heavy' rare earth element and a silver-gray metal — one so reactive that, cut into tiny pieces, it can burn spontaneously in air. Though it is not classically regarded as a nutrient, he lists it among the plant-derived minerals of humic shale that, in his view, meet the criteria to be called essential. That places yttrium in the family of rare earths he argues humans should be getting.
claims.verbatim:
Yttrium is a silver-gray metal that is reactive enough to
burn spontaneously in air w hen it is cut into tiny pieces.

claims.subject: yttrium
claims.question: Where does the name yttrium come from?
claims.answer_short: Yttrium was first identified in 1789 by Johan Gadolin, who named it for Ytterby, a small Swedish village near Stockholm.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that yttrium was first identified in 1789 by Johan Gadolin, who named the new element after Ytterby, a small Swedish village near Stockholm. He classes yttrium as a 'heavy' rare earth element and notes it is found only in small quantities in the earth's crust.
claims.verbatim:
Yttrium
was first identified in 1789 by Johan Gadolin; he named it for
the small Swedish village of Ytterby, near Stockholm.

claims.subject: yttrium
claims.question: Did the Apollo astronauts find yttrium on the moon?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says yttrium is scarce in the earth's crust, but moon rocks the Apollo astronauts brought back had a surprisingly high level of it.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that yttrium is found only in small quantities in the earth's crust, yet the rocks the Apollo astronauts brought back from the moon carried a surprisingly high level of it. Down on earth, he says, the greatest quantity of yttrium is extracted from monazite sand.
claims.verbatim:
Rocks brought back from the moon by the Apollo
astronauts had a surprisingly high level of yttrium.

claims.subject: arsenic
claims.question: What is arsenic?
claims.answer_short: Arsenic is a semimetal or metalloid that occurs mostly in mineral compounds such as realgar and orpiment, both of which are mixes of arsenic and sulfur.
claims.answer: In Wallach's account, arsenic is usually classed as a semimetal or metalloid. Only a small quantity occurs in nature in its free (pure) form; most arsenic is locked up in mineral compounds such as realgar and orpiment, both of which are mixes of arsenic and sulfur. He notes the substance has been known since ancient China, Greece and Rome, and that its name traces to the Latin arsenicum for orpiment, a common, widely used gold-like yellow pigment.
claims.verbatim:
Arsenic is often thought of as a semimetal or metalloid.
Although a small quantity of arsenic does occur in nature in
its free form, most arsenic is found in a number of mineral
compounds such as realgar and orpiment - both compounds
are mixes of arsenic and sulfur.

claims.subject: lutetium
claims.question: Where does the name lutetium come from?
claims.answer_short: The name comes from Lutetia, the ancient name for the city of Paris, coined by the French scientist Georges Urbain.
claims.answer: Wallach traces the name lutetium to Lutetia, the ancient name for the city of Paris; it was chosen by the element's French co-discoverer, Georges Urbain. Its other co-discoverer, the Austrian mineralogist Carl Auer von Welsbach, had instead picked the name 'cassiopium,' drawn from the constellation Cassiopeia. Because of that rival christening, Wallach notes that many German scientists still refer to the element as cassiopium rather than lutetium.
claims.verbatim:
Urbain created the name for the new element from
Lutetia, the ancient name for the city of Paris. Welsbach
had chosen the name cassiopium, a name derived from the
constellation Cassiopia. Many German scientists still refer to
lutetium by the name cassiopium.

claims.subject: lutetium
claims.question: Who discovered lutetium?
claims.answer_short: Lutetium was discovered in 1907 by the Austrian mineralogist Carl Auer von Welsbach and the French scientist Georges Urbain, with American chemist Charles James believed to have found it independently the same year.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that lutetium was discovered in 1907 by the Austrian mineralogist Baron Carl Auer von Welsbach and the French scientist Georges Urbain, who spotted it as an impurity in a mineral sample they had thought was pure ytterbium. There was also a third, quieter claimant: the American chemist Charles James -- nicknamed 'King James' by his colleagues and students -- is now believed to have identified the element independently that same year, though he never published his findings.
claims.verbatim:
Though he never published his findings, the American
chemist Charles James, known to his colleagues and students
as “King James,” is now believed to have independently
identified lutetium in 1907.

claims.subject: niobium
claims.question: What is niobium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes niobium as a soft, steel-gray metal found mainly in the ore columbite.
claims.answer: In Immortality, Wallach describes niobium as a soft, steel-gray metal that occurs primarily in the mineral columbite — an ore that also contains iron and manganese. He gives the element its own encyclopedic entry and includes it among the 60 essential elements and the plant-derived minerals of high-quality humic shale that, in his framework, the body needs. Wallach traces it through nature from igneous rocks and shale down to land plants and marine animals.
claims.verbatim:
Niobium is a soft, steel-gray metal that is primarily
found in the mineral columbite, an ore that also contains iron
and manganese.

claims.subject: niobium
claims.question: Who discovered niobium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says niobium was discovered by the Englishman Charles Hatchett in 1801.
claims.answer: According to Wallach in Immortality, niobium was discovered in 1801 by the Englishman Charles Hatchett, who came upon it while analyzing a sample of columbite owned by the British Museum in London. Columbite is the ore in which the soft, steel-gray metal chiefly occurs, alongside iron and manganese. Wallach recounts the discovery as part of the individual encyclopedic entry he devotes to niobium in his trace-mineral surveys.
claims.verbatim:
Niobium was discovered by the Englishman
Charles Hatchett in 1801, while he was analyzing a sample of
columbite that was owned by the British Museum in London.

claims.subject: niobium
claims.question: Where does the name niobium come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the element was named niobium for the mythological goddess Niobe.
claims.answer: In Immortality, Wallach explains that the newly discovered element was named niobium for the mythological goddess Niobe. In the same book he notes that Niobe was, in Greek mythology, the queen of the city of Thebes and the daughter of Tantalos — the figure for whom the element tantalum is named. Wallach folds this naming story into the individual entry he gives niobium, the metal he says Charles Hatchett discovered in 1801.
claims.verbatim:
The new element was named niobium for the mythological
goddess Niobe.

claims.subject: praseodymium
claims.question: What is praseodymium?
claims.answer_short: Praseodymium is a soft, silvery-white 'light' rare earth metal that tarnishes to a green oxide, one of the rare-earth minerals Wallach counts among the essential nutrients.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework praseodymium is one of the 'light' rare earth elements — a soft, silvery-white metal that tarnishes to form a green oxide. He notes it was not produced in its pure elemental form until 1931. Wallach counts it among the plant-derived rare-earth minerals he holds the human body needs.
claims.verbatim:
Praseodymium
was not produced in its pure elemental state until 1931. Itisa
soft, silvery-white metal that tarnishes to form a green oxide.

claims.subject: praseodymium
claims.question: Who discovered praseodymium?
claims.answer_short: Praseodymium was isolated in 1885 by the Austrian baron Carl Auer von Welsbach, who split the mineral didymium into two new elements.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that praseodymium was isolated in 1885 by Carl Auer von Welsbach, an Austrian baron who had a passion for mineralogy. Von Welsbach separated a mineral called didymium into two new and distinct elements, one of which contained praseodymium; the other was neodymium. Wallach adds that the pure elemental metal was not produced until 1931.
claims.verbatim:
Praseodymium was isolated in 1885 by Carl Auer
von Welsbach, an Austrian baron who had a passion for
mineralogy. He separated a mineral called didymium into
two new and distinct elements, one of which contained
praseodymium;

claims.subject: praseodymium
claims.question: Where does the name praseodymium come from?
claims.answer_short: The name comes from the Greek 'prasios' (green) and 'didymos' (twin), for the green color of the element's oxide.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that praseodymium was named from two Greek words — prasios, meaning 'green,' and didymos, meaning 'twin.' The name refers to the green color of the element's oxide. The element came from splitting the mineral didymium in two, and its sibling element was named neodymium.
claims.verbatim:
it was named from two Greek words, prasios,
which translates to “green,” and didymos, which translates to
“twin.” The name refers to the green color of the element's
oxide; the second element was neodymium.

claims.subject: titanium
claims.question: What is titanium?
claims.answer_short: Titanium is the ninth most abundant element in the earth's crust — a trace mineral discovered in 1791 and named for the Titans of Greek myth.
claims.answer: In Wallach's mineral survey, titanium is the ninth most abundant element in the earth's crust, making up 0.6 percent of the earth's mass. He records that it was first identified in 1791 by an amateur English mineralogist, the Reverend William Gregor, and named for the Titans of Greek mythology. Its common mineral sources, he notes, are rutile and ilmenite.
claims.verbatim:
Titanium is the ninth most abundant element in the
earth’s crust, and making up 0.6 per cent of the earth’s mass.
It was discovered in 1791 by an amateur English mineralogist,
the Reverend William Gregor, titanium was named for the
Titans of Greek mythology. The minerals rutile and ilemnite
are the common sources of titanium.

claims.subject: titanium
claims.question: Where does the name titanium come from?
claims.answer_short: Titanium is named for the Titans of Greek mythology.
claims.answer: Wallach records that titanium takes its name from the Titans of Greek mythology. The element was first identified in 1791 by an amateur English mineralogist, the Reverend William Gregor. In the same survey Wallach notes titanium is the ninth most abundant element in the earth's crust, drawn from the common minerals rutile and ilmenite.
claims.verbatim:
the Reverend William Gregor, titanium was named for the
Titans of Greek mythology.

claims.subject: titanium
claims.question: What is titanium used for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach points to titanium's industrial scale — each Boeing 747 jet engine holds 10,000 pounds of it.
claims.answer: Beyond being a trace mineral, titanium is also a heavily used industrial metal. Wallach notes that each jet engine from a Boeing 747 contains 10,000 pounds of titanium and its compounds. He records that it is the ninth most abundant element in the earth's crust and that its common sources are the minerals rutile and ilmenite.
claims.verbatim:
Each jet engine from a Boeing 747 contains 10,000

pounds of titanium and its compounds.

claims.subject: scandium
claims.question: What is scandium?
claims.answer_short: Scandium is a rare element that makes up only about 0.0025% of the earth's crust and occurs at an even higher rate in the sun and a few other stars.
claims.answer: In Wallach's element survey, scandium (symbol Sc) is described as a rare element that makes up only about 0.0025% of the earth's crust — and, unusually, it occurs at a higher rate in the sun and a few other stars than it does on Earth. Some geochemists group scandium with the rare-earth metals, a class Wallach holds to be vital to health and longevity. Within the body it appears only in trace amounts, where it concentrates in the heart and bone.
claims.verbatim:
Scandium is a rare element that is found in the crust of
the earth at 0.0025%, it is found in a higher rate in the sun and a
few other stars.

claims.subject: scandium
claims.question: Who discovered scandium?
claims.answer_short: Scandium was predicted by Mendeleyev in 1871 from the periodic chart and then discovered in 1879 by Lars Fredrik Nilson.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that scandium's existence was predicted by Mendeleyev back in 1871, worked out from the periodic chart before the element had ever been isolated. It was then actually discovered eight years later, in 1879, by Lars Fredrik Nilson. Scandium is therefore one of the elements Mendeleyev foresaw from his chart and that was later confirmed to be real.
claims.verbatim:
Scandium, using the periodic chart in 1871, was
one of the elements that Mendeleyev predicted would exist. In
1879, scandium was discovered by Lars Fredrik Nilson, who
named the element after his homeland. Scandinavia.

claims.subject: scandium
claims.question: Where does the name scandium come from?
claims.answer_short: When Lars Fredrik Nilson discovered scandium in 1879 he named it after his homeland, Scandinavia.
claims.answer: When Lars Fredrik Nilson discovered scandium in 1879, Wallach notes, he named the new element after his own homeland — Scandinavia. So the name 'scandium' is a direct nod to the Scandinavian region the chemist came from.
claims.verbatim:
In
1879, scandium was discovered by Lars Fredrik Nilson, who
named the element after his homeland. Scandinavia.

claims.subject: rhenium
claims.question: What is rhenium?
claims.answer_short: Rhenium is one of the rarest elements on Earth — so scarce that a million pounds of ore yields only a single gram.
claims.answer: In Immortality, Wallach calls rhenium one of the most rare of all earthly elements. To show how scarce it is, he notes that producing a single gram takes one million pounds of molybdenite ore. He records that this extreme rarity carried a price of $10,000 per gram back in 1928.
claims.verbatim:
Rhenium is one of the most-rare of all earthly elements.
It takes one million pounds of molybdenite ore to produce
one gram of rhenium, resulting in a price of $10,000 per gram
in 1928.

claims.subject: rhenium
claims.question: Who discovered rhenium?
claims.answer_short: Rhenium's existence was predicted and then discovered in 1925 by German chemists Ida Tacke, Walter Nodack, and Otto Carl Berg.
claims.answer: In Immortality, Wallach recounts that in 1925 the existence of rhenium was first predicted and then discovered by three German chemists: Ida Tacke, Walter Nodack, and Otto Carl Berg. The same three researchers gave the newly found element its name. Wallach relays this alongside his account of rhenium as one of the most rare elements on Earth — so scarce, he notes, that a single gram cost $10,000 in 1928.
claims.verbatim:
In 1925, the existence of rhenium was predicted by and
then discovered by the German chemists Ida Tacke, Walter
Nodack, and Otto Carl Berg.

claims.subject: rhenium
claims.question: Where does the name rhenium come from?
claims.answer_short: Rhenium is named from the Latin word Rhenus, which translates to the Rhine River.
claims.answer: In Immortality, Wallach explains that the name rhenium comes from the Latin word Rhenus, which translates to the Rhine River. The three German chemists who discovered the element in 1925 — Ida Tacke, Walter Nodack, and Otto Carl Berg — chose the name. It is one of several elements whose names Wallach traces back to their Latin and Greek roots in the same survey.
claims.verbatim:
They named rhenium from the
Latin word Rhenus, which translates to the Rhine River.
topics: where does the name come from

claims.subject: dysprosium
claims.question: What is dysprosium?
claims.answer_short: Dysprosium is a soft, shiny, silvery rare-earth metal — soft enough to be cut with a knife and fairly stable in air.
claims.answer: Dysprosium (Dy) is one of the rare-earth metals in Dr. Wallach's roster of essential elements. He describes it as a soft metal — soft enough to be cut with a knife — that is shiny and silvery and stays fairly stable when exposed to air. In his classification it belongs to the yttrium/ytterbium group of the rare earths, the same plant-derived mineral family he argues the human body needs.
claims.verbatim:
Dysprosium is a metal that is soft enough to be cut
with a knife; it is a shiny, silvery element that is fairly stable
in air.

claims.subject: dysprosium
claims.question: What is dysprosium used for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes dysprosium forms alloys whose magnetic features help compact discs function efficiently.
claims.answer: Wallach's encyclopedic entry for dysprosium notes a modern industrial use for the rare-earth metal: it forms alloys whose magnetic features are put to work helping compact discs function efficiently. It is the same soft, shiny, silvery element he catalogs among the essential rare earths, here singled out for the magnetic-alloy properties that make it useful in compact-disc technology.
claims.verbatim:
Dysprosium forms alloys whose magnetic features are
employed to help compact discs function efficiently.

claims.subject: thulium
claims.question: What is thulium?
claims.answer_short: Thulium is a soft, bright silvery 'heavy' rare-earth metal, so soft it can be cut with a knife, and one of the scarcest of the rare earths.
claims.answer: Wallach describes thulium (symbol Tm) as a 'heavy' rare earth belonging to the yttrium/ytterbium group of rare-earth metals. He calls it extremely rare and pictures it as a bright, silvery metal so soft that it can be cut with a knife. Although Wallach counts thulium among the rare earths he considers essential plant-derived trace minerals, it occurs in nature only in minute amounts.
claims.verbatim:
Thulium is a bright silvery metal that is soft that it can
be cut with a knife.

claims.subject: thulium
claims.question: Who discovered thulium?
claims.answer_short: Thulium was discovered in 1879 by the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, who isolated its greenish oxide from the mineral erbia.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve discovered thulium in 1879 by isolating its greenish oxide from the mineral erbia. Cleve then named the new element for Thule, the ancient name for Scandinavia. Wallach classes thulium among the 'heavy' rare earths of the yttrium/ytterbium group.
claims.verbatim:
The Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve discovered the
element in 1879 by isolating its greenish oxide from the mineral
erbia.

claims.subject: thulium
claims.question: Where does the name thulium come from?
claims.answer_short: Thulium is named after Thule, the ancient name for Scandinavia, chosen by its discoverer Per Teodor Cleve.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that thulium takes its name from Thule, the ancient name for Scandinavia. It was the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve who chose the name, having discovered the element in 1879 by isolating its greenish oxide from the mineral erbia.
claims.verbatim:
He named his new element for Thule, the ancient name
for Scandinavia.

claims.subject: thulium
claims.question: Where does thulium come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says thulium's main source is the mineral monazite, found in river sands in India and Brazil and in beach sand in Florida.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, the main source of thulium is the mineral monazite, which is only about seven thousandths of one percent thulium. Monazite contains all of the rare-earth elements along with thorium and calcium. Wallach says it is found in the river sands of India and Brazil and in the beach sand of Florida.
claims.verbatim:
The main source of thulium is the mineral monazite,
which consists of approximately seven thousandths of one
percent thulium. Monazite, which contains all of the rare earth
elements in addition to thorium and calcium, is found in the
river sands in India and Brazil and in beach sand in Florida.

claims.subject: samarium
claims.question: Who discovered samarium and when?
claims.answer_short: Samarium was discovered in 1879 by the French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that samarium, which he calls the fifth most abundant of the rare earth elements, was discovered in 1879 by the French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran. He identified the new element by correctly reading its spectral absorption lines in a mineral called samarskite. Commercially, Wallach notes, samarium is drawn from the ores monazite and bastnasite, with monazite found in the river sands of India and Brazil and in Florida beach sand.
claims.verbatim:
elements, it was discovered in 1879 by the French chemist
Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, who correctly identified

claims.subject: samarium
claims.question: Where does the name samarium come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says samarium was identified in a mineral called samarskite, which was itself named for a Russian army officer, Colonel Samarski.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, when samarium was discovered in 1879 its spectral absorption lines were first identified in a mineral called samarskite. He notes that samarskite itself was named for a Russian army officer, Colonel Samarski, tying the mineral in which the element was found back to that officer.
claims.verbatim:
spectral absorption lines in a mineral called
samarskite, which has been named for a Russian army officer,
Colonel Samarski.

claims.subject: ytterbium
claims.question: Where does the name ytterbium come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says ytterbium was discovered in 1878 by French chemist Jean de Marignac and named after the small Swedish village of Ytterby.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, ytterbium was discovered in 1878 by the French chemist Jean de Marignac, who found it within the mineral erbia -- which, in his telling, made it the first 'rare earth' element ever discovered. Its name comes from Ytterby, a small Swedish village. Wallach adds that the main source of ytterbium is monazite sand -- a material that holds all of the rare earths along with thorium and calcium -- recovered from river sand in India and Brazil and from beach sand in Florida.
claims.verbatim:
The French chemist Jean de Marignac discovered this
element in 1878 as a part of the mineral known as erbia and
was the first “rare earth” element discovered. It was named for
the Swedish village of Ytterby. The main source of ytterbium
is monazite sand which contains all of the rare earths, thorium
and calcium and is found in river sand from India and Brazil
and beach sand from Florida at three hundredths of one per
cent.

claims.subject: holmium
claims.question: Who discovered holmium?
claims.answer_short: Two Swiss chemists first spotted holmium's spectral lines in 1878 but couldn't identify it, and Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve isolated and named it in 1879.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that holmium was first detected in 1878, when two Swiss chemists noticed its characteristic spectral lines but could not identify the element responsible, so they referred to it only as "element X." A year later, in 1879, the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve isolated and identified it and gave it the name Holmia, after his home town of Stockholm. In Wallach's survey holmium is one of the rare-earth trace minerals, scattered thinly through rocks, plants and animals and collecting mainly in bone in land animals.
claims.verbatim:
In 1878, two Swiss chemists noticed holmium’s
characteristic spectral lines, but could not identify them, so
they referred to the unknown element as “element X.” In 1879,
a Swedish chemist, Per Teodor Cleve isolated and identified
the element and called it Holmia, Latin for his home town of
Stockholm.

claims.subject: holmium
claims.question: Where does the name holmium come from?
claims.answer_short: Holmium is named Holmia -- Latin for Stockholm, the home town of Per Teodor Cleve, the Swedish chemist who isolated it in 1879.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, holmium takes its name from Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm, the home town of the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, who isolated and identified the element in 1879. The element had first been noticed a year earlier, in 1878, through its distinctive spectral lines, before Cleve pinned it down and named it. So the name of this rare-earth trace mineral is essentially a Latin tribute to Cleve's own home town.
claims.verbatim:
In 1879,
a Swedish chemist, Per Teodor Cleve isolated and identified
the element and called it Holmia, Latin for his home town of
Stockholm.

claims.subject: tantalum
claims.question: Where does the name tantalum come from?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts that the Swedish chemist Anders Gustav Ekeberg, who discovered the element in 1802, named it after Tantalos, the father of Niobe in Greek mythology.
claims.answer: In Immortality, Wallach traces tantalum's name to Greek mythology. Its discoverer, the Swedish chemist Anders Gustav Ekeberg, found the new element in 1802 near the Swedish town of Ytterby, and named it for Tantalos, the father of Niobe. Wallach notes that Ytterby played an important role in the history of chemistry, serving as a source of minerals for the discovery of the rare earths. So the element carries a mythological namesake tied to one of science's most important mineral-discovery locales.
claims.verbatim:
Anders Gustav Ekeberg, aSwedish chemist, discovered
the new element in 1802 near the Swedish town of Ytterby,
which played an important role in the history of chemistry,
particularly as a source of minerals for the discovery of rare
earths.

Ekeberg named his new element for Tantalos, the father

claims.subject: tantalum
claims.question: Was tantalum confused with niobium?
claims.answer_short: For nearly 50 years after Ekeberg announced it, many chemists thought he had mistaken tantalum for niobium, and pure tantalum metal was not produced until 1903.
claims.answer: Wallach relates that tantalum had a rocky start as a recognized element. For almost 50 years after Ekeberg announced his discovery, many chemists believed he had actually confused tantalum with niobium. The matter was not settled until pure tantalum metal was finally produced in 1903 -- more than a century after the 1802 discovery. Wallach frames the mix-up within the element's mythological pedigree, noting it was named for Tantalos, the father of Niobe, queen of the city of Thebes.
claims.verbatim:
of Niobe, who, in Greek mythology, was queen of the city of
Thebes. For almost 50 years after Ekeberg’s announcement
of his new element, many chemist thought he had confused
tantalum with niobium. Pure tantalum metal was not
produced until 1903.

claims.subject: tantalum
claims.question: What is tantalum used for?
claims.answer_short: Wallach notes that tantalum -- whose principal ore is columbite -- is used for dental and joint prosthesis.
claims.answer: In his survey of tantalum, Wallach reports that the element is used for dental and joint prosthesis. Its principal ore is the mineral columbite, which he says is widely distributed throughout the world, with large deposits in Africa, Thailand, Portugal and Canada. These are among the few concrete real-world uses and sources Wallach records for this rare, plant-derived trace mineral.
claims.verbatim:
The principal ore of tantalum is the mineral columbite,
which is widely distributed throughout the world, with large
deposits in Africa, Thailand, Portugal and Canada. Tantalum
is used for dental and joint prosthesis.

claims.subject: hafnium
claims.question: What is hafnium?
claims.answer_short: Hafnium is a bright, silvery-white metal so chemically bound to its 'twin' zirconium that the two are almost impossible to separate, and Wallach counts it among his essential trace minerals.
claims.answer: In Wallach's account, hafnium is a bright, silvery-white metal whose elemental properties and history are inseparable from those of its 'twin,' the element zirconium. Hafnium is actually more dense than zirconium, yet the two metals are so chemically similar that it is almost impossible to work with one without working with the other. Wallach also lists hafnium among his 60 essential elements and among the plant-derived minerals of a high-quality humic shale, trace minerals that, though not 'classically' considered essential, he holds meet the criteria of an essential nutrient.
claims.verbatim:
Hafnium is a bright, silvery-white metal, its elemental
properties and history are joined with the element zirconium.

claims.subject: hafnium
claims.question: Where does the name hafnium come from?
claims.answer_short: Hafnium is named for Copenhagen; its finders Coster and von Hevesy honored Bohr's native city using its Latin name, Hafnia.
