claims.answer: Wallach recounts that hafnium was finally found by Dirk Coster, a Dutch physicist, and George Karl von Hevesy, a Hungarian physicist. To honor Bohr, the two named their new element after his native city, Copenhagen, using the Latin translation of that city's name, Hafnia. So the metal's name is a tribute both to the city of Copenhagen and to Bohr himself.
claims.verbatim:
Ultimately, Dirk Coster, a Dutch
physicist and George Karl von Hevesy, a Hungarian physicist
found the element. To honor Bohr, Coster and de Hevesy
named their new element for his native city, Copenhagen,
using the Latin translation, Hafnia.

claims.subject: zirconium
claims.question: What is zirconium?
claims.answer_short: Zirconium is a mineral Wallach counts among the essential trace elements and rare earths; its best-known form is the gemstone mineral zircon, a crystalline zirconium silicate.
claims.answer: Zirconium is a mineral Wallach counts among the essential trace elements and rare earths, and its best-known and most familiar form is the mineral zircon -- a crystalline compound of zirconium silicate. Zircon occurs in a wide variety of colors, and once cut and polished it is prized as a semiprecious gem. Because it has a very high index of refraction, bending light through large angles, colorless zircon crystals are so brilliant that they are often used as a diamond substitute in imitation jewelry.
claims.verbatim:
Zircon is a crystalline compound of zirconium silicate
(ZrSiO,). Itis found ina variety of colors, and when the crystal
is cut and polished, the stone is regarded as a semiprecious
gem. Zircon has a very high index of refraction, which means
that it has the property of bending light through large angles.
Because the colorless crystals of zircon have a high brilliance
they are oftentimes used as a diamond substitute in faux

jewelry.

claims.subject: zirconium
claims.question: Who discovered zirconium?
claims.answer_short: Zirconium was discovered in 1787 by the German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, though its best-known compound, zircon, had been known since ancient times.
claims.answer: Zirconium was discovered in 1787 by the German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. Its best-known compound, the mineral zircon, is far older as a known substance -- it has been recognized since ancient times and is even referred to in the Bible. So while the element itself was a comparatively late chemical discovery, the stone that carries it had been prized long before.
claims.verbatim:
Zirconium was discovered in 1787 by the German
chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The best known compound
of zirconium is the mineral zircon. This mineral has been
known since ancient times and is even referred to in the Bible.

claims.subject: zirconium
claims.question: Where does the name zirconium come from?
claims.answer_short: The name zirconium comes from 'zargun,' the Arabic word for zircon, which translates to 'gold color.'
claims.answer: Zirconium takes its name from the mineral zircon, and 'zircon' in turn comes from 'zargun,' the Arabic name for the stone. 'Zargun' translates to 'gold color.' So the element's name traces back through Arabic to a word describing the color of the crystal it was first known in.
claims.verbatim:
Zirconium derives its name from zargun, which is the Arabic
name for zircon and translates to “gold color.”

claims.subject: zirconium
claims.question: Is zirconium related to hafnium?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- zirconium and hafnium are chemical twins, so alike that Wallach says it is almost impossible to work with one without working with the other.
claims.answer: Wallach describes zirconium and hafnium as closely bound twin metals. Although hafnium is more dense than zirconium, the two are chemically so similar that it is almost impossible to work with one without working with the other. Their elemental properties and history are intertwined -- zirconium's ever-present, diamond-like presence long overshadowed hafnium, which is one reason hafnium was not discovered until 1923 even though it is a common, abundant metal.
claims.verbatim:
Hafnium, is more dense than zirconium, however, the two
metals are chemically similar and it is almost impossible to
work with one without working with the other.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: Is there real proof that rare-earth minerals extend life?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach cites lab studies where adding rare-earth minerals to animals' diets doubled their expected lifespan, and argues that because these minerals are stripped from our food, daily supplementation is the only reliable way to get them.
claims.answer: Wallach points to controlled feeding studies as his hard evidence for the rare earths. When rare-earth minerals were added to laboratory animals' diets — on top of the recognized major and trace minerals — the animals' expected lifespan doubled across several different species. He holds these same rare earths are vital to animal (and most probably human) health and longevity, yet they have been stripped from our modern food supply, so in his framework daily supplementation is the only reliable way to get enough.
claims.verbatim:
Rare Earths added to laboratory animal's diets as a
supplement to the well recognized major and trace minerals
have doubled the expected life span of several different
species.

claims.subject: nitrates
claims.question: Are nitrates in processed meat bad for you?
claims.answer_short: Salt compounds added to cured meats and canned food to block bacteria and keep meat red; Wallach warns the stomach converts them into cancer-causing nitrosamines and they suppress the thyroid, making them a goitrogen.
claims.answer: Nitrates are salt compounds formed when nitric acid is neutralized by bases such as sodium or potassium hydroxide. Wallach explains they are added to canned foods and cured, preserved meats to prevent bacteria from growing and to keep the meat colored red. His health concern is what happens after you eat them: in the acid environment of the stomach, nitrates (and the related nitrites) are converted into nitrosamines, compounds that can become cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens) and can suppress thyroid function. For that reason he classes both dietary nitrates (deli slices, sandwich meats) and water-borne nitrates among the "goitrogens" — substances that interfere with normal thyroid metabolism and can produce thyroid disease.
claims.verbatim:
When nitric acid is neutralized with bases including
sodium and potassium hydroxide, it forms compounds called
nitrates. Nitrates and nitrites are added to canned foods and
preserved meats to help prevent the growth of bacteria and to
color meat red.

Nitrates and nitrites are converted to nitrosamines in
the acid environment of the stomach; these compounds can
be converted to cancer causing chemicals (carcinogens) and
can suppress thyroid function.

claims.subject: nitrites
claims.question: Are nitrites in bacon and cured meat bad for you?
claims.answer_short: Preservatives added with nitrates to cured meats to block bacteria and redden meat; Wallach warns the stomach converts them into cancer-causing nitrosamines, they suppress the thyroid, and he counts them as a dietary free radical to avoid.
claims.answer: Nitrites are preservative compounds added, alongside nitrates, to canned foods and cured or preserved meats — bacon, ham, sausage, bologna, salami, pepperoni, jerky and deli meats — to stop bacteria from growing and to keep the meat looking red. Wallach's warning is about what happens once they are eaten: in the acid environment of the stomach, nitrites (and nitrates) are converted into nitrosamines, compounds that can turn into cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens) and can suppress thyroid function. He therefore counts nitrites among the "goitrogens" that interfere with normal thyroid metabolism, and lists them among the dietary free radicals a person should cut down on to slow aging.
claims.verbatim:
Nitrates and nitrites are added to canned foods and
preserved meats to help prevent the growth of bacteria and to
color meat red.

Nitrates and nitrites are converted to nitrosamines in
the acid environment of the stomach; these compounds can
be converted to cancer causing chemicals (carcinogens) and
can suppress thyroid function.

claims.subject: berylliosis
claims.question: What is berylliosis?
claims.answer_short: A painful, sometimes fatal lung disease caused by inhaling beryllium oxide dust from mining and industry; its chronic form resembles pulmonary sarcoidosis.
claims.answer: Berylliosis is a painful and sometimes fatal lung disease caused by inhaling beryllium oxide dust, which is released as a contaminant during the mining and industrial handling of the metal. Beryllium itself is a mineral — the scientific name of the gemstone beryl is beryllium aluminum silicate — so the hazard comes not from the element in food but from breathing its powdered oxide. Wallach describes two forms: an acute form (acute beryllium disease, or chemical pneumonitis) first reported in Europe in 1933 and in the United States in 1943, and a chronic form — chronic berylliosis — that resembles pulmonary sarcoidosis, another chronic lung disease.
claims.verbatim:
Inhalation of beryllium oxide dust (mining and
industrial contaminants) can lead to “berylliosis,” a painful
and sometimes fatal lung disease.

claims.subject: rare_earth_elements
claims.question: What are the rare earth elements?
claims.answer_short: Wallach defines the rare earths as a large family of chemically very similar metal oxides, drawn from minerals that are widely distributed but relatively scarce.
claims.answer: Wallach describes the rare earths as a whole category of chemically very similar metal oxides, not a single element. He says they are drawn from minerals that are widely distributed across the earth yet relatively scarce, and treats this large family of related metals as one class.
claims.verbatim:
The term, rare earths, refers to any of a large series of
very similar oxides of metals obtained from widely distributed
but relatively scarce minerals.

claims.subject: high_fructose_corn_syrup
claims.question: Why do I crave soda and soft drinks?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says craving high-fructose-corn-syrup soft drinks first (and water last) is a sign of chromium and vanadium deficiency, which drives intense thirst and carbohydrate hunger.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, reaching first for high-fructose-corn-syrup-laden soft drinks is a sign of mineral deficiency rather than simple thirst. Chromium and vanadium deficiencies manifest as an intense thirst for liquid — and minerally deficient people reach for HFCS soft drinks first and plain water last — together with a hunger for carbohydrates such as soft drinks, sweetened coffee and tea, alcohol, pasta, desserts, and bread.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium and vanadium deficiencies are manifested
by an intense thirst for liquid (high fructose corn syrup laden
soft drinks being the usual first choice and water the last for
minerally deficient humans) and hunger for carbohydrates
(i.e. - soft drinks, coffee and tea with added sugar, alcohol,
pasta, deserts, bread, etc.).

claims.subject: high_fructose_corn_syrup
claims.question: What is high fructose corn syrup?
claims.answer_short: It is a manufactured sweetener made from corn, sugar beet, and sugar cane, built from glucose and fructose (levulose), the sweetest of the natural sugars.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that high-fructose corn syrup is a manufactured sweetener made from grains (corn) as well as from sugar beet and sugar cane. Fructose — also called levulose or fruit sugar — occurs naturally with glucose and sucrose in honey and fruit and is the sweetest of the natural sugars; sweeteners containing glucose and levulose are processed from these crops to make high-fructose corn syrup.
claims.verbatim:
Fructose: (levulose, fruit sugar) is found together with
glucose and sucrose in honey and fruit. It is the sweetest of the
natural sugars. Sweeteners containing glucose and levulose
can be made from grains (corn) as well as from the sugar beet
and sugar cane to make high-fructose corn syrup.

claims.subject: intermittent_fasting
claims.question: Does intermittent fasting help you live longer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites a 1940s Carlson and Holzol study in which rats fasted every other, third, or fourth day extended their maximum life span 20 to 30%, from 800 to 1,000-1,100 days.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in the 1940s professors A.H. Carlson and F. Holzol added a "creative twist" to the caloric-restriction (CR) longevity approach by testing intermittent periods of fasting in rats. The animals were free-choice fed a high-quality diet rich in vitamins and minerals in unlimited amounts, but were fasted completely every other day (one group), every third day (another group), or every fourth day (a third group). As Wallach reports the result, the un-fasted rats reached a maximum life span of 800 days, while all three intermittently fasted groups extended maximum life span to 1,000 to 1,100 days — a 20 to 30% increase. Wallach presents intermittent fasting here as a variant of his "under-nutrition without malnutrition" theme: the fasting is paired with a nutrient-dense diet on the eating days, not with starvation.

claims.subject: twenty_thousand_autopsies
claims.question: Why did Wallach start doing autopsies?
claims.answer_short: An NIH-funded project set out to see whether pollution caused deaths in zoo animals and humans; the autopsies pointed instead to nutritional deficiency.
claims.answer: Wallach's autopsy program grew out of a $7.5 million grant from the National Institutes of Health, secured by zoo director Marlin Perkins and Washington University botany professor Dr. Barry Commoner. The project, the Center for the Biology of Natural Systems, was created to autopsy zoo animals and urban-dwelling humans who had died of natural causes, to determine whether environmental pollution or food contamination might be a factor in their deaths. What the autopsies actually found was that every animal and every human dying of natural causes died of a nutritional deficiency disease rather than of pollution.

claims.subject: stem_cells
claims.question: Who kept chicken heart cells alive for 34 years?
claims.answer_short: Dr. Alexis Carrel grew fibroblast 'stem cells' from chicken hearts that kept multiplying for 34 years, giving rise to the idea of cellular immortality.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that in 1912 Dr. Alexis Carrel, a Nobel laureate for pioneering end-to-end anastomosis (the suturing together of blood vessels), began growing undifferentiated fibroblasts, connective-tissue cells he calls 'stem cells,' from chicken hearts in flasks at the Rockefeller Institute. Fed on filtered extracts of blended chicken embryos, these cultures kept multiplying and growing for 34 years, including two years after Carrel's own death. Wallach presents this as the basis of 'cellular immortality': the theory that cells are inherently immortal if they are fed a perfect diet and kept in a perfect environment.

She earned an MS in transplantation immunology from Zhongshan Medical University in Canton and, like all Chinese doctors, was trained in Traditional Chinese Medicine (acupuncture, herbs, manipulation, food medicine, massage, and hydrotherapy) before entering Western-style medical school. claims.subject: vanadium
claims.question: What are the signs of vanadium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Diabetes and hypoglycemia. Wallach counts vanadium (with chromium) as essential to blood-sugar control, so its deficiency drives insulin up — producing type II diabetes and low blood sugar — and shows up day-to-day as thirst and relentless carbohydrate and sugar cravings.
claims.answer: Wallach frames adult-onset (type II) diabetes as, at root, a simple mineral-deficiency disease in which vanadium — alongside chromium — is central. When dietary intake or absorption of chromium and vanadium is insufficient, blood insulin climbs, and that excess insulin in turn produces hypoglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, and pre-diabetes. So in his framework the signs of a vanadium deficiency are precisely diabetes and low blood sugar (hypoglycemia); at the everyday level the deficiency also shows up as thirst, an obsessive hunger for carbohydrates and sugar, and the 'munchies.'
claims.verbatim:
VANADIUM DEFICIENCY
diabetes
hypoglycemia
ZINC DEFICIENCY
acne

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Do muscle cramps and eye twitches mean low calcium?
claims.answer_short: Wallach teaches that muscle cramps and twitches, including eyelid twitches, signal calcium deficiency even when blood calcium reads normal, because calcium is drained from the cells before blood levels ever fall.
claims.answer: Wallach teaches that muscle cramps and twitches — including eyelid (eye) twitches — are signs of calcium deficiency even when the blood calcium reading stays within the "normal" range. He explains that calcium is depleted from the cells (severely enough to cause life-threatening convulsions) before blood calcium levels ever fall, so a normal blood calcium does not rule out deficiency. Calcium's reference range is 9–10.8 mg per 100 ml.

claims.question: Can a blood test detect calcium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: No — Wallach says your blood calcium stays in the normal range even during a raging calcium deficiency, so a standard blood test misses it.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that most blood values are held within a narrow range by homeostatic mechanisms, so a person can be seriously ill yet show a "normal" blood test. Calcium is his prime example: someone can be suffering spontaneous fractures from raging osteoporosis while their blood calcium still reads normal. He states that in a typical audience of 1,000 or more people they will all have a "normal" blood calcium (a below-normal level would itself cause convulsions) yet most of them are calcium deficient.

claims.answer_short: Wallach's take: its successes come mostly from accidentally cutting gluten - people with hidden celiac disease finally absorb minerals, vitamins and fats. The value is nutritional, not the yin/yang theory.

The explanation he gives is nutritional — resolving malabsorption — rather than the yin/yang imbalance that macrobiotic philosophy holds to be the cause of all disease.

claims.subject: chiropractic
claims.question: What is chiropractic?
claims.answer_short: A drug-free, surgery-free physical medicine holding that many ills come from 'subluxations' (misaligned vertebrae) pressing on spinal nerves - the West's most accepted alternative therapy.
claims.answer: Wallach describes chiropractic as a physical, drug-free and surgery-free form of medicine. Its philosophy holds that many diseases — especially physical discomfort and many visceral (internal-organ) malfunctions — are caused by "subluxations" (partial misalignments) of the vertebral joints pressing on spinal nerves. He notes chiropractic is the most accepted alternative therapy in the Western world, licensed in all 50 U.S. states with comprehensive insurance and Medicare coverage.

claims.question: Where does chiropractic come from?
claims.answer_short: Spinal manipulation is ancient (Egypt, China, Babylon); it reached the West in 1895 when D.D. Palmer cured a janitor's deafness, and chiropractors won a 1987 antitrust case against the AMA.

Palmer cured his janitor's deafness with cervical (neck) manipulation; in 1987 chiropractors won a landmark U.S. antitrust case against the American Medical Association (AMA).

claims.subject: somatic_therapies
claims.question: What is osteopathy?
claims.answer_short: A manipulation-based healing art of body and spine, founded ~130 years ago by engineer Andrew Still after he lost all three children to orthodox medicine; today most D.O.s practice much like M.D.s.
claims.answer: Wallach describes osteopathy as a manipulation-based healing art (of body and spine) developed over 100 years ago by Andrew Still — an engineer who, after losing all three of his children to orthodox medicine during a meningitis outbreak, concluded that disease results from a mechanical breakdown of the body. He notes most modern Doctors of Osteopathy (D.O.s) are now hard to distinguish from M.D.s in the orthodox "burn, cut and poison" approach, though a few offer chelation therapy instead of rushing into bypass surgery.

Osteopathy originated as a type of manipulation of body and spine to heal disease.

claims.subject: somatic_therapies
claims.question: What is reflexology, and how is it meant to work?
claims.answer_short: An ancient Chinese and East Indian system: 'zones' on the soles and palms map to the internal organs, so 10-30 minutes of thumb compression on a point is meant to treat the organ it stands for.
claims.answer: Wallach describes reflexology as an ancient Chinese and East Indian diagnostic and treatment system in which the soles of the feet and palms of the hands carry "zones" or "points" that represent the visceral (internal) organs and systems. Treatment is 10-30 minutes of compression massage with the thumb or index finger; it works particularly well for physiological or functional disease, and the practitioner searches the foot or hand for "crystals" or "nodules" to work out.

Reflexology is an ancient Chinese and
east Indian diagnostic and treatment system.
The soles of the feet and palms of the hands

claims.subject: somatic_therapies
claims.question: What is Rolfing (structural integration)?
claims.answer_short: A deep, uncomfortable connective-tissue massage devised by Ida Rolf to break down 'pathological' tissue and correct posture - said to leave patients half an inch to an inch taller.
claims.answer: Wallach describes Rolfing (structural integration) as a deep body-massage therapy — named after Ida Rolf, a biological-chemistry graduate of Barnard College (1920) — used to break down pathological connective tissue. Before-and-after photos track posture; treatments are very uncomfortable but most patients feel the gains are worth it, and releasing the muscles, ligaments and connective tissue makes patients half an inch to one inch taller.

claims.subject: ayurveda
claims.question: What is Ayurveda, and how old is it?
claims.answer_short: Possibly the most ancient medical art - 'ayur' (life) + 'veda' (science), recorded ~1200 BC. 80-90% of Indians use it, and Wallach says the Greeks (even Pythagoras) learned medicine from the East Indians.
claims.answer: Wallach describes Ayurvedic medicine as possibly the most ancient of all medical arts. The word translates to 'life sciences' (ayur = life, veda = science) and is recorded in the Atharva Veda around 1200 BC; the 'Sambuta' encyclopedia of medicines was written about 500 BC. Eighty to ninety percent of people in India are treated with Ayurvedic medicine. Wallach notes that although Western medicine is generally thought to come from the Greeks, the Greeks learned it from the East Indians, and that Pythagoras, one of Hippocrates' early teachers, obtained his whole system from India.
claims.verbatim:

sciences." Ayur = life, veda = science is recorded in the Atharva veda 1200 BC

claims.subject: ayurveda
claims.question: How does Ayurveda explain health and disease?
claims.answer_short: The body is seven tissues (Dhatus) kept in balance by food, so 'wrong food' causes disease; it works with the energies Pitta, Kapha and Vaya and five elements, treating imbalances rather than diagnoses.
claims.answer: Wallach explains the Ayurvedic model of health: the human body is made up of seven tissues (Dhatus), and a person is healthy when the Dhatus are in balance. Food, after digestion, feeds the Dhatus, so any imbalance in food creates disease — Ayurvedic medicine places great emphasis on 'wrong food' as a cause of disease, while also recognizing that physical activity, sleep, sexual habits, climate, emotional status, surroundings, age, and gender influence disease. At the level of the individual mind it describes three activities (Rojas, Tamas, Satva) and the energies Pitta (heat), Kapha (phlegm/cold), and Vaya (air); the human being and the universe are composed of five elements or Bhutas (ether, air, fire, water, earth). Ayurveda treats 'imbalances' rather than arriving at a Western-style diagnosis.
claims.verbatim:
Ayurveda expects the patient to take
part in his own cure. According to Ayurveda,
the human body is made up of seven tissues or
Dhatus; if the Dhatus are in balance, the individual is healthy. Food after digestion feeds the
Dhatus; any imbalance in food creates disease
in the Dhatus. Ayurvedic medicine puts great
emphasis on "wrong food" as a cause of disease

claims.subject: homeopathy
claims.question: What are Schuessler cell salts (Biochemics)?
claims.answer_short: A 19th-century system from Dr. Wilhelm Schuessler, who analyzed the ash of cremated bodies and found twelve mineral 'salts' he called essential to health; given in homeopathic (highly diluted) doses. Later workers added ~30 trace elements.
claims.answer: Wallach describes Biochemics (Schuessler Cell Salts), a 19th-century system of medical therapy devised by the physician and chemist Dr. Wilhelm Heinrich Schuessler. Schuessler based it on analyzing the ashes of cremated human bodies, in which he found twelve mineral 'salts' he considered basic and essential to human health. Influenced by the chemist Dr. Liebig, he held that the body's cells are composed of organic material, water, and 'salts.' In more recent times an additional 30 trace elements have been recognized and added to the original twelve cell salts.
claims.verbatim:
Biochemics (Schuessler Cell Salts) is
a system of medical therapy devised in the last
century by a physician and chemist, Dr.
Wilhelm Heinrich Schuessler. He based his
"science" on the analysis of the ashes of cremated human bodies. In these ashes Schuessler
found twelve (12) "salts" (minerals) basic and
essential to human health

claims.subject: homeopathy
claims.question: What are Bach flower remedies?
claims.answer_short: Homeopathic-style flower preparations from bacteriologist Edward Bach (1880-1936), who first collected sun-warmed flower dew; aimed at emotional imbalance rather than physical disease, taken as four drops four times a day.
claims.answer: Wallach describes Bach Flower Remedies, conceived by Edward Bach (1880-1936), who began his career as a bacteriologist at University College Hospital, London, and as pathologist and bacteriologist at the London Homeopathic Hospital. Bach initially collected sun-warmed dew from flowers, later expanding his 'remedies' to a homeopathic-like water preparation of flowers; traditionally the patient takes four drops of the diluted remedy four times per day. Wallach notes Bach's remedies were designed to address emotional imbalances rather than physical disease. (Scope note: Bach flower therapy is a homeopathy-class system using highly diluted preparations; included as Wallach's descriptive account of the modality.)
claims.verbatim:
Bach Remedies (Bach Flower Remedies) were conceived by Edward Bach (1880-
1936). Bach started his career as a bacteriologist in the University College Hospital in London and as the pathologist and bacteriologist
to the London Homeopathic Hospital

claims.subject: color_therapy
claims.question: What is color therapy?
claims.answer_short: Using colored lights or panels for a healing effect — recorded in ancient Egypt and used in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine; Wallach frames it as a form of light therapy.
claims.answer: Wallach describes color therapy as the use of colored lights or panels to create a positive healing effect. It was originally recorded in the Greek Healing Temples of light and color at Heliopolis, Egypt, and color healing is also used in Ayurvedic and Traditional Chinese medicine (the gem therapy of Ayurvedic medicine is a close parallel in theory and methodology). Wallach notes it is well documented that our response to color is emotional while our response to shape is intellectual, and that blue appears to be the universally favored color, followed by red. He reports that color therapy is considered by many to be another form of light therapy.
claims.verbatim:
Color therapy is the use of colored
lights or panels to create a positive healing
effect. Color therapy was originally recorded
in the Greek Healing Temples of light and
color at Heliopolis, Egypt.

claims.subject: color_therapy
claims.question: What does each color treat in color therapy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's color map: blue for blood pressure, fever, cuts and burns; red for low blood pressure; orange for stones; yellow for diabetes; green for ulcers, colds and breast cancer.
claims.answer: Wallach gives a color-by-color map of what each color is used to treat in color therapy. Blue reduces blood pressure and alleviates teething, boils, fever, inflammation, dysentery, colic, and jaundice, and heals cuts and burns. Red alleviates low blood pressure (hypotension) and certain forms of paralysis. Yellow/Violet alleviates anxiety and arthritis. Orange alleviates gallstones and kidney stones. Yellow is used for diabetes and constipation. Green is used for ulcers, colds, flu (influenza), and breast cancer.

claims.subject: color_therapy
claims.question: How is color therapy actually done?
claims.answer_short: Six techniques — the Kilner diagnostic screen, reading tissue colors, sun-charged salt bags, colored foods, 'rainbow' sun-charged water, and meditative color breathing.
claims.answer: Wallach lists six color-therapy techniques. (1) Kilner screen — a diagnostic tool of two glass plates holding a dicyanin (indigo/violet) solution, through which the therapist views the patient to determine which colors are needed. (2) Tissue colors — a diagnostic tool observing the color of the sclera (white of the eye), nails, urine, and stool. (3) Solar-chrome salt bags — a therapy tool: massaging the patient with colored salt in a cheesecloth sack 'charged' by sun or sunlamp exposure. (4) Food colors — a therapy tool: selecting colored food groups whose 'chemicals' (vitamins and minerals) the patient needs. (5) Rainbow healing — a therapy tool: water placed in colored glasses and exposed to sunlight, which the patient then drinks. (6) Color breathing — a therapy tool: a meditative style of retiring and awakening.
claims.verbatim:

Consists of two (2) plates of glass with a
solution of dicyanin (indigo/violet solution);
the color therapist views the patient through
the screen to determine which colors are
needed

claims.subject: faith_healing
claims.question: What is faith healing (laying-on-of-hands)?
claims.answer_short: Using a person to mediate healing through belief - recorded in ancient China and Egypt and in Christianity today. Wallach notes 20-60% of patients improve on placebo when positive thought is induced.
claims.answer: Wallach describes laying-on-of-hands (spiritual and faith healers) as the use of a human being to mediate healing. 'Healers' were recorded in ancient China and Egypt, and appear in various forms today in Christianity. A spiritual healer works on the premise that whatever one believes can be made to happen by belief in God. Wallach notes that 'positive thinking' is practiced by Christians and alternative physicians alike — Robert Schuller considered positive thinking to be a form of prayer — and that twenty to sixty percent of patients will recover with placebos if positive thought is induced.
claims.verbatim:
Laying-on-of-hands (spiritual and
faith healers) - the use of a human to mediate
healing. "Healers" were recorded in ancient
China, Egypt and in various forms today in
Christianity.

claims.subject: faith_healing
claims.question: Who are the Christian Scientists, and what is 'therapeutic touch'?
claims.answer_short: A Christian sect founded in 1879 by Mary Baker Eddy that holds 'healing is proof of God's love'; Wallach says they outlive other Westerners (and get lower insurance rates). Its modern nursing form is 'therapeutic touch.'
claims.answer: Wallach notes the Christian Scientists, a sect of orthodox Christians founded in 1879 by Mary Baker Eddy (Church of Christ, Scientist), who believed that 'healing is proof of God's love for man'; statistically Christian Scientists live longer than any group of western people and, as a result, have special lower insurance premiums. He adds that Kirlian photography shows a significant increase in the healer's hand 'aura' during laying-on-of-hands, and that a new-age form of laying-on-of-hands is 'therapeutic touch,' practiced by nurses and massage therapists on patients with poor circulation and debilitating diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Christian Scientists are a sect of orthodox Christians founded in 1879 by Mary Baker
Eddy (Church of Christ, Scientists) who believed that "healing is proof of God's love for
man

claims.subject: herbal_medicine
claims.question: What is herbal medicine?
claims.answer_short: An ancient system using plants to prevent and cure disease - the root of Chinese, Ayurvedic, American Indian and naturopathic medicine, traced back to Chinese pharmacopeias around 3000 BC.
claims.answer: Wallach describes herbal medicine as an ancient system of medicine that uses plants to prevent and cure disease. He notes that Traditional Chinese medicine, Ayurvedic medicine, American Indian medicine, American folk medicine, Eclectic medicine, and naturopathic medicine all have strong roots in herbal medicine, and traces its history back to the Chinese (large pharmacopeias around 3000 BC), the Persians (plants used medicinally some 6,000 years ago), the Assyrian king Asurbipal (a list of 250 plant drugs around 2500 BC), and Nicholas Culpeper's 'Complete Herbal' (1653).
claims.verbatim:
Herbal medicine is an ancient system
of medicine that uses plants to prevent and
cure disease. Traditional Chinese medicine,
ayurvedic medicine, American Indian medicine, American folk medicine, Eclectic medicine and naturopathic medicine all have strong
roots in herbal medicine

claims.subject: herbal_medicine
claims.question: Do real drugs come from herbs?
claims.answer_short: Yes - Wallach notes over 30% of orthodox pharmaceuticals derive from plants (digitalis from foxglove, the cancer drug vincristine from periwinkle), and praises herbs' relative safety and millennia of use.
claims.answer: Wallach notes that even today more than thirty percent of 'orthodox' pharmaceuticals are derived from herbal compounds (for example digitalis and foxglove, and vincristine, a cancer therapy from the Madagascar periwinkle). He cites the seventeenth-century 'Doctrine of Signatures' (the theory that a plant or plant part resembling a human organ was a 'God-given clue' to its medicinal value) and says herbal medicines have the advantages of relative safety and thousands of years of experience.

claims.subject: hydrotherapy
claims.question: What is hydrotherapy?
claims.answer_short: Healing with water - practiced since Roman times across all medicine, from sitz baths for hemorrhoids to whirlpools for injuries and mineral baths for arthritis; insurance often covers it if prescribed.
claims.answer: Wallach describes hydrotherapy as a healing art that began in Roman times and is widely used today by all forms of healing arts, including 'orthodox' medicine. Medicinal baths take many forms — from sitz baths for hemorrhoids and whirlpool for muscle injuries to mineral baths for arthritis — and insurance companies will often pay for some form of hydrotherapy if it is prescribed by a licensed physician of any healing art.

claims.subject: hydrotherapy
claims.question: What are the different kinds of hydrotherapy?
claims.answer_short: Cold baths cut swelling; hot baths ease soreness; mineral baths help arthritis; steam baths detox heavy metals; sitz baths for hemorrhoids; epsom for edema; water fasts and colonics for detox.
claims.answer: Wallach lists the forms hydrotherapy takes and what each is used for: cold bath reduces swelling; hot bath relieves soreness and improves circulation for chronic diseases and injuries; mineral bath for chronic disease such as arthritis; steam bath to detoxify heavy metals; sitz bath for hemorrhoids; epsom salt bath produces sweating, relieves edema and soreness, and cleans infected wounds; water fast for detoxification of food allergies (and as a prelude to diagnosing them); colonic irrigation for constipation and to detoxify patients with any chronic disease or liver ailment (infectious hepatitis being an exception); and 'knipping' — walking or jogging in knee-deep lake or ocean water to stimulate circulation and the immune system.

claims.subject: negative_ion_therapy
claims.question: What is negative ion therapy?
claims.answer_short: Using negatively charged air particles to prevent and treat disease - abundant in forests and at the beach (300-1,000 per cubic meter) but low in AC'd rooms; too many POSITIVE ions bring anxiety and depression.
claims.answer: Wallach describes negative ion therapy as the use of negatively charged air particles to prevent and cure disease. Sources include 'negative ion generators' for home and office and spending time in forests, mountains, and at the seashore for 'free' supplies. Pure outside air holds about 300-1,000 negatively charged ions per cubic meter (higher at the beach), while air-conditioned office or classroom air typically has only 150-500. He notes that excessive levels of positive ions in the air produce anxiety, depression, and restlessness.
claims.verbatim:
Negative ion therapy is the use of
negatively charged air particles to prevent and
cure disease. Sources of negative ions include
"negative ion generators" for home and office
use and frequenting forests, mountains and
seashores for "free" supplies.

claims.subject: negative_ion_therapy
claims.question: What does negative ion therapy do?
claims.answer_short: Six effects - it lowers heart rate/BP, deepens breathing, speeds respiratory cilia, boosts glands and steadies brain rhythm - and Wallach says it especially helps asthma, allergies and cystic fibrosis.
claims.answer: Wallach lists six effects of negative ions: they (1) reduce heart rate and blood pressure, (2) increase respiratory volume, (3) increase ciliary beat in the respiratory epithelium, (4) increase the efficiency of the endocrine glands, (5) normalize brain rhythm, and (6) reverse the effects of positive ions. He says negative ion generators are particularly good for patients with inhalant allergies, asthma, respiratory disease, and cystic fibrosis, with two to four treatments per day of 45 minutes each (or overnight use) being typical.
claims.verbatim:
Negative ions 1) reduce heart rate and
BP, 2) increase respiratory volume, 3) increase
ciliary beat in respiratory epithelium, 4) increase efficiency of endocrine glands, 5) normalize brain rhythm, 6) reverse effects of
positive ions

claims.subject: urine_therapy
claims.question: What is urine therapy?
claims.answer_short: Injecting a patient's own urine back into them to boost immunity - the same idea as an allergist's shots; Wallach says MD allergists used it for 50 years until prepared allergens became profitable.
claims.answer: Wallach describes urine therapy as a method of improving a patient's immune system by injecting the patient's own urine back into him. He says the basis is the same principle the 'modern' allergist uses when injecting allergens to 'treat' allergies, that the technique is simple and can be done at home or via a naturopathic physician (N.D.), chiropractor (D.C.), or osteopath (D.O.), and that medical-doctor allergists used the technique for 50 years until pharmaceutical companies found they could make money with prepared allergens.
claims.verbatim:
Urine therapy is a method of improving the patients immune system by injecting
his own urine back into him. The basis of the
therapy is exactly the same as the "modern"
allergist uses when he injects allergens into the
patient to "treat" allergies

claims.subject: urine_therapy
claims.question: How is urine therapy performed?
claims.answer_short: Urine is centrifuged and filtered to remove cells and bacteria, then 5-10 mL is injected under the skin (procaine stops any sting); Wallach cites use for allergies, asthma, migraine and arthritis.
claims.answer: Wallach explains how urine therapy is performed: the patient's urine is centrifuged and then filtered through a 'millipore' filter to remove any cells and bacteria, after which five to ten milliliters are injected subcutaneously (any burning can be eliminated by adding procaine to the filtered urine). He states the urine injection technique is very useful for allergies, asthma, migraine headache, and arthritis, and that a nonspecific increase in immune capacity has been recorded in cancer patients given urine therapy.
claims.verbatim:
The urine injection technique is very
useful for allergies, asthma, migraine headache and arthritis. A nonspecific increase in
immune capacity has been recorded in cancer
patients given urine therapy

claims.subject: homeopathy
claims.question: What is homeopathy?
claims.answer_short: A system on two principles: 'like cures like' (a substance that causes symptoms in the healthy can cure a disease with those symptoms) and 'minimum dose' - using extremely diluted preparations.
claims.answer: Wallach describes homeopathy as a widely practiced medical art with two basic principles: (1) 'let like be cured by like' and (2) the principle of 'minimum dose.' Agents (herbs, chemicals, etc.) that produce certain symptoms in normal healthy people ('proving') are then used to cure diseases that produce those same 'proved' symptoms. (Scope note: homeopathy is a homeopathy-class system using highly diluted preparations; included here as Wallach's descriptive account of the modality, not as a dosing protocol.)
claims.verbatim:
Homeopathy is a widely practiced
medical art that has two basic principles:
1) "let like be cured by like"
2) principle of "minimum dose"
Agents (herbs, chemicals, etc.) produce certain symptoms in normal healthy humans
("proved") - these agents are then used to cure
diseases that produce the "proved" symptoms

claims.subject: homeopathy
claims.question: Who founded homeopathy, and does the dilution really work?
claims.answer_short: Samuel Hahnemann, who found Cinchona bark gave healthy people malaria-like symptoms; oddly, more dilute often meant a stronger effect - though past about 12C not one molecule of the original remains.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that Dr. Samuel Hahnemann, a physician from Leipzig, Germany, 'proved' that Cinchona bark (a malaria cure of the day) gave malaria symptoms to healthy people, and went on to 'prove' hundreds of medications and substances. Hahnemann found that very often the more dilute the preparation, the more dramatic the clinical effect — a long-controversial observation that Wallach notes a 1988 article in Nature magazine supported. Homeopathic dilutions are expressed as 'potencies' on decimal/centesimal scales (e.g. 1X/2X, 1C/2C, with European 1D/2D designations); at a 12C dilution there may be one molecule of the original substance or none (Avogadro's Law), yet Wallach says the 'remedy' still has a homeopathic medical effect.
claims.verbatim:
Dr. Samuel Hahnemann, a physician
from Leipzig, Germany, "proved" that Cinchona bark (a malaria cure of the day) gave
malaria symptoms to healthy people.
Hahnemann went on to "prove" hundreds of
medications and substances

claims.subject: naturopathy
claims.question: What is naturopathy?
claims.answer_short: A whole system of natural medicine (N.D.) built on 'FIRST DO NO HARM' and the body's own healing power - covering herbs, hydrotherapy, homeopathy, nutrition and natural childbirth, but not major surgery or most drugs.
claims.answer: Wallach describes naturopathy, practiced by naturopathic physicians (N.D.), as distinguished by its underlying principle — FIRST DO NO HARM. Naturopathic medicine recognizes the body's inherent healing ability and emphasizes the prevention of disease. Its scope of practice varies by state but, as taught, covers the full practice of medicine except major surgery and most prescription ('legend'/allopathic) drugs — including natural hygiene, botanical (herbal) medicine, physical medicine (hydrotherapy, heat, cold, manipulation), homeopathy, counseling, gynecology/obstetrics (natural childbirth), minor surgery, public health, immunization, and laboratory/clinical diagnosis. Wallach notes it is claimed Hippocrates was the father of modern naturopathic medicine since he was an herbalist.
claims.verbatim:
Naturopathy is practiced by
naturopathic physicians (N.D.). What distinguishes naturopathic medicine is that its "practice" emerges from its underlying principle -
FIRST DO NO HARM. Naturopathic medicine
recognizes an inherent healing ability of the
body. Naturopathic physicians emphasize
the prevention of disease

claims.subject: macrobiotics
claims.question: Where did macrobiotics come from?
claims.answer_short: George Ohsawa created it in 1946 Japan, using it to heal his own tuberculosis, then opened a healing center and toured the world teaching a philosophy of health through eating.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that macrobiotics originated in Japan in 1946, created by George Ohsawa, who developed the healing art to heal himself of tuberculosis (which he did) before opening a macrobiotic healing center in Hiyoshi, Japan, teaching from 1946 to 1952 and then taking a world lecture tour (Africa, India, Europe, the United States). Ohsawa taught a philosophy of life and eating habits meant to unify people through health practices.
claims.verbatim:
Macrobiotics originated in Japan in
1946. George Ohsawa created this healing art
to heal himself of tuberculosis (which he
did!!); after curing himself, he opened up a
macrobiotic healing center in Hiyoshi, Japan

claims.subject: macrobiotics
claims.question: What is the macrobiotic diet?
claims.answer_short: An eating system built on balancing 'yin' (fruit, drinks, sweet) and 'yang' (meat, grains, dense) foods; reported to help food allergies, diabetes and - when wheat is dropped - grain sensitivity.
claims.answer: Wallach explains that macrobiotics is based on wholesome behavior and eating habits, with macrobiotic philosophy maintaining that all disease and illness is caused by an imbalance of 'yin' (tends to be feminine; drinks, fruit, sweet/sour/hot flavors, green/blue/purple) and 'yang' (tends to be masculine; meat, cereals, some vegetables, hard/dense, orange/yellow). The macrobiotic diet (popularly the 'brown rice' diet) has many reported successes with food allergies, emotional problems, and chronic diseases such as arthritis and diabetes; he explains the increased health as individuals who are unaware they have gluten sensitivity (celiac disease) getting benefit from eliminating wheat from their diet and beginning to absorb trace minerals, vitamins, and essential fatty acids.
claims.verbatim:
Macrobiotics is based on wholesome
behavior and eating habits. Macrobiotic philosophy maintains that all disease and illness
is caused by an imbalance of "yin" and "yang

claims.subject: vitamins
claims.question: What is megavitamin (orthomolecular) therapy?
claims.answer_short: Using vitamins at very high 'pharmacologic' doses - the 1968 'megavitamin theory' that Linus Pauling named 'orthomolecular medicine' and Abram Hoffer extended to psychiatry, reportedly for colds, depression and schizophrenia, though orthodoxy never endorsed it.
claims.answer: Wallach describes megavitamin therapy as one of the major friction points between 'orthodox' medical philosophy and the alternative healing arts. The 'megavitamin theory' was created in 1968 and became the center of what Dr. Linus Pauling (a double Nobel Prize winner) called 'orthomolecular medicine'; Dr. Abram Hoffer then created 'orthomolecular psychiatry.' Pauling and Hoffer used vitamins at 'pharmacologic' or 'therapeutic' ('mega') levels for a variety of conditions — including colds, alcoholism, hyperactivity, drug addiction, osteoarthritis, neuritis, schizophrenia, depression, various psychoses, and food allergies — with what they reported as excellent results, while the orthodox community declined to endorse the approach. (Note: these are Pauling and Hoffer's orthomolecular megadose protocols, presented here as Wallach's descriptive account of the modality — they are not Wallach's own dosing targets, and the specific megadoses are not surfaced as recommendations.)
claims.verbatim:
Megavitamin therapy is one of the
major friction points between "orthodox"
medical philosophy and alternative healing
arts. The "megavitamin theory" was created in
1968 and was the center of what Dr. Linus
Pauling (double Nobel Prize winner) called
"orthomolecular medicine." Dr. Abram Hoffer
then created "orthomolecular psychiatry."

claims.subject: abrasions
claims.question: How do you treat a scrape or abrasion?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recommends cleaning with soap and water, disinfecting with hydrogen peroxide, bathing in an herbal wash of aloe, plantain, or comfrey, taking vitamin C orally to bowel tolerance (1-5 grams), and covering with non-stick dressings to prevent infection.
claims.answer: For abrasions (scrapes), Wallach recommends cleaning the wound with soap and water, disinfecting with hydrogen peroxide, and bathing it in an herbal wash or poultice such as aloe, plantain (Plantago major), or comfrey (Symphytum officinale), plus vitamin C orally to bowel tolerance (1-5 grams) and covering with non-stick dressings to help prevent infection.
claims.verbatim:
Wounds may be bathed in a
variety of herbal washes or poultice - our
choice is aloe, plantain (Plantago major) or
comfrey (Symphytum officinale). Vitamin C
orally to bowel tolerance (anywhere from 1-5
grams). Covering abrasions with nonstick
dressings will help prevent infection.

claims.subject: abscess
claims.question: How do you treat a boil or abscess?
claims.answer_short: Wallach advises bringing the abscess to a head with a compress or poultice (a sitz bath if near the anus) using 3% boric acid, or echinacea or sand sagebrush; once opened, flush it clean, pack with gauze if large, and take vitamin C to bowel tolerance.
claims.answer: For an abscess (boil), Wallach advises bringing it to a head with a compress or poultice (a sitz bath if near the anus or buttock) using a 3% boric acid solution; herbal alternatives are echinacea (Echinacea angustifolia) or sand sagebrush (Artemisia filifolia). Once opened, the cavity is flushed clean, packed with gauze if large, and vitamin C is taken orally to bowel tolerance.
claims.verbatim:
bring abscess to "a head" (a
soft point in the center) with a compress or
poultice (sitz bath if near the anus or buttock)
using a 3% solution of boric acid

claims.subject: absence_attacks
claims.question: How do you treat petit mal seizures?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's protocol for absence attacks is choline 4 grams per day, taurine 500 mg three times daily, dimethyl glycine 100 mg twice daily, and phosphatidyl choline plus vitamin B-6 at 100-300 mg per day.
claims.answer: For absence attacks (petit mal seizures, in which the patient briefly stops, rapidly blinks the eyes, then resumes activity), Wallach's protocol is choline 4 grams per day, taurine 500 mg three times daily, dimethyl glycine 100 mg twice daily, and phosphatidyl choline plus vitamin B-6 at 100-300 mg per day.
claims.verbatim:
ABSENCE ATTACKS (petit mal): patient
stops what he is doing and rapidly blinks eyes
then starts the activity again where he left off.
Treatment should include choline 4 gm/day;
taurine 500 mg t.i.d.; dimethyl glycine 100 mg
b.i.d., phosphytidyl choline and B-6 100-300
mg/day.

claims.subject: achalasia
claims.question: How do you treat achalasia?
claims.answer_short: Wallach suggests small liquid meals and controlled air swallowing, elevating the head of the bed at night to reduce the risk of vomiting while asleep, and surgery for severe cases.
claims.answer: For achalasia (megaesophagus, a failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to open that causes regurgitation of undigested food), Wallach suggests small liquid meals and controlled air swallowing to relieve it, elevating the head of the bed at night to reduce the risk of vomiting while asleep, and surgery for severe cases.
claims.verbatim:
Night time elevation of head of the bed
will reduce risk of vomiting while asleep.
Surgery may be required to relieve severe
cases.

claims.subject: digestion
claims.question: What happens if you don’t fix low stomach acid?
claims.answer_short: Untreated achlorhydria costs you B-12, calcium and protein, and brings on new food allergies as half-digested protein fragments get absorbed. Treatment is 75–250 mg betaine HCl 15–20 minutes before each meal, or 1–2 oz of vinegar with gentian if you have none.
claims.answer: For achlorhydria (loss of stomach acid, common with aging and stress, with 75% of people over age 50 requiring supplementation, and which untreated leads to vitamin B-12, calcium, and protein deficiencies plus new food allergies), Wallach's treatment is betaine hydrochloride (betaine HCl) 75-250 mg taken 15-20 minutes before each meal; in its absence, 1-2 oz of vinegar with gentian (Gentian) before meals; plant-derived colloidal minerals also help the stomach produce acid.

food allergies as a result of absorption of
partially digested polypeptides (relatively large

claims.subject: acne
claims.question: How do you treat acne naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach attributes acne mainly to essential-fatty-acid deficiency plus too much saturated fat, and treats it by eliminating fast food, fat, and sugar, checking for food allergies, and adding flaxseed oil, vitamin A as beta carotene, B-6, zinc, topical vitamin E, and ultraviolet light.
claims.answer: Wallach attributes acne primarily to an essential fatty acid deficiency combined with too much saturated fat. His protocol: eliminate fast foods, fat, and sugar; check for food allergies (wheat, milk, soy); betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes; essential fatty acids (flaxseed oil 1 tablespoon twice daily); vitamin A 300,000 units per day as beta carotene for five months; vitamin B-6 100 mg three times daily; zinc 50 mg three times daily; topical vitamin E oil on lesions; and ultraviolet light directly on the acne for 1-6 minutes.
claims.verbatim:

claims.subject: gluten
claims.question: What does celiac disease do to absorption, and can the gut heal?
claims.answer_short: Wheat gluten can destroy up to 70% of the intestine's absorptive surface (90% by age 45–50). Wallach says removing the offending grain lets the gut repair over 90 days.
claims.answer: Celiac disease is a loss of the small-intestine villi and scarring of the supporting tissue that can destroy up to 70% (and by age 45-50 up to 90%) of the absorptive surface, classically from a wheat-gluten sensitivity — though cow's-milk albumen and soy protein cause the same damage. Wallach calls it the basic cause of many diseases through malabsorption (diabetes from chromium and vanadium, cancer from zinc, vitamin A and selenium, and muscular dystrophy and cystic fibrosis from selenium). Diagnosis and treatment use the pulse test for allergies and then eliminating or rotating the offending allergen (especially wheat, cow's milk, and soy); it takes 90 days to repair the injured gut.

claims.answer_short: Wallach notes midwives who knew contraception herbs were once branded 'witches' and burned; he ranks birth control (abstinence, barriers, hormones - least desirable, IUDs, surgery) and bluntly calls sex outside marriage 'Russian roulette.'

claims.answer: Hepatitis means any inflammation of the liver, but in daily use refers to three liver viruses: Hepatitis A (fecal-oral contamination), Hepatitis B (blood contamination via dirty needles; more severe, potentially fatal), and Hepatitis C (blood-transfusion-associated, causing chronic liver disease). Wallach stresses prevention through hand-washing and avoiding community needles. His treatment of hepatitis includes bed rest, plenty of fluids including chicken soup, avoiding sugar/fat/alcohol, vitamin B-12 at 1,000 micrograms a day, folic acid at 5-10 milligrams a day, catechin at 1.5 grams a day, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, herbs including licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra), chicory (Cichorium intybus), and dandelion (Taraxacum officinale), germanium at 25-50 milligrams a day, selenium at 200-500 micrograms a day, and SuperOxy Plus at one ounce on awakening and retiring.

claims.subject: hiatal_hernia
claims.question: How do you treat a hiatal hernia?
claims.answer_short: Wallach usually manages a hiatal hernia by controlling gas and dyspepsia with small meals and sleeping with the head of the bed raised, reserving surgical repair for a large diaphragm defect to prevent strangulation.
claims.answer: Hiatal hernia is usually a congenital birth defect (not genetic) but can also be caused by crushing the chest or abdomen, as in a car accident; gas, dyspepsia, reflux, and chest pain that mimics a heart attack are common symptoms, and Wallach notes more than 40% of the USA population has asymptomatic hiatal hernia by x-ray survey. Treatment is usually restricted to managing the gas and dyspepsia: small meals, and sleeping with the head of the bed elevated to prevent nighttime esophageal reflux. When there is a large defect in the diaphragm (paraesophageal hiatal hernia), surgical repair is recommended to prevent strangulation of portions of the stomach, intestine, or liver.

claims.subject: hiccoughs

claims.answer_short: Wallach treats hiccups by holding your breath, sipping water or orange or lemon juice slowly, pressing on the closed eyes with the heels of your hands, and applying pressure to the phrenic nerves behind the collarbone joint.
claims.answer: Hiccoughs are distracting and bothersome but rarely fatal — the result of spasmodic contractions of the diaphragm followed by a sudden closure of the glottis, sometimes started by swallowing hot or irritating substances. Wallach's treatment includes holding your breath (high blood carbon dioxide inhibits hiccoughs), drinking a large glass of water or orange or lemon juice slowly, applying pressure on the closed eyes with the heels of your hands, and applying digital pressure to the phrenic nerves just behind the sternoclavicular joint (where the collarbone joins the sternum).

claims.answer: Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is, in Wallach's view, almost always caused by food allergies that produce celiac-type intestinal changes and malabsorption of chromium and vanadium, and/or a high intake of purified sugar and refined flour that increases urinary chromium loss by up to 300%; untreated, it frequently develops into diabetes. claims.answer: Impetigo (ecthyma) is a form of dermatitis in children — blisters filled with straw-colored fluid or pus, or skin ulcers, mainly on the face, arms, and legs. claims.answer_short: Wallach says infection depends on both an infective dose of organisms and low host resistance, and treats it with the baseline nutrient program plus echinacea, goldenseal, garlic, vitamin C, vitamin A, zinc, and selenium.

claims.answer_short: Wallach says jaundice comes from bile-duct blockage or red-blood-cell destruction and treats it with ultraviolet light, a liver flush, vitamin C, vitamin A as beta carotene, selenium, vitamin E, and herbs like licorice.
claims.answer: Jaundice (icterus, yellow eyes) can be caused by blockage of the bile-duct system in the liver (gallstones, tumor, hepatitis) and/or destruction of red blood cells (Rh factor, blood parasites, malaria); diagnosis is critical. Treatment: exposure to ultraviolet light to speed elimination; a liver flush (three days of apple juice, then a cup of olive oil and a cup of lemon juice); vitamin C to bowel tolerance; vitamin A at 300,000 international units per day as beta carotene; selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day; vitamin E at 800-1,200 international units per day; and herbs licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra), agrimony (Agrimonia eupatoria), celandine (Chelidonium majus), and chionanthus (Chionanthus virginica).

claims.answer_short: Wallach prevents and treats kernicterus by feeding the infant frequently to reduce bile-pigment absorption and exposing the baby to blue and ultraviolet light to photo-oxidize the bilirubin.

claims.question: How do you treat ketoacidosis or ketosis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats ketoacidosis by resolving the underlying disease (diabetes, hypoglycemia, alcoholism, or starvation), increasing complex carbohydrates, and adding chromium and the baseline nutritional program.

Treatment: resolve the basic disease process (diabetes, hypoglycemia, alcoholism, starvation), increase complex-carbohydrate intake, chromium at 50-200 micrograms three times daily, and the baseline nutritional program.

Treatment: avoid lactose-containing foods and/or predigest the lactose by adding lactase enzyme to milk-containing foods.

claims.subject: lead_poisoning
claims.question: How do you treat lead poisoning naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats lead poisoning with vitamin C, EDTA or D-penicillamine chelation, and the baseline supplement with colloidal minerals to replace minerals lost during chelation, noting selenium is of particular value.
claims.answer: Lead poisoning (plumbism) can cause a wide variety of symptoms — learning disabilities, kidney disease, stunted bone growth, headaches, and gastrointestinal disease; often the lead is eaten because of 'pica', a compulsive eating of unusual things driven by mineral deficiencies. claims.question: How do you treat Legionnaires' disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says Legionnaires' disease is treated specifically with erythromycin at 500 milligrams to 1 gram orally or intravenously every 6 hours for three weeks.
claims.answer: Legionnaires' disease is caused by infection with Legionella pneumophila; it is characterized by pneumonia, high fever, slow heart rate, dry cough, chills, pleuritis, and diarrhea. A relatively new disease (discovered in 1976), it is fatal in 80% of untreated cases and is diagnosed by growing the organism on charcoal-yeast extract from sputum; immunosuppressed patients (those on chemotherapy, transplant patients, AIDS patients) are most susceptible. Treatment is specific: erythromycin at 500 milligrams to 1 gram orally or intravenously every 6 hours for three weeks.

claims.subject: leptospirosis
claims.question: How do you treat leptospirosis or Weil's disease?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says leptospirosis (Weil's disease) responds best to antibiotics started within four days of onset, with tetracycline at 500 milligrams four times daily being effective.
claims.answer: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease, infectious jaundice) is an infectious disease caused by Leptospira, a spirochete bacterium carried by dogs, rats, and various wild animals; people are infected through urine-contaminated water or cuts while skinning or butchering infected animals. Symptoms include anemia, jaundice, proteinuria, hematuria, and occasionally aseptic meningitis, with fever and chills consistent; diagnosis needs blood tests or urine cultures. Treatment with antibiotics is most effective if started within four days of onset — tetracycline at 500 milligrams four times daily is effective.

claims.answer: Leukemia (blood cancer) is a cancer of the blood-forming tissues of the bone marrow; no exact cause is proven, though viruses, radiation, and chemicals such as benzene are implicated. It produces a defect in white-blood-cell maturation, flooding the circulation with immature white cells; diagnosis comes from a blood test showing anemia, low platelets, increased lymphoblasts, and an elevated total white-cell count, and symptoms include weakness, joint pain, anemia, enlarged lymph nodes, and an enlarged spleen. Wallach's treatment includes Laetrile, hydrogen peroxide, intravenous dimethyl sulfoxide (said to mature the immature cells), Onco-Tox, shark liver extract, hydrazine sulfate, cesium chloride, polyerga, germanium, carbamide, and as needed micro-dose chemotherapy, intravenous amino acids, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day, and vitamin A at 300,000 international units as beta carotene.

claims.answer: Leukorrhea (vaginal discharge) is a nonspecific vaginal discharge containing mucus and white blood cells, occasionally blood-tinged; it can be caused by Candida albicans, Hemophilus vaginalis, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus (the organism behind toxic-shock syndrome with incorrectly used tampons), or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. claims.answer: Lice (pediculosis) can infest the head (Pediculus humanus capitis), body (P. h. corporis), and pubic area (Phthirius pubis); the eggs (nits) are white, oval, seed-like objects attached to the base of the hairs, and adult lice can be seen scuttling through the hair. Itching and irritated skin are the most common symptoms, and diagnosis depends on finding adult lice or nits. Treatment: a hair wash of Labrador tea (Ledum latifolium) or field larkspur (Delphinium consolida), and a special fine-toothed comb to 'harvest' the nits, done daily for fourteen days to break the lice life cycle. the lice.

claims.subject: longevity
claims.question: How long can humans live?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says 120-130 years, vs the ~72-78 of actuary tables. He credits the Hunza's ~100-year average to plant-derived colloidal minerals, and says filters, digestive aids and the baseline program add ~20 years.
claims.answer: Wallach holds that the potential lifespan for humans is 120-130 years, yet insurance actuary tables put the average at only 72 for males and 78 for females -- a 40-50 year gap to work toward. He says home water-filtration systems, air filters and conditioners, and the baseline nutrition program can together add ten years, and that digestive aids (betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes) add another ten -- about twenty added years when pursued actively. He attributes the Hunza secret of longevity (averaging 100 years, up to 140) to the daily consumption of plant-derived colloidal minerals, and warns that exercise alone -- without attention to food allergies, digestive aids, the baseline program, colloidal minerals, and avoiding pollutants -- will only shorten life. He also notes that 40% of hospital patients are there because of iatrogenic (doctor-caused) disease. (Captured for the search corpus as Wallach's general longevity guidance.)

claims.answer: For liver disease (cirrhosis and nonviral hepatitis), Wallach says it is diagnosed by blood tests showing elevated liver-function markers (the SGOT, SGPT and GGT enzymes, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin), with elevated urine ketones, jaundice, delayed clotting, a swollen tender liver under the right ribs, dry itchy skin (an essential-fatty-acid problem), anemia (iron-storage and vitamin B-12/folic-acid deficiency), weight loss and ketosis (he adds: also see gallbladder disease). claims.subject: tetanus
claims.question: How do you prevent and treat tetanus (lockjaw)?
claims.answer_short: Wallach stresses prevention — make a puncture wound bleed, clean with soap and water, disinfect with 3% hydrogen peroxide, and take cramp bark tea — and says once lockjaw develops it needs tetanus antitoxin, wound cleaning, IV penicillin or tetracycline, sedation, and IV fluids.
claims.answer: For lockjaw (tetanus) — caused by the toxin of Clostridium tetani, a normal inhabitant of animal manure that enters through puncture wounds and paralyzes the voluntary muscles including the jaw (masseter) muscles — Wallach stresses prevention as the best option: make the puncture wound bleed by squeezing it, open small foot or hand punctures to clean with soap and water, then disinfect with 3% hydrogen peroxide, and take cramp bark tea (Viburnum opulus) in tablespoon doses as needed; he says these minimal steps prevent lockjaw almost 100% of the time. Once it develops, treatment requires tetanus-neutralizing (non-fixed) antitoxin, cleaning and disinfecting the infected wound with hydrogen peroxide, penicillin at two million units intravenously every 6 hours OR tetracycline at 500 milligrams intravenously every 6 hours, sedation to control muscle spasms, and intravenous fluids and electrolytes until the patient can eat and drink on their own.

claims.answer: For lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, SLE) — a connective-tissue disease with 90% of cases in women in their 30s — Wallach argues the autoimmune antibody attack is a result of the disease and its abnormal proteins, not its cause. claims.answer: For Lyme disease (Lyme arthritis) — a spirochete bacterial infection transmitted by ticks, first described in 1975 in Lyme, Connecticut — Wallach notes that 3 to 32 days after an infected tick bite a skin lesion called erythema chronicum migrans appears on the thigh, buttock or axilla and expands up to 50 cm, with recurring attacks of arthritis, fatigue, chills, fever, stiff neck, sore muscles, nausea and vomiting, and heart involvement (an enlarged heart and atrioventricular [AV] block) in 8% of patients. It occurs most in children who play in grass or deep woods or who have a dog that brings home the Ixodes dammini tick, clusters along the U.S. northeastern coast and in Wisconsin, California and Oregon, and is often misdiagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis. His treatment is tetracycline at 250-500 milligrams four times a day for 20 days; in children, whose teeth tetracyclines discolor, penicillin at 20 million units per day intravenously in divided doses.

claims.subject: colloidal_minerals
claims.question: If someone can't absorb nutrients from food, what's the best way to get minerals in?
claims.answer_short: Liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals, Wallach says — the most efficient way to get minerals into malnourished people. He frames malnutrition-from-malabsorption (celiac changes or low stomach acid) as the common denominator of almost all degenerative disease, so the absorbable colloidal form is his answer.
claims.answer: Wallach defines malnutrition as occurring either as an overt nutritional deficiency, secondary to extended use of medications that interfere with nutrient absorption, or as malabsorption from celiac disease or low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria). He argues conventional doctors think of malnutrition only as protein/calorie deprivation and miss macro- and micro-nutrient deficiencies (singly or in combination, especially early), and miss that celiac changes in the small-intestine lining arise from subclinical allergies to wheat, cow's-milk albumen and soy (and rye, barley, beef, eggs). In his framework many degenerative diseases are really malabsorption: diabetes and hypoglycemia as chromium/vanadium deficiencies, cystic fibrosis as a selenium and essential-fatty-acid deficiency, arthritis as a calcium deficiency worsened by excess dietary phosphorus, and cancer as a depleted immune system run out of repair nutrients. He concludes malnutrition from malabsorption is the common denominator of almost all degenerative disease, and that liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals are the most efficient way to get minerals into malnourished people.

His treatment is topical over-the-counter anti-itch products (for example Caladryl) plus herbs: salves of marigold (Calendula officinalis), and taken orally columbine (Aquilegia vulgaris), yarrow (Achillea millefolium) and pleurisy root (Asclepias tuberosa).

claims.answer_short: Wallach warns rubella is dangerous in pregnant women and can cause spontaneous abortions and birth defects; he treats it with the same symptomatic care as ordinary measles and gives his editorial opinion that rubella vaccines should be avoided during pregnancy.
claims.answer: German measles (rubella, three-day measles) is a contagious viral disease that causes mild symptoms in children, including swollen lymph nodes of the head and neck; its incubation is 14-21 days and overt symptoms may be absent in teenagers and adults. Wallach's treatment is the same symptomatic therapy used for ordinary (nine-day) measles. claims.subject: meningitis
claims.question: Is meningitis a medical emergency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach warns that meningitis is not a self-help disease — if you suspect it, get the patient to an emergency room immediately and demand help, because patients often die after waiting hours to be seen.
claims.answer: Meningitis (infection of the covering of the brain and spinal cord) can be caused by many organisms — bacteria (Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus/Diplococcus pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes), fungi, and hundreds of viruses. Wallach stresses it is especially dangerous because infants often show only fever and lethargy, and the blood-brain barrier keeps most medications out of the meninges and brain. Symptoms vary but usually include sore throat, fever, headache, stiff neck and vomiting, and children and adults can become critically ill within 6-24 hours of the first symptoms. He warns emphatically that this is NOT a self-help disease: if you suspect meningitis, get the patient to an emergency room immediately and demand help, because patients often die after waiting hours in a waiting room. Treatment requires rapid diagnosis (spinal tap) and injection of antibiotics into the subdural space (under the meninges), total intravenous fluid and electrolyte support, and frequently mechanical respirators.

claims.answer_short: Wallach attributes meningocele — severe birth defects like spina bifida and anencephaly — to a deficiency of folic acid, vitamin B-12, or zinc and vitamin A during early pregnancy, so correcting those deficiencies before and during pregnancy is the way to prevent them.
claims.answer: Meningocele (severe anencephaly or spina bifida) is a severe birth defect in which the brain or spinal cord and its coverings (meninges) are exposed because the vertebrae form improperly. Wallach attributes it to a deficiency of folic acid, vitamin B-12, or zinc and vitamin A during early pregnancy — deficiencies that may stem from a poor diet and/or malabsorption in the mother. Severe cases may be debilitating or fatal. Treatment is limited to surgery, so he emphasizes that prevention — correcting these deficiencies before and during early pregnancy — is the goal.

claims.question: How do you treat mercury poisoning naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats mercury poisoning by removing the source (including mercury-amalgam fillings), CaEDTA chelation with IV nutrition, and sauna sweating, and notes selenium-containing colloidal minerals are very effective at removing mercury from tissues.
claims.answer: Mercury poisoning can result from ingesting or inhaling any mercurial compound and from off-gassing of mercury vapor from mercury-amalgam dental fillings. Symptoms include gastroenteritis, salivation, burning mouth pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, colitis, kidney disease, gingivitis, mental and emotional disturbances and nerve deficits; Wallach notes many dentists and alternative practitioners think multiple sclerosis may result from mercury poisoning, and that the mental/emotional effects in Victorian 'hatters' gave rise to 'as mad as a hatter.' Diagnosis is easy via hair analysis plus a history of a mercury source. His treatment: remove the mercury source (including mercury-amalgam fillings), chelation with calcium-EDTA (with complete intravenous nutrition), and sweating (sauna), since mercury is excreted in sweat; he adds that selenium-containing colloidal minerals are very effective at removing mercury from the tissues.

claims.subject: be_your_own_doctor
claims.question: What is 'metabolic therapy'?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's umbrella term for curing disease by fixing whole-body metabolism - through nutrition, herbs, homeopathy, acupuncture, manipulation and hydrotherapy.
claims.answer: 'Metabolic therapy' is Wallach's umbrella term for his whole approach to healing. He defines it as resolving or curing disease processes by correcting the body's overall metabolism — rather than treating one symptom — using a combination of nutrition, herbs, homeopathy, acupuncture, manipulation, and hydrotherapy. The definition reflects his central premise: that chronic disease is best addressed by fixing whole-body nutrition and metabolism, not by isolating a single organ or complaint.

claims.subject: opiate_withdrawal
claims.question: How do you get through opiate withdrawal?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recommends doubling the baseline nutrition program for 30 days to help a patient through opiate withdrawal, then dropping to the baseline supplement program, noting opiate withdrawal is self-limiting and not life-threatening.
claims.answer: Methadone is the drug used to ease opiate withdrawal, classically given in just enough amount (usually 20 mg/day) to prevent the most severe withdrawal symptoms; Wallach notes opiate (opium, morphine, etc.) withdrawal is self-limiting and not life-threatening (though addicts in withdrawal often feel otherwise). He recommends doubling the baseline nutrition program for 30 days to help the patient through withdrawal, then dropping to the baseline supplement program and staying on it; do the pulse test for food sensitivities/allergies and a six-hour glucose tolerance test, since people addicted to drugs and/or alcohol frequently have 'addictive allergies' to food and sugar.

patient's ability to get through the withdrawal

claims.subject: migraine
claims.question: How do you treat migraine headaches naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds that migraines come from food allergies rather than blood vessels, and treats them by avoiding the identified food allergens plus rotation diets, urine therapy, digestive enzymes, vitamin C, and bioflavonoids.
claims.answer: Migraine headaches are often heralded by flashes of light and tingling, occur between ages 10-30, and are more common in women; symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, digital cyanosis (blue fingers from poor circulation/oxygen), irritability and photophobia (light sensitivity). Wallach rejects the conventional blood-vessel theory, holding that migraines result from food allergies — the 'target' tissue being the arteries (the elastic arteries in the brain constrict while the muscular scalp arteries dilate); use the pulse test to identify the offending foods. Treatment and prevention: avoid the identified food allergens, rotation diets, autoimmune urine therapy, betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 mg three times a day, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, bioflavonoids at 200 mg twice a day, and the baseline nutrition program.
