claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Can a zinc deficiency cause a miscarriage?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds that zinc is one of the nutrients essential to maintaining a pregnancy, and that deficiencies of it (along with vitamin A, folic acid, selenium and protein) are a common cause of miscarriage.
claims.answer: Miscarriage (spontaneous abortion) is usually due to deficiencies of vitamins, trace minerals and/or protein — in particular vitamin A, zinc, folic acid, selenium and complete proteins, all essential to maintaining pregnancy. Wallach attributes the underlying malnutrition to restricted diets (weight-loss, incomplete vegetarian or rotation diets) and malabsorption syndromes (such as celiac-type intestinal injury) in the mother, and says these cause both miscarriages and birth defects; use the pulse test to identify offending food allergens. Treatment and prevention: the baseline nutrition program for six months before attempting conception, plus herbs cramp bark (Viburnum opulus), blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides) and alfalfa.

claims.answer: Mitral valve prolapse is a common, progressive change in the left atrioventricular (mitral) valve and the surrounding heart tissue. Most people have no symptoms; some have non-anginal chest pain, palpitations, fatigue and/or breathing problems, and a late systolic heart murmur is sometimes heard during squatting exercises. If you have no symptoms, your activities need not be restricted. Wallach's treatment is selenium at 500 to 1,000 micrograms a day, magnesium at 1,000 milligrams three times a day, salmon oil (a source of omega-3 essential fatty acids) at 1 to 5 grams three times a day and the herb hawthorne (Crataegus oxyacantha), in addition to the baseline nutritional supplement program. He says you can expect significant improvement in 30 to 60 days.

claims.subject: monckebergs_arteriosclerosis
claims.question: How do you treat Monckeberg's arteriosclerosis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach attributes Monckeberg's arteriosclerosis to excess vitamin D and treats it with EDTA chelation, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, selenium at 500-1,000 mcg a day, and the baseline nutritional supplement program.
claims.answer: Monckeberg's arteriosclerosis is a circular calcification of the media — the middle muscular/elastic layer — of the small arteries. Wallach says this disease is caused by excess vitamin D (hypervitaminosis D), and its symptoms include high blood pressure (hypertension) and angina. His treatment is EDTA chelation, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, selenium at 500 to 1,000 micrograms a day and the baseline nutritional supplement program.

claims.subject: down_syndrome
claims.question: Can Down syndrome be prevented or treated?
claims.answer_short: Wallach attributes Down's syndrome to a zinc deficiency at the earliest moment of conception and says it can be prevented and treated with the baseline supplement program and zinc — expecting IQ to rise 15-20 points as long as the program is followed.
claims.answer: Mongolism (Down's syndrome) is a birth defect that Wallach attributes to a zinc deficiency in the earliest moments of conception (he notes one third of the extra chromosome comes from the father). Orthodox doctors instead view it as a chromosomal defect whose risk rises with the mother's age. Newborns are 'floppy', lacking muscle tone; physical and mental maturation is delayed (average intelligence quotient, or IQ, around 50), with a small domed-forehead head, a flattened nose bridge, slanted eyes with epicanthal folds, and Brushfield's spots around the iris. Prevention: follow the baseline nutritional supplement program for 90 days before attempting conception and use the pulse test to find and eliminate the food allergies that block zinc absorption. Treatment: zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day plus the baseline program, again using the pulse test to identify and avoid offending foods. Wallach says you can expect the intelligence quotient to rise by 15 to 20 points and physical features to improve as long as the program is followed; stopping it loses all the gains.

claims.answer: Morning sickness is the nausea that occurs in the first three months of pregnancy because of rising progesterone levels. Wallach says eating a complex-carbohydrate or protein snack on awakening relieves much of the nausea. He also suggests herbal teas of dogwood (Cornus sericea) and mint (Mentha sativa); vitamin B-6 together with a B-complex at 25 milligrams three times a day; essential fatty acids at 1,000 milligrams three times a day; and the baseline nutritional supplement program.

claims.answer: Mosquitoes can be kept out of the home with screen windows and doors and electric 'zapper' lights placed 15-25 yards from the back door (the violet light draws mosquitoes away from the house). Wallach notes mosquitoes carry serious human diseases — meningitis and encephalitis in North America; malaria, yellow fever, meningitis and encephalitis in South America. Beyond over-the-counter flying-insect sprays, he says the herb pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium) oil rubbed on the skin and vitamin B-1 (thiamine) at 500 milligrams a day will also help repel mosquitoes.

claims.question: How much phenylalanine does Wallach recommend for multiple sclerosis (MS)?
claims.answer_short: For MS, Wallach's protocol includes D-phenylalanine at 500 mg three times a day, alongside removing mercury fillings, fish and flaxseed oil, and other steps.
claims.answer: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive disease of the central nervous system marked by scattered zones of demyelination (loss of the fatty insulating layer on nerves). Symptoms start between ages 20 and 40 — usually tingling or numbness in the arms or legs (a 'stocking and glove' pattern) — and progress to weakness, clumsiness, visual and balance problems, dizziness and bladder-control trouble; intention tremor, nystagmus and 'scanning' speech form Charcot's triad. Wallach links MS to mercury (he cross-references mercury poisoning) and to the loss of cholesterol-rich myelin. He criticizes the orthodox cortisone/prednisone approach and instead recommends: avoid animal fats; a high intake of fish oil (cod liver or salmon oil) at 5 grams three times a day and flaxseed oil at one tablespoon twice a day (said to raise survival by 50 percent); removal of mercury (amalgam) fillings; calcium 2-aminoethylphosphate (CaEAP) one dose four times a day; octacosanol two capsules three times a day; daily snake-venom injections; D-phenylalanine at 500 milligrams three times a day; betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day; avoidance of known food allergens with rotation diets; and avoiding vitamin C supplements (using green vegetables and juices as a natural source instead). Wallach says the same regimen has also worked for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, or Lou Gehrig's disease).

claims.question: How do you treat mumps?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats mumps symptomatically with pain relief (codeine, Tylenol, aspirin), bed rest, a liquid diet, and the herb mullein for symptom relief.
claims.answer: Mumps is a contagious viral disease that causes painful enlargement of the salivary glands, especially the parotids; the virus is highly aggressive and is present in saliva up to six days before illness is felt. Symptoms include fever (up to 104°F), chills, and tender, shiny, swollen skin over the salivary glands in front of and below the ear. In about 20 percent of adult males it causes a painful testicular infection, and testicular atrophy may follow (though hormone production and fertility are rarely affected). Wallach's treatment is symptomatic: pain relief (codeine, acetaminophen/Tylenol, aspirin), bed rest, a liquid diet (chicken rice soup, sugarless Jello, Gatorade, juices) and the herb mullein (Verbascum thapsus) for symptom relief.

claims.subject: muscular_dystrophy
claims.question: How does Wallach treat muscular dystrophy?
claims.answer_short: Wallach calls muscular dystrophy a preventable selenium-deficiency disease (like livestock 'white muscle disease') and treats MD and Keshan disease with oral/IV/IM selenium, vitamin E, sulfur amino acids, essential fatty acids, avoiding food allergens, keeping fat under 20% of calories, choline as soy lecithin, and avoiding exercise the first month.
claims.answer: Muscular dystrophy (MD) is, in Wallach's view, a preventable selenium-deficiency disease — he points out it has been eliminated in livestock ('white muscle disease') by giving selenium to pregnant females and fast-growing young animals. Adequate selenium in preconception women maintains pregnancy and prevents all forms of MD (Duchenne, Erb, Leyden-Moebius, Landouzy-Dejerine, Becker's and Gowers), and he adds Keshan disease (a selenium-deficiency heart-muscle dystrophy) to the list. Food-allergy-driven celiac-type changes in the small intestine are a common cause of the tissue selenium deficiency, so do a pulse test. He says giving selenium and vitamin E by intramuscular or intravenous injection at the very first symptoms can arrest or cure the disease. Treatment of MD and/or Keshan disease: selenium orally (as plant-derived colloidal minerals), intravenously or intramuscularly at 50-1,000 micrograms a day (by weight); vitamin E intramuscularly at 80 milligrams a day; selenium orally at 250-1,000 micrograms a day; vitamin E 800-1,200 (orally); sulfur amino acids (a complete amino-acid infusion intravenously, plus free amino acids orally) and sugarless Jello; essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times a day; avoid food allergens; keep fat under 20 percent of daily calories; choline as soy lecithin at 10-20 grams a day; and avoid exercise for the first month of treatment to protect compromised muscle.

They range from a subtle eyelid twitch or muscle flutter (fasciculations) in the arms or legs to hard cramps of the feet, calves, back and neck. Prevention is the baseline nutritional supplement program; do a pulse test for food allergies that can cause celiac-type changes and malabsorption, and a hair analysis to check mineral status. Treatment can include liquid colloidal calcium, magnesium and potassium, plus betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day before meals.

claims.subject: neuralgia
claims.question: How do you treat neuralgia or nerve pain naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's treatment addresses every underlying cause and adds a B-complex, vitamin B-12, essential fatty acids (EPA and flaxseed oil), calcium and magnesium, antivirals for viral cases, acupuncture, and herbs such as St. John's wort and white willow.
claims.answer: Neuralgia (which includes Bell's palsy and neuropathy) is an irritation of a nerve that can stem from many causes — trauma; nutritional deficiencies (vitamin B-12, folic acid, vitamin B-1, vitamin B-6); infections (herpes, shingles); alcoholism; diabetes; and multiple sclerosis. Treatment requires addressing every underlying condition and should also include a B-complex at 50 milligrams three times a day, vitamin B-12 at 1,000 micrograms a day, essential fatty acids as EPA at 5 grams three times a day and flaxseed oil at one tablespoon twice a day, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000 milligrams a day, and — for viral neuralgias such as herpes and shingles — the antivirals Isoprinosine at 500-1,500 milligrams a day and Ribavirin at 250-1,500 milligrams a day, plus acupuncture and the herbs lavender (Lavandula angustifolia), oats (Avena sativa), rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis), St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) and white willow (Salix alba).

claims.subject: night_blindness
claims.question: How do you treat night blindness naturally?
claims.answer_short: Night blindness is caused by vitamin A deficiency, and Wallach treats it with high-dose vitamin A as beta carotene plus zinc.
claims.answer: Night blindness (xerophthalmia) is caused by vitamin A deficiency — whether from an outright dietary lack, fat malabsorption (vitamin A is fat-soluble), or zinc deficiency, which impairs the liver's conversion of carotene to vitamin A. Cystic fibrosis, celiac disease and food allergies cause intestinal changes that block absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, E, D and K) and essential fatty acids. The symptom is delayed or complete failure of adaptation to darkness. Wallach's treatment is specific: 25,000-300,000 IU of vitamin A per day as beta carotene and zinc at 15-50 milligrams three times a day.

Wallach uses the pulse test and a six-hour glucose tolerance test to find the cause, noting blood sugar bottoms out about 4 to 4.5 hours after eating (especially sugary foods), so night terrors tend to strike roughly four hours after a bedtime snack such as cookies and milk. Bedwetting in children often accompanies night terrors and likewise stems from food allergies (usually milk) and hypoglycemia. Treatment: avoid offending food allergens and sugar, chromium at 25-200 micrograms three times a day, a high-animal-protein diet, the baseline nutritional supplement program, and avoid caffeine.

claims.answer: Numbness and tingling in both hands (carpal tunnel syndrome) can be caused by neuralgia (diabetes, vitamin B-12 deficiency), circulation problems and the carpal tunnel itself; food allergies can also cause it, and multiple sclerosis should be considered. Tinel's sign (tapping the wrist to elicit pain) is a clue, and orthodox neurologists favor carpal tunnel surgery. Wallach's treatment is aggressive diagnosis and treatment of any underlying condition plus vitamin B-12 at 1,000 micrograms a day, vitamin B-6 at 200-300 milligrams three times a day, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000 milligrams a day, zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day, and colloidal minerals.

claims.subject: obesity
claims.question: How do you lose weight according to Wallach?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says starvation backfires, so eat at least 1,000 calories a day with moderate exercise; he says empty-calorie diets trigger pica-driven bingeing, so he adds colloidal minerals, tests for food allergies and hypoglycemia, and uses salmon and flaxseed oil, fiber, glucomannan, digestive enzymes, and thyroid.
claims.answer: Obesity (overweight) is, at its simplest, consuming and storing more calories than you use — but Wallach stresses it is not simple. Starvation backfires (the body conserves energy), so eat at least 1,000 calories a day for gradual, permanent loss, with moderate exercise (walking, tennis, golf, swimming, low-impact aerobics). He says 90 percent of obese people overeat and binge because empty-calorie diets trigger 'pica' — a nibbling driven by the body's search for trace minerals — so use colloidal minerals. Test for food allergies (pulse test) and do a six-hour glucose tolerance test for hypoglycemia or diabetes. His program: avoid food allergens, sugar (solid and liquid), caffeine and carbonated drinks (phosphates promote osteoporosis); drink filtered spring water, 8-10 glasses a day; use potassium salt with kelp; don't skip meals (large breakfast, moderate lunch with animal protein, light soup-and-salad dinner); salmon oil at 5 grams three times a day, flaxseed oil one tablespoon twice a day, two tablespoons of nutritional fiber before bed, glucomannan at 1 gram before meals, betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day before meals, and thyroid starting at 1-3 grains (adjust to avoid jitteriness; needing over six grains suggests celiac-type malabsorption). Herbal laxatives or diuretic teas and subliminal weight-loss tapes can also help.

claims.subject: airway_obstruction
claims.question: What do you do when someone is choking?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's treatment is to manually remove the obstruction with a finger, perform a Heimlich maneuver, and as a last resort perform an emergency tracheotomy, followed by CPR if the heart has also stopped.
claims.answer: Obstruction of the airways (choking) is heralded by the 'universal choking sign' — both hands clutched at the throat and loss of speech; it happens often in restaurants (a 'restaurant coronary' mistaken for a heart attack). Prevention: don't talk while chewing and swallowing, especially meat and firm raw vegetables. Treatment: (1) put a finger into the back of the throat and manually remove the obstruction; (2) perform a Heimlich maneuver (stand behind the patient, lock your arms around them with hands just below the xiphoid cartilage and thrust sharply; for babies use hands only). If the obstruction cannot be cleared, Wallach describes an emergency tracheotomy as a last-resort lifesaving measure — a dead-center incision midway between the base of the larynx and the notch where the collarbones meet the breastbone, large enough for the empty barrel of a ballpoint pen to maintain airflow — followed by CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) if the heart has also stopped.

claims.subject: oligospermia
claims.question: How do you increase a low sperm count naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says low sperm count usually comes from nutritional deficiencies or malabsorption, and treats it by avoiding food allergens, doubling the baseline supplements for 30-60 days, acupuncture, and herbs like ginseng.
claims.answer: Oligospermia (low sperm count) is usually the result of nutritional deficiencies and/or malabsorption syndromes; do a pulse test for food allergies and celiac-type changes. Infertility is the usual red flag that prompts a sperm-count check — on a semen sample under high power, healthy live sperm should be highly motile, moving in swirling waves. Wallach's treatment: avoid offending food allergens, double the baseline nutritional supplementation for 30-60 days, acupuncture, and herbs including ginseng (Panax ginseng) and herbal combinations such as Zumbani.

claims.subject: omphalocele
claims.question: How do you treat an umbilical hernia (omphalocele) without surgery?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says omphalocele (umbilical hernia) is a birth defect caused by maternal deficiencies of vitamin A and/or zinc; small ones (about a fingertip's width) can be healed at home by taping wool over the hernia and massaging the ring three times a day, while larger ones need surgery.
claims.answer: Omphalocele (umbilical hernia) is a birth defect — a grape- to basketball-sized, peritoneum-lined skin sac at the navel that may contain fat and/or loops of intestine that can be pushed back into the abdomen. Wallach says it is a common birth defect caused by maternal (and therefore fetal) deficiencies of vitamin A and/or zinc. Treatment: surgery is needed if the hernial ring (the defect in the belly wall) is larger than a fingertip; if it is about a fingertip's diameter it can be healed at home without surgery by taping a golf-ball-sized ball of virgin wool firmly over the hernia and, three times a day, removing it, pushing the fat back in with the fingertip and rubbing the ring in a rotary motion for several minutes to irritate it — over weeks to months the defect fills in and heals.

claims.subject: organic_brain_syndrome
claims.question: How does Wallach treat organic brain syndrome?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats organic brain syndrome — his umbrella for disorders like depression, schizophrenia, dementia, and hyperactivity — by correcting nutritional deficiencies and toxicities with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes, niacin, essential fatty acids, chromium, and zinc plus the baseline supplement program, after a pulse test and a six-hour glucose tolerance test.
claims.answer: Organic brain syndrome is Wallach's umbrella term for a group of nutritionally-driven mental and behavioral disorders — pellagra, alcoholism, dementia, depression, hyperkinesis (hyperactivity), hypoglycemia, diabetes, premenstrual syndrome (PMS), paranoia, schizophrenia, and learning disabilities. He says they are caused by a wide variety of nutritional deficiencies (niacin/vitamin B-3, vitamin B-1, vitamin B-12, folic acid, chromium and others) and toxicities (alcohol, lead poisoning, and mercury poisoning from dental amalgam fillings). Work-up: do a pulse test to see whether food allergies are involved, and a six-hour glucose tolerance test to rule diabetes or hypoglycemia in or out (a single fasting blood-glucose reading misses 99.9 percent of hypoglycemia and 85 percent of diabetes). Treatment takes serious dedication to find and correct the underlying problems, and should include avoiding food allergens, rotation diets, betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day fifteen minutes before meals, niacin (vitamin B-3) at 450 milligrams three times a day as time-release tablets, essential fatty acids as salmon and flaxseed oils three times a day, chromium at 25-200 micrograms three times a day, zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day, plus the baseline nutritional supplement program.

claims.subject: ornithosis
claims.question: How do you treat parrot fever (ornithosis)?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats ornithosis (parrot fever) with the antibiotic tetracycline by mouth at 250-500 mg four times a day for 10-14 days, controlling the cough with codeine and enforcing strict bed rest.
claims.answer: Ornithosis (parrot fever) is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Chlamydia psittaci. It is caught by inhaling contaminated dust from the feathers, cage bedding, or droppings of infected birds — parrots, parakeets, lovebirds, canaries, and pigeons — and produces an 'atypical pneumonia.' Symptoms include fever, chills, weakness, loss of appetite, and a dry cough that becomes productive; early on it can be mistaken for flu, Legionnaires' disease, or Q fever, so exposure to birds (especially sick ones) is the key diagnostic clue, confirmed by a blood test. Treatment is the antibiotic tetracycline by mouth at 250-500 milligrams four times a day for 10-14 days, with the cough controlled by codeine and strict, enforced bed rest — untreated, parrot fever can be fatal.

claims.subject: osteitis_fibrosa
claims.question: How do you treat Paget's disease of bone?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's treatment aims to correct the dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio — cutting red meat and phosphate soft drinks, lowering vitamin D and sun exposure, raising calcium to 2,000 mg and magnesium to 1,000 mg a day, adding betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals, and following the baseline supplement program.
claims.answer: Osteitis fibrosa (nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism), also known as Paget's disease of bone, is a bone disease — more common in men — in which hard bone is lost and replaced by fibrous connective tissue. It often shows up first in the jaw (separating and loosening the teeth), then in the weight-bearing bones of the pelvis, femur, and tibia, with loss of height and a 'dowager's hump' (kyphosis). Mainstream medicine calls the cause unknown, but in animals it comes from a reversed dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio together with relatively large amounts of vitamin D. It is diagnosed by x-ray and by elevated blood alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone. Treatment should include a vigorous effort to correct the dietary calcium/phosphorus ratio: reduce or eliminate red meat, avoid phosphate-containing soft drinks and supplements, reduce vitamin D intake and sun exposure (hats, long sleeves), raise calcium and magnesium intake to 2,000 milligrams and 1,000 milligrams per day, take betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day fifteen minutes before meals, and follow the baseline nutritional supplement program.

claims.subject: osteoporosis
claims.question: How do you treat osteoporosis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats osteoporosis with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg a day, and colloidal minerals with boron — criticizing estrogen (possibly contraindicated for cancer risk) and fluoride as inadequate.
claims.answer: Osteoporosis is a loss of bone that usually develops in older people, more often in women. Wallach is critical of the standard push for estrogen and fluoride — he says those two alone do not solve the problem, and that estrogen may be contraindicated because of its potential to cause breast and uterine cancer. In his experience osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure with proper supplementation of stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) and calcium. He recommends a pulse test to find any food allergens that could be causing celiac-type changes and malabsorption. Symptoms include bone pain, joint pain, a 'dowager's hump,' and 'spontaneous' fractures; he calls osteoporosis the 12th most frequent cause of death in adults. Treatment should include betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day fifteen minutes before meals, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 milligrams and 1,000 milligrams per day (or more for the first 30 days), and plant-derived colloidal minerals that include calcium, magnesium, and boron.

claims.subject: otitis
claims.question: How do you treat earaches without antibiotics?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says 95 percent of earaches come from milk allergy and treats otitis with hydrogen peroxide or mullein eardrops, strict avoidance of cow's milk, and the baseline supplement, reserving antibiotics for cultured strep throat or inner-ear infection.
claims.answer: Otitis (earache) is inflammation of the ear — externa affecting the outer eardrum and ear canal, interna affecting the inner eardrum and the eustachian tube. The standard ear-nose-and-throat approach is antibiotic eardrops and oral antibiotics for acute cases and surgically inserted 'tubes' through the eardrum for chronic ones. Wallach says that in reality 95 percent of all earaches are the result of a milk allergy, which can cause severe fever, painful earaches, and even burst eardrums if not corrected — so do a pulse test before the eardrums are pierced and weakened unnecessarily. Treatment should include hydrogen peroxide or mullein eardrops to relieve local inflammation, strict avoidance of cow's milk in all forms, and the baseline nutritional supplement program; aspirin or acetaminophen (Tylenol) may be needed for pain. Antibiotics are justified only when a streptococcal sore throat or an internal ear infection is cultured.

claims.subject: palpitations
claims.question: What causes heart palpitations and how do you treat them?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says palpitations can come from heart disease, food allergies (such as MSG sensitivity), nutritional deficiencies (B-1, B-3, selenium, potassium) or hypoglycemia, and treats them with EDTA chelation, IV hydrogen peroxide, avoiding caffeine and sugar, B-vitamins, vitamin C, and calming herbs.
claims.answer: Palpitations (irregular heartbeat) can come from organic heart disease (easily checked with an electrocardiogram, EKG/ECG), food allergies (such as Chinese Restaurant Syndrome, an allergy to MSG/monosodium glutamate), nutritional deficiencies (for example vitamin B-1, vitamin B-3, selenium, potassium), and/or hypoglycemia. Treatment should include EDTA chelation for cardiovascular disease, intravenous hydrogen peroxide, and avoiding caffeine, offending food allergens, sugar, and processed foods; vitamin B-1 at 100 milligrams three times a day, vitamin B-3 at 450 milligrams three times a day as time-release tablets, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, and the baseline nutritional supplement program; plus herbs including hawthorn (Crataegus oxyacantha), lily-of-the-valley (Convallaria majalis), hops (Humulus lupulus), lavender (Lavandula angustifolia), motherwort (Leonurus cardiaca), valerian (Valeriana officinalis), and foxglove (Digitalis purpurea).

claims.subject: parasites
claims.question: How do you get rid of intestinal parasites and worms?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats parasites with garlic, peach, and walnut, and for heavy infestations lists stronger drugs — pyrantel pamoate for roundworms, niclosamide for tapeworms, and metronidazole for protozoa.
claims.answer: Parasites (worms) include roundworms (ascaris, hookworms, pinworms, whipworms), tapeworms, and microscopic single-celled organisms (amoeba, flagellates). Symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anal itching, weakness, and — with tapeworm — vitamin B-12 deficiency. Diagnosis is by a microscopic fecal exam for most intestinal parasites, except pinworms, which need a scotch-tape test. Treatment includes garlic (Allium sativum), peach (Prunus persica), and walnut (Juglans nigra); for heavy infestations needing stronger medication, Wallach lists pyrantel pamoate (for roundworms), niclosamide (for tapeworms), and metronidazole (for protozoa).

claims.subject: leucine
claims.question: How much leucine does Wallach recommend for Parkinson's disease?
claims.answer_short: For drug-induced Parkinsonism, Wallach's protocol includes leucine at 10 grams a day, alongside octacosanol, L-methionine, L-tyrosine, DL-phenylalanine, B-vitamins, essential fatty acids, and digestive enzymes.
claims.answer: Parkinsonism (shaking palsy) is caused by degeneration of the basal ganglia of the brain; its symptoms are relentlessly progressive and include muscular rigidity, lack of purposeful movement, and a 'pill rolling' tremor of the thumb and index finger. The cause of true Parkinson's disease is unknown, but many things can cause Parkinsonism-like symptoms: certain drugs (phenothiazines, haloperidol, reserpine), carbon-monoxide poisoning, and excessive manganese supplementation. For drug-induced Parkinsonism, treatment should include eliminating the offending drug, then octacosanol at 300 micrograms three times a day, Neuro-Gen, leucine 10 grams a day, L-methionine 5 grams a day, essential fatty acids one tablespoon twice a day, L-tyrosine 100 milligrams a day, DL-phenylalanine 100 milligrams three times a day, vitamin B-1 at 200 milligrams three times a day, vitamin B-6 at 100 milligrams three times a day, betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day before meals, and the baseline nutritional supplement program. He warns that the standard L-Dopa and carbidopa aggravate and speed up Parkinson's in a significant number of cases and have no benefit in more than half.

claims.question: How do you treat pica (craving dirt or paint)?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says pica is a symptom of nutritional deficiency and treats it with the baseline program including plant-derived colloidal minerals, using hair analysis to assess mineral status and EDTA chelation if lead or cadmium is elevated.
claims.answer: Pica (craving dirt or paint) is a symptom of one or more nutritional deficiencies: adults often crave ice, while children eat dirt and/or paint — the latter extremely dangerous because many paints contain lead or cadmium. claims.answer_short: Wallach links pilonidal cysts to a deficiency of zinc, vitamin A or folic acid, and treats them with a poultice of plantain and comfrey or boric acid twice a day until the cyst opens, with surgery needed only on rare occasions.
claims.answer: A pilonidal cyst is a midline congenital defect in the sacral area (lower back, near the tailbone), which Wallach links to a deficiency of zinc, vitamin A, or folic acid. The pit often contains hair and the tract is usually symptom-free unless it becomes plugged and turns into a cyst. Treatment should include a poultice of plantain (Plantago major) and comfrey (Symphytum officinale), or boric acid, twice a day until the cyst opens up; on rare occasions surgical opening of the cyst is required, needing only local anesthesia and a scalpel blade for this relatively minor surgery.

claims.answer: In his home-medicine guide, Wallach lists two traditional herbs for strengthening labor during childbirth: red raspberry (Rubus idaeus) and blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides), both long used in folk midwifery to encourage effective uterine contractions. He discusses them alongside the tools for controlling postpartum bleeding, such as ergot, in his practical chapter on remedies.

claims.subject: preeclampsia
claims.question: How do you prevent and treat preeclampsia (pregnancy toxemia)?
claims.answer_short: Wallach blames pregnancy toxemia on the low-protein, low-salt diets women were put on, and treats preeclampsia with a high-animal-protein meal plan (150+ grams), no salt restriction, vitamin B-6 (100 mg/day), the baseline supplement program, and 10-12 glasses of water or juice a day.
claims.answer: Pregnancy toxemia (eclampsia) is, in Wallach's view, the result of the low-protein, low-salt diets women were put on to limit weight gain in pregnancy. Pre-eclampsia symptoms include sudden weight gain (fluid accumulation from low blood protein), high blood pressure, and albuminuria (protein in the urine); eclampsia adds convulsions and/or coma, and both characteristically occur after the 20th week of pregnancy. Against the orthodox approach (hospitalize, watch for convulsions, then give barbiturates), treatment of pre-eclampsia should include a high-animal-protein meal plan (150 grams or more, versus the RDA — Recommended Dietary Allowance — of 40 grams), not restricting salt, vitamin B-6 at 100 milligrams per day (dropping to 50 milligrams at birth if you plan to breast-feed, since high B-6 levels reduce breast-milk production), the baseline nutritional supplement program, and 10-12 glasses of water and/or juice per day, especially in the warm summer months.

claims.subject: q_fever
claims.question: How do you treat Q fever?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats Q fever with tetracycline by mouth at 250 mg every 4 hours, using chloramphenicol in small children to avoid the tooth discoloration tetracycline can cause.
claims.answer: Q fever is an acute rickettsial disease caused by Coxiella burnetii, marked by sudden onset, fever, headache, weakness, and pneumonitis (lung inflammation). It has a worldwide distribution and is kept endemic in domestic animals — sheep, goats, and cattle are the primary reservoirs for human infection, which spreads through bites from the infected tick (Dermacentor andersoni) and from drinking infected raw milk; diagnosis is by a positive blood test. Treatment should include tetracycline by mouth at 250 milligrams every 4 hours (chloramphenicol may be used in small children to avoid the tooth discoloration tetracycline can cause).

claims.subject: psoriasis
claims.question: How do you treat psoriasis naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach attributes psoriasis to celiac-type intestinal changes causing malabsorption and treats it with pulse testing to avoid trigger foods, folic acid, vitamin A as beta carotene, lecithin, flaxseed oil, vitamin E, zinc, copper, selenium, and digestive enzymes.
claims.answer: Psoriasis is a cosmetically disfiguring dermatitis ('the heartbreak of psoriasis'), marked by dry, sharply demarcated, silvery scaling plaques that appear mainly behind the joints (elbows and knees), on the scalp, and behind the ears. Wallach attributes it to celiac-type changes in the intestines that cause malabsorption of essential nutrients, and advises a pulse test to identify specific food allergens. Treatment should include avoiding offending food allergens, rotation diets, folic acid at 15-25 milligrams per day, vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, lecithin at 2,500 milligrams three times a day with meals, flaxseed oil at one tablespoon twice a day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day, copper at 2 milligrams per day, selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day, and betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams per day. Topical herbal washes and topical vitamin A & D creams are of palliative value.

claims.subject: quinsy
claims.question: How do you treat quinsy (a peritonsillar abscess)?
claims.answer_short: Wallach urges patients to refuse a tonsillectomy and save their tonsils, treating quinsy with vitamin A (300,000 IU/day as beta carotene), zinc (50 mg three times a day), vitamin C to bowel tolerance, herbal gargles, and penicillin.
claims.answer: Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is an infection of the tonsil, between the tonsil and the pharyngeal constrictor muscle. It is rare in children but common in young adults. The 'orthodox' ear-nose-and-throat doctor will want to do a tonsillectomy — Wallach urges patients to save their tonsils and refuse it. Treatment should include vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, gargles with herbal washes, and penicillin G or V at 250 milligrams every 6 hours for 12-14 days.

IUper day as beta carotene, zinc at 50 mg t.i.d.,
vitamin C to bowel tolerance, gargles with

claims.subject: tularemia
claims.question: How do you treat tularemia (rabbit fever)?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats tularemia with intramuscular streptomycin at 500 mg every 12 hours until the fever normalizes, then oral tetracycline at 250 mg four times a day for 10-12 days.
claims.answer: Rabbit fever (tularemia) is caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis, contracted by skinning and dressing infected rabbits or ground squirrels (87 percent of cases). It first appears as a local ulceration at the infection site, then goes systemic into a typhoid-like illness with diarrhea and pneumonia, with high fever and recurring chills and drenching sweats; sputum cultures are highly infectious, so labs should be warned. Treatment of tularemia is with streptomycin intramuscularly at 500 milligrams every 12 hours until the temperature drops into the normal range, then tetracycline by mouth at 250 milligrams four times a day for 10-12 days.

claims.subject: rabies
claims.question: How do you treat rabies?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says rabies treatment must be started quickly to succeed and includes the well-known "rabies shots" every day for ten days plus respiratory support in a hospital, with preventive vaccination available for high-risk research personnel.
claims.answer: Rabies (hydrophobia) is a highly dangerous viral disease transmitted through the blood, tissue (including transplanted corneas, livers, kidneys, or hearts), urine, or saliva of infected animals or people. Besides bites from rabid bats, foxes, skunks, and unvaccinated dogs, Wallach notes many fatal cases follow tissue transplants, because rabies in humans is a progressive paralytic disease often misdiagnosed as stroke. He also points out the incubation period is fourteen days, so if you have had the biting pet for three weeks or more, rabies is an impossible diagnosis. Treatment should be started quickly if it is to succeed, and includes the well-known 'rabies shots' every day for ten days plus respiratory support in a hospital setting; high-risk research personnel can get preventive vaccination.
claims.verbatim:

treatment includes the well known "rabies
shots" every day for ten days and respiratory
support in a hospital setting

claims.subject: rickets
claims.question: What is rachitic rosary and how is it treated?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes rachitic rosary, beading where the ribs meet the rib cartilage in indoor children lacking vitamin D, as a sign of rickets, treated with oral vitamin D (400-1,000 IU/day), calcium and magnesium, and at least 30 minutes of daily sun.
claims.answer: Rachitic rosary is the beading at the junction of the ribs and rib cartilage, seen exclusively in small children kept indoors without an oral source of vitamin D; it is easily felt on examination. Wallach treats it as a sign of rickets (vitamin D deficiency). Treatment should include oral vitamin D at 400-1,000 IU per day plus the baseline nutritional supplement program including calcium and magnesium; once the abnormal bony changes normalize, drop the vitamin D dose to 250-400 IU per day, and afford daily sun exposure for at least 30 minutes.

claims.subject: radial_nerve_palsy
claims.question: How do you treat Saturday night palsy (radial nerve palsy)?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats radial nerve palsy — a wrist drop from compressing the radial nerve against the arm bone — with a B-complex 50 three times a day, topical DMSO, acupuncture and hydrotherapy.
claims.answer: Radial nerve palsy ('Saturday night palsy') results from compressing the radial nerve against the humerus — classically by draping the arm over the back of a hard-backed chair for an extended period during a drunken stupor or deep sleep — producing a wrist 'drop,' weakness extending the wrist and fingers, and sometimes a loss of sensory function between the first and second fingers. Treatment should include a B-complex 50 three times a day, topical dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), acupuncture, and hydrotherapy.

claims.subject: raynauds_disease
claims.question: How do you treat Raynaud's disease naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats Raynaud's disease with calcium and magnesium (2,000 mg and 1,000 mg/day), vitamin E (800-1,200 IU/day), essential fatty acids, L-tryptophan, avoiding food allergens and caffeine, acupuncture, chiropractic and circulation herbs like cayenne pepper.
claims.answer: Raynaud's disease is marked by tingling and numbness in the fingers (and sometimes the nose and tongue) caused by spasms of the small arteries; the orthodox approach is to cut sympathetic nerves and give anesthetics and tranquilizers. Wallach notes food allergies can be the precipitating factor when arteries are the target tissue (do a pulse test), and to rule out thoracic inlet syndrome. Treatment should include calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, avoiding offending food allergens and caffeine (coffee, tea, soft drinks, chocolate), vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times a day, L-tryptophan at 500 mg three times a day, acupuncture, chiropractic, and circulation-boosting herbs such as cayenne pepper (Capsicum minimum).

claims.question: What causes rectal itching and how do you treat it?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says rectal itching can come from candidiasis, food allergies, hemorrhoids, crabs, fleas or pinworms, and can be relieved with herbal washes, Preparation H, sitz baths with herbal washes or hydrogen peroxide, and specific treatment of the underlying parasites.
claims.answer: Rectal itching can be caused by candidiasis, food allergies, hemorrhoids, crabs, fleas, or pinworms; Wallach advises a pulse test for food allergies, a self/blood/skin test for candidiasis, the Scotch-tape test to identify pinworm eggs, and a mirror to self-examine the anal folds for fleas or hemorrhoids. claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Can vitamin C be given intravenously?
claims.answer_short: Yes, for Reye's syndrome Wallach uses intravenous vitamin C at 5-10 grams per day.
claims.answer: Reye's syndrome occurs most often in young teens, usually in fall and winter, and is thought to be caused by consuming aflatoxin (a toxin of the grain mold Aspergillus flavus); it is marked by pneumonitis, nausea and vomiting, a sudden change in mental status to deep depression, amnesia, agitation progressing to coma and convulsions, fixed dilated pupils, and death in 42-80% of cases. Treatment includes barbiturate anesthesia to lower intracranial pressure, intravenous fluids and electrolytes, pulmonary support, exchange transfusions, and dialysis, plus vitamin C intravenously at 5-10 grams per day, B-complex and B-12 intravenously or intramuscularly, and selenium intramuscularly or intravenously at 250-500 mcg per day.

claims.subject: rheumatic_fever
claims.question: How do you treat rheumatic fever?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says treating rheumatic fever early prevents heart damage, using aspirin for joint pain plus oral sulfadiazine (500-1,000 mg/day for 1-2 years) or penicillin G or V (250,000 units twice daily for two years).
claims.answer: Rheumatic fever is caused by a Streptococcus Group A infection (usually starting as a 'strep throat') and is marked by arthritis, skin rash, fever, heart-valve inflammation, and brain signs (chorea); the residual heart-valve damage is the most dangerous consequence of untreated disease, and diagnosis rests on the typical symptoms plus positive Group A Streptococcus cultures. Treatment early in the course prevents the heart damage and should include aspirin for joint pain and sulfadiazine orally at 500-1,000 mg per day for 1-2 years, or penicillin G or V orally at 250,000 units twice a day for two years.

claims.subject: histidine
claims.question: How much histidine does Wallach recommend for rheumatoid arthritis?
claims.answer_short: For rheumatoid arthritis, Wallach's protocol includes L-histidine at 1,000 mg three times a day, alongside treatment for Mycoplasma and many other nutrients.
claims.answer: Wallach holds that rheumatoid arthritis is not primarily an immune-system disease but is initially caused by infection with a Mycoplasma (PPLO, a pleuropneumonia-like organism) that causes an upper-respiratory infection and then attacks the joint membranes of the fingers and toes, and later the larger joints — a cause he says has been recognized and eliminated in veterinary medicine. Orthodox treatment (aspirin, gold shots, steroids) only relieves symptoms, though he notes 75% of patients improve in the first year with no treatment at all. Treatment should include specific treatment for Mycoplasma/PPLO (Tylosin, tetracyclines, etc.) for six months to one year, intravenous and/or oral hydrogen peroxide, chelation, acupuncture, enterically coated bromelain at 40 mg four times a day, autoimmune urine therapy, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), L-histidine at 1,000 mg three times a day, essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times a day, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, selenium at 500-1,000 mcg per day, copper at 2-4 mg per day, B-6 at 100 mg three times a day, cartilage at 5 grams three times a day, hydrotherapy, and herbs (topical camphor, black mustard, dandelion, devil's claw, juniper, stinging nettle, sweet vernal grass), plus plant-derived colloidal minerals.

claims.answer: Rickets is caused by a deficiency of vitamin D and is marked by stunted growth, joint pain, and deformed long bones (bow legs, dropped wrists, 'sickle shins,' barrel chest, rachitic rosary). Treatment includes supplementation with vitamin D at 400 IU orally, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, and exposure to sunshine for 30 minutes per day; advanced cases will require orthotic correction and, in some cases, orthopedic surgery.

claims.subject: ringworm
claims.question: How do you get rid of ringworm?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says ringworm is a fungal infection and treats it with oral Griseofulvin, vitamin A as beta carotene, zinc, vitamin E, ultraviolet light on the lesion, and topical herbs like plantain and castor oil.
claims.answer: Ringworm is caused by fungi (most often Microsporum/Tinea capitis or Trichophyton/Tinea cruris, 'jock itch') that invade the skin, nails, and hair, producing the characteristic circular lesions; cats, rabbits, and children are the most common sources, and diagnosis is by the typical lesions, fungal culture, and a positive Wood's lamp test (Microsporum lesions fluoresce a bright pastel green). Treatment should include Griseofulvin orally at 250 mg four times a day for four months, vitamin A at 25,000-300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, zinc at 50 mg three times a day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, ultraviolet light directly to the lesion for up to six minutes per day, and topical herbs including plantain (Plantago major) and castor oil (Ricinus communis).

claims.subject: rocky_mountain_spotted_fever
claims.question: How do you treat Rocky Mountain spotted fever?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says treatment should not wait for a positive blood test and includes tetracycline at 500 mg four times a day (orally or IV) plus supportive IV fluids and electrolytes.
claims.answer: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (tick fever) is caused by a rickettsia (Rickettsia rickettsii) transmitted by the bite of an infected tick (wood, dog, or lone-star tick); it occurs May through October during tick season, mostly along the Eastern seaboard, and affects small children with access to wooded areas (often via the family dog). Symptoms follow 7-12 days after a bite — headaches, chills, weakness, muscle pain, fever, dry cough, and a skin rash starting on the wrists, ankles, palms, soles, and forearms then spreading. Wallach warns: do NOT wait for a positive blood test before starting treatment, as death may occur as quickly as 4-10 days after symptoms appear. Treatment should include tetracycline at 500 mg four times a day orally, or intravenously if the patient cannot swallow capsules, plus supportive intravenous fluids and electrolytes.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of RMSF should include tetracycline at 500 mg q.i.d. orally or IV if the patient
can't swallow capsules. Supportive treatment
with rv fluids and electrolytes is essential to
rapid and full recovery

claims.subject: roseola
claims.question: How do you treat roseola in a child?
claims.answer_short: Wallach directs treatment at reducing the fever enough to prevent convulsions, plus topical poultices on the rash (as for measles).
claims.answer: Roseola is an acute viral disease of infants and toddlers marked by high fever (up to 105 F) and a rash that predominates on the belly and chest and lightly on the face and limbs; convulsions may occur during the high-fever periods, and after 3-4 days the child feels completely well even though the rash persists. Treatment is directed to reducing the fever sufficiently to prevent convulsions, plus topical poultices on the rash (see measles).

Treatment of roseola is directed to reducing
the fever sufficiently to prevent convulsions
and topical poultices on the rash (see measles).

claims.answer_short: Wallach's treatment is a total-body application of 1% lindane or 25% benzyl benzoate cream in adults, and 5-10% sulfur ointment in infants (to avoid neurotoxicity), with poke usable topically as a natural alternative.
claims.answer: Scabies ('itch') is caused by an almost microscopic mite (Sarcoptes scabiei) that burrows into the skin; it is very contagious person-to-person, and the original infestation usually comes from an infected animal or contaminated animal bedding. Treatment includes total-body application of 1% gamma benzene hexachloride (lindane) or 25% benzyl benzoate cream in adults, and 5-10% sulfur ointment in infants to avoid potential neurotoxicity; poke (Phytolacca decandra) may be used topically as a natural alternative.

claims.answer: Scarlatina (scarlet fever) is caused by a Streptococcus Group A throat infection; the organism releases a toxin that produces a rash most common on the belly, sides, and skin folds, plus a red pulpy 'strawberry' tongue, with fever common in the early stages. Aggressive treatment is recommended to prevent death or rheumatic fever, and diagnosis rests on the characteristic lesions plus positive Group A Streptococcus throat cultures. Treatment of scarlatina is oral penicillin V at 250 mg four times a day for 10-14 days.

claims.question: How do you treat sciatica naturally?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats sciatica with hydrotherapy, chiropractic, acupuncture, inversion-gravity therapy, calcium and magnesium, and the baseline supplement program with colloidal minerals.
claims.answer: Sciatica (low back pain radiating down the buttocks and legs) can be caused by subluxations of the lumbar vertebrae, thinning of a lumbar intervertebral disc, or even a thick wallet in one back pocket; in its most severe form it may result from a ruptured intervertebral disc. claims.subject: scoliosis
claims.question: Can scoliosis be treated with nutrition?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties scoliosis to uneven spinal-muscle degeneration and malabsorption, says early aggressive supplementation can bring a complete cure, and treats it with avoiding trigger foods, vitamin E, selenium, calcium and magnesium, colloidal minerals, and chiropractic.
claims.answer: Scoliosis (curvature of the spine) occurs in preteens and teens (80% in girls) during rapid growth; it may be benign or herald early muscular dystrophy, and Wallach attributes it to one set of spinal muscles being stronger than the other from muscle degeneration, with celiac-type intestinal damage and malabsorption as a possible cause. Treatment in the early stages will result in a complete cure, while failure to aggressively supplement leads to persistent damage requiring back braces and surgery. Treatment should include avoidance of offending food allergens, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, selenium at 500-1,000 mcg per day, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, and the baseline supplement program including plant-derived colloidal minerals; chiropractic can be very useful for the associated back-muscle spasms.

claims.answer: Scurvy (bleeding gums) is caused by a vitamin C deficiency and may occur concurrently with gingivitis. Treatment should include vitamin C to bowel tolerance, increased intake of green leafy vegetables and fruit, and herbs including dog rose (Rosa canina).

claims.subject: sebaceous_cyst
claims.question: How do you treat a sebaceous cyst?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's treatment is a stab incision at the lowest edge of the cyst, evacuating the contents and flushing with hydrogen peroxide; large cysts need the cyst wall removed and a gauze drain over 7-10 days.
claims.answer: A sebaceous cyst (wen, steatoma) is a slow-growing benign cystic skin 'tumor' containing sebaceous material, frequently found on the scalp (wen), ears, back, or scrotum; it ranges from pea- to golf-ball-sized, is firm (like a soft-shell egg), and painless. Treatment includes a 'stab' incision at the lowest edge of the cyst, evacuating the contents, and flushing with hydrogen peroxide; large cysts require removal of the cyst wall to prevent refilling, placing a sterile gauze drain in the empty cyst and gradually removing it over 7-10 days.

evacuate the contents; flush with hydrogen

claims.answer_short: Wallach's treatment for seborrheic dermatitis (dandruff) includes biotin, folic acid, vitamin B-6, vitamin E, essential fatty acids, vitamin A as beta carotene, zinc, and topical Selsun Blue shampoo, noting celiac-type malabsorption can underlie it.
claims.answer: Seborrheic dermatitis (dandruff) is a scaling dermatitis of the scalp and face with normal sebum composition and amount; celiac-type intestinal lesions can be the underlying cause of a malabsorption syndrome. Treatment should include biotin at 100 mcg three times a day, folic acid at 15-25 mg per day, B-6 at 100 mg three times a day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times a day, vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, zinc at 50 mg three times a day, and Selsun Blue shampoo topically.

SEBORRHEIC DERMATIS (dandruff): is a
scaling dermatitis of the scalp and face; the

claims.answer: Wallach holds that pregnancy is a normal biological process, not a disease, and that hospitalizing women to deliver babies is rarely medically necessary (exceptions such as Rh incompatibility or placenta previa aside). He says home birth is the safest, least expensive option and brings the family together, noting that more infections occur in newborns and post-delivery mothers in the hospital than at home, and that the United States ranks 23rd in newborn mortality among industrialized nations (World Health Organization). He invokes the history of Dr. Ignaz Semmelweis, who showed that orthodox doctors who failed to wash their hands between the autopsy room and the delivery room caused far higher newborn mortality (about 80%) than hand-washing midwives (about 5%) at the Vienna Children's Hospital between 1774 and 1836.

claims.subject: cystic_fibrosis
claims.question: Is cystic fibrosis really genetic?
claims.answer_short: Wallach's signature thesis: no - it's a selenium and essential-fatty-acid deficiency from the mother's malabsorption. He cites 1972 Cornell chicks cured in 21 days by selenium, and 450 patients treated since 1978.
claims.answer: Wallach's signature thesis: cystic fibrosis is not a genetic disease but a selenium and essential-fatty-acid deficiency in the fetus and/or breastfed newborn, initiated by the mother's malabsorption of selenium from subclinical celiac disease and food allergies. Selenium deficiency produces the classic cystic-fibrosis lesions of the pancreas; affected infants are born with normal lungs and a negative 'sweat test' that only turns positive over the first months of life as they lose the essential fatty acids their mother gave them as a fetus. He notes the sweat test (introduced by Dr. Paul di Sant'Agnese of the National Institutes of Health in 1958) is non-specific, also turning positive in eight other conditions such as celiac disease, allergies and starvation. He marshals evidence: Dr. Klaus Schwartz reported selenium as an essential nutrient in 1958 and recorded cystic-fibrosis-like pancreatic changes in deficient rats; in 1972 Cornell University found chicks from selenium-deficient hens developed classic cystic fibrosis that was totally cured within 21 days when selenium was given within 30 days of hatching; in 1978 Wallach reported the first agreed-upon non-human cystic fibrosis in NASA monkeys (and says he was fired with 24 hours' notice, 10 days after his wife died). Since 1978 he reports treating 450 cystic-fibrosis patients with excellent results. A joint study with Harbin Medical University and Shanghai First Medical University examined 1,700 Chinese children who died of Keshan disease (a selenium-deficiency heart disease); 595 — 35% — had classic cystic-fibrosis pancreatic lesions, and of over 400 cystic-fibrosis autopsies, 79 had Keshan heart disease.

claims.answer_short: Wallach warns that rare beef can transmit toxoplasmosis, especially dangerous for pregnant women because the infection will cause birth defects in the fetus — brain defects, blindness and mental retardation.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that eating rare beef can transmit toxoplasmosis, which is of particular danger to pregnant women because infection will cause birth defects in the fetus — brain defects, blindness and mental retardation.

claims.subject: pork
claims.question: Can eating pork trigger a gallbladder attack?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- pork ranks just behind eggs (which Wallach blames for 93% of gallbladder attacks) and onions as a leading food trigger of gallbladder attacks.
claims.answer: Yes. Wallach names pork among the foods most likely to precipitate a gallbladder attack. He says eggs precipitate 93% of all gallbladder attacks, with onions and pork following closely behind -- so eating pork ranks near the very top of his list of foods that set off gallbladder attacks.
claims.verbatim:
Eggs are known to precipitate 93%
of all gallbladder attacks, followed closely by
onions and pork.
Treatment of gallbladder disease and gallstones

claims.subject: pork
claims.question: Can you get parasites or tapeworms from pork?
claims.answer_short: Yes -- raw pork is one of Wallach's named tapeworm sources (alongside raw beef, raw fish, and contaminated watercress); once eaten, the larvae grip the intestinal wall with the hooks or suckers on their head.
claims.answer: Wallach warns that raw pork is one of the foods that transmits tapeworm; the encysted larvae hatch in the gut and latch onto the intestinal wall.
claims.verbatim:
Tapeworms are contracted by eating
contaminated watercress, raw fish, raw beef
or raw pork. The encysted larvae are released
into the digestive tract and attach to the intes-
tinal wall by suckers or hooks in their head.

claims.subject: fish
claims.question: How does fish oil help cholesterol / heart health?
claims.answer_short: The EPA in fish oil (and flax oil) raises protective HDL cholesterol — the fraction that ferries cholesterol to the liver for disposal — while refined sugar drives HDL down to dangerous levels.
claims.answer: The EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) in fish oil (and flax oil) raises protective HDL cholesterol — the fraction that ferries cholesterol to the liver for disposal — while refined sugar drives HDL down to dangerous levels.
claims.verbatim:
HDLs are increased by consumption of
eicosapentanoic acids (EPA - fish oils or flax
seed oils). Refined sugars in your diet will
lower this valuable substance to dangerous
levels.

claims.subject: detox
claims.question: Do supplements help protect against heavy metals and pollution?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says plant-derived colloidal minerals do double duty — preventing disease and reducing your risk of damage from heavy metals and pollution in the environment.
claims.answer: Wallach's answer is his signature supplement — plant-derived colloidal minerals — which he says do not just prevent deficiency disease but 'reduce your risk of damage from heavy metals and pollution in the environment.' Colloidal here means the minerals exist as ultra-fine particles (Angstrom scale) that a plant has already pulled from the soil and rebuilt into a living, absorbable form — which is why he rates them about 98% absorbable and makes them the base of any 'public health program.' The logic is protective as much as nutritional: a body kept fully mineral-replete is, in his framing, more resistant to the toxic metals and pollutants it is inevitably exposed to.
claims.verbatim:
Be sure to include plant derived colloidal minerals into your public health program
- they prevent disease and reduce your risk of
damage from heavy metals and pollution in
the environment!

claims.subject: detox
claims.question: How does Wallach say to reduce my exposure to environmental toxins?
claims.answer_short: Take control of your household environment: grow some of your own organic food and filter your home's water and air — a bone-charcoal filter, he says, removes hydrocarbons and heavy metals.
claims.answer: Wallach frames environmental toxins as something you have to take personal control of — 'we must take matters into our own hands.' His program for dropping your 'personal pollution load': grow a portion of your own organic food (which also cuts the pollution you take in through food), and treat home water and air treatment as necessities, not luxuries. He is most insistent on water — he claims more than 3,000 chemicals survive municipal treatment, most carcinogenic and undetectable by taste ('just because the water is clear doesn't mean that it is safe'), and that a bone-charcoal filter 'will remove all of the hydrocarbons and heavy metals.' The through-line: you spend a third or more of your day at home, so cleaning up that micro-environment is high-leverage — do not wait for a 'Love Canal' in your own community.
claims.verbatim:
This means dropping our
personal pollution load to a minimum by
growing a certain amount of our own "organic" food, we must have home water treatment systems and air conditioning systems in
the fullest sense (not just cooling)

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: How much selenium does Wallach recommend a day?
claims.answer_short: For everyday maintenance, Wallach's Base Line program sets selenium at 200 mcg a day — with a much higher short-term therapeutic range (500–3,000 mcg) reserved for actively treating disease.
claims.answer: In his Base Line Nutritional Supplement Program, Wallach lists selenium's daily maintenance target (“True Supplement Need”) at 200 mcg — pointedly leaving the official RDA column as a question mark, since he rejects government RDAs as too low to prevent disease. In his Epigenetics dosing he frames it by body weight: roughly 100–200 mcg per 100 lb per day. Above maintenance he defines a 30-day “pharmacologic” range of 500 to 3,000 mcg for actively reversing a deficiency disease, and for cancer specifically names 1,000–3,000 mcg/day. He also stresses form over milligrams: plant-derived colloidal selenium, he says, is far better absorbed than the cheap metallic kind — so the number on the label only matters if your gut can take it up.
claims.verbatim:
SELENIUM ? 200 mcg 500 to 3,000 mcg
SODIUM 1,100 mg 3,300 mg 300 to 3,000 mg

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: Can you take too much selenium?
claims.answer_short: Yes — although Wallach uses high therapeutic doses, he also lists clear signs of selenium excess: hair loss, brittle nails, a garlic odor on the breath, a metallic taste, and arthritis, with kidney and liver dysfunction at more serious levels.
claims.answer: Selenium is one of the minerals where the gap between “enough” and “too much” genuinely matters, and Wallach documents both ends. The tell-tale signs of selenium toxicity, in his listing, are alopecia (hair loss), brittle nails, a distinctive garlic odor on the breath, a metallic taste in the mouth, and arthritis — with kidney and liver dysfunction at more serious excess. It's the necessary counterweight to his high therapeutic doses: the 500–3,000 mcg ranges he cites are deliberate, time-limited treatment levels rather than open-ended daily habits, and these symptoms are the body's signal to pull back.
claims.verbatim:
SELENIUM TOXICITY
alopecia
arthritis
brittle nails
garlic breath
metallic taste
kidney dysfunction
liver dysfunction

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Does zinc help acne?
claims.answer_short: Zinc is part of Wallach's acne protocol at 50 mg three times a day — though he considers acne primarily an essential-fatty-acid deficiency combined with too much saturated fat.
claims.answer: Wallach treats acne as primarily an essential-fatty-acid deficiency combined with eating too much saturated fat, so his first moves are cutting fast foods, fat and sugar and checking for food allergies to wheat, milk and soy. Within that protocol he includes zinc at 50 mg three times a day, along with essential fatty acids (flaxseed oil 1 tablespoon twice a day), betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes, 300,000 units of vitamin A as beta carotene for five months, and B-6 100 mg three times a day. He also suggests topical vitamin E oil and brief ultraviolet light on the affected areas.

claims.subject: zinc
claims.question: Does zinc help the immune system?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says zinc, together with vitamins A, C and E and selenium, is of great value in restoring immune status when fighting infections like thrush.
claims.answer: Wallach treats thrush — a Candida yeast overgrowth that turns pathogenic when the body's defenses drop (malnutrition, chemotherapy, AIDS, or antibiotics that wipe out competing organisms) — by rebuilding immunity. He states that vitamin C, selenium, vitamin E, vitamin A (as beta carotene), and zinc (50 mg, three times a day) are of great value in restoring immune status. In his framework zinc is a core nutrient for shoring up the body's ability to defend itself against infection.

vitamin A at 25,000-
300,000 IU per day as beta carotene and zinc
at 50 mg t.i.d. are of great value in restoring the
immune status.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: What causes joint pain?
claims.answer_short: Wallach lists nutritional deficiencies — including calcium, magnesium, sulfur, sulfur-bearing amino acids and copper — among the causes of joint pain, alongside conditions like arthritis, gout and food allergies.
claims.answer: Among the many causes of joint pain, Wallach names various nutritional deficiencies — calcium, magnesium, sulfur, sulfur-bearing amino acids and copper — so magnesium deficiency is one of several nutritional shortfalls he holds responsible. He says joint pain can also stem from disease processes such as arthritis, osteoporosis, rickets, gout and obesity, as well as food allergies and sensitivities. Correcting the underlying deficiency (magnesium among them) is part of his approach.

JOINT PAIN: can be caused by a variety of
disease processes including arthritis,
osteoporosis, rickets, gout,obesity and vari-
ous nutritional deficiencies (i.e. , calcium, mag-
nesium, sulfur, sulfur bearing amino acids and
copper) and food allergies/ sensitivities.

claims.subject: magnesium
claims.question: Will taking calcium supplements give me kidney stones?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says no — even heavy calcium supplementation will not cause kidney stones as long as you take magnesium along with it.
claims.answer: Wallach directly addresses the common fear that big calcium doses cause kidney stones: he says heavy calcium supplementation will not cause stones if you take magnesium with it. In the passage he is using calcium at 2,000 mg with magnesium at 1,000 mg (for gum disease), and advises cutting the calcium back to 2,000 mg per day once the acute problem resolves. In his framework magnesium is the safeguard that makes generous calcium supplementation safe.

2,000 mg/day after the teeth tighten up.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Can omega-3 / essential fatty acids help cystic fibrosis?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says cystic fibrosis is prevented in animals by adequate selenium and essential fatty acid nutrition in the mother, and treated in people with flaxseed oil and selenium.
claims.answer: Wallach reports that the veterinary profession has prevented cystic fibrosis in pet, farm and laboratory animals by ensuring adequate selenium and essential fatty acid nutrition in the preconception, pregnant, and nursing mother. In people he treats it early with selenium and flaxseed oil at 5 gm three times a day.

The prevention of CF has been accomplished

veterinary profession by assuring adequate
levels of selenium and essential fatty acid
nutriture to the preconception, pregnant and
nursing mother.

claims.subject: omega-3
claims.question: Does omega-3 help with PMS?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says PMS is driven by essential fatty acid deficiency acting with the monthly hormone cycle, and he includes EFAs in his PMS treatment.
claims.answer: Wallach states it is now known that deficiencies of essential fatty acids, working together with a woman's cyclical hormone patterns, produce the classic PMS picture — fragile emotions, irrational behavior, mania, depression, and debilitating pelvic cramps. Essential fatty acids are part of his PMS treatment program.

tional behavior, mania, depression and debili-
tating pelvic "cramps."

claims.subject: vitamin-c
claims.question: Can vitamin C deficiency cause nosebleeds?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says nosebleeds are usually the result of vitamin K and/or vitamin C deficiencies.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, nosebleeds (epistaxis) are usually caused by a deficiency of vitamin K and/or vitamin C. He is critical of orthodox ear-nose-throat doctors who cauterize (burn) capillaries in the nasal membranes to stop the bleeding rather than correct the underlying deficiency.

claims.question: How much vitamin C should I take when I'm sick?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recommends taking vitamin C 'to bowel tolerance' - and, if you already have diarrhea, 1,000 mg time-release tablets hourly through the day.
claims.answer: For illness, Wallach's instruction is to take vitamin C 'to bowel tolerance' - as much as the gut will take. In treating the flu he adds that if you already have diarrhea you should take 1,000 mg time-release tablets hourly during your waking day, keeping vitamin C levels up while the body fights the infection.

tablets hourly during your waking day)

claims.subject: vitamin-a
claims.question: Can low vitamin A cause infertility?

claims.subject: iron
claims.question: What does iron deficiency look like on a blood test?
claims.answer_short: Iron deficiency shows up as decreased hemoglobin and small red cells — the picture of a microcytic anemia.
claims.answer: On a complete blood count, Wallach says iron deficiency shows up as decreased hemoglobin (HGB), the protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen and carbon dioxide. It also produces very small red blood cells and a reduced mean corpuscular volume (MCV) — the classic picture of a microcytic anemia. By contrast, larger cells or elevated values point instead to B-12 or folic acid deficiency.

HGB (hemoglobin) is the specialized protein
in the RBC that actually binds with oxygen and
carbon dioxide. Increased values are seen in
B-12 deficiency (because there are fewer cells)
and decreased values are characteristic of iron
deficiency.

It sits alongside vitamin E at 800 to 1,200 IU per day, selenium at 500 to 1,000 mcg per day, and essential fatty acids (salmon and flaxseed oil) in his protocol for heavy or painful menses.

claims.subject: calcium
claims.question: Is arthritis caused by a calcium deficiency?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds that arthritis is fundamentally a calcium deficiency made worse by too much phosphorus in the American diet.
claims.answer: In Wallach's framework, arthritis is, in fact, a deficiency of calcium complicated by the excess phosphorus in the American diet. He places it alongside other degenerative conditions he traces to specific nutrient shortfalls—diabetes and hypoglycemia to chromium and vanadium deficiencies, cystic fibrosis to selenium and essential fatty acid deficiency, and cancer to an immune system starved of essential nutrients. His overarching claim is that malnutrition resulting from malabsorption is the common denominator of almost all degenerative disease.

common denominator of almost all degenerative disease.

claims.subject: vitamin-b3

claims.answer_short: In orthomolecular medicine, niacinamide is given at 3,000 mg per day for psychosis — far above the tiny 1.5 mg RDA for niacin.
claims.answer: Wallach describes the 'megavitamin' approach — the basis of what Linus Pauling called orthomolecular medicine and Abram Hoffer extended into orthomolecular psychiatry — which uses vitamins at pharmacologic doses. claims.subject: potassium
claims.question: What is a normal potassium level in a blood test?
claims.answer_short: Wallach gives a normal blood potassium range of 3.5 to 4.4 mEq/L.

claims.subject: sodium
claims.question: What does sodium do in the body?
claims.answer_short: Sodium is an essential macro-mineral that maintains acid-base balance, fluid pressure in the blood and tissues, and neuromuscular function.
claims.answer: Wallach classifies sodium (Na) as an essential "macro" mineral required in the diet. It maintains proper acid-base balance in the blood and tissues, regulates fluid pressure in the blood vessels and cells, and supports neuromuscular function. Elevated blood sodium points to dehydration, kidney disease, or adrenal dysfunction, while low blood sodium is typical of excessive water intake, diabetes, or pituitary disorders; the normal blood range is 135-147 mEq/L.

claims.answer_short: Wallach gives a normal blood phosphorus range of 3.1–4.5 mg%, kept within narrow limits by parathyroid hormone.

claims.answer_short: Wallach gives a normal blood chloride range of 95–110 mEq/L; low levels point to diarrhea, infection, diabetes, or weak adrenals.

claims.subject: nitrogen
claims.question: What is BUN (blood urea nitrogen) and what does it mean?
claims.answer_short: BUN, or blood urea nitrogen, is a barometer of how well the liver and kidneys process the by-products of protein metabolism.

claims.answer_short: Wallach frames his whole self-care approach around one purpose: giving you enough information to avoid unnecessary doctor or hospital visits.

claims.subject: selenium
claims.question: How did Wallach discover selenium's role in cystic fibrosis?
claims.answer_short: By accident. A selenium-deficient diet fed to a Yerkes monkey colony produced the first non-human cystic fibrosis in 1978, and Wallach found the disease could be reproduced at will by removing selenium -- pointing to prenatal selenium deficiency as the cause.
claims.answer: Wallach discovered it as a veterinary pathologist at the Yerkes Regional Primate Research Center. In 1978 he made the first universally accepted diagnosis of cystic fibrosis in a non-human -- an infant rhesus monkey -- from its pancreas and liver. The decisive clue was that this CF monkey and two age-peers had developed the disease iatrogenically, by accident, after a selenium-deficient diet was fed to a normal breeding colony, and the CF could then be reproduced at will with that same selenium-deficient diet. Cross-checking a computer literature search of veterinary journals on the tissue changes of pure selenium deficiency against his own observations of the pancreas, liver, and heart of the selenium-deficient monkeys, Wallach proposed that the pancreatic, liver, and heart lesions of CF were in fact the result of a prenatal selenium deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
a trace mineral, Selenium, in the etiology and
prevention of Cystic Fibrosis while a research veterinary pathologist
