claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: What do high chloride levels in a hair mineral analysis mean?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says elevated hair sodium, potassium, and chloride point to an essential fatty acid deficiency, not a true excess.
claims.answer: On a hair mineral analysis, Wallach reads elevated levels of sodium, potassium, and chloride as a sign of essential fatty acid deficiency. He explains that without enough EFAs the skin glands malfunction and leak electrolytes instead of conserving them, so the high readings are false. These false elevations return to normal once the person is properly supplemented with minerals and essential fatty acids.
claims.verbatim: Elevated hair levels of sodium, potassium and chloride indicate deficiencies of essential fatty acids, with resultant malfunctions of the skin glands which loose electrolytes instead of conserving them. These false “elevations” return to normal following the proper mineral and essential fatty acid supplementation.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: What causes the body to lose chloride?
claims.answer_short: Wallach ties chloride (as NaCl) loss to conditions like cystic fibrosis and Addison's disease, which disturbs the body's acid-base balance.
claims.answer: Discussing how the body manages hydrogen ions and pH, Wallach notes that large amounts of hydrogen ions can build up during disease — or through the loss of chloride ions. He links chloride (NaCl) loss to salt deficiency, cystic fibrosis, and Addison's disease. In his account, losing chloride is one of the ways acid-base balance gets thrown off.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Does sodium chloride control water balance in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach describes sodium chloride (the cell salt Natrum Mur) as regulating cellular moisture by attracting and distributing water.
claims.answer: Wallach presents sodium chloride — known in cell-salt terms as Natrum Mur, the chloride of soda — as a constituent of every liquid and solid part of the body. He says it regulates the moisture inside cells by attracting and distributing water, and since the body is about 70% water, that water would be inert and useless without it. A deficiency, in this account, throws off the body's water balance, leaving a watery, bloated appearance.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Where does the body get chloride?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says ordinary table salt (sodium chloride) is the universal source of chloride ions.
claims.answer: Wallach identifies sodium chloride — ordinary table salt — as the universal source of chloride ions. In his framework the diet's chloride comes from salt, which ties chloride intake directly to salt consumption.
claims.verbatim:
Sodium chloride or salt is the universal
source of chloride ions.

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Isn't chlorine a poisonous gas—how can it be essential?
claims.answer_short: Wallach opens his minerals chapter with a quote noting salt joins an explosive metal (sodium) and a lethal gas (chlorine), yet becomes an absolute necessity for life.
claims.answer: To frame chlorine's paradox, Wallach opens his minerals chapter with a quote from G. Young in National Geographic: salt is a blend of sodium—a metal so unstable it bursts into flame in water—and chlorine, a lethal gas. When swallowed, the quote notes, the blend forms hydrochloric acid in the stomach; rather than being suicidal, it is an absolute necessity for life. Wallach uses the passage to underscore that a dangerous element becomes indispensable in its dietary form.
claims.verbatim:
Even its basic makeup defies logic. Salt is a blend
of sodium and chlorine - the first a metal so un-
stable that it bursts into flame when exposed to
water; the second a lethal gas. When we swallow
the blend, it forms hydrochloric acid in our stom-
achs. Suicidal? No, an absolute necessity for life.”

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Is salt bad for you?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says salt itself is not harmful, contrary to popular belief, though relying on it can fool the body into thinking it's getting minerals.
claims.answer: Contrary to popular belief, Wallach maintains that salt consumption is not in and of itself harmful. The real problem he points to is different: because processed salt makes the body think it is getting minerals, it works like an empty-calorie diet — satisfying a craving without delivering the trace minerals the body is actually seeking. Historically, he notes, unprocessed salt was valuable precisely because it did carry trace minerals and rare earths.

ful; it does present the problem of allowing
our bodies to think we are getting minerals
(the equivalent of the “empty calorie diets”,
i.e.- processed food calories without vita-

claims.subject: chloride
claims.question: Who discovered that chloride had medical value?
claims.answer_short: Wallach credits Paracelsus, whose research into minerals and disease led him to the medical value of chloride.
claims.answer: Wallach credits the physician Paracelsus with discovering the medical value of chloride. He describes Paracelsus's research into minerals and disease as leading him to the curative value of chloride along with sulfate of mercury, flowers of sulfur, and antimony. This is part of Wallach's broader account of how minerals came to be recognized as medicine.

fur and antimony.

claims.subject: tyrosine
claims.question: What does tyrosine have to do with hair and skin color?
claims.answer_short: Tyrosine is the raw material for melanin, the pigment in hair and skin; the enzyme tyrosinase acts on it with copper as a cofactor, so a copper shortage can turn hair white, silver, or gray.
claims.answer: Tyrosine is the starting material the body uses to make melanin, the pigment that colors hair and skin. The enzyme tyrosinase acts on tyrosine to build the pigment, and this reaction requires copper as a cofactor. Wallach points out the practical consequence: when copper is deficient, the reaction stalls and hair turns white, silver, or gray. He also notes that red hair is a different case -- its pigment (tricosiverin) is an iron-based compound rather than ordinary melanin.

claims.subject: tyrosine
claims.question: Who discovered thyroxin, the thyroid hormone?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts that in the first quarter of the 20th century a chemist he names as Kenall isolated a crystalline iodine-tyrosine complex, about 65% iodine, and called it thyroxin -- the thyroid hormone.
claims.answer: The bond between tyrosine and the thyroid has a discovery story. Wallach recounts that in the first quarter of the twentieth century, after low iodine content had been tied to endemic goiter, a chemist he names as Kenall isolated a crystalline complex of iodine and the amino acid tyrosine -- roughly 65% iodine -- and named it thyroxin, the thyroid hormone. It was direct chemical proof that the thyroid's hormone is built from iodine bonded to tyrosine, which is why Wallach counts a tyrosine shortage among the causes of goiter.

claims.subject: hydrogen
claims.question: How does the body use hydrogen peroxide to fight infection?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says neutrophils (white blood cells) make hydrogen peroxide as a 'lethal weapon' to destroy germs and cancer cells, while the enzyme catalase protects healthy tissue from the excess.
claims.answer: Wallach describes hydrogen peroxide as one of the body's own built-in weapons. Neutrophils, the white blood cells that hunt down viruses, bacteria, yeast, fungi, parasites and cancer cells, are packed with tiny organelles called peroxisomes whose only job is to make hydrogen peroxide and eject it onto the captured target to destroy it. Because neutrophils are 'sloppy' and spill their excess peroxide into the bloodstream, Wallach notes the body is protected by an enzyme, catalase, that coats the red blood cells and blood-vessel walls and rapidly breaks stray hydrogen peroxide down into water and singlet oxygen.
claims.verbatim: Neutrophils, a type of white blood cell that help defend us by identifying, engulfing and destroying invading micro-organisms (i.e.- virus, bacteria, yeast, fungus, etc.), parasites and cancer cells, use hydrogen peroxide as their “lethal weapon.” Neutrophils are packed with small organelles ( microscopic organs) called peroxisomes, whose sole function is to produce hydrogen peroxide and eject it onto the captured pathogen or cancer cell for the specific purpose of destroying it. Neutrophils tend to be very sloppy, dribbling their over-production of hydrogen peroxide freely into the blood stream.

claims.subject: nitrogen
claims.question: Where is nitrogen found and how much is in the body?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports nitrogen rising from about 20 ppm in igneous rock to 100,000 ppm in land animals, showing it concentrates strongly in living tissue.
claims.answer: Wallach traces nitrogen's concentration across nature: about 20 ppm in igneous rock, 0.23 ppm in fresh water and 0.5 ppm in sea water, rising to 1,000 ppm in soils (99% bound as non-basic nitrogen in humus). It climbs far higher through the living world -- 15,000 ppm in marine plants, 30,000 ppm in land plants, 75,000 ppm in marine animals, and 100,000 ppm in land animals. In other words, nitrogen concentrates dramatically in living tissue.
claims.verbatim: N - Nitrogen is found in igneous rocks at 20 ppm; fresh water at 0.23 ppm; sea water 0.5 ppm; soils 1,000 ppm (99 % present as non-basic N bound in humus); marine plants at 15,000 ppm; land plants at 30,000 ppm; marine animals at 75,000 ppm; land animals at 100,000 ppm.

claims.subject: silica
claims.question: What parts of the body contain silica?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says silica is present in the blood, bile, skin, hair and nails, and forms part of the connective tissue, bones, nerve sheaths and mucus membranes.
claims.answer: Wallach describes silica as a substance found abundantly throughout the plant kingdom — especially in grasses, grains and palms — and, less commonly, in the animal world. In the body it is present in the blood, bile, skin, hair and nails, and it forms part of the connective tissue, bones, nerve sheaths and mucus membranes. This broad presence across connective and hard tissues is why Wallach ties silica so closely to the strength and quality of the bones, skin, hair and nails.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: Why are newborn babies given silver drops in their eyes?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts that in 1884 Carl Sigmund Crede began the practice of putting a single prophylactic drop of 2% silver nitrate in every newborn's eyes to prevent gonorrheal eye infection at birth.
claims.answer: Silver's germ-killing power gave rise to one of medicine's most enduring newborn safeguards. Wallach relays from the older medical literature that in 1884 Carl Sigmund Crede, a German professor of obstetrics, instituted the practice of placing a single prophylactic drop of 2% silver nitrate in each eye of every infant at the moment of birth, to prevent infantile (gonorrheal) conjunctivitis -- the eye infection then called ophthalmia neonatorum. It grew out of a longer tradition of using silver nitrate, or 'lunar caustic,' to treat wounds, ulcers, and inflamed eyes.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: Why is silver linked to the moon and lunacy?
claims.answer_short: In Wallach's history of medicine, silver was tied to the moon -- believed to rule the head and emotions -- so 'Tincture of the moon' (a silver preparation) was long used for epilepsy, melancholia, and mania.
claims.answer: Silver carried a centuries-old link to the moon and the mind. Wallach recounts that in ancient times silver was associated with the moon, which was believed to control the head and the emotions -- the root of words like 'moonstruck' and 'lunacy' -- a relationship firmly entrenched by the chemical doctors of the 16th century. Because of it, 'Tincture of the moon' (Tinctura luna, a silver preparation) was long a popular remedy for epilepsy, melancholia, and mania, and in 1637 Angelus Sala used silver nitrate ('lunar caustic') as a purgative and for brain and uterine illnesses.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: What conditions can colloidal silver help with?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites a 1917 British Medical Journal report by J. Mark Hovell that colloidal silver helped ear, nose and throat problems -- blocked eustachian tubes, nasal catarrh, mouth/throat/ear infections -- plus septicemia, cystitis, whooping cough and shingles.
claims.answer: Colloidal silver had a broad clinical record in the pre-antibiotic era. Wallach cites a report by J. Mark Hovell in the British Medical Journal (December 15, 1917) that colloidal silver was beneficial for permanently restoring the patency of the eustachian tubes and for reducing nasopharyngeal catarrh. Hovell also reported it used successfully in septic conditions of the mouth (including pyorrhea and Rigg's disease), the throat (including tonsillitis), and the ear, as well as in generalized septicemia, leucorrhea, cystitis, whooping cough and shingles. Wallach presents these older reports as background to his view of silver as a broad-spectrum, non-toxic germ-killer.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: Does colloidal silver survive stomach acid when you swallow it?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says that taken internally, colloidal silver particles resist the dilute acids and alkalis of the stomach and intestine, so they keep their catalytic action and pass into the intestine unchanged.
claims.answer: According to Wallach, swallowed colloidal silver is not neutralized by digestion the way many substances are. Taken internally, the particles of colloidal silver are resistant to the action of the dilute acids and alkalies of the stomach and intestine, so they continue their catalytic action and pass into the intestine unchanged. That stability is part of why he frames silver as a systemic disinfectant -- its germ-killing action can survive digestion and reach the gut intact.

claims.subject: silver
claims.question: Has silver been used to treat cancer?
claims.answer_short: Wallach reports that Dr. Bjorn Nordstrom of Sweden's Karolinska Institute has used silver in his alternative cancer therapy programs.
claims.answer: Silver's medical use has reached even into cancer care, in Wallach's account. He reports that Dr. Bjorn Nordstrom of the Karolinska Institute in Sweden has used silver in his alternative cancer therapy programs. Wallach cites this alongside silver's broader credentials -- a broad-spectrum antibiotic said to kill over 650 disease-causing organisms while remaining non-toxic to humans at standard rates of consumption. He presents Nordstrom's work as a report, not as a protocol of his own.
claims.verbatim:

claims.subject: aluminum
claims.question: Was aluminum ever more valuable than silver?
claims.answer_short: Yes - Wallach recounts that aluminum was once worth more than silver, until Charles Hall's 1886 electrolysis process made it cheap.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts aluminum's fall from precious rarity to everyday metal. In 1884 an American metallurgist cast a 100-ounce pyramid of pure aluminum - the largest single lump ever made at that point - to cap the 555-foot Washington Monument; it was first displayed at Tiffany's in New York, where aluminum was worth more than silver and eight platinum lightning rods guarded it. Napoleon III had personally sponsored aluminum smelting research, yet the metal stayed semiprecious until 1886, when 22-year-old Charles Hall ran battery electricity through a molten mixture to isolate aluminum cheaply - the Hall-Heroult process that still makes nearly all of it today.

claims.subject: gold
claims.question: Was gold one of the first metals humans discovered?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds that gold, silver and copper were probably the first metals discovered in their native nugget form -- with gold likely the very first.
claims.answer: Wallach holds that gold, silver and copper were probably the first metals humans discovered, encountered in their native nugget form. He reasons gold was likely first of all, being the most widely distributed metal found as nuggets in nature; because gold resists corrosion, the bright color of a nugget would catch a primitive person's eye, and its refusal to chip or break like ordinary tool-making rocks would spark curiosity. Its beauty made gold a prized ornament long before it had any practical use.
claims.verbatim:
Gold, silver and copper were probably
the first metals (minerals) discovered in
their native nugget form.

claims.subject: cerium
claims.question: Was cerium ever used as a medicine?
claims.answer_short: Yes — in the 1800s physicians used cerium salts to control morning sickness and severe vomiting.
claims.answer: Cerium has a documented history as a medicine. Wallach recounts that in 1854 James Young Simpson, a professor of obstetrics at the University of Edinburgh, supported using oxalate of cerium to treat the morning sickness of early pregnancy. In 1860 Charles Lee, a house physician at Blockley Hospital in Philadelphia, reported successfully using cerium to control the vomiting associated with phthisis (pulmonary tuberculosis), pyrosis (severe heartburn), hysterical vomiting, and atonic dyspepsia — a lack of muscular tone in the gastrointestinal tract.

claims.subject: nickel
claims.question: Was nickel ever used as a medicine?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts that bromide of nickel was used in the 1800s as a therapy for epilepsy and similar diseases.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts that a Dr. Costa reported using bromide of nickel as a therapy for epilepsy and similar diseases. He notes that in an 1884 'controlled' study at the Jefferson Medical College Hospital in Philadelphia, nickel was reported to work best in cases where the attacks came regularly and at long intervals, and where the case had a hysterical or hypochondriacal feature.

claims.subject: barium
claims.question: Was barium ever used as a medicine?
claims.answer_short: Yes — Wallach recounts that 18th-century physician Adair Crawford used chlorinated barium to treat 'scrophulous' (TB of the cervical lymph nodes), believing it improved appetite and general health, though it could cause nausea and vertigo.
claims.answer: Wallach recounts the historical medicinal use of barium: the 18th-century physician Adair Crawford, at St. Thomas Hospital, investigated 'borytes' (chlorinated barium) and found it useful in certain cases of scrophulous — tuberculosis of the cervical lymph nodes — and believed it usually improved the appetite and general health. Barium was also reported to act as an evacuant and a deobstruent, though it carried toxic side effects including nausea and vertigo. Today, he notes, barium's medical role is different: barium sulfate serves as the opaque contrast medium for X-rays of the digestive tract.

claims.subject: arsenic
claims.question: Isn't arsenic a poison — why would I need it?
claims.answer_short: Wallach holds that although arsenic is feared as a poison, in trace levels it is in fact an essential element for optimal health and longevity.
claims.answer: Wallach pushes back on the idea that arsenic is nothing but a poison. He recounts that arsenic stayed an active medicine well into the 20th century — research into its medical uses remained vigorous until 1945, when penicillin took over as the preferred treatment for syphilis — and that it is still used today for sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis) and amoebic diseases. His conclusion: it is now generally accepted that, in trace levels, arsenic is in fact an essential element for optimal health and longevity.
claims.verbatim:

remained very active until 1945 when peni-
cillin came into general medical use and was
thought to be a superior treatment for syphi-
lis with fewer side effects. Arsenic is still used
today for the systemic treatment of sleeping
sickness (Trypanosomiasis) and amoebic
diseases. It is now generally accepted that
arsenic is in fact in trace levels an essential
element for optimal health and longevity.

claims.subject: tin
claims.question: How was tin used in medicine historically?
claims.answer_short: Wallach recounts that in the Middle Ages Paracelsus recommended tin to expel worms, and tin was also used as a sweat-inducer and a purgative for fevers, PMS, and venereal disease.
claims.answer: Wallach traces tin's long medicinal history. In the Middle Ages, Paracelsus first recommended tin to expel intestinal worms, and it was also used as a sweat-inducer and as a purgative for fevers, hysterical complaints (which Wallach glosses as PMS), and venereal diseases. He notes alchemists even alloyed tin with mercury and distilled it with sulfur and ammonium chloride to make a gold-colored pigment they called mosaic gold.

expel worms in the Middle Ages. Alchemists
produced mosaic gold (aurum musivum) by
alloying tin with mercury and then distill-

chloride. The resultant gold-like color gave

claims.subject: tuna
claims.question: Does canned tuna contain lead, and is it safe to eat?
claims.answer_short: Wallach cites a study finding canned tuna carries nearly double the lead of fresh tuna — the lead leaches in from the sealant used to close the seams of steel and tin cans.
claims.answer: In his chapter on toxic metals, Wallach lists canned foods as a hidden dietary source of lead: the sealant used to close the seams of steel and tin cans leaches lead into the food sitting inside. He points to tuna as the clearest example, citing a study in which canned tuna carried nearly double the level of lead found in the same fish sold fresh. He frames this as just one of several everyday routes — alongside leaded-gasoline residue settled on crops, chipping old lead paint, and lead-glazed imported pottery mistakenly used for food — by which lead, which he calls one of the most universally dangerous toxic metals, quietly enters the body.
claims.verbatim:
Another source of lead in our food chain
is the sealant materials used to close the
seams in steel or tin canned foods. One
study showed that canned tuna has nearly
double the level of lead as fresh tuna.

claims.subject: silver-nitrate
claims.question: What is silver nitrate (lunar caustic) and what has it been used for?
claims.answer_short: Silver nitrate, historically called 'lunar caustic,' has centuries of medicinal use — as a purgative, a cautery for wounds and tumors, and famously a 2% drop placed in newborns' eyes from 1884 to prevent gonorrheal blindness.
claims.answer: Silver nitrate — historically called 'lunar caustic,' a name rooted in silver's ancient association with the moon (the same link behind words like 'moonstruck' and 'lunacy') — has a long medicinal history. In 1637 Angelus Sala used it as a purgative and for brain and uterine illness, and Robert Boyle rolled silver nitrate and nitre into bread-crust pills the size of small peas as a laxative. Beginning in 1826, John Higginbottom of Nottingham, England used lunar caustic to treat wounds and ulcers (from needles, hooks, bayonets, saws, leech and rabid-animal bites, and insect stings), to remove tumors, and to cauterize surgical wounds, and later described its use against erysipelas, varicose ulcers, diabetic (senile) gangrene, and burns. Its most enduring application came in 1884, when the German obstetrician Carl Sigmund Crede began placing a single drop of 2% silver nitrate in each newborn's eyes at birth to prevent gonorrheal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum); a diluted 1/2% solution became a standard burn treatment only after Carl A. Moyer's work in 1965.
claims.verbatim:
Angelus Sala (1637) em-
ployed silver nitrate (lunar caustic) as a
purgative and in brain and uterine illnesses.
Robert Boyle concocted pilulae lunara by
creating a mixture of silver nitrate and nitre,
dried and formed with bread crusts into pills
the size of small peas as a laxative.

claims.subject: testosterone
claims.question: Does testosterone cause teenage violence or aggression?
claims.answer_short: Wallach argues the puberty testosterone surge (ages 14–18), landing on top of mineral deficiencies and a high-sugar diet, is an 'explosive' driver of teen crime and murder.
claims.answer: Wallach ties adolescent violence partly to hormones interacting with nutrition. He points to the surge of the 'male hormone testosterone' during puberty, roughly ages 14 to 18, and argues that when it lands on top of specific mineral deficiencies — he names copper, chromium, vanadium and lithium — and a high-sugar diet (fruit juices, sodas, candy, ice cream, sugary cereals), the result fills jails and death rows with teenage killers. He calls testosterone surges, high sugar intake and mineral deficiencies 'as explosive a mixture as matches, nitroglycerine and gun powder combined.' It is a characteristic Wallach stance: behavior conventionally blamed on psychology or environment, reframed as a fixable hormonal-and-nutritional problem.

claims.subject: honey
claims.question: Is honey bad for you?
claims.answer_short: Wallach treats honey as a sugar to avoid - sugar loads flush minerals out of the body in sweat and urine by 300% for 12 hours, so no supplement can keep up.
claims.answer: Wallach counts honey as a sugar to eliminate, not a health food. He argues that sugar loads - natural and processed alike - raise the body's normal rate of mineral loss in sweat and urine by 300% for 12 hours, so honey on your English muffin at breakfast, ice cream at lunch, and a pastry at dinner will flush minerals out faster than any amount of supplementation or dieting can replace. He places honey squarely on his 'no' list alongside molasses, table sugar, and sweet juices, and notes that giving up sugar also sheds weight, clears thinking, reduces irritability, and moves anyone with hypoglycemia halfway toward fixing their problem.

claims.subject: mediterranean_diet
claims.question: What does Dr. Wallach think of the Mediterranean diet?
claims.answer_short: Wallach says the Mediterranean diet, like every other named diet, makes no difference unless you also supplement all 90 essential nutrients daily.
claims.answer: Wallach holds that no named diet makes the real difference to health, because "we are what's in (or isn't in) the food we eat." He lists the Mediterranean Diet alongside the Beverly Hills, Atkins, Fit for Life, Immune Power, Pritikin, Macrobiotic, Life Extension and 120 Year diets, veganism, an Eskimo blubber diet, and eating dozens of burgers a day, and says it does not matter which you follow: unless you supplement daily with optimal amounts of each of the 90 essential nutrients, you throw away 50 to 75% of your life as surely as if you had jumped in front of a speeding train.
